​
On behalf of Community Economic Development Association of Michigan (CEDAM) and the community
development organizations and communities we serve across the state, we appreciate the opportunity
to comment on the joint proposal issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) on July 31, 2026, to revise Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) regulations. We note that the Federal Reserve did not join this proposal.
CEDAM is a nonprofit membership trade association, with more than 300 members that span across the
state of Michigan. Billions of dollars in community development investment are at stake for the
organizations and communities we serve, and we submit these comments to ensure that any
modernization of CRA strengthens, rather than weakens, bank accountability for meeting the credit
needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.
Our preliminary view is that the proposal would narrow bank accountability and weaken the community
development infrastructure that helps capital reach LMI people and places in our state. Modernization
should make CRA more responsive to how banks operate today; it should not reduce responsibility or
transparency.

According to the National Community Reinvestment Coalition, if this rule goes into effect, the 69 largest
OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks, which currently make $102 billion a year in total community
development loans and investments inside their assessment areas, would be able to justify decreasing
their community development financing to just $15 to $31 billion, a $71 billion to $87 billion annual
loss.1 Below we outline six provisions most directly tied to community and economic development,
guided by the analysis outlined by the Community Opportunity Alliance.
1. Community needs should drive CRA credit​
CRA credit should prioritize documented community needs and measurable impact, not simply whether
an activity fits an eligible category.
1 https://ncrc.org/cra/

2. CRA responsibility must reflect modern banking​
CRA assessment areas should reflect where banks actually lend and operate, not just where they have
branches. The agencies should consider Retail Lending assessment areas and other approaches to ensure
meaningful market activity carries CRA responsibility.
3. Do not weaken community development requirements by increasing asset thresholds​
Higher asset thresholds could reduce community development accountability, particularly in rural and
underserved markets. The current proposal would categorize banks below $1B as small banks and banks
from $1B-$10B as intermediate. Many banks that are currently categorized as "large" would drop down
to intermediate, reducing their CRA obligations and responsibility. The agencies should preserve distinct
community development evaluations for banks currently subject to them.
4. Preserve flexible grants​
Flexible operating grants are essential to sustaining community development organizations and
infrastructure. The agencies should preserve CRA credit for these grants and eliminate the proposed 15%
overhead documentation requirement.
5. CRA must address race and redlining​
Race and income are not interchangeable. CRA should use available data to identify racial disparities in
access to credit and coordinate with fair lending enforcement.
6. Adopt one interagency CRA framework​
The OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve should adopt a single, consistent CRA framework to avoid regulatory
fragmentation and strengthen accountability.


Why does this matter for Michigan? ​
​
The proposed changes would have meaningful
consequences for Michigan financial institutions and,
in turn, for the communities and organizations that
depend on CRA-motivated capital. Michigan has a
diverse banking market that includes large regional
institutions, intermediate-sized banks, and smaller
community banks that play important roles in
financing affordable housing, small businesses,
community facilities, and other community
development activities. Reducing the community
development obligations applicable to these
institutions would likely reduce the amount of capital
available for these activities, particularly in rural
communities and smaller cities where individual
financial institutions can be critical community
development partners.
In Michigan, 15 of 64 banks would
lose any community development obligation, the
28th highest reduction in the country. Michigan
would also see a 34.5% reduction in banks with
large-bank status, dramatically lowering
standards for lending, investing, and services.
Michiganders would risk a 10.3% reduction in banking
branches in communities of color and 9.2% of small
business data lost. 2
The reduction in CRA obligations could translate
directly into fewer grants and other forms of flexible community development support available to
Michigan nonprofits. Community-based organizations rely on these resources not only to implement
individual projects but also to maintain the staff capacity, partnerships, technical expertise, and
infrastructure necessary to identify opportunities and successfully deploy capital. A reduction in
CRA-motivated grantmaking would therefore have effects beyond the loss of individual grants: it could
weaken the broader ecosystem that enables community development projects to move from concept to
implementation.
These impacts are particularly concerning in Michigan's affordable housing market. Minimum wage
workers in Michigan would have to work 60 hours a week at the state's minimum wage of $13.73/hr to

afford a modest one bedroom rental home at $1,070 per month which is Fair Market rent; this increases
to 74 hours a week to afford a two bedroom rental home at $1,327 per month.3 Housing continues to get
more expensive and out of reach for both renters and prospective homeowners. Reducing the obligation
for banks to invest in housing that is in reach for Michigan residents will have dire effects on our low- and
moderate-income communities for years to come. ​
​
Currently, CRA investments and grants frequently complement Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC),
New Market Tax Credits (NMTC) and other public and private sources of financing needed to make
affordable housing developments financially feasible. As published in the 2026 Incentive to Impact report
released by National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders, 80% of Low Income Housing Tax Credit
equity and 98% of New Markets Tax Credit equity comes from CRA-incentivized investors.

Banks can help fulfill their CRA obligations by investing in LIHTC projects, directing private capital toward
affordable housing in LMI communities. In return, banks receive valuable tax benefits while earning CRA
consideration for supporting qualified community development investments. This creates a mutually
beneficial relationship: LIHTC provides developers with critical equity to build affordable housing, while
banks satisfy CRA requirements through their investment. If the proposed rule reduces the incentive for
financial institutions to provide community development investments, grants, and other flexible
capital, affordable housing developers will face larger financing gaps and greater difficulty assembling
complete project capital stacks. For the few projects that are able to find investment, they will face
larger financing gaps as tax credit pricing will likely plummet due to the decreased demand for tax
credits. Ultimately, there will be significant reduction in the number of projects that can move
forward, and projects that do will face even more financing obstacles.
The concern is not simply the amount of CRA capital associated with any individual transaction.
CRA-motivated investment can help fill gaps in financing, make projects more competitive for public
resources, and provide the flexible capital necessary to move complex developments forward. When that
capital becomes less available, the effect can compound across the development pipeline. Fewer viable
projects can mean fewer applications for LIHTC and other public resources, even as Michigan continues
to face substantial needs for affordable housing and community investment.

Since 2010, CRA qualified lending has channeled $120 billion to LMI Michiganders pursuing

downstream effects before adopting changes that would reduce the community development
responsibilities of financial institutions.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that
banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit
services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining,
disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.

Further, MBA is very concerned about the potential regulatory fragmentation that may arise from
the Agencies pursuing regulatory changes (i.e., finalizing this NPR) without the Federal Reserve
Board. In the past, we have cautioned against CRA rules that are not jointly issued by all three
banking Agencies. In addition to creating confusion, disjointed rulemaking increases the same
regulatory burdens the Agencies seek to reduce and creates an uneven playing field for banks.
A central goal of all three Agencies' efforts should be to improve the processes that allow banks
to meet the credit needs of their communities under the CRA. Therefore, any proposed
changes or improvements to the existing framework should ensure that the rules and
regulations governing the processes are clear, consistent, unambiguous, and aligned.
II.
BACKGROUND
Congress enacted the CRA in 1977 to encourage regulated banks to help meet the credit needs
of the local communities in which they are chartered. In 1978, the Agencies promulgated the
first major regulatory framework to implement the statute. These regulations have been revised
over the years, including the last major revision in 1995, and a less substantive modification in
2005. Since then, the Agencies have embarked on various joint and individual efforts to update
the regulations to align with changes in the banking industry.
In 2019, the OCC and FDIC published a joint NPR3 on the CRA regulatory framework. The
OCC issued a final CRA rule in May 2020.4 Neither the FDIC nor the Federal Reserve Board
joined in the issuance of the final rule resulting in inconsistent and unaligned rules from the
Agencies. The OCC rule was ultimately rescinded.
On May 5, 2022, the Agencies issued an NPR to modernize the CRA framework.5 On October
24, 2023, the Agencies issued their final CRA rule;6 however, prior to the rule going into effect,
the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas issued an order in March 2024 enjoining
the final rules from going into effect. The Agencies subsequently withdrew the rule – effectively
reverting to the 1995 framework.
III.
MBA COMMENTS
The Agencies identify several goals in the NPR, including better aligning CRA regulations with
the statute; ensuring that community development grants reach the communities they are
intended to benefit; reducing burdens for banks (particularly community banks); and providing
greater clarity on how banks will be evaluated for CRA consideration. In furtherance of these
goals, the Agencies place greater emphasis on lending while diminishing the impact of deposit
services in CRA evaluation. According to the Agencies, a larger focus on lending (rather than
deposit services) should be the focus of CRA as this better reflects how a bank meets the
community's credit needs as prescribed by the statute. As discussed below, while MBA
supports these outlined goals, we strongly recommend that the Agencies focus on the
unintended consequences as well as the operational difficulties that would result from some of
the provisions prior to finalizing any rules. The Agencies have requested responses and
comments on a host of specific questions and issues addressed in the NPR. We have limited

A.
Regulatory Uniformity And Process Improvement
(i)
Uniformity and Certainty
MBA supports efforts to reduce regulatory reporting burdens for banks, and we reiterate the
importance of achieving this goal through clear, concise, and uniform regulations, rather than
fragmented rules that result in friction or ambiguity. To that end, we strongly urge all three
banking Agencies to work together on aligned CRA rules to ensure that all banks subject to the
rules are operating under the same requirements and processes.
Past instances of the banking Agencies not working together on a joint rule have resulted in
inconsistent and unaligned rules, leading to confusion for banks, and eventually prompting
withdrawal or rescission. To avoid another withdrawal or rescission, we urge the three
Agencies to work on a unified CRA regulatory framework to establish a more efficient and
streamlined process for banks and community stakeholders alike. Just as important, we urge
the Agencies to ensure that any final rules issued incorporate industry feedback and largely
focus on improved compliance processes for banks, with the major components addressing
certainty in the administration of the rules by regulators and greater flexibility governing the
delivery of services to the community. These components—compliance, certainty, and flexibility
in the delivery of services—should be developed in a manner that facilitates innovation by banks
and would benefit the communities they serve.
CRA is a vital tool for both banks and their communities, and we believe that operating under
uniform rules is an important part of ensuring that banks continue to meet their CRA obligations.
A CRA rule that is subject to constant change or not supported by all three Agencies deprives

appropriately planning for the future.
While we appreciate efforts by the bank regulators acting individually to spur progress on long
overdue CRA reforms, it is important to acknowledge that these actions have resulted in
uncertainty, lack of clarity or direction, and frustration not just for the banks that have to

rules. It is therefore imperative that all three banking Agencies strive for complete collaboration

D.
Assessment Area
(i)
Delineating Assessment Area
The Agencies propose two options for determining if a surrounding census tract involves a
"substantial portion of a bank's loans" and therefore should be included in a bank's assessment

CRA rule language that allows the Agencies to broaden assessment areas to include

appropriately differ depending on an institution's business model. For institutions with a
meaningful branch and deposit-taking presence, assessment areas should continue to be based

subdivisions, which provide stable and predictable geographic boundaries.

significant and sustained presence, such as a "substantial portion of a bank's loans." The
Agencies should avoid requiring branch-based institutions to expand assessment areas solely
because of lending activity in surrounding census tracts, as such an approach introduces
unnecessary complexity and uncertainty without improving CRA outcomes.

G.
Other Issues
(i)
Treatment of HELOCs for Purposes of CRA Evaluations
HELOCs differ fundamentally from closed-end mortgages in their purposes, structure, and risks.
Unlike closed-end mortgages, which primarily finance home purchases or refinance existing
mortgage debt, HELOCs provide revolving credit for debt consolidation, unexpected costs,
home improvement, and short-term cash-flow needs.
Therefore, because the two products serve different purposes, involve different eligibility
requirements, and respond to different borrower demand, the Agencies' 2023 CRA final rule did
not combine HELOCs and other open-end home mortgage loans with closed-end mortgages in
the Retail Lending Test's quantitative distribution analysis.
We urge the Agencies to re-affirm the 2023 final rule's separation of HELOCs from closed-end
mortgages, thereby clarifying that close-end mortgage distribution is not an appropriate proxy
for expected HELOC distribution. Given their distinct purposes, eligibility constraints, borrower
demand, revolving structure, and risk profile, HELOCs and other open-end home mortgage
loans should not be benchmarked against closed-end mortgage distribution. Thus, any
quantitative assessment should compare a bank's HELOC distribution only with aggregate
HELOC distribution—not with the distribution of closed-end mortgages.
(ii)
Community Development
MBA supports enhanced clarity in the definitions of CD activities, which will ensure greater
certainty regarding qualification standards. The Agencies should ensure that any final rules
further the intended CD goals of the statute, rather than disrupting existing channels or
diminishing the ability of banks to respond to the needs of their local communities.

The Agencies propose consideration of prior-period CD loans as a way to create parity with the
current treatment of CD investments. While MBA supports CRA consideration for prior-period
loans, investments, grants and other CD activities, including loan renewals, extensions and
long-term commitments that continue to provide community benefits, we urge the Agencies to
allow such consideration to be at the option of the bank, rather than a requirement for all banks.
This optionality standard will ensure that sustained capital deployment in underserved
communities is not discouraged, and at the same time, allow a bank to opt out of the
burdensome exercise of tracking and reporting loans that may have multiple records due to
renewals and possibly loan size changes across multiple years and exam cycles.
MBA supports the proposed expansion of CD services to include activities related to either
financial services or an employee's professional services. However, we recommend against
any unnecessarily restrictive eligibility standards for CD qualification, such as a requirement that
the CD investment or service be complex. A complexity requirement would narrow CRA
qualification and improperly exclude activities and services that have a clear community
development purpose and have historically delivered meaningful community impact.
Complexity should not determine CRA eligibility but rather attract enhanced consideration. In
effect, any activity that is innovative, impactful, or otherwise responsive to a community need as
required by the statute, should receive CRA consideration – with complex activities receiving
enhanced consideration.
Finally, MBA recommends that the final rules preserve CD eligibility for lending, investments,13
and services that support affordable housing, community development intermediaries, workforce
development, small business technical assistance, revitalization and stabilization activities and
other high-impact CD activities. The rules should provide greater clarify and flexibility without
narrowing CRA eligibility for activities that meaningfully benefit the intended beneficiaries of the
statute.
(iii)
High-Cost Markets & Definitions
Rather than prescribing a single methodology, the final rule should provide flexibility for banks to
demonstrate high-cost market conditions using objective, supportable measures appropriate to
the transaction being financed. Depending on the activity, those measures could include
housing-cost burden data, affordability metrics, housing development cost indicators, or
established federal designations such as HUD Difficult Development Areas and FHFA High
Opportunity Areas. The final rule should also expand affordable housing eligibility to include
middle-income and mixed-income rental housing in high-cost markets and confirm that naturally
occurring affordable housing may qualify based on affordability and benefit without requiring
location in an LMI census tract. If the Agencies retain a county-based housing-cost-burden
methodology, the threshold should be reduced from 40 percent to more than 30 percent so that
markets with significant affordability challenges are not unintentionally excluded.
Grandfathering and transition provisions recommended in this letter should ensure that a

loans, investments, or legally binding commitments.
(iv)
Wholesale Banks
MBA urges the Agencies to retain the current standard for determining whether a bank qualifies
as a wholesale bank, including retaining the current standard for determining whether a bank
makes retail loans only on an incidental basis. Currently, the 2016 Interagency Questions &
Answers state that a bank is considered to extend retail loans on an incidental basis when those
loans make up an insignificant portion of the institution's assets and income. Under the
Agencies' proposal, "incidental basis" would instead be defined as retail loans making up less
than five percent of the bank's loans. This is a substantial shift from the current policy and could
cause significant changes in CRA exams and additional regulatory burden for banks currently
defined as wholesale banks.
H.
Implementation Period and Grandfathering
(i)
Implementation Period
As the Agencies are aware, recent proposals to update CRA have either been withdrawn,
rescinded, or challenged in court. Given this, industry has been in a constant state of
uncertainty on when, whether, or how to best to approach implementation of "final" CRA rules in
the last several years. Many banks have had to unwind or rescind CRA strategies and policies
that were implemented based on issued final rules only to revert to the 1995 framework – after
investing time and dollars in attempting to comply with the new rules. To avoid such
deadweight compliance costs, MBA strongly requests that the Agencies ensure that any final
rules under this NPR be accompanied by at least a two-year implementation period. Any
changes under the rules should be effective no earlier than January 1st of the third calendar
year following the effective date of the final rule.
(ii)
Grandfathering
(a)
Strategic Plans Approved before the New Rule is Implemented
The Agencies should take all appropriate steps to ensure that Strategic Plans that were
approved under the existing framework are grandfathered and therefore allowed to be
implemented and evaluated under the original approval framework. This would reflect an
acknowledgement of the effort and resources already expended by depositories and allow them
to achieve consideration based on the criteria that was in place when the Agencies approved
their plan.
(b)
Strategic Plans in an Open Exam Period
We urge the Agencies to also clarify that a bank with a Strategic Plan that is in an open exam
period will continue through its open exam period under the framework that was in place when
the exam period started. In effect, any criteria established under the new rules would not be
applied to such bank, but rather, be applicable or effective for such bank after the current exam
cycle. For instance, if a bank is in an open exam cycle on the date the final rules are issued, the
bank should be allowed to complete that exam cycle under the existing 1995 framework, which
was the applicable framework when the exam cycle started. After the exam cycle is complete,

Regenerate California Innovation (RCI) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed
changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. We are a community serving

Fresno, and contribute to organizing, growth and impact of numerous affordable housing, small
business, sustainable agriculture and clean energy development initiatives in the San Joaquin
Valley.

Central California has substantial entrepreneurial talent and opportunities for small business
growth. Yet many owners encounter limited access to conventional business credit, particularly
in rural communities and underserved urban neighborhoods. The unemployment rate in August
2026 was 7.8 percent in Fresno County and 8.4 percent in Kern County, according to
California's Employment Development Department. These local figures underscore the
importance of small businesses as a source of jobs and economic opportunity.[1]
A 2022 Fresno Small Business Capital Flows and Gaps Analysis commissioned by RCI partner
Access Plus Capital and others estimated at least $3 billion in annual unmet small business
financing demand in Fresno County. That estimate includes both unmet demand from financing
applications and latent demand from businesses that needed financing but were discouraged,
considered credit too costly, or found the search too difficult. It is an estimate of demand at the
time of the study, not a projection that every dollar could immediately be financed. The study
also identified gaps in business records, financial readiness, language access, and available

developed together.[2]

Other research points in the same direction. An Urban Institute analysis of investment from 2010

Bank financing supplies lending capital, while grants can pay for the work that makes that capital

To Whom It May Concern:
Scale Link is writing in response to the request for comments on the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation regarding the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
This letter is organized in the following manner:
1. Information about Scale Link and our perspective
2. General feedback on the proposal
3. Specific feedback on numbered questions
4. Feedback on questions not asked in the proposal

1. About Scale Link

Scale Link is a nonprofit marketplace that creates liquidity to support small business
access to capital for communities in need. Scale Link's purpose is aligned with the CRA –
we work to expand access to lending in underserved communities. Scale Link
accomplishes this in two ways. First, Scale Link purchases small business loans from
Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) to replenish their capital and
continue lending. Second, Scale Link sells most of those loans to banks seeking to ensure
that capital flows to businesses in their assessment areas, especially to businesses they
are unlikely to serve in the course of their regular business. Banks provide capital and take
on the risk of loss for each loan. This marketplace of loans expands lending capacity in
banks' assessment areas.
Scale Link has purchased loans in 39 states and continues to grow its footprint. It has
worked with more than 35 banks and 30 different CDFIs. As a marketplace, Scale Link
understands the needs of small businesses served by CDFIs and how banks can better
serve small business owners.
Because of Scale Link's focus on small business lending and CDFIs, we will largely limit our
specific responses to questions that fit that focus.

2. General Feedback on the Proposal
As a partner to banks and CDFIs, we see firsthand how consistency benefits communities.
Consistent rules and enforcement give banks a stable foundation for making long-term
capital commitments to their communities.
This is not an argument against change, but an argument for consistent change. A rule
proposed by two of the three CRA regulators would create inconsistency and confusion
that harms lending under CRA. Years of confusion and regulatory rent-seeking would
ensue. As the OCC and FDIC both note a concern about rent-seeking behavior among non-
profits, we are sure you will understand that having different CRA rules will mean rent-
seeking by for-profit banks seeking the regulatory framework that requires the least of
them. The banks will spend time not in creating value or lending, but in plotting the best
strategy to play the regulatory structures against themselves.
Any new CRA rule should apply across all three regulators. If the OCC and FDIC cannot
achieve that buy-in, the rule should not be changed.
Our second general concern is simply that under the current rule, too many banks are given
passing grades on CRA when we know they are not doing their best to lend. We see this
firsthand in banks with "satisfactory" performance who do not serve their assessment

areas well. The facts also bear this out: 98% of banks pass their exam.1 The new proposed
rule does nothing to hold banks more accountable and does not appear likely to produce
greater differentiation among banks with materially different levels of performance. Given
already weak CRA accountability, changes in the asset thresholds that define CRA exam
types should be made carefully and avoid changes that will further dilute CRA
examinations.
Finally, the OCC and FDIC have withdrawn support for the 2023 CRA rule and are asking the
Eastern District of Texas to declare that future CRA regulations cannot evaluate retail
lending outside areas where banks maintain deposit-taking facilities or assess deposit
products under an expansive interpretation of "credit needs." While a federal district court
preliminarily enjoined the 2023 rule in 2024 after finding that plaintiffs were likely to
succeed on the merits, that ruling was not a final determination of CRA's meaning and did
not establish binding limits on future rulemaking. We urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw
their request for a judgment restricting future regulatory authority, especially as one CRA
regulator – the Federal Reserve – did not accept this interpretation. If the OCC and FDIC
intend to proceed with a flawed process that does not include one of the three regulators,
they should at least limit changes to those that are in line with previous interpretations of
the law rather than introducing novel, and not yet settled, views.

3. Specific Feedback on Numbered Questions
Scale Link has only chosen to respond to the questions where it believes its perspective is
most likely to support better rulemaking.
Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less
than $30 billion as a threshold for certain supervisory approaches, such as being
considered a community bank or being subject to the continuous examination
process, should the agencies consider adjusting the intermediate bank asset size
threshold to include all banks with an asset size of less than $30 billion that do not
qualify as small banks? If the agencies establish $30 billion as the appropriate
threshold to delineate between intermediate banks and large banks, should the
agencies also adopt a larger threshold for small banks, such as the $10 billion
currently proposed as the intermediate bank threshold?
We do not believe the asset thresholds should be advanced to $30 billion for large banks as
those thresholds for other supervisory methods have no direct relevance to the CRA. In

1 As noted here, https://ncrc.org/cra-overhaul-did-the-agencies-do-enough-to-cure-ratings-inflation/

fact, we believe the opposite. Removing all asset thresholds and holding all banks to the
obligations currently reserved only for large banks would be closest to the original intent
and purpose of CRA. In terms of capacity to serve their CRA obligations and meet data
burdens, it has never been easier given advances in software and core banking systems.
And after 50 years of work, CRA knowledge and expertise is now widespread across banks
of all sizes. Asset thresholds are an outdated approach that does not serve the targets of
CRA. The original rule in 1977 had no asset thresholds and there should be no asset
thresholds now.
With regards to the reference of other rules using a $30 billion threshold, they are not
directly applicable to CRA. CRA impact in communities is driven by the number and dollar
amount of financial products more fairly distributed across a bank's footprint. A bank with
$100 million in assets can have a profound impact just like a bank that has $30 billion in
assets. The latter is likely to touch more communities given its size. Other supervisory
approaches are not driven by looking at the impact on communities, but by assessing risk
at the bank and for the financial system. The right asset size for assessing risk is not likely
to be the same asset size for assessing the approach and extent of community impact for
CRA.
Adjusting the asset thresholds for the banks is also justified in the NPR based on a desire to
align the proportions of banks in different categories historically with the proportions today.
Given industry consolidation, maintaining those proportions is tricky. The asset thresholds
proposed are nearly 6 times higher than an inflation-only driven change in the asset
thresholds.
The more critical question for asset thresholds is not which thresholds are used for risk-
based assessment (these are largely irrelevant to community impact) or how to maintain
the proportions of banks in each category (it is not clear why this should be a target). The
critical question is which threshold preserves the same level of CRA obligation relative to
bank capacity as when the CRA was originally passed or substantially updated. In other
words, a $1 billion bank in 1995 might have the same capacity to conduct CRA today as a
bank with $100 million of assets. This is an exceedingly difficult question to answer.
However, advances in technology, efficiency, and CRA knowledge mean the thresholds
should be moving in the opposite direction – as even the smallest banks now have the
means and tools to target CRA activity and meet their obligations in a way that large banks
in 1977 and 1995 could only dream of.
For these reasons, the asset thresholds should not be moved higher and instead should be
removed entirely. All banks should be held to the same tests and requirements as large
banks. For peer comparisons in the evaluation, banks could still be compared to those of

similar sizes. Alternatively, peers could be determined based on major product focus and
strategy in addition to asset sizes. As an added benefit, since all banks would be required
to report more data, peer comparisons would be much easier and accurate to assemble.
Question 9: Are there alternative standards the agencies should consider relying on in
the context of limiting indirect costs for CD grants? Do the proposed guardrails do
enough to ensure the majority of grant and donation funds go directly towards
benefiting the bank's assessment area(s)?
Before responding directly to this question, we would note that no objective evidence is
presented that a problem needs to be fixed and there is no evidence being gathered to
determine whether the proposed remedy – changes to grant administration - has any
benefit.
In the following discussion, we make the case that there should be no indirect cost rate
administered and tracked by banks. If the regulators do move forward with an indirect cost
rate, we request 15% be treated as intended by the OMB – as a de minimus indirect cost
rate. Finally, we propose an approach to demonstrating the extent to which grants benefit
an assessment area that follows the approach used by the CDFI Fund. The latter approach
will increase efficiency of the process.
The CRA rule does not review whether banks are efficient at meeting their obligations or
how they choose to operationalize lending efforts. It focuses only on results. It reviews
whether sufficient volume and dispersion of loans occur relative to the bank's deposits and
business model. This approach was a very intentional change made in 1995 to move from
process focus to results.
The same approach is the most effective for CD grants. If a bank believes a grant is an
efficient way to aid its community and fits its CRA strategy, then that should be sufficient
evidence. Requiring banks to measure and police indirect costs themselves is a misguided
and inefficient approach that will have no discernible impact on bank assessment areas.
The requirements to track and gather cost information further impair efficiency by
increasing the regulatory burden on banks. In fact, this inefficiency may actually limit
grants from going where they are most needed as banks may prefer to avoid small grants in
light of the documentation burden. In practice, this approach makes banks regulators of
nonprofit financial statements. There should be no new indirect cost method or gathering
of additional budgets (or already publicly available 990s).
Finally, there is considerable evidence that targeted overhead rates actually reduce
efficiency at the nonprofit partners. A uniform indirect-cost ceiling is not an evidence-
based measure of nonprofit efficiency. Empirical research indicates that the relationship

between overhead and outcomes is nonlinear, that many nonprofits underinvest in
organizational infrastructure, and that appropriate indirect costs vary substantially by
mission, business model, scale, and stage of development. A flat ceiling may therefore
lower program effectiveness, encourage expense reclassification, increase compliance
costs, and favor organizations based on accounting presentation rather than community
impact. Much of the research on this issue questions the benefit of specifying a level of
overhead, but when there is a target, finds optimal rates in the 30-40% rate. As one
researcher states, "Emphasis on overhead diverts attention away from more informative
data on charitable outcomes and hinders organizations from achieving impact."2
If a new indirect cost method is adopted, it should first be implemented in line with the
OMB citation from the rule. In that case, 15% is the minimum amount automatically
granted when there is no negotiated rate. It is expected and common that the rate may be
much higher than 15%. The OCC and FDIC should allow grant recipients to set a rate and
provide justification without placing the burden of approving a higher rate on federal
agencies.
Furthermore, if a new indirect cost method is adopted, it should be simple for banks to
implement so as not to add unnecessary cost or complexity to either the grantor or the
recipient (especially since there is no evidence of a need for a change and therefore no
clear value from the change). Grant recipients should be able to simply sign an attestation
that they will abide by the rate declared in the attestation, which may be more than 15% if
justification is provided.
Finally, with regards to assessment areas, we do not dispute the value in attempting to tie
grants back to impact in the assessment area of the grantor. However, making that process
overly burdensome for banks and grantees would add unnecessary inefficiency. Much like
the CDFI Fund Target Market, nonprofits receiving funds should sign an attestation that
more than 60% of the funds, or an equivalent amount to 60% of the funds, will go to the
assessment areas of the bank (unless the bank is expressly looking to deploy funds outside
its assessment area). The nonprofit should be able to show the amount across a three-year
period. The dollars should simply be earmarked to support the activity but need not be
tracked directly as long as the activity occurs and dollars are not earmarked for more than
one funder.

2 Altamimi, H., & Liu, Q. (2022). The nonprofit starvation cycle: Does overhead spending really impact program
outcomes? Nonprofit and Voluntary Sector Quarterly, 51(6), 1324-1348.
https://doi.org/10.1177/08997640211057404

Question 10: As an alternative, should the agencies eliminate all grants and donations
from CRA consideration?
Before responding directly to this question, we would note that no objective evidence is
presented that a problem needs to be fixed and there is no evidence being gathered to
determine whether the proposed remedy – changes to grant administration - has any
benefit. There is no reason to consider this question in the first place.
It is also essential to recognize that there are many types of lending and support that are
positive for the community but do not generate sufficient profit to cover their expenses.
This is the exact reason banks choose to partner with nonprofits – because the banks will
not provide those products themselves. Grants and donations help ensure that work can
occur. As long as the work fits within the targets of CRA, grants and donations are clearly a
way to reinvest in communities.
Question 26: Should any of the example government programs included in the third
category of economic development (proposed §ll.12, definition of economic
development paragraph (3)(iii)) be removed from the list of examples? Should
additional programs, projects, or initiatives be included in the list of examples?
The list as written should remain. Additional programs that should be included would be
state-based efforts, such as the federally funded State Small Business Credit Initiative
(SSBCI).
Question 34: If the rules were to permit banks to receive consideration for CD
activities outside of assessment areas in States, multistate MSAs, or at the bank level
without requiring that the bank meet or exceed the geographic flexibility standard(s) in
all assessment areas, in determining when consideration would be permitted outside
assessment areas, should the agencies rely on the ''substantially met'' standard in
proposed §ll.27 or should another standard apply?
Flexibility should be reserved only for those with an exemplary CRA track record.
Determining a definition of "substantially met" is difficult without completing a full CRA
exam. Additionally, choosing a quantitative threshold based on barely exceeding "Needs to
improve" should not be considered "substantially met." Substantially is an unclear
threshold but should imply better than satisfactory performance. The quantitative
approach proposed can also result in frequent changes to the threshold as the bank grows
and evolves, making planning activities outside of the assessment area more difficult.
A simpler, and more justifiable, approach would be that a bank that receives an overall
outstanding rating for a CRA exam should then be allowed to include efforts outside its

assessment area throughout its entire next exam period. This would show that the bank has
a history of substantially meeting its local credit needs and then provide a longer time
horizon to thoughtfully deploy funds outside the assessment area.
After the first time it is permitted to include activities outside its assessment area, the bank
should be required to continue to demonstrate at least Satisfactory performance on
lending within all its assessment areas and an overall rating of Outstanding to continue to
receive geographic flexibility in the subsequent exam periods.
Question 58: Throughout this SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION the agencies
referenced the guidance in the Interagency Questions and Answers. Several aspects
of this proposal were based on codifications of the existing guidance. The agencies
request feedback on how to address the Interagency Questions and Answers going
forward.
Creating an Interagency Question and Answer will be impossible if there are two different
systems for CRA. It would be unwieldy and not useful as all answers would end up multiple
choice (and especially given two different asset threshold systems). The FDIC and OCC
should simply not create a new rule without the Federal Reserve.

4. Feedback on non-Numbered Questions

Re: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
(Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57; RIN 3064-AG31)
The Financial Technology Association (FTA)1 appreciates the opportunity to comment on the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) (together, the Agencies) to amend their
regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) (the Proposal). FTA supports
the CRA's core purpose of encouraging banks to help meet the credit needs of the communities
they serve, including low and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods, and welcomes the
Agencies' stated goals of reducing unnecessary burden and improving clarity.
Banks with digital or branch-light business models serve customers in ways that do not always
map neatly onto a framework designed around physical branches and a set of standardized
products. For these institutions in particular, the Strategic Plan option has been an important
tool for setting CRA commitments that are both meaningful to communities and grounded in
how the bank actually operates.
We encourage the Agencies to incorporate a few targeted adjustments that preserve flexibility,
reduce unnecessary burden, and give banks greater certainty as they plan their community
investments. In particular, FTA recommends that the Agencies:
•
Preserve Strategic Plan flexibility and provide clear transition relief;
•
Preserve flexibility in the treatment of consumer lending and major product lines;
•
Preserve flexibility in Community Development goal structure and geographic allocation;
•
Increase certainty and predictability for qualifying Community Development activities;
and
•
Harmonize expectations across the banking industry.

1FTA is a network of fintech leaders shaping the future of finance. We champion the power of technology-driven
financial services to catalyze innovation and advocate for modernized policies and regulations that reflect this digital
transformation.

2

I.
The Agencies Should Preserve Strategic Plan Flexibility and Provide Clear
Transition Relief
FTA supports retaining the Strategic Plan as a flexible alternative to the standard large-bank
performance tests. The Strategic Plan option exists precisely because a single set of
standardized tests cannot capture the full range of bank business models. A bank that lends
nationally through digital channels, or that concentrates in a small number of consumer
products, may serve its communities in ways the standard tests are not designed to measure.
The Strategic Plan allows such a bank to propose, and the Agencies to approve, measurable
goals that reflect its actual business model, product mix, and the communities it serves.
FTA appreciates that the Proposal seeks to clarify how banks submit, amend, and implement
Strategic Plans and what content those plans must contain, and that it would add a prefiling
communications provision under which the Agencies would give substantive feedback on draft
plans, including on the merits of proposed measurable goals. As the Agencies finalize these
provisions, FTA urges them to keep the focus on clarifying process rather than prescribing plan
design. Specifically, the Agencies should preserve each bank's ability to design measurable
goals around its business model, product mix, and communities served, rather than requiring
Strategic Plan banks to replicate the structure of the standard performance tests.
FTA also urges the Agencies to provide clear transition or grandfathering treatment for Strategic
Plans that are already in development or under agency review when the final rule takes effect.
Developing a Strategic Plan requires significant advance planning, including community needs
analysis, internal governance and board approval, public comment, and sustained engagement
with agency staff. The Agencies should not require a bank that has invested in that process
under the existing framework to restart it because the governing rules changed midstream. FTA
recommends that the final rule:
•
Permit a bank whose plan the Agencies approved, or that the bank formally submitted
for approval, before the final rule's effective date to continue that plan under the
framework in place at submission for the full plan term;
•
Allow banks with plans in active development to elect whether to complete those plans
under the existing framework or the new framework, within a 12-month window after the
effective date; and
•
Clarify that a bank may, but is not required to, amend an existing plan to conform to the
new framework before the plan expires.
Clear transition treatment would avoid unnecessary disruption, protect the investment that
banks and communities have already made in plan development, and support a smooth
implementation of any final rule.

3

II.
The Agencies Should Preserve Flexibility in the Treatment of Consumer
Lending and Major Product Lines
As an initial matter, we request that the Agencies further consider the proposed standard for
designating consumer lending as a major product line. In particular, replacing the current
qualitative "substantial majority" standard with a bright-line majority test could have unintended
consequences for certain financial institutions.
FTA also urges the Agencies not to evaluate consumer lending by type of consumer loan, as
contemplated in Question 5(a) of the Proposal, which asks whether the Agencies should
consider consumer lending "[b]y type of consumer loans, rather than in the aggregate."2
Product-by-product evaluation could materially increase complexity for banks with diversified
consumer-lending businesses, which may offer personal loans, credit cards, student loan
refinancing, and other products to the same customers through the same digital platform.
Separate goals, benchmarks, and data analyses for each product would multiply the compliance
work without necessarily producing better information. Products with modest volumes can
generate statistically unreliable results, and isolating each product can obscure how the bank
serves LMI borrowers across its consumer business as a whole.
The Agencies recognized these same limitations in the 2023 CRA final rule, when they declined
to evaluate consumer loans other than automobile loans as major product lines. The Agencies
explained that the "heterogeneity of consumer loan products" made them difficult to evaluate
under a distribution analysis, and that disaggregating them into separate categories risked
leaving banks with too few loans in any one category to evaluate meaningfully, while adding
"additional metrics, benchmarks, and weights, thereby increasing the complexity of the
evaluation."3 That reasoning applies equally here.
FTA therefore recommends that, where consumer lending is evaluated, the Agencies retain the
Proposal's approach of considering it in the aggregate rather than by type of consumer loan.
III.
The Agencies Should Preserve Flexibility in Community Development Goal
Structure and Geographic Allocation
The Agencies should allow banks using Strategic Plans to determine the appropriate mix of
Community Development (CD) lending, investments, grants, and services based on community
needs and bank capabilities. FTA supports the flexibility in proposed § __.27(b)(2), which would
allow a bank to emphasize a performance category other than lending where doing so responds
to community credit needs, and to exclude measurable goals for a performance category where
its performance context supports that choice. We urge the Agencies to preserve this flexibility in
the final rule and to clarify that a bank may set combined goals, such as a single goal covering
CD lending and investments, rather than separate goals or fixed allocations for each activity
type. That approach would be consistent with the elective goals in the OCC's Simplified

2 91 Fed. Reg. 52125.
3 89 Fed. Reg. 6574, 6797.

4

Strategic Plan Process for Community Banks, which Question 42 asks whether to extend to all
banks.
Banks can address community needs through different forms of CD activity. In one community,
the most pressing need may be capital for affordable housing, best met through a CD loan. In
another, it may be operating support for a financial counseling program, best met through a
grant or a CD service that provides technical expertise. A bank's own capabilities matter too: a
bank with deep underwriting expertise in a particular asset class may deliver far more impact
through lending than through passive investment. Requiring separate, predetermined goals for
each activity type would push banks to direct resources toward filling categories rather than
toward the activities most responsive to community needs.
A combined CD goal, or a goal structure the bank proposes and justifies in its plan, would give
the Agencies a clear and measurable commitment while preserving the flexibility that makes
Strategic Plans valuable. The public comment and agency approval process already provides a
check that the proposed mix is responsive to community needs.
The same principle should apply to geographic allocation. FTA supports the Proposal's
approach of allowing banks, at their option, to receive consideration for CD activities outside
their assessment areas once they meet the applicable geographic flexibility standard. In
response to Questions 44 and 46, we further encourage the Agencies to go beyond this and (i)
consider CD activities not otherwise considered in connection with any measurable goals in
concluding whether the bank should receive a "satisfactory" rating; and (ii) permit banks to
specify measurable goals for CD activities outside of their assessment area. FTA also
recommends keeping the broader statewide or regional area concept, and confirming that a
program operating across a state or region that includes a bank's assessment area meets §
__.13(d)(1)(ii) even if the assessment area is not specifically identified, and that a bank with only
one assessment area receives full credit there for such a program.
IV.
The Agencies Should Increase Certainty and Predictability for Qualifying
Community Development Activities
FTA supports the Proposal's codification of a process to publish a non-exhaustive illustrative list
of activities that do and do not qualify for CD consideration, as well as a formal process for
banks to confirm the eligibility of activities. Stakeholders welcomed similar provisions when the
federal banking agencies included them in the 2023 CRA rules, and FTA encourages the
Agencies to retain them in any final rule.
Uncertainty about whether an activity will receive CRA consideration discourages banks from
committing to it, particularly for newer or less conventional structures. That uncertainty falls
hardest on innovative partnerships, such as collaborations between banks, community
development financial institutions, and technology providers, that may be among the most
effective ways to reach underserved communities. Greater upfront certainty helps banks plan
and structure their CD investments and partnerships with confidence that the activities will
receive CRA consideration.

5

To make these tools as useful as possible, FTA recommends that the Agencies:
•
Update the illustrative list regularly, at least annually, to add activities confirmed through
the eligibility process, with appropriate protection for confidential information;
•
Codify the proposed 90-day response timeframe such that if the agency does not
respond within 90 days, the activity would be deemed to qualify for CRA purposes; and
•
Allow banks to rely on a confirmation for the life of the activity, absent a material change
in its terms.
Furthermore, FTA urges the Agencies to reconsider the proposal to exclude small business
financing "primarily used for ongoing operating liquidity" from the definition of economic
development. Working capital often lets a small business retain employees through temporary
disruptions, which is the kind of preservation the definition otherwise recognizes. These
businesses, particularly newer and thinly capitalized ones, are the ones the CRA is most
intended to reach. Crediting working capital that sustains jobs and operations would keep CRA
incentives pointed toward the small businesses that most need access to capital.
V.
The Agencies Should Lead Efforts Toward A Single Interagency CRA Rule
We appreciate the Agencies' leadership on this issue and emphasizes the importance of clear
CRA standards across the entire banking system in order to ensure that covered entities are
evaluated under the same expectations, regardless of their charter or primary federal regulator.
Divergent rules would create uneven compliance burdens, and inconsistent standards could
make it harder for financial technology companies that partner with multiple banks to design
products and programs that support those banks' CRA obligations, since the same activity could
receive different credit depending on which agency supervises the partner bank. A single rule,
issued jointly by all three federal banking agencies with common definitions, performance
measures, and data requirements, would give banks and their partners the certainty they need
to calibrate their programs appropriately. We therefore urge the Agencies to work with the
Federal Reserve Board toward one harmonized final rule that applies consistently across the
banking system.
*



*



*
FTA appreciates the Agencies' efforts to modernize the CRA framework and to clarify and
simplify procedures for Strategic Plans. Preserving the flexibility that defines Strategic Plans,
providing clear transition relief, calibrating evaluation appropriately, increasing certainty around
qualifying CD activities, and working toward a single interagency rule would help ensure the
final rule encourages meaningful community investment by banks of all business models,
including technology-driven banks that serve customers nationwide.



6

Thank you for your consideration of these comments. We would welcome the opportunity to
discuss them further.
Respectfully submitted,




Angelena Bradfield
Head of Policy

The National Urban League writes in strong opposition to the proposed changes to the
regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). We urge the Federal

collectively referred to as the agencies, to withdraw the provisions discussed below, or at
minimum to complete and publish the community impact analysis the current record lacks before
issuing a final rule.
The National Urban League is one of the nation's oldest civil rights and urban advocacy
organizations, with 93 affiliates across 36 states and the District of Columbia, serving more than
two million people each year. Over the course of our 116-year history, we have consistently
advocated for policies that promote equitable access to credit, housing counseling,
homeownership assistance, entrepreneurship support, workforce development, and financial
education. Our affiliates work directly with families, homeowners, entrepreneurs, small
businesses and the communities the CRA was written to serve. Many are themselves recipients
of the bank grants and investments this proposal would change.
For almost fifty years, the CRA has helped ensure that federally regulated banks meet the credit
needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.
Congress found that the convenience and needs of communities include the need for deposit
 services along with credit services1. These protections remain particularly important in
communities that have experienced government-sanctioned redlining, disinvestment, branch loss,
unequal access to mortgage and small business credit, and persistent barriers to mainstream
financial services.
The CRA is more than a bank examination framework. It reflects Congress's recognition that
access to credit and financial services is essential to the economic well-being of communities
long excluded from mainstream investment. For the National Urban League, the effectiveness of
CRA must be measured not only by institutional compliance, but by whether families can obtain
responsible mortgage financing, entrepreneurs can secure capital, and neighborhoods can attract
the investment needed to sustain housing, businesses, and economic opportunity. Community
organizations are an important part of that infrastructure: they help financial institutions identify
and respond to unmet needs through counseling, financial education, technical assistance, and
trusted relationships with residents.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would

identifies several of the possible harms described below, including reduced standardized data and
comparability, reduced support for nonprofits and intermediary activities, and potential

savings to banks in detail while quantifying none of these consequences for communities. That
discrepancy, rather than any failure to anticipate the effects, is our central concern with the
record supporting this rule. A narrower examination framework may permit an institution to earn
a satisfactory rating even while serious community credit and investment needs remain unmet.

that consideration of community development activities outside of the assessment area could
override the current geographic limitation that applies to a bank's CRA examination.
We recognize that some communities outside any bank's assessment areas, including those in
rural communities and neighborhoods with limited branch presence, are underserved and have
serios unmet needs. Geographic flexibility could direct resources to those places. But neither
alternative directs out-of-area activity toward those communities. Once eligibility for out-of-area
consideration has been established, banks may have incentives to pursue projects that are easier
to originate rather than to undertake more difficult development within their assessment areas.
NCRC analyzed 69 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks among the 100 largest and found they
currently conduct about $102 billion a year in assessment-area community development lending
and investment. The proposed benchmark applied to the same banks comes to about $14.8

29 91 Fed. Reg. at 52,117, 52,127

30 91 Fed. Reg. at 52,139-40
31 91 Fed. Reg. at 52,120
 billion, roughly 85 percent less than the current activity.32 A floor set that far below current
practice risks becoming the target.
The agencies should analyze where community development activity is likely to relocate under
each alternative and whether the community's losing capital is disproportionately low-and
moderately low-income. The solution to underinvestment in communities outside assessment
areas should not be to reduce accountability within assessment areas.
The proposal works against the public welfare investment authority Congress expanded
weeks earlier
The agencies should account for the 21st Century ROAD To Housing Act before finalizing this
rule. Section 203 of the Act, enacted July 11, 2026, raised the aggregate public welfare
investment limit from 15 to 20 percent of capital and surplus and directed the Comptroller and
the Federal Reserve Board to report biennially to Congress on public welfare investments
made.33 The agencies issued this proposal twenty days later, on July 31, 2026. It would remove
the investment test from banks between $1.649 billion and $10 billion in assets.
These two actions point in opposite directions. Congress expanded banks' capacity to make
public welfare investments and asked to be told how that capacity is used. The agencies propose
to remove the examination that gives many banks a reason to use it. The Act appears nowhere in
the proposal.
The proposal also leaves a technical inconsistency in place, it updates cross references in the
OCC's public welfare investment regulations but leaves untouched the provision capping those
investments at 15 percent of a bank's capital and surplus, which now conflicts with the 20
percent limit Congress enacted. The OCC should update that cap to match the statute and explain
how removing the investment test for these banks is consistent with what Congress enacted.
The comment period should be reopened once the agencies select operative text
The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages and leaves core questions unresolved,
including two alternative geographic flexibility standards, two alternative approaches to major
product lines34, an alternative $850 million small-bank threshold35, and an alternative $3.252
billion intermediate threshold.36 The agencies also ask whether the large-bank threshold should
be $30 billion.37 Commenting on a proposal without definitive operative text is significantly

 more difficult, especially for community organizations and local affiliates without dedicated
regulatory staff. We urge the agencies to reopen the comment period once they have selected
among these alternatives.
Conclusion
The CRA exists to ensure that banks serve their entire communities. This proposal would reduce
the number of banks held to that standard, narrow what examiners look at, loosen what counts as
community development, and end the data reporting needed to see the results. The National
Urban League urges the agencies to withdraw these provisions.
If the agencies proceed, they should first complete and publish for comment an analysis that
identifies which LMI communities would receive less CRA scrutiny; quantifies the branches,
lending, investments, and deposit services that would fall outside evaluation; assesses the
permanent loss of lending data; and determines whether these effects concentrate in communities
that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment. They should also conform to the
indirect-cost limit to federal cost principles, retain a demonstrated-benefit requirement for
economic development credit, and reconcile the rule with Section 203 of the 21st Century ROAD
to Housing Act.
Where precise quantification is difficult to obtain, the agencies should not assume the
community's effect is insignificant. They should identify available evidence, acknowledge its
limitations, assess reasonably foreseeable consequences, and explain why the benefits outweigh
those risks.
