Re: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking Regulation BB – Community Reinvestment Act Regulations

To Whom It May Concern:

Hancock Whitney is a $36 billion state-chartered traditional brick and mortar financial institution
with 35 Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) assessment areas. Since the late 1800s, Hancock
Whitney has embodied core values of Honor & Integrity, Strength & Stability, and Commitment to
Service, Teamwork, and Personal Responsibility. Hancock Whitney offices and financial centers in
Mississippi, Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, and Texas offer comprehensive financial products and
services, including traditional and online banking; commercial and small business banking; private
banking; trust and investment services; healthcare banking; and mortgage services. The company
also operates combined loan and deposit production offices in the greater metropolitan areas of
Nashville, Tennessee, and Atlanta, Georgia. The Bank is evaluated under the CRA Large Bank Test by
its primary regulator, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC).

Hancock Whitney is grateful for the opportunity to comment in response to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking under the CRA. We applaud the efforts of the FDIC and the Office of the Comptroller of
the Currency (OCC) (collectively, the "Agencies") for the endeavor to streamline and modernize the
regulation while attempting to align with its original statute. Hancock Whitney supports the Agencies
intent to create efficiency, transparency, and consistency within banking and support for low- and
moderate-income communities and to low- and moderate-income individuals and small businesses.

The Agencies effort to further clarify the definition of community development and related activities
by codifying specific preexisting Interagency Questions and Answers is commendable. Furthermore,
the proposal's expansion of activities under the revised community development definition will help
broaden the banking industry's opportunity to create greater impact among the communities we
serve.

While we recognize these and other benefits found in the proposal, there are several areas requiring
further attention and consideration.

 2
Community Reinvestment Act Framework
The CRA has been the foundation for much of the community renewal as we know it today. Research
has shown significant impact over the course of its 49-year history. The Agencies have chosen at this
time to provide additional clarity around the definition of community development and to include
several notable expansions. Much of the proposal speaks to the original spirit of the regulation and
the statute's aim to increase the availability of credit across all communities including low- and
moderate-income communities. At its core the intention of the CRA is to improve the lives and
financial well-being of individuals, families, and businesses across the nation. Through this aim
much innovation has been credited to the original act and the Agencies oversight of the banking
industry in this regard.
Thresholds
To begin, the current asset size thresholds (small, intermediate small, and large) and associated
bank evaluation procedures have provided for predictability in exam proceedings, fairly consistent
regulatory oversight, and a strategic framework in which banks of all sizes are able to reasonably
establish goals and internal benchmarks in order to manage to the given objectives. This
longstanding framework has created rigor, discipline, and collective purpose among practitioners.
The proposed rule seeks to establish similar thresholds, namely small, intermediate, and large, with
the goal of simplifying the related asset requirement and aligning with similarly situated thresholds
as set forth in the 1995 rule. We commend the Agencies foresight in realigning the sizing to more
accurately reflect today's business models and institutional capacity. Unlike the 1995 rule, however,
the proposed rule would remove reporting requirements from all but large banks.
In the proposed rule the Agencies estimate that the revised asset thresholds would result in
approximately 79.8 percent of institutions being classified as small banks, 17.8 percent as
intermediate banks, and only 2.4 percent as large banks. As a result, only 2.4 percent of institutions
would remain subject to the large bank CRA reporting framework, significantly reducing the
availability of CRA data across the remaining 97.6 percent of the industry. Today, aggregated CRA
data serves as an important resource for financial institutions, public stakeholders, researchers and
the Agencies themselves to ascertain the degree to which community credit needs are being served.
This data also helps to inform strategies to expand credit availability, identify lending gaps, and
encourage the development and adoption of products and services that address community needs.
While the reduction in available CRA data presents one concern, a secondary potential impact is the
degree to which the community could lose current investment levels as a result of the loss of broad-
based bank accountability. Many financial institutions, as a core value, are committed to being good
community stewards; however, the proposed rule could have the unintended consequence of
decreasing CRA-focused resources and, therefore, CRA-related activities among the majority of
institutions, particularly small and intermediate banks. As a large bank, Hancock Whitney recognizes
that public, private, and nonprofit partnerships matter. These partnerships are key to creating
impactful and lasting community improvement. Often, multiple banks of varying sizes are
instrumental in working collectively toward community improvement through infrastructure projects,
neighborhood revitalization initiatives, economic development incentives, loan pools, and community
education programs. This collaboration allows banks to leverage their individual resources alongside
those of other financial institutions and community partners, 1resulting in greater investment and
impact.
 3

An unintended consequence of the proposal could result in fewer opportunities for large banks to
leverage their resources with other financial institutions, thereby creating additional responsibility on
a smaller number of institutions to help meet community credit needs. Community development is
not the role of one; it is the role of many. It requires collaboration across multiple stakeholders,
including financial institutions, community organizations, public entities, and private industry. The
most successful community development initiatives are often the result of these collective efforts
and partnerships.


Community Development

Affordable Housing

As a cornerstone of the CRA, the affordable housing guidance has been quintessential in addressing
housing stock shortages, housing cost burden, the availability of safe and affordable options, and
has helped spurn affordable housing development nationwide. We recognize the proposed rule's
intention of maintaining the success of this element of the rule and further clarifying and codifying
direction. We support the proposed baseline standards for multifamily developments, including rents
not to exceed 30 percent of 80 percent of area median income and the new allowance for high-cost
areas utilizing a baseline of 30 percent of 120 percent of area median income. The inclusion of
middle-income individuals in high-cost areas allows for an expansion of community development
supports to an often overlooked segment of the population for whom housing affordability is a
consistent problem and yet few resources exist to cover the gaps.


Economic Development

The current rule has established several baseline requirements for determining CRA activity based
on economic development aims. Currently it requires both a size test and purpose test. The
proposed rule seeks to further streamline and clarify what constitutes economic development by
removing the purpose test and more specifically eliminating the requirement to prove job creation
and retention. The proposed rule does, however, retain the initial intent of promoting the financing of
small businesses and small farms and the initiatives which support them. We ask however that
additional consideration be given to retaining operating liquidity in the revised definition. For small
businesses the availability of operating liquidity allows flexibility to make needed upgrades, purchase
equipment, purchase new technology, create efficiencies in operations, and provide momentum
toward overall business growth and sustainability.


Revitalization and Stabilization

As a financial institution uniquely situated along the Gulf South, our bank has weathered many
storms throughout our history. We have locked arms with our community and helped support
individual and community recovery. Disaster recovery is one of the ways we show up and meet
community needs whether those needs are food, water, gas, or emergency loans, we show up. We
are often in lockstep with local community organizations and local government on the ground
working collaboratively toward the same goals. We thank the Agencies for continuing the focus on
revitalization and stabilization for our communities and for being intentional around disaster
recovery. One additional consideration is worth noting, however, which is the extent to which local
and state government serve as the first response to natural disasters. Because of this localized
response and intelligence, states are often first to declare disaster in impacted areas followed by the
 4

Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). We ask that the Agencies consider adding state-
level declarations of disaster as an additional qualifier for CRA activities.


Community Development Loans

Community Development Lending has long been a staple offering at our institution and has offered
an opportunity for the bank to participate in all forms of the Community Reinvestment Act including
affordable housing, revitalization and stabilization, economic development and support of essential
community services. The bank intends to continue to lead these efforts across the communities we
serve and further commend the Agencies recognition of the importance of the work by proposing the
change to allow prior period loans in the same manner as prior period investments are evaluated
today. This change is welcomed and honors the risk, along with the initial responsiveness and
complexities which come with providing these loans.


Community Development Investments

Community development investments serve a vital role in responding to community credit needs and
supporting organizations whose missions are to improve economic opportunity and quality of life
within underserved communities. The current rule has provided a great deal of flexibility to banks in
helping to meet these needs through a variety of forms and at the bank's discretion with appropriate
guardrails. The proposed rule seeks to redefine community development investment by separating
elements of the current definition which includes eligible securities, deposits, donations, and grants.
In the proposal donations and grants would receive consideration under the new term Community
Development Grant. According to the proposed rule these bank contributions would be treated much
in the same way as a traditional grant offered by federal agencies and private foundations. Further,
the proposed rule would significantly expand the reporting requirements and impose a budgetary
restriction and oversight obligations to banks. In addition, the proposed will require banks to report
annually, to collect tax documentation, to confirm that funds do not exceed 15% of an organization's
operating budget and have data publicly available on their giving.

The comparison of the federal grantmaking process to a bank's charitable giving efforts is at its core
problematic. Most banks lack the staffing and technological resources to support a comprehensive
grantmaking operation. Most public, private, and nonprofit grantmaking entities are equipped with
full-time teams, and sophisticated grant portals for facilitating grantmaking. These teams also
employ skilled and experienced fund development professionals to manage their processes and
provide daily oversight of their grantmaking activities. A bank, on the other hand, exists
fundamentally to provide credit and deposit facilities in order to best serve its communities. Further
the philanthropic efforts of financial institutions are a part of their intention to provide goodwill and
serve as a community steward.

The inclusion of donations and grants in the current rule has provided banks the unique
responsibility and role of meeting community organizations "where they are". These organizations
supply real time on the ground response to communities in need. They represent a diverse mix of
budgets, staff size, programmatic capacity, and fund development acumen. No two organizations are
alike. In many instances a bank's support of an organization is intended to provide much needed
gap funding and serve as leverage between other funding sources and the cost of providing the
services. Without funding to support staffing, technology, facilities, the community needs simply
 5

cannot be met. The current rule has provided a much needed olive branch to many meaningful
causes and initiatives and the organizations which lead them for over 49 years. We ask that the
Agencies eliminate the administrative cap of 15 percent in the proposed rule and the requirement
for the bank's oversight of this component. We further ask that banks be allowed to continue to
support community organizations which are meeting the needs of low- and moderate-income
communities and small businesses in a way that provides the industry flexibility and self-directed
action.


Data Requirements & Reporting

In addition, we also ask that the proposed annual submission requirement for community grants be
reconsidered as well as the related public availability of that information which could open banks up
to potential reputational and other unforeseen risks. The current rule mandates annual reporting
based on associated thresholds and for large banks requires loan activity reporting namely across
small business, small farm, mortgage, and community development loans. We ask that those
requirements remain in place as they exist today. Further we request that the internal annual data
collection and maintenance of community development investments and grants remain the same.

The proposed rule also amends the current requirements around the physical availability of the
public file. The change would require banks to post the public file on the website and offer digital
availability. This approach would create efficiencies in the management and availability of the public
file. Likewise, the Agencies commitment to develop and publish a non-exhaustive list of qualified
community development activities along with a universal process for inquiries is much appreciated.
We further encourage the Agencies to consider the operational challenges associated with
implementing new or modified data collection and reporting requirements, particularly for
institutions with multiple lending platforms and business lines. Clear data definitions, consistent
reporting standards, and adequate implementation periods are essential to ensuring data accuracy,
effective quality control, and reliable regulatory reporting. These considerations become particularly
important for institutions experiencing growth through mergers and acquisitions, where system
integration and data consistency may present additional challenges.

Final Rule Implementation

The proposed rule in its aim to clarify and streamline the regulation offers some much-improved
opportunities for banks to continue the work of community development. However, several of the
proposed amendments as previously notated could stand to substantially change the community
development landscape and the availability of credit facilities to the most vulnerable communities.
We ask that the Agencies revisit the noted items and consider modifications where applicable.
Similarly, we ask for a review of the new proposed reporting requirements for large banks,
specifically those surrounding the proposed community development grant reporting which would
impose extensive data collection and recordkeeping. In addition, these changes would require adds
to staff due to the time-consuming nature and expertise required. Lastly these changes would
involve permanent budget increases.

We also acknowledge the Agencies question around alignment with reporting requirements for
section 1071 loans and although we understand there will be some duplication we would not
 6

recommend replacing the current small business data collection as it exists today with 1071 data
reporting. Small business and small farm data currently presents some similarities to 1071 reporting
requirements however the two data sets are not equivalent across data points and replacing one for
the other may result in the exclusion of certain small business loans from submission eligibility.

We further applaud the Agencies desire to preserve flexibility in assessment area delineation and
performance evaluation, particularly for institutions operating across multiple geographic markets or
experiencing changes in their branch networks through mergers and acquisitions, or other business
developments. CRA performance expectations should appropriately consider an institution's physical
presence, lending opportunities, market demographics, and demonstrated responsiveness to
community needs. A consistent, risk-based approach would promote meaningful community
reinvestment while recognizing differences in market conditions and institutional operating models.

As a final note we recommend a substantial implementation timeline of at least 24 months in sync
with historic timelines of recent rulings to allow for proper onboarding, testing, and clarification
period. Thank you for consideration of our comments we appreciate the opportunity to respond to
the new proposed rule and we look forward to a review of the final outcome.

Sincerely,

Ashley Aubrey Harrison,
Senior Vice President, Corporate CRA Officer
Director Community & Economic Development

October 13, 2026
Chief Counsel's Office
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street, SW
Washington, DC 20219
Jennifer M. Jones
Deputy Executive Secretary
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street NW
Washington, DC 20429
Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; OCC
RIN 1557-AF57; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31
The CDFI Coalition appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
proposed amendments to Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
The CDFI Coalition is the unified national voice of Community Development Financial
Institutions (CDFIs) and their partners. CDFIs work with regulated financial institutions
throughout the country to finance small businesses, affordable housing, community
facilities, rural communities, Native communities, and other borrowers and projects that
often face difficulty accessing conventional credit. CRA has been instrumental in
supporting these partnerships and in bringing private bank capital into communities where
credit needs remain substantial.
The Coalition supports the agencies' efforts to provide greater clarity regarding qualifying
community development activities and to modernize geographic eligibility for regulated
financial institutions.
At the same time, several provisions would significantly weaken incentives for banks to
engage in community development activities and could discourage bank partnerships with
CDFIs. We urge the agencies to revise the final rule to explicitly recognize banks
partnerships with CDFIs. We also urge the agencies to preserve meaningful community
development obligations, maintain geographic flexibility, and avoid restrictions on grants
that would discourage support for effective community development organizations.
I. Bank Thresholds and Community Development
The agencies propose changing the small bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion,
creating an intermediate bank category between $1 billion and $10 billion, and raising the
large bank threshold to $10 billion. The Coalition strongly opposes both proposals, which
would be devastating to community development finance. In place of a wholesale overhaul
of banks' CRA responsibilities, the Coalition recommends that the agencies make an effort
to index the thresholds to inflation.
 Large banks ($10B+): The proposed thresholds would reduce the number of large banks
facing rigorous CRA scrutiny by 417. The proposal also narrows the large bank test to focus
exclusively on its two largest "major product lines" (based on loan count and volume). The
Coalition does not support this proposal, which could leave tens of billions in bank
products and services unexamined.
Intermediate Banks ($1-$10B): The proposal would also dilute the community
development test for 417 newly classified intermediate banks by allowing them to receive
an overall "satisfactory" rating based on satisfactory lending performance even if their
community development performance is less than satisfactory. The Coalition opposes
this proposal. If today's CRA status quo produces homogenous scoring, this would only
increase the opacity of banks' performance serving the credit needs of their footprint.
Small Banks (Under $1B): Increasing the small bank threshold to $1 billion would
eliminate the community development obligations of over 814 banks.
The effect of these changes would be to make community development performance less
consequential for a substantial number of institutions. Industry experts estimate that
these changes could put at least $2 billion per year in current community development
loans and investments at risk.1 It would also substantially reduce the amount of data
available to determine whether the credit needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI)
communities are being met.
All these changes would reduce the incentive for partnerships with CDFIs, particularly in
rural areas that already lack access to brick-and-mortar banking facilities and have seen a
wave of closures and consolidation over the past two decades. For many rural families,
CDFIs are the only lender of note, and they rely on assistance from the few banks who
serve underinvested areas.
II. The 15 Percent Indirect-Cost Cap and CRA Consideration for Grants
The Coalition strongly opposes the proposed 15 percent indirect-cost cap for grants.
Under the proposal, for a grant to qualify as a community development activity, it would
have to be directly used by the recipient for a qualifying community development program,
project, or initiative. In addition, a large bank could receive CRA consideration only if the
recipient's indirect costs associated with administering the grant do not exceed 15 percent.
Banks would be expected to collect written commitments, attestations, Form 990
information, and operating and program budgets to validate compliance.

1 https://www.ncrc.org/cra/
 In response to Question 92, the Coalition recommends that the agencies eliminate the 15
percent cap rather than substitute another arbitrary organization-wide overhead limit. This
proposed change would create paperwork and headaches for banks and cash-constrained
nonprofits and would have a chilling effect on banks' willingness to use grants as a
qualifying community development activity.
There is plenty of research on the efficacy of capacity building grants for nonprofits. For
example, researchers examined 15 years of data from a major foundation, covering roughly
400 nonprofit applicants. Organizations receiving capacity-building grants experienced
about 10% financial growth over the following three years, compared to those that received
traditional grants.3
For CDFIs in particular, accounting, compliance, information technology, loan servicing,
underwriting systems, audit expenses, and other operational costs are essential to
providing products and financial services. Treating those costs as evidence that a CDFI is
diverting resources away from community development misunderstands how financial
institutions operate.
Operating support acts as a multiplier for a financial institution serving markets with deep
credit needs. A recent study of operating grants for CDFIs4 found the following:
• Total CDFI assets increased 56% on average and net assets 38%.
• The number of outstanding loans increased 78% on average.
• Meanwhile, staffing only increased 25% on average.
• The grantees enabled CDFIs to strengthen balance sheets and attract additional
capital.

The CDFIs studied used flexible grant assistance for improved technology, new staff, new
financial products and services, geographic expansions, and other activities that ordinary
debt capital typically does not support. As Department of Treasury explains, Technical
Assistance awards (analogous to capacity building grants) are used for "capacity
development that is integral to a CDFI's organizational sustainability."
At a minimum, the final rule should continue to permit general operating and capacity-
building support to organizations whose mission and activities satisfy the rule's final
community development definition. Grants help CDFIs better serve the communities CRA
is designed to support. They can hire locally based loan officers, improve service delivery

2 Question 9: Are there alternative standards the agencies should consider relying on in the context of limiting
indirect costs for CD grants? Do the proposed guardrails do enough to ensure the majority of grant and
donation funds go directly towards benefiting the bank's assessment area(s)?
3 Faulk & Stewart (2017), "As You Sow, So Shall You Reap?"
4 Sarah Wolff et al., Building Organizational Capacity and Deepening Impact with PRO Neighborhoods Grants
(Abt Associates, 2020).
 through better technology systems, increase loan-loss capacity, expand technical
assistance, and invest in other institutional resources to expand the breadth and quality of
their financial products and services. Artificially separating those functions from
"community development" would discourage precisely the institutional investment
necessary to expand lending.
In response to Question 105, the Coalition strongly opposes eliminating grants and
donations from CRA consideration for large banks. Grants perform functions that debt and
equity capital cannot, and they are particularly important during periods of economic
dislocation and upheaval when CDFIs need additional resources to meet growing demand.
Grants to CDFIs support technical assistance, new or expanded lending products,
financial counseling, predevelopment work, operating capacity, loan-loss reserves, and
activities that do not generate sufficient revenue to support risk-based capital.
III. Explicitly Recognize the Full Range of Bank Financing Provided to
Certified CDFIs
The proposal appropriately recognizes CDFIs that finance small businesses and small
farms within its economic development definition. The Coalition strongly supports
retaining this provision.
The final rule should go further and, as the OCC and FDIC proposed in 2019, expressly
recognize capital investments, loan participations, and other financing undertaken in
cooperation with certified CDFIs. CDFIs finance much more than small businesses and
farms. They finance affordable housing, new manufacturing plants, health centers and
hospital upgrades, commercial real estate, nonprofit organizations, infrastructure, and a
variety of other eligible community development projects. This explicit regulatory
recognition would codify what is already spelled out in the agencies' CRA Q&A, as the
proposal notes.
The final rule should make clear that qualifying bank support for certified CDFIs may
include loans, deposits, equity and equity-equivalent investments, loan participations,
loan guarantees and credit enhancements, grants, donations, and other forms of capital.
Bank support for certified CDFIs should automatically receive CRA consideration.
Providing clear treatment of CDFI financing would also reduce red tape by eliminating
unnecessary tracing and documentation. Treasury certification already establishes that
CDFIs (as organizations) are a financing entity with a primary mission of promoting
community development. Certified CDFIs must meet requirements for accountability,
target markets, and development services. Banks should not be required to trace capital
flows and prove a community development use every time they provide support to a

5 Question 10: As an alternative, should the agencies eliminate all grants and donations from CRA
consideration?
 certified Community Development Financial Institution. By injecting unwarranted risk and
uncertainty into the process, many of the proposed rules would increase the cost of
providing capital for CDFIs, and, correspondingly, the cost of capital in underinvested rural
and urban markets.
IV. Prior-Period Community Development Loans
The Coalition supports the proposal to provide CRA consideration for prior-period
community development loans, which would incentivize longer-term financing (as the
agencies recognize in their proposed rule). The Coalition supports annual consideration for
qualifying community development loans and investments that remain on a bank's
balance sheet.
Community development activities benefit tremendously from patient, long-term financing.
Affordable housing, community facilities, and small-business loan funds often require
capital extending well beyond a single CRA evaluation period. Annual recognition better
reflects the continuing commitment of bank capital.
However, the agencies should not provide full credit for loans that are simply reissued.
V. Native Land Areas
The Coalition supports the proposal's recognition of Indian country and other Tribal and
native lands as targeted geographic areas for community development activities.
According to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, 46.4 percent of the population
living in majority American Indian and Alaska Native census tracts lived in banking deserts
in 2023, more than 12 times the national average.6
The proposal defines "Indian country" and "other Tribal and native lands" using several
statutory and Census geographic designations. The Coalition recommends that the
agencies instead adopt the broader "Native Land Area" definition used in the 2023 CRA
rule, as contemplated by Question 557. That definition more comprehensively captures
Native communities that may not fall neatly within a single statutory or Census geographic
designation.
Additional approaches (beyond geographic prioritization) are also needed to encourage
banks to meet credit needs in these communities.

6 Alaina Barca and Harry Hou, U.S. Bank Branch Closures and Banking Deserts, Federal Reserve Bank of
Philadelphia (February 2024).
7 Question 55: Are there alternative approaches the agencies should consider to encourage banks to meet
the credit needs of Indian country and other Tribal and native lands? For example, should the agencies use
the definition of Native Lands in the 2023 CRA rules? Are there any difficulties or unintended consequences
that banks might encounter with the definitions as proposed?
 The final rule should provide additional qualitative consideration for bank branches on
Native lands. It should also provide broad geographic flexibility for activities undertaken
through Native CDFIs and other financial institutions with demonstrated expertise serving
Native communities.
These changes are welcome. However, we are deeply concerned that the changes to the
bank thresholds will lead to a major reduction in both bank lending and data collection in
Native communities.
VI. Primary-Purpose Guidance
The Coalition supports clear guidance regarding the definition of the "primary purpose"
standard requested in Question 11.8 We agree with the agencies' approach in adopting
language from the CRA Q&As while providing additional clarity on the definition of
"responsiveness."
Clear guidance would reduce the costs borne out of uncertainty for banks and CDFIs. The
guidance should avoid requiring banks or CDFIs to trace every dollar through pooled
financing vehicles with a community development purpose.
For certified CDFIs, the agencies should provide a safe harbor wherein banks can point to
reasonable evidence demonstrating that the activity supports a qualifying community
development activity.
In terms of the definition of responsiveness, we urge the agencies to weigh a community
development loan or investment's impact over its transactional complexity. Instead of
rewarding complex financial instruments, qualitative measures should provide preference
for the extent to which an activity addresses community needs.
VII. Preserve Investor Demand for Community Development Tax
Incentives
The proposed changes to the CRA thresholds could cause a significant decline in investor
demand for community development tax incentives, including the Low-Income House Tax
Credit (LIHTC) and the New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC).
By shifting over 400 large banks into the intermediate category, the new thresholds limit
the number of banks subject to the Investment Test measuring their equity investments.
Large, CRA-motivated banks are the primary investors in the NMTC and LIHTC. Reduced
demand for these credits would reduce their efficiency. For example, NMTC pricing

8 Question 11: Should the agencies provide guidance regarding how primary purpose would be determined
for each CD purpose in the definition of "community development"?
 corresponds directly with the amount of subsidy reaching a qualified business. A decline in
LIHTC pricing reduces the equity available for affordable housing.
VIII. Economic Development Definition
The Coalition generally supports the proposal's effort to make the economic development
definition clearer and more objective. However, in response to Question 259, the agencies
should retain an LMI-benefit requirement for this category but should not make job
creation or retention the exclusive means of demonstrating that benefit.
Job creation is an important measure of impact, but it need not be the only measure.
Financing may enable a small business to purchase equipment, acquire property, stabilize
operations, expand product lines, or survive a temporary disruption or natural disaster.
CDFIs also frequently serve entrepreneurs and sole proprietors. A loan that preserves the
viability of their business has a significant impact in itself.
In response to Question 2610, the Coalition strongly supports retaining CDFIs among the
expressly identified examples of entities presumed to promote economic development.
The final rule should also make clear that the list is non-exhaustive and should
accommodate new Federal, State, local, and Tribal programs as they develop.
In response to Question 2911, the final rule should not exclude working-capital financing for
ongoing operating liquidity. For small businesses served by CDFIs, working capital
financing allows a business to expand, grow, or stabilize.
IX. Geographic Flexibility
The Coalition supports greater geographic flexibility in CRA evaluations to encourage
banks to invest in underserved communities, particularly rural areas and smaller markets
that have historically struggled to attract bank investment. Under the current regulatory
framework, CRA unintentionally shifts lending away from certain geographies.
However, we are concerned that Option 1 of the proposal would establish a numerical
threshold that could substantially weaken incentives for community development lending
and investment. Option 1 would allow banks to receive CRA consideration for community
development activities outside their assessment areas after meeting annual thresholds of

9 Question 25: Should the agencies retain the requirement that the activity create, improve, or retain jobs for
LMI individuals or in an LMI area in the first category of economic development?
10 Question 26: Should any of the example government programs included in the third category of economic
development (proposed § __.12, definition of economic development paragraph (3)(iii)) be removed from the
list of examples? Should additional programs, projects, or initiatives be included in the list of examples?
11 Question 29: Are there activities that would be considered economic development under the current rules
that would not qualify under the proposed definition of economic development?
 0.625% of allocated Tier 1 capital for community development loans and another 0.625%
for investments and grants within their assessment areas. According to an analysis by the
National Community Reinvestment Coalition, 69 large OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks
currently provide approximately $102 billion annually in community development lending,
investments, and grants within their assessment areas, compared to just $14.8 billion
represented by the proposed thresholds. Although intended to provide geographic
flexibility, these relatively low thresholds could become benchmarks (in all but name only)
that weaken incentives for banks to maintain their current levels of community
development lending and investment.
While the low thresholds are concerning, geographic flexibility is an important piece of any
CRA overhaul, particularly for rural and Native communities with significant credit needs
but few bank branches or CRA assessment areas. The current regulatory framework
incentivizes the concentration of community development capital in metropolitan areas
(where bank branches are largely located).
X. Maintain Consideration of Affordable Deposit Services
The proposal would eliminate consideration of deposit services in the retail banking
evaluation. The agencies describe their intent to "shift CRA-motivated activity toward
lending and credit services and away from certain CD activities, in particular grants and
deposit services."
We addressed the importance of grants earlier, but the Coalition also disagrees with the
decreased emphasis on deposit services.
The Coalition urges the agencies to restore evaluation of deposit services. CRA
consideration of the availability, cost, and features of deposit products provides banks
with a regulatory incentive to offer affordable accounts that can help bring unbanked and
underbanked households into the banking system.
XI. Provide a Reasonable Transition
In response to Question 5912, the agencies should provide reasonable transition periods for
material changes in data collection, documentation, and reporting. Banks and their CDFI
partners should not be disadvantaged for transactions entered under existing CRA
expectations, and activities that qualified when undertaken should continue to receive
consideration during the applicable evaluation period.

12 Question 59: Should the agencies include transition provisions providing for deferred applicability dates
for any of the proposed provisions? In particular, should the rules include transition provisions for the
proposed: (1) consideration for eligible CD activities provision; (2) strategic plan provisions; (3) new data
collection, maintenance, and reporting provisions; or (4) public notice provisions?

 XII. Unified Framework
The Coalition urges the federal banking agencies to adopt a single, jointly issued
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule rather than proceeding with separate or
inconsistent regulatory frameworks. For decades, the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC
have maintained consistent CRA regulations, providing banks, regulators, and community
development organizations with a unified regulatory framework. Divergent rules would
create unnecessary compliance burdens, introduce uncertainty for banks operating under
different federal supervisors, and undermine the consistency and effectiveness of CRA.
Inconsistent standards could also distort competition among financial institutions and
create confusion for CDFIs and other community development partners seeking long-term
financing and investment commitments. The Coalition therefore urges the agencies to
coordinate closely, secure the participation of all three federal banking regulators, and
issue a unified final rule that preserves consistent CRA standards across the banking
system.
XIII. General Comment: Bank–CDFI Partnerships at Risk
As previously noted, the threshold changes will eliminate CRA as a motivating factor for
community development for 417 large banks and dilute it for hundreds more. The
proposed changes will weaken incentives for banks to provide capital and support to
CDFIs, increasing the cost of capital in LMI communities. These longstanding CDFI-bank
partnerships include:
•
Loans and revolving lines of credit to capitalize CDFI lending activities;
•
Equity-equivalent investments (EQ2s) and other long-term, patient capital;
•
Subordinated debt and other investments that strengthen CDFI balance sheets;
•
Deposits in CDFI banks and credit unions;
•
Loan participations, loan purchases, and secondary-market arrangements;
•
Credit enhancements, guarantees, and loan-loss reserves;
•
Warehouse financing and bridge loans;
•
Multibank lending consortiums and pooled community development investments;
•
Joint financing of affordable housing, small businesses, commercial real estate,
and community facilities;
•
New Markets Tax Credit investments and financing partnerships;
•
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit investments and affordable housing financing;
•
Financing partnerships supporting Native CDFIs, rural CDFIs, and specialized
community development lenders;
•
Employee volunteer services, including board participation, credit committee
service, underwriting assistance, and financial expertise; and
•
Referrals of borrowers who cannot obtain conventional bank financing to CDFIs
offering more flexible underwriting and specialized technical assistance.

 CDFI-bank partnerships, many of which have been explicitly recognized and encouraged
by the OCC and FDIC, support affordable housing, small-business development, childcare,
health care, manufacturing, community facilities, food access, homeownership, and other
essential community development activities. While the proposal would not eliminate CRA
consideration for all these arrangements, reducing the number of banks subject to
meaningful community development evaluations would weaken the incentives supporting
them.
Conclusion
CRA has helped build durable partnerships between banks and CDFIs and has directed
substantial private capital toward small businesses, affordable housing, community
facilities, and communities with significant unmet credit needs. The final rule should
strengthen those partnerships rather than make them more difficult.
The CDFI Coalition therefore urges the OCC and FDIC to maintain meaningful community
development expectations for a broad range of banks; reject a $10 billion large-bank
threshold; require satisfactory community development performance from intermediate
banks; expressly recognize the full range of qualifying financing provided to certified CDFIs;
eliminate the proposed 15 percent indirect-cost cap; preserve CRA consideration for
grants and operating support; provide annual consideration for long-term community
development loans and investments; provide meaningful geographic flexibility; preserve
recognition of CDFIs under the economic development definition; strengthen
consideration for activities serving rural and Native communities; and protect the viability
of community development tax incentives.
We appreciate the agencies' consideration of these comments and look forward to
working with the OCC and FDIC to ensure that the final CRA regulations continue to
encourage safe and sound bank financing that meets the credit needs of communities
throughout the country.
Sincerely,
Hank Helton
President, CDFI Coalition

Entrepreneur Works Fund is a community development finance institution (CDFI) that provides

financing and support to make a project or service possible. CRA has helped make banks dependable
partners in that work. NCO is concerned that several parts of the proposal could weaken those
partnerships and make it harder for local organizations to respond to the housing and credit needs of the
communities they serve.
NCO supports clear and workable regulations, but regulatory simplification should not come at the cost
of reducing meaningful expectations that banks serve the full range of credit and community development
needs in their communities. We urge the agencies to reconsider the proposal before finalizing it and to
assess its likely effects on housing production, homeownership, nonprofit capacity, and access to services
in Ohio communities.





1. Preserve meaningful community development expectations for community and regional banks
The proposed increase in the large-bank asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion would move
many community and regional banks out of the framework that includes a separate Investment Test. That
change matters to organizations working at the local level. Banks do not contribute only one kind of
support: depending on the community and the project, they may provide loans, equity, grants, financial
education, and other forms of partnership. A bank's community development investment can be the piece
that allows a housing development or community initiative to move forward.
Ohio communities should not lose those incentives simply because a bank's assets fall below a
substantially higher threshold. Smaller and rural markets can have fewer potential sources of financing
and less competition for housing transactions. In those places, the participation of a locally engaged bank
may be especially important. A national market-wide estimate of available capital would not, by itself,
demonstrate that financing will remain available on workable terms in each local market.
NCO therefore urges the agencies to retain meaningful, distinct expectations for community development
lending and investment. If the agencies decide to increase the large-bank threshold, NCO supports the
more limited $3.252 billion alternative over the proposed $10 billion threshold. The agencies should not
adopt the $30 billion alternative, which would place an even larger share of community development
activity outside the strongest evaluation framework.

2. Recognize that housing finance requires more than conventional lending
Housing projects frequently require a combination of public resources, private financing, and equity.
Conventional loans are important, but they cannot replace equity when a development's costs exceed the
rents or sale prices that households can afford. The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) is a central
source of equity for affordable rental housing, and CRA-related incentives have helped sustain
participation by banks of different sizes. Changes that weaken the incentive for community and regional
banks to make these investments could reduce competition, worsen financing gaps, or make some
projects infeasible.
The same principle applies beyond rental development. NCO affiliates work across homeownership,
housing counseling, rehabilitation, and neighborhood revitalization. These activities depend on local
partnerships and on a range of financing and support that reflects local needs. CRA should continue to
recognize the different roles of lending, investment, grants, and services rather than treating one form of
activity as a substitute for another.

3. Protect grants that help community organizations deliver results
Community-based organizations need operational capacity to deliver effective programs. Staff,
technology, compliance, financial management, resident outreach, and program administration are not

peripheral to community development; they are part of how services are delivered responsibly and
consistently. Housing counseling, financial education, homeownership preparation, and support for local
revitalization all require this capacity.
The proposal's restrictions on qualifying grants, including a proposed 15 percent limit on administrative
costs, risk discouraging support for organizations whose work responds directly to community needs. A
fixed overhead percentage is not a reliable measure of an organization's effectiveness or the value of its
work. The agencies should instead evaluate whether a grant supports an eligible community development
purpose, responds to an identified need, and is subject to appropriate accountability. NCO urges the
agencies to preserve CRA consideration for grants that support qualifying activities, including reasonable
operating and capacity-building support.

4. Keep low- and moderate-income households and communities at the center
Ohio faces a range of housing challenges, including a shortage of homes affordable to lower-income
households, barriers to sustainable homeownership, and neighborhoods where reinvestment remains
difficult. Middle-income households also experience affordability pressures, but broadening CRA eligibility
without clear safeguards could redirect limited CRA-motivated resources away from low- and moderate-
income people and places—the central focus of the statute.
NCO encourages the agencies to maintain a clear connection between CRA consideration and
demonstrated community need. Any expansion of eligibility for naturally occurring affordable housing or
other activities should include meaningful affordability standards and protections against displacement
of resources from households with the greatest needs. The final rule should also preserve support for the
counseling, education, and other services that help households prepare for homeownership and remain
stably housed.

5. Evaluate the practical consequences before finalizing the rule
The proposal would change bank classifications, evaluation methods, geographic considerations, and the
treatment of grants and community development activities. NCO urges the agencies to assess how these
changes would affect actual lending, investment, services, and branch access in low- and moderate-
income communities, including rural areas and smaller Ohio markets. That assessment should identify
which communities would receive less CRA-related activity and whether the effects would be
concentrated in places already facing barriers to housing development and access to credit.
Given the breadth of the proposed changes and their potential effect on local organizations and residents,
the agencies should extend the comment period by at least 60 days and provide a meaningful opportunity
for affected communities to assess the proposal and submit evidence. If the agencies do not extend the
period, NCO urges them to delay final action until they have completed and publicly explained a thorough
assessment of the proposal's likely community-level effects.


Recommendations
In summary, we recommend that the FDIC and OCC:
•
Retain meaningful and distinct expectations for community development lending and investment.
•
If the large-bank threshold is increased, adopt the $3.252 billion alternative rather than $10
billion, and reject the $30 billion alternative.
•
Preserve CRA eligibility for grants supporting qualifying community development purposes,
including reasonable operating and capacity-building costs, without a rigid 15 percent
administrative-cost cap.
•
Maintain a clear focus on low- and moderate-income households and communities, with
safeguards for any expanded eligibility categories.
•
Extend the comment period by at least 60 days or delay final action until the agencies have
assessed and publicly explained the likely effects on local housing and community development
activity.
CRA works best when it creates a durable expectation that financial institutions will be attentive to the
needs of the communities where they do business. For Ohio's NeighborWorks affiliates, that expectation
helps sustain local partnerships that support affordable homes, responsible homeownership, and stronger
neighborhoods. NCO encourages the agencies to pursue clarity and proportionality while preserving the
incentives and accountability that make those outcomes possible.
Thank you for considering NCO's comments.
Sincerely,


Stacy Brown
Chair, NeighborWorks Collaborative of Ohio

Thank you for the opportunity for the Illinois Housing Development Authority (IHDA) to provide
feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). As Illinois' housing
finance agency, IHDA allocates the majority of Illinois' Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC) to
create or preserve housing for low- and moderate-income renters across the state. Over the past
five years, IHDA has utilized LIHTC to finance 147 developments, resulting in the creation or
preservation of 7,541 much-needed affordable housing units.

Since 1977, CRA has motivated banks to extend private capital financing to the local communities
they serve, combating the legacy of redlining, promoting equitable lending, and facilitating
reinvestment in low- and moderate-income communities and people. CRA has spurred lending
and investments in homeownership, small businesses, healthcare, childcare, and other
community needs, but nowhere is its impact more pronounced than in the effect CRA has had on
financing the creation of affordable housing through LIHTC.

LIHTC, the nation's most important tool to produce affordable rental housing, relies heavily on
investments from banks subject to CRA to create equity to make the developments financially
feasible. In fact, 80 percent of equity investments in LIHTC each year come from CRA-motivated
 bank investors.1 Banks make these investments not only to receive the return provided by the tax
advantages, but also because the full CRA examination for large banks includes a distinct
investment test. LIHTC investment yields are typically modest, banks often still choose to invest
in LIHTC because it helps them meet their CRA obligations.

IHDA is concerned that the OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with assets ranging from
$1.649 to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks could reduce competition in
the LIHTC equity market, leading to lower pricing on credits and less housing produced. Of the
642 banks currently classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain that designation under the
proposal, a decline of over 60 percent, according to the National Association of Affordable
Housing Lenders (NAAHL). This leaves only six percent of banks in the current large bank
classification subject to the full CRA exam. According to a survey by the Affordable Housing Tax
Credit Coalition (AHTCC), banks with assets in the $1.649 billion to $10 billion range invested at
least $1.6 billion in LIHTC equity over a five-year survey period. Extrapolating these results to the
full LIHTC market, banks in this asset range invested up to $2 billion in LIHTC equity over the past
five years. Quite frankly, with this proposed change, the probability that the market for LIHTC
equity investments would collapse is quite high.

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, the newly classified intermediate banks would no longer
need to invest in the low- and moderate-income communities they are supposed to serve because
they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having more general
community development obligations as an intermediate-sized bank. This is because, for various
reasons, it is often easier for banks to support community development activities through lending
rather than equity investment.

Moreover, the proposed rulemaking undercuts recent congressional action to strengthen and
expand LIHTC and facilitate more bank investment in the program. House Resolution 1 included
a substantial increase in LIHTC authority and supply, while the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act
raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to increase their LIHTC
investments. The lifting of the PWI cap would impact many of the same banks that would be
reclassified as intermediate banks if the rule is passed.

Lastly, the consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to smaller communities that
now benefit from being in the CRA assessment area of one or more large banks but may no longer
be if the definition of large bank is changed. In Illinois, this would include a large swath of our
state that is made up of smaller towns and rural communities. A survey by AHTCC found that
approximately a third of LIHTC equity invested through syndicators by banks in the $412 million
to $10 billion asset range supported rural markets between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these
banks play an outsized role in investing in smaller communities. We have seen that to be true in
Illinois.

Conclusion
IHDA strongly encourages the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under

RE: Docket No. OCC-2026-0694, Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
To Whom It May Concern:
Housing Forward submits these public comments to express our strong opposition to
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and the Office of the Comptroller of
the Currency's (OCC) joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding proposed
amendments to the implementing regulations for the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) of 1977.
Operating in Suburban Cook County, Illinois, since 1992, Housing Forward is a nonprofit
service leader offering a coordinated response to help individuals and families
experiencing a housing crisis resolve their situation quickly. Our comprehensive housing
model transitions individuals and families out of housing crises into long-term stability
through permanent supportive housing, rapid rehousing, street outreach, interim
shelter, and medical respite care. In 2025 alone, Housing Forward utilized federal, state,
local and private resources to impact the lives of 2,232 vulnerable people.
While Housing Forward supports regulatory efficiency, we strongly reject the proposed
changes to the CRA regulations. If finalized as written, these revisions will severely
undermine the financial ecosystem that supports our permanent housing solutions,
community development partnerships, and supportive services across West Suburban
Cook County, including Maywood, Broadview, and Oak Park.
1. Drastic Increases to Asset Thresholds Exempt Dozens of Illinois Banks from
Community Development Obligations
The proposed rule would dramatically raise the asset threshold for "large banks" to over
$10 billion and intermediate banks to over $1 billion. In Illinois, this will result in nearly 40%
of intermediate and large banks being bumped down a category, stripping them of
mandatory community development obligations.
For Housing Forward and the communities of Maywood, Broadview, and Oak Park, this
 2
rollback is devastating. Banks operating in our region rely on these regulatory guardrails
to maintain robust community development lending and investments. Letting mid-sized
and large institutions off the hook means a sharp reduction in private capital flowing into
affordable housing development, local economic stabilization, and vital permanent
supportive housing initiatives that keep vulnerable households out of emergency
shelters.
2. Restrictions on Community Development Grants and Punitive Overhead Caps
Threaten Non-Profit Infrastructure
The NPRM proposes strict new restrictions on community development grants and
donations, including a mandate that funds be "directly used" for specific programs and
an arbitrary 15% cap on a non-profit recipient's indirect or administrative costs.
Housing Forward strongly opposes these provisions. Non-profit organizations do not
operate as extractive "middlemen," as suggested by the agencies; rather, they form the
crucial operational bridge connecting financial institutions to low- and moderate-
income (LMI) neighborhoods. Flexible grant funding and administrative overhead
support are essential to maintaining organizational infrastructure, complying with
complex public-private funding requirements, and deploying vital services on the
ground. Restricting grants and penalizing administrative capacity will destabilize local
non-profits, reduce flexible capital, and directly impair our ability to serve families
navigating housing crises in West Suburban Cook County.
3. Lowered Performance Benchmarks and Devaluation of the Community Development
Test
Under the proposed rule, intermediate banks could achieve a "satisfactory" rating solely
by passing a retail lending test, and large bank performance expectations would be
lowered to a mere 0.625% of Tier 1 capital dedicated to community development
grants/investments and 0.625% for lending.
These benchmarks are drastically lower than current industry medians and historical
performance averages. By lowering performance standards, the rule creates a "race to
the bottom" that diminishes the role of community development in CRA examinations.
Permanent supportive housing development, Community Development Financial
Institution (CDFI) partnerships, and local homelessness prevention programs rely heavily
 3
on the higher accountability standards currently embedded in the CRA.
4. Regulatory Fragmentation and Conflict with State Frameworks (Illinois CRA)
The absence of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors from this joint NPRM creates a
fractured regulatory framework, resulting in different federal standards depending on a
bank's primary regulator. Furthermore, this fragmentation directly conflicts with state-
level regulations, such as the Illinois Community Reinvestment Act, which was carefully
designed to align with unified federal asset thresholds and performance standards.
Imposing misaligned federal rules will generate widespread regulatory confusion,
multiply compliance burdens for covered institutions, and disrupt the stability of state-
level community reinvestment monitoring.
Conclusion
Housing Forward urges the FDIC and OCC to rescind the NPRM and refrain from moving
forward with changes that weaken the CRA's core statutory purpose. The proposed
revisions will reduce critical capital flows for affordable housing, destabilize community
development non-profits, and impair our ability to end homelessness across West
Suburban Cook County.
Thank you for your time and consideration of our perspective.
Sincerely,
Lynda Schueler
Chief Executive Officer
lschueler@housingforward.org

evaluates the degree to which lenders make credit available to all portions of
their service area, particularly low- and moderate-income, distressed rural,
and remote (underserved) rural census tracts. For community development
activity to qualify for CRA consideration, it must occur in a "high credit need"
area. In 2025, federal regulators designated 8,099 rural and small town census
tracts as having high credit needs. These census tracts are home to 25.4
million people, about 42 percent of rural and small town residents, but they
received roughly 35 percent of rural and small town mortgage originations in
2025. In addition, these high credit need rural and small town areas had high
rates of loan denials and high interest rate lending.
Summary of HAC's Major Comments

HAC strongly supports the following four basic principles, which are well stated in a
comment letter spearheaded by the National Association of Affordable Housing
Lenders.


Maintain meaningful community development responsibilities for banks
of all sizes. Raising the asset thresholds for CRA evaluation would not serve
the communities CRA is intended to support. Smaller lenders are key
providers of community development resources, particularly in rural and
underserved areas. Reducing their community development work by
redefining them would remove private support at a time when affordable
housing, local businesses, and community infrastructure are badly needed
nationwide.

Preserve strong expectations for community development lending and
investment. Communities need loans, equity, and other capital to meet their
varied needs. Banks should not be incentivized to support only the needs that
can be met through lending.

Protect grants and other support for nonprofit and community-based
organizations. CRA-qualifying grants support housing provision, financial
education, small business assistance, food access, health services, and more.
The organizations that provide such services can be particularly important in
rural places where local government staffing and capacity are limited.

Keep low- and moderate-income people and communities at the center of

affordability challenges, the need for support is most acute for those with the

Increasing asset size thresholds hurts rural America the most.

"Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less

effective CRA oversight for underserved markets, limiting the CRA's ability to fulfill its
statutory purpose as a catalyst for community development and investment.

CRA strongly impacts the pricing and use of Low-Income Housing Tax Credits

Lending cannot meet all community needs.

While HAC agrees that CRA activity should not include bloated administrative
expenses, the NPR uses blunt instruments where a more careful approach is
warranted. The NPR suggests that bank grants and donations should receive CRA
credit only if they are "directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or

The nation's banks know that communities need not only loans, but also equity and
other capital to meet their varied needs. Low-income residents need services such as
financial counseling that might not be considered a specific project, yet they benefit
not only families but also banks, by increasing the financial knowledge of their
customers. CRA-qualifying grants have supported housing provision, financial
education, small business assistance, food access, health services, and more. Such
support for local organizations can be particularly important in rural places where
local government staffing and resources are limited.

development grant classification. Nor does HAC support eliminating all grants and
donations from CRA consideration.

these requirements. Requiring more oversight and documentation for grants than
for loans would likely discourage banks from making grants, even in the low-income

A single cap on indirect costs is inappropriate.

The NPR proposes to limit indirect costs to 15 percent when a large bank makes a
grant or donation for community development purposes, and proposes to require
collection of extensive supporting documentation. HAC believes the agencies should
use different methods to ensure that overhead costs are not excessive. While the
Office of Management and Budget's Uniform Guidance14 has adopted a 15 percent
de minimis indirect cost rate, the NPR provides no information on the current rates
paid by banks, any abuses that may have occurred, or any research that may
indicate what rate is appropriate for nonprofits doing community development
work. The only explanation given is that, "in their supervisory experience, the
agencies have found that [grants and donations to nonprofit entities] may be
susceptible to rent extraction" – a vague and general charge stated without any
support.

On the contrary, research on the subject indicates that 15 percent is often too low,
even far too low, to cover indirect costs for nonprofits. Researchers in the early 2000s
coined the term "nonprofit starvation cycle" to describe the effects of funders' limits
on overhead costs.15 One study found that this cycle led to a drop in reported
average overhead costs from 20.9 percent in 1985 to 18.3 percent in 2014, leading to
reduced salaries for non-executive staff and artificial deflation in reporting to
funders.16 A 2015 study of nonprofits receiving support from an unnamed large
foundation found that their indirect costs ranged from 21 percent to 89 percent. The
median rate for direct-service organizations was 25 percent.17 When the MacArthur
Foundation commissioned a study using IRS Form 990 data from over 130,000
nonprofits based in the U.S., they found that the minimum indirect cost rate
associated with financially healthy organizations was 29 percent. MacArthur adopted
that finding as a policy.18

Overhead costs may be higher for small and rural nonprofits than for larger
organizations. In fact, one research study found that the largest overhead ratios were
experienced by the smallest and largest nonprofits.19 Small organizations have fewer
programs and funding sources among which to divide the costs of overhead items
such as rent and technology, for example. They cannot always afford to hire staff
with expertise in a field such as program compliance or, in a remote rural area, such
staff may be unavailable. Small local groups may also have difficulty providing the
documentation that would be required under the NPR's rules.

activity. There could also be a cutoff at which the outside assessment area activity
represents too much of a lender's overall CD work.

To ensure that any modified approach works, there must be greater certainty in
determining whether any given CD activity will be considered CRA eligible. If this is
the case, lenders will know how much CRA CD activity they have engaged in, what it
is worth, and how outside assessment area activity may be used for their final rating.
For example, the institution could know if it exceeded the outside assessment area
CD threshold so it would not count additional activity towards the rating. The
simpler this is to administer, the more successful it is likely to be.

"Question 57: Should the agencies replace the requirement to include census tracts
where the bank does a substantial portion of lending in the bank's assessment
area(s) with an alternative such as a radius-based standard discussed above[?] If
so, how should the agencies determine the appropriate radius? Should it vary by
geographic area (e.g., MSA or nonmetropolitan area)?"

The process of determining lender assessment area, other than the standard
inclusion of census tracts with deposit-taking bank branches, is unclear. What
constitutes a substantial portion of lending is difficult to determine. If this could be
cleared up it would improve the CRA and the public's understanding and interaction
with the regulations.

As of now, it is likely best to continue using as the foundation all census tracts with a
deposit-taking bank branch. To this, add adjacent census tracts if these census tracts
include reported bank lending activity. A radius might work but it may also fall short
because it would not necessarily reflect communities where a lender is providing
services. Regardless of the final approach, the entire process would be improved by
the release of a publicly available assessment area data file. This way there would be
certainty as to whether a community is or is not within the boundaries of a lender's
assessment area.

This approach, though it is likely, is not a viable long-term solution given the
continued decline in bank branches. The increased use of on-line banking means
that a better way to determine assessment areas will be needed. It may be deposit
based, as has been previously noted in recent CRA rule promulgation, but in most
 Housing Assistance Council comments on CRA
October 13, 2026
Page 20

cases the issue of setting a threshold will likely continue until an equilibrium is
achieved in how banks provide services.

Unique provisions are needed to support Indian Country.

Question 55: "Are there alternative approaches the agencies should consider to
encourage banks to meet the credit needs of Indian country and other Tribal and
native lands? For example, should the agencies use the definition of Native Lands in
the 2023 CRA rules? Are there any difficulties or unintended consequences that
banks might encounter with the definitions as proposed?"

HAC fully supports efforts to increase investment in Native American Lands. The CRA
has struggled to incentivize lending in Tribal lands, many of which are sparsely
populated and geographically isolated. CRA's reach is limited because few bank
branches are located in these communities. Giving lenders CRA credit for
community development and investment activities that occur in Native American
Lands, even when those lands are not within their assessment areas – as was put
forth in the 2020 and 2023 CRA modernization efforts – is a good start.

A challenge here is to ensure that the definition of Native American Lands accurately
captures Tribal lands. The NPR proposes using the Census Bureau's American Indian,
Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian Areas (AIANNHA) geography. This geography
includes most government recognized Tribal lands, but it may also include some
communities that are not predominantly Native American. The 2023 CRA final rule's
provisions explicitly designed to increase bank investment in Tribal Nations and
Native communities should be incorporated in this rule. These include, first, the 2023
rule's conferral of automatic, enhanced CRA credit for a bank's entire loan, grant,
investment, or service if it involves a Treasury-certified Native Community
Development Financial Institution. Second, the 2023 rule established "Native Land
Areas" (NLAs) as a stand-alone CRA place-based category investment area. Third, it
provided additional consideration for branches and further incentivized community
development activity benefiting Native communities. More details about these
provisions are provided in a comment letter spearheaded by the Native CDFI
Network.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Development's Native CDFI Relending
Demonstration Program25 provides proof that qualified, carefully credentialed
intermediaries can make the difference between success and failure in delivering
financial services. USDA RD makes loans to Native CDFIs, which make and service
mortgage loans to Native homebuyers. The CDFIs have dramatically improved USDA
RD's ability to support Native homeownership.26 Similar arrangements, appropriately
overseen by the regulatory agencies, could allow banks to reach Native American
borrowers and communities.

October 13, 2026
Page 21

Online posting can be helpful, but many rural places still lack reliable internet
access.

"Question 60: The agencies request comment on whether they should maintain the
location of public information requirements in current 12 CFR ___.43(c) or adopt a
website requirement as proposed. The agencies also invite comment on whether
requiring banks to include their public file requirements on a bank's website would
impose costs on banks, results in cost savings for banks, or have a significant
impact on public access to banks' public file information. In addition, the agencies
invite comments on whether banks should be required to provide for inspection of
the public file at all branch locations or only at certain branch locations in a State."

HAC supports allowing banks to post their CRA required information/documents on
their websites. Many rural areas, however, still lack consistent and adequate
broadband service, so HAC recommends that banks also be required to provide their
CRA files at all branch locations.
Conclusion

Meaningful CRA reform should balance reducing regulatory burden and improving
regulatory clarity with boosting lending and access to banking for underserved
communities. Access to credit for individuals and community leaders remains a
challenge in many rural communities. The CRA can do a better job of helping these
rural communities; however, this NPR would not achieve such improvements.

This NPR recommends things that can be helpful. Improving regulatory clarity is
needed and, in many cases, HAC supports these efforts. The NPR falls short, however,
in important areas. The proposal to increase the small/intermediate bank thresholds
would mean less CRA oversight and fewer incentives for community investments in
underserved areas. This change alone would be damaging to many rural
communities.

Once again, the Housing Assistance Council appreciates this opportunity to provide
comments on the NPR. The CRA's past successes are impressive and its future
possibilities to effect real and measurable change, particularly for those
communities who still lack the means of acquiring capital, are inspiring. HAC looks

CRA for all communities – urban and rural. Please do not hesitate to contact me if
