Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould:

Connect Humanity appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the
Community Reinvestment Act regulations.

Connect Humanity is a nonprofit lender and impact investor focused on expanding affordable,
reliable broadband in rural, low-income, Tribal, and other historically underserved communities. We
finance broadband infrastructure, work directly with communities and locally rooted providers to
develop investable projects, and are pursuing CDFI certification as we expand this community
development finance work.

Our experience financing broadband points to two barriers particularly relevant to this rulemaking.
First, broadband projects need clear treatment as qualifying essential infrastructure across the range
of ownership and financing models used in the sector. Second, many communities with the greatest
broadband financing gaps have limited overlap with major-bank assessment areas, creating a
geographic mismatch between communities that need capital and institutions capable of providing
it.

I. Essential telecommunications infrastructure should expressly include broadband

Connect Humanity strongly supports the proposal's express recognition of essential
telecommunications infrastructure as essential infrastructure. We request explicit recognition of
broadband within the CRA framework. This can help bring private capital into projects that
otherwise face persistent financing gaps and can help build a more durable market for broadband
finance beyond time-limited public grant programs.

Reliable broadband is foundational infrastructure for economic participation. It enables access to
employment, education, healthcare, financial services, entrepreneurship, government services, and
other opportunities. Yet many rural, low-income, Tribal, and economically distressed communities
1

continue to face both inadequate broadband infrastructure and limited access to appropriately
structured capital. We, therefore, encourage the agencies to clarify in the final rule or accompanying
guidance that broadband infrastructure is included within "essential telecommunications
infrastructure."

Further, the proposed definition includes "essential telecommunications infrastructure" in a list that
concludes with "other similar infrastructure that is provided as part of a public and private
partnership."1 Because it is unclear whether the public-private partnership language is intended to
apply only to "other similar infrastructure" or more broadly to the listed infrastructure categories,
we encourage the agencies to clarify that qualifying broadband infrastructure does not need to be
delivered solely through a public-private partnership.

Recommendation: The agencies should clarify that broadband is included within essential
telecommunications infrastructure and confirm that qualifying telecommunications infrastructure is
not conditioned on use of a public-private partnership structure.

II. Meaningful geographic flexibility can help CRA-motivated capital reach rural
broadband projects outside major-bank assessment areas

Connect Humanity supports the proposal's goal of enabling community development capital to
reach communities with significant unmet needs but relatively few bank assessment areas.

Many communities in which we work face a double disadvantage: they lack adequate broadband
infrastructure, and they also have little or no overlap with the assessment areas of banks capable of
providing significant community development capital. That geographic mismatch can make it
difficult to attract private financing even when a broadband project has a clear community
development purpose and is otherwise viable. Some of the communities with the greatest
infrastructure needs are also places where relatively few financial institutions have a substantial
CRA footprint.

The proposal creates pathways for banks to receive consideration for qualifying community
development activities outside their assessment areas once applicable standards within their own
assessment areas have been met.2 Connect Humanity supports meaningful geographic flexibility, but
our support should not be understood as support for lowering the level of community development
activity expected of banks within their own assessment areas. Geographic flexibility should
supplement, rather than replace, strong community development performance where banks already
operate.

Any standard used to unlock consideration for activity outside assessment areas should therefore
reflect meaningful community development performance within a bank's own assessment areas, not
merely the minimum level of activity the agencies indicate would generally be expected to avoid a
"Needs to Improve" rating.3

Once that safeguard is met, however, the pathway for outside-assessment-area activity should be
workable in practice. Broadband projects are often regional rather than confined to a single
municipality or census tract, and networks may cross county and other jurisdictional boundaries. A
qualifying rural broadband project may be ready for financing even though it lies outside the
assessment areas of institutions interested in supporting community development. If the rules make
outside-area consideration technically available but practically difficult to use, CRA-motivated
capital may continue to concentrate in markets with significant bank presence while rural
communities with demonstrated financing needs remain harder to serve.

Conversely, meaningful geographic flexibility can allow banks and specialized intermediaries to
direct responsible private capital toward qualifying infrastructure projects in communities where
both broadband access and conventional financing remain limited.

Recommendation: The agencies should preserve a meaningful pathway for CRA consideration of
qualifying community development activity in rural and other underserved markets outside bank
assessment areas, but only after a bank has demonstrated meaningful community development
performance within its own assessment areas. Geographic flexibility should expand the reach of
CRA-motivated capital, not reduce existing community development activity.

Conclusion

The proposed rule presents an opportunity to strengthen the role of private community development
capital in financing broadband infrastructure. Done well, the final rule can help community
development finance become a more durable source of broadband capital alongside — and beyond
— time-limited public grant programs.

Thank you for considering these comments and the financing needs of rural and underserved
communities.

Prosperity Indiana is our state’s association for 200+ community economic development organizations and professionals across Indiana’s 92 counties. We appreciate the opportunity to comment expressing our opposition to the proposed amendments to the regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), and we thank the undersigned Prosperity Indiana members and partner organizations for joining us to affirm our concerns and considerations in the rulemaking process. 

Our members work across Indiana in communities of all sizes developing affordable housing, operating shelters and transitional housing, and providing a variety of services ranging from homeownership education to food assistance to support in sealing evictions. Our members also include funders, conveners, capacity builders and financial institutions.

Financial institutions join our network because they benefit from the expertise of local service providers in understanding the full picture of the local economy, as well as community needs. They join our network because they take community reinvestment seriously, as a legal and civic commitment, and as a strategic investment in their own long-term success. They join our network because they share our goal of strengthening the communities in which we work to support a prosperous Indiana for generations to come.  
Through decades of partnership, we have seen how CRA fosters long-term relationships and promotes the strategic deployment of capital to meet community needs as they evolve. The CRA brings our banking partners to the table, and we stay at the table together because we make each other stronger and more effective in our respective roles.

It is with great respect for these partnerships, all the good that has come from them, and all the good that has yet to come, that we oppose these proposed changes to the CRA. Please find our full comment letter attached, including signatures from members and partners across the state, and contact us at info@prosperityindiana.org if we can provide any additional information as you consider these changes to the Community Reinvestment Act. With respect, we want to reiterate that we oppose these changes that would jeopardize $87 billion in community investment by current estimates. The harm would only grow with time.

No Longer Subject to the Investment Test

The proposal compounds this problem by weakening how community development

framework, an intermediate bank generally must receive at least a "satisfactory" rating on both

the proposal, strong lending performance could compensate for weak community development
performance in the overall rating. Because Housing Credit equity serves a function that cannot
be replaced with additional debt, allowing lending to substitute for investment removes the last
structural reason many mid-sized banks would continue making Housing Credit investments at

This proposal also runs directly counter to H.R. 1's effective expansion of tax-exempt bonds
used to create affordable homes along with the 4% and 9% Housing Credits that are projected
to finance 1.22 million additional affordable rental homes over the next decade. The proposed
rule also undermines Section 311 of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act which raised the

1. Retain the current $1.649 billion large bank threshold, consistent with the 1995 CRA
framework and the direction the Federal Reserve, the third federal bank regulator,
appears to be taking.
2. If the agencies proceed with raising the large bank threshold, instead adopt the $3.252
billion alternative rather than the proposed $10 billion threshold. AHTCC survey data
show this alternative would reduce the number of affected Housing Credit investors by
approximately 63 percent (from 108 banks to 40 banks) and reduce the estimated five-
year Housing Credit equity impact from roughly $2 billion to approximately $272 million
because banks with assets above $3.252 billion already account for approximately 86
percent of the Housing Credit equity investment made by banks between $1.65 billion
and $10 billion. The $3.252 billion threshold is also the inflation-adjusted successor to
the OCC's 2020 $2.5 billion threshold and has a clearer regulatory basis than an
untested $10 billion cutoff.
3. Reject the $30 billion alternative threshold discussed in the proposal outright. NAAHL
estimates that a $30 billion threshold would cut the number of large banks with
investment requirements by half or more in 17 states, and AHTCC survey data show that

much Housing Credit debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and

primary proposal.

6. Phase in any threshold increase rather than implementing it as a single cutover, to avoid

Development Finance

The proposed rule changes would allow a bank devoting just 0.625 percent of its Tier 1 capital
to community development loans, and separately 0.625 percent to community development
investments, to receive a passing CRA rating. This bar is set far below what banks currently do.
NCRC found that among the largest 100 OCC and FDIC supervised banks, the median bank
devotes 6.8 percent of Tier 1 capital annually to community development lending in its
assessment areas, and a median of 3.6 percent of Tier 1 capital to CRA-qualified investments.8
If banks instead did only the minimum necessary to meet the proposed 0.625 percent
thresholds, NCRC estimates that combined community development lending and investment
activity would fall to approximately $14.8 billion annually, a decrease of approximately $87.2
billion, or 85 percent, from current levels. There is no justification consistent with CRA's purpose
for setting a floor this far below current market performance; doing so functions less as a
minimum standard than as a signal to banks that current levels of community development
activity are unnecessary.

We ask the agencies to:

1. Reject the proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital floor or set any minimum activity threshold at
a level consistent with current market performance rather than a fraction of it.

We oppose the proposed standard for granting CRA community development credit to
unsubsidized, naturally occurring affordable housing ("NOAH"). Under the proposal, NOAH
properties would qualify for CRA credit if the market rents they charge at the time of the bank's

essentially market rate properties. Increasing the rent threshold in "high-cost areas" to 30
percent of 120 percent of AMI would mean middle-income individuals, who can currently afford
market rents in all 58 California counties, would also qualify as CRA beneficiaries, giving banks
huge incentives to shift investments from serving lower income households to moderate
income households without any meaningful benefit to the communities the statute is intended
to serve.

Data compiled in the Partnership's Losing California's Unsubsidized Affordable Homes (April
2026) puts the scale in perspective: as of 2025, California has an estimated 1,076,484
unsubsidized/NOAH affordable homes, compared with only 594,055 government-regulated
(subsidized) affordable rental homes, meaning NOAH already outnumbers the state's entire
deed-restricted affordable housing stock by roughly 80 percent.9 If financing this existing stock
becomes CRA-creditable under a "clear benefit or likely benefit" standard, a bank could satisfy a
large share of its affordable-housing consideration through ordinary-course lending on buildings
it would have financed regardless.

Compounding the deleterious effects of this change, "affordability in NOAH properties, unlike
Housing Credit properties, which carry recorded, government-monitored affordability covenants
lasting 55 years in California, can disappear at the next lease turnover, renovation, or sale. The
Partnership's data shows how unstable this housing is: since mid-2020, an estimated 268,113
formerly unsubsidized affordable homes (19.9 percent of the 2020 stock) have already lost their
affordability, and as of 2025 an additional 78,133 homes are at very high risk of imminent loss,
with 354,332 to 433,166 more at high or moderate risk within five years, a pattern present in 43
of California's 58 counties.10 Crediting banks today for financing volatile NOAH housing would

inevitably mean granting CRA credit for outcomes that evaporate before the next CRA exam
cycle.

1. Not adopt the proposed NOAH standard as drafted, or, at minimum,
2. Require a recorded affordability covenant or regulatory agreement with a duration
comparable to a Housing Credit extended-use period of at least 30 years so that credit is
tied to a lasting public commitment rather than a moment in time market snapshot; and
3. Reject the addition of a "high-cost area" definition up to 120% AMI housing, which not
only would extend CRA "affordable housing" credit well beyond the LMI populations the
statute is intended to serve, but also provide no meaningful or lasting community
benefit.

Given banks' outsized role as Housing Credit's primary capital source, if the agencies intend to
proceed with adding any version of a NOAH investment or lending standard, they should
conduct and publish an economic analysis of its likely effect on Housing Credit investment and
lending volume and pricing and allow public comment before finalizing the rule.

IV. Preserve CRA-Qualifying Grants and Nonprofit Capacity

The proposal would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring an
established nexus to a specific community development project and capping grantee overhead
and administrative costs at 15 percent, with new documentation requirements to demonstrate
compliance. The agencies also ask whether CRA eligibility for grantmaking should be
eliminated entirely. Many of our members rely on operating grants to ensure the long-term
financial viability of deeply affordable housing units, which often have operating costs that
exceed the rents collected from extremely low-income households. Adding any such
restrictions will lead to most smaller, local, and rural community development organizations
(the ones who are the most important to their communities and the least able to absorb new
reporting burdens ineligible for CRA grants. Bank contributions of this kind represent a small
share of overall CRA activity, but their loss would be felt disproportionately by the organizations
best positioned to do the hardest preservation and community development work in
underserved parts of the state.

We ask the agencies to preserve CRA eligibility for general operating support, capacity-building
grants, and sponsorships to nonprofit organizations engaged in community development,
without imposing new project-level nexus or overhead-tracking requirements that fall hardest on
smaller and rural organizations.

www.scanph.org
V. Geographic Flexibility Should Complement, Not Replace, Assessment-Area Obligations

The proposed rule changes would allow banks, at their option, to receive CRA credit for
qualifying community development activity outside their assessment areas, up to the state or
multistate level, after adequately meeting needs inside their assessment areas. We support the
goal of directing more private capital to California's rural and underserved "CRA deserts," where
few banks maintain a physical presence or assessment area, and agree this flexibility could help
address the pricing gap between competitive urban "CRA hot spots" and underserved rural
markets. However, this flexibility should not become a mechanism for banks to redirect capital
away from the communities where they take deposits and hold assessment-area responsibility
in the first place.

We ask the agencies to condition any out-of-assessment-area credit on a bank first
demonstrating it has adequately met the community development needs within its own
assessment areas, and prioritize this flexibility for LIHTC, CDFI, and other high-impact
investment that would not otherwise reach underserved rural California communities.

SCANPH's membership includes numerous organizations that would be impacted, but more
importantly low-income families in California and across the U.S. would face even longer odds
of attaining high quality, affordable housing. Our members already navigate difficult financial,
land use, and operational challenges, not to mention rising costs of construction, materials, and
labor that make building and operating affordable housing increasingly difficult. SCANPH has
seen firsthand what CRA-motivated investment makes possible in the Southern California
region, and what is put at risk when that investment weakens. We urge the OCC and FDIC to
preserve the standalone investment test, reject the proposed activity floor, reject the NOAH
standard, and ensure that any final rule strengthens, rather than diminishes, the effectiveness
and positive investment that CRA has made possible in California for nearly 50 years.

Dear Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation:

On behalf of WestCare, thank you for the opportunity to submit comments on the Joint
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding proposed amendments to the
implementing regulations for the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) of 1977.

WestCare is a national nonprofit provider of behavioral health services including
substance use disorder (SUD) treatment, mental health services, crisis intervention,
housing, reentry, and supportive services—operating across 17 states and multiple U.S.
territories. As a safety-net behavioral health provider deeply integrated into local
communities, WestCare concludes independently that while regulatory modernization
and administrative efficiency are important goals, future policy directions must not
disrupt the vital financial ecosystem that supports integrated care, affordable housing
development, and community development partnerships.

We appreciate that financial institutions play an essential role in fueling local housing and
supportive service infrastructure. Drawing on our direct operational experience across
diverse state and local landscapes, we offer key recommendations to ensure that any
CRA regulatory updates preserve capital flows for permanent supportive housing,
protect safety-net nonprofit infrastructure, and maintain rigorous accountability
standards for community development.

1. Drastic Increases to Asset Thresholds Exempt Key Banking Institutions from
Community Development Obligations
The proposed rule would dramatically raise the asset threshold for "large banks" to over
$10 billion and intermediate banks to over $1 billion. In many regions, this shift will result
in a significant percentage of intermediate and large banks being bumped down a
category, stripping them of mandatory community development obligations.
 WestCare • CRA NPRM Comments (OCC-2026-0694)
2
For WestCare and the communities we serve, this rollback is devastating. Banks
operating in our regions rely on these regulatory guardrails to maintain robust
community development lending and investments. Letting mid-sized and large
institutions off the hook means a sharp reduction in private capital flowing into
affordable housing development, local economic stabilization, and vital permanent
supportive housing initiatives that keep vulnerable households out of emergency
shelters. Long-term housing stabilization requires stable, predictable private capital
investments to sustain infrastructure and prevent individuals from cycling through crisis
response systems.

2. Restrictions on Community Development Grants and Punitive Overhead Caps
Threaten Non-Profit Infrastructure
The NPRM proposes strict new restrictions on community development grants and
donations, including a mandate that funds be "directly used" for specific programs and
an arbitrary 15% cap on a non-profit recipient's indirect or administrative costs.

WestCare opposes these provisions. Non-profit organizations do not operate as
extractive middlemen; rather, they form the crucial operational bridge connecting
financial institutions and public resources to low- and moderate-income (LMI)
neighborhoods. Flexible grant funding and administrative overhead support are
essential to maintaining organizational infrastructure, complying with complex public-
private funding requirements, and deploying vital behavioral health and housing services
on the ground. Restricting grants and penalizing administrative capacity will destabilize
local safety-net providers, reduce flexible capital, and directly impair our ability to serve
individuals navigating housing and behavioral health crises.

3. Lowered Performance Benchmarks and Devaluation of the Community Development
Test
Under the proposed rule, intermediate banks could achieve a "satisfactory" rating solely
by passing a retail lending test, and large bank performance expectations would be
lowered to a fraction of capital dedicated to community development grants,
investments, and lending.

These benchmarks are drastically lower than current industry medians and historical
performance averages. By lowering performance standards, the rule creates a race to
the bottom that diminishes the role of community development in CRA examinations.
 WestCare • CRA NPRM Comments (OCC-2026-0694)
3
Permanent supportive housing development, Community Development Financial
Institution (CDFI) partnerships, and local homelessness prevention programs rely heavily
on the higher accountability standards currently embedded in the CRA framework.

4. Regulatory Fragmentation and Conflict with State Frameworks
Discrepancies in federal regulatory standards create a fractured framework, resulting in
different compliance burdens depending on a bank's primary regulator. Furthermore,
misaligned federal rules can directly conflict with state-level community reinvestment
regulations designed to align with unified asset thresholds and performance standards.
Imposing fragmented rules generates widespread regulatory confusion, multiplies
compliance burdens for covered institutions, and disrupts the stability of state-level
community reinvestment monitoring.

Conclusion
WestCare encourages the agencies to refrain from moving forward with changes that
weaken the CRA's core statutory purpose. The proposed revisions will reduce critical
capital flows for affordable housing, destabilize community development non-profits,
and impair our ability to help vulnerable individuals achieve long-term stability and
recovery.

Thank you for your time and consideration of WestCare's perspective.

Sincerely,

Ken Ortbals
Chief Executive Officer

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould:
Genesee Co-op Federal Credit Union (Genesee Co-op) respectfully submits the following
comments in response to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) and Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed rule, "Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
Regulations." We appreciate this invitation to provide input on the CRA revisions and help
promote impactful and effective community development finance. Generally, we are concerned
that the proposed changes would result in a substantial decline in community development
activity, curtail successful bank-CDFI partnerships, and leave low- and moderate-income (LMI),
rural, Native, and other underserved communities with fewer resources and reduced access to
capital.
Genesee Co-op is a CDFI-certified credit union serving over 4,500 members in Rochester, NY, one
of the poorest cities in the country. While Genesee Co-op does not currently have investments
from CRA banks, the credit union has been a member of the Greater Rochester Community
Reinvestment Coalition for over 20 years—encouraging banks to support the Rochester
community. CRA requirements have helped bring millions of dollars in lending into the
communities that Genesee Co-op serves.
For almost 50 years, the Community Reinvestment Act has enabled investments that reduce the
number of unbanked Americans and build savings and wealth in low-income, previously
disinvested communities. The partnerships built through CRA efforts have strengthened
communities, sustained local and regional economies, and expanded economic opportunity

 2
across the nation, demonstrating what is possible when financial institutions are encouraged to
invest in all the communities they serve.
Genesee Co-op advises against the adoption of the proposed rule, based on its departure from
the core objectives of CRA as well as how it would weaken productive relationships between
banks and the communities in which they operate. The CRA was originally enacted to address
disinvestment in underserved communities by establishing a continuing and affirmative obligation
for banks to help meet the credit needs of their local communities, including LMI communities,
consistent with the safe and sound operations of the institutions. The proposed rule would move
away from this core purpose by scaling back CRA's coverage, drastically reducing regulatory
expectations of CRA activity, and weakening the CRA mechanisms for holding banks accountable
for serving the needs of the full communities in which they operate. This would have far-reaching
implications not only for CDFI credit unions, but also for affordable housing organizations, small
businesses, local and state governments, and the general public, who all benefit from strong,
well-functioning housing markets and business communities. In light of these concerns, Genesee
Co-op respectfully offers the following recommendations for the agencies' consideration, if
rulemaking does go ahead:
Maintain the existing bank size thresholds.
The proposed rule would increase the CRA bank size thresholds from under $412 million to under
$1 billion for small banks and from under $1.649 billion to under $10 billion for intermediate
banks. If this change is adopted, the number of banks subject to community development
standards would be significantly reduced, since only large banks' overall CRA ratings would be
impacted by community development tests.
Defining small and intermediate banks as those with less than $10 billion in assets would mean
that more than 1,500 banks, or 36% of all banks nationwide, would no longer be incentivized to
provide community development loans or investments in the places where they operate.1 These
banks provided nearly $27 billion in community development loans in one year, making up 35% of
loan volume nationwide, and they also play an essential role as investors in Low-Income Housing
Tax Credits (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) ).2, 3 Both programs are critical to


1 https://naahl.org/news/naahl-statement-on-proposed-cra-rule
2 Ibid.
3 https://www.taxcreditcoalition.org/weigh-in-with-regulators-on-cra/

 3
incentivizing affordable housing investment and development in low- and moderate-income (LMI)
communities.
As more banks move into lower asset-size categories, fewer would be evaluated for community
development lending, investment, and services, resulting in less capital flow to LMI communities,
especially rural communities and smaller markets. Raising the large bank threshold to $10 billion
would also reduce banks' accountability for branches and basic banking services because 417
banks would no longer undergo separate branch evaluations.4 Bank branches are especially
important for older adults, people with limited internet access in rural areas, and customers
needing language assistance. More than 5,000 branches in LMI census tracts—30% of all LMI
branches nationwide—would lose CRA scrutiny under these changes, and studies have found
that CRA consideration makes branches less likely to close.5 Beyond the loss of in-person
banking services, branch closures are associated with declines in small-business lending and
relationship-based banking, particularly in LMI neighborhoods.6
Further, an analysis of the proposed rule's impact across states found that the states most
affected—Alaska, Iowa, Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Mississippi, and Wisconsin, where more
than 40% of banks would lose community development (CD) obligations—are all states where
more than a quarter of the population lives in rural areas.7 This suggests that the proposed
changes could have a disproportionate impact on rural communities as more banks in those
areas would lose the obligation to reinvest in local CD activities like affordable housing and small
business or small farm support.
The effect would be felt directly in the Rochester, New York area. According to the Greater
Rochester Community Reinvestment Coalition (GRCRC), five large banks serving the Rochester
MSA—Canandaigua National Bank, The Lyons National Bank, Nextier Bank, Tompkins Community
Bank, and Woodforest National Bank—would be reclassified as intermediate banks.8
Canandaigua National Bank is the region's second-largest bank by deposits, with 16.7% of the
market, and in 2024 it was the leading mortgage and CRA small business lender among the area's


4 https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/
5 Ibid.
6 https://ncrc.org/relationships-matter-small-business-and-bank-branch-locations/
7 https://www.ncrc.org/cra/
8 Greater Rochester Community Reinvestment Coalition, Comments on OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations (Oct. 13, 2026), citing FDIC Summary of Deposits (June 30, 2026), HMDA data, and CRA small business lending data.

 4
eight largest banks. Lyons National Bank ranked second in mortgage lending and fourth in small
business lending among those banks. Together, the two banks operate 11 branches designated as
serving low- and moderate-income areas. Under the proposal, neither bank would undergo a
separate service test or be required to report its small business lending, so the public would lose
data on the area's top and fourth-largest CRA small business lenders.
The current framework works. GRCRC's tracking shows that as Canandaigua National Bank's
Rochester deposits grew 228% between 2007 and 2024, its annual community reinvestment grew
471%, twice as fast.9
Given the above findings, we recommend that the agencies preserve the existing bank size
thresholds and retain bank branch evaluations in order to maintain service levels across the
country, particularly in rural areas.

Maintain rigor of CRA standards by (a) continuing to evaluate all relevant retail lending
activity, rather than limiting assessment to a bank's major product lines, and (b) continuing
to factor intermediate banks' community development test ratings into overall ratings.
In addition to reducing participation in the CRA's most substantive tests, the proposed rule also
reduces the rigor and weight of some of the CRA tests themselves, particularly for the lending test
and the community development (CD) test.
Under the proposed changes, the scope of the lending test would be narrowed such that a bank
could be evaluated on just one or two of its major retail lending product lines. However, this
approach would create gaps in oversight for lending categories that, while smaller in scale, could
be particularly important to local communities. The relative importance of a lending product
within a bank's portfolio does not necessarily correspond with its importance to communities
where the bank operates. For example, small farm loans may represent a small portion of a
bank's retail lending while being central to the economic health of a rural community, or
affordable mortgages may be critical to meeting housing needs in a high-cost market, even if they
would not be considered a "major product line" under the proposed framework. Given that the
founding purpose of CRA was to ensure banks helped meet the credit needs of the communities


9 Ibid.; see also https://empirejustice.org/resources_post/grcrc-comments-on-canandaigua-national-banks-cra-performance-2/

 5
where they operate, particularly in LMI communities, CRA evaluations should continue to
examine lending across the four product lines regardless of dollar volume or loan count.
Secondly, the proposed rule would allow an intermediate bank to receive a "satisfactory" or
"outstanding" rating overall, provided that it receives at least a "satisfactory" rating on the lending
test. This standard effectively makes the CD test irrelevant for intermediate banks. However, the
lending test alone does not sufficiently capture the breadth of CD activities that banks undertake
to meet community needs. Banks' investments in local CDFIs, affordable housing development,
and other community projects are an important complement to retail lending in order to fill
financing gaps and address broader community-level needs. If the CD test is removed from
impacting the overall CRA rating, intermediate banks will no longer be incentivized to participate
in non-retail CD activities, significantly narrowing the ways in which banks engage with and
support local communities.
To keep CRA focused on meeting community needs, we recommend continuing to evaluate all
relevant retail lending activity and continuing to consider intermediate banks' CD test ratings in
overall ratings.

Preserve the existing treatment of qualifying grants and donations as community
development (CD) activities without capping indirect costs.
The proposed rule imposes a 15% cap on indirect costs that recipients can incur as part of
administering a grant or donation from a large bank and states that the remaining 85% must be
"directly used by the recipient to deploy the funds to meet community credit needs." This
requirement that funds be directly used to meet community credit needs is not clear about what
CD activities would qualify, and without clarity, banks may be reluctant to provide grants for
activities that are important to community development but do not fit neatly within a narrow
reading of this provision. For example, banks currently support financial or housing counseling or
small business training via grants to community-based organizations (CBOs). These are critical
community services that create jobs and help borrowers succeed with their capital, strengthening
local economies and capital markets. However, it is unclear whether such activities would qualify
as a direct use of funds to meet community credit needs under the proposed rule.
In addition, the proposed 15% cap on indirect costs is overly restrictive, as it could substantially
limit the effectiveness of bank partnerships with CDFIs and other CBOs that help banks reach LMI
and underserved borrowers, particularly where banks lack specialized expertise and local

 6
relationships. While a 15% cap on indirect costs may be appropriate for some grants, it could
disproportionately affect CDFI and CBO partnerships in rural and smaller communities, which
can cost more to reach and serve. The cap would also be particularly challenging for small local
organizations, for which economies of scale are limited and administrative costs naturally
represent a larger share of operating budgets. Further, funding indirect costs can be integral to
meeting community credit needs, as they support the infrastructure and capacity building often
necessary to deploy funds effectively in high-need communities.
Imposing a cap also drives up administrative costs for both banks and grantees, as banks may
need to collect and review additional documentation from grantees to verify compliance, diverting
resources away from the actual CD activities the grants are intended to support.
We therefore recommend that the agencies preserve the existing treatment of qualifying grants
and donations and remove the proposed cap on indirect costs, which would disincentivize banks'
investments in smaller organizations and increase administrative burdens.

Explicitly recognize loans, investments, and services to CDFIs as CD activity eligible for CRA
credit.
The proposed rule does not explicitly recognize activities undertaken with certified CDFIs as
eligible CD activities. In the 2020 and 2023 CRA rules as well as the Q&A accompanying the 1995
rule, loans, investments, and services provided to CDFIs were specifically identified as examples
of eligible CD activities. However, in the current proposed rule, financing undertaken through a
CDFI may only qualify where the activity financed satisfies the applicable CD and geographic
requirements.
This approach imposes a duplicative compliance burden to trace downstream CDFI activities,
even though CDFIs have already undergone a rigorous certification process by the US Treasury
Department to demonstrate that they carry out a primary mission of promoting community
development and serving LMI communities. Clear, entity-based treatment of CDFIs would reduce
uncertainty and compliance burden for banks while more effectively facilitating the flow of capital
to CDFIs as proven conduits for serving the credit and CD needs of LMI communities.

Preserve the purpose test for economic development activity to ensure financing continues
to be directed to small businesses and small farms that benefit LMI communities.

 7
Under current CRA rules, an activity generally must satisfy both a size test and a purpose test to
qualify as economic development. The purpose test asks banks to demonstrate that an activity
creates, retains, or improves jobs for LMI people, benefits LMI areas, or works through qualifying
intermediaries. The proposed rule would dilute this definition of "economic development" by
eliminating the purpose test, thus reducing the quality and impact of CRA eligible activity.
Under this change, banks would be able to receive CRA credit even for activities that do not
benefit LMI communities. For example, a loan to a wealthy small business owner in an upper-
income census tract could still qualify for CRA credit, even if the business creates no jobs and
does little to address local economic needs. This outcome would be antithetical to CRA's original
intent.
In their rationale, the agencies cite concerns that the focus on job creation for LMI individuals in
the purpose test does not account for the quality of those jobs, but eliminating the purpose test
would not address this concern. If anything, it would weaken the connection between qualifying
activities and quality jobs, as banks would be less incentivized to ensure that their activities
meaningfully benefit LMI individuals and communities. Preserving the purpose test would help
ensure that CRA-eligible economic development activities remain responsive to the needs of LMI
communities.

Maintain the current approach to considering discriminatory and illegal credit practices in
CRA ratings.
The current CRA framework permits examiners to consider discriminatory or other illegal credit
practices identified through the supervisory process, including violations cited in examination
reports, when determining whether a bank's CRA rating should be adversely affected. The
proposed Option 1 for § __.28(c)(2) would limit consideration to violations reflected in a public
federal or state enforcement action or qualifying judicial order, such that any violation is exempt if
addressed through nonpublic supervision. In effect, this means that a bank could receive an
Outstanding CRA rating despite having engaged in serious illegal or discriminatory credit
practices, so long as those practices are addressed through nonpublic supervision. Such an
outcome is difficult to reconcile with the CRA's purpose of addressing redlining and other forms
of disinvestment and credit discrimination. The agencies should therefore retain the current
approach, which allows examiners to consider violations identified through the supervisory
process when evaluating a bank's CRA performance, regardless of whether those violations result
in a public enforcement action.

 8

If the agencies establish a geographic flexibility standard, it should preserve or increase
existing activity, and the agencies should set a goal of 10% of tier 1 capital for Outstanding
performance by large banks.
The proposed geographic flexibility standard would allow a large bank to receive CRA credit for
community development (CD) activity outside its assessment areas, but only after it meets two
thresholds inside those areas: CD loans equal to 0.625% of its tier 1 capital, and a separate
0.625% for CD investments and grants.
We support giving banks clearer rules for investing in underserved areas outside their assessment
areas, including rural communities without branches. However, the proposed thresholds are far
below what banks do today. A National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) study of 69
large OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks found they provide about $102 billion a year in CD loans,
investments, and grants within their assessment areas.10 At the proposed thresholds, the same
banks would need to provide only about $14.8 billion, roughly 85% less.
Although the agencies state that meeting the thresholds would not by itself establish satisfactory
performance, this would be the only CD dollar figure written into the rule. In practice, banks are
likely to treat it as the amount that is "enough."
Instead, expectations should reflect what banks already achieve. NCRC's data show that the
median large bank provides CD lending equal to about 6.8% of tier 1 capital and CD investments
and grants equal to about 3.6%, roughly 10% combined.11 We therefore recommend that the
agencies (1) state in the rule text that meeting the geographic flexibility standard does not by itself
indicate satisfactory CD performance; and (2) establish, for large banks, a goal of CD loans,
investments, and grants within assessment areas equal to 10% of tier 1 capital annually as the
level associated with Outstanding performance. A goal tied to current practice would reinforce,
rather than weaken, CRA's incentive for banks to invest in their communities.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment. For any questions regarding these comments, please
contact Daniel Apfel at dan@genesee.coop.


10 https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-risk/
11 Ibid.

 9

Sincerely,
Daniel Apfel
CEO, Genesee Co-op Federal Credit Union

Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-
AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
On behalf of the City of Milwaukee, I submit this comment in opposition to the Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller
of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)[1] because it would
significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before
making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-
income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the
agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
Over a dozen Milwaukee, WI based nonprofit organizations and community development
corporations are members of the National Community Reinvestment Coalition, demonstrating
significant local support for this issue.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-



income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both
credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that
have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream
financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
We are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. As stated earlier, Milwaukee has strong contingent of affordable
housing development organizations and supporters that are following this issue and are
concerned about the possible effect of this rule on community development resources available
to the serve the public.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling,
workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through
grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be
particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships with residents and
understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller
organizations.[2] For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff,
rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to
deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and
funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits
operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial records, budgets or program
documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks
conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may
redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or redirect bank
support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with limited administrative
capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects would ultimately reduce
resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.



More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of reducing
perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what the changes
mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.
Additionally, under the current rule, large banks are generally evaluated on their home mortgage,
small business and small farm lending. The proposal outlines two options for regulators to focus
on products designated as a bank's "major product lines" based either on the largest two product
lines by all lending volume, or based on the type of lending a bank does more of in a particular
assessment area.[3] Either option would allow weak performance in a lower volume product to
escape meaningful scrutiny even when that credit is important locally.
For example, in Milwaukee, there is a strong need for new affordable homeownership options
and opportunities. The City of Milwaukee has invested millions of dollars in creating and
incentivizing these opportunities. For example, the City of Milwaukee's Homes MKE program
renovates city-owned vacant houses in need of significant repairs and sells them at an affordable
price, prioritizing owner-occupants. These types of programs and opportunities often require
smaller dollar mortgages than standard lending products support. The current proposal may
discourage lenders from offering these unique products tailored to local community needs. If that
type of lending is not a major part of a large bank's business, regulators will not evaluate
whether the bank is meeting our crucial local community need. Absent such evaluation, the bank
will likely deprioritize making such loans.
In addition, under the current rule banks above the large bank threshold generally collect and
report on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans and
assessment areas. But because of the proposed change in the threshold, banks with $10 billion or
less in assets would no longer be required to collect and report such CRA data. Nationwide, that
will result in a 11% reduction in CRA small business lending data. Without meaningful data,
communities, regulators, and researchers will not be able to identify credit deserts, compare
performance or understand whether local credit needs are being met.
Before narrowing the activities subject to CRA examination and eliminating data reporting
requirements, the agencies should analyze the impact of doing so will have for people with low-
and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income communities, including whether it could
result in a reduction in the types of lending that would meet community needs. In addition, the
agencies should explain why this change would be consistent with the CRA's requirement to
assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods.
In conclusion, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
under the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color;



● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability; and

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to
prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days.
The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes
to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit
grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on
October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not
have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected
organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the
communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base
any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment
deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,

and communities have the opportunity to thrive. We rely on CRA to incentivize private

in the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program.

Most of Oakland's housing is profoundly unaffordable to large segments of our community. As of
July 2026, Oakland's median rent is $2,270, whereas the median annual household income for
Black households is $69,000, and for Hispanic/Latino households, it is $49,500. There are more
than 17,500 severely rent-burdened and extremely low-income tenants in Oakland, and our tax-
credit affordable housing developments have long waitlists.





While the CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest, and provide services in
underserved communities like Oakland, there is still a long way to go before these communities
have equitable access to capital and financial services. Rather than addressing these gaps, the
proposed CRA rule changes will pull investment and support away from, worsening Oakland's
affordable housing and homelessness situation.

The scale of housing need in Oakland makes the stakes of this proposal especially high for our us.
Oakland has over 4,400 homeless individuals living in our City. Furthermore, across Alameda
County, the County in which Oakland is situated, there are 110,000 low-income renter households
but only 52,000 homes and apartments renting for levels affordable to these community members.
The rest – over 57,000 households - face untenable rents and overcrowded conditions as a result.
Oakland and Alameda County are reflective of many parts of the United States: we are suffering
a profound and urgent affordable housing crisis.

Oakland is a committed partner and investor with CRA investors, ensuring that tax credit equity
performs well and serves those most in need. Over the past 5 years, the Oakland Department of
Housing and Community Development has invested over $300 million of local sources into
affordable housing, and the Department oversees a pipeline of new projects that will result in over
1,350 new affordable units by the end of 2027.

Thanks to the passage of H.R. 1 in July 2025, California has doubled production of affordable
rental homes in the past year. Private bank participation in affordable home production and
preservation has been absolutely critical to this progress. Given that the participation of federally
chartered banks in California has been motivated almost entirely by CRA, the proposed rule change
to exempt many banks from CRA tests would be devastating and undermine a singular
achievement of H.R. 1.

Unfortunately, the proposed CRA rule changes would significantly worsen the situation by
reducing the number of banks incentivized to make CRA loans and investments in Oakland and
California.

According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 banks active in
California would see their CRA reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal, with 25
banks active in California shedding their CRA community development responsibilities entirely.1
Forty-five banks active in California would no longer be subject to the investment test, which has
successfully driven crucial investment in Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC).2 Commercial
banks account for an estimated 85 percent of LIHTC investors nationally, making this test a critical
driver of affordable housing capital.3

RE: Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Regulations (Docket OCC-2026-0694)

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould:

Inclusiv, Inc., a national 501(c)(3) organization and Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI),
respectfully submits the following comments in response to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's
(OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed rule, "Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) Regulations." We appreciate this invitation to provide input on the CRA revisions and help promote
impactful and effective community development finance. Generally, we are concerned that the proposed
changes would result in a substantial decline in community development activity, curtail successful bank-
CDFI partnerships, and leave low- and moderate-income (LMI), rural, Native, and other underserved
communities with fewer resources and reduced access to capital.

About Inclusiv
Inclusiv is the leading network of community development credit unions with a primary mission of
promoting financial inclusion and independence for low-income people and communities. The Inclusiv
network represents more than 450 credit unions serving nearly 20 million people in predominantly low-
income urban, rural, and reservation-based communities across the United States, including Puerto Rico,
Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Inclusiv channels capital to and builds the capacity of community
development credit unions dedicated to serving low-income people and disinvested communities that
mainstream financial institutions fail to serve.
For almost 50 years, the Community Reinvestment Act has enabled Inclusiv to raise and deploy capital to
grassroots community development financial institutions that connect low-income consumers with
affordable loans, savings opportunities, and counseling and guidance that help them financially succeed. In
that time, we have directly invested more than $500 million to build the balance sheets of these institutions,
which have collectively mobilized more than $300 billion in savings and deployed more than $250 billion in
loans that revolve in their communities. These investments reduce the number of unbanked Americans and
build savings and wealth in low-income, previously disinvested communities, and the capital has been raised

primarily through banks, which proudly report these outcomes as part of their regular CRA reporting and
examinations. The partnerships built through CRA efforts have strengthened communities, sustained local
and regional economies, and expanded economic opportunity across the nation, demonstrating what is
possible when financial institutions are encouraged to invest in all the communities they serve.
It is from this longstanding experience that Inclusiv advises against the adoption of the proposed rule, based
on its departure from the core objectives of CRA as well as how it would weaken productive relationships
between banks and the communities in which they operate. The CRA was originally enacted to address
disinvestment in underserved communities by establishing a continuing and affirmative obligation for banks
to help meet the credit needs of their local communities, including LMI communities, consistent with the
safe and sound operations of the institutions. The proposed rule would move away from this core purpose
by scaling back CRA's coverage, drastically reducing regulatory expectations of CRA activity, and weakening
the CRA mechanisms for holding banks accountable for serving the needs of the full communities in which
they operate. This would have far-reaching implications not only for CDFI credit unions, but also for
affordable housing organizations, small businesses, local and state governments, and the general public,
who all benefit from strong, well-functioning housing markets and business communities. In light of these
concerns, Inclusiv respectfully offers the following recommendations for the agencies' consideration:

1. Maintain the existing bank size thresholds.
The proposed rule would increase the CRA bank size thresholds from under $412 million to under $1
billion for small banks and from under $1.649 billion to under $10 billion for intermediate banks. If this
change is adopted, the number of banks subject to community development standards would be
significantly reduced, since only large banks' overall CRA ratings would be impacted by community
development tests.
Defining small and intermediate banks as those with less than $10 billion in assets would mean that
more than 1,500 banks, or 36% of all banks nationwide, would no longer be incentivized to provide
community development loans or investments in the places where they operate.1 These banks provided
nearly $27 billion in community development loans in one year, making up 35% of loan volume
nationwide, and they also play an essential role as investors in Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC)
and New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC).2, 3 Both programs are critical to incentivizing affordable housing
investment and development in low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.
As more banks move into lower asset-size categories, fewer would be evaluated for community
development lending, investment, and services, resulting in less capital flow to LMI communities,
especially rural communities and smaller markets. Raising the large bank threshold to $10 billion would
also reduce banks' accountability for branches and basic banking services because 417 banks would no
longer undergo separate branch evaluations.4 Bank branches are especially important for older adults,

people with limited internet access in rural areas, and customers needing language assistance. More
than 5,000 branches in LMI census tracts—30% of all LMI branches nationwide—would lose CRA
scrutiny under these changes, and studies have found that CRA consideration makes branches less likely
to close.5 Beyond the loss of in-person banking services, branch closures are associated with declines in
small-business lending and relationship-based banking, particularly in LMI neighborhoods.6
Further, an analysis of the proposed rule's impact across states found that the states most affected—
Alaska, Iowa, Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Mississippi, and Wisconsin, where more than 40% of banks
would lose community development (CD) obligations—are all states where more than a quarter of the
population lives in rural areas.7 This suggests that the proposed changes could have a disproportionate
impact on rural communities as more banks in those areas would lose the obligation to reinvest in local
CD activities like affordable housing and small business or small farm support.
Given the above findings, we recommend that the agencies preserve the existing bank size thresholds
and retain branch evaluations to support continued banking access across the country, particularly in
rural areas.

2. Maintain rigor of CRA standards by (a) continuing to evaluate all relevant retail lending activity, rather
than limiting assessment to a bank's major product lines, and (b) continuing to factor intermediate
banks' community development test ratings into overall ratings.
In addition to reducing participation in the CRA's most substantive tests, the proposed rule also reduces
the rigor and weight of some of the CRA tests themselves, particularly for the lending test and the
community development test.
Under the proposed changes, the scope of the lending test would be narrowed such that a bank could
be evaluated on just one or two of its major retail lending product lines. However, this approach would
create gaps in oversight for lending categories that, while smaller in scale, could be particularly
important to local communities. The relative importance of a lending product within a bank's portfolio
does not necessarily correspond with its importance to communities where the bank operates. For
example, small farm loans may represent a small portion of a bank's retail lending while being central to
the economic health of a rural community, or affordable mortgages may be critical to meeting housing
needs in a high-cost market, even if they would not be considered a "major product line" under the
proposed framework. Given that the founding purpose of CRA was to ensure banks helped meet the
credit needs of the communities where they operate, particularly in LMI communities, CRA evaluations
should continue to examine lending across the four product lines regardless of dollar volume or loan
count.
Secondly, the proposed rule would allow an intermediate bank to receive a "satisfactory" or
"outstanding" rating overall, provided that it receives at least a "satisfactory" rating on the lending test.
This standard effectively makes the community development (CD) test irrelevant for intermediate

banks. However, the lending test alone does not sufficiently capture the breadth of CD activities that
banks undertake to meet community needs. Banks' investments in local CDFIs, affordable housing
development, and other community projects are an important complement to retail lending in order to
fill financing gaps and address broader community-level needs. If the CD test is removed from impacting
the overall CRA rating, intermediate banks will no longer be incentivized to participate in non-retail CD
activities, significantly narrowing the ways in which banks engage with and support local communities.
To keep CRA focused on meeting community needs, the agencies should continue to evaluate all
relevant retail lending activity and consider intermediate banks' CD test ratings in overall ratings.

3. Preserve the existing treatment of qualifying grants and donations as community development (CD)
activities without capping indirect costs.
The proposed rule imposes a 15% cap on indirect costs that recipients can incur as part of administering
a grant or donation from a large bank and states that the remaining 85% must be "directly used by the
recipient to deploy the funds to meet community credit needs." This requirement that funds be directly
used to meet community credit needs is not clear about what CD activities would qualify, and without
clarity, banks may be reluctant to provide grants for activities that are important to community
development but do not fit neatly within a narrow reading of this provision. For example, banks
currently support financial or housing counseling or small business training via grants to community-
based organizations (CBOs). These are critical community services that create jobs and help borrowers
succeed with their capital, strengthening local economies and capital markets. However, it is unclear
whether such activities would qualify as a direct use of funds to meet community credit needs under the
proposed rule.
In addition, the proposed 15% cap on indirect costs is overly restrictive, as it could substantially limit the
effectiveness of bank partnerships with CDFIs and other CBOs that help banks reach LMI and
underserved borrowers, particularly where banks lack specialized expertise and local relationships.
While a 15% cap on indirect costs may be appropriate for some grants, it could disproportionately affect
CDFI and CBO partnerships in rural and smaller communities, which can cost more to reach and serve.
The cap would also be particularly challenging for small local organizations, for which economies of
scale are limited and administrative costs naturally represent a larger share of operating budgets.
Further, funding indirect costs can be integral to meeting community credit needs, as they support the
infrastructure and capacity building often necessary to deploy funds effectively in high-need
communities.
Imposing a cap also drives up administrative costs for both banks and grantees, as banks may need to
collect and review additional documentation from grantees to verify compliance, diverting resources
away from the actual CD activities the grants are intended to support.
We therefore recommend that the agencies preserve the existing treatment of qualifying grants and
donations and remove the proposed cap on indirect costs, which would disincentivize banks'
investments in smaller organizations and increase administrative burdens.

4. Explicitly recognize loans, investments, and services to CDFIs as CD activity eligible for CRA credit.
The proposed rule does not explicitly recognize activities undertaken with certified CDFIs as eligible CD
activities. In the 2020 and 2023 CRA rules as well as the Q&A accompanying the 1995 rule, loans,
investments, and services provided to CDFIs were specifically identified as examples of eligible CD
activities. However, in the current proposed rule, financing undertaken through a CDFI may only qualify
where the activity financed satisfies the applicable CD and geographic requirements.
This approach imposes a duplicative compliance burden to trace downstream CDFI activities, even
though CDFIs have already undergone a rigorous certification process by the US Treasury Department to
demonstrate that they carry out a primary mission of promoting community development and serving
LMI communities. Clear, entity-based treatment of CDFIs would reduce uncertainty and compliance
burden for banks while more effectively facilitating the flow of capital to CDFIs as proven conduits for
serving the credit and CD needs of LMI communities.

5. Preserve the purpose test for economic development activity to ensure financing continues to be
directed to small businesses and small farms that benefit LMI communities.
Under current CRA rules, an activity generally must satisfy both a size test and a purpose test to qualify
as economic development. The purpose test asks banks to demonstrate that an activity creates, retains,
or improves jobs for LMI people, benefits LMI areas, or works through qualifying intermediaries. The
proposed rule would dilute this definition of "economic development" by eliminating the purpose test,
thus reducing the quality and impact of CRA eligible activity.
Under this change, banks would be able to receive CRA credit even for activities that do not benefit LMI
communities. For example, a loan to a wealthy small business owner in an upper-income census tract
could still qualify for CRA credit, even if the business creates no jobs and does little to address local
economic needs. This outcome would be antithetical to CRA's original intent.
In their rationale, the agencies cite concerns that the purpose test's focus on job creation for LMI
individuals does not account for the quality of those jobs, but eliminating the purpose test would not
address this concern. If anything, it would weaken the connection between qualifying activities and
quality jobs, as banks would be less incentivized to ensure that their activities meaningfully benefit LMI
individuals and communities. Preserving the purpose test would help ensure that CRA-eligible economic
development activities remain responsive to the needs of LMI communities.

6. Maintain the current approach to considering discriminatory and illegal credit practices in CRA ratings.
The current CRA framework permits examiners to consider discriminatory or other illegal credit
practices identified through the supervisory process, including violations cited in examination reports,
when determining whether a bank's CRA rating should be adversely affected. The proposed Option 1 for
§ __.28(c)(2) would limit consideration to violations reflected in a public federal or state enforcement
action or qualifying judicial order, such that a violation is exempt if addressed through nonpublic
supervision. In effect, this means that a bank could receive an Outstanding CRA rating despite having
engaged in serious illegal or discriminatory credit practices, so long as those practices are addressed


55 Broadway 29th Floor, New York, NY 10006 | T. 212 809 1850
inclusiv.org | info@inclusiv.org

through nonpublic supervision. Such an outcome is difficult to reconcile with the CRA's purpose of
addressing redlining and other forms of disinvestment and credit discrimination. The agencies should
therefore retain the current approach, which allows examiners to consider violations identified through
the supervisory process when evaluating a bank's CRA performance, regardless of whether those
violations resulted in a public enforcement action.

7. If the agencies establish a geographic flexibility standard, they should ensure that it preserves or
increases existing activity.
One of the proposed options for considering CD activities would set a geographic flexibility standard for
large banks of 0.625% of tier 1 capital for CD lending and a separate 0.625% for CD investments and
grants. As highlighted in the National Community Reinvestment Coalition's (NCRC) comments, this
benchmark is about 85% below what banks provide today. An NCRC study of 69 large banks supervised
by the OCC and FDIC found that those banks currently provide approximately $59.1 billion annually in
CD lending and $42.9 billion in CD investments and grants within their assessment areas—about $102
billion combined.8 Applying the proposed 0.625% benchmark to the same banks produces
approximately $14.8 billion combined, about 85% below current levels. A benchmark set so far below
current practice would surely weaken CRA's incentive for banks to maintain their existing levels of
community development financing.
While the agencies state that meeting these thresholds would not automatically establish satisfactory
CRA performance, it may be difficult in practice to maintain a meaningful distinction between a
numerical threshold written into the rule and the amount of CD activity banks come to view as
sufficient. If adopted, a geographic flexibility standard should be set at a level that would reinforce,
rather than weaken, the CRA's incentive for banks to engage in CD activity.

 Financial Access Coalition. We are greatly concerned that the current proposal would

 community-based organizations harder to support. This part of the proposed changes

As the OCC and the FDIC note in their Proposed Rule, the CRA is meant to encourage financial
