Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on proposed changes to the Community
Reinvestment Act. As a mission-driven community development bank and Community
Development Financial Institution ("CDFI"), we bring both the practical perspective of a
regulated bank responsible for implementing CRA and the experience of working with
community partners to expand access to credit, investment, and economic opportunity.
That experience leads us to strongly oppose this proposed rule in its current form and to urge
the agencies to pursue reforms that strengthen, rather than dilute, CRA's fundamental focus
on low- and moderate-income ("LMI") people and communities.

I. Introduction
Beneficial State Bank ("BSB") is an Oakland, California-based, state-chartered, federally
insured Community Development Financial Institution ("CDFI") serving communities across
California, Oregon, and Washington. BSB believes banks can and should be a force for good
in the communities they serve, and its mission is reflected in how it lends, invests, offers
banking products and services, and partners with community organizations. BSB's approach
to CRA is grounded in its Beneficial Banking Mission Framework, which guides the Bank's
impact goals and consists of six pillars: Unite for Economic Mobility; Regenerate the
Environment; Build a Better Banking System; Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging; Engagement
Docusign Envelope ID: 223BC957-D6E1-8306-8090-1985C100BF4A


2

and Agency; and Accountability and Integrity. These principles inform BSB's approach to this
proposed rulemaking, including its focus on expanding economic opportunity, ensuring that
LMI people and communities remain at the center of CRA, promoting transparency and
accountability, supporting meaningful community engagement, and building a banking
system that responsibly directs capital toward community needs.

BSB brings several complementary perspectives to this rulemaking. First, we are a regulated
bank that must build systems, allocate resources, collect data, and design programs to
comply with the Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA") and prepare for CRA examinations.
Second, BSB is also a mission-driven CDFI that sees firsthand how CRA requirements direct
capital and resources toward LMI communities. BSB has also been a certified B Corporation
since 2012, reflecting its commitment to a triple bottom line of equally prioritizing people,
planet, and profit.

BSB recognizes that CRA was enacted in response to redlining and disinvestment, practices
deeply intertwined with systemic discrimination against Black, Hispanic, Asian American,
and other communities of color. This history remains central to CRA's purpose today. The
agencies should consider not simply whether an activity technically qualifies for CRA
consideration, but whether it produces durable benefits for the LMI people and communities
the statute is intended to serve. The agencies must preserve meaningful incentives for
community development, affordable housing, responsible financial services, and support
for community-based organizations, while ensuring that new investment does not
accelerate gentrification and displacement or leave longtime residents behind, including in
communities of color.

Six years ago, BSB urged the agencies to approach CRA reform with care, because changes
to the framework have real consequences for banks that implement it and, more
importantly, for the communities the CRA serves.1 BSB writes again with many of the same
concerns. Let us be clear, BSB supports modernizing the CRA, but modernization must
provide rules that are clear, durable, and predictable, and remain focused on serving the
needs of LMI communities and small businesses. Over the past several years, banks have
faced repeated changes in CRA rules and supervisory expectations, and BSB has
experienced that uncertainty directly. It moved from intermediate small bank to large bank
status, made the investments necessary to comply with the large-bank framework, and
completed a large-bank CRA examination, only now to face the possibility of being
reclassified again under the proposed rule. Repeated changes of this kind make it
exceedingly difficult for banks to build long-term compliance programs and, more

on LMI communities).

importantly, to plan the community-development strategies and investments that CRA is
intended to encourage.

perspectives to this rulemaking, BSB shares many of the concerns raised in the Foundation's
comment letter and likewise opposes the proposed rule in its current form.

The experience of the past six years underscores the importance of durability, which also
requires consistency among the agencies. In our prior CRA comments, BSB urged the federal
banking agencies to reach interagency consensus and cautioned that divergent regulatory
approaches were not workable over the long term. The regulatory history since then has only
reinforced that concern. In particular, durable CRA reform requires the OCC, FDIC, and
Federal Reserve to work together toward a consistent framework. The current proposal,
without participation by the Federal Reserve, risks again subjecting similarly situated banks
and communities to different CRA frameworks depending on their federal regulator. BSB
therefore urges the agencies to return to the interagency approach that has historically been

of providing stable and consistent rules of the road over time.

Responsive to Questions 18–23 concerning affordable housing, high-cost areas, and
naturally occurring affordable housing.

BSB supports CRA incentives that bring responsible investment into LMI communities, but
investment in an LMI geography does not necessarily mean that existing LMI residents
benefit from that investment. BSB has long urged regulators to focus on people rather than
place when determining whether an activity advances CRA's purposes.12 That principle is
particularly important in communities experiencing rapid appreciation and displacement,
where substantial new investment can coexist with declining affordability and opportunity
for existing residents. BSB has previously cautioned that financing the acquisition or
rehabilitation of naturally occurring affordable housing can contribute to gentrification and
displacement when rents rise and incumbent LMI residents are priced out of their
communities. CRA should not reward investments that increase property values without
preserving affordability for the residents the statute is intended to serve. CRA should
therefore encourage investment that allows LMI residents to remain in their communities
and participate in the economic opportunity that investment can create, rather than treating
the location of an investment as sufficient evidence of community benefit.13

existing affordable housing can offer an important model for limiting displacement and
ensuring lasting benefits for LMI residents. BSB financed the construction of 54 homes for
LMI families through a partnership between Kulshan Community Land Trust and Habitat for
Humanity. The Kulshan Community Land Trust has created permanently affordable
homeownership opportunities for LMI families, and BSB in 2025 awarded $850,000 in grants
to support the preservation of 1,271 affordable housing units across the West Coast. 14
Research demonstrates that community land trusts and affordable housing preservation
can help maintain affordability and prevent displacement in rapidly appreciating markets.15

mortgage credit in predominantly Black neighborhoods, while Hispanic and Asian American

including LMI neighborhoods.24 CRA's core historical purpose cannot be separated from the
racial discrimination that contributed to its enactment, nor should it. The agencies should
therefore ensure that CRA evaluations account for the continuing effects of that
discrimination and whether historically underserved residents actually benefit from
community reinvestment.

The proposal makes this issue more important, not less. Higher bank-size thresholds and
reduced reporting could make it more difficult for banks, regulators, and communities to
identify racial disparities in lending. Changes to affordable housing and community-
development standards could direct additional investment into historically underserved
neighborhoods without ensuring that incumbent residents share in the resulting benefits.
And the proposed treatment of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices could limit the
extent to which serious discriminatory conduct identified through the supervisory process
affects a bank's CRA rating.25

BSB therefore urges the agencies to preserve the data necessary to identify disparities,
analyze the effects of the proposed changes by race, ethnicity, and geography using
available HMDA, CRA, Census, and other appropriate data, and preserve meaningful
consideration of discriminatory practices in CRA evaluations. In particular, BSB opposes an
approach under which serious discriminatory conduct would be excluded from
consideration merely because it was identified and addressed through nonpublic
supervision rather than a public enforcement action.26

investment in a historically underserved community does not necessarily mean that the
residents who experienced the original disinvestment receive the benefit of that investment.

BSB recognizes that the agencies must implement CRA consistently with the statute and

A modern CRA framework must make it easier, not harder, for banks to direct capital to
communities with unmet needs, including through CDFI partnerships and support for local
nonprofits. BSB supports the proposal's recognition that banks should be able to receive
CRA consideration for qualifying community-development ("CD") activities outside their
assessment areas when community-development needs exist elsewhere. BSB also
supports the proposed CD activity confirmation process, which would provide greater
certainty for banks considering novel or other qualifying activities. At the same time, BSB is
concerned that other aspects of the proposal, particularly its treatment of CDFIs and CD
grants, could discourage community-development capital and partnerships.

sufficient time to implement material changes. Banks make long-term investments in
systems, personnel, data collection, community partnerships, and lending and investment
programs based on the CRA framework that applies to them. BSB's own experience moving
between CRA classifications demonstrates the difficulty of making those investments when
the applicable framework and supervisory expectations repeatedly change. Clear rules and
a workable transition are therefore not merely matters of regulatory convenience. They are
necessary if banks are to plan responsibly and communities are to rely on the incentives CRA
creates.

In response to Question 58, BSB urges the agencies to publish updated Interagency
Questions and Answers concurrently with any final rule and clearly identify which existing
Q&As remain operative. 33 The Proposed Rulemaking relies in several places on existing

consistent with CRA's statutory text and applicable law, to respond to changes in how banks
serve customers and communities. Durable regulation should provide stable rules of the
road while retaining the capacity to adapt when the banking system itself changes.

VIII. Conclusion
In the past few decades, the banking system has evolved in an unprecedented manner,
including through the growth of digital banking and the many ways that consumers access
financial services. CRA must be capable of evolving with it. BSB supports modernization of
the CRA, but modernization should strengthen the statute's ability to meet community credit
needs while providing banks with clear and durable rules.

Banks need sufficient certainty to build compliance programs, make long-term investments,
develop community partnerships, and allocate resources responsibly. Communities
likewise need confidence that CRA incentives will continue to generate meaningful lending,
investment, services, and other support. Regulatory burden can and should be reduced
where appropriate, but greater efficiency should not come at the expense of accountability,
transparency, or meaningful community reinvestment. The experience of the past several
years also demonstrates why durable reform requires a consistent interagency approach
among the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve. Banks and communities should not have to
repeatedly recalibrate their programs, investments, and expectations as the CRA framework
changes from one rulemaking or administration to the next. A durable framework should
provide enough certainty for long-term planning while preserving the flexibility necessary to
respond to changes in banking and community needs.

are being met, and agencies should use the full extent of their lawful authority to identify and
address those disparities. Ultimately, CRA's history underscores why racial disparities must

banks to plan around, flexible enough to reflect changes in banking and community needs,

implementing these requirements and a mission-driven CDFI committed to expanding

Dear Regulators:
On behalf of Community Housing Network, I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the
proposed revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations issued by the Office of
the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC).
Community Housing Network is a nonprofit housing organization serving low- and moderate
income (LMI) individuals and families throughout Southeast Michigan. Our work includes
affordable housing development including homeownership opportunities, homebuyer education,
foreclosure prevention, renter education, and financial education. These programs that are
designed to help LMI families become self-sufficient and successful homeowners and renters are
made possible through grants and investments provided by financial institutions seeking to fulfill
their CRA obligations. We are deeply concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule
would significantly weaken the positive impact on local communities the CRA was designed to
have.
Serving Local Communities Needs
CRA's central purpose is to ensure that banks help meet the credit and community development
needs of the communities they serve, particularly LMI communities. We encourage regulators to
emphasize demonstrated responsiveness to documented community needs when evaluating
community development activities.
The most effective community development projects are those designed in partnership with local
stakeholders and tailored to local conditions. CRA credit should prioritize activities that produce
sustainable benefits for LMI residents, preserve affordable housing, expand homeownership

To Whom it May Concern:
AARP, which advocates for the more than 125 million Americans age 50 and older, appreciates
the opportunity to provide comments on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM or
proposed Rule) regarding the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) by the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
(collectively, Agencies).1 The incentives created by the CRA are critical to ensuring access to
credit and banking services in low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities, and in generating
investments in and for the benefit of those communities. These activities are essential to ensuring
older adults, particularly those living in LMI communities, have access to housing and essential
services. AARP is concerned that a number of the contemplated changes would weaken the
incentives financial institutions have to engage in community development, and/or are likely to
make community development more difficult or less effective. AARP therefore urges the
Agencies not to implement the proposed Rule as drafted, as discussed in more depth below.
AARP has long advocated for improvements to CRA regulations. As AARP has noted in
previous comments, the preeminent goal of CRA modernization must be to promote equitable
reinvestment of deposits and resources held in banking and lending institutions in geographic
communities with aging infrastructure, buildings, and populations, and to transform such
communities into vibrant places in which older adults can live and work affordably and with
stability.2 As AARP's work shows, the majority of adults prefer to stay in their home and/or
community as they age, but a significant number would need to modify their home to

accommodate future physical limitations.3 Only approximately half of adults are fully confident
that their community will continue to meet their needs as they age.4 Access to reliable utilities,
quality health care, and streets and sidewalks that are well-maintained and safe is highly
important.5 Nearly half of adults cite moving to an area that has high-quality health care facilities
and health care providers as a reason to move out of their current community.6
Any modernization or modification of CRA regulations should be designed to promote:
(1) providing credit to develop a range of housing types, including multifamily housing options,
dispersed throughout the community to enable older homeowners to relocate to more suitably
sized, affordable housing with access to transportation; (2) offering affordable financing for older
individuals to make necessary modifications to their homes and to pay for necessary home
maintenance; (3) protecting homeowners in LMI communities from displacement as
neighborhoods are redeveloped; (4) ensuring that older adults continue to have access to
conveniently located local bank branches serving their needs; and (5) encouraging flexible
servicing options, including repayment and loan assistance, for borrowers with low and moderate
incomes who face financial hardship.7 The NPRM, if implemented, will not serve these goals,
and will instead hamper the availability of affordable, age-friendly housing for older Americans;
reduce the availability of age-friendly banking products; and constrict investment in the
community centers, health and supportive services, and transportation services upon which older
Americans rely. The proposed changes would also limit the availability of data on financial
institutions' activities, harming transparency and rendering it more difficult to assess and seek to
improve the state of financial and programmatic support for older Americans by financial
institutions.
I.
Background
The CRA was passed in 1977 and requires that banking regulators encourage certain federally
insured depository institutions, including banks and thrifts (collectively "banks" or "financial
institutions"), to help meet the credit needs of the communities where they do business, including
LMI neighborhoods. In enacting the CRA, Congress found that "regulated financial institutions
are required by law to demonstrate that their deposit facilities serve the convenience and needs of
the communities in which they are chartered to do business," and that "the convenience and
needs of communities include the need for credit services as well as deposit services."8 For
decades, supervisory agencies have considered financial institutions' track records of branch

support lending and banking activities in LMI areas.
The Agencies must ensure that the CRA is implemented in a manner that serves the needs of
older adults. According to census data, nearly one in four adults age 50 and older lives in an LMI
census tract.9 A significant and growing number of older adults live below the poverty line.10
And the American population is aging, with the share of the population who are older adults
projected to increase in the coming decades.11 At the same time, our nation faces an affordability
crisis affecting all aspects of daily living, including housing and health care.12 Indeed, among the
greatest challenges faced by older adults is access to affordable housing—including housing that
meets the needs of the older and aging population, who can face challenges with mobility,
transportation, and access to basic services.13 Older adults are more likely to be disabled or face
mobility challenges than the general population, which creates additional difficulty when seeking
accessible housing and transportation.
Older adults also have specific needs related to the provision of financial services. As income
sources change, lending needs can evolve; likewise, affordable deposit account features, along
with safeguards to help prevent and detect elder financial abuse, fraud, and scams, are important
to meet the needs of older Americans.

III.
Changes to Lending Test
Under current CRA regulations, large banks are generally evaluated for their home mortgage,
small business, and small farm lending,27 while small and intermediate banks are generally
evaluated on their major (retail) product lines.28 The proposed Rule would adopt a major product
line approach across size categories.29 This proposed change has the potential to exclude
mortgage lending from evaluation for certain institutions.
As noted above, affordable housing is a key concern for older Americans. Access to credit,
particularly for LMI populations, is critical in ensuring older Americans' ability to afford and
maintain housing. Without evaluation of mortgage lending, banks could face less accountability
for failing to meet mortgage credit needs in their communities. This is particularly the case if
determination of major product lines is based on a bank-wide, quantitative approach, as in the
proposed Option 1.30 But even under the assessment-area based, mixed approach the Agencies
provide as Option 2, large banks' mortgage activity could remain unexamined if it is not already
a product line that "meaningfully contributes to the bank's record of meeting the credit needs of
that assessment area."31 AARP recommends that mortgage lending remain a central part of the
CRA inquiry for all large banks.
Likewise, the NPRM proposes not to evaluate a bank's consumer lending even if consumer
lending is a major product line, unless consumer lending is the majority of the bank's business or
the bank affirmatively chooses to be so examined.32 In addition to mortgage lending, other
consumer loans can be critical tools for allowing older adults to age in place by giving them the
funds necessary to repair their homes or make improvements to account for changing mobility
and other needs.

[the] communities [banks serve] include the need for credit services as well as deposit
services."33 Congress found that regulated financial institutions "are required by law to

In addition to the changes brought about by operation of the NPRM's proposed modified asset-
size thresholds, the NPRM proposes to allow intermediate banks to receive an overall
"satisfactory" CRA rating even if they do not receive a "satisfactory" or better rating on their

loosening of the requirement to receive a "satisfactory" rating on the intermediate-bank
community development test would significantly limit the incentives intermediate banks have to
undertake community development activities across the board. Without facing CRA rating
consequences for weak community development performance, intermediate institutions have
fewer incentives to engage in community development activities. This increases the risk that
institutions will pare back community development activities or forego them entirely, to the
detriment of older adults' access to housing and services.

The proposed Rule contemplates a number of changes relative to which activities can receive

development.41 The Agencies' view that use of CRA funds to cover indirect or general costs is

provide vital funding to organizations that provide critical services in their communities,
including services that benefit older adults.

I. The CRA Was Enacted to Combat Redlining and Require Bank Support for Low-

steering and improper compensation models for mortgage loan originators, establishes
certain standards for servicing, guarantees appraisal independence and includes core
elements of a right to appeal an appraisal, allows consumers to dispute billing errors, caps
unauthorized card charges, establishes fair rules for credit cards, and sets standards for
qualified mortgages to prevent risky loan terms, among other things.
The CRA Proposal would narrow consideration of TILA violations to just those involving a
consumer's right of rescission. Taking TILA's other protections off the table for
consideration of a CRA downgrade does not ensure banks meet their continuing and
affirmative obligation to meet the credit needs of local communities.40 It disincentivizes
banks from maintaining strong compliance programs to protect consumers' significant
rights under TILA.
C. Removing Consideration of the Root Cause, Severity of the Harm,
Duration of Violations, and Pervasiveness of Violations

The current CRA regulations provide that the agencies consider highly relevant factors
about evidence of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices when determining if a
downgrade is warranted including:
• the root cause or causes of any such violations of law, rule, or regulation;
• the severity of any harm to any communities, individuals, small businesses, and
small farms resulting from such violations;
• the duration of time over which the violations occurred; and
• the pervasiveness of the violations.41
Consideration of these factors ensures that violations that harm individuals and
communities, longstanding violations, and pervasive violations get the evaluation they
deserve and are more likely to result in CRA rating downgrades. However, the CRA Proposal
eliminates all these factors from consideration. Additionally, the CRA Proposal would
replace an existing factor which holistically considers the effectiveness of a bank's
compliance management system (CMS) and ability to self-identify and reduce risks42 with a
new factor that merely considers a bank's policies and procedures to prevent
discriminatory or other illegal credit practices and any corrective actions the bank has
taken or committed to take. With the removed factors and proposed replacements, a
bank's rating turns on its paperwork and post-hoc remediation rather than on how much

damage was actually done or how long it went on — a materially weaker standard.
Consideration of the bank's CMS and the other removed factors provides a superior view.
D. The Agencies Should Consider Non-Public Examination Violations for
CRA Downgrades, and Should Consider Enforcement Actions by
Individuals and Private Organizations, Including Fair Housing
Organizations

The CRA Proposal gives two options for eligible sources of evidence of unlawful
discriminatory or other illegal credit practices that would be considered by the agencies.
The first option would consider only public enforcement actions and judicial orders. The
second would permit consideration of violations cited in an examination.
Both options limit consideration to actions by Federal or State agencies, or judicial orders
to which they are a party. Under either option, evidence of discriminatory or other illegal
credit practices from individual lawsuits or enforcement actions by private organizations,
including qualified fair housing enforcement organizations and fair housing enforcement
organizations, would be excluded.43 Especially given the current retreat from Federal
enforcement of fair housing laws44 and the targeting of State enforcement of fair housing
laws,45 this limitation is insufficient to ensure banks fulfill the purposes of the CRA as
outlined in part I and do not receive high marks under CRA while violating the law. There is
no statutory basis for limiting consideration only to governmental lawsuits, and relevant
laws themselves permit private enforcement.46
Similarly, evidence cited in examinations by both Federal and State regulators should be
considered. Because the FDIC and the OCC themselves control when they choose to cite a
violation in an examination versus pursuing a public enforcement action, excluding
examination violations would permit the agencies to exclude particular violations from
consideration for a downgrade under the CRA Proposal.
V. The CRA Proposal Should Incorporate Support for Special Purpose Credit
Programs

Special purpose credit programs (SPCPs) are authorized under the ECOA,47 and help banks
serve their "entire community" while complying with fair lending laws. In a prior CRA rule,

the FDIC and the OCC included special purpose credit programs as part of the rule.48 That
inclusion was "universally" supported by commenters.49 The current proposal does not
include special purpose credit programs.
SPCPs have helped strengthen the mortgage banking sector, expand opportunities for
consumers, and increase the breadth of mortgage products lenders can offer to people.
From 2022 to 2024, special purpose credit programs backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie
Mac helped nearly 58,000 economically disadvantaged persons of all backgrounds fairly
access homeownership and the ability to build wealth for their families. According to the
Federal Housing Finance Agency, those loans generated $17.2 billion in positive economic
impact.50
SPCPs provide a proven method to help banks address the effects of redlining and
disinvestment in the communities they operate in, while broadening their customer base of
creditworthy borrowers. Incorporating SPCPs as qualifying for CRA credit would ensure that
the proposal is consistent with the purposes of CRA and complements fair lending law as
discussed in part I above.

VI. Conclusion

For the reasons described above, NFHA urges the FDIC and the OCC to withdraw the CRA
Proposal. Alternatively, the FDIC and OCC should:
• maintain rigorous CRA requirements for banks with assets below $30 billion;
• not impose onerous restrictions on grants to community nonprofits and fair housing
agencies;
• maintain strong standards for fair housing, fair lending, and consumer protection
violations; and
• incorporate SPCPs, which were "universally" supported by commenters in a prior
rulemaking.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
National Trust Community Investment Corporation (NTCIC) appreciates the opportunity to
comment on the proposed rule issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) (together, the agencies) to
amend the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. NTCIC is a mission-driven
impact investment and asset management firm, financing community development,
historic preservation and renewable energy initiatives nationwide. Since 2000, NTCIC has
brought together investors and developers for highly impactful community development
initiatives. From historic theaters and iconic hotels to childcare and community facilities
delivering critical social service programming, NTCIC has successfully financed over 200
impactful projects across the country, using Historic Tax Credits, New Markets Tax Credits
and Renewable Energy Tax Credits.
We support the agencies' goals of improving clarity and reducing unnecessary burden.
However, we are concerned that three provisions of the proposal would together reduce
bank participation in community development, particularly the equity investments that
finance affordable housing, community revitalization, small businesses, and community
facilities in rural and underserved communities.
I. Increases to Asset-Size Thresholds (NPRM Section IV.A; Questions 1–3)
The proposed changes in bank asset-size thresholds are concerning. The rule would
classify banks as small if they hold less than $1 billion in assets, replacing the current
threshold of less than $412 million. Intermediate banks would hold between $1 billion and
$10 billion, compared with the current intermediate small bank range of $412 million to
 $1.649 billion. Only institutions with more than $10 billion in assets would be treated as
large banks, up from the current $1.649 billion threshold.
These changes would significantly reduce the number of banks subject to a separate
evaluation of their community development activities. Currently, banks receive CRA credit
for qualifying loans, investments, grants, services, and technical assistance that are
determined to be community development activities. Intermediate-small banks are
evaluated under a community development test, while large banks face separate lending,
investment, and service tests. Based on the agencies' data, approximately 800 banks
would move from intermediate to small bank status and therefore lose the community
development test entirely. As a result, nearly 80 percent of the banks the agencies
supervise would not be subject to the community development test.
Another 376 banks would shift from large bank to intermediate bank treatment. Those
institutions would no longer face a standalone investment test or the associated data
collection and reporting requirements. Instead, their community development lending,
investments, and services would be combined into a single test. This could weaken
incentives for banks to make equity investments using the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
(LIHTC), the New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC), and qualifying the Historic Tax Credit (HTC)
transactions, even as Congress has increased LIHTC access and investment opportunities
and made the NMTC permanent in the tax code.
The loss of standardized reporting from these banks would also reduce the public data
available to communities, researchers, and federal regulators to assess whether banks are
meeting local needs. Weakening these thresholds could therefore mean fewer affordable
homes, less financing for businesses and community facilities, and less capital reaching
underserved communities.
Recommendation: We urge the agencies to retain the current asset-size and reporting
thresholds.
II. Reducing Intermediate Banks' Participation in Community Development (Appendix
A, Paragraph (d)(3))
Under the proposal, an intermediate bank could receive an overall Satisfactory rating
based solely on a Satisfactory lending test rating, without also earning a Satisfactory rating
on the community development test. This would remove a major incentive for intermediate
banks to participate in community development activities, especially in areas where
market-rate capital is difficult to attract.
The agencies suggest that because banks do not know their ratings in advance, the change
will not encourage them to scale back community development activity. We respectfully
 disagree. Banks plan their CRA programs around examination standards. When community
development performance can no longer prevent an overall Satisfactory rating, it becomes
the natural place to reduce resources, particularly for institutions with limited CRA staff.
Recommendation: We urge the agencies to retain the current requirement that an
intermediate bank receive at least a Satisfactory rating on both the lending test and the
community development test to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
III. The Proposed Definition of "Complexity" Overlooks Equity Investments (Proposed §
__.14)
The proposed definition of "complexity" would link qualifying activities primarily to lending.
An investment, grant, or service would be considered complex when it is a component of a
multicomponent financing transaction involving a loan, or when a community development
loan or certain investments require specialized lending expertise. This narrower definition
could exclude activities currently recognized as complex if they do not include a
community development loan. For example, sophisticated LIHTC-HTC or NMTC-HTC
twinned equity investments without an accompanying loan might no longer qualify as
complex, potentially reducing CRA recognition of, and bank incentives for, these important
community development investments. These transactions routinely require specialized
underwriting, structuring, compliance, and asset management expertise.
Recommendation: We urge the agencies to revise the definition so that community
development equity investments, including LIHTC, NMTC, and HTC investments, qualify as
complex on their own merits when they require specialized investment, structuring, multi-
layered financing, or underwriting expertise, whether or not they are accompanied by a
loan.
IV. Illustrative List of Qualifying Activities and Confirmation Process
We strongly support the proposed requirement that the agencies maintain an illustrative
list of eligible CRA activities and the proposed formal process for banks to seek advance
confirmation that a community development activity qualifies. These provisions would
provide valuable certainty to banks and their community partners. We encourage the
agencies to update the list regularly and to make confirmation determinations publicly
available so that all banks and community organizations can benefit from them.
Recommendation: Specifically, we encourage the agencies to identify as eligible activities
twinned HTC-LIHTC, and HTC-NMTC investments and qualifying HTC (not twinned)
investments that create affordable housing, address disinvestment through revitalization,
and bring job opportunities and community services to economically distressed areas
through the adaptive reuse of historic properties.
 NTCIC appreciates the agencies' consideration of these comments. We urge federal
regulators to preserve the incentives that currently draw bank capital into community
development, especially the tax credit equity investments that are often the only way to
finance affordable housing, job creation, small business incubation as well as community
and health facilities in underserved areas.
Sincerely,
David Clower
President/CEO
National Trust Community Investment Corporation

To preserve CRA's effectiveness in encouraging NMTC investment, the NMTC
Working Group respectfully recommends that the Agencies:

investment component for banks between the current large-bank threshold and

weight for NMTC equity investments from 100 percent to 20 percent and not
apply a risk weight higher than 50 percent under any circumstances, so that
capital treatment and reduced CRA incentives do not collectively discourage bank
investment.

October 13, 2026

CRA Is a Material Driver of Bank Demand for NMTC Equity
Since enactment of the NMTC in 2000, CRA has encouraged regulated financial
institutions to invest equity in projects and businesses serving low-income communities.
Through September 2026, the NMTC program had generated nearly $83 billion of
qualified equity investment, according to the U.S. Department of the Treasury1. The
2026 Progress Report of the NMTC Coalition reports that 372 projects receiving $4.8
billion of NMTC allocation generated $8 billion of private-sector investment in 2025.
The report also states that 29.7 percent of 2025 NMTC financing went to
nonmetropolitan counties and that NMTC financing supported 101 manufacturing and
industrial businesses. 2 Together, these investments supported businesses, health care
providers, community facilities, nonprofit organizations, and other community
development activities in urban and rural communities.
Regulated financial institutions motivated in substantial part by CRA
considerations provide the predominant share of annual NMTC equity investment.
NMTC Working Group members that arrange, underwrite, and place NMTC equity
consistently report that CRA consideration is a material factor in regulated banks'
NMTC investment decisions. CRA does more than recognize activity that would occur in
any event. It creates a distinct regulatory incentive for banks to commit equity to
transactions that often involve complex structures, long investment periods, and
projects that cannot be financed solely with conventional debt.
A reduction in the number of banks with a distinct CRA investment incentive
could affect the NMTC market in several related ways. If fewer banks have a distinct
CRA incentive to make community development investments, the number of current
and prospective NMTC equity investors is likely to decline, reducing competition and
potentially limiting the amount of NMTC equity available to finance qualifying
businesses and projects. Reduced competition can weaken equity pricing. Lower pricing
produces less net private capital from a fixed amount of NMTC allocation, increases
project financing gaps, and may prevent financially marginal projects from proceeding.
These effects are likely to be most consequential in smaller and rural markets, where the
pool of interested investors is already more limited.

operating businesses, manufacturers, health care providers, and community facilities.
Those loans often include more flexible terms than conventional financing would
provide. Preserving the CRA incentive for NMTC equity is therefore consistent with,
rather than contrary to, the Agencies' emphasis on lending.
Congress Has Encouraged Broader NMTC Investment
Congress has recently taken two significant steps that support broader bank
participation in the NMTC market. First, Congress made the NMTC permanent with $5
billion of annual allocation authority, providing the long-term certainty needed for
additional financial institutions to develop the personnel, systems, and expertise
required to become NMTC investors.4 Second, Congress increased the public welfare
investment limit from 15 percent to 20 percent of a bank's capital and surplus,
expanding the capacity of banks, including regional banks, to make qualifying
investments such as NMTC investments.5 The CRA regulations should reinforce, rather
than diminish, the incentive for those institutions to use that additional capacity to
support community and economic development.
The CRA regulations should reinforce Congress's efforts to broaden NMTC
investment by preserving incentives for banks to use their expanded capacity. A broad
and competitive investor base supports stronger equity pricing and increases the private
capital generated by each dollar of NMTC allocation.
The Proposed $10 Billion Threshold Would Weaken the Incentive for
Regional-Bank Investment
The proposal would raise the large-bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10
billion in assets. The Agencies identify 126 OCC-supervised banks and 250 FDIC-
supervised banks that would move from the large-bank framework to the intermediate-
bank framework. Those 376 banks would no longer be evaluated under a separate
investment test as part of the three-part large-bank CRA test. Instead, they would be
evaluated under an intermediate-bank community development test that permits

The Agencies request comment on alternative large-bank thresholds of $3.252

than the proposed $10 billion threshold. It would therefore better balance the Agencies'

enter and remain in the NMTC equity market.
The $30 billion alternative would produce the opposite result. Under that
alternative, only the very largest institutions would remain subject to the large-bank
framework and its separate investment test, concentrating the CRA investment
incentive in a small group of banks that already hold the substantial majority of industry

small number of large institutions will materially affect equity availability and pricing.
The NMTC Working Group therefore recommends a large-bank threshold no higher
than $3.252 billion.

Under the current intermediate-small-bank framework, a bank generally must
receive at least a Satisfactory rating on both the lending test and the community
development test to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. Under the proposal, stronger
lending performance could compensate for weaker community development
performance. The Agencies state that this change is intended to emphasize lending
performance.7
That interaction becomes more consequential if hundreds of banks move into the
intermediate-bank category. The final rule should require meaningful community
development performance as a condition to an overall Satisfactory or Outstanding rating
and should separately recognize investments within the community development test.
This approach would preserve flexibility while ensuring that community development
investment remains a meaningful component of CRA performance. Specifically, the final
rule should retain the current requirement that an intermediate bank receive at least a
Satisfactory rating on the community development test in order to receive an overall
Satisfactory rating. That requirement is familiar to examiners and institutions and
would preserve the existing ratings safeguard without imposing the separate data
collection and reporting requirements applicable to large banks.
Clarify That NMTC Ownership Interests Remain Eligible Community
Development Investments
The proposal would define a "community development investment" by reference
to a "security," deposit, or membership share that meets the rule's other requirements.
The preamble explains that "security" broadly includes equity investments and debt
instruments, but the proposed text does not expressly identify partnership interests,
limited liability company interests, or interests in NMTC investment funds.8

7 Id. at 52127.
8 Id. at 52128.

October 13, 2026
Page 7 of 10


A bank investing in an NMTC transaction generally acquires an ownership
interest in an entity or fund. The tax credit is a benefit associated with that investment,
not the instrument the bank purchases. Express clarification is therefore needed to
avoid uncertainty about common NMTC structures and to ensure consistent treatment
among examiners and institutions.
The NMTC Working Group recommends that the final rule or accompanying
interpretive guidance provide:
"For purposes of this section, a community development investment includes a
direct or indirect ownership interest in a partnership, limited liability company,
corporation, fund, or similar entity, including a legally binding commitment to
acquire such an interest, where the investment finances one or more activities
having a primary purpose of community development."
Eligibility would continue to depend on whether the underlying activity has a
primary purpose of community development and satisfies the other requirements of the
rule. The requested clarification would not expand the substantive scope of qualifying
activity. It would confirm that established investment structures remain eligible.
For NMTC transactions in which QEI proceeds are deployed through QLICIs in
multiple geographic areas, the final rule should permit a bank to use a reasonable and
consistently applied methodology, supported by the CDE's records, to attribute
qualifying activity among the applicable assessment areas.
The NMTC Working Group also requests that the Agencies confirm that qualified
equity investments in NMTC transactions may qualify under the proposed definition of
a complex community development investment when the applicable requirements are
met. The proposal would treat a community development investment that is a necessary
or otherwise beneficial component of a multicomponent financing transaction involving
a loan as complex, and therefore responsive. NMTC transactions fit this definition
particularly well because they commonly combine investor equity and leverage debt to
fund a qualified equity investment, the proceeds of which the CDE then uses to make
qualified low-income community investments in the operating business or project.
Express confirmation in the final rule or accompanying guidance would provide
institutions and examiners with a clear and administrable standard without expanding
the scope of qualifying activity.
 Response to the 2026 Community Reinvestment Act NPR
October 13, 2026
Page 8 of 10


Preserve CRA Consideration for Service on CDE Boards
Section 45D of the Internal Revenue Code requires a CDE to maintain
accountability to residents of the low-income communities it serves, commonly through
representation on a governing or advisory board.9 Bank employees often contribute
their community development expertise to these boards and CRA recognition can
encourage institutions to make qualified personnel available for this work.
Raising the large-bank threshold would remove the separate service test for
affected institutions and could reduce the incentive for bank employees to serve on CDE
boards. The Agencies should preserve meaningful consideration for such service where
it supports a CDE's community accountability, underwriting, portfolio oversight, or
delivery of capital to low-income communities.
Preserve Grants That Build Community Development Capacity
The proposed rule would limit consideration of community development grants
to amounts directly used for a qualifying program, project, or initiative and would
impose additional documentation requirements, including, for large banks, a 15 percent
limitation on recipients' indirect costs. These restrictions could disproportionately affect
smaller and rural nonprofit organizations that have limited administrative capacity but
play an important role in developing projects, building local pipelines, and providing
services needed for successful NMTC investments. The Agencies' own economic analysis
acknowledges that the proposal may reduce support for some nonprofit and
intermediary activities.10 The NMTC Working Group's experience confirms that this
effect would be felt most acutely by the organizations least able to absorb it.
The Agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating support,
capacity-building grants, and sponsorships provided to nonprofit organizations
primarily engaged in qualifying community development activities. Eligibility should
turn on the organization's documented community development purpose and use of
funds, without inflexible project-level tracing or overhead requirements that make
modest grants impractical to administer.

Consider the Combined Effect of CRA Incentives and Bank Capital
Requirements
CRA treatment and regulatory capital treatment affect different components of
bank demand for NMTC equity. CRA affects the strength of the incentive to invest, while
capital treatment affects the capacity and cost of making the investment. In its June 18,

The NMTC Working Group supports appropriate reductions in unnecessary
regulatory burden, but those reductions should not eliminate the CRA features that

organizations to conduct qualifying community development activities. Finally, the
