shift the bank's focus away from these vital activities;

3. Changes to the rules with respect to grant-making will be detrimental to CDFIs, intermediaries
and non-profit recipients of funding that rely on grant funding to support general operations as
well as program delivery.

4. Changes to the definitions of qualifying community development activities will shift funding
away from the activities that most benefit low-income people (LIP)and residents of low- and
moderate-income (LMI) communities towards broader economic activities that are less
impactful.

SECTION-BY-SECTION RESPONSES

A. Asset Size Thresholds

The regulators propose raising the threshold definitions of small banks from the current asset cap of
$412 million to a cap of $1 billion in assets, and of intermediate banks (formerly called intermediate
small banks) from a cap of $1.649 billion in assets to a cap of $10 billion in assets. While this may help
meet the regulators' stated goals of reducing "the associated data collection, maintenance, and
reporting requirements for many smaller banks", we are concerned that this will ultimately lead to the
loss of billions of dollars of investments in community development activities, including most notably in
smaller and rural communities with limited bank presence already; as well as the loss of critical
reporting data from intermediate sized institutions.

According to the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC), raising the small bank threshold
from $412 million to $1 billion would eliminate community development evaluations for roughly 814
banks, or about 40% of the banks currently subject to that requirement. Similarly, the proposal would
reclassify another 417 banks by raising the intermediate bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10
billion. This would eliminate the separate investment and service tests and combine community
development loans, investments and services into one evaluation, reducing their distinct scrutiny
purposes.

As a result, only the largest 6% of banks would face separate reviews of their community
development loans/investments and branch services or of their CRA small-business loan reporting
requirements – considerably reducing their incentive to make community development investments
including investments in affordable housing, Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs),
community development tax credits like LIHTC and NMTCs, and crucial community facilities like health
care centers, daycare centers and charter schools that often struggle to attract bank capital.

 4

As noted by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), removing the investment test
requirement for banks under the $10 billion threshold would remove an incentive for a significant
number of banks to invest in the Housing Credit. In an AHTCC survey, over 108 banks below the $10
billion threshold invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over the five-year survey period.
Extrapolating these results to the full Housing Credit market, banks under the $10 billion threshold
invested approximately $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over those five years – investments that may
be in jeopardy without the incentive of a separate investment test.

What's more, banks under the $10 billion threshold play a particularly important role in financing
affordable housing in rural communities. AHTCC survey data show that approximately one-third of
Housing Credit equity investments from banks under $10 billion in assets supported rural markets,
indicating that banks in this asset range play an outsized role in investing in rural communities. By
comparison, roughly 8 percent of all Housing Credit equity in a CohnReznick industry-wide sample was
invested in nonmetro counties, a proxy for rural and small-town markets.

While LISC supports adjustments to asset thresholds, the threshold levels proposed by the regulators
are excessively high. The small bank threshold was initially set at $250 million in 1995, which would
equate to approximately $500 million in today's dollars – significantly smaller than the $1 billion
proposed by regulators. It is also notable that even the major bank trade associations have proposed
much smaller thresholds than what the regulators currently propose. In their public response to the
agencies' requests for Economic Growth and Regulatory Paperwork Reduction Act (EGRPRA) comments
in October of 2025, the American Bankers Association recommended threshold levels of up to $850
million for small banks and up to $4.7 billion for intermediate banks; and the Independent Community
Bankers Association recommended threshold levels of up to $850 million for small banks and $3 billion
for intermediate banks.

In short, the levels currently proposed by the regulators – much less the proposal to increase the
intermediate bank threshold to $30 billion – are much higher than what would be reasonable based
upon inflationary adjustments and what the industry itself believes to be adequate thresholds and, as
noted, will lead to a significant retreat of capital from low income and distressed communities. To this
end, LISC would support a small bank threshold of $850 million, and the intermediate bank threshold of
$3.252 billion that was proposed as an option by the regulators. LISC would also support annual
inflationary adjustments for these figures.

B. Performance Tests

Retail Lending Product Lines: LISC supports narrowing the CRA focus to the bank's main business lines,
as determined at a national level (rather than at each assessment area); but would recommend that all
banks should be evaluated, at a minimum, on mortgage and small business/small farm loans. We
would also recommend that consumer loans be evaluated in all instances where they constitute one of
the two largest product lines for the bank, not just in those instances where the dollar volume and loan
count exceed 50% of the bank's portfolio.

 5

Range of Retail Services: LISC believes that the regulators should continue to examine deposit account
products as part of the CRA examination. Deposit account products, including overdraft fees and fees
for failing to maintain a minimum balance, can significantly impact a consumer's ability to avoid
excessive debt, build savings, and access credit. Consistent with the CRA statute, we believe that a
bank that is charging excessive fees to its customers is not "meeting the credit needs of its entire
community", in that it could negatively impact that customer's ability to access credit.

Intermediate Bank Ratings: LISC opposes the regulators' proposal to allow intermediary banks that fail
to meet at least a satisfactory rating on the community development test to receive an overall score of
satisfactory. Community development loans and investments are every bit as essential as retail lending
when capturing the totality of a bank's investment activities in low-income communities. In fact, they
are arguably more important, in that they specifically target activities that benefit low-income families
and revitalize LMI communities. The current practice of assigning equal weighting and consideration to
each set of activities should be maintained.

Other Changes to Performance Tests: LISC does not agree with the regulators' proposal to remove
factors that require specific consideration of serving the credit needs of highly disadvantaged areas
and low-income people. The authorizing statute for the Community Reinvestment Act requires
regulators to assess whether a bank is meeting the credit needs of "its entire community". This
includes families at all income levels, not just those at moderate income levels and higher. Similarly,
banks should also be required to report the portion of lending to communities characterized by high
distress, as measured by census tracts with low median family incomes (at or below 80% of the area
median) and/or high poverty rates (20% or higher).

C. Community Development Activities

Community Development Loans: LISC supports proposals that would permit legally binding
commitments to qualify for CRA credit, as well as the consideration of prior period community
development loans that continue to be on the bank's balance sheets. Under the current regulations,
there is a practice of churning short-term loans to CDFIs, for example, so that the bank can get credit
for originating a new loan in each assessment period. These short-term loans aren't nearly as impactful
as longer-term loans, particularly in a volatile interest rate environment.

Community Development Investments: LISC has significant concerns with proposed changes to the
definition of Community Development Investments, as noted below:

1. Definition of Qualified Investment

The proposed regulations would define a community development investment as "a security or
a deposit or a membership share in a financial institution, including a legally binding
commitment to invest, that: (1) Has as its primary purpose community development, (2) Is
permissible under applicable laws, rules and regulations, and (3) Except as specified in 25.13(e),
benefits the banks or savings association's service area(s)."

 6

We believe that there is a drafting error here, as it currently could be interpreted that to qualify
for consideration, a security must be in a "financial institution". This could be solved by
including a comma after the word security.

The agencies should also clarify that the proposed definition of a community development
investment preserves CRA consideration for banks' investments in funds, limited partnerships,
limited liability companies, and similar entities that finance qualifying community development
activities, including LIHTC and NMTC investments.

Lastly, as noted in comments submitted by the National Association of Affordable Housing
Lenders (NAAHL), the final rule should also expressly preserve investment consideration for
qualifying equity equivalent investments (EQ2s) in nonprofit CDFIs and other community
development lenders. EQ2s provide deeply subordinated, long-term capital that supports
financing for community needs in the hardest to serve parts of the market. Long-standing
interagency interpretive guidance recognizes appropriately structured EQ2s that retain equity-
like characteristics as qualified investments, even if they are documented as a note or
subordinated obligation. This clarification would carry forward existing policy.

2. Definition of Grants

The regulators are proposing significant changes to the treatment of grants to nonprofit
recipients that strikes at the heart of the safety and soundness of the nonprofits the serve the
hardest to reach populations in the banking industry.

Operating grants: The regulators are proposing that operating grants made by large banks to
nonprofits cannot qualify for CRA credit. Nonprofits are the preferred partners of large banks
that wish to serve low-income communities in their assessment areas -- providing a host of
services ranging from housing development to small business technical assistance to
homeownership counseling that the bank simply cannot provide in such an intensive and
targeted fashion across multiple assessment areas. Operating grants are the lifeblood of
nonprofit entities, supporting everything from staff salaries to training resources to simply
building net assets and making them stronger borrowers for the banks; and these tend to be
the most difficult funds to raise. Cutting off this source of funding to nonprofits focusing on
housing and economic development activities in LMI communities would negatively impact the
safety and soundness of bank CRA lending. LISC therefore recommends that banks continue to
get CRA credit for making operating grants to nonprofit entities that provide services consistent
with the regulation's definition of community development.

Pass-through grants from intermediaries: LISC strongly opposes the regulators' proposal to
eliminate pass-through grants to intermediaries as a qualifying CRA investment. As noted in this
letter from over one dozen intermediary organizations including LISC, intermediaries play an
essential role in the delivery of grants, capital, training and technical resources to local
nonprofit institutions; supporting critical housing and community development projects at the
local level. A nonprofit intermediary may aggregate funding from multiple banks and other
 7

sources, conduct due diligence on community organizations, provide technical assistance,
monitor performance, and distribute grants or low-cost capital to organizations that themselves
conduct qualifying community development activities. We also play a valuable role in collecting
shared outcome data from across multiple sites and advising banks and other funders on best
practices that can inform future funding efforts. Properly structured nonprofit intermediaries
are not an obstacle between banks and the communities they serve, but rather the connective
tissue – aligning national, regional and local banks alike with an efficient and accountable
mechanism for supporting community-based organizations in their local assessment areas.

For example, LISC supports a network of over 120 Financial Opportunity Center sites in 29
different urban and rural markets throughout the country. FOC programs provide employment
and career counseling, one-on-one financial coaching and education and low-cost financial
products to LMI families to help build credit, savings and assets safely. They also connect clients
with income supports such as food stamps, utilities assistance and affordable health insurance
to bridge gaps as they work towards new career goals. The cornerstone of the FOC model is
providing these services in an integrated way—rather than as stand-alone services— with a
long-term commitment to helping clients achieve financial success. Through the client data
we've collected at these sites, we've been able to demonstrate that integrated, or "bundled"
services, lead to concrete gains in net income and job retention. Notably, research shows that
FOC clients who take advantage of all three combined services are 50 percent more likely to
land a well-paying job than people receiving employment services alone.

LISC launched its FOC programming work over 15 years ago, and much of the funding has come
in the form of grants from large national banks that have received CRA credit for their
investments in our model. LISC in turn uses these funds to provide:

(1) pass-through grants to help community-based organizations staff and run FOC
programming, covering everything from start-up to operating costs;

(2) technical assistance and training to help FOC staff attain credentials and offer more
effective coaching and job counseling

(3) data collection tools and analysis that help FOC coaches tailor support for individual
clients, and that reports client outcomes – helping LISC and our funders to identify
practices that can inform future program design.

(4) professional networking support in the form of national and regional meetings,
collaborative groups and an online library of resources on the FOC model's continued
innovations.

The FOC model is just one example of national programming that we deliver to nonprofits
working in banks' local assessment areas. We also provide pass-through grants and technical
assistance dollars to hundreds of nonprofit housing developers in local communities annually;
as well as to Business Development Organizations working to revitalize urban commercial
 8

corridors and rural main streets through commercial improvements, business loans, and
counseling to small businesses. This is high touch work that banks are happy to partner with
LISC to support, since they do not otherwise have the resources and boots on the ground to
deliver these services and monitor the outcomes across all their assessment areas. This is the
unique role that intermediaries like LISC play, and the reason that banks have been eager to
partner with us over the years.

For the reasons stated above, LISC strongly recommends that the regulators continue to allow
intermediary organizations to make pass through grants to nonprofits that support community
development activities in banks' assessment areas. If the regulators are concerned about funds
not flowing through to the community partners, they could develop a requirement that the
intermediary record how the money was utilized (e.g., pass-through grants vs. program
expenses vs. overhead), as well as the names of all nonprofit entities which received pass-
through funding, to demonstrate that they serve the banks' assessment area(s).

Administrative costs: LISC appreciates the regulators wanting to limit the amount of funding
spent on overhead expenses, versus direct program delivery. In most instances, the hard cap of
15% for "indirect" expenses should be sufficient, but we would recommend that the regulators
raise this to 20% to ensure that all nonprofit entities can appropriately administer the grants.

Alternatively, the regulators should consider specifying that the bank can receive partial credit
for a grant in instances where more than 15% is used for indirect expenses. For example, under
the current proposal, if a bank makes a grant and 20% is used by the recipient for indirect
expenses, the bank will not receive any credit for this investment. However, if the regulators
were to state that the bank could not receive any credit on amounts used to cover indirect
expenses greater than 15%, then in this instance, the bank could receive credit for 95% of the
grant amount (the 80% supporting programs and the allowable 15% covering indirect expenses)
but could not claim the additional 5% that was used to cover indirect expenses above the
stated cap.

Reporting requirements: LISC is concerned that the additional reporting requirements
proposed by the regulators will further dissuade banks from making grants to nonprofits. We
believe that banks should get automatic approvals for investing in CDFIs (since these are
independently verified to be community-based financing entities), and that for all other entities,
retention of the nonprofit's IRS form 990 is sufficient to demonstrate the mission and
geographic service area of the entity. Banks should not be otherwise required to retain annual
operating budgets or program budgets but rather should be able to rely on self-certifications
from beneficiaries or the initial grant proposal to demonstrate the appropriate use of funding.

Primary Purpose of Community Development: LISC believes that the regulators need to put more
guardrails around the primary purpose definition, particularly with respect to investments in general
infrastructure and community facilities that are not specifically targeted to serving low-income
individuals or low-income community residents. LISC does not generally believe that banks should
receive CRA credit for investments that are not specifically targeted to LMI communities or LIP and/or
 9

where less than the majority of funding directly benefits these populations; and is concerned that with
the changes proposed in the regulations there could be a huge substitution effect away from projects
that by their very purpose are designed to serve low-income communities or low-income families (e.g.,
LIHTC and NMTC investments) in favor of municipal bonds that may only incidentally serve these
populations.

Qualitative Factors: LISC appreciates the regulators' continued focus on qualitative reviews, as
performance context and responsiveness should continue to be an important consideration for a CRA
examination. To increase transparency, the regulators should also provide an illustrative list of higher
impact community development investments, as was included in the 2023 regulations. In this manner,
banks and community partners would have a signal as to which investments are likely to be viewed
most favorably by regulators with respect to their qualitative reviews. Notably, the 2023 regulations
emphasized that investments in high need areas, in CDFIs, and in community development tax credits
would receive favorable consideration from the regulators.

D. Community Development Definition

Affordable Housing: LISC supports the inclusion of Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing (NOAH) as
affordable housing in certain circumstances, but recommends adopting the standards that were
included in the 2023 final regulations that were released by the regulators, which included for
consideration housing that met affordability standards and at least one of the following four
characteristics: (1) is located in LMI census tracts; (2) is located in a census tract in which the median
renter is low-moderate income and the median rent does not exceed 30% of area median income; (3)
is purchased, developed, financed, rehabilitated, improved or preserved by any nonprofit organization
with a stated mission of, or that otherwise directly supports, providing affordable housing; or (4) the
bank can provide documentation that a majority of the units are occupied by LMI individuals or
families.

LISC does not support the proposal to allow NOAH housing in high-cost areas to qualify as affordable
housing even if it serves middle-income individuals – unless a majority of the units are determined to
serve LMI families.

LISC does, however, support higher income thresholds with respect to owner occupied homes – given
that the market for first time homebuyers includes low-, moderate- and even middle-income
homeowners that are increasingly priced out of homeownership. We believe that banks should be
given credit for community development products (construction loans, grants to nonprofits) that
facilitate homeownership for families making up to 120% of AMI, even if the homes are not located in
LMI communities – particularly if the investments align with a federal, state or local government
initiative.


 10


Economic Development: LISC believes that to qualify for credit under the economic development
definition, the bank investment must provide benefits to LIP or LMI communities. Simply allowing any
small business loan, regardless of the location of the business, to qualify for CRA credit undermines the
statutory imperative that banks provide credit in all their communities. LISC believes that if the
business itself is not located in a LMI community, then the bank must demonstrate that the loan will
reasonably support creating or retaining jobs for LMI persons.

Revitalization and Stabilization: LISC does not support codifying the FAQ language around "essential
infrastructure" into the regulations; much less the clarifications that investments can qualify if they
benefit entire communities "including low-income communities". This would essentially allow banks to
fulfill CRA investment requirements by giving them full credit for purchasing municipal bonds that
support water/sewers, roads, broadband, etc. that only incidentally serve low-income communities.
Unless the project is specifically targeted to serve LMI families or communities and/or they are the
majority beneficiaries of the investment, it should not be eligible for credit under CRA.

LISC does support the inclusion of areas targeted by government agencies for redevelopment as
proposed in the revised regulations and concurs that the regulations should not identify which
programs will automatically qualify, since as noted, this could inadvertently exclude promising
programs enacted after the regulations are published.

For example, there is significant bipartisan support in Congress to enact the Neighborhood Homes
Investment Act, which would create a new community development tax credit to support the
development and rehabilitation of single-family homes, primarily in distressed communities. This
would create an excellent opportunity for bank investment and should be eligible for CRA credit but
won't likely be enacted until after these regulations are published. The regulations therefore need to
be flexible enough to allow for innovative initiatives such as this one to be eligible for CRA credit upon
enactment.

E. Consideration of Community Development Activities

Illustrative Lists: LISC supports proposals by the regulators to publish an illustrative list of qualifying CD
activities, and to provide banks with an opportunity to seek pre-approvals from regulators. But as
noted previously in these comments, LISC believes that regulators should also provide an illustrative
list of activities that will demonstrate "complexity and responsiveness", so banks will know that these
investments will be given preferential treatment by examiners. This is where regulators could
differentiate between, and favor, products that have direct benefits to LIP and LMI communities (e.g.,
affordable housing, federally qualified health centers, a grocery store in a food desert) vs. those that
may only have marginal or incidental benefits (MBS purchases, infrastructure investments).

Community development activities outside of assessment areas: LISC supports efforts by the regulators
to better clarify when activities undertaken outside of a bank's assessment area(s) will qualify for CRA
credit. However, we are concerned that attempting to align specific measurable outcomes on an
annual basis and in every single assessment area in a bank's footprint may prove unmanageable for
 11

large, branch-based banks. LISC prefers the approach taken by regulators in the final regulations
released in 2023, which created a sliding scale based upon the bank's delivery model (i.e., branch-based
banks would be more heavily scored on activities within their assessment areas, whereas wholesale
banks would have heavier weighting for activities outside of their assessment areas).

Alternatively, the regulators should consider deciding whether activities outside of an assessment area
will be permitted in a future exam cycle. That is, upon completing an exam cycle and demonstrating
satisfactory accountability to its assessment areas, the bank may, on a going forward basis, be
permitted to make more investments outside of its assessment areas. In fact, banks should be
encouraged to use this flexibility to make investments in underbanked communities, including CRA
deserts, as a way of demonstrating "responsiveness".

F. Strategic Plans

LISC supports the agencies' proposals with respect to institutions choosing to submit strategic plans.
We believe that these proposals will generally benefit both banks and community stakeholders, by
providing clarity, transparency and accountability to the strategic plan process.

That said, as noted in LISC's public comments from February of 2026, we do have concerns with the
OCC's proposed development of a streamlined strategic plan template for banks of over $30 billion. To
the extent the OCC moves forward with streamlined strategic plans, at the very minimum, the
streamlined plans should only be offered to small or intermediate size banks.

G. Data Collection, Reporting and Disclosure

LISC supports the comments submitted by the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders
(NAAHL) with respect to the proposed collection of information regarding grants to nonprofits. As
noted in its comments, banks already exercise their own due diligence to make impactful grants to
organizations working in their communities. Requiring documentation of organizational budgets,
written attestations of operating costs, and bank oversight of operating expenses will impose new
oversight responsibilities that fall outside of banks' area of expertise and could raise liability concerns.
Further, requiring public disclosure of grantees and award amounts would compromise both banks'
and grantees' privacy. Together, these burdens could disincentivize grants that amplify impact and
drive new credit opportunities nationwide.

It is also notable that, unlike other parts of the proposed regulations which seek to reduce CRA burden
on banks, this proposal would add significantly more reporting requirements for both banks and
nonprofit recipients of grants.


 12

CONCLUSION

In conclusion, while LISC generally supports efforts to modernize the Community Reinvestment Act and
applauds certain specific proposals offered, we do not support these proposed regulations because, on
balance, they would limit both the quality and quantity of community development investments
provided by the banking sector.

As the single most critical driver of private capital into underinvested urban, rural, and tribal
communities, the CRA must not be diluted by unnecessarily high asset thresholds, by prohibitions on
certain types of grantmaking, or by consideration of activities under the community development test
that do not target LIP or LMI communities. We strongly encourage the agencies to adopt LISC's
recommendations to recalibrate these asset caps, preserve robust community development testing,
and safeguard the vital partnerships between financial institutions, CDFIs, and affordable housing
intermediaries.

By striking the proper balance between regulatory modernization and rigorous community
accountability, the agencies can ensure that the updated CRA remains a powerful engine for economic
growth, wealth-building, and opportunity for the low-income families and distressed communities that
rely on it most.

We appreciate the opportunity to submit these comments and stand ready to serve as a resource to
the agencies throughout this rulemaking process. Please contact mjosephs@lisc.org if you would like
additional information on any of these proposals.

Sincerely,


Matt Josephs
Senior Vice President for Policy

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Working Solutions CDFI submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
("OCC") and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies")1.
The proposed changes would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In
addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the
OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences
for low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the
analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current
comment deadline by 60 days.
Working Solutions is a nonprofit community development finance institution (CDFI) serving low-
and moderate-income entrepreneurs throughout the state of California. Our organization
provides affordable financing and technical assistance to small businesses, helping expand
economic opportunity and strengthen local communities across the state. We are a member of
Opportunity Finance Network (OFN), the National Coalition for Community Reinvestment
(NCRC), the Responsible Business Lending Coalition (RBLC), the Credit Builders Alliance (CBA),
the National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders (NALCAB), and the California
Coalition for Community Investment (CalCCI).
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-
income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both
credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).


2
have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss, and unequal access to mainstream
financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services, and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities, on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment, and on the
nonprofit CDFIs and organizations that serve them.
REDUCTION IN COMMUNITY INVESTMENT EXPECTATIONS FOR ALL BANKS
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In California
communities, from 2010-2024, banks made $488,125,184,000 in CRA qualified mortgage
lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and $144,603,550,000 in CRA qualified lending
to small businesses.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the percentage the National
Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the largest banks currently devote to
community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC and
FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently
conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development loans and investments
inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of annual community
development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of Tier 1 capital, and a median of 3.6% of
Tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each bank instead conducted only the
amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community
development lending and investments, combined activity would fall to approximately $14.9
billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal
encourages banks to use strategic plans to make their CRA compliance easier and more

2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks
surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of its Tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise
0.625% for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the
practical effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk,
(Sept. 10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-
development-activity-at-risk/.


3
predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set strategic plan benchmarks for CRA
performance well-below historical levels of community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and
loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to
the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for entire communities. For
example, in California, families and businesses continue to face significant affordability
challenges, from rising housing and childcare costs to increased barriers to access capital.
Through our work with banking partners, CDFIs like Working Solutions help address these
challenges by providing responsible, flexible financing that supports affordable housing, small
business starts and growth, community facilities, and other local investments that improve
quality of life and create economic opportunity. Working Solutions' priority entrepreneurs are
building businesses without traditional financial safety nets—making access to restorative CDFI
capital and supportive networks and resources especially catalytic in accelerating their growth
and resilience.
Right-sized, right-timed capital helps businesses succeed. For example, Working Solutions loans
were the right match to help a family grow their bakery from a home kitchen to a successful
storefront earning national recognition by supporting equipment purchases and build-out needs
without overextending the business. Beyond capital, the entrepreneur received guidance and
ongoing check-ins from Working Solutions Business Consulting staff to support long-term,
sustainable business growth. CDFIs like Working Solutions provide financial solutions tailored to
help communities thrive, beyond what banks can provide directly.
It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs. Before
finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce
lending, services, or investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and
whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be
disproportionately affected.
LESS COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT SCRUTINY OF BANKS
The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (Docket ID: OCC-2026-0694 / RIN 3064-AG31)

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould:

The Native CDFI Network (NCN), the only national membership organization solely dedicated to supporting the
nearly 100 Native community development financial institutions (CDFIs) serving Tribal Nations and Native
communities across the country, welcomes this opportunity to provide comments to the FDIC and OCC regarding
their Proposed Rule governing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). Our comments are formally supported
by the 26 co-signatory Native CDFIs, Tribal Nations, other Native organizations, and Indian Country partners listed
at the end of this document.

The Vital Role Native CDFIs Play in Catalyzing Economic Growth in Indian Country

As the CDFI Fund explains on its website, Native CDFIs' origins can be traced to the Congressional legislation
authorizing the Fund's creation more than 30 years ago, which contained among its provisions the mandating of a
study examining lending and investment practices in Native communities. Titled the Native American Lending Study,
it identified 17 major barriers to investment in Indian Country1, and "affirmed the importance of developing Native
CDFIs to play a key role in the broader effort to lead Native Communities into the nation's economic mainstream."2
A recent federal study found that 46 percent of Native communities are located in banking deserts, "over 12 times
the national average of 3.8 percent."3 Established in large part to address these deserts, Native CDFIs are often the
only financial institutions serving these communities, providing access to capital, credit, and financial education
where no alternatives exist. Over the past two-plus decades, Native CDFIs have proven themselves to be vital
engines for fueling the growth of healthy, vibrant Native economies and communities, particularly those located in


rural America. In the CDFI Fund's own words, Native CDFIs are making a "considerable impact" by "helping to
transform their communities. They are creating businesses and jobs in places that desperately need them...They are
helping to change the lives of the people they serve." Below are some more details about how they do so:

• Native CDFIs provide a range of critical supports: According to a recent federal study, to directly address
the acute capital access gaps Native communities have long faced, as of 2025, 65 percent of Native CDFIs
provide business loans and 73 percent provide micro loans for businesses, and many (69 percent) also
provide consumer loans to foster economic activity in local communities. In addition, 29 percent of Native
CDFIs provide mortgage loans – including U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Section 184
loans designed to facilitate homeownership in Native American communities – and 39 percent provide home
improvement loans.4 Meanwhile, a 2021 federal study revealed that Native CDFIs help to substantially
increase the credit scores of Native people "in credit distress."5

• Uniquely positioned and equipped to cultivate Native homeownership: In 2018, the USDA Section 502
Direct Home Loan Program's demonstration project affirmed the unique ability of Native CDFIs to help Native
people become homeowners on Tribal lands by making two Native CDFIs eligible borrowers and enabling
them to relend to qualified families for the construction, acquisition, and rehabilitation of affordable housing
on tribal trust land. In just one year, those CDFIs doubled the number of low-interest home loans that USDA
had provided on two Indian reservations in South Dakota during the previous decade – an outcome that has
prompted bipartisan efforts to make this program permanent and expand it nationwide. This is particularly
critical given that data shows Native people living on reservations who want to buy homes are significantly
more likely to have high-priced mortgages, and those mortgage rates average nearly two percentage points
higher than for non-Native people outside reservations.6

• An extraordinary and reliable return on investment: According to the Treasury Department, investments
made in Native and non-Native CDFIs generate significant additional capital for affordable housing and
homeownership, small business, and consumer lending by leveraging limited federal resources to attract
private sector investments. CDFIs also are safe investments, with a loan default rate of 0.36% in 2023, roughly
half the rate of traditional banks.7

Simply put, Native CDFIs are among the most efficient and impactful financial institutions in the nation, stretching
limited resources to drive economic and job growth in some of the country's most economically distressed
communities, especially across rural America (the vast majority of Native CDFIs are based in and serve rural
communities).

The CRA: A Five-Decade Record of Failing Tribal Nations and Native Communities

Congress passed the CRA in 1977 to encourage banking institutions to serve the credit needs of the communities in
which they operate, specifically low- and moderate-income areas and populations. The Act also aimed to curb
discriminatory credit and lending practices against those populations, a practice commonly known as "redlining."
With many Native communities located in the poorest parts of the country, and with a substantial percentage of the
Native population deemed to be low or moderate income, the CRA on paper should have significantly enhanced the
ability of Tribal Nations, their enterprises, Native-owned small businesses, Native homebuyers, and Native
consumers to access capital and credit through CRA-qualifying banking institutions.

Unfortunately, however, to date the CRA has failed to compel or effectively incentivize banking institutions'
investment in Tribal Nations and Native communities. Since its founding in 2009, NCN has collected extensive
anecdotal evidence confirming that banking institutions' redlining of Native nations and communities continues
largely unabated, a dynamic exacerbated in recent years by the widely documented consolidation of the banking
industry and the ensuing retraction of bank branches away from Tribal Nations and Native communities. As the CDFI


Fund's landmark "Access to Capital and Credit in Native Communities" report points out, while the CRA "was not
intended to exclude Native Communities living on tribal lands...in practice it often does," and banks under the Act's
current regulations can easily satisfy CRA requirements without having to do business in or with Native nations and
communities if they so choose (as most do), and they are not required to affirmatively disclose that they have failed
to make CRA-qualified investments in Tribal Nations and Native communities.8

This has contributed to some predictable, persistent, and sobering outcomes. With the CRA largely excluding Tribal
Nations and Native communities, large swaths of Indian Country continue to exist as credit desert epicenters where
no banking services are available. This has left many Native people to instead turn to nearby high-cost predatory
lenders that trap them in endless debt cycles and rob them of their ability to grow their personal and familial assets
and wealth and, collectively, community prosperity. As the Native American Finance Officers Association explains,
"An alignment of a banking and credit deserts map with a map of tribal communities reveals a crisis for tribal citizens
and governments attempting to access cost-effective capital and banking services."9 A recent study of this state of
affairs in Arizona and New Mexico, meanwhile, found that (among other things) traditional mortgage lending is failing
Native families "egregiously," Tribal lands received less than one cent for each dollar loaned to small businesses in
those two states, and Tribal areas have far higher quantified financial need than other rural areas.10

The CRA Proposed Rule: What It Will Mean for Indian Country

NCN has been actively involved in the federal government's various attempts in recent years to modernize the CRA,
particularly as it pertains to Tribal Nations and Native communities and the ability of Native CDFIs to serve them.
Based on our collective analysis of the Proposed Rule and how its provisions are bound to specifically impact Tribal
Nations and Native communities, NCN and our co-signatories to these comments are opposed to the Proposed Rule
on three primary grounds:

(1) it will structurally and dramatically de-incentivize bank lending and investment in Tribal Nations and
Native communities generally and Native CDFIs specifically, all but eliminating the modest benefits the
CRA currently generates for these recipients;

(2) it will render impossible to track the nature and degree of CRA-qualifying bank activity involving
Tribal Nations, Native communities, and Native CDFIs at a national, local, or individual bank level,
further reducing banks' public accountability to Indian Country under the CRA; and

(3) it will make it exceedingly difficult to amend the CRA regulations in the future to strengthen CRA to
increase bank lending and investment in Indian Country (the Proposed Rule, coupled with the agencies'
current effort to secure court decisions that would prevent future administrations from amending CRA
regulations to examine lending beyond banks' footprints or evaluate deposit products, threatens to
permanently restrict the CRA's reach).

Our Joint Positions on the Overarching Provisions of the Proposed Rule

We oppose finalization of the Proposed Rule in its current form based on our collective analysis of how the Rule's
key provisions will specifically manifest themselves across Indian Country. Below is a detailed explanation of several
ways the CRA Proposed Rule will reduce CRA-qualified lending and investment in Tribal Nations, Native
communities, and Native CDFIs:

1. Substantially reducing the number of banks required to satisfy the CRA's most rigorous requirements by
increasing bank asset thresholds: Under the Proposed Rule, banks with less than $1 billion in assets would now
be considered "small banks" (up from the current threshold of $412 million), while banks with between $1 billion
and $10 billion (up from $1.649 billion) in assets would now be considered intermediate small (hereafter,
intermediate) banks. Combined, these two new thresholds will serve to dramatically reduce the number of large


banks under CRA, meaning far fewer would remain subject to the full large bank CRA examination with its separate
lending, investment, and service tests. Removal of these accountability measures will de-incentivize hundreds of
regional and community banks from channeling vitally needed CRA-qualified capital into Indian Country and other
rural areas. For Native CDFIs, fewer banks subject to the most rigorous CRA requirements will mean fewer banks
inclined to actively pursue loans, investments, deposits, grants, and other partnerships with Native CDFIs.

Of grave concern to Native CDFIs and the Tribal Nations and Native communities we serve is the significant
reduction in bank accountability to invest in community development that these proposed asset threshold changes
will cause. First, raising the ceiling threshold for small banks from $412 million to $1 billion will eliminate community
development evaluations under CRA for roughly 814 banks, or about 40% of the banks currently subject to that
requirement, which is projected to prompt the loss of at least $500 million dollars annually in CRA-qualifying
community development loans and investments from those banks.11 Meanwhile, the more than 400 banks moving
from large bank to intermediate bank status would eliminate the separate investment and service tests they must
now satisfy and combine community development loans, investments and services into one evaluation, reducing
their distinct scrutiny purposes. As a result, only the largest 6% of banks would face separate reviews of their
community development loans/investments and branch services or of their CRA small-business loan reporting
requirements.

In addition, under proposed Option 1 in the Proposed Rule, a large bank would generally qualify for broader
geographic consideration of community development loans after meeting a benchmark equal to 0.625% of Tier 1
capital allocated to its assessment areas. The same 0.625% benchmark would apply separately to CD investments
and grants. A recent analysis of this measure concluded that this could endanger as much as 85% of the current
CRA-based community development activity.12

Together, these provisions also will put financing for affordable housing at risk, especially in smaller markets that
include much of Indian Country, worsening the nation's housing crisis. Notably, the Proposed Rule will reduce
demand for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) at a time when Congress just increased the supply of LIHTCs
through the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (which won't matter much if more than 800 banks no longer have
community development requirements, with another 400 no longer being separately evaluated for investments).

2. Reducing bank branches in LMI areas: Raising the classification threshold for large banks six-fold to $10 billion
eliminates for a total of 417 banks the service test that currently examines the distribution, opening, and closing of
bank branches and whether they are adequately accessible to LMI communities. More than 5,000 branches of these
banks are located in LMI census tracts (30% of all LMI branches nationwide) and more than 4,000 of their branches
are located in majority-people-of-color census tracts (23% of all such branches) – these branches would no longer
be evaluated by this vital accountability measure. CRA's branching requirements are a primary reason that banks
have maintained the share of their branches located in LMI communities at relatively steady levels – about 24%
nationwide. With this compulsory mechanism removed, the number and share of branches maintained by affected
banks in LMI areas are likely to decline precipitously. This is particularly significant in Indian Country, where bank
branch access is already extremely limited (see Figure 1 above). Majority-Native American counties average just two
bank branches, compared with nine in rural counties generally and 27 across all counties.

3. Decreasing bank investment in Native CDFIs and non-profit organizations: Currently, some Native CDFIs and
CDFI intermediaries and a greater number of Native non-profits receive CRA-based investments from banks in the
form of grants and donations designed to support qualifying community development initiatives. Often these
investments are for general operating support to help these entities sustain and grow their operations and diversify
and expand the lending and other services they provide to meet their communities' evolving needs. Under the
existing CRA regulations, there is no cap on what the recipients of those investments can spend on indirect or
administrative costs, which in the case of Indian County gives Native entities great flexibility to tailor those dollars to
most impactfully meet their communities' distinct needs. For Native CDFIs, this notably supports the cost of staff
providing deep technical assistance to consumer, small business, and home mortgage loan clients to help them
become credit worthy and prepare them to take and make good on the loan.

The Proposed Rule, however, requires grant funds from all banks to be tied to a specific community development
project or program to receive CRA credit. It also institutes a 15% cap on indirect and administrative costs that is
bound to disincentivize large banks' investments in Native CDFIs and non-profits, particularly smaller ones who
need these investments most but whose indirect and administrative costs comprise a larger – and under the
Proposed Rule, disqualifying – percentage of their annual operational budgets. This cap will compel Native CDFIs
and non-profits to spend more time pursuing project-specific grants from banks and less on designing and offering
critical CRA-eligible community development services, such as helping families become first-generation
homeowners and providing technical assistance to small businesses. It also will make Native CDFIs and non-profits
more vulnerable to economic downturns by making it more difficult to cover fixed overhead costs when there are
reductions in other sources of revenue.

4. Elevating bank strategic plans that will serve to reduce community development financing: The Proposed
Rule expands the ability of – and incentives for – banks to opt to be evaluated under a regulator-approved CRA
strategic plan instead of the normal CRA tests. In addition, it allows CRA regulators to coach banks on the adequacy
of their proposed strategic plan goals before public input is solicited and gathered, diminishing the importance of
the public comment process, and allows banks that fail to achieve their self-selected goals to fall back on the regular
CRA test. Meanwhile, recently the OCC issued guidance fixing annual community development loans and
investments equal to just 0.12% to 0.24% of assets as "Satisfactory" and 0.20% to 0.40% as "Outstanding,"
percentages that are significantly less than the historical medians of 0.70% for OCC-supervised banks with assets
of $30 billion or less and 0.64% for banks with assets of $1 billion or less.13 Combined, the Proposed Rule and the
OCC guidance will enable banks to commit substantially less to communities while still earning passing, or even
outstanding, CRA ratings. For example, if just 10% of banks reduced their annual activity from their historical median
level to the OCC's new 0.24% benchmark, nearly $100 million in community development financing will be lost
annually.14

5. Reducing transparency of banks' CRA performance by decreasing required small business and other
lending data: Currently under CRA, large banks generally must collect and report data on small business loans,
small farm loans, community development loans, and assessment areas, which is critical for understanding where,


how, and to what degree those banks are investing in LMI communities. Under the Proposed Rule, however, a
significant number of once-large banks will no longer be required to collect and share this data with federal
regulators. This will lead, for example, to an estimated 11% decrease nationally in CRA small business lending data,
with particularly large losses in rural states (see Figure 1 above for the projected data reductions in key states that
are of particular importance to Native CDFIs and Tribal Nations). Losing CRA data from regional and community
banks will make it harder for Native CDFIs, Tribal Nations, and their advocates to: (1) determine which banks are
lending in Indian Country, where, and in what amounts; (2) compare banks' institutional commitments to Indian
Country; (3) identify credit gaps; and (4) demonstrate unmet needs during CRA exams, mergers, or community-
benefit negotiations. The data loss will be especially significant in rural Western and Plains states where smaller
banks make up a larger share of the banking market.

6. Lessening the impact of CRA-qualifying dollars by diluting the definition of "economic development": Under
the current CRA regulations governing economic development, an activity must generally satisfy both a size test and
a purpose test, including showing that it creates, retains or improves jobs for LMI people, benefits LMI areas, or works
through qualifying intermediaries. However, the Proposed Rule weakens this standard for earning CRA credit for
economic development activities by eliminating the purpose test – meaning banks will be able to receive CRA credit
without proving that the business financing they are providing actually creates, preserves or improves jobs for LMI
people or communities. For example, a bank could now receive CRA credit for financing a limited liability company
(LLC) established by a wealthy business owner in an upper-income census tract, even if the business creates no jobs
for low- and moderate-income people – which is wholly contrary to the CRA's original intent. Specific to Indian
Country, this would directly harm the employment prospects of Tribal citizens as Tribal and non-Tribal businesses
reliant on CRA-qualified start-up or growth capital that are located in or near Native communities or otherwise
dependent on Native labor would no longer be attractive to banks for CRA purposes.

7. Disincentivizing bank investments in critically needed infrastructure projects in LMI people and
communities: Currently, bank investments in infrastructure projects in an LMI area typically will only receive CRA
credit when they work to retain or attract residents or businesses to that area. The Proposed Rule weakens this LMI
accountability measure by enabling banks to get credit for such projects that benefit or serve a targeted area, even
when they produce few if any meaningful benefits for LMI residents or the community writ large. This means banks
could get CRA credit for infrastructure projects that primarily benefit affluent communities or private companies at
the expense of LMOI people and communities. For Indian Country, this would actively suppress place-based
infrastructure development, which is the prerogative of Tribal Nations and Native communities, and ensure reduced
opportunities for Tribal Nations and Native CDFIs to attract private financing for desperately needed large-scale
infrastructure projects that benefit not just Tribal but also surrounding communities.

Our Joint Positions on Specific Questions Posed in the Proposed Rule

Question 55: Are there alternative approaches the agencies should consider to encourage banks to meet the credit
needs of Indian country and other Tribal and native lands? For example, should the agencies use the definition of
Native Lands in the 2023 CRA rules? Are there any difficulties or unintended consequences that banks might
encounter with the definitions as proposed?

Yes, if the FDIC and OCC ultimately decide to advance this Proposed Rule to finalization, it should be substantively
overhauled to integrate the key provisions contained in the 2023 CRA Final Rule15 explicitly designed to increase
bank investment in Tribal Nations and Native communities. These include:

1. The 2023 rule's conferral of automatic, enhanced CRA credit for a bank's entire loan, grant, investment, or
service if it involves a Treasury-certified Native CDFI.16 It is critical that this automatic credit not be abridged or
limited in any way by any other, potentially conflicting provisions contained within the FDIC and OCC's Final Rule.



2. Its establishment of "Native Land Areas" (NLAs) as a stand-alone CRA place-based category investment
area and, critically, its additional consideration for branches and further incentivizing community
development activity benefiting Native communities. As referenced above on pages 1-3, "Indian country" and
"other Tribal and Native lands" exhibit significant disparities in access to capital and bank services. For example,
the National Community Reinvestment Coalition recently found that the average census tract on Tribal land
received just five small business loans, compared to 82 such loans made on average in non-Tribal tracts.17 The OCC
and FDIC acknowledge that "communities in Indian country or other Tribal and native lands face significant and
unique CD [community development] challenges", but their proposed rule's approach to addressing those
challenges falls short in comparison to the 2023 CRA Final Rule.18 The OCC and FDIC are currently offering to include
"Indian country or other Tribal and native lands" as an eligible geography under the revitalization and stabilization
category of community development, but the 2023 CRA Final Rule took it a critical step further by awarding
additional qualitative consideration for bank branches on Native Lands and creating an impact and responsiveness
factor for community development activities that "benefits or serves residents of Native Land Areas" (see below).19
CRA performance evaluations under the 2023 rule would have included how much of a bank's community
development activities fit into each impact and responsiveness factor, creating a meaningful incentive for banks to
pursue community development in Native Lands and other high-need areas so as to avoid having nothing to report
in specific categories.20 The 2023 rule also would have made it easier for banks to pursue community development
financing outside of their branch networks by not requiring banks to first demonstrate they have adequately served
their assessment areas and instead to weight activities inside and outside facility-based assessment areas based
on where a bank lends and takes deposits.21 Given these factors, we request the OCC and FDIC use the 2023 rule's
definition of Native land areas as it is more comprehensive.22 This definition also should be expanded to cover the
formal service areas of certified Native CDFIs that fall outside of these lands.

3. Its inclusion of CDFIs and NLAs among the CRA's impact and responsiveness review factors (in the 2023 Final
Rule, two of the 12 factors considered in evaluating the impact and responsiveness of a bank's community
development loan, investment, or service was whether it (1) "supports a...CDFI, excluding certificates of deposit
with a term of less than one year" and (2) "benefits or serves residents of Native Land Areas").

NCN and our co-signatories also believe the Proposed Rule should be amended to require banks, as part of their
CRA evaluations, to collect and report data on their community development financing activities in "Indian country"
and "Other Tribal and native lands" and with entities such as Native CDFIs and tribal governments that serve
American Indian, Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian communities. The agencies should publicly share that data
with Native CDFIs, tribal governments, and other key Indian Country stakeholders annually, and should also annually
provide to these groups an updated longitudinal analysis of CRA-qualified community development financing
activity trends within those lands and involving American Indians, Alaska Natives, and Native Hawaiians.

Furthermore, banks should be required to collect and report data as part of their CRA evaluations that documents
where within "Indian country" and "Other Tribal and native lands" their CRA-qualified activities took place (specific
geographic location, whether an activity took place on Tribal trust land or non-trust land, etc.). This disaggregated
data will enable Native CDFIs, Tribal governments, and other key Indian Country stakeholders to evaluate the true
commitment of a particular bank in practice to invest in the most underserved and under-resourced parts of Indian
Country and hold those banks who are not living up to the spirit of the CRA accountable.

Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less than $30 billion as a threshold for
certain supervisory approaches, such as being considered a community bank or being subject to the continuous
examination process, should the agencies consider adjusting the intermediate bank asset size threshold to include
all banks with an asset size of less than $30 billion that do not qualify as small banks? If the agencies establish $30
billion as the appropriate threshold to delineate between intermediate banks and large banks, should the agencies
also adopt a larger threshold for small banks, such as the $10 billion currently proposed as the intermediate bank
threshold?



No. We categorically oppose the proposal to adjust "the intermediate bank asset size threshold to include all banks
with an asset size of less than $30 billion that do not qualify as small banks," as we oppose the Proposed Rule's
raising of the asset threshold size for large banks to $10 billion. We also, therefore, categorically oppose the ensuing
proposal to "adopt a larger threshold for small banks, such as the $10 billion currently proposed as the intermediate
bank threshold." If the $30 billion threshold was adopted, it would jeopardize over $26 billion in community
development loans and $267 million in investments per year, while 42 states would have their number of banks with
local community development requirements cut in half or more, and 21 states would lose two thirds of the banks
currently required to reinvest in local community development under CRA.

Question 9: Are there alternative standards the agencies should consider relying on in the context of limiting indirect
costs for CD grants? Do the proposed guardrails do enough to ensure the majority of grant and donation funds go
directly towards benefiting the bank's assessment area(s)?

As discussed in detail in point #3 on page 5 of this comment letter, the agencies should remove this problematic
provision from the Proposed Rule altogether, as it will significantly harm the ability of Native CDFIs and non-profits
to secure bank investments that will help them meet the distinct needs of their service communities.

Question 10: As an alternative, should the agencies eliminate all grants and donations from CRA consideration?

No. Grants and donations currently constitute an important sources of CRA-qualifying support for LMI communities
and the organizations that serve them, and they should be retained as pathways for achieving CRA credit.

Question 25: Should the agencies retain the requirement that the activity create, improve, or retain jobs for LMI
individuals or in an LMI area in the first category of economic development?

Yes, for the reasons outlined in points #6 and #7 on page 6 of this comment letter.

Question 30: Are there other programs that should be presumed to promote economic development, such as
programs that support Indian country residential development? Alternatively, should these activities be presumed
to qualify as community development but instead be considered as a revitalization and stabilization activity that
helps to attract or retain businesses or residents (see discussion of revitalization and stabilization activities below)?

Programs that support Indian country residential development should be presumed to promote economic
development and community development under CRA guidelines, as should any other bank lending and
investments in Tribal Nations, Native communities, Native CDFIs, and Native non-profit organizations.

Conclusion

On the whole, the Proposed Rule will serve to greatly weaken CRA's accountability to Indian Country when it so
desperately needs to be strengthened. The CRA is one of many vehicles through which the federal government can
and should fulfill its eternal trust and treaty obligations to Tribal Nations, their citizens, and, by extension, Native
entities like CDFIs that serve and support them. Any changes to the regulations governing CRA, therefore, should be
formulated in partnership with them through meaningful, ongoing consultation, and should be precisely designed
to shift the calculus for banks to prioritize lending and investment – directly and through intermediaries like Native
CDFIs – in Tribal Nations and Native communities as opposed to the status quo of considering such lending and
investment as a luxury or last resort.

NCN is deeply committed to supporting Native CDFIs' collective mission of creating ample and fair access to capital
and resources for Native people, primarily those in LMI communities. That mission aligns with the enduring spirit of
the CRA, which includes addressing fairness and access to credit for homeownership, small business development,
infrastructure development projects, and other wealth-building activities in Native communities.



We look forward to continuing to engage directly with the FDIC and OCC to ensure that any new CRA regulations
fully – and finally – incentivize substantially increased investments by banks in Tribal Nations and Native
communities across this country.

Dear Comptroller and FDIC Leadership:
On behalf of NeighborWorks Waco, I am writing to oppose provisions of the proposed
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations that could weaken incentives for financial
institutions to invest in low- and moderate-income communities and partner with nonprofit
community development organizations.
NeighborWorks Waco expands access to affordable housing, sustainable homeownership,
financial education, counseling, and economic opportunity throughout Waco, McLennan
County, and Central Texas. We have received funding from financial institutions for
preservation of our rental units, development of rental units and funding to assist families
purchasing a home for this first time as well as grant funding that support our work.
CRA has helped create the conditions for banks to provide mortgage, construction, permanent,
and community development financing and to consider the full needs of a transaction—not
only its conventional return. CRA consideration can help bring financial institutions to the table
when an affordable housing transaction is difficult, layered, smaller in scale, or dependent on
flexible terms. In our market, that engagement is often essential to moving a project or a family
from readiness to closing.
Bank support extends beyond lending. Grants and investments help fund homebuyer
education, financial counseling, down payment and closing cost assistance, technology,
reporting, and program delivery. These resources allow NeighborWorks Waco to prepare
borrowers, manage public and private funds responsibly, and remain involved when a
transaction requires additional time or coordination.

If CRA incentives are reduced, banks may have less reason to participate in complex affordable
housing transactions, provide grants, offer patient or flexible capital, or invest in nonprofit
capacity. The likely result would be fewer financing partners, larger funding gaps, longer
development timelines, fewer families reaching homeownership, and greater difficulty
producing or preserving affordable housing in Central Texas.
The hardest capital to replace is often not standard market-rate debt. It is flexible, below-
market, patient, subordinate, or gap financing; predevelopment and acquisition capital;
construction financing suited to affordable projects; equity-like investments; and grants that
can support services, operating costs, and transaction expenses that other sources will not
cover. Losing these tools can make otherwise viable projects infeasible.
Operating support and nonprofit capacity are equally important. Affordable housing and
homeownership programs require qualified staff, sound financial management, compliance
systems, technology, reporting, counseling, and long-term stewardship. These are not
incidental administrative expenses; they are the infrastructure that protects families, lenders,
investors, and public resources. Without adequate capacity, nonprofits cannot assemble
layered financing, manage risk, meet regulatory obligations, or sustain effective programs.
We are therefore concerned that placing greater emphasis on lending volume could reduce
incentives for grants, community development investments, technical assistance, and flexible
capital. We urge the OCC and FDIC to preserve strong CRA consideration for affordable
housing development, rehabilitation, and preservation; affordable mortgage and community
development lending; down payment and closing cost assistance; homebuyer and financial
education; nonprofit grants and investments; capacity-building; technical assistance; and
programs serving low- and moderate-income families and communities.
We also urge the agencies to carefully consider changes to bank asset thresholds. Community
and regional banks are important partners in Central Texas. Reducing regulatory burden should
not come at the expense of meaningful investment in the communities CRA was designed to
serve.
CRA should continue to ensure that financial institutions meet the credit and community
development needs of their entire communities, particularly low- and moderate-income
families and neighborhoods. Any modernization or simplification should strengthen—not
weaken—the incentives for banks to lend, invest, provide grants, share expertise, and build
durable community partnerships.

For these reasons, NeighborWorks Waco respectfully opposes provisions that could diminish

Dear OCC and FDIC staff:

typeA/planB works with banks and community development organizations to deliver technical assistance to small businesses, including through technology platforms that document beneficiary eligibility and program activity at the time the activity occurs. We write to support four elements of the proposed rule and to answer several of the agencies' feedback questions.

1. The community development activity confirmation process (proposed §__.13(b)). We strongly support codifying an optional confirmation process. Small-business technical assistance is increasingly delivered through channels the 1995 framework never contemplated, and banks reasonably decline to build or fund innovative programs when eligibility can only be learned at examination. A confirmation process usable "primarily for novel potential CD activities" is exactly the right tool. In response to Question 32: yes — a bank should retain the notification of eligibility until completion of its next CRA examination, and for balance-sheet activities, for the period the activity remains on the bank's books. In response to Question 33: yes — the agencies should set an outer limit on extensions; an additional 30 days, specified in the agency's notification, is appropriate.

2. The illustrative list (proposed §__.13(a)). We support codifying a public, non-exhaustive list, and we ask the agencies to include an explicit example recognizing that technical assistance to small businesses may be delivered through digital platforms and tools, not only in person. The proposed economic development definition already covers "[t]echnical assistance and supportive services, such as shared space, technology, or administrative assistance" for size-eligible businesses; stating on the list that such assistance may be technology-delivered would prevent the list from unintentionally chilling the most scalable delivery channel — the concern the agencies themselves flagged about list-driven conservatism.

3. Eliminating the purpose test for economic development (Questions 27–29). We support the proposal. The subjective purpose test has historically diverted bank resources into after-the-fact narrative reconstruction rather than service delivery. Replacing it with objective criteria — activity type plus the SBA size standards or the $1 million gross-annual-revenue threshold — makes eligibility administrable and auditable. In response to Question 28, we are not aware of activities that would newly qualify that should be excluded; the size standards are a sound outer boundary. We encourage the agencies to pair the objective test with a clear expectation that banks retain documentation of business size eligibility and activity type, so that examinations remain verifiable without reintroducing subjectivity.

4. Community development grant accountability (proposed §__.13(e) and related documentation requirements). We support the direct-use requirement, the 15 percent indirect-cost limitation calculated consistent with the OMB Uniform Guidance, and the requirement that large banks obtain written commitments and attestations from grant recipients. Grant-funded technical assistance delivered by nonprofit intermediaries is one of the most responsive channels for reaching small businesses; requiring recipient-level documentation will professionalize that channel rather than burden it, and tooling to produce such documentation already exists.

We appreciate the agencies' work to provide greater clarity on CRA consideration and would welcome the opportunity to discuss these comments.

Respectfully submitted,

The GroundBreak Coalition is a first-in-the-nation economic development initiative working to
mobilize $5.4 billion in the Minneapolis-Saint Paul region to close wealth gaps, build a more
equitable financial system, and revitalize our regional economy. In partnership with banks,
community development financial institutions (CDFIs), foundations, and nonprofits,
GroundBreak has an ambitious plan over the next 10 years to reach 11,000 new homeowners,
5,000 businesses, and 60 neighborhood developments.

To date, GroundBreak has deployed over $17.3 million in flexible capital through its regional
loan pools, unlocking over $100 million from banks for 399 new homeowners, 56 early- and
growth-stage businesses, and seven neighborhood developments.

Investment trends show 1930s federal lending policy is still impacting communities
The CRA has made a significant difference by ensuring people and communities historically
underserved by financial systems have access to capital from regulated financial institutions and
through CDFIs that receive loans from regulated financial institutions.


Current regulations have served as a bedrock for helping communities access financing for
homeownership, small businesses, and property ownership, as well as affordable housing
production.

However, many low- and moderate-income Minnesotans are still facing significant barriers to
financial access, especially in places historically affected by discriminatory lending practices.
GroundBreak's data shows that even though our work to remove financial barriers is currently
focused on underinvested people and places across the seven-county metropolitan area, families
and entrepreneurs are leveraging GroundBreak investments in specific neighborhoods.

When mapped together, 55 percent of GroundBreak's financial products for homeownership,
businesses, and developments are landing in the same handful of ZIP codes in North
Minneapolis, East St. Paul and Midway, Brooklyn Park, Brooklyn Center, and Fridley that
federal lending policy graded "hazardous" in the 1930s. This is the result of financial products
following the same unmet demand today.

Strong federal regulations are still needed today. We urge the agencies to uphold the legislative
intent of the Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 by preserving meaningful community
development requirements to help ensure banks meet the credit needs of low- and
moderate-income Americans.

Raising bank-size thresholds threatens economic progress and growth
