communities that depend on the partnership between CDFIs and banks for capital.

2 NCRC.

The HomeOwnership Center, a program of County Corp, submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)   because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).  

The HomeOwnership Center is a HUD-approved housing counseling agency that has operated in the Dayton-Springfield, OH MSA for nearly 25 years.  

We are concerned about the proposal’s treatment of community development grants and nonprofit organizations.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.  For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.

The HomeOwnership Center (HOC) has seen firsthand the role that bank grants and partnerships can play in supporting community development. This funding provides a critical gap funding for housing counseling services to be able to continue between government contract and grant agreements.  For example, HOC has been waiting for HUD to award its FY25 Comprehensive Housing Counseling funding.  The NOFO for the grant was issued in March 2026.  On September 25, 2026, the Trump administration enacted a pocket appropriation rescission of the funding.  In the meantime, HOC has been maintaining its HUD-required client management software, along with HUD’s quality assurance protocols necessary for a HUD-approved housing counseling agency.  Our current grant funding is covering a considerable administrative cost burden while assisting with the country’s national objectives of addressing American’s housing needs.  Attached is a letter from one of our community partners regarding the impact that the HomeOwnership Center has on her work.  
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond the banks themselves.

The HomeOwnership Center believes that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

On behalf of the members of the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) Working Group, we

the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) published by the Office of the Comptroller of the

Working Group are participants in the affordable housing community from a variety of
stakeholder perspectives who work together to help resolve technical LIHTC policy issues and
provide recommendations to make the LIHTC even more efficient in delivering benefits to help
build and preserve affordable housing and serve low-income residents. Our group includes
nonprofit and for-profit developers, syndicators, investors, lenders, lawyers and other affordable
housing professionals. Moreover, we represent a number of banks that invest in LIHTC equity
annually, for which the CRA is a crucial incentive. According to the Affordable Housing Tax Credit
Coalition, the LIHTC equity market in 2025 was estimated at about $29 billion, of which about
71% were attributed to CRA-motivated financial institutions.
Summary of Recommendations

To preserve CRA's effectiveness in encouraging LIHTC investment, the LIHTC Working Group
respectfully recommends that the Agencies:
 Response to the Community Reinvestment Act NPR
October 13, 2026


2

•
Adopt a large-bank threshold no higher than $3.252 billion. If the Agencies retain the
proposed $10 billion threshold, preserve a distinct and meaningful investment
component for banks between the current large-bank threshold and $10 billion;
•
Give community development performance meaningful and separately identifiable
weight in the overall CRA rating of an intermediate bank;
•
Expressly confirm that direct and indirect ownership interests in LIHTC funds,
partnerships, limited liability companies, and similar entities, including legally binding
commitments to acquire those interests, are eligible community development
investments when the underlying activities otherwise qualify;
•
Confirm that banks may use documented written allocation agreements and other
reasonable, consistently applied methodologies to attribute investments among
assessment areas without case-by-case uncertainty;
•
Provide a clear and predictable pathway for CRA consideration of qualifying LIHTC
investments outside a bank's assessment areas, particularly in rural and underserved
markets; and
•
Consider the combined effect of CRA incentives and regulatory capital requirements on
banks' capacity and willingness to invest in LIHTC equity and, consistent with the
LIHTC Working Group's recommendations in the Basel III capital rulemaking comment
letter, support a more risk-sensitive capital framework that reduces the risk weight
applicable to LIHTC equity investments from 100 percent to 20 percent to better reflect
their demonstrated performance and risk characteristics.

CRA Is a Material Driver of Bank Demand for LIHTC Equity

Ever since the promulgation of the revised CRA regulations in 1995, the CRA has helped make the
LIHTC the most successful affordable rental housing production and preservation incentive in the
nation's history. The LIHTC is the most important source of capital for affordable rental housing
finance, annually financing virtually all newly constructed or substantially rehabilitated
affordable rental housing since its inception. From 1987 through 2025, the LIHTC has generated
more than $280 billion in equity investment, financed 4.28 million affordable rental homes, and
housed nearly 10 million low-income households, according to data from the National Council of
State Housing Agencies (NCSHA) and analysis from the National Association of Home Builders
(NAHB). It has also supported the creation of more than 7.2 million jobs for one year, generated
more than $815 billion in wages & business income, and spurred more than $293 billion in tax
revenue.
Not only does the LIHTC have a strong record of economic impact, it also targets the lowest
income households. According to HUD's latest LIHTC Tenant Report, the median LIHTC
household earned less than $19,000 annually. Furthermore, more than 57% of the households
earned at or below 30% of the area median income (AMI), and more than 72% earned at or below
40% AMI.
 Response to the Community Reinvestment Act NPR
October 13, 2026


3

Despite this tremendous record of achievement, there are more than 12 million low-income
renters nationwide that are severely cost-burdened, i.e., paying more than 50 percent of their
income on rent, according to Harvard's Joint Center on Housing Studies (JCHS) State of the
Nation's Housing report. While those at the bottom of the income spectrum—nearly 83% of
renters with incomes at or below $15,000 are severely cost burdened—fare the worst, those cost
burdens are increasingly affecting middle-income renters, with a 10% increase in the incidence of
cost burdens among renters with incomes between $30,000 and $45,000. Given this rental
affordability crisis, and as the premier resource for affordable rental housing production, we
cannot afford to reduce LIHTC investment by reducing the CRA incentive for affordable housing
investment and lending.
While we believe the proposed regulatory framework as outlined in the NPR represents an
improvement over the regulations published by the OCC in June 2020, we are concerned that if
the NPR is acted upon without significant changes, the LIHTC and affordable rental housing
production and preservation could be harmed, and urge you to make changes to the NPR to ensure
that the CRA continues to robustly support affordable rental housing production and preservation
through the LIHTC. We believe our comments and suggestions, if incorporated into your proposal,
will ensure the CRA continues to support and possibly increase LIHTC investment and the
affordable rental housing production and preservation it finances to address the nation's growing
rental housing crisis.
In July 2025, Congress voiced its support for increased LIHTC investment by permanently
increasing 9% LIHTC allocations by 12% and lowering the private activity bond financing
threshold from 50% to 25% of land and building costs, which Novogradac estimates will finance
1.22 million more affordable rental homes over a decade than otherwise would have been possible.
As a result, Novogradac's estimate of the 2027 newly minted LIHTC allocations is at least $37
billion. At a median LIHTC equity price of 82 cents per LIHTC dollar, which was the approximate
median LIHTC equity price in 2026,1 that would result in $30.3 billion of LIHTC equity in 2027.
If CRA regulations were to diminish the incentive for banks to invest in LIHTC equity, the efficacy
of the newly authorized LIHTC to finance affordable rental housing would be significantly
diminished.
Preserving CRA Incentives Is Essential to Sustaining LIHTC Investment
and Addressing the Affordable Housing Shortage
The nation continues to face a severe shortage of affordable rental housing. According to the Joint
Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University, the number of homes renting for less than
$1,000 per month, adjusted for inflation, declined by more than 7 million between 2014 and 2024.
The National Low Income Housing Coalition likewise reports a shortage of more than 7 million
homes that are affordable and available to extremely low-income renters. These conditions
underscore the importance of preserving regulatory policies that support the private investment
needed to finance affordable rental housing.

1 See https://www.novoco.com/resource-centers/affordable-housing-tax-credits/lihtc-equity-pricing-trends
 Response to the Community Reinvestment Act NPR
October 13, 2026


4


Congress recently increased the capacity of banks to make public welfare investments, including
LIHTC investments, by raising the public welfare investment cap from 15 percent to 20 percent
in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Regional banks are among the institutions best
positioned to use this additional authority. The CRA regulations should reinforce, rather than
diminish, the incentive for those institutions to deploy that capacity in support of affordable
housing.

Maintaining a broad and diverse investor base is also critical to the efficient operation of the
LIHTC market. Competition among investors supports stronger equity pricing, thereby increasing
the amount of private capital generated by each LIHTC allocation and reducing the amount of
other financing required to complete a development. Stronger pricing can also make financially
marginal developments feasible and allow limited LIHTC resources to support additional
affordable housing production.

Given these circumstances, we are concerned that the proposed rule would materially weaken
CRA incentives for regional-bank investment in the LIHTC. The proposal would raise the large-
bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion in assets. As a result, hundreds of OCC- and
FDIC-supervised banks that are currently evaluated under a separate investment test as part of
the three-part large-bank CRA test would instead be evaluated under the intermediate-bank
community development test, which would permit a bank to satisfy its community development
obligation entirely through community development loans. The Agencies also request comment
on alternative thresholds of $3.252 billion and $30 billion. To evaluate the likely effect of each
threshold on the LIHTC market, the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC) surveyed
LIHTC syndicators. As discussed below, the survey results provide market-based evidence
regarding both the amount of private capital and the number of active LIHTC investors associated
with each threshold. We urge the Agencies to consider this evidence carefully and to adopt a
threshold that preserves a meaningful incentive for banks to make LIHTC equity investments.
The Proposed $10 Billion Threshold Would Remove the Investment Test
for 376 Banks

Under the proposal, 376 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks currently classified as large would
move to the intermediate bank framework and would no longer be subject to a separate
investment test. The Agencies identify 126 OCC-supervised banks and 250 FDIC-supervised
banks in this category. The AHTCC survey captured more than 108 active LIHTC investors from
banks within the affected asset range. Those banks invested at least $1.595 billion in LIHTC equity
during the five-year survey period. Extrapolated to the full syndicated market, the corresponding
five-year amount is approximately $2.0 billion.

These institutions are not incidental participants in the LIHTC market. Regional banks frequently
invest through multi-investor funds alongside larger institutions. Their commitments can help
complete fund raises that deploy capital across multiple properties and markets and, by sharing
exposure across a broader investor pool, can support additional participation by larger
institutions, broadening the reach of LIHTC investments. Because multi-investor funds often
 Response to the Community Reinvestment Act NPR
October 13, 2026


5

limit each investor's share of the fund, the loss of one investor cannot always be replaced dollar-
for-dollar by other investors, meaning the departure of community and regional banks can reduce
the overall amount of equity a fund is able to raise, with effects that can extend beyond the banks
directly affected by the proposed threshold change.
A $3.252 Billion Threshold Would Preserve More LIHTC Investment Than the
$10 Billion or $30 Billion Alternatives

The Agencies requested comment on alternative large bank thresholds of $3.252 billion and $30
billion. AHTCC survey data show that the choice among these thresholds would have materially
different implications for both the number of banks investing in the LIHTC and the amount of
LIHTC equity investment implicated.

Applying the $3.252 billion threshold instead of the proposed $10 billion threshold reduces the
number of affected banks investing in the LIHTC over the survey period from more than 108 to
40, a reduction of approximately 63 percent.

The distribution of investment within the affected range is also concentrated above $3.252 billion.
AHTCC survey data show that approximately 86 percent of LIHTC equity investment from OCC-
and FDIC-regulated banks with consolidated assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion comes
from banks with assets above $3.252 billion. Accordingly, the associated estimated five-year
LIHTC equity impact declines from approximately $2.0 billion under the proposed $10 billion
threshold to $272 million under the $3.252 billion alternative.

The $3.252 billion alternative would have a significantly less damaging impact on
LIHTC investment by leaving the separate investment test in place for banks
representing a much larger share of the LIHTC equity.

The $3.252 billion figure also has a distinct historical basis in the CRA framework. It is the
inflation-adjusted equivalent of the OCC's 2020 $2.5 billion threshold, which was calibrated to
preserve the relative shares of banks classified as small and intermediate.

The Agencies also requested comment on a $30 billion large bank threshold, which AHTCC survey
results show could significantly reduce LIHTC investments. The survey captured more than 140
banks with consolidated assets between $1.65 billion and $30 billion that invested at least $3.575
billion over the five-year survey period. Extrapolated to the full syndicated market, that amount
is approximately $4.5 billion, more than twice the amount associated with the proposed $10
billion threshold and roughly 16 times the amount associated with the $3.252 billion alternative.

Recurring direct LIHTC investment is concentrated among banks with more than $30 billion in
consolidated assets. Direct LIHTC investment by banks with less than $30 billion in assets is
generally made on a one-off basis, while direct investments facilitated through syndicators may
already be reflected in the LIHTC Working Group survey responses, providing a high degree of
confidence in the representative coverage of this sample.

The LIHTC Working Group strongly encourages the Agencies to adopt a lower large bank
threshold in order to minimize the loss of a significant number of investors and their associated
investments from the LIHTC market who would no longer be subject to a separate investment
test. To the extent that the CRA requirements related to the investment test will change for certain
banks, the $3.252 billion large bank threshold would be significantly less damaging to the LIHTC
than the $10 billion threshold, which is also significantly less damaging than the proposed
alternative $30 billion threshold.
Regional Banks Provide Disproportionate LIHTC Investment in Rural and
Small Metropolitan Markets

In addition to the number of banks affected and the amount of their investments in the LIHTC,
the geographic distribution of investment is especially relevant to the threshold discussion. Our
survey found that community and regional banks direct a disproportionately high share of their
investments to rural areas, which could be diminished if these banks lose the current incentives
to invest in the LIHTC.

For the analysis of impacts in rural areas, the AHTCC survey was able to identify geographic
investment activity for a subset representing 54.9 percent of the LIHTC equity reported by survey
respondents providing bank-level data. Within that subset, approximately one-third of LIHTC
equity from OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks with assets between $412 million and $10 billion
supported rural markets during 2021 through 2024. By comparison, 8.1 percent of LIHTC equity
in a CohnReznick industry-wide sample during the same period was invested in USDA-defined
nonmetro counties. Although the two measures are not identical, the contrast is directionally
significant and indicates that community and regional banks in the affected asset range account
for a comparatively large share of investment in rural markets.

This pattern is consistent with how the LIHTC market operates. Community and regional banks
often have business relationships and market knowledge in smaller communities. Maintaining a
broad and deep investor base therefore matters not only for aggregate equity demand but also for
the geographic distribution of that demand.

As stated above, the LIHTC Working Group encourages the Agencies to adopt a lower large bank
threshold so that these community and regional banks retain the incentive to make investments
in the LIHTC, particularly in underserved rural areas.
Clarify That LIHTC Ownership Interests and Written Allocation
Agreements Remain Eligible for CRA Consideration
The proposed rule comes up with a new definition of "community development investment" which
now pivots off of "security" as defined by the SEC. At 91 Fed. Reg. 52128, the agencies propose
to define a community development investment as a security, or a deposit or membership share
in a financial institution, that meets the other specified requirements. The preamble says "security"
broadly includes equity investments and debt instruments such as bonds, and cites the definitions
 Response to the Community Reinvestment Act NPR
October 13, 2026


7

in the Securities Act of 1933 and Securities Exchange Act of 1934. It also says loans would be
considered under the applicable CRA lending tests rather than as community development
investments.

LIHTC investments. A low-income housing tax credit is itself a tax benefit for a bank, not the
instrument the bank purchases. Banks generally obtain LIHTCs through an ownership interest in
a partnership or LLC that owns the housing, directly or through a fund. Such an interest may
qualify as a security, but the proposed text does not expressly identify LIHTC partnership or LLC
interests. The agencies should confirm that these interests, including interests in LIHTC funds,
remain eligible community development investments when the other requirements are met.

The agencies should clarify that the proposed definition of a community development investment
preserves CRA consideration for banks' investments in funds, limited partnerships, limited
liability companies, and similar entities that finance qualifying community development activities.
These structures are central to financing projects involving Low-Income Housing Tax Credits,
New Markets Tax Credits, Historic Tax Credits, and renewable energy tax credits. A bank
generally invests in an entity or fund; the tax credit is a benefit associated with that investment,
not itself the security the bank acquires. The proposed definition's reference to a "security" should
expressly encompass direct and indirect ownership interests in these entities, including interests
acquired through multi-investor funds and legally binding commitments to acquire them.
Eligibility would continue to depend on whether the underlying activity has a primary purpose of
community development and satisfies the rule's other requirements. The preamble's broad
description of equity investments is helpful, but express clarification in the final rule would give
banks and their community development partners greater certainty.
-----
The other issue pertains to side letters and whether they can continue to be used. The proposal's
geographic allocation provisions are in proposed § 25.13(d) for OCC-supervised banks and the
corresponding FDIC provision. Under § 25.13(d)(3), a bank may use a reasonable methodology,
subject to agency approval, for allocating community development financing among multiple
assessment areas. The preamble specifically asks whether additional examples of reasonable
methodologies should be provided.

The LIHTC Working Group requests the Agencies provide explicit confirmation that banks may
continue to rely on written allocation agreements, including side letters with community
development investment funds, to establish the geographic attribution of qualifying investments
to individual bank investors, provided that the same investment is not improperly claimed by
multiple banks and the allocation is supported by appropriate documentation.
Give Community Development Performance Distinct Weight in Intermediate-
Bank CRA Ratings

The proposal would also change how intermediate bank CRA performance is combined into an
overall rating. Under the current intermediate small bank framework, a bank generally must
receive at least a Satisfactory rating on both the lending test and the community development test
to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. Under the proposal, stronger lending performance could
 Response to the Community Reinvestment Act NPR
October 13, 2026


8

compensate for weaker community development performance. The Agencies acknowledge that
this change may increase the relative incentive for banks to devote CRA resources to lending
activities. That change would necessarily weaken the relative incentive to devote resources to
community development activities.

That interaction becomes more consequential if substantially more banks are moved into the
intermediate bank category. LIHTC equity is a community development investment that performs
a function not supplied by additional debt. If the separate investment test no longer applies to a
bank, the structure of the community development test becomes the principal mechanism within
the CRA evaluation for recognizing the bank's investment activity. The final rule should therefore
ensure that community development performance receives meaningful and distinct weight in the
overall evaluation of intermediate banks.
Allow Predictable CRA Credit Beyond Assessment Areas to Direct Capital to
Underserved Markets

The proposal would provide additional flexibility for banks to receive CRA consideration for
qualifying community development activities outside their assessment areas after satisfying
applicable geographic standards or where performance context demonstrates that local
community development needs have been adequately addressed. The Agencies note that the
existing framework can contribute to distortions in the market known as CRA "hot spots" and
"deserts," including in rural areas where relatively few banks have a physical presence.

A framework that preserves a bank's responsibility to serve its local assessment areas while also
recognizing qualifying activity beyond those areas can broaden the pool of capital available to
communities with fewer CRA-motivated investors. In the LIHTC market, greater geographic
flexibility can also reduce localized pricing distortions. Where more investors are able to compete
for investments outside their immediate footprints, pricing can become more consistent across
markets, strengthening the efficiency of the national LIHTC market without displacing the
importance of local performance.

The proposal presents more than one method for implementing this flexibility. From the
perspective of LIHTC investment, the key consideration is that the final framework provides a
workable and predictable path for meaningful CRA consideration of qualifying community
development investments outside a bank's assessment areas. Either a qualitative or quantitative
framework can be evaluated against that objective.

The final rule should provide a clear and predictable pathway for qualifying community
development activities conducted on a broader statewide or regional basis to receive CRA
consideration. A bank that received a Satisfactory or Outstanding rating on its most recent CRA
evaluation should be presumed to have adequately served the needs of its assessment areas and
therefore be eligible to receive consideration for qualifying activities outside those areas
throughout its next examination cycle. This approach would preserve accountability for meeting
local needs while supporting sustained investment in rural and underserved communities where
 Response to the Community Reinvestment Act NPR
October 13, 2026


9

affordable housing needs and financing markets often extend beyond individual assessment-area
boundaries.
Align Bank Capital Treatment with LIHTC Risk to Support Investor Capacity and
Demand

Although separate from this rulemaking, we encourage the Agencies to consider the impact of
bank capital requirements on the capacity of regulated institutions to invest in the LIHTC. The
LIHTC Working Group has separately submitted comments regarding the capital treatment of
LIHTC investments in the Agencies' Basel III rulemaking. The historical performance and risk
characteristics of LIHTC investments are relevant to that work, and the interaction between CRA
incentives and regulatory capital requirements will influence the amount and composition of bank
demand for LIHTC equity.

The CRA proposal and the capital proposals affect different sides of that equation. Changes to
CRA requirements may reduce the incentive for some banks to invest in the LIHTC, while more
risk-sensitive capital treatment could increase banks' capacity to invest. The Agencies have
emphasized that the capital proposals are intended to better align regulatory capital with risk,
reduce burden, and better support banks' ability to deploy capital while maintaining safety and
soundness. Applying those principles to LIHTC investments could materially expand bank
capacity to supply equity to the market.

The LIHTC Working Group therefore encourages the Agencies, as they consider these related
regulatory changes, to recognize the combined effect of CRA incentives and capital requirements
on LIHTC demand. A lower risk weight that more accurately reflects the demonstrated
performance of LIHTC investments would complement the Agencies' broader deregulatory and
risk-sensitive objectives and could significantly expand banks' capacity to invest in LIHTC equity.

Conclusion

The LIHTC Working Group supports the Agencies' broader efforts to modernize bank regulations,
reduce unnecessary regulatory burden, and better tailor requirements to institutions of different
sizes and business models. Those objectives can be advanced while preserving and, where
appropriate, strengthening the incentives and capacity for private investment in affordable
housing through the LIHTC.

The CRA has been a crucial incentive for banks to invest in LIHTC equity and affordable rental
housing production and preservation since 1995, and with an appropriate revised regulatory
framework, will continue to be an essential incentive to help address the nation's affordable rental
housing crisis, one that pre-dated the pandemic and has been exacerbated by it. We urge the
agencies to carefully consider the impact of any CRA regulatory reform that may limit or harm the
incentive to invest in LIHTC and affordable rental housing.

The need for housing people can afford is higher than ever. Rents have risen 28.4% over the

and mitigate catastrophic risks. Executive orders focused on housing supply, the expansion of
the Housing Credit in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (also known as the Working Families Tax

If retained in a final rule, Enterprise believes that the operating support exclusion and overhead
cap would substantively curtail bank operating support for CDFIs and community development
corporations (CDCs), as well as for other nonprofits like housing counselors, all of which rely on
CRA-motivated bank support to build their capacity or support their overhead costs that are not
directly linked to program delivery. Rather than result in more CRA grant funds flowing into local
communities, the rule could enervate nonprofits and lead to less CD activity, rather than more.

Recognizing the Value of Intermediaries
The proposed rule, for the first time, would preclude banks from seeking CRA credit for
community development investments made in the form of grants to intermediary organizations
 7

who pass through the funding to other nonprofit organizations working on the ground on CD-
eligible activities. The rationale provided for this unprecedented change rests on a series of
assumptions that do not accord with our on-the-ground experience as an intermediary working
directly with communities and local organizations. Banks value the efficiencies and cost savings
available to them by working through intermediaries rather than making direct grants and
investments themselves.
In short, rather than discouraging investment through intermediary organizations, the final rule
should recognize their unique role in expanding the reach, effectiveness, and long-term impact
of CRA that would enable banks to support more local organizations efficiently without
duplicating the intermediary's infrastructure or weakening CRA eligibility standards.
Intermediaries like Enterprise are not barriers between banks and communities; they are the
infrastructure that helps banks reach local organizations effectively and responsibly, often
leveraging philanthropic funds to provide needed training, grants and capital, technical
assistance, and capacity-building support to create the enabling environment needed to drive
private capital to meet community needs. These efforts support critical affordable housing and
community development projects on the ground. Nonprofit intermediaries often consolidate
funding provided by multiple financial institutions (and other sources), conduct due diligence on
community organizations, and monitor performance, in addition to providing the aforementioned
technical assistance and delivery of low-cost capital.
But one example of how we work as an intermediary to magnify CD activities: Enterprise
launched the New Orleans Community Development Organization Fund in 2021 to provide
flexible operating support, technical assistance, peer learning, and collective policy support to
neighborhood-based nonprofits. The Fund illustrates a successive-funder model: early bank and
foundation support established a flexible capacity platform that later attracted additional
philanthropy and renewed bank participation, resulting in more than $2 million disbursed
through the first two phases to 12 organizations, yielding 245 homeowner and rental homes
created or preserved as a direct result of CDO Fund support. In addition to the homes created
and preserved, the funding increased organizational and project capacity. Cohort organizations
used the support to strengthen staffing and systems, advance real estate pipelines, expand
homebuyer and financial education, create eviction-prevention programming, and pursue
additional grants and capital. This added capacity has led to stronger organizations that can
participate in more complex activities that are responsive to local needs, including qualifying for
loans and equity for a new early childhood learning center with affordable housing in a formerly
vacant firehouse in New Orleans, which was rehabilitated by the NMTC.
Intermediaries also collect crucial quantitative and qualitative data from multiple projects, sites,
and partner organizations, which are used to inform and advise banks, other funders, policy
officials, and other stakeholders on best practices, future funding initiatives, and policy solutions.
Intermediaries act as the connective tissue between banks and communities they serve,
working to align banks of all sizes and in all locations with accountable and efficient
mechanisms for supporting community organizations in their assessment areas. Banks have
historically valued partnering with intermediaries precisely because of these efficiencies.
 8

Enterprise appreciates the interest of the agencies in ensuring the maximum flow of capital to
local community projects; Enterprise knows from experience the importance of having strong
community organizations execute these projects with the technical assistance and pass-through
grants provided by intermediaries. In order to ensure that such money is spent effectively and
efficiently, especially using high-quality data that intermediaries are uniquely capable of
gathering, CRA should encourage, rather than discourage, the role of nonprofit intermediaries.

Supporting LMI Communities and Areas of Unmet Needs
The agencies propose broadening the list of eligible activities in such a way that could reduce
the focus on and support for LMI communities and individuals, including offering credit for
serving households at 120% of AMI and for considering a bank's total dollar support for wide-
scale community-serving infrastructure rather than allocating credit on a pro rata basis by LMI
population if the majority of the service area is not LMI.
The agencies also discuss examples of qualifying activities that could be particularly impactful in
expanding access to affordable housing. Clarifying that financing for resilience against natural
disasters is a CRA-qualifying activity will help address the growing need to protect families and
communities from extreme weather and rising property insurance costs, and we urge the
agencies to include this in any illustrative list.
In highly cost-burdened markets, support for middle-income rental housing (with and without
public subsidy) would be considered eligible for CRA credit. The statutory focus of CRA must
remain on LMI communities and individuals (even though cost-burdens and shortages of
available housing might be significant for some middle-income families). CRA evaluations are
not the appropriate mechanism to encourage support from the banking system for capital to flow
to that segment of the market.
We support the agencies' interest in providing banks with greater certainty about the eligibility of
CD activities through illustrative lists and the ability to receive confirmation of CD activity
eligibility in advance.

Basel III
Enterprise would like to take this opportunity to reiterate comments submitted earlier this year
regarding Basel III. Enterprise urges the banking regulators to apply a risk weight of 20% to
equity investments and loans backed by Housing Credit properties, and in no case should the
 9

risk weight exceed 50%.11 Similarly, Enterprise urges federal banking regulators to change the
100% risk weight for NMTC equity investments to as low as 20% but no more than 50%.12

Conclusion
For nearly the past 50 years, the CRA has been a critical tool to direct private-sector lending
and investment to LMI individuals and communities that would otherwise be poorly served by
the banking system. Enterprise strongly encourages the agencies to partner with the Federal
Reserve to conduct joint rulemaking that would avoid regulatory arbitrage. Should the agencies
pursue a final rule based on this proposal, we urge them to maintain the asset thresholds in
their current forms, retain banks' autonomy in selecting and supporting nonprofit partners—
including intermediaries—in their community development activities, and maintain primary
purpose for community development activities as currently defined to ensure an ongoing focus
on LMI communities.
We look forward to working with the agencies and other stakeholders to address these concerns
and the others identified in our comments so that CRA can even more meaningfully support the
financing and community development needs of low- and moderate-income individuals and
communities, consistent with recent Congressional actions.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments. If you have any questions, please do not
hesitate to reach out to Max Brossy (mbrossy@enterprisecommunity.org) or me
(ajakabovics@enterprisecommunity.org).

Response to Question 8:
We urge the agencies to clarify that the proposed definition of a community development
investment preserves CRA consideration for investments in affordable housing and economic
development. Banks' investments in funds, limited partnerships, limited liability companies, and
similar entities are central to financing projects involving Housing Credits and NMTCs, as well
as equity-equivalent investments (EQ2s), preservation funds, and other real estate funds that
expressly invest in properties serving LMI households. These investments play a central role in
affordable housing and community development, but may not involve a "security" as referenced
in the proposed definition.
In Housing Credit and NMTC transactions, a bank generally invests in an entity or fund; the tax
credit is a benefit associated with that investment, not itself the security the bank acquires. The
proposed definition's reference to a "security" should expressly encompass direct and indirect
ownership interests in these entities, including interests acquired through multi-investor funds
and legally binding commitments to acquire them. Any final rule should also expressly preserve
investment consideration for qualifying EQ2s in nonprofit CDFIs and other community
development lenders, which provide deeply subordinated, long-term capital that supports
financing for community needs in the hardest to serve parts of the market. Long-standing
interagency interpretive guidance recognizes appropriately structured EQ2s that retain equity-
like characteristics as qualified investments, even if they are documented as a note or
subordinated obligation. These clarifications would carry forward existing policy.

Response to Questions 9-10:
We reiterate our strong opposition to the agencies' proposed treatment of operating grants and
indirect costs.
The proposed rule seeks to remove grants from the definition of community development
investments and place them in a separate category subject to constraints not applicable to other
activities also evaluated under the CD Investment test. In a rule intended to reduce regulatory
burdens, the separate treatment of CD grants stands apart from nearly all other proposed
changes in imposing costs (rather than savings) on banks, noting the costs will especially
impact large banks and create "secondary burdens for nonprofit organizations and community
development intermediaries."
CD grants would be ineligible for credit if designated for oft-needed general operating support,
and even for programmatic grants made by large banks, indirect costs for grant recipients would
be capped at 15% of the total grant amount. The current average overhead cost for nonprofits is
approximately 35%; slashing reimbursement for those costs by more than half would be
significantly problematic.
Grants are a critical way for nonprofits to support and maintain the necessary infrastructure for
their organizational strength and success. This allows them to be better borrowers themselves,
support better borrowers (banks' customers), and more reliably repay their loans. Complexity,
responsiveness, and innovation all require strong nonprofit counterparts to facilitate banks' CD
activities; operating support and reimbursement of overhead are two components that enable
those outcomes.
In practice, some banks have decided to exclusively provide operating grants, and not
programmatic grants, because they do not want to get involved in program or project decisions.
Typically, operating grants are comparatively small by dollar amount, but they regularly result in
an outsized impact from a qualitative perspective, as they allow nonprofits to build capacity in
order to make meaningful changes in the communities they serve.
The proposed rule states that the 15% limitation on indirect costs is based on OMB guidance on
indirect costs that are intended to serve as a floor, not a ceiling. The proposed rule, in footnote
131, clarifies that "OMB guidance guarantees a de minimis rate for indirect costs of 15 percent
to 'allow for a more reasonable and realistic recovery of indirect costs, particularly for new or
inexperienced organizations that may not have the capacity to undergo a formal rate negotiation
but still deserve to be fully compensated for their overhead costs.'"23 The intent of the OMB
guidance is that all organizations "deserve to be fully compensated for their overhead costs."
Indeed, entities that contract with or receive grants from the federal government may enter into
a negotiated indirect cost rate agreement (NICRA) under the terms of 2 CFR Part 200 to cover
their indirect costs on federal grants. Should the agencies seek consistency with the Uniform
Guidance for Federal Awards, banks' private agreements with nonprofits engaging in CD-eligible
activities should be eligible for CRA credit if an existing NICRA rate (or its methodology) is
applied.
Better yet, the agencies could reduce compliance burdens on banks and recipients as a simpler
way to ensure the majority of grant funds support community development by leaving grants

Response to Question 11:
The primary purpose standard incorporated in the existing Interagency Q&A should be
maintained. It is well understood and has been successfully implemented across banks'
activities in communities throughout the country. Should the agencies seek to incorporate
guidance into the rule, we strongly recommend adopting the language from the Interagency
Q&A and ensuring that the focus of CRA-eligible activities remains LMI individuals and
communities. Borrowing from the 2023 CRA final rule, we recommend banks receive credit for
any entire loan, investment (inclusive of a grant that facilitates organizational capacity to
construct, rehabilitate, or provide), or service that involves a Housing Credit property.
Partial credit should remain available for activities that do not meet the primary purpose
standard; we encourage the pro rata allocation of credit for large-scale economic development
activities that benefit only a minority of LMI individuals or communities rather than weaken the
primary purpose requirement for full consideration.
Relatedly, "The proposed rules would clarify that subsidized housing may have a mixed-income
component, in which case the pro rata dollar amount of the total activity would be based on the
percentage of units set aside for affordable housing to LMI individuals." The clarification should
indicate that the pro rata calculation would apply when less than 50% of the units are affordable
to LMI households. Otherwise, the primary purpose standard would apply and allow for credit for
the full activity.

Response to Questions 12-17:
Complexity, responsiveness, and innovativeness all require strong organizations for banks to
work with in deploying capital into LMI communities. The agencies should be mindful of the
impacts that changes to CD grants will have on banks' ability to successfully deploy capital for
CD lending and investment in ways that are quantitatively and qualitatively impactful in
response to demonstrated community needs.

Response to Question 18:
Increasing the supply of housing affordable to middle-income households (going up to 120% of
AMI) is unquestionably a worthwhile activity that should be supported by the financial system,
but it is largely beyond the scope of CRA and should not be automatically eligible for credit.
Moreover, the agencies have not provided supporting evidence that the reason that middle-
income housing production has declined is due to a lack of capital (particularly lending). That is
not to say that in certain circumstances—potentially in markets where capital for middle-income
housing is otherwise limited—housing affordable to middle-income households could be
considered for credit. Indeed, the Interagency Q&A expressly allows for it based on qualitative
and quantitative factors. Should the final rule include the proposed process for confirmation of
eligibility of a proposed activity, a mechanism would exist for appropriate consideration of
middle-income rental housing where appropriate.
To be clear, however, the places where CRA-motivated financial support can address markets'
failures to provide middle-income housing may not be the "high-cost areas" that the proposed
rule envisions. The proposed rule references the 2020 5-year American Community Survey
(ACS), finding that 39% of families nationally are LMI, using it as rationale for setting the "high-
cost area" threshold at 40% of a county with monthly housing costs above 30% of income.
This reasoning is flawed, however. Cost burdens reflect the ratio of housing cost to household
income, while the LMI definition is a function of income distribution (and independent of housing
cost). Using Table B25106 from the 2024 5-year ACS, we find only 41 counties nationwide
where the share of households paying 30% or more for housing is greater than 40%.24 Among
those 41 counties, the incidence of cost burden averages over 20 percentage points higher for
households earning 60%-80% of AMI than for households earning 80%-120% of AMI at the
county level. In Brazos County, TX, for example, we estimate25 that 51.2% of households
between 60%-80% of AMI are cost-burdened, compared to 32.5% of households between 80%-
120% of AMI. (When limiting the analysis to renter households in those counties, the average
difference between the two income bands increases to 26 percentage points, rather than the
18.7 percentage-point difference across all households.)

affordable workforce housing, a high-cost area with high incomes (along with high housing

costs) may support high enough rents or house prices such that middle-income housing could

middle-income households may not earn enough for new construction to be financially viable.

Response to Questions 19-20:
For the sake of clarity and consistency, Enterprise discourages the agencies from establishing a
standalone definition of high-cost areas or high-opportunity areas. The agencies should allow
banks to use extant definitions such as HUD Fair Market Rents or Small Area Fair Market
Rents, especially given the likely intersection between bank-supported lending and investment
and federal housing programs. Alignment of requirements across funding sources improves
programmatic and operational efficiencies.

Response to Questions 21-22:
Eligibility for credit consideration should be a function of the affordability of the property,
irrespective of ownership. Nonprofit status should not be an exemption from the requirements.
More generally, Enterprise recommends that the agencies adopt the definition of affordable
housing included in the 2023 final rule issued by all three banking regulators, which establishes
clear guidelines for consideration of subsidized and unsubsidized affordable housing.

Enterprise commends the agencies for including "(iii) Programs, projects, or initiatives that
assist individuals and communities with preparing for, adapting to, or withstanding natural
disasters" in the definition of Revitalization or stabilization of targeted geographies given the
vulnerability of many LMI communities and individuals to natural disasters and the
disproportionate impact that natural disasters can have on these places and populations. Bank
support for disaster preparedness is a valuable investment in communities; by preventing
damage and displacement in the first place, the public and private costs of natural disasters can
be substantially reduced.
Since so many communities across the country have been severely damaged by natural
disasters in recent years, Congress recognized the need to reform federal disaster-recovery
processes. In the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, Congress significantly reformed and
extended the reauthorization of the Community Development Block Grant – Disaster Recovery
(CDBG-DR) program. Similarly, periodically throughout the past two decades, legislation to
temporarily increase allocations of Housing Credits and NMTCs in certain disaster areas has
been introduced in Congress in order to accelerate the revitalization of destroyed communities.

rebuilding and minimize the negative impact that natural disasters have on rental markets,26 the

recovery.

policy, as discussed below. Some elements of CRA, including an illustrative list of qualifying

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Branches, Inc. submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced
above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we
also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely
consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the
analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment
deadline by 60-days.
Branches, Inc. (Branches) is a Miami-based nonprofit founded in 1973 as the urban and social justice
agency of what is now the South East District of the United Methodist Church. Today, Branches
partners with families in Miami-Dade County to build educational and financial assets, community and
hope, using a two-generation approach that serves parents and children together. Our Achieve program
provides the largest free financial coaching service in Miami; we lead the Miami VITA Free Tax
Preparation Coalition, one of the largest in the nation; and we spearhead the Bank On Miami Coalition,
which connects residents to safe, affordable bank and credit union accounts. Branches is a member of
the Community Reinvestment Alliance of Florida.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that
banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit
services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining,
disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.
1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 2
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how
regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. We
are concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely
effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment.
These concerns are acute in Florida. Analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition
indicates that the proposal's new benchmark could put approximately 85 percent of current community
development activity by the largest banks at risk, and our partners at the Community Reinvestment
Alliance of Florida estimate that bank investment in affordable housing in Florida could fall by
approximately 20 percent in the first year alone if the proposal is finalized. Philanthropy, sponsorships,
social services and small business lending that support Miami-Dade families would face similar
pressure.
BANK BRANCHES AND ACCESS TO BANKING SERVICES
By raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion, 417 banks would no longer receive the full large-bank
examination, including a separate service test that evaluates branch delivery systems and banking
services. We are concerned that approximately 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census
tracts would no longer be evaluated as part of the large-bank CRA service test under the proposal, and
more than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census tracts would also lose CRA
consideration. In 28 states, at least one-third of branches located in LMI census tracts would no longer
receive any CRA evaluation.2
The proposal would also narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service test. Today,
examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information about the costs and
features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit services, removing deposit
products such as checking and savings accounts from direct evaluation under the service test.3 As such,
examiners would no longer evaluate whether those products are affordable and responsive to community
needs even though 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are
underbanked.4 CRA review of the cost and features of deposit products has played an important role in
encouraging banks to address these disparities by providing affordable products.
Our organization works with communities where access to mainstream banking services remains a
serious concern. Many of the families we serve in Miami-Dade County rely on costly alternative
financial services to receive income and pay bills. Through our free financial coaching and the Miami
VITA Free Tax Preparation Coalition, we regularly work with low- and moderate-income working
families, including immigrant families who file taxes with Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers,
who receive paychecks and tax refunds without a safe, affordable account in which to deposit them. For
these households, a bank or credit union account with no overdraft fees and a low opening deposit is
often the first step toward saving, building credit and achieving financial stability.
2 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-
rollbacks/.
3 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,126 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
4 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-
rollbacks/.
 3
For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from access to
credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely receive income, build
savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit.
That is why Branches spearheads the Bank On Miami Coalition, part of the national Bank On movement
supported by the Cities for Financial Empowerment Fund (CFE Fund). Bank On Miami brings together
27 partner banks and credit unions with Miami-Dade County, United Way Miami and community
organizations to connect residents to Bank On certified accounts. These accounts meet the Bank On
National Account Standards, which were inspired by the FDIC's own Model Safe Accounts: they charge
no overdraft fees, require a low opening deposit, and offer debit card access, online and mobile banking,
and fee-free direct deposit and bill payment. Coalition partners also connect account holders to free
money management training.
The stakes for our clients are significant. According to the CFE Fund, the average unbanked person
spends about 5 percent of net income on unnecessary fees for alternative financial services, which can
amount to $40,000 over a lifetime, and unbanked financial counseling clients were less than half as
likely to be able to save, and over a third less likely to establish credit, as banked clients.5 CRA
examination of deposit products has been an important incentive for banks to develop and offer certified
accounts and to partner with local coalitions like ours. Many of our financial institution partners are
examined by the OCC or the FDIC, and their participation in Bank On Miami is a meaningful way they
respond to the needs of low- and moderate-income residents. If examiners no longer evaluate whether
banks offer affordable checking and savings accounts, we are concerned that the incentive to offer,
maintain and promote these accounts in Miami-Dade County will weaken, and the progress our coalition
has made will be put at risk.
We are therefore concerned that under the proposal, examiners will no longer evaluate whether banks
that are still subject to the service test offer affordable checking and savings accounts. By reducing the
importance of deposit services and branch performance in CRA evaluations, the proposal eliminates
incentives for banks to offer basic products that help unbanked and underbanked households. Before
finalizing these changes, the agencies should identify which communities would receive less scrutiny of
bank branches and services, determine whether the effects would fall disproportionately on low- and
moderate-income communities or communities of color, and explain why the changes are justified
despite those consequences.
CONCLUSION
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
●
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under
the proposal;
●
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development
activities subject to CRA evaluation;
●
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color;
5 Cities for Financial Empowerment Fund, The Bank On Movement (2022), www.cfefund.org/bankon.
 4
●
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the OCC
and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and
released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant
declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The
proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank
classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core
elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from community
organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated
regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected organizations to
evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and
provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request
that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Sincerely,
Branches, Inc.
