​



October 13, 2026

National CAPACD, along with the undersigned coalition members and partners, write in
opposition to the joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to amend their
regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) (Docket ID
OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57; RIN 3064-AG31).

We are a coalition of community-based organizations (CBOs), an intermediary, and the
country's leading organization advancing community development and advocating against
gentrification and displacement of Asian American and Pacific Islander (AA and PI)
communities. We represent and support more than 160 CBOs in advancing their local strategies
for housing and economic opportunity, and we back their efforts by advancing national policies.

Reforms to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) should focus on its core
purpose: to ensure the financial industry serves the credit needs of underinvested
and traditionally overlooked communities.
National CAPACD is concerned that the proposed revisions do not prioritize the fundamental
purpose of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). Congress enacted the CRA in 1977 to
establish an affirmative obligation on financial institutions to meet the credit needs of the
communities where they do business, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) households,
communities of color, and neighborhoods and communities that have historically been
underserved by the financial system.
It was in direct response to redlining, the historic practice of denying credit and investment to
communities, disproportionately communities of color, based on where they lived rather than
their creditworthiness. The statute's core purpose has always included addressing the history of
disinvestment in communities of color, and CRA examinations have long served as one of the
few regulatory tools requiring banks to demonstrate they are serving these communities rather
than excluding them.
The market alone does not ensure equitable access to credit and financial services. Low-income
individuals and other underinvested households face barriers to capital and financial services
that are shaped by patterns of disinvestment, unequal access to finance and credit, historic and
systemic discrimination, and segregation. Equitable access and investment allow these
traditionally overlooked families to remain housed, start and grow businesses, build wealth, and
create greater financial stability across generations. Although the CRA cannot remedy these
longstanding inequities on its own, it remains an important tool for ensuring the banking system
contributes to addressing them rather than reinforcing existing patterns of disinvestment.
 ​

The proposed rule moves the CRA framework away from this core purpose. Rather than asking
whether banks are meaningfully meeting the credit needs of disinvested communities, it reduces
the number of banks subject to meaningful community development obligations, reduces
scrutiny of branches serving historically overlooked communities, and limits engagement with
them. Notably, while the FDIC and OCC consider the proposal's effect on the population of
banks subject to CRA obligations, they do not offer a comparable analysis of how these changes
are expected to affect the actual volume of lending, investment, and services flowing to LMI
communities and communities of color. A reform of this scale, moving the framework away from
its statutory core, should provide evidence that the communities the CRA was designed to serve
will not be harmed by the changes.
The CRA should preserve a strong, community-centered framework that ensures banks
equitably invest in the communities where they operate, with particular attention to those that
have historically faced barriers to credit and financial services, such as LMI households and
communities of color.
The OCC and FDIC should not increase the asset thresholds or change
performance ratings in a manner that reduces meaningful CRA obligations for
banks serving underinvested households.
The proposal would significantly raise the asset thresholds that determine which CRA tests
apply to specific banks. The small bank threshold would rise from approximately $412 million to
under $1 billion, the intermediate bank category would apply to banks with $1-$10 billion in
assets, and the large bank threshold would rise to $10 billion from $1.649 billion. This would
substantially reduce the number of financial institutions subject to the most rigorous CRA
community development obligations, weakening the regulatory incentive for these banks to
invest in the communities CRA was intended to benefit.
According to the agencies' own analysis in the proposal, approximately 798 banks currently
classified as intermediate small banks and subject to a community development test would
become small banks under the proposed threshold and would no longer face any CD
requirements, and an additional 376 banks would move from the large-bank category, where
they are evaluated on three separately-scored tests, Lending (50 percent), Investments (25
percent), and Services (25 percent), into the intermediate category, which has a single blended
community development test (all CD loans, investments, and services examined under the same
test). Overall, the agencies estimate that approximately 79.8 percent of all banks subject to the
CRA would be classified as small banks under the proposal, meaning more than 75 percent of all
banks could be exempt from any community development test.
In addition to the threshold changes, the proposal would remove the current requirement that
intermediate banks pass both their lending test and their community development test to
receive an overall satisfactory CRA rating. Under this framework, banks could receive an overall
satisfactory rating based on lending performance alone, regardless of their performance on the
community development test. Intermediate banks that would face reduced community
 ​

development obligations under the threshold changes will have even fewer reasons to prioritize
community development activity once it is no longer necessary to achieve a passing rating.
Affordable housing developments, small business financing, community facilities, neighborhood
revitalization, and other community development activities can involve higher perceived risks,
longer time horizons, or might have lower returns than other investment opportunities. CRA
helps ensure that these activities remain part of the broader investment strategies that banks
adopt. Banks that no longer receive CRA credit for these projects may have less reason to
maintain relationships with community development organizations, participate in affordable
housing transactions, invest in community development financial institutions (CDFIs), or
provide financing for other projects and services that address the needs of LMI communities.
These proposed changes are particularly concerning because the OCC and FDIC have not shown
that the communities affected by the proposed changes have less need for community
development investment. In fact, LMI communities continue to face significant challenges
related to housing affordability, displacement, access to capital, small business development,
and neighborhood stabilization.
National CAPACD is especially concerned about the implications for smaller community-based
organizations serving low-income households and communities of color. These organizations
often lack relationships with, or access to, larger mainstream banks and more robust sources of
capital. Community development activity like affordable housing finance and investment in
economic revitalization is disproportionately concentrated in low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods because of historic redlining and ongoing disinvestment patterns and practices.
When banks have meaningful CRA obligations, community organizations have an important
avenue to engage financial institutions around unmet local needs. Weakening those obligations
can diminish both the resources available to communities and the leverage community
organizations have to advocate for investment.
The OCC and FDIC should preserve strong CRA incentives for bank investment in
Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs).
Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) are mission-driven entities that serve
low-income and underinvested communities that mainstream banks often overlook. Banks
receive CRA credit for loans, equity investments, and grants supporting operations and capacity
for CDFIs and other mission-driven financial entities. National survey data collected by
Opportunity Finance Network found that its members received nearly $6.2 billion in funding
from traditional banks in FY 2024, representing approximately 46 percent of total borrowed
funding, or around half the financing available to those surveyed.1
1 https://www.ofn.org/blog/2026-proposed-changes-to-the-community-reinvestment-act/ [OFN Annual
Member Survey FY24]
 ​

In turn, CDFIs invest capital into small businesses, affordable housing, and community facilities
in neighborhoods that banks either cannot or will not serve. CDFIs often have the flexibility,
relationships, and community knowledge necessary to highlight viable opportunities that banks
are unable to identify. This helps direct capital to the disinvested neighborhoods and
populations the CRA is created to support in ways that increase the likelihood of project success
and lower the investment risk for banks.
The CDFI Fund, which is administered by the U.S. Treasury, describes the CDFI model as
financial institutions working on a local level that know their communities the best.2 It is not
uncommon for CDFIs to be headquartered in, staffed, and governed by representatives of the
specific neighborhoods and populations they serve, giving them a depth of local knowledge,
cultural competency, and trust that traditional banks often lack.
This relationship benefits banks as well. Rather than building this local neighborhood
knowledge in-house at significant cost, a bank can invest in or lend to a CDFI and reach the
same borrowers indirectly, which they receive CRA credit for under the current framework.
CDFI capital is also leveraged, meaning banks' investments often have a multiplier effect that
increases impact. Every $1 in public funding invested generates $8 in private investment,
leading to much more robust financing and resources for important community development
projects and programs that support underinvested communities.3 Moreover, CDFIs are in
demand and have a demonstrated track record of success,4 and CDFI clients can become future
mainstream bank customers as their credit and capacity grow.
The changes to asset thresholds, the investment test, and the new operating grant structure
being proposed would result in fewer mission-driven financial institutions like CDFIs receiving
the funding and resources they need to serve the under-resourced and overlooked communities
they are well-positioned to support. As mentioned earlier, the proposed changes to the asset
thresholds mean community development obligations will either disappear or be diluted for a
significant number of banks. The proposal also calls for a new definition of "complexity" that
disadvantages equity-like investments not paired with an accompanying loan, which is not
uncommon for CDFI-supported projects and services. Restrictions on grants and donations
(discussed further below) would reduce flexible operational funding for national and regional
CDFIs and further limit the impact and reach of these important mission-driven entities.
CDFIs exist to serve markets and borrowers that conventional financial institutions have
historically underserved, like small businesses without conventional collateral or credit history,
affordable housing developers, and households or neighborhoods that banks disproportionately
overlook. This focus aligns well with the core purpose of the CRA. These mission-driven
financial institutions have deep-seated knowledge of the communities they support and provide
4
https://www.richmondfed.org/region_communities/regional_data_analysis/cdfi_survey/survey_results/cdfi_
survey_key_findings_2025
3 https://www.ofn.org/us-treasury-cdfi-fund/
2 https://www.cdfifund.gov/system/files/documents/cdfi_brochure-updated-dec2017.pdf
 ​

tailored services to meet their unique needs. Mainstream banks benefit from investing in and
building relationships with CDFIs, and finalizing a rule that could significantly reduce their
reach and impact would be harmful and short-sighted.
The OCC and FDIC should protect the CRA's role in sustaining Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) investment.
The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) is the primary tool for financing the construction
and preservation of affordable rental housing, and the CRA plays a critical role in driving
investment into LIHTC-funded projects. The Congressional Research Service confirms that
financial institutions and banks are responsible for the majority of LIHTC investment, in part
due to the favorable CRA consideration these investments receive.5 CohnReznick's 2024 LIHTC
Equity Market Volume Survey found that bank investors accounted for approximately 80
percent of total LIHTC equity surveyed that year, and one that exists in significant part because
CRA credit, not market return alone, makes LIHTC an attractive investment for banks.6
As with the impact on investment in CDFIs, the asset threshold shifts and the change in the
definition of "complexity" for the Investment Test outlined in the proposal could have a chilling
effect on LIHTC-funded affordable housing development. As discussed, a significant number of
large banks would be reclassified as intermediate under the proposal and downgraded to a
single, blended community development test, rather than the more rigorous three-test
examination for large banks. Banks can satisfy CD obligations primarily through lending under
the blended test, with little or no LIHTC investment, and still pass. The new definition of
"complexity" under the responsiveness assessment, which centralizes loan-based financing, also
disadvantages LIHTC development. A meaningful share of LIHTC investment activity consists of
standalone equity investments without an accompanying loan component, compounding the
harm caused by the proposed asset threshold changes. There are similar concerns about the
impact on development financed by New Market Tax Credits (NMTC).
Given the significant shortage of safe, affordable housing, weakening the primary financing
mechanism for affordable rental housing is short-sighted. According to the National Low
Income Housing Coalition's (NLIHC) most recent annual Gap report, the country is facing a
shortage of 7.2 million affordable and available rental homes for extremely low-income renter
households, which is only 35 affordable and available homes for every 100 households.7 Cities
and states struggle to provide an adequate supply of affordable rental housing for the
lowest-income renters, and nearly three-quarters of extremely low-income renters are severely
cost-burdened, spending more than half their income on housing. LIHTC-financed housing
takes years to plan, finance, and build, and regulatory choices made now will shape the pipeline
of affordable housing available for years to come.
7 https://nlihc.org/gap
6 https://www.cohnreznick.com/insights/2024-lihtc-equity-market-volume-survey
5 https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RS22389#fn21
 ​

It also does not seem like a sound policy decision to reduce LIHTC financing given the recent
enactment of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. This legislation raises the statutory cap on
bank investment in public welfare projects such as LIHTC from 15 percent to 20 percent of a
bank's capital, a bipartisan legislative choice to unlock additional bank capacity for affordable
housing investment and help address the national affordable housing shortage. The public
welfare boost will not help to meaningfully address the affordable housing shortage if the CRA is
modified to disincentivize LIHTC-funded affordable housing construction.
Our coalition members include affordable housing developers that rely on LIHTC equity to
finance new construction and preserve affordable rental housing in the communities we serve.
The experience of Asian Community Development Corporation (ACDC), a National CAPACD
coalition member, illustrates the high demand for affordable housing and the importance of
maintaining a strong LIHTC investment market. In Boston's Chinatown, ACDC is currently
developing 55 Hudson Street, a community-driven project that will create 110 affordable homes
(66 rental units and 44 homeownership units), along with a permanent Boston Public Library
branch. Construction began in September 2025, with completion currently anticipated in 2027.
The project will transform a site used as a city-owned parking lot for about two decades into
permanently affordable housing and community space.
Demand for these homes is reflected in interest in ACDC's previous affordable housing
developments in Chinatown. According to ACDC, earlier rental developments received
approximately 4,400 applications for 95 units, while approximately 1,600 applications were
submitted for 51 affordable condominium units. This demand illustrates the severe shortage of
affordable housing in Chinatown and the need to create more opportunities for safe, affordable
housing.
The 55 Hudson project was financed through a LIHTC syndicator that pools equity from
multiple bank investors. As a result, ACDC does not know which individual banks invested in
the project. ACDC selected the syndicator based on the most favorable pricing available. Bank
demand for LIHTC investments helps create competition for credits, which improves the pricing
available to affordable housing developers, meaning they receive a more favorable cost-benefit
ratio (high value for money).
If the proposal is finalized, it could lead to fewer affordable housing developments like 55
Hudson being built, longer waitlists, and a reduced capacity to preserve existing affordable
housing before it is lost to market-rate conversion. This would be a step in the wrong direction,
exacerbating, rather than alleviating, the persistent and well-documented shortage of affordable
rental housing.


 ​

The OCC and FDIC should reject the proposed restrictions on community
development grants and donations, which would weaken organizations' capacity to
serve low- and moderate-income communities effectively.
The proposal would require CD grants to be "directly used" for a specific program, project, or
initiative, and it would cap grant recipients' indirect and administrative costs at 15 percent for
large banks. Together, these provisions represent a shift away from flexible, general operating
support toward narrowly restricted, project-specific funding. We are concerned this shift reflects
an outdated and empirically unsupported view of how effective nonprofits actually operate, and
that it will weaken, not strengthen, the ability of community organizations to serve low- and
moderate-income communities.
The premise underlying project-based funding has been extensively studied and increasingly
abandoned by leading philanthropic institutions in recent years. Research has indicated that the
minimum rate associated with financially healthy organizations in the dataset was 29 percent,
nearly double the 15 percent ceiling this proposal would impose.8
Research summarized by PEAK Grantmaking in 2024 also shows that smaller organizations
often have higher indirect costs and less access to unrestricted funding, and they tend to serve
communities of color and underserved areas.9 Given this, a 15 percent cap could particularly
harm these small community-anchored organizations that disproportionately serve traditionally
underinvested households that the CRA is intended to benefit.
Flexible, general operating support allows organizations to retain and develop staff, maintain
the technology and data systems increasingly required by funders and regulators, respond to
emerging community needs that cannot be incorporated into a pre-defined project, and weather
funding gaps between restricted grants without disrupting services. For small, community-based
nonprofits, this flexibility often allows them to remain viable and able to support their
communities adequately.
The OCC and FDIC should not allow a rent formula alone to determine whether
housing counts as "affordable" for CRA purposes and should not prioritize
middle-income housing over lower-income.
The proposal would establish a specific regulatory definition for naturally occurring affordable
housing (NOAH), which is housing that is not subsidized by the government. But the specific
definition the agencies chose falls short of what is needed to ensure this credit actually reaches
low- and moderate-income (LMI) renters.
9
https://www.peakgrantmaking.org/insights/rethinking-indirect-cost-rates-to-support-nonprofit-financial-heal
th/
8 https://www.macfound.org/about/our-policies/indirect-cost-policy/
 ​

The proposed regulatory text states that housing qualifies if it is "likely to be inhabited by low-
or moderate-income individuals or families as demonstrated by median rents that do not and
are not projected at the time of the transaction to exceed 30 percent of 80 percent of the area
median income." Under this approach, a rent formula becomes the only evidence required to
show that a property is reaching LMI tenants. There is no mandate to verify whether it serves
LMI households. This is misaligned with the longstanding "primary purpose" guidance, which
cautions against crediting a project based on a rent formula alone.
The 2023 CRA rule coupled the same rent formula with a requirement that the property meet at
least one additional criterion: location in an LMI census tract or one where renter income is
LMI, development in partnership with an affordable housing nonprofit, or bank-verified
documentation that a majority of tenants are LMI. We believe the agencies should adopt this
stronger model, rather than finalizing a formula-only standard.
The proposal also includes housing for middle-income renters, or 30 percent of 120 percent of
area median income, above the 80 percent threshold definition of moderate income. By
definition, 120 percent of area median income is a middle-income standard. We understand the
purpose is to support "workforce housing" in high-cost metropolitan areas, but we are
concerned that LMI-focused investment could be passed over in favor of middle-income
housing. This provision should be structured so that credit for high-cost middle-income housing
is available in addition to, not in place of, bank investment in housing affordable to LMI
households in the same areas. A bank should not be able to claim CRA credit that prioritizes
tenants with more resources than low-income communities and other underinvested
households.
The regulators should preserve the requirement that economic development and
infrastructure activities create, retain, or strengthen opportunities for LMI
residents and businesses.
For community facilities and other neighborhood improvement projects financed under the
revitalization and stabilization category, current guidance requires that an activity "help to
attract new or retain existing businesses or residents" in an eligible census tract. The proposal
would replace this with a broader test that would provide CRA credit for a program or project
that "benefits or serves" an LMI census tract or another targeted redevelopment area, with no
requirement that the project benefits residents or businesses.
Under this amended standard, an infrastructure or commercial redevelopment project could
receive full CRA credit by being located in or near an LMI census tract, even if it creates few
permanent jobs for existing residents, drives up rents and property values, and ultimately
contributes to the displacement of the LMI households and small businesses our coalition works
to keep housed and in business.
It raises concerns similar to the ones associated with the Opportunity Zone program. Eligibility
for OZ tax benefits is determined by whether an investment is located within a designated
 ​

low-income census tract, not by whether the investment actually benefits the low-income
residents living there. Investment has flowed disproportionately to tracts that were already
gentrifying or economically improving, rather than the most distressed communities the
program was designed to reach.10 We do not think the CRA, which was enacted specifically to
direct capital toward LMI communities, should adopt a similar standard.
Robust small business and community development lending data reporting
requirements should be maintained, which are essential tools for identifying
credit gaps and holding banks accountable to the communities they serve.
Under the current framework, large banks are required to collect, maintain, and annually report
data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, along with
the census tracts that make up their assessment areas. Raising the large-bank threshold from
$1.649 billion to $10 billion would remove an estimated 376 banks from this reporting
requirement entirely, according to figures cited earlier. Many of the banks that could be
downgraded operate across multiple states and communities with meaningful lending volume.
Once a bank moves into the intermediate category, it is no longer required to collect small
business, small farm, and community development lending data.
Small business, small farm, and community development loan data, broken out by geography
and loan size, is one of the few tools available to identify which neighborhoods and borrower
categories bank credit reaches (and which they do not). Without this reporting, gaps in lending
activity become harder to locate, making it more difficult to direct limited resources to the places
that need them most. Funders, policymakers, and community organizations can better target
their own investments when they can see where bank credit is being deployed.
This reporting requirement also benefits banks themselves. Banks use their own CRA lending
data for strategic planning, to identify underserved markets or lending opportunities within
their footprint, and to compare their performance with similarly situated financial institutions
and lenders. Data that supports public accountability also informs bank strategy and operations.
National CAPACD, our coalition members, and our partners work with small businesses and
communities that have historically faced barriers to credit and financial services. Being able to
identify where these gaps exist helps pinpoint the places and populations with the most need,
which can inform our programming, technical assistance, and advocacy. Reducing the number
of banks required to report small business and community development data makes it harder for
organizations to target resources toward the policies, programming, and practices that improve
the economic and social well-being of these disinvested communities.
This proposal also coincides with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's (CFPB's) recent
narrowing of small business lending data collection under Section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act.
This rule was enacted to bring the same kind of geographic and demographic transparency to
small business lending that the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act provides for home mortgages. In
10 https://www.urban.org/projects/opportunity-zones
 ​

2026, the CFPB significantly narrowed the reporting requirements under Section 1071,
including raising the reporting threshold to exclude banks with smaller business loan
originations, narrowing the number of businesses that are covered, and removing the mandate
to collect and maintain disaggregated data on borrowers' race and ethnicity.
The proposed reporting restrictions for the CRA would be another significant setback for small
business data reporting. These two data sources can provide a robust picture of who small
business credit serves. Narrowing both through separate rulemakings could substantially
diminish the capacity to identify and respond to small business credit gaps. It would also reduce
transparency and accountability.
The OCC and FDIC should be coordinating with the Federal Reserve to avoid a CRA
framework that is not consistently applied across the banking system.
The OCC and FDIC issued this proposal jointly, without the participation of the Board of
Governors of the Federal Reserve System (the Board), the other major federal banking agency
responsible for CRA oversight. Unless the Board joins or adopts a similar rule, banks supervised
by the Federal Reserve would remain subject to the current 1995 framework while OCC- and
FDIC-supervised banks would operate under the narrower standard outlined in this proposal.
A fractured CRA landscape, in which a bank's community development obligations depend on
which agency happens to supervise it rather than on communities' credit needs, creates practical
confusion for banks, examiners, and the community organizations that rely on consistent CRA
standards to advocate on behalf of the communities they serve. It also highlights the lack of
interagency consensus among influential and important banking regulators on highly
consequential reform. It is troubling that banking reforms with potentially significant
consequences would not have support from all the regulators.
Conclusion
The CRA has long been one of the few regulatory tools requiring banks to demonstrate that they
are meeting the credit needs of low- and moderate-income households and communities of
color. National CAPACD urges the OCC and FDIC to withdraw this proposal. Changes to the
CRA framework should strengthen, rather than weaken, the obligations of banks to the
historically redlined and disinvested communities this legislation was created to reach. We
appreciate the opportunity to comment and welcome the opportunity for further engagement as
this rulemaking moves forward.


Sincerely,

National CAPACD

Dear OCC and FDIC Leadership:

On behalf of Baltimore Green Justice Workers Cooperative (BGJWC), I am writing to express
strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). BGJWC
is deeply concerned that weakening bank obligations to invest in low- and moderate-income (LMI)
communities in the United States (U.S.) will further undermine the economic stability of frontline
neighborhoods throughout the U.S. and threaten the sustainability of grassroots nonprofits like
BGJWC.

BGJWC operates at the intersection of adult literacy, green workforce development, environmental
justice, climate resilience and cooperative economic development. Through its Clean, Green &
Beautiful Baltimore Community Change Collaborative (CG2B3C), BGJWC partners with 12 other
neighborhood associations and community-based nonprofits in Baltimore, MD to strengthen
neighborhood leadership, advance community greening initiatives and build climate resilience
across nine frontline neighborhoods/communities in Baltimore, MD.

Organizations like BGJWC and our CG2B3C partners already face significant challenges in
securing the funding necessary to sustain our staff, facilities, initiatives, programs and
administrative infrastructure. CRA-related investments, grants and banking partnerships serve as
essential resources that help grassroots organizations build capacity to make positive change.
Weakening and/or reducing these incentives will restrict access to much needed funding for adult
education, green workforce training, community revitalization, affordable housing, small business
development, cooperative ownership initiatives and other types of community-centered programs
that fuel positive change in high-need communities.

BGJWC is especially concerned that the proposed changes to the CRA will result in:

e The loss of over $26 billion in community development loans annually;
e The loss of $267 million in investments annually;
 e Fewer grants, investments and funding opportunities to community organizations;

e Less financing for community development, rehabilitation and preservation efforts; and

e Weaker oversight of the commitment of banks to invest in the health of frontline
communities.

Without a doubt, these rollbacks will significantly weaken the financial support and accountability
that frontline communities rely on to ensure affordable housing, economic opportunities and
neighborhood revitalization. We respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to:

1. Withdraw or substantially revise the proposed rule to preserve strong community
reinvestment and accountability obligations;

2. Maintain meaningful transparency, public reporting and accountability requirements for
banks; and

3. Strengthen incentives for banks to invest directly into frontline communities, grassroots
organizations and nonprofits.

The financial sustainability of grassroots organizations and nonprofits is inseparable from the
economic resilience and well-being of the frontline communities we serve. At a time when our
nation is witnessing troubling setbacks in efforts to confront systemic racism, reverse generations
of disinvestment, and advance social and economic justice, we need the OCC and FDIC to
strengthen, not weaken, the Community Reinvestment Act. Our communities cannot afford
policies that deepen existing inequities or undermine decades of hard-fought progress.

It is for these reasons that I urge the OCC and FDIC to honor both the letter and spirit of the
Community Reinvestment Act by strengthening the responsibility of financial institutions to invest
equitably, meaningfully, and consistently in the communities they serve. Community reinvestment
is not simply a regulatory obligation; it is a commitment to economic justice, shared prosperity,
and ensuring that frontline communities have the resources to thrive.

Sincerely,

pecti—

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould:

Citizens Tri-County Bank appreciates the opportunity to provide comment and recommendations to the Notice
Of Proposed Rulemaking with regard to Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. We support the
Agencies efforts and initiatives to better align CRA with its statutory mandate, reduce unnecessary burden, and
improve clarity. We offer the following comments in support of that process.

© Question 56: Should the agencies replace the requirement to include census tracts where the bank does a
substantial portion of lending in the bank's Assessment Area(s) with an alternative such as the radius-based
standard discussed above. If so, how should the agencies determine the appropriate radius? Should it vary by
type of geographic area (e.g., MSA or nonmetropolitan area)?

The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) seeks feedback on whether banks should have continued
or further flexibility in Assessment Area delineation. The NPRM is true that agencies and the banks they
supervise have often confronted ambiguity as to when a bank meets the "substantial portion of its
loans" standard, triggering the obligation to include additional census tracts within a bank's Assessment
Area. The NPRM opines whether a transparent threshold would make it easier for banks to discern
when they incur obligations to include areas that are not the census tract in which their main office or
home office, as applicable, branches, or deposit-taking ATMs or remote service facilities, as applicable,
are located. However, we support the alternative or option to the "substantial portion of its loans"
standard as mentioned in the NPRM, a radius-based standard, that requirements for banks include all
census tracts within a radius of a bank's main office, branches, or deposit-taking ATMs or remote service
facilities. The option of this approach substantiates a core principal under the Community Reinvestment
Act, that banks delineate Assessment Areas to reflect where they can reasonably be expected to serve
their community's credit and financial needs.

 The Assessment Area framework in the rules requires banks to identify areas around their physical
locations within which the agencies evaluate the bank's record of helping to meet the credit needs of
its community. We agree that Assessment Areas should remain tied primarily to physical infrastructure,
such as where a bank maintains its main office, branches, and deposit-taking ATMs. We did not support
the 2023 rule which attempted to mandate the creation of new lending-based Assessment Areas where
a bank had a concentration of loans but could have little or no substantiated footprint.

We recommend that the regulations be revised so an Assessment Area would not be delineated or
expanded in a manner beyond a bank's realistic operational capacity. A bank's limitations include its
asset size, reduced knowledge of diverse markets, ability to offer products and services dissimilar from
its core strength and success, depth of capital, and staffing capabilities (both in number and expertise).
We also recommend the regulations recognize that an Assessment Area should not be created or
expanded into an area a bank cannot effectively compete in a saturated market, where multiple banks
or banks with multiple branches compete for a fixed number of qualifying low to moderate-income
applicants, projects, and opportunities. Competition also grows from fintech and pure online lenders
and branchless banks. Credit unions with expansive and sprawling fields of membership contest
aggressively on price by being unencumbered by tax or profit responsibilities or concerns). Banks whose
focus is on relationship banking and compete through localized market knowledge may simply not be
capable of meeting the diverse credit demands of an expanded population and geography. An
arbitrarily broadened Assessment Area doesn't take these considerations into account and obliges a
bank to account for community needs it cannot physically or fiscally address or support.

Artificially expanding Assessment Area boundaries without operational foundations can create false
conclusions of a Bank's record of addressing community needs, skewing benchmarks in the performance
context. In other words, an exaggerated Assessment Area can generate a poor CRA performance
because the bank may be compared against those within markets it cannot realistically serve. For an
example not pertaining to lending performance, the NPRM observes that Community Development
services are inherently tethered to geographies in which employees conducting the service are located.

For these reasons above, we believe the performance context should incorporate all factors that can
encumber a bank from competing with institutions entrenched in all or separate portions of a county.
An expansion of any bank's Assessment Area to encompass an entire county could be an operational
hazard. A bank with few locations would, for example, unlikely have local loan officers or established
county relationships (for example, with local CDFls) to proactively source low to moderate-income
loans, community investments, or community services at scale.

A radius-based concept provides a simple and common-sense approach to establishing an Assessment
Area, removing numerical calculations with results that otherwise can be elusive, ambiguous, or
misinterpreted by banks and the agencies. After all, if a bank operates along the perimeter of a county
for example, and deposits are not received in equal proportion throughout that county, it is highly
doubtful that the bank is simply operationally capable or it lacks brand presence to obtain or attract
covered loan applications, or even sustain community development throughout that county, from a
county or massive metropolitan footprint. Further, it would be difficult for a bank to design or draw
Assessment Area boundaries to deliberately avoid low-income or minority-majority neighborhoods with
a radius-based approach. Moreover, the radius-based approach could also mitigate misinterpretations
by regulators or community groups who may contend that if a bank serves part of a metropolitan area,
it must expand its Assessment Area to cover a county's entire market or be stretched into a county's
market without supportable operational or internal infrastructure, particularly without a physical
branch presence, as well as lacking market knowledge, contacts, and area governance (thereby

2
 generating unrealistic institutional expectations). It would also assist regarding the nonspecific text
within the Interagency Questions and Answers on discrimination and Assessment Area development.
For example, by establishing a radius-based Assessment Area of which a bank can focus its attention
based on the factors discussed in this response, the Community Reinvestment Act's regulation should
then not be misapplied to assert a lack of services to residents of distant specific neighborhoods based

on race or ethnicity that are physically outside of a bank's capacity, capability, competency, and
branching to serve.

We therefore support the option of an alternative radius-based standard in establishing Assessment
Areas. As to determining an applicable radius surrounding these bank locations, we suggest a flexible
methodology to be employed. For example, census tracts in rural areas tend to be much large then
areas of denser metropolitan areas. Therefore, a concentric fixed distance for banks, regardless of the
bank's location could be impractical in some but not all cases. It could also be problematic if a bank's
location adjoins a natural or physical feature (for example, a mountain's escarpment or a
river/waterway without bridging infrastructure or lacking convenient transit points); in these cases, a
natural geographical formation or landscapes could reasonably serve as a boundary of an Assessment
Area. As a result, census tracts that encompass the border of a municipality could be an option for a
bank. A county border should not be discounted as an option if appropriately based on the bank's
business hub and branch reach as previously discussed above. Optionally, the radius could be largest
for rural locations (in or out of MSAs), or an intermediary radial size that encompasses suburban
locations, and the smallest size for locations when a main office or branching footprint principally serves
a city or municipality within a county or MSA.

® Comment on Option A and Option B with regard to the handling of discriminatory practices in Community
Reinvestment Examinations.

It's been long established that existing law and the implementing regulations for the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) require the consideration of discrimination in examination. An institution's CRA
rating can be adjusted downward based on "evidence of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices,"
which includes violations of the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and the Fair Housing Act. However, the
usage of this requirement has been subject to disagreements in examination settings. In addition,
opinions differ in recent years if banks feel accused of discriminatory practices using metrics and
statistical models, when a bank asserts a position that there was no evidence of overt bias or intent to
discriminate. Initial _redlining involved explicitly drawing lines on maps to exclude minority
neighborhoods from receiving loans; newer considerations have been based on statistical redlining
accusations, if a bank's lending area shows a mathematical shortage in minority tracts compared to its
peers.

The proposal seeks to mitigate conflict with two options:
¢ Option 1 (a formal enforcement action standard), or
* Option 2 (a broad compliance examiner standard)

Under Option 1, evidence of discriminatory and other illegal credit practices must be formally cited as
a violation of a law, rule, or regulation within a public enforcement action taken by a Federal or State
agency, or a judicial order to which a Federal or State agency is a party. A financial institution is
benefitted by a gaining a bright-line standard and predictability, not subject to examiner discretion or
possible downgrades based on open-ended Fair Lending accusations during an exam. Discrimination
allegations would be thoroughly investigated and formalized into a matter of legal record by a
regulatory body or court. Option 1 ensures corporate strategies are not derailed by unadjudicated or

3
 preliminary examiner findings, separating a bank's Fair Lending compliance track from its CRA
evaluation track. It also eliminates a burden on CRA examiners to evaluate ambiguous fair lending
issues, allowing them to focus entirely on performance data. However, Option 1 can be detrimental to
a bank, as an enforcement action assures a devastating twofold impact, an enforcement penalty plus a
CRA downgrade. Also, the substantive costs of defending even a preliminary or unproven charge are
significant (financial capital, administrative resources, and organizational focus). Even before a case
goes to court or a settlement is discussed, a bank must spend money to investigate and respond to a
preliminary charge. Expensive corporate defense counsel would be retained and managing an
accusation would be formidable (retrieving data, conducting internal interviews and research, replicate
the agency's statistical models, drafting formal responses to agencies, and attention being periodically
averted from managing loans and other bank services). While under the shadow of a preliminary
regulatory cloud, planned expansions, new loan product rollouts, or merger and acquisition discussions
are paused, as regulators are unlikely to approve expansions with an open, unresolved discrimination
inquiry. Further, If the preliminary charge leaks or advances, the long-term financial consequences
escalate as a bank manages reputation harm; a downgraded rating bars a bank from opening new
branches or acquiring other institutions.

The Option 2 alternative preserves the ability of examiners or agency to downgrade a CRA rating. It can
be beneficial to an institution that can voluntarily correct a preliminary finding, discuss findings with
additional information and data, or contest a ratings reduction, possibly without facing an enforcement
action. Option 2 is also desirable in that it would provide if the citation is a violation of law, rule, or a
regulation, it remains confidential supervisory information, and the agencies will not disclose this
information in the public section of a bank's CRA Performance Evaluation. This prevents banks from
premature reputational harm while an issue is being resolved. This confidentiality can also encourage
cooperation between banks and the agencies to address any possible perceived discriminatory practices
or misunderstands of either party without initiating an adversarial position. Yet this subjectivity of

examiners and agencies personnel can also have its downsides, such as ambiguity of inconsistent
evaluations.

We recommend, however, that both options can be employed, first Option 2, and if unresolved the
bank can elect that Option 1 be implemented. We also recommend that additional definitive guidance
is provided to the industry, more than the current guidance in the regulation, examination procedures,
and the Interagency Questions and Answers regarding Community Reinvestment. Inconsistent
evaluations can be mitigated by further detailed guidance to curtail ambiguity. A good example is in the
NPRM, the ability to obtain advance agency confirmation that specific activities qualify as community
development, that reduces CRA compliance risk. The proposition of an alternative radius-based
standard in establishing Assessment Areas is another example, taking into consideration an institution's
financial condition and capacity to effectively operate, compete, and market.

* Proposal to expand other illegal credit practices into the scope of Community Reinvestment Act rating system.

We disagree that additional consumer protection laws be incorporated into the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) examinations. These laws are the Home Ownership and Equity Protection Act,
section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act (UDAP), section 8 of the Real Estate Settlement
Procedures Act (RESPA), the Truth in Lending Act provisions regarding a consumer's right of rescission
(TILA), Military Lending Act (MLA), Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (SCRA), and section 1031 of the
Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (UDAAP)
 The Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 was enacted with an obligation to encourage financial
institutions to help meet the credit needs of the communities in which they are chartered, particularly
low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods. Its focus is fundamentally community development.
The NPRM proposes to introduce individual consumer protection and disclosure laws that would involve
evaluating technical compliance and consumer law violations under a divergent purpose and focus of
the CRA (credit availability, services, investment, etc.). The CRA transforms from being an incentive
process for community growth and progress to being an umbrella enforcement mechanism.

There are already dedicated, highly specialized examination tracks designed exclusively to vigorously
review, monitor, and enforce UDAAP, RESPA, TILA, and military lending protections (of which already
contains enforcement actions, including restitution, civil money penalties, and consent orders).
Enforcing these laws in the CRA process invites double penalization, imposing a downgraded CRA rating,
This could occur even for an isolated and inadvertent infractions (without taking into consideration an
institution's processes of mitigation, cure, and remediation in any instance).

The adoption of these laws into the CRA scope can also distort an institution's performance. For
example, a downgraded CRA rating could occur for a mis-signed document even though an institution's
performance exhibits an exemplary record of providing affordable housing opportunities, deploying
capital for communities in need, or sound branch accessibility.

Lastly, CRA examinations rely heavily on those trained in evaluating geographic and comparative data,
community demographic research and metrics, investment portfolios, and analysis of each bank's
unique circumstances, abilities, and impediments. Conversely, enforcement of the proposed statutes
requires a completely different base of analytical methodologies and training of examiners. The
introduction of this proposed regulatory redundancy mires both banks and examiners in operational
inefficiencies, which could lead to inconsistent or unpredictable examination results.

| © Question 7: If the agencies adopt Option 1, should the agencies determine a bank's major product lines by
Assessment Area, as opposed to at the institution level as proposed?

We support that a bank's major product lines could optionally be by Assessment Area, or carve-outs if
multiple Assessment Areas are involved, if circumstances indicate divergent product offerings impacted
by differing populations, geographies, or demand. As an example, if a bank's Assessment Areas consist
of branches in several counties, each county Assessment Area could emphasize distinctive products
based on demand or other circumstances (for instance, if any particular county contained land-use
restrictions, a military installation, a university, large farming tracts, or a manufacturing plant employing
a substantive percentage of the working public).

© Question 34: If the rules were to permit banks to receive consideration for CD activities outside of Assessment
Areas in States, multistate MSAs, or at the bank level without requiring that the bank meet or exceed the
geographic flexibility standard(s) in all Assessment Area(s), in determining when consideration would be
permitted outside Assessment Area, should the agencies rely on the "substantially met" standard in proposed
__.27 or should another standard apply?

| We generally agree with visiting the treatment and consideration of Community Development (CD)
| activities that benefit the "broader statewide or regional area that includes the assessment area(s)"
| concept. The introduces a flexible framework allowing banks to count qualifying CD activities anywhere
| outside Assessment Areas (at the State or multistate MSA level). However, we have concern that with
the "substantially met" qualifier.

A downside of the "substantially met" qualifier is that a bank's CD activities outside its Assessment Areas
would not automatically qualify for CRA credit. Instead, banks face a conditional and potential
regulatory obstruction for this geographic flexibility. If a bank fails to clear benchmarks in its Assessment
Area, its entire portfolio of regional or state-level CD activities could be disqualified from receiving any
CRA credit. In fact, one reason banks have engaged in outside Assessment Area activities in the past is
that CD opportunities in their Assessment Areas are simply lacking. As result, a bank may be reluctant
to provide CD benefits to areas outside its Assessment Areas if it determines it will be discounted
regardless.

The proposal provides two options to which a bank can receive credit outside its Assessment Areas.
Option 1, a quantitative benchmark, would require a large bank reach a specific threshold (0.625% of
Tier 1 capital allocated to Assessment Areas) to qualify for CD activities outside its Assessment Area
(1.25% of Tier 1 capital for intermediate banks). An Option 2 (qualitative benchmark) evaluation would
rely on a qualitative examiner review to determine if the bank has maintained an "adequate" and
responsive level of CD activity within its defined Assessment Areas.

Option 1 has its advantages in that a transparent benchmark is available for which a Bank can assess
and plan its CD activities, not merely speculating on how an examiner would consider a bank's CD
pursuits and actions. However, as with any numerical benchmark or standard, testing Option 1 in real-
world circumstances before implementation in the regulation would be desirable to avoid unintended
consequences or unseen impediments. The application of this standard would need to be refined and
flexible, as it does not take into account unique circumstances in any bank's market footprint (for
example, the economic health of its communities, or simply a limited number or amount of
opportunities in an Assessment Area ). Another example, if a Bank's Tier 1 capital in 2026 is used to
base its ability to pursue CD activity outside its Assessment Area in 2026, there would be a disconnect
in that investments with long term community benefits originated in prior years and might not be
recognized. Also, highly capitalized banks could face unduly high dollar thresholds to qualify for outside
CD credit. It would also be worthwhile that examination cycles be used to determine if Option 1's use
would actually reduce CD activity when a bank would have otherwise engaged in more CD activity.

Option 2 has its advantages in that banks with unique footprints or who could struggle to reach capital
metrics could rely on examiners to recognize these banks' unique circumstances or constraints, also
perceiving the differences in a bank's market area. It utilizes supervisory training, experience, and
flexibility within the performance context, recognizing different levels of CD needs and opportunities in
different areas of the Assessment Areas. The downside is the uncertainly and subjectivity of how a
bank's CD performance is gauged in examinations, even from examination cycle to the next.

Regardless if Option 1 or Option 2 paths are used, or any iterations thereof, we recognize and welcome
written and formalized frameworks under which to operate. Either method has its advantages and
disadvantages; a balance is needed. Afterall, if regulations are adopted that actually encourage outside
CD activity, it is possible that pressures in examination settings can transform a voluntary option into a
functional equivalent of an expanded Assessment Area. Consequently, subject to a thorough evaluation
and testing of Option 1 with or versus Option 2, we concur that qualifying CD initiatives may be
conducted beyond designated Assessment Areas, provided that the "substantially met" standard can
be waived or moderated, as any possible local alternatives can be limited, or even unavailable,
unfeasible, unviable, or impractical for an institution to engage. Waiver can include scenarios where
other institutions have already established a CD foothold or relationship, and duplicative CD efforts are
impractical, unfeasible or unneeded. Moreover, a pass-fail threshold of Tier 1 capital should be tested

6
 | before implementation to assess the ability of smaller capitalized institutions to soundly reach that
threshold, or even a range of Tier 1 capital, relative to their Assessment Areas. Similarly, well-capitalized
institutions may be located in areas where Community Development is limited or impractical, but
appreciate where regional assistance could be welcomed (for example if nearby counties suffer from a
weather-rated catastrophe). For this reason, we recommend consideration for CD activities outside of
Assessment Areas and the "substantially met" standard being met be based on either Option 1 or Option
2 criteria as chosen by the institution at each examination (after Option 1 efficacy is tested).

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Acts Housing submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would
significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC,
before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low-
and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis
and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current
comment deadline by 60-days.
Acts Housing is a HUD-certified housing counseling agency serving Milwaukee and
Rock Counties in Wisconsin. Acts Housing's mission is Empowerment Through
Homeownership, providing homebuyer coaching, real estate services, down payment
assistance, lending services, and more to first-time homebuyers.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 2
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.
REDUCTION IN COMMUNITY INVESTMENT EXPECTATIONS FOR ALL
BANKS
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In our
communities, from 2010-2024, banks made $27,578,322,000 in CRA qualified mortgage
lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and $6,916,917,000 in CRA qualified
lending to small businesses.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1
capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough
to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the
OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these
banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development
loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital,
and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each
bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625%
of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined activity
would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make
their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set

2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks
surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625%
for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical
effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk,
(Sept. 10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-
development-activity-at-risk/.
 3
strategic plan benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of
community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments
and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be
accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for
communities. For example, while Acts is proud of the impact its programs continue to
have, it is disappointing that of the 1500+ families who begin homebuyer coaching each
year through Acts, only 300-350 become homeowners. Many families who seek out Acts
services have 1-3 years of work to do before they can qualify for a mortgage. This seems
like an eternity to families who have low-to-moderate income and are juggling work and
family obligations. Moreover, for many of our families, they do not have enough trust in
us or the banking system to put in several years of hard work focused on homeownership,
for fear that they eventually will be told there is some loophole that will prevent them
from owning. It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet
community needs. Banks have been strong partners to Acts Housing and its affiliates,
originating mortgage loans to Acts families, donating and lending money to Acts, and
providing Acts with skilled volunteers. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should
analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or investment
available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether communities that have
experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately
affected.
LESS COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT SCRUTINY OF BANKS
The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small
banks, while banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be
evaluated under the less demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more
comprehensive tests applied to large banks.5 The proposal would also eliminate several
CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks for
institutions with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on small-business,
small-farm and community development lending.6

4 NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept 1,
2026), https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.

5 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,120–23 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
6 Id. at 52,120.

Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation
because the proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1
billion.7 The 417 banks newly classified as intermediate rather than large would no
longer be examined under separate CRA investment and services tests and instead would
be evaluated based on their combined community development loans, investments and
services. These reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development
obligations for over 800 banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks, may
worsen the housing crisis by reducing the demand for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC).
In Wisconsin, this means:
• 43.4% of banks will lose community development obligations, no longer having
to reinvest in local community development projects such as affordable housing,
small business support, workforce development, community healthcare and
education services.
• 55% of banks will lose large-bank status facing easier community development
tests and longer having to maintain branches in LMI neighborhoods, volunteer
with local nonprofits or report small business lending data each year.
This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and
moderate-income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to
affordable mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain
responsible small-business financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in
affordable housing, small businesses and other community development.
The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the
CRA obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify
the banks that would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the
communities those institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development
activity that would receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be
concentrated in low- and moderate-income communities or communities that have
experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
BANK BRANCHES AND ACCESS TO BANKING SERVICES
By raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion, 417 banks would no longer receive the
full large-bank examination, including a separate service test that evaluates branch
delivery systems and banking services. We are concerned that approximately 5,000
branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts would no longer be evaluated as part
of the large-bank CRA service test under the proposal, and more than 4,000 branches in
majority-people-of-color census tracts would also lose CRA consideration. In 28 states, at

least one-third of branches located in LMI census tracts would no longer receive any
CRA evaluation.8 In Wisconsin, 45.9% of branches (130 full-services branches) in LMI
neighborhoods are in jeopardy. This proposal also jeopardizes 32.9% of full-services
branches in communities of color in Wisconsin, communities who have already
experienced a lengthy history of disinvestment and barriers to economic prosperity.

The proposal would also narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service
test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and
information about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit
this criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings
accounts from direct evaluation under the service test.9 As such, examiners would no
longer evaluate whether those products are affordable and responsive to community
needs even though 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19
million are underbanked.10 CRA review of the cost and features of deposit products has
played an important role in encouraging banks to address these disparities by providing
affordable products.
Our organization works with communities where access to mainstream banking services
remains a serious concern. We have seen how detrimental it can be to a community when
there is a lack of reliable, trustworthy full-service bank branches available nearby.
Communities with limited access to affordable bank accounts are more likely to rely on
check cashers or other alternative financial services, which often sets them back when
they are working toward their dream of homeownership. We believe that presence
matters – having physical, full-services branches in underserved communities promotes
neighborhood and community stability.
For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate
from access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families
can safely receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain
responsible credit. We are therefore concerned that under the proposal, examiners will no
longer evaluate whether banks that are still subject to the service test offer affordable
checking and savings accounts. By reducing the importance of deposit services and
branch performance in CRA evaluations, the proposal eliminates incentives for banks to
offer basic products that help unbanked and underbanked households. Before finalizing
these changes, the agencies should identify which communities would receive less
scrutiny of bank branches and services, determine whether the effects would fall
disproportionately on low- and moderate-income communities or communities of color,
