Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, RIN 3064-AG31 / Docket ID OCC-2026-0694

To Whom It May Concern:

On July 31, 2026, the OƯice of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation ("FDIC") (together, "the agencies") issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking proposing major
revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA") regulations. The Michigan CDFI Coalition ("Coalition")
appreciates the agencies' eƯorts to reform CRA and supports several provisions that could increase
responsible capital in underserved communities. However, we have serious concerns about the proposed
increases in asset thresholds and the restrictions on operating grants, as well as several interacting
provisions that together would weaken the flow of capital to Michigan's most underserved communities.

About the Coalition and Michigan CDFIs
Our Coalition brings together Michigan's community development financial institutions ("CDFIs") to
increase lending capacity, share best practices, strengthen the sector, and speak with a common voice
on public policy. More than 40 certified CDFIs operate in Michigan, including loan funds and credit
unions. We serve low- and moderate-income ("LMI") neighborhoods in Detroit, Flint, Lansing, and Grand
Rapids, as well as small towns and rural communities across our state, and communities with Tribal and
Native lands. Since 2005, our members have deployed more than $6.3 billion in financing that supported
more than 18,000 housing units (72% aƯordable), created and retained more than 50,000 jobs, more than
1,500 projects, and supported more than 26,000 small businesses. In 2024 alone, our members deployed
$164,033,626 in financing that supported 1,281 aƯordable housing units, created or retained 2,464 jobs,
and supported 381 small businesses.

Banks are critical partners in our work. Michigan CDFIs rely on banks to serve as lenders, investors,
depositors, grant makers, and co-lenders through loans, lines of credit, Equity Equivalent Investments
(EQ2s), and loan participations. They are also essential partners in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
("LIHTC") and New Markets Tax Credit ("NMTC") projects across the state. The partnership works both
ways: banks rely on CDFIs to reach borrowers they cannot eƯiciently serve directly and to meet
community credit needs, and CDFI borrowers often graduate into mainstream bank relationships.

CRA has long given banks the incentive to build and sustain these relationships. Michigan has also
invested its own resources in this ecosystem through the Michigan CDFI Fund, which gives CDFIs flexible
capital to leverage into private lending. We are concerned that the proposal would weaken CRA

incentives, reducing the capital reaching Michigan communities and reducing the return on that
public investment. We focus our comments on the three issues we believe matter most.

1. All three banking agencies should follow the same CRA rules

For decades, the OCC, the FDIC, and the Federal Reserve have evaluated banks' CRA performance under
a generally consistent interagency framework. This proposal breaks from that practice: it was issued by
only two of the three agencies, and banks supervised by the Federal Reserve would continue to be
evaluated under diƯerent rules.

As a result, two similar banks serving the same Michigan community could face diƯerent CRA
expectations based only on their primary federal regulator. For example:

An investment in a Michigan CDFI could count one way for an OCC- or FDIC-supervised bank and
another way for a Federal Reserve-supervised bank.

 A grant to a CDFI could be subject to the 15% indirect-cost cap and new documentation
requirements from one bank partner but not another.

Banks competing in the same market could also face diƯerent asset thresholds, performance
tests, and lists of eligible activities.

We are concerned that this split would create confusion, weaken accountability, and invite regulatory
arbitrage, where banks choose a charter or regulator based on which CRA rules are easier to meet. A
fragmented system works against the agencies' stated goals of clarity, predictability, and reduced burden.
Regulatory simplification should not come at the cost of regulatory consistency. This matters to Michigan
CDFIs because they work with many bank partners supervised by diƯerent regulators. Under the
proposal, U.S. Bank would follow the new OCC and FDIC rules, while Independent Bank and Chelsea
State Bank would remain under the Federal Reserve's rules. That would make it harder to bring several
banks together on a single project, to explain what will qualify, and for communities to compare bank
performance.

Recommendation: We encourage the OCC and FDIC to continue working with the Federal Reserve
toward one consistent interagency framework, keeping consistent standards, definitions, examination
expectations, and performance measures, including a single interagency illustrative list of eligible
activities.

2. Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance
Section IV.A; Questions 1–3

The proposal would define small banks as those under $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks as those
between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as those above $10 billion. Nationally, about 800
banks would lose their separate community development ("CD") test, and about 400 large banks would
lose the separate lending, investment, and service tests and many data-reporting obligations. In
Michigan, an estimated 15 banks (23.4% of the state's banks) would no longer receive a separate
community development evaluation, and 10 of the existing 29 large banks (34.5%) would lose large-bank
status, reducing the pool of CRA dollars flowing to LMI Michigan communities. The eƯects would be felt
most in rural Michigan and smaller cities, where there are fewer banks and fewer alternative sources of
capital, and losing even one or two CRA-motivated partners can decide whether an aƯordable housing
project, small business, or community facility gets financed.

The concern is not that every aƯected bank would cut CD financing, but that fewer institutions would face
explicit incentives to sustain the specialized loans, investments, grants, and services CDFIs need. The
agencies themselves acknowledge that a CD test typically leads banks to adjust their CRA programs. The

consequences would be greatest in rural Michigan, where the loss of even one or two CRA-motivated
partners can determine whether a project is financed. Precision Hardwoods, a sawmill in Onaway,
illustrates the point: a $13 million expansion financed by Michigan Community Capital, PNC Bank, and
NMTC allocations retained seven jobs and created 20 new ones in a region where several mills have
closed and traditional financing is scarce.

The change also runs counter to Congress's recent bipartisan eƯorts to expand LIHTC and make NMTC
permanent. Both are evaluated under the large-bank investment test, which carries a distinct 25% weight.
Michigan CDFIs have deployed more than $1.8 billion in NMTC investment across 156 projects. Folding
investments into a single blended CD test would let banks emphasize lending over LIHTC and NMTC
investment, reducing demand for the very tools Congress just strengthened.

For our members, the consequences would be direct. The agencies acknowledge that banks typically
adjust their CRA programs when they become subject to a community development test, and the reverse
is also true: when the test goes away, much of the incentive goes with it. The result would be fewer CRA-
motivated dollars and more organizations competing for them. Under less pressure, banks will
reasonably seek the simplest way to meet their remaining obligations, favoring large, routine transactions
over the smaller, more complex, and more patient financing that CDFIs provide.

Recommendation. We urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds, which are already indexed
annually to CPI-W, and to reject all alternatives, including the substantially higher thresholds raised in
Question 1. "Restoring proportionality to 1995" does not explain how higher thresholds serve CRA's
statutory purpose of meeting the credit needs of LMI communities. The agencies also apply the concept
inconsistently: the small-bank threshold is justified by the share of banks (nearly 80%), yet under that
same logic nearly 20% of banks were large in 1995, versus a little over 2% under the proposal. The large-
bank threshold is instead justified by share of industry assets. Matching a 1995 distribution does not
show the categories fit today's consolidated industry, in which banks with several billion dollars in assets
have far greater lending, investment, data, and operational capacity than their 1995 counterparts.

3. Restrictions on Community Development Grants
Section IV.C; Questions 9–11

We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on CD grants, which would (1) require that a qualifying grant
be used directly by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of community
development; (2) cap recipients' indirect administrative costs at 15% for large banks; and (3) require large
banks to collect written use-of-funds commitments, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Forms 990, and
operating and program budgets. We also oppose the alternative in Question 10 to eliminate grants and
donations from CRA consideration. We share the goal of ensuring that grants meaningfully benefit
communities, but these requirements misunderstand the role of flexible operating support. For CDFIs,
staƯing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk management, data systems, and technical
assistance are not ancillary to community development; they are the infrastructure that makes
community development lending possible.

A fixed 15% indirect-cost limit is also a poor proxy for impact. Costs vary with an organization's size,
geography, product mix, regulatory obligations, and technical-assistance model. The cap would fall
hardest on small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar loans, and organizations
that provide intensive borrower technical assistance, which describes many of Michigan's smaller loan
funds and credit unions.





Recommendation. The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-
building grants as under the 1995 framework, and let banks provide the form of support that best
responds to community needs without undue compliance burdens.


Interacting Provisions That Would Further Reduce Community Development Incentives
Intermediate-bank ratings (Section IV.B). Today an intermediate bank must earn at least Satisfactory
on both its lending and CD tests to receive an overall Satisfactory. The proposal would let strong lending
offset weak CD performance, and with higher thresholds moving hundreds of large banks into this
category, incentives for CDFI loans, investments, and grants would fall. We urge the agencies to require
at least Satisfactory CD performance for an overall Satisfactory rating.
Complexity (Section IV.C; Questions 12–17). Defining complexity by whether an activity is part of a
multicomponent loan is too narrow. CDFI investments involve layered capital, subordinate positions,
guarantees, and patient terms that make them complex even when unpaired with a bank loan. We
oppose a lending-centric definition, mandatory complexity for CD investments or services, and treating
complexity as more responsive than innovation, flexibility, or impact.
Retail lending substituting for CD lending (Sections IV.B and IV.C). The agencies should require a
meaningful CD nexus so ordinary-course small-business or small-farm lending does not substitute for
specialized CD lending that depends on CRA incentives.
Essential community infrastructure (Section IV.D; Question 25). We support consideration for rural,
Indian Country, and distressed areas, but eliminating the requirements to show that infrastructure helps
attract or retain residents or businesses, and to allocate benefit to LMI individuals, risks letting large
conventionally financed deals compete with affordable housing and CDFI financing.
Strategic plans (Section IV.F; Questions 38–53). Goals should respond to demonstrated needs,
approximate the rigor of the standard tests, be measurable, and be subject to meaningful public
engagement. We urge strong standards in response to Question 53.
Outside-assessment-area activities (Section IV.E; Question 34). Geographic flexibility can direct
capital to CRA deserts, including rural and Tribal communities in Michigan, but it should supplement, not
displace, activity in banks' own assessment areas. Option 1 would allow outside-area credit once a large
bank reaches 0.625% of allocated Tier 1 capital in CD loans and in CD investments and grants, roughly
the minimum to avoid a "Needs to Improve" rating. The National Community Reinvestment Coalition
found that for 69 large banks, current assessment-area CD activity totals about $102 billion annually,
while that benchmark yields about $14.8 billion, roughly 85% less. The standard should reflect
satisfactory performance, and any "substantially met" exception should be limited to documented lack
of opportunity.

Provisions We Support
Prior-period CD loans (Question 8). We strongly support consideration of qualifying CD loans
outstanding from prior evaluation periods, matching the treatment of investments. We recommend using
average outstanding balances that reflect both amount and duration, with repeated renewals of
substantially the same loan treated as one exposure.
Illustrative list and advance confirmation (Questions 32-33). We strongly support a public, non-
exhaustive, ideally single interagency illustrative list and a formal advance-confirmation process,
including retention of determinations while an activity remains on a bank's balance sheet and a
maximum 30-day extension of the 90-day review. Determinations should include written rationales, allow
 reconsideration, provide a channel for community stakeholders to raise material concerns, be published
in anonymized form, and remain subject to verification at examination.
Allocation across assessment areas (Section IV.E). Greater flexibility in allocating CD activity that
serves multiple assessment areas would better reflect the impact of statewide and regional CDFIs.
Assigning an entire bank investment to a headquarters location would misstate who benefits.
Indian Country and Tribal and Native lands (Sections IV.D and IV.I; Question 54). Michigan is home to
twelve federally recognized Tribes, and we strongly support expressly recognizing these areas as targeted
geographies. We support adopting the 2023 rule's "Native Land Area" definition and retaining its explicit
recognition of qualifying CD activities, which appropriately treated these areas as a distinct place-based
category. Adopting the definition alone, however, is insufficient. The agencies should preserve
meaningful consideration of the impact and responsiveness of activities benefiting Native communities
and support bank partnerships with certified Native CDFIs. We also recommend extending eligibility to
the service areas of certified Native CDFIs located outside Native Land Areas, with clear standards for
how activities benefit the Native communities served, consistent with the Native CDFI Network's
recommendation.
Disaster preparedness and resilience (Question 31). We support recognizing activities that help
communities prepare for and withstand disasters, including the flooding and severe storms that have
repeatedly damaged Michigan housing and small businesses. CDFIs finance housing, homeowners,
small businesses, and community facilities before and after disasters, and CRA should reward
preparation, not only recovery.

Conclusion
CRA has built a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities we serve. Modernization
should result in more responsible capital reaching communities with unmet credit needs, as the statute
intends. We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposed asset-threshold increases and
the restrictions on CD operating grants; to preserve the intermediate-bank CD requirement; to adopt a
lending-independent definition of complexity; and to adopt the guardrails described above on strategic
plans, infrastructure, and outside-assessment-area activity. Thank you for considering these comments
and the impact of the proposed changes on the communities we serve.


Sincerely,






Elissa Sangalli




President & CEO, Northern Initiatives

Chair, Michigan CDFI Coalition

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations RIN 3064-AG31 / Docket ID OCC-2026- 0694

To Whom it May Concern,
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") shared a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, proposing
major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). CRA encourages banks to
make community investments through loans, grants, and other support that provides access to capital in
underserved areas.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support some of the agencies'
provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in underserved
communities. However, we are very concerned about the increases in the asset thresholds that determine
how banks are evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on operating grants. Additionally, we believe
several interacting provisions could further weaken community development incentives that will
undoubtedly impair the flow of much needed capital in the most underserved communities.
Established in 1993, Neighborhood Development Center (NDC) is a community development financial
institution (CDFI) whose mission is to empower entrepreneurs and community partners to transform low-
income neighborhoods from within. Our goal is to empower aspiring entrepreneurs in low to middle income
neighborhoods with business knowledge and access to opportunity to develop successful businesses that
allow them to create jobs, build wealth, and develop and transform their own neighborhoods. To do this, we
provide access to capital, training, business services, and affordable commercial real estate to around 500
entrepreneurs each year.
Banks are critical partners in our work. We currently have relationships with banks that provide grants,
technical assistance and loan capital for NDC assisted entrepreneurs, and New Market Tax Credits (NMTC)
for NDC affordable commercial development projects. These partnerships have allowed NDC to infuse




over $42 million in affordable, flexible loan capital into our communities since 1993, and have helped small
business clients of NDC create over 4,000 estimated existing jobs and return around $93,000,000 to their
neighborhoods each year.
These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital and resources to CDFIs,
banks rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, develop borrowers, and cultivate future bank
customers. Though we work with mainly micro-businesses, some NDC-assisted businesses have grown
exponentially, establishing various locations across the Twin Cities. When NDC clients reach this point,
they can transfer to mainstream financing options, which provides clients for large banks and reinforces
partnerships between NDC and the banking community of Minnesota. The CRA has long helped create
incentives for banks to build and sustain these relationships, strengthening the broader community
development ecosystem. We are therefore concerned that several provisions in the proposal could weaken
these incentives, reducing bank engagement with CDFIs and ultimately the flow of capital to the
communities we serve.
Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section IV.A, "Asset
Thresholds"; Questions 1–3
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks as
institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with more than $10
billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate community development test as intermediate small
banks would become small banks and lose that requirement. Another approximately 400 banks that are
currently evaluated as large banks would become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-bank
lending, investment, and service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements.
In Minnesota, the impact of these proposed changes will be drastic: 50 of 107 banks, comprising 46.7% of
all the banks in the state would no longer be required to reinvest in local community development projects
such as affordable housing, small business support, workforce development, community healthcare and
education services. About 19 of 36 banks, comprising 52.8% of all banks in the state would lose their large
bank status, thereby jeopardizing 49.6% of low-and moderate-income (LMI) census tracts in Minnesota.1
Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance
These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development performance is evaluated
and therefore affect the strength of banks' incentives to engage in community development. The agencies
acknowledge in the proposal that when banks become subject to a CD test under the current framework,
the explicit evaluation of their CD activities typically results in banks adjusting their CRA programs.
Banks moving down asset sizes and losing incentives for community development activities would have a
direct impact on our partnerships. For example, NDC currently partners with banks to provide gap funding
for entrepreneurs to achieve their projects. Under this model, a traditional bank will lead the loan process,
and NDC will provide supporting capital to meet the gap between what the bank can offer and the amount
the entrepreneur needs to accomplish the project. Frandsen Bank and Northeast Bank have often been
partners in these loans, and through this structure, in the past two years NDC and these partners have




funded projects totaling over $3 million. Under the new proposal, Frandsen Bank would lose its large-bank
status, and Northeast Bank would lose its community development obligations. They are two crucial
partners that provide funding for all entrepreneurs to successfully establish or expand businesses that
have positive effects on the Twin Cities' economic health.
NDC and CDFIs across the nation frequently rely on regional and community banks for patient debt,
deposits, investments, lines of credit, grants, and other forms of capital that allow us to reach borrowers
and projects that conventional financial institutions cannot efficiently serve directly.
Misalignment with Congressional Priorities on Affordable Housing and New Markets Tax Credit
(NMTC)
The change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
(LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) which are two bipartisan, popular federal tax tools with a long
track record of success in our communities. While Congress expanded LIHTC and made NMTC permanent,
the proposal undermines these important investment tools.
LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the standalone investment
test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted component of their CRA evaluation
devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into the lower size category would mean these transitioned
banks would only be subject to a diluted evaluation that considers all CD in one test. This means a bank
may have greater ability to emphasize CD lending rather than maintain the same level of LIHTC or NMTC
investment because investment performance no longer receives a separate rating. Through this weakened
regulatory incentive, bank demand for these investments would decrease.
Our organization, for example, has worked with banks that have provided $9,006,686 of NMTC investments.
That critical investment led to the creation of NDC's new headquarters at the intersection of key streets
Selby Ave and Dale Street, these headquarters provided increased capacity for the organization to serve
about 200 more entrepreneurs in the span of three years.
Significance of CRA data and transparency: Section IV.G, "Data Collection, Reporting, and
Disclosure"
The threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to large-bank
CRA data requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs, policymakers, and regulators
to identify credit gaps, compare bank performance, assess geographic disparities, and understand whether
community credit needs are being met. We are concerned that aggregate community development finance
data is already difficult to track and the proposal would excerbate the coverage of data, making it difficult to
identify and understand where credit is flowing.
Recommendation
For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and reject all
alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for consideration in Question 1).
The current thresholds are already annually indexed to CPI-W, so they are not beholden to 1995 asset
levels. Moreover, the justification of "restoring proportionality to 1995" that the agencies use in the
proposal does not adequately explain why raising asset thresholds better serve the statutory intent of the
CRA—which is to ensure that credit needs of LMI communities are met. For the small bank threshold, the




proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the number of banks such that nearly 80% of all banks
would be considered small, similar to what it was in 1995. While that's true, by the same logic, nearly 20%
of banks in 1995 were considered large whereas under the proposed large bank threshold, only a little over
2% of all banks would be considered large. Instead, the agencies selectively use total banking industry
share to justify the large bank threshold saying large banks would under this proposal, and similar to 1995
cover about 85% of all total bank industry's assets. Matching a 1995 distribution through either method
does not necessarily demonstrate that the resulting categories are appropriate for the modern banking
system. The industry has consolidated dramatically, bank business models and geographic reach have
changed. Banks with several billion dollars in assets today may have substantially greater lending,
investment, data, and operational capacity than institutions that were treated as small or intermediate,
three decades ago. The fact that assets happen to sit above a chosen threshold does not by itself establish
that banks below that threshold should lose the separate investment/service tests or associated data
requirements.
Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community Development Activities
— CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which: 1) requires a
qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a primary
purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, caps grant recipient's indirect administrative costs
to 15%; 3) requires that large banks obtain documentation from grant recipients including written
commitments regarding use of funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and operating and program
budgets. We also strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and
donations from CRA consideration entirely.
While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit
communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and misunderstand
the role that flexible operating support plays in community development finance. For CDFIs, staffing,
underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk management, data systems, financial management,
technical assistance, and product development are not ancillary to community development. They are the
infrastructure that makes community development lending possible.
Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA eligibility. An

Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section IV.B,

undoubtedly impair the flow of much needed capital in the most underserved communities.

institution (CDFI) whose mission is to empower entrepreneurs and community partners to transform low-
income neighborhoods from within. Our goal is to empower aspiring entrepreneurs in low to middle income
neighborhoods with business knowledge and access to opportunity to develop successful businesses that
allow them to create jobs, build wealth, and develop and transform their own neighborhoods. To do this, we
provide access to capital, training, business services, and affordable commercial real estate to around 500
entrepreneurs each year.

technical assistance and loan capital for NDC assisted entrepreneurs, and New Market Tax Credits (NMTC)

development ecosystem. We are therefore concerned that several provisions in the proposal could weaken

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Louisiana Appleseed appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC).1 We share the agencies' interest in a Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
framework that is clear, predictable, and workable for banks of every size. At the
same time, we are concerned that several provisions of the proposal could
unintentionally reduce the lending, services, and community development
partnerships that low- and moderate-income (LMI) Louisianans rely on. Given the
complexity of the rule and the scope of the changes, we respectfully request that
the OCC and FDIC, before finalizing any changes, carefully analyze the likely
consequences for LMI communities, provide an opportunity to comment on that
analysis and the evidence supporting any changes, and extend the current
comment deadline by 60 days.

1Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 Page 2 of 10

Since 2007, Louisiana Appleseed has worked to address the root causes of the
problems facing Louisiana's most vulnerable communities by creating access to
justice, opportunity, and education. As a member of a network of 20 Appleseed
public interest law centers, we mobilize pro bono attorneys and other professionals
to develop practical, lasting solutions. Through our Access to Opportunity program,
we help families protect and build wealth by clearing title to heirs' property,
hosting free will and estate planning clinics across the state, expanding access to
mainstream financial institutions, and supporting homeownership as a foundation
for disaster recovery and economic stability. Much of this work is possible because
of our partnerships with financial institutions, and we see banks as essential
partners in building strong Louisiana communities.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has provided a shared framework through which
banks, regulators, and communities work together to meet the credit needs of
entire communities, including LMI neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that
communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. That framework
is especially valuable in Louisiana, where many communities are still recovering
from hurricanes and flooding, where rural parishes have limited access to bank
branches, and where families in historically underserved neighborhoods continue
to face barriers to mainstream financial services.
We recognize the importance of reducing unnecessary regulatory burden, and we
support efforts to make CRA compliance more efficient. Our comments are offered
in that spirit. Our concern is that some of the proposed changes to how regulators
evaluate community development, bank services, and support for nonprofit
organizations could reduce the incentives for, and recognition of, the kinds of bank–
community partnerships that have worked well in Louisiana—and that these
effects have not yet been fully analyzed.
1. Maintaining Meaningful Community Investment Expectations
CRA expectations have encouraged banks to invest in communities throughout
Louisiana. In our state, from 2010 to 2024, banks made over $27 billion in CRA-
qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $19
billion in CRA-qualified lending to small businesses. This lending has helped
Louisiana families become first-time homeowners, rebuild after storms, and start
and grow small businesses, and it has supported the affordable housing and

Under the current rule, large banks are generally evaluated on their home
mortgage, small business, and small farm lending. The proposal outlines two
options for focusing examinations on a bank's "major product lines," based either
on its two largest product lines by overall lending volume or on the type of lending
the bank does most in a particular assessment area.13 Either option could leave

largest lines would tend to leave it outside CRA review. Home mortgage lending in

report data on small business, small farm, and community development lending.

in assets, meaning that over 400 banks would no longer collect and report this

business lending data nationwide. In Louisiana, 9 of the 18 large banks (50%)
would lose their community development obligations. Here, that means 320 bank
branches across the state would no longer provide meaningful data on the
communities they serve and the impact of their services.
Public CRA data benefits banks and communities alike. Louisiana Appleseed uses
publicly available data in our research and advocacy mapping to understand where
families face the greatest barriers and where partnerships with financial
institutions can have the greatest impact. Banks likewise use this information to
identify unmet needs, design products, and demonstrate the value of their
community investments. Without it, communities, regulators, researchers, and
banks would have less information to identify credit deserts, compare
performance, and understand whether local credit needs are being met.

services to the communities that need them most. Using GIS, parcel-level tax roll

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
I, Zoe Schwingel-Sauer, submit this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would
significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, I also request that the OCC and FDIC, before
making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-
income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the
agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.
I am a resident of Philadelphia and have lived here for over 22 years. I am committed to making
sure Philadelphia stays affordable for all residents, and that the regulatory bodies in charge also
honor the necessity of an equitable, healthy, and prospering Philadelphia. Every person deserves
the opportunity buy their first home or start a business and it is these very opportunities that
allow our city to flourish.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-
income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both
credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that
 have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream
financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. I am concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia
metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to
LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small
businesses.
I am concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote to
community investments and loans and I fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually,
but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million – an 80% loss.
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example,
across communities, a reduction in community development investments and loans
disproportionately affects first-time homebuyers, small-business owners, and residents who have
limited relationships with mainstream financial institutions. It is crucial to continue the
investment in Philadelphians and their communities. Not only are there numerous individual
benefits for these investments—which everyone is deserving of—but increasing home ownership
and strengthening the presence of small businesses in Philadelphia also extend benefits to the
broader community.
It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities.
Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would
reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and
whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be
disproportionately affected.
 The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business,
community development lending.
A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or
small banks under the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the country, may worsen the
housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC), and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for
home repairs.
Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service
test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and
information about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this
criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts
from direct evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate
whether those products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though
approximately 15% of Philadelphians – over 100,000 households – remain unbanked or
underbanked. Moreover, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these
households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and
features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address these
disparities by providing affordable products, and it must continue to do so.
For the people across Philadelphia communities, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts
are not separate from access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether
families can safely receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain
responsible credit. Punishing neighborhoods that have lost bank branches or residents who must
travel substantial distances to reach a branch reinforces cycles of economic inequality. The
Community Reinvestment Act is vital to acting as a buffer against these detrimental cycles and
increasing opportunity for every Philadelphian.
This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business
financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.
 The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
I am also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships
with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.
For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the
underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources
over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with
limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program documentation in the precise
format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves. These rules should be motivated by the needs of the communities CRA is
intended to serve and not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.
To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying
small business must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation,
retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income
communities.
The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could
earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs
for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. This
change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development credit and the
 people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying
business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an
underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.
I am also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and
report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks
with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA
data on small business loans and community development loans.
Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs
are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision
making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This proposed change is
inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the
final rule.
Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
●
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
under the proposal;
●
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
●
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color; and
●
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes
that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
 consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
I also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. I therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
I, Zoe Schwingel-Sauer, submit this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would
significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, I also request that the OCC and FDIC, before
making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-
income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the
agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.
I am a resident of Philadelphia and have lived here for over 22 years. I am committed to making
sure Philadelphia stays affordable for all residents, and that the regulatory bodies in charge also
honor the necessity of an equitable, healthy, and prospering Philadelphia. Every person deserves
the opportunity buy their first home or start a business and it is these very opportunities that
allow our city to flourish.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-
income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both
credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that
 have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream
financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. I am concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia
metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to
LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small
businesses.
I am concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote to
community investments and loans and I fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually,
but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million – an 80% loss.
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example,
across communities, a reduction in community development investments and loans
disproportionately affects first-time homebuyers, small-business owners, and residents who have
limited relationships with mainstream financial institutions. It is crucial to continue the
investment in Philadelphians and their communities. Not only are there numerous individual
benefits for these investments—which everyone is deserving of—but increasing home ownership
and strengthening the presence of small businesses in Philadelphia also extend benefits to the
broader community.
It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities.
Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would
reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and
whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be
disproportionately affected.
 The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business,
community development lending.
A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or
small banks under the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the country, may worsen the
housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC), and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for
home repairs.
Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service
test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and
information about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this
criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts
from direct evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate
whether those products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though
approximately 15% of Philadelphians – over 100,000 households – remain unbanked or
underbanked. Moreover, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these
households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and
features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address these
disparities by providing affordable products, and it must continue to do so.
For the people across Philadelphia communities, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts
are not separate from access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether
families can safely receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain
responsible credit. Punishing neighborhoods that have lost bank branches or residents who must
travel substantial distances to reach a branch reinforces cycles of economic inequality. The
Community Reinvestment Act is vital to acting as a buffer against these detrimental cycles and
increasing opportunity for every Philadelphian.
This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business
financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.
 The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
I am also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships
with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.
For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the
underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources
over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with
limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program documentation in the precise
format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves. These rules should be motivated by the needs of the communities CRA is
intended to serve and not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.
To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying
small business must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation,
retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income
communities.
The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could
earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs
for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. This
change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development credit and the
 people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying
business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an
underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.
I am also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and
report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks
with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA
data on small business loans and community development loans.
Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs
are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision
making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This proposed change is
inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the
final rule.
Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
●
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
under the proposal;
●
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
●
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color; and
●
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes
that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
 consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
I also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. I therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Sincerely,
Zoe Schwingel-Sauer

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) (collectively, the agencies)'s
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking proposing major revisions to the Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA).
ROC USA is a nonprofit social enterprise working to preserve and expand resident
ownership of manufactured home communities. ROC USA and its network of nine state-
based partner organizations provide technical assistance, business coaching, and
financing options to 365 Resident Owned Communities in 22 states, preserving the
affordability of totaling more than 24,700 manufactured home sites. Each ROC formed not
only permanently preserves critically important affordable housing, but it also gives
residents the power to preserve and improve their community – setting rents and other
policies and making investments in community infrastructure and improvements.
ROC USA's affiliate ROC USA Capital (a Community Development Financial Institution)
offers acquisition and construction loans to resident owned communities (ROCs), making
it possible for resident cooperatives to purchase the land beneath their homes and repair
the infrastructure so that the communities remain safe, high-quality, and affordable. More
than 87% of the residents of these communities are low-income, and sixty percent are
very-low income. About half of ROCs are in rural communities, which are often
underserved by banks. ROC Capital fills a clear market gap, providing credit to a group of
borrowers that conventional lending institutions had largely declined to serve, and we do


this work successfully: making loans where borrowers succeed and providing consistent
mission-adjusted returns to our partners.
ROC USA Capital has provided $550 million in financing since 2008 and has $400 million in
assets under management. Network-wide, ROC financing exceeds $1 billion – a lending
total that is only possible because of an ecosystem of financing partners that includes
banks, other CDFIs, state housing finance agencies, insurance companies, and impact
investors. Bank partners provide the majority of balance sheet debt that ROC Capital
leverages to make loans. Banks are also critical partners to ROC USA Capital through loan
participations, and to ROC USA by providing operating grant support that enables us to
provide on-the-ground technical assistance to ROC borrowers, invest in our lending
technology systems, research and launch new products, and other critical functions.
The Community Reinvestment Act has provided a durable incentive for banks to provide
loans, investments, grants, and services in communities that have historically lacked
access to capital, and banks achieve this in part by partnering with CDFIs like ROC USA
Capital. These partnerships are transformational for ROC USA Capital, as they facilitate
access to capital that is critical in enabling resident ownership. We are therefore greatly
concerned that the agencies' proposal would largely weaken the CRA framework, reduce
incentives for banks to build and sustain relationships with CDFIs, and ultimately impair
the flow of capital in underserved communities.
Below, we describe our three largest concerns with the agencies' proposed rule. We urge
the agencies to withdraw these proposals.
The Proposed Asset Thresholds Threaten Housing and Community Development
Investment and Financing
Under the proposed rule, banks with assets between $1.649 billion and $10 billion would
no longer receive the full large-bank examination threshold with separate lending,
investment and service tests. This will reduce scrutiny and transparency on community
development investments and likely result in fewer bank investments serving CRA-eligible
populations. As a result of the proposal, only the largest 6% of banks would face separate
reviews of their community development loans/investments.
These concerns are not theoretical. About $19 million (12.5%) of ROC USA Capital's
balance sheet investments are provided by banks that would be reclassified from large to
intermediate institutions under this proposal.
In addition, the proposal to raise the small bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion
would eliminate community development evaluations for roughly 814 banks, or about 40%
of the banks currently subject to that requirement.


How a bank's community development performance is evaluated has a large effect on the
strength of banks' incentives to engage in community development. We urge the agencies
to retain the current thresholds and reject all alternatives offered. The current thresholds
are already annually indexed to CPI-W, so they are not beholden to 1995 asset levels. As a
principle of any reforms going forward, we urge the agencies to maintain meaningful
community development responsibilities for banks of all sizes.
The Proposed Restrictions on Grants Will Severely Weaken Community Development
Finance Activities
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants,
including: 1) the requirement that a qualifying grant be directly used by the recipient for a
community development program, project, or initiative; 2) for large banks, caps on a grant
recipient's indirect administrative costs; 3) and the requirement that large banks obtain
documentation from grant recipients including written commitments regarding use of
funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and operating and program budgets. We
also strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and
donations from CRA consideration entirely. Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15%
indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA eligibility. An organization's administrative-cost
percentage is not an appropriate proxy for community impact. The proposal would also
significantly increase compliance burden, which directly contradicts the agencies' stated
goals for the proposed rulemaking.
While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully
benefit communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective
grantmaking and misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in enabling
community development finance. Grant support to invest in ROC USA Capital's lending
technology systems are critical for risk management and ultimately help lower transaction
costs through greater efficiency. Grant support enabling ROC USA to provide technical
assistance to ROC borrowers is critical for delivering on our mission of empowering
residents while also protecting investors. And grant support that allows ROC USA Capital to
research and launch new products helps us expand our impact while fully assessing risks
and rewards in advance.
The Proposal Weakens Expectations for Community Development
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a
Satisfactory rating on both its lending test and its community development test to receive
an overall Satisfactory rating. The proposal would require a Satisfactory or better lending-
test rating but would allow lending performance to compensate for weaker community


development performance. If weak community development performance does not
prevent an overall Satisfactory rating, banks may have less regulatory incentive to make
CDFI loans and investments, provide grants, or undertake other community development
activities. This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset
thresholds. We urge the agencies to retain a requirement that intermediate banks
demonstrate at least Satisfactory community development performance to receive an
overall Satisfactory rating.
Conclusion
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve the Community Reinvestment Act, which
remains a cornerstone of community development finance and provides strong incentives
for banks to provide credit in underserved communities. As the agencies consider further
reforms, we urge you to withdraw the three proposals described above.
- Emily Thaden, Chief Executive Officer, ROC USA
