3064-AG31]
Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould,
Growth Homes opposes any weakening of the 1995 Community Reinvestment Act framework.
Keep it. Enforce it. Decline the parts of this proposal that loosen it. Enforce it, not to embrace an
ideology, but to ensure that banks remain focused on helping Americans afford reasonably-
priced homes.
We are a homebuilder. We build homes for working families in Birmingham, Atlanta, Dallas–Fort
Worth, Columbus, OH, and other markets, and we price them to be within reach. That mission
runs on capital largely supplied by CRA-regulated banks. Land does not develop itself. Lots do
not finance themselves. A buyer earning 80-120% of area median income does not close unless
a lender is willing, and expected, to say yes. CRA-regulated banks, concerned about the
scrutiny that comes from the current enforcement scheme, offer portfolio loans with terms
designed to ensure that the loans are sustainable but fair, often eliminating PMI (private
mortgage insurance) and offering assistance to buyers in the form of down payment, closing
costs, or interest-rate buydown assistance.
In our experience, much of that willingness comes from one place. It comes from a bank that
knows an examiner will look at what it did for the community and will write down the answer.
Quite simply, their incentive to provide these kinds of portfolio loans will be reduced in
proportion to the reduction in enforcement and oversight provided by the OCC and FDIC.
What we have seen
We do not comment on this rulemaking as theorists. We comment as a builder who uses the
system as it exists today.
Capital shows up where examiners are looking. Land acquisition and horizontal development
are the hardest dollars to raise for affordable communities. Banks that are evaluated on
community development lending and investment have been willing to fund them.
 Travis Hill
Jonathan V. Gould
October 13, 2026
Page 2
Since our inception in 2015, we have built 1200 new, or acquired and rehabilitated existing,
homes in 20 cities/regions. Through an increase in investment and lending capital from CRA-
regulated banks, we have recently raised sufficient capital to build an additional 6,000 affordable
homes between now and 2034-35. Motivated by CRA and the enforcement/oversight provided
by the prudential regulators, 35 banks have invested in funds designed to create starter and first
move-up homes in communities that had been largely redlined before enactment of CRA in
1977. For example, we are building 53 single-family homes in the ShadowBrook neighborhood
of the Pratt community in Birmingham, Alabama. This is the first significant investment in that
community since tornados devastated it in 2011. Along with developments in two other
neighborhoods, we are the largest builder in the City of Birmingham, and we are focused on
bringing more mixed-income development to that city (and the others we invest in) in an effort
that is framed by the current standards applied by prudential regulators.
Buyers need more than a mortgage rate. First-time buyers need counseling, down payment
help, and a lender who knows the product. Our Growth Homes for Community Heroes program,
which opens homeownership to military families and veterans as well as first responders,
teachers, and nurses in Birmingham, works because partners treat these buyers as a market to
serve and not a risk to avoid. Two of our banks in Birmingham have agreed to co-invest by
offering terms for mortgages that recognize the unaffordability of current interest rates. Without
their flexibility, many of the homes we build would be unaffordable to the homebuyers cities
need most – police, fire, EMT, nurses, teachers, and others who deserve an opportunity to live
affordably in the cities they serve. It is the consistent enforcement of CRA, through the current
regulatory process, that provides the correcting lens in how banking institutions view
neighborhoods that otherwise have historically been largely avoided.
Branches and deposit relationships matter. A family does not become a homeowner on the day
of closing. It happens years earlier, at a teller window or on a first savings account. The three-
part test of the 1995 rule measures that whole path.
Banks respond to exams, not exhortations. A rule that is read, tested, and enforced changes
behavior. A rule that can be satisfied on paper does not.
Where the proposal loosens the 1995 framework
The agencies call these changes targeted. Taken together, they move the line -- backwards. Six
concern us most:
The large bank threshold. Raising it from $1.649 billion to $10 billion would take the regional
banks that lend in markets like ours out of the lending, investment, and service tests. Those are
the banks closest to the neighborhoods we build in. Fewer banks held to the investment test
means less equity and patient capital for affordable homeownership.
The intermediate bank rating. As we read the proposal, an intermediate bank could earn a
Satisfactory or Outstanding rating on the strength of its lending test. Community development
would become optional in practice. Optional work gets done last, and in a downturn, it does not
get done at all.
The service test. Limiting it to credit services drops deposit products and the distribution of
branches. Branch closures in lower-income neighborhoods are often the first sign of
disinvestment. An examiner should be able to see them and score them.
 Travis Hill
Jonathan V. Gould
October 13, 2026
Page 3
Community development grants. A 15% cap on indirect costs and a direct-use requirement
sound like fiscal discipline. In practice, they punish the small counseling agencies and
intermediaries that carry real overhead. Banks will fund fewer of them. The first thing cut will be
homebuyer counseling, the work that makes a first-time buyer mortgage-ready. Building starter
homes "on spec" requires a pipeline of mortgage-ready borrowers. If we care about building
starter homes in this country, meaning with sustainable mortgages, we cannot threaten our best
sources of training to help potential homeowners become full-fledged participants in the
American Dream. [As evidence of the tide that we and cooperating banks are facing: note that in
the 1970s the US was building 440,000 starter homes/year and by 2016 that number had fallen
to 65,000 per year. Reference: NAHB]
The litigation judgment. We understand the agencies intend to ask the court for a judgment
that would bar future rules from taking an expansive view of the "entire community" or of "credit
needs." A statute written by Congress should not be narrowed by agreement between a
regulator and the plaintiffs. Future agencies must keep the freedom to read the Act as written.
One more point. This proposal applies to banks supervised by the OCC and the FDIC and
leaves Federal Reserve banks on the 1995 rules. Two standards for the same statute invite
banks to choose the lighter one. CRA has worked best as a uniform, interagency standard.
Why a strong rule pays off locally
A well-enforced CRA is not a cost to a community. It is an investment that a city or region gets
back. Homeownership not only assists the families that directly benefit, it stabilizes and helps
redevelop communities that would otherwise be dominated by rental units. Of course, the
disparity in wealth building for those families that rent instead of own is so wide that the
communities that CRA was intended to benefit will remain, at best, in stasis and, at worst, with
accelerated deterioration owing to a lack of investment. CRA-regulated banks offer hope to
these communities in ways that other statutes and federal policies simply don't begin to touch.
Bank capital is patient and local. It tends to arrive alongside public and philanthropic dollars,
such as HOME and CDBG funds, tax credits, and state housing trust funds, and it makes those
dollars go further. A mayor who can count on that capital can plan a neighborhood. One who
cannot is left hoping.
The returns are concrete. New homeowners become taxpayers and customers on a main street.
Their children occupy schools that in many cities are threatened with extinction. Stable
workforce housing helps local employers hire and keep people. Owned homes anchor blocks
that would otherwise empty out, and a family's equity becomes the next generation's start.
These benefits depend on banks believing that performance will be measured and that results
will have consequences. Weaken the measure and the capital goes elsewhere.
What we ask of the agencies
•
Treat the 1995 framework as the floor. Finalize nothing that reduces the number of
banks examined, the tests applied, or the weight given to community development.
•
Keep the large bank threshold at its current inflation-adjusted level, and keep the annual
adjustment.
•
Require performance on the community development test for any intermediate bank to
earn a Satisfactory or Outstanding rating.
•
Keep deposit services and branch distribution in the service test.
 Travis Hill
Jonathan V. Gould
October 13, 2026
Page 4
•
Drop the 15% indirect cost cap and the direct-use requirement. Let banks continue to
support qualified intermediaries and counseling agencies, with transparency in place of a
hard limit.
•
Do not seek or agree to a judgment that limits how future agencies may read the statute.
•
Keep the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve on one interagency standard.
The 1995 rule has helped us build homes that working families can own. It has helped
communities we serve see investment they would not otherwise have seen. Please do not trade
that away for burden relief. We would welcome the chance to walk agency staff through our
projects and share what we have learned.
Respectfully submitted,
Ed Gorman
Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer
Growth Homes

NHSIE Comment — Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 / RIN 3064-AG31 · Page 1
 About NHSIE
For more than four decades, NHSIE has helped working families in San Bernardino and Riverside Counties
become and remain homeowners. Our two-county service area is home to more than 4.6 million people
across roughly 27,000 square miles, and it is one of the most housing-stressed regions in California. NHSIE is
a certified Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI), a HUD-approved housing counseling agency,
a Community Housing Development Organization (CHDO), and a charter member of NeighborWorks
America. We bring HUD-approved counseling and homebuyer education, down payment assistance, our
Empire Builder matched savings program, CDFI lending, and attainable homeownership development
together on a single path from renting to owning.
Our work is concentrated where the market has not reached on its own: four neighborhoods in the City of
San Bernardino — the 13th Street corridor, 49th Street, 6th and G, and Arrowhead Grove — along with the
High Desert and the Hemet/San Jacinto area. In 2025 alone, NHSIE served 662 households, delivered 435
one-on-one counseling sessions, graduated 206 adults from our eight-hour HUD-approved homebuyer
education course, distributed $381,000 in down payment assistance, and helped 106 families close on a
home. Eighty-two percent of our clients were approved for a mortgage, up from 71 percent the year before,
and 82 percent of the households we served were led by women. Since 2011, we have educated 8,950
households and created 3,790 new homebuyers; since 1991, NHSIE clients have purchased more than $1.06
billion in homes across the Inland Empire.
Banks Are Essential Partners in This Work
Banks are critical partners in everything described above. Our bank relationships include down payment
assistance grants — among them a $500,000 commitment from a national bank partner — program and
operating grants that sustain our counseling and education staff, deposit relationships, first-mortgage lending
partnerships that turn our clients into borrowers, and active discussions with large banks about
equity-equivalent (EQ2) investments to capitalize our loan fund. Bank support works alongside significant
public capital, including a $621,000 CDFI Fund Financial Assistance award to launch a first-mortgage program
and $2 million in down payment assistance through the Southern California Association of Governments. In
our experience, bank participation is often what makes public dollars deployable: public programs fund the
assistance, and bank support funds the counseling, underwriting, and closing capacity that turns assistance
into keys.
These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing capital and resources to CDFIs, banks
rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, develop borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers.
Every NHSIE client who completed our programs in 2025 opened or maintained a bank and savings account.
Forty-four percent of our counseling clients raised their credit scores, up from 10 percent the prior year.
Households that arrive at our door unbanked, credit-invisible, or declined for a mortgage leave as account
holders and qualified borrowers — customers our bank partners could not have efficiently developed on
their own. CRA has long created the incentives for banks to build and sustain these relationships. We are
therefore concerned that several provisions in the proposal would weaken those incentives, reduce bank
engagement with CDFIs, and ultimately reduce the flow of capital to the communities we serve.
NHSIE Comment — Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 / RIN 3064-AG31 · Page 2
 Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section IV.A, "Asset
Thresholds"; Questions 1–3
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks as
institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with more than $10
billion. According to the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC), roughly 814 banks — about 40
percent of the banks currently subject to a community development requirement — would lose community
development evaluation entirely, and another 417 banks would drop from large to intermediate status,
losing the separate investment and service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements. Only
about 6 percent of banks would retain a separate community development review.2
The effect reaches directly into LMI neighborhoods. NCRC estimates that more than 5,000 bank branches in
LMI census tracts — roughly 30 percent of all LMI-area branches nationally — and more than 4,000 branches
in majority-people-of-color neighborhoods would lose separate evaluation under the proposal. In the Inland
Empire, regional and community banks are among the institutions that know our market best, and several of
the regional banks we work with or are actively evaluating as partners fall squarely within the asset bands
the proposal would reclassify.
California has just enacted its own Community Reinvestment Act, covering state-chartered banks, credit
unions, mortgage lenders, and financial technology firms.3 That law is a meaningful step, but it cannot reach
the nationally chartered banks the OCC supervises. The federal framework remains the floor for community
reinvestment in our state, and the proposal would lower that floor at precisely the moment communities are
working to build on it.
Impact on High Desert and Smaller Markets
The consequences are especially significant in the smaller and more remote markets we serve. Communities
in the High Desert and the Hemet/San Jacinto area have fewer financial institutions, thinner branch networks
relative to population, and longer distances between residents and services than the urban core of the
region. In these communities, the loss of even one or two CRA-motivated bank partners can determine
whether a homebuyer education cohort runs, whether a down payment assistance file closes, or whether a
senior homeowner gets the repair loan that keeps her housed. For markets with fewer sources of private
capital to begin with, losing a handful of CRA-motivated lenders and investors would have an outsized effect.
Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance
These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development performance is evaluated,
and therefore the strength of a bank's incentive to engage in community development at all. The agencies
acknowledge in the proposal that when banks become subject to a community development test under the
current framework, the explicit evaluation of their community development activities typically leads them to
adjust their CRA programs. The reverse is equally true.
For NHSIE, the exposure is direct. Our lending strategy depends on bank EQ2 investments and grants that are
planned around banks' CRA examination cycles. When a bank's separate investment test disappears, so does
much of the internal case for a patient, subordinated investment in a community-based CDFI loan fund.
When community development performance is folded into a single diluted test — or eliminated for banks

 below $1 billion — the bank officers who champion partnerships with organizations like ours lose the
regulatory standing that makes those partnerships possible.
The dollar amounts at stake for any single bank may appear modest. For our community, they are not. In
2025, 435 counseling sessions and 206 homebuyer education graduates produced 106 new homeowners —
families whose purchases add to the more than $1 billion in homes NHSIE clients have bought in the Inland
Empire. That pipeline runs on counseling staff, and counseling staff are funded in large part by flexible bank
support. CDFIs frequently rely on regional and community banks for patient debt, deposits, investments,
lines of credit, grants, and other forms of capital that allow us to reach borrowers and projects that
conventional financial institutions cannot efficiently serve directly.
Significance of CRA Data and Transparency: Section IV.G, "Data Collection, Reporting, and
Disclosure"
The threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to large-bank CRA
data requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs, policymakers, and regulators to
identify credit gaps, compare bank performance, assess geographic disparities, and understand whether
community credit needs are being met. Aggregate community development finance data is already difficult
to track, and the proposal would further erode its coverage.
Place-based strategies like NHSIE's depend on public lending data. We are concentrating counseling,
rehabilitation lending, and down payment assistance in specific San Bernardino neighborhoods and outlying
markets so that investment compounds rather than scatters. Deciding where to work, and demonstrating to
public and private funders that it is working, requires visibility into where mortgage and small business credit
is and is not reaching. Removing hundreds of institutions from data reporting would blind communities and
lenders alike to the very gaps CRA exists to close.
Recommendation
For the reasons above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and reject all alternatives
offered, including the substantially higher thresholds raised for consideration in Question 1. The current
thresholds are already indexed annually to CPI-W, so they are not tied to 1995 asset levels. Moreover, the
agencies' stated justification of "restoring proportionality to 1995" does not explain why raising asset
thresholds better serves the statutory purpose of CRA — ensuring that the credit needs of LMI communities
are met. For the small bank threshold, the proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the number of
banks, such that nearly 80 percent of all banks would be considered small, as in 1995. By the same logic,
however, nearly 20 percent of banks were considered large in 1995, whereas under the proposed large-bank
threshold only a little over 2 percent would be. The agencies instead use share of total industry assets to
justify the large-bank threshold. Matching a 1995 distribution by either method does not demonstrate that
the resulting categories are appropriate for the modern banking system. The industry has consolidated
dramatically, and bank business models and geographic reach have changed. A bank with several billion
dollars in assets today may have substantially greater lending, investment, data, and operational capacity
than institutions treated as small or intermediate three decades ago. The fact that a bank's assets sit below a
chosen threshold does not by itself establish that it should lose the separate investment and service tests or
associated data requirements.
NHSIE Comment — Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 / RIN 3064-AG31 · Page 4
 Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community Development
Activities — CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants, which would (1) require a
qualifying grant to be used directly by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a primary
purpose of community development; (2) for large banks, cap a recipient's indirect administrative costs at 15
percent; and (3) require large banks to obtain documentation from grant recipients, including written
commitments regarding use of funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and operating and program
budgets.
Question 10: Grants and donations must remain creditable
We most strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and donations
from CRA consideration entirely. Grants are the only form of bank support that can fund the counselors,
educators, and underwriters who make community development lending and homeownership possible.
Loans and investments must be repaid or returned; the capacity to originate, prepare, and support
borrowers must be paid for by someone. Eliminating CRA consideration for grants would not redirect that
support into lending — it would simply remove it, and with it the borrower pipeline that bank lending
depends on.
The proposal disqualifies the work it should be encouraging
In explaining the 15 percent indirect-cost limit, the agencies offer as their example of a grant that would no
longer qualify a grant to a community development organization directly providing homeownership
counseling to LMI individuals (91 Fed. Reg. at 52119). That is precisely what NHSIE does. HUD-approved
housing counseling is among the most rigorously regulated and outcome-tested community development
services in the country, and Congress has just strengthened HUD's oversight of it through new performance
reviews, retesting, and certification requirements in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (P.L. 119-101). A
rule that treats this work as an illustration of what CRA should not support has its priorities reversed.
The proposal measures indirect costs under OMB Uniform Guidance or a comparable methodology, yet
discards the Uniform Guidance's own central principle: that a federally negotiated indirect cost rate is the
legitimate rate for an organization administering federal programs. Fifteen percent is the Uniform Guidance
de minimis rate for entities without a negotiated rate. A multi-program HUD grantee and CDFI with audit,
compliance, data, and certification obligations will properly exceed it. The test is also all-or-nothing rather
than pro-rata: a grant that exceeds the limit by a single percentage point fails to count entirely.
While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit communities,
these requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and misunderstand the role that
flexible operating support plays in community development finance. For CDFIs, staffing, underwriting,
servicing, compliance, technology, risk management, data systems, financial management, technical
assistance, and product development are not ancillary to community development. They are the
infrastructure that makes community development lending possible.
NHSIE uses flexible bank support to pay for exactly that infrastructure: HUD-certified counselors and
homebuyer educators; the client data system that tracks every household from intake to closing; compliance
with HUD housing counseling requirements; and the underwriting capacity behind our down payment
assistance and CDFI lending. That infrastructure is why 662 households were served and 106 families became
homeowners in 2025, and it is why our mortgage approval rate rose from 71 to 82 percent in a single year.
None of it fits neatly inside a single program budget, and none of it is overhead in any meaningful sense.
NHSIE Comment — Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 / RIN 3064-AG31 · Page 5
 Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15 percent indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA eligibility. An
organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for community impact. Costs vary
with an organization's size, geography, product mix, regulatory obligations, technical-assistance model, and
populations served. The cap would disproportionately harm small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs
making small-dollar loans, organizations providing intensive borrower counseling and technical assistance,
CDFIs developing new products or entering underserved markets, and organizations making necessary
investments in technology, compliance, data, and risk management. The documentation requirements would
compound that harm by shifting compliance burden from banks onto the smallest, most locally rooted
grantees.
We also note that the proposal contains no analysis of the aggregate effect of these provisions on grant
volume, on general operating support, or on the capacity of smaller nonprofits. It offers the disqualification
of housing counseling as an illustration without estimating its consequences. Before finalizing any restriction
of this magnitude, the agencies should analyze and publish its expected effects on the organizations and
communities CRA is meant to serve.
One provision that helps locally rooted organizations
We do want to acknowledge one feature of the proposal that serves communities well. Requiring that
large-bank grants serve the bank's own assessment areas favors organizations rooted in the communities
they serve over distant intermediaries. For an agency headquartered and working in San Bernardino and
Riverside Counties, that is a sound principle, and we encourage the agencies to retain it.
Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building grants, as is
currently the case under the 1995 framework, and should reject the alternative in Question 10. If the
agencies retain any indirect-cost test, a recipient's federally negotiated indirect cost rate — or, for a
HUD-approved housing counseling agency or certified CDFI, its cost allocation as reviewed by its federal
regulator or auditor — should be deemed to satisfy it, and the test should apply pro-rata rather than
all-or-nothing. Documentation requirements should rely on information grantees already produce, such as
audited financial statements and Form 990s, rather than new attestations. CRA should give banks the
flexibility to provide the form of support that best responds to identified community needs, without
imposing undue compliance burdens on the organizations doing the work.
Interacting Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community Development Incentives
Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section IV.B, "Performance
Tests — Intermediate Bank Ratings"
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a Satisfactory
rating on both its lending test and its community development test to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
The proposal would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would allow lending performance
to compensate for weaker community development performance.
This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset thresholds, which would
move hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-bank framework into the intermediate
category. In NHSIE's experience, bank decisions about CDFI investments, grants, and partnerships are closely
tied to CRA examination cycles; the prospect of a community development rating that carries real
consequences is often what brings those conversations to the table. If weak community development
NHSIE Comment — Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 / RIN 3064-AG31 · Page 6
 performance no longer prevents an overall Satisfactory rating, banks will have less reason to make CDFI loans
and investments, provide grants, or undertake other community development activities. We urge the
agencies to retain the requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate at least Satisfactory community
development performance to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
Complexity definition anchored to lending is too narrow: Section IV.C, "Qualitative Factors"; Questions
12–17
The proposal would define complexity for community development investments, grants, and services largely
by whether an activity is a necessary or beneficial component of a multicomponent financing transaction
involving a loan. We oppose a lending-centric definition of complexity. Investments in CDFIs can involve
specialized expertise, layered capital, subordinate positions, public subsidies, risk sharing, guarantees,
tax-credit structures, patient repayment terms, or other features that make transactions complex even when
they are not paired with a particular bank loan. We also oppose requiring community development
investments or services to be complex, as contemplated in Question 14, or treating complexity as
categorically more responsive than innovation, flexibility, or impact, as contemplated in Question 15.
An EQ2 investment in NHSIE's loan fund illustrates the problem. Such an investment is long-term, deeply
subordinated, and structured to leverage a CDFI Fund award, public down payment assistance, and
first-mortgage financing from other institutions. It is complex by any reasonable measure — yet it would not
be a component of a multicomponent transaction involving a loan by the investing bank. The proposal is also
silent on EQ2 investments altogether, despite their long record as one of the most effective tools for
capitalizing CDFIs. The agencies should assess complexity, innovativeness, flexibility, impact, and
responsiveness based on the characteristics and community value of the activity itself, rather than its
association with a lending transaction, and should expressly recognize EQ2 investments in CDFIs.
Prevent ordinary retail lending from substituting for specialized CD lending: Section IV.B, "Retail Lending
Product Lines," Questions 4–7; and Section IV.C, "CD Loans"
The proposal would evaluate retail lending only in a bank's major product lines, and would allow a loan in a
retail product line that is not evaluated as a major product line to receive consideration as a community
development loan if it otherwise satisfies the community development definition. We agree that genuinely
community-development-oriented financing should not lose CRA consideration simply because its product
line is excluded from the retail evaluation. However, this interaction creates a risk that ordinary-course
small-business, small-farm, or other retail lending could substitute for more specialized community
development lending that depends more directly on CRA incentives. The agencies should require a
meaningful community development nexus and ensure that this provision does not allow banks to satisfy
community development expectations primarily through activity they would undertake in the ordinary
course of business.
Essential community infrastructure and facilities should retain a meaningful CD nexus: Section IV.D,
"Community Development Definition — Revitalization and Stabilization"; Question 25
We support CRA consideration for essential community facilities and infrastructure, particularly in rural
communities, Indian Country, distressed areas, and other markets with limited access to conventional
capital. The proposal, however, would broaden eligibility for essential community infrastructure and facilities
serving specified targeted areas so that these activities would no longer need to demonstrate that they help
attract or retain businesses or residents, and community-wide infrastructure could receive consideration
without allocating a particular share of the benefit to LMI individuals. We are concerned that large
infrastructure transactions routinely financed in the conventional market could crowd out affordable
NHSIE Comment — Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 / RIN 3064-AG31 · Page 7
 housing, CDFI financing, homeownership assistance, small-business lending, and other activities more
dependent on CRA incentives. The agencies should preserve flexibility where infrastructure addresses a
genuine community development or financing gap, while ensuring that ordinary-course infrastructure
transactions do not displace more targeted community development activity.
Strategic plans require strong guardrails: Section IV.F, "Strategic Plan"; particularly Questions 38–53
We support efforts to provide greater clarity regarding strategic plans and measurable goals. Because
strategic plans allow banks to develop individualized CRA performance standards, however, strong guardrails
are essential to ensure that banks do not circumvent the rigorous and reasonably consistent expectations
applied to similarly situated institutions. The agencies should require strategic-plan goals to be responsive to
demonstrated community needs; sufficiently rigorous to approximate the performance expected under the
standard CRA tests; transparent and measurable; subject to meaningful public engagement; and evaluated
against clear standards for determining whether the goals adequately address assessment-area credit needs.
We particularly urge the agencies to establish strong standards in response to Question 53, which asks when
measurable goals should be considered inadequate to address assessment-area needs. Given the proposal's
automatic approval of plans on agency silence, those standards are all the more important.
Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E, "CD Activities Outside
Assessment Areas"; proposed § __.13(e); Question 34
We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with significant unmet needs
but relatively few bank assessment areas. Greater geographic flexibility could be particularly beneficial for
reaching CRA deserts. Parts of NHSIE's own service area — including High Desert communities and the
Hemet/San Jacinto area — have bank footprints that are thin relative to their population and need, and they
have historically struggled to attract CRA-motivated capital on the scale of the region's urban core.
However, flexibility should supplement rather than displace community development activity in banks' own
assessment areas. With respect to Question 34, we support greater geographic flexibility where it can direct
CRA-motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas outside traditional
assessment areas, but only after a bank has demonstrated meaningful community development
performance within its own assessment areas.
The quantitative standard proposed under Option 1 is too low to meet that objective. For large banks, the
proposal would allow outside-assessment-area consideration once a bank reaches 0.625 percent of allocated
Tier 1 capital in community development loans and 0.625 percent in community development investments
and grants. The agencies themselves explain that these thresholds generally reflect the minimum level of
activity needed to avoid a "Needs to Improve" rating and are not, by themselves, sufficient to demonstrate
satisfactory performance. NCRC's analysis illustrates the gap: among 69 large OCC- and FDIC-supervised
banks, current annual assessment-area community development lending, investments, and grants totaled
approximately $102 billion, while applying the proposed 0.625 percent benchmarks to the same institutions
yields roughly $14.8 billion — about 85 percent below current activity. NCRC also found median
assessment-area community development lending equal to 6.83 percent of Tier 1 capital and median
qualified investments and grants equal to roughly 3.5 percent, both far above the proposed benchmarks.4
A standard intended to determine when a bank has adequately served its own communities should be
calibrated to meaningful, satisfactory community development performance — not the minimum necessary
to avoid a failing rating. We encourage the agencies to adopt a more rigorous standard that considers both
4National Community Reinvestment Coalition, analysis of 100 largest OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks (Sept. 10, 2026).
NHSIE Comment — Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 / RIN 3064-AG31 · Page 8
 the level of activity and its responsiveness to identified community needs, and we caution against allowing a
broadly defined "substantially met" standard to weaken this safeguard. Any exception should be narrowly
tailored to circumstances in which a documented lack of community development opportunities or other
performance-context factors explain a shortfall, rather than allowing weak performance in individual
assessment areas to be offset by activity elsewhere.
Allocation of CD activities across assessment areas: Section IV.E, "Assessment Area Allocation, Assigning
Assessment Area Weights"
We support greater flexibility in allocating community development activities that benefit multiple
assessment areas. This would better accommodate regional CDFIs whose community impact is not
accurately represented by the location of their headquarters. NHSIE, for example, is headquartered in the
City of San Bernardino, but our clients live across San Bernardino and Riverside Counties — from the High
Desert to Hemet and San Jacinto. Assigning an entire bank investment in NHSIE to our headquarters location
would not accurately represent the communities benefiting from that capital.
Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development Finance
Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD Loans"; Question 8
We strongly support providing CRA consideration for qualifying community development loans that remain
outstanding from prior evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-period investments.
Community development borrowers frequently need long-term, patient financing, and CRA should
encourage banks to structure loans around community needs rather than examination cycles. With respect
to Question 8, we recommend evaluation-period-based consideration because it better recognizes patient,
long-term financing, provides a more representative measure of capital committed throughout the
examination period than an annual snapshot, and brings parity to the treatment of loans and investments.
The agencies should base consideration on the average outstanding balance, or otherwise account for both
the amount and duration of the exposure, and should treat repeated renewals of substantially the same loan
as a single exposure.
Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process: Section IV.E, "Illustrative List" and
"Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions 32–33
We strongly support establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of eligible community
development activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of eligibility. This is among the most
constructive features of the proposal. The OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve should seek to maintain consistent
standards and, ideally, a single interagency list.
The proposal is silent on several activities that are central to LMI homeownership and that banks need
certainty to support. We urge the agencies to name the following expressly on the illustrative list: (1)
HUD-approved housing counseling and homebuyer education, including general support to HUD-approved
counseling agencies; (2) down payment and closing cost assistance for LMI and first-time homebuyers; (3)
matched savings and individual development account programs, such as NHSIE's Empire Builder program; (4)
equity-equivalent (EQ2) investments, loans, and grants to certified CDFIs; (5) financial capability and
credit-building services for LMI individuals; and (6) low-cost, safe deposit accounts meeting recognized
national standards, which the proposal otherwise removes from the service test.
With respect to Questions 32–33, we support requiring banks to retain eligibility determinations for as long
as the applicable activity remains on their balance sheet, and establishing a maximum 30-day extension
NHSIE Comment — Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 / RIN 3064-AG31 · Page 9
 beyond the proposed 90-day review period. Eligibility determinations should include a clear written rationale
and, where appropriate, identify the facts or conditions on which eligibility depends. The agencies should
provide a reconsideration process through which banks or community development partners can supply
additional information, as well as a mechanism for community stakeholders to raise material concerns about
activities determined eligible. Nonconfidential or anonymized determinations and their rationales should be
made public to promote transparency and consistent treatment, and determinations should remain subject
to verification during examinations where an activity is ultimately implemented differently than represented.
Recognize Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and
Stabilization"; Section IV.I; Question 54
We strongly support expressly recognizing Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands as targeted
geographies within the revitalization and stabilization component of community development. Inland
Southern California is home to numerous Tribal nations, and capital access on Tribal lands remains severely
constrained.
Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: Section IV.D, "Designated Disaster Areas"; Question 31
We support expressly recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt to, and
withstand natural disasters. The Inland Empire faces recurring wildfire risk, extreme heat, and a deepening
homeowners insurance crisis that threatens both new purchases and existing owners' ability to stay in their
homes. CDFIs and housing counseling agencies provide financing, counseling, and recovery assistance before
and after disasters to homeowners, affordable housing, small businesses, and community facilities. CRA
should recognize responsible investments that strengthen vulnerable communities before disasters occur —
including home hardening, insurance navigation, and resilience-oriented repair lending — not only financing
provided after damage occurs.
Conclusion
CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities we serve. We
appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility. Modernization, however, should result in
more responsible capital reaching communities with unmet credit needs, as the CRA statute intends — not
less.
We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to:
1. Withdraw the proposed increases to the asset thresholds and retain the current, CPI-indexed thresholds,
rejecting all higher alternatives raised in Question 1.
2. Withdraw the restrictions on community development grants; preserve CRA consideration for general
operating and capacity-building support; and reject the alternative in Question 10 to eliminate CRA credit for
grants and donations.
3. If any indirect-cost test is retained, deem a federally negotiated indirect cost rate to satisfy it and apply the
test pro-rata — and in no case treat HUD-approved homeownership counseling as an example of
non-qualifying activity.
4. Expressly name housing counseling and homebuyer education, down payment assistance, matched
savings, financial capability services, safe deposit accounts, and EQ2 investments in CDFIs on the illustrative
list of qualifying activities.
NHSIE Comment — Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 / RIN 3064-AG31 · Page 10
 5. Retain a Satisfactory community development rating as a condition of an overall Satisfactory rating for
intermediate banks; define complexity by the activity itself rather than its link to a loan; and raise the
out-of-assessment-area benchmark to reflect satisfactory, not minimally passing, performance.
6. Retain the requirement that large-bank grants serve the bank's assessment areas, and adopt the proposed
prior-period loan consideration, illustrative list, advance-confirmation process, and recognition of Indian
Country and disaster resilience, with the guardrails described above.
Thank you for considering these comments and the impact of the proposed changes on the families and
neighborhoods of the Inland Empire. We would welcome the opportunity to discuss them further.
Sincerely,
Kailin Scott Peoples
Chief Executive Officer and Executive Director
Neighborhood Housing Services of the Inland Empire
kailin.peoples@nhsie.org

AIC | CRA Comment Letter | 1

October 13, 2026
RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations—Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57 / RIN 3064-AG31
To Whom It May Concern:
Allivate Impact Capital (AIC) appreciates the opportunity to provide the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) with comments on the proposed
regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
Allivate Impact Capital is an impact investment manager whose mission is to use innovative capital solutions
to elevate communities, alleviate poverty, and activate entrepreneurial ecosystems.
AIC is a product of the community development (CD) investment ecosystem the CRA has helped foster. The
organization was born out of industry-leading CD investing and the recognition CRA-motivated bank capital
can accomplish more than fund individual projects. When deployed strategically, it can serve as foundational
and catalytic capital capable of attracting additional investors and expanding the overall pool of private
capital available to underserved communities.
Today, AIC builds on this experience by using CRA-motivated bank capital alongside capital from other like-
minded investors. Its impact investment strategies address needs including affordable and workforce
housing, permanent supportive housing, employee ownership, community revitalization, and other forms of
economic opportunity.
This experience informs the comments contained herein. AIC has seen firsthand how CRA-motivated
investment capital is not interchangeable with conventional lending. Patient investment capital can fill gaps
that debt cannot, enable complex CD transactions to proceed, seed new investment strategies, and attract
additional private capital into communities that have historically lacked adequate investment.
AIC is concerned with several provisions of the proposed rule, taken together, would weaken the investment
incentives that have helped create and sustain the CD capital ecosystem. Patient investment capital is
essential to help reverse the lasting effects of redlining and disinvestment that have constrained access to
capital, weakened neighborhood economies, and limited opportunities to build wealth. Reducing regulatory
burden should not come at the expense of that capital or the community organizations necessary to translate
investment into lasting benefits for underserved communities.
AIC respectfully recommends the following changes to the proposed rule.
1. Preserve meaningful investment incentives across the proposed asset-size categories.
The proposal raises the Large Bank threshold to $10 billion and the Small Bank threshold to $1 billion. Its
estimates imply 376 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks would move from Large to Intermediate Bank
treatment, eliminating a separate CRA evaluation of qualified investments. Further, 798 would move from

AIC | CRA Comment Letter | 2

intermediate-small to Small Bank treatment, eliminating a separate evaluation of CD activities. These totals
exclude Federal Reserve-supervised institutions. [1]
These changes create two compounding reductions in investment incentives. The first removes a distinct
examination reason for a larger number of substantially sized banks to maintain qualified investment
portfolios and specialized investment expertise. The second removes a separate CD activity evaluation for an
even larger group of banks. Neither prohibits investment, but both will weaken the business case for
allocating resources to it.
AIC is concerned about the cumulative effect on funds, Community Development Financial Institutions
(CDFIs), housing developers, and other intermediaries that depend upon commitments from banks of
different sizes. Community development investment requires sustained organizational capacity: personnel
who can identify opportunities, structure commitments, assess risk, and document community benefits.
Once the incentive for maintaining that capability is reduced, rebuilding it will be substantially more difficult
than adjusting an annual allocation.
The proposed Appendix A also permits stronger retail Lending Test performance to compensate for weaker
CD Test performance among Intermediate Banks. Indeed, the proposal permits Intermediate Banks with less
than Satisfactory CD Test rating to still achieve overall Satisfactory CRA ratings based on their Lending Test
performance alone. This further weakens the signal that CD investments and financing warrant sustained
attention. Although examination outcomes remain uncertain, banks must still make resource-allocation
decisions in advance; the relative importance of each test informs those decisions.
AIC recommends retaining a distinct, meaningful investment component for institutions moving out of Large
Bank treatment, with proportionate documentation requirements. The agencies should also retain an
expectation of at least Satisfactory CD Test performance for an Intermediate Bank to receive an overall
Satisfactory rating. For institutions moving into Small Bank treatment, the agencies should preserve a
practical, consequential mechanism for recognizing CD investment leadership. Voluntary participation alone
should not substitute for examining the aggregate loss of investment incentives caused by the new
thresholds.
2. Ensure the combined Community Development Test preserves patient investment
capital.
The Intermediate Bank CD Test continues to consider investments alongside lending, grants, and services.
AIC's concern is the economic substitution that can occur within that combined framework.
Loans and investments are complementary, but they perform different functions. A bank may be able to
meet a community development need through a secured loan with contractual repayments and a
comparatively short maturity. An equity investment or fund commitment may, by contrast, require a
multiyear holding period, involve illiquidity, demand specialized underwriting, and expose the investor to


AIC | CRA Comment Letter | 3

project or business risk without a guarantee or underlying collateral. Such commitments provide capital that
is often scarce precisely because it cannot be supplied on conventional lending terms.
If banks can obtain comparable examination outcomes through either instrument, they may favor shorter-
duration secured lending. This is a foreseeable incentive risk, not a claim that all loans are short term or all
investments are more complex. In many transactions, reducing equity does not produce more lending; it
produces a financing gap that prevents the transaction from proceeding.
Atrium Court in Seattle illustrates the distinct role of equity. An investment vehicle jointly sponsored and
managed by AIC and CEI-Boulos Capital Management invested $15 million as the project's largest and
majority equity investor, alongside a $16 million low-interest loan from the Amazon Housing Equity Fund.
The project created 271-unit affordable and workforce housing development with income restrictions across
multiple affordability levels and 99-year affordability requirements. The equity and loan serve
complementary purposes. Recognition of the equity component should preserve the incentive to supply that
capital rather than assume that additional debt can replace it.
AIC recommends separately identifying investment performance within the CD Test and giving material
qualitative recognition to duration, illiquidity, financing gaps addressed, complexity, responsiveness, and
catalytic effect. Exceptional investment performance should be capable of materially improving overall CRA
evaluations beyond the limited confines of the CD Test. Evaluation should also recognize sustained patient
commitments across examination cycles, with clear safeguards against duplicative credit. The framework
should reward continued leadership rather than create an effective ceiling once a bank has undertaken
enough other CD activity to satisfy the test.
3. Protect operating support for community organizations and remove the proposed 15
percent indirect-cost cap.
For Large Bank grants, the proposal imposes a 15 percent indirect-cost cap and requires increased reporting,
including recipient commitments, attestations, Forms 990, and operating/program budgets. While AIC shares
the agencies' objective of ensuring community benefits, a universal indirect-cost ceiling poses a significant
threat to the organizations that make financed projects successful. Administrative staff, financial
management, technology, insurance, utilities, and mortgage or rent payments support reliable service
delivery. Their treatment as direct or indirect costs depends on the function and allocation involved; their
necessity does not disappear because an accounting framework labels them as overhead.
The Bread of Life Permanent Supportive Housing Project in Houston demonstrates the connection between
investment and nonprofit capacity. AIC CEI-Boulos Opportunity Fund made a majority equity investment in
the adaptive reuse of a damaged former youth center into 31 units of permanent supportive housing for
individuals experiencing homelessness. Temenos Community Development Corporation is the nonprofit
partner responsible for providing services, including case management, mental health counseling, substance
abuse treatment, life skills training, and nutrition assistance. Financing the building is only part of the
solution. Community organizations, like Temenos, must have the staff, systems, and operating stability to

AIC | CRA Comment Letter | 4

support residents over time. Flexible funding helps sustain that capacity, particularly where restricted
program grants fail to cover shared infrastructure.1
The proposed new documentation requirement adds costs (both financial and time) for both banks and
recipients. For a modest grant, collecting and assessing budgets, tax filings, attestations, and cost allocations
can consume a disproportionate share of the resources involved. Smaller organizations may have less
capacity to produce grant-specific calculations even when they are effective community partners. Banks may
consequently concentrate funding among larger recipients or reduce smaller grants.
AIC recommends eliminating the cap and expressly permitting general operating and capacity-building
support where a bank reasonably documents a primary CD purpose. Documentation should be proportionate
to grant size and complexity and should permit reliance on ordinary organizational records and reasonable
recipient certifications. Accountability should focus on qualifying purpose and community benefit, with
targeted inquiry where concerns arise, rather than a universal ratio that treats organizational infrastructure
as a diversion from impact.
4. Recognize the additional capital mobilized by CRA-motivated investments.
The effects of reduced investment incentives extend beyond the dollars withdrawn by a bank. Bank capital
can anchor a fund, establish confidence in an emerging strategy, and inspire other investors to participate.
AIC's origin and current approach demonstrate this connection: CRA investing helped create a platform that
can now bring like-minded capital from individuals, family offices, foundations, corporate treasury, pension,
and endowments into CD strategies.
Sharswood Ridge in Philadelphia illustrates how equity supports a broader capital stack. The Woodforest CEI-
Boulos Opportunity Fund (AIC's predecessor fund) was the majority private equity investor and the first
equity investor to commit to the neighborhood's broader revitalization plan. Financing also included
community-sourced capital, New Markets Tax Credits, public-sector loans, and state grants. The project
delivered much needed affordable and workforce housing alongside a grocery store run by a local owner
operator, a federally qualified healthcare clinic, a bank branch, and more. This multi-layered investment was
innovative, complex, and responsive in a neighborhood that was previously considered a medically
underserved food and banking desert in need of quality housing.
The regulatory question is therefore not only how much bank CD investments might decline, but how much
total downstream project capital may never materialize. Equity that closes a capital-stack gap can make other
financing deployable. An anchor fund commitment can support a strategy's scale and institutional viability.
These contributions should receive qualitative consideration without assigning a bank dollar-for-dollar credit
for capital supplied by others.


1 This example illustrates the importance of operating support; it does not suggest that Bread of Life or Temenos has
any particular indirect-cost ratio or would necessarily fail the proposed standard.

AIC | CRA Comment Letter | 5
AIC recommends recognizing documented catalytic contributions, such as early commitments, financing gaps
filled, and additional capital attracted. The agencies should preserve clear treatment of qualifying
investments through professionally managed funds and pooled vehicles, with predictable eligibility standards
and practical documentation of qualifying deployment. Geographic treatment should support viable regional
and national strategies while retaining meaningful responsiveness to banks' local communities. These
features would help CRA capital work alongside institutional capital at a scale that individual transactions
cannot always achieve.
The final rule must preserve the distinct capital channels on which successful community development
depends: lending, patient investment, and flexible support for community organizations. AIC urges the
agencies to revise the proposal to sustain those channels and the investment incentives necessary to help
reverse the lasting effects of redlining and decades of disinvestment.
The proposed thresholds, combined evaluation incentives, and grant restrictions should be assessed
together. Their cumulative effect would change the amount and the composition of capital available to
underserved communities. Preserving meaningful investment recognition and nonprofit operating support
would help ensure that reduced compliance burden does not come at the expense of the financing and
organizational capacity needed to deliver lasting outcomes.
AIC appreciates the opportunity to comment and would welcome the opportunity to provide additional
information about the role of CRA-motivated capital in our investment strategies.
Sincerely,
Noelle Lentz
Chief Executive Officer & Co-Founder
Allivate Impact Capital
Doug Schaeffer
Board Chair & Co-Founder
Allivate Impact Capital

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
The African American Alliance of CDFI CEOs (the Alliance) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed
amendments to their regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The Alliance is a
national membership organization representing Black-led community development financial institutions (CDFIs)
and works to strengthen their capacity to expand access to capital and financial opportunity in underserved
communities. Alliance members finance affordable housing, small businesses, community facilities, and other
community needs, including in markets where conventional sources of capital may be limited.
I. The Final Rule Should Preserve Meaningful Community Development Incentives
Congress enacted CRA on the premise that regulated financial institutions have a continuing and affirmative
obligation to help meet the credit needs of their local communities, consistent with safe and sound operations. The
statute directs each appropriate Federal financial supervisory agency to assess an institution's record of meeting
the credit needs of its entire community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.1
CDFIs operate as financial intermediaries. Bank relationships can include loans, investments, deposits, grants,
participations, and other forms of support. CDFIs, in turn, can help banks originate and finance loans, build
borrower and project pipelines, provide specialized underwriting and technical assistance, share risk, service
financing, and reach markets the bank may have difficulty serving directly. When CRA changes the regulatory
value of those activities, it can change the incentives surrounding bank-CDFI partnerships. CRA does not require
a bank to fund a CDFI, and CDFI status does not make every transaction CRA-qualifying, but where a bank-CDFI
relationship supports qualifying activity, the CRA framework affects the regulatory value of that relationship.
Several proposed changes should be considered together. The proposed asset thresholds would substantially
expand the intermediate bank category. The proposed rating framework would reduce the consequence of below-
Satisfactory community development performance for institutions in that category. The proposed grant rules
would also narrow CRA consideration for a form of support that can finance the operating capacity necessary to
originate, underwrite, service, and manage community development financing. Each provision raises a separate
issue, but their combined effect matters because they all bear on the relative value of community development
activity under CRA.
The Alliance therefore urges the agencies to focus the final rule on the changes necessary to improve clarity and
administration without weakening community development accountability or the incentives that support bank-
CDFI partnerships. The principal recommendations are:
•
preserve CRA consideration for qualifying grants and donations, remove the proposed 15 percent categorical
eligibility ceiling for large bank grants, and reject the Question 10 alternative of eliminating grant

The Alliance focuses these comments on the provisions most likely to affect community development financing
and bank-CDFI partnerships. The proposal also contains useful clarifications, several of which we identify below.
Those improvements do not resolve the concerns raised by the proposed changes to grants, asset thresholds,
ratings, and related community development incentives.
II. Preserve Qualifying Grants and Do Not Finalize the 15 Percent Eligibility Ceiling
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for qualifying grants and donations, remove the proposed 15
percent indirect cost ceiling for large bank grants, and reject the Question 10 alternative of eliminating grant
consideration. CRA eligibility should turn on documented qualifying use, not a single accounting percentage. If
the agencies nevertheless retain a percentage-based standard, the Alliance recommends at least a 30 percent safe
harbor, with higher documented rates permitted under a negotiated or consistently applied cost allocation
methodology.
The proposal would create a separate definition of "community development grant." To qualify, a grant or
donation would have to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a primary
purpose of community development and satisfy the applicable geographic requirements. For a grant made by a
large bank, the preamble states that the grant would not qualify if the recipient's indirect costs to administer it
exceed 15 percent of the grant or donation dollar amount; the proposed regulatory text also provides that the 15
percent limit is to be calculated consistent with the Uniform Guidance for Federal Awards or a comparable
standard.2
A. Direct recipient use addresses the pass-through concern; the 15 percent ceiling raises a different
question.
The direct use requirement asks who is carrying out the qualifying activity. The indirect cost requirement asks
how that recipient classifies and allocates its costs. A recipient can directly operate a qualifying lending or
community development program while incurring both direct and indirect costs. An organization also could have
relatively low administrative costs while principally passing funds to another entity that actually performs the
work.
The direct use requirement addresses the intermediary or pass-through component of the agencies' concern.
Requiring the recipient itself to carry out the qualifying activity creates a clear connection between the grant and
the community development work for which CRA consideration is sought. It does not, by itself, establish why a
categorical 15 percent indirect cost ceiling is necessary.
For CDFIs, operating capacity can be part of the machinery that turns capital into financing. Origination,
underwriting, servicing, portfolio management, compliance, data systems, financial management, borrower
support, and technical assistance require staff and systems. A grant that supports underwriting capacity, servicing
systems, compliance infrastructure, borrower technical assistance, or product development may support the
recipient's own delivery of a qualifying program even though some associated expenses are classified as indirect.

B. Treasury's CDFI programs reinforce the connection between capacity and financial intermediation.
The Department of the Treasury's CDFI Fund provides relevant evidence on that point. The CDFI Program
expressly uses Technical Assistance grants to build CDFI organizational capacity. The CDFI Fund's Small Dollar
Loan Program separately provides Loan Loss Reserve and Technical Assistance grants, with Technical Assistance
supporting technology, staff support, and other eligible activities to enable a Certified CDFI to establish or expand
a small dollar loan program.3
Those federal programs do not determine whether a private bank grant qualifies under CRA. They show, however,
that staffing, systems, policies, technology, financial management, and borrower support can be inputs into the
delivery of financial products. A CRA rule designed to ensure that grants reach qualifying community
development activity should account for that operating model, because, especially for a CDFI, lending requires
more than principal available for disbursement.
C. Operating support can help keep mission driven capital affordable.
Operating support also matters because the economics of mission driven lending do not always allow a CDFI to
recover the full cost of delivering a product from the borrower. CDFIs may choose to subsidize interest rates,
make smaller or more complex loans with relatively high delivery costs, and provide technical assistance or other
borrower support that adds to those costs. External subsidy can therefore be part of the model that keeps capital
affordable while sustaining the staff and systems needed to lend. Limiting operating support can affect not only
administrative capacity, but also a CDFI's ability to offer affordable capital and services in the markets it serves.4
D. The 15 percent ceiling is not adequately supported by the Uniform Guidance benchmark the agencies
cite.
The agencies invoke OMB's Uniform Guidance in explaining the 15 percent condition and note that OMB
increased the de minimis indirect cost rate to 15 percent.5
Under 2 C.F.R. § 200.414(f), however, the 15 percent figure is an optional de minimis indirect cost rate for
recipients and subrecipients without a current federally negotiated rate, and it is applied to modified total direct
costs. Recipients and subrecipients are not required to use that rate. It is a cost recovery method under Federal
awards, not a finding that indirect costs above 15 percent are unreasonable.6
The proposal therefore creates a methodological problem the agencies should resolve. The preamble compares the
recipient's indirect costs with the grant or donation dollar amount, while the proposed text directs that the 15
percent limit be calculated consistent with Uniform Guidance. Section 200.414(f), by contrast, applies the elected
rate to modified total direct costs. At minimum, the final rule should make the calculation unambiguous. More
fundamentally, the agencies have not explained why a Federal award cost recovery methodology should determine
whether an otherwise qualifying private bank grant receives CRA consideration.
E. Independent nonprofit evidence and the agencies' own analysis support a more tailored rule.
Independent nonprofit evidence also cautions against treating 15 percent as a general measure of reasonable
organizational cost. The John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation reports that, in an analysis using IRS
Form 990 data from more than 130,000 nonprofits, 29 percent was the minimum indirect cost rate associated with
financially healthy organizations in the dataset. The MacArthur research does not measure the administrative cost
of individual CRA grants and does not establish an appropriate CRA rate. Its relevance is narrower in that it
undermines the premise that costs above 15 percent are, without more, a reliable indicator of inefficiency or
inadequate community benefit.7

The agencies' own record identifies the practical concern. The FDIC states that the direct use requirement, large

support, capacity building grants, and intermediary grants supporting multiple downstream projects. It also
recognizes that smaller and newer nonprofits, and organizations serving hard to reach populations, may have
greater difficulty providing the required documentation or operating cost information.8 That concern is especially
relevant to community financial institutions, because a rule intended to prevent unsupported administrative costs
could reduce CRA-motivated support for the operating capacity that enables a CDFI to originate, underwrite,
service, and manage qualifying financing.
The proposed reliance on Form 990 information also has limits. Form 990 Part IX reports expenses by function at
the organization level and permits allocation under the organization's normal accounting method or another
reasonable method. By itself, it does not establish how costs associated with a particular bank grant were
allocated.9 Documentation requirements should be tied to the facts necessary to establish qualification rather than
to information that may not answer the grant-level question.
F. Replace the hard ceiling with a documented use of funds standard and a 30 percent fallback safe harbor.
The agencies can address their targeting concern more directly. A bank should establish that the grant has a
qualifying community development purpose, that the recipient itself carries out the qualifying activity, that
applicable geographic requirements are satisfied, and that the recipient documents its use and allocation of grant
funds using a consistently applied accounting methodology. Where indirect cost allocation is required, the
agencies could recognize an applicable negotiated indirect cost rate, the Uniform Guidance methodology, or
another comparable accounting standard. CRA consideration should turn on whether the documentation
establishes qualifying use of the funds, rather than whether one cost category crosses a categorical percentage
ceiling. If the agencies nevertheless retain a percentage-based screen, the MacArthur evidence at least supports
considering a 30 percent safe harbor rather than a 15 percent hard ceiling. The final rule should also permit higher
documented rates where supported by a negotiated rate or a consistently applied cost allocation method.
Question 10 should be answered in the negative. Eliminating CRA consideration for grants would not solve the
targeting problem the agencies identify. It would remove CRA recognition from qualifying grant activity
regardless of recipient, purpose, geography, documentation, or demonstrated community benefit. Loans and
investments are not substitutes for every need a grant can address. Where the qualifying need involves borrower
support, product development, technology, staffing, or other capacity that cannot prudently be financed with debt,
a grant may be the appropriate tool.
The agencies should preserve qualifying grants, reject the Question 10 alternative, and replace the 15 percent
ceiling with a substantive use of funds and documentation standard. If they retain a percentage-based approach,
the Alliance recommends a 30 percent safe harbor using a clearly defined cost base, with higher documented rates
remaining eligible.
III. Retain Existing Thresholds Absent a Stronger Record for Reclassification
The proposed thresholds do more than reduce compliance or examination burden. They determine which banks
remain subject to a separate Community Development Test, which banks remain subject to separate Investment
and Service Tests, and which data obligations apply. Those consequences require their own analysis.
For institutions supervised by the OCC and FDIC, the proposal would create a substantially larger intermediate
bank category, generally covering institutions from $1 billion to $10 billion. That result comes from moving the
lower boundary up from the current small bank threshold and moving the upper boundary up from the current
large bank threshold. The effects at those two boundaries are different and should be evaluated separately.

A. At the lower boundary, hundreds of current intermediate banks would lose a separate Community
Development Test.
The proposal would increase the small bank threshold from less than $412 million to less than $1 billion. Banks
below the proposed threshold generally would be evaluated under the small bank Lending Test rather than the
intermediate bank framework that includes a separate Community Development Test.10
The OCC estimates that 194 OCC-supervised intermediate banks would be reclassified as small banks and
generally would no longer be assessed separately on community development activities. The FDIC separately
estimates that 604 FDIC-supervised small institutions would become small banks and lose a separate Community
Development Test.11 That is more than a change in examination mechanics. A separate Community Development
Test gives community development loans, investments, and services an independent role in the institution's CRA
evaluation. Removing that test changes the regulatory significance of those activities.
The agencies should therefore justify why banks newly classified as small no longer should have a distinct
community development evaluation, rather than treating the administrative savings from simplified examinations
as sufficient by themselves.
B. At the upper boundary, hundreds of current large banks would move into the intermediate framework.
Raising the large bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion has a different effect. Current large banks
below $10 billion would retain community development evaluation, but would move from the current large bank
structure of separate Lending, Investment, and Service Tests to a Lending Test and Community Development
Test. They also would no longer be subject to the data obligations that apply to large banks.12
The OCC estimates that 126 currently large OCC-supervised institutions would move to intermediate treatment.
The FDIC estimates that 250 currently large FDIC-supervised institutions would do so.13
This change does not eliminate community development accountability, but it changes its structure. Investments,
grants, loans, and services would be evaluated together through the intermediate bank Community Development
Test rather than carrying the same separate role they have under the large bank framework. That can change the
relative value of particular activities even where community development remains part of the examination.
C. The threshold proposal and the intermediate bank rating proposal should be evaluated together.
The proposed thresholds would make the intermediate bank framework applicable to a substantially larger group
of institutions. The proposed rating change discussed in Section IV would simultaneously remove the current
requirement that an intermediate bank achieve at least Satisfactory performance on its Community Development
Test before receiving an overall Satisfactory rating.
Those changes interact. Current large banks that move into the expanded intermediate category would not only
move from separate Investment and Service Tests into a combined Community Development Test; they also
would enter a rating structure in which below-Satisfactory community development performance no longer
automatically prevents an overall Satisfactory rating.
The agencies should assess that combined effect directly. Reclassification determines which test structure applies.
The rating rule determines the consequence of weak performance within that structure. Examining those
provisions separately risks understating the change in community development incentives for institutions moving
into the new $1 billion - $10 billion category.
D. The agencies' asset concentration rationale does not answer the community development question.
The agencies note that only approximately 2.4 percent of the banks they supervise, 86 institutions based on 2024
and 2025 Call Report data, would remain large under the proposal, but those institutions would hold
approximately 85.4 percent of total industry assets. They compare that figure with 1995, when institutions treated

A regional institution can represent a small share of national banking assets and still be an important provider of
