should address what community development requirements and incentives change when those institutions move
categories, not only the percentage of national assets that remains subject to large bank treatment.
E. The agencies should retain the existing thresholds unless they establish a stronger basis for moving them.
The Alliance recommends retaining the existing small and large bank thresholds unless the agencies develop a
stronger record explaining why reclassification at $1 billion and $10 billion is warranted in light of the resulting
changes in community development requirements and incentives. The agencies have identified compliance and
examination savings from reclassification, but the record does not establish that every substantive consequence
attached to those proposed lines is necessary to achieve those savings.
If the agencies nevertheless raise the thresholds, they should separate burden relief from avoidable reductions in
community development accountability. At the lower boundary, they should consider preserving a separate
community development evaluation for institutions that otherwise would lose it. At the upper boundary, they
should consider whether investment, service, data, reporting, recordkeeping, or examination requirements can be
tailored rather than eliminated solely because an institution moves below $10 billion. They also should not adopt a
still higher large bank threshold, including the $30 billion alternative raised in Question 1, without a substantially
stronger analysis of the additional consequences of reclassification.15
IV. Retain a Satisfactory Floor on Both Intermediate Bank Tests
The agencies should not finalize the proposed intermediate bank rating structure. An intermediate bank should
continue to receive at least a Satisfactory rating on both its Lending Test and its Community Development Test
before it can receive an overall Satisfactory CRA rating.
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank must receive at least Satisfactory on both tests to receive
an overall Satisfactory rating. The proposal would retain Satisfactory lending as a minimum but remove the same
floor for community development. The Community Development Test would remain, but a below-Satisfactory
rating on that test would no longer, by itself, prevent an overall Satisfactory rating. That change reduces the
consequence attached specifically to inadequate community development performance.16
A. The FDIC's own analysis identifies the incentive problem.
The agencies explain that banks do not know their precise ratings before an examination is complete and therefore
may not be able to calibrate activity to a particular result. They suggest that added flexibility could improve
incentives to perform well on both tests because stronger performance on one test would no longer be constrained
by a categorical minimum on the other.17
The FDIC's own analysis identifies the other side of that incentive change. It recognizes that banks with limited
CRA resources may shift effort toward lending and away from activities evaluated under the Community
Development Test, and that allowing stronger lending performance to compensate for weaker community
development performance may increase the relative incentive to devote CRA resources to lending.18
Once below-Satisfactory community development performance no longer blocks an overall Satisfactory rating, the
categorical consequence of weaker community development performance is reduced. The FDIC itself recognizes

Retaining a Satisfactory floor on both tests would not diminish the role of lending. A bank with below-

The agencies have chosen to retain a separate Community Development Test for intermediate banks. If

The agencies can provide flexibility in how banks demonstrate community development performance, clarify

V. Keep Locally Important Small Business Lending and Essential CRA Information
Visible
The final rule should not allow lending that is important to a local market to disappear from meaningful CRA
evaluation solely because it is not one of the institution's largest product lines nationally.
The agencies acknowledge that narrowing the product lines evaluated may reduce CRA incentives for lending
outside designated major product lines. The FDIC states that some institutions may reallocate resources away
from lending categories that are not evaluated, although it expects the overall effect to be modest.19
That risk is particularly relevant to small business and small farm lending. A product line that is modest at the
institution-wide level may still be important to meeting credit needs in a particular assessment area. The agencies'
own alternative approach recognizes local significance by considering the bank's lending volume and strategy, its
capacity to lend locally, and whether the product line meaningfully contributes to meeting the credit needs of that
assessment area.
The Alliance therefore favors a major product line methodology that preserves local significance. If the agencies
adopt an institution-level quantitative approach, the final rule should provide an assessment area-level backstop or
equivalent mechanism for a product line that materially contributes to local credit needs. A de minimis threshold
also should not exclude a product line that remains materially important in a particular market. The agencies
should consider both loan count and dollar volume so that small dollar lending is not obscured by a small number
of larger transactions.20
The same concern applies to information. Reclassifying current large banks will reduce some CRA data
obligations. The agencies themselves identify reduced standardized data and comparability as a potential
secondary effect of the threshold changes, while also stating that they intend, to the fullest extent feasible, to use
Section 1071 data to eliminate duplicative CRA requirements. The Alliance supports eliminating genuinely
duplicative requirements when Section 1071 or another federal source provides substantially equivalent
information in coverage, geography, quality, timing, and accessibility. However, the agencies should identify what
information is lost when a bank is reclassified and whether another source actually replaces the function that
information served.21 A source that covers different products, lacks sufficient geographic detail, is unavailable for

VI. Geographic Flexibility Should Expand Access to High-Need Markets Without
Becoming a Performance Floor
The Alliance supports a clearer path for qualifying community development loans, investments, and grants outside
a bank's assessment areas. Greater geographic flexibility can help direct capital to rural, Native, regional, and
other high-need markets where relatively few banks maintain branches. It also can make regional and national
CDFI partnerships more workable where a responsive activity falls outside a bank partner's assessment area
footprint.
The broader pathway should remain supplemental to meaningful performance in the communities where a bank
has local CRA obligations.
A. A numerical trigger for broader consideration should not become a measure of satisfactory
performance.
The proposal offers quantitative and qualitative approaches for determining when a bank has conducted enough
community development activity within its assessment areas to receive broader geographic consideration. Under
the quantitative option, the agencies state that meeting the geographic flexibility threshold would permit broader
consideration but would not be sufficient to support a conclusion on the bank's community development
performance in an assessment area.22
If the agencies retain a numerical trigger, they should make clear that the number is not a measure of satisfactory
community development performance. A published threshold may influence internal goals and budgets even when
it is not formally a rating benchmark. The final rule should therefore explain how the threshold was set and make
clear that meeting it means only that outside area activity may be considered, not that the bank's local community
development performance is satisfactory. Meeting that trigger also should not displace examiner consideration of
identified community needs, institutional capacity, historical performance, and other relevant performance context
factors.
B. Question 34 should be resolved with a substantial performance safeguard rather than an all or nothing
gate.
The proposal also conditions broader consideration at the State, multistate MSA, or bank level on satisfying the
applicable geographic flexibility standard in all assessment areas within the relevant geography. Question 34 asks
whether broader consideration should be available without requiring that result in every assessment area.23
Additional flexibility is warranted. A bank can meaningfully serve community development needs across most of
a State or multistate MSA while falling short in a limited number of assessment areas. An all or nothing
prerequisite can prevent otherwise responsive financing in another high-need market even where the remaining
local weakness is isolated.
Outside-assessment area activity, however, should not substitute for material unmet needs in the bank's own
assessment areas. The agencies should allow broader consideration where the bank has substantially met its
community development responsibilities across the relevant geography and any remaining shortfall is limited
rather than material. That approach preserves local responsibility while making the broader pathway usable for
responsive financing in underserved markets.

VII. Retain Useful Clarifications, With Narrow Guardrails
Several parts of the proposal would improve certainty and should be retained.
The Alliance supports a non-exclusive illustrative list of qualifying community development activities and an
optional confirmation process through which banks can seek greater ex ante certainty. The list should remain non-
exclusive so that absence from it does not imply that an innovative activity is ineligible. The proposal's 90-day
response period, subject to notice if additional time is needed, and its requirement that the agency provide the
rationale for a determination are useful features that should be retained.24
The proposal's reliance protections for activity that was eligible when conducted and its clearer treatment of
qualifying loans and investments that remain on the balance sheet also should be retained. Multi-year financing
should not become less attractive because a later interpretive change retroactively alters eligibility. Final guidance
should address outstanding balances, commitments, renewals, and refinancings with enough precision for banks
and community partners to structure patient capital with confidence.25
The affordable housing provisions also provide useful clarity. Clearer treatment of subsidized housing, naturally
occurring affordable housing, and mixed-income projects can reduce uncertainty around qualifying transactions.
The proposed expansion to include middle-income rental housing in high-cost areas, however, should preserve
CRA's focus on low- and moderate-income households and should not displace financing addressing more acute
LMI housing needs.26
The proposed economic development framework can improve administrability by using more objective criteria for
qualifying small business and small farm activity. The proposal separately recognizes technical assistance and
supportive services to qualifying small businesses and farms and certain financing through CDFIs that finance
small businesses or small farms. The agencies should retain those clarifications while providing examples that
distinguish financing used principally for ongoing operating liquidity from working capital financing that
stabilizes, preserves, or expands productive capacity.27
Strategic plans can become more usable, but public participation must remain meaningful. The proposal would
permit more substantive prefiling feedback, including on the adequacy of a draft plan and the merits of measurable
goals, before the formal public comment process. The agencies themselves ask in Question 49 how to permit that
guidance without implying preapproval. Prefiling engagement should not effectively settle the adequacy of
substantive goals before affected communities have had a meaningful opportunity to comment.28
A strategic plan establishes the goals against which a bank's CRA performance may be judged for the plan period.
Any elective goals or benchmarks therefore should be transparent and subject to meaningful public review before
the agencies determine that they are adequate.
The proposal would continue to recognize innovativeness, flexibility, impact, quality, and other responsiveness
considerations even as it narrows the definition of complexity toward lending-related activity. The final rule
should make clear that formal linkage to a particular loan is not the only route to qualitative recognition for
activity that demonstrably enables community development finance.29
VIII. Phase In Genuinely New Requirements After Guidance Is Available
The proposal's reliance principle should be retained. Under that provision, an activity that was eligible when
conducted would continue to receive consideration in the evaluation period in which it was conducted, and a
qualifying loan or investment remaining on the bank's balance sheet could continue to receive consideration in
later periods. Requirements that would require banks or community partners to change documentation, systems,
contracts, or compliance processes should receive targeted transition.30

IX. Conclusion
The Alliance urges the agencies to revise the proposal so that community development remains a meaningful
component of CRA performance and the rule does not weaken the bank-CDFI partnerships that help capital reach
underserved communities.
The agencies should preserve qualifying grants and reject the proposed 15 percent ceiling and Question 10
alternative; if a percentage-based grant standard is retained, use at least a 30 percent safe harbor with higher
documented rates permitted; retain the existing small and large bank thresholds absent a stronger record for
moving them, and preserve community development accountability if the thresholds are raised; retain a
Satisfactory community development floor for the substantially expanded intermediate bank category; and make
the targeted changes described above to major product lines, data, geography, strategic plans, and transition.
These recommendations would preserve clearer rules and workable administration while maintaining meaningful
incentives for loans, investments, grants, services, and other forms of support that help community financial
institutions meet local credit needs. The Alliance appreciates the agencies' consideration of these comments.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In our community, from

 of approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic

and providing little direct benefit to residents.

 lines by all lending volume, or based on the type of lending a bank does more of in a particular

 e consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,
The undersigned organizations thank you for the opportunity to comment on the notice of
proposed rulemaking concerning Community Reinvestment Act Regulations.1
A person's ZIP code should not determine their destiny. The Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) was enacted to ensure broad credit access throughout the nation with a powerful
principle – regulated financial institutions have a continuing and affirmative obligation to help
meet the credit needs of local communities in addition to simply accepting deposits.2 While the
United States is a vast nation with a national banking system that has grown with its prosperity,
the CRA reminds us that credit needs are fundamentally local and every community has its own
specific needs.
In a prior CRA rule, the FDIC and the OCC included special purpose credit programs authorized
under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) as part of the rule.3 That inclusion was broadly
supported by commenters.4 The current proposal does not include mention of special purpose
credit programs.

4 2024 CRA Final Rule at 6939.
 Special purpose credit programs have proven to be quite beneficial for local communities,
borrowers, and businesses. These programs have helped strengthen the mortgage banking
sector, expanding opportunities for consumers, and increasing the breadth of mortgage
products lenders can offer to people. From 2022 to 2024, special purpose credit programs
backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac helped more than 57,000 economically disadvantaged
households fairly access homeownership and the ability to build wealth for their families.
According to the Federal Housing Finance Agency, those loans generated $17.2 billion in
positive economic impact.5
Special purpose credit programs are permitted by the Equal Credit Opportunity Act include:
(1) any credit assistance program expressly authorized by law for an economically
disadvantaged class of persons;
(2) any credit assistance program administered by a nonprofit organization for its
members or an economically disadvantaged class of persons; or
(3) any special purpose credit program offered by a profit-making organization to meet
special social needs which meets standards prescribed in regulations by the
[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau].6
The undersigned organizations urge the FDIC and the OCC to include reference to "programs
authorized under 15 U.S.C. § 1691(c)(1), (2), or (3)" in the non-exhaustive list of programs that
banks may support under the definition of "civic assistance."7 This will provide regulatory clarity
and alignment between ECOA and CRA regulations and enable banks to fulfill the central
principle of CRA – supporting communities at the most local level with programs tailored to
their community members' needs.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Community Reinvestment Advisors, LLC, appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed
Community Reinvestment Act regulations. We support clearer standards, practical administrative
relief, and a framework that strengthens banks' responsiveness to community credit needs. We
urge the OCC and FDIC to pursue these improvements in coordination with the Federal Reserve.
As a former bank regulator and a banker with more than 30 years of experience in CRA leadership
and community development, | have worked with institutions supervised by all three agencies. Our
firm advises financial institutions, nonprofit organizations, and municipalities on CRA strategy,
Strategic Plans, examination readiness, and community development. We offer four
recommendations.

Maintain a harmonized framework across all three agencies.

We urge substantially consistent CRA regulations, interpretations, examination practices, and
implementation timelines across the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve. A common framework can
accommodate differences in bank size, business model, institutional capacity, and community needs
through appropriate tailoring and performance context.

If finalized without corresponding Federal Reserve changes, divergent standards could require
banking organizations with differently regulated subsidiaries to operate separate compliance
systems, impair comparisons of CRA performance, and complicate partnerships among banks and

Community Reinvestment Advisors, LLC | 1
 community organizations. Harmonization should extend to examiner training, qualifying-activity
determinations, Strategic Plan approvals, and transition guidance.

This concern has longstanding support. In 2020, the Consumer Bankers Association called for
substantially identical agency rules; the Conference of State Bank Supervisors warned of dual
compliance systems. In July 2021, the three agencies jointly recognized the value of a consistent
framework. The OCC's 2020 rule and subsequent 2021 rescission also illustrate the uncertainty
associated with changes that lack durable interagency alignment. These precedents support
coordinated modernization today. [1-3]

Balance lending emphasis and threshold relief with community accountability.
Lending is central to CRA's purpose. Investments, accessible banking services, financial counseling,
and capable community partners can also enable households and businesses to obtain and sustain
access to credit. The agencies should preserve consideration for these contributions when they
demonstrably support eligible community needs.

The proposed $1 billion small-bank and $10 billion intermediate-bank thresholds could provide
administrative relief. We recommend that the agencies explain the supporting analysis and assess
effects on community development activity and public lending data. Threshold relief should
preserve meaningful accountability and provide sufficient transition guidance for affected
institutions.

Evaluate grant effectiveness and provide reliable eligibility guidance.

We support accountability for grants and donations intended to benefit low- and moderate-income
communities. However, the proposed requirement for large banks to document that grant
recipients' overhead does not exceed 15 percent could exclude effective organizations whose
staffing, compliance, technology, and administrative infrastructure are necessary to deliver services.
We recommend replacing a rigid cutoff with proportionate due diligence that considers reasonable
organizational costs, documented use of funds, and measurable community outcomes. If the
agencies retain an overhead test, they should define the calculation, treatment of shared costs,
measurement period, and acceptable documentation, and provide reasonable exceptions. Banks
and nonprofit recipients should not face duplicative verification requirements.

An illustrative qualifying-activity list and confirmation process can improve certainty. These tools
should allow innovative activities with demonstrated community benefits. The agencies should
coordinate determinations, publish useful examples, and protect reasonable reliance on eligibility
decisions when banks make commitments.

Make Strategic Plans more predictable and responsive

We support substantive prefiling feedback, clear submission requirements, written completeness
determinations, and transparent review procedures. These improvements could make Strategic
Plans more useful for community banks, de novo institutions, and digital banks while retaining
meaningful public participation.

The final framework should establish a deadline for determining technical completeness, require
specific explanations of deficiencies, and provide written reasons and reasonable limits for

Community Reinvestment Advisors, LLC | 2
 extensions of review. Agencies should publish consistent examples of measurable goals and clarify
how annual interim goals and goals covering the full plan term will be evaluated.

Guidance should explain how performance context supports tailoring among lending, investment,
and service goals, and how material changes in business strategy, institutional capacity, or
assessment areas may justify amendments. Banks need predictable procedures that support
measurable commitments responsive to community needs.

We encourage the agencies to adopt practical improvements within a durable, harmonized
framework that provides predictable expectations and supports sustained community investment.
Thank you for considering our comments.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in communities. For
example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community
development loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that
percentage is far lower than the percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC)
determined the largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC and FDIC
supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently conduct

qualified investments.3 If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate
thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing
the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or
investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether communities that have
experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
The Community Development Bankers Association ("CDBA") respectfully submits the following
comments on the joint notice of proposed rulemaking ("NPR" or "proposed rule") published in the
Federal Register on August 12, 2026, to amend the Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA")
regulations. CDBA is the national trade association for banks certified by the U.S. Department of
Treasury as Community Development Financial Institutions ("CDFIs"). Our members share a
primary mission of serving low- and moderate-income ("LMI") communities and underserved
markets. The CRA is central to the ecosystem of capital, deposits, and grants that support that
mission.
CDBA welcomes many of the proposed changes that provide greater flexibility and reduce
regulatory burden for community banks. However:
• We strongly encourage the agencies to ensure a final rule reflects a consensus of all
regulators to minimize the risk of continuous changes to the rule. Continuously shifting
policies carry material costs for banks and regulatory change has a disproportionate impact
on small community banks. Our members, who are community banks serving LMI
communities, are acutely affected by these shifts and desire a lasting and stable rule.
• The cumulative impact of many proposed changes threaten the viability of the
community development finance ecosystem and pose substantial harm to economic
conditions in LMI communities.
RECOGNITION FOR ALL CDFIs:
CDBA strongly urges that the proposed rule be amended to eliminate geography as a factor in
CRA eligibility of CDFI support.
We recommend:
 • Explicitly including CDFI-related activity as a qualifying community development
category for all types of CDFIs.
• Aligning the treatment of proposed § 25.12(3)(iii)(E) and § 25.13(e) so that CDFI-related
loans, investments, and grants are not subject to a stricter geographic test than the one
Congress and the agencies have applied to Minority Depository Institutions ("MDIs"),
Women-owned Depository Institutions ("WDIs"), and low-income credit unions
("LICUs").
Discussion: For more than 20 years, for-profit CDFI banks have sought regulatory clarity that
financial institutions' support for CDFIs qualify for consideration under the CRA. The lack of clarity
and inconsistent regulatory interpretation between nonprofit and for-profit CDFIs has meaningfully
diminished financial institutions' engagement in supporting CDFI banks.
The 2023 rule addressed this issue by explicitly stating that support that a financial institution
provided to any CDFI qualified under CRA. In addition, the rule stated that support for all CDFIs
was CRA eligible regardless of the geography the CDFI served. This clarification aligned CDFI
banks' treatment with that of MDIs, WDIs, and LICUs. The entire banking industry and its
prudential regulatory agencies all expressed strong support for this provision in public
comment letters.
The proposed 2026 rule does not include this provision for CDFI banks, though it does give CRA
consideration for activities that support nonprofit organizations (including nonprofit CDFIs), MDIs,
WDIs, and LICUs without regard to geography. Although CDFIs remain a recognized category for
"economic development" purposes under proposed § 25.12(3)(iii)(E), Community Development
("CD") activity involving a CDFI would still need to satisfy the general assessment-area
requirement, or the new geographic flexibility standard in proposed § 25.13(e), to receive credit.
This asymmetry has no clear policy justification. The CRA exists to direct capital to LMI
communities, and CDFI banks are, by certification and mission, institutions organized specifically to
serve those communities without regard for a particular supporting bank's assessment area. This
exclusion is keenly felt by CDFI banks, which must attract deposits, investments, and partnerships
from traditional banks outside their immediate assessment areas. The pool of potential traditional
bank partners for CDFI banks in regions without large money-center or super-regional institutions is
severely curtailed by removing that flexibility.
ASSET THRESHOLDS
CDBA supports regulatory relief for small banks but strongly urges recalibration of the Large
Bank Threshold. Specifically:
• We support increasing the small bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion in
assets– an increase of 143%.
• The proposed increase from $1.649 billion to $10 billion in assets for the large bank
threshold would disrupt the community development finance ecosystem and access to
 credit in LMI communities. We support a threshold that does not exceed $3.25 billion,
as outlined in the proposed rule's Scenario B.
• We support indexing asset thresholds to inflation based on nominal GDP.
Discussion: CDBA supports adjusting outdated asset thresholds and reducing compliance burden for
smaller institutions. Moving the small-bank threshold to $1 billion would provide genuine relief for
many CDBA members currently classified as intermediate small banks. However, CDBA believes
the proposal does not adequately balance reducing compliance burden and preserving the model of
community development finance that the current rule supports. In particular, raising the large-bank
threshold to $10 billion exempts a significant number of banks from the investment test — the
principal mechanism through which banks place capital and deposits with CDFI and MDI banks.
Banks currently subject to the investment test placed approximately $661.9 million in deposits with
MDI and CDFI banks; of that amount, approximately $108.8 million — 16.4% — came from banks
with between $1.6 billion and $10 billion in assets1, precisely the population that would no longer be
evaluated under the investment test at the proposed threshold. That would reduce the regulatory
incentive to renew or originate these placements, likely leading to attrition at a time when
competition for deposits is already intense. At the same time, banks that drop out of the large-bank
category no longer have investments graded on their own. Instead, lending, investment, and service
are all folded into one combined test. Investment activity still counts, but it carries less weight.

Bank counts by asset-size category under the current and proposed definitions (–531 large banks;
+995 small banks). Source: CDBA analysis; see NAAHL Summary, p. 7.
Share of residents nationwide with access to a
large-bank branch
35.5% → 29.6% (≈ 20.8 million fewer
residents)
The NPR acknowledges that it has not settled on a final threshold and requests comment on two
alternatives.

1 Intrafi Network analysis, 2026.
 CDBA strongly believes a large-bank threshold of $10 billion and the proposed $30 billion
alternative goes further than what would be necessary to achieve meaningful burden reduction, and
would harm CDFI and MDI banks. This risk is compounded by a provision in the 21st Century
ROAD to Housing Act, enacted July 11, 2026, that raised the statutory cap on bank public welfare
investments from 15% to 20% of capital and surplus. That provision was designed to unlock
additional bank capital for affordable housing and other community development investment,
including through Low-Income Housing Tax Credits. Shrinking the population of banks subject to
the CRA investment test at the same time that Congress just expanded banks' statutory capacity to
make these investments will work at cross-purposes.
We urge the agencies to assess the combined effect of the two changes on the overall supply of bank
capital available for affordable housing and community development before finalizing a large-bank
threshold
COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT GRANTS
CDBA strongly opposes the 15% administrative cost cap and sub-granting limitations. We
instead propose:
• Substantially increasing the administrative-cost cap and indexing it to a recognized
external benchmark for nonprofit overhead (for example, benchmarks used in
government grantmaking commonly permit administrative and overhead costs between
25% and 45%).
•
Retaining bank discretion to exercise reasonable business judgment regarding which
community organizations to support and how, consistent with the goal of reducing, not
increasing, regulatory micromanagement of CRA-qualifying activity.
• No administrative caps or sub-grant limitations for grants to CDFIs, nonprofits, and
other intermediaries supporting CDFIs. The activities of CDFIs by law are fully aligned
with the proposed rule's goals of providing access to credit and financial services in
LMI communities.
•
Preserve credit for sub-granting arrangements, in which an intermediary organization
re-grants bank funding to smaller nonprofits in its network — a common and effective
structure for reaching CDFIs and community organizations that lack the scale to
receive or administer bank grants directly.
• Scale back new documentation requirements, particularly the universal requirement
for IRS Form 990 filings and written attestations, in recognition of the added burden on
smaller and newer grant recipients.
Discussion: The agencies' economic analysis anticipates many of our concerns. Section VI of the
preamble, under "Reduced Support for Some Nonprofit and Intermediary Activities," states that the
community development ("CD") grant restrictions "could also create secondary burdens for
nonprofit organizations and community development intermediaries," and that "smaller nonprofits,
 newer organizations, or organizations serving hard-to-reach populations may face greater difficulty
providing the documentation or operating-cost information needed to support CRA consideration"
(Fed. Reg. NPR, Section VI.A (Economic Analysis)).
CDBA strongly believes the proposed narrowing of the community development grant
definition, particularly the 15% cap on a recipient's indirect and administrative costs and the
related documentation requirements, defeats the proposed rule's stated goal of reducing
regulatory burden.
CDBA members are, first and foremost, community banks. Proximity is what allows them to
identify effective, locally responsive ways to meet their communities' needs. They should be given
greater flexibility in assessing what those communities need, not less. Several of the proposed
restrictions on CD grants move in the opposite direction, substituting a rigid, centrally set standard
for a bank's own judgment about its community. The loss of flexibility is not merely burdensome;
it risks the kind of unintended consequences that can follow when a national rule displaces
local knowledge of what a community needs.
The proposed 15% cap also treats seasoned CD grant recipients the same as first-time federal
grantees, despite the distinction in the federal government's own general grants framework. Under 2
CFR 200.414(f), the 15% "de minimis" rate applies only to organizations that have never held a
federally negotiated indirect cost rate agreement — in other words, entities without a demonstrated
track record. That same framework explicitly permits negotiated rates well above 15%, commonly in
the 25% to 65% range, for organizations with an established relationship and documented
performance history. CD grant recipients working with CDBA member banks are frequently long-
standing partners with a demonstrated track record of program delivery, not first-time, unproven
grantees. Applying the federal government's own "unproven grantee" standard uniformly to
organizations with years of established performance ignores the very distinction the federal
government's own grants policy is built around, and penalizes exactly the kind of durable, locally
rooted partnerships the CRA is meant to encourage.
The agencies' preamble illustrates the problem. Section III.B of the NPR cites a real-world grant to
an organization providing homeownership counseling and homelessness services, with
administrative costs of approximately 25%, as an example of a grant that would no longer qualify for
CRA credit under the proposed cap. That is precisely the kind of legitimate, mission-driven
organization CRA is intended to support, and the agencies' economic analysis in Section VI
acknowledges that the grant restrictions "could also create secondary burdens for nonprofit
organizations and community development intermediaries," and that "smaller nonprofits, newer
organizations, or organizations serving hard-to-reach populations may face greater difficulty
providing the documentation or operating-cost information needed to support CRA consideration."
CDBA believes the agencies should weigh their own economic analysis seriously in finalizing this
provision.
We perceive tension between the rule's stated goal of reducing burden and its practical effect: a bank
that already exercises reasonable business judgment about which nonprofits to support, and that
reports basic detail about its CD grants, would now be asked to obtain written commitments,
 administrative-cost attestations, and IRS Form 990 filings from every grant recipient. That
documentation burden falls disproportionately on smaller and newer organizations, again, by the
agencies' own analysis, and does not serve their goal of reducing regulatory burden or increasing
clarity.
IV. Other Definitional and Technical Changes Warranting Reconsideration
Several additional provisions, while individually narrower in scope, work in combination to reduce
flexibility for CDBA member banks and the institutions and communities they serve.
• Economic development "purpose test": The proposal removes the current requirement that
economic development financing be linked to job creation or retention for LMI persons or in
LMI geographies, replacing it with a size-based eligibility standard (SBA/SBIC size standards
or revenue at or below $1 million). This is a different mechanical test, not necessarily a more
flexible one, and could permit credit for activity with a weaker connection to LMI benefit than
under current practice. The agencies should preserve the current purpose test linking economic
development financing to job creation/retention for LMI persons or LMI geographies, and
provide additional CRA consideration, such as enhanced weighting or presumptive
qualification, for activity originated by mission-driven lenders, including U.S. Treasury-
certified CDFIs, that already satisfy both the size and LMI-benefit standards.
• Primary purpose standard: The NPR proposes to retain current guidance rather than tighten
the primary-purpose standard, which could result in less LMI targeting than under current
supervisory practice for some CD activities. CDBA encourages the agencies to use this
rulemaking to reinforce, rather than leave ambiguous, the LMI-benefit expectation.
• Affordable Housing / Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing (NOAH): CDBA supports
clarifying the treatment of naturally occurring affordable housing, but believes that extending
credit to housing affordable to middle-income households in undefined "high-cost areas,"
without a required percentage of LMI benefit, could shift some CRA-motivated investment
away from LMI households. The agencies should define "high-cost areas" narrowly and
consider a minimum LMI-benefit threshold for any CD credit tied to this category.
• Consortium loans: Removing retail-loan treatment for loans made through a lending
consortium eliminates an option CDBA members and other banks currently use to support
retail lending in their communities. The agencies should retain the option to treat qualifying
consortium loans as retail loans.
• Retail services test: Narrowing the services test to evaluate only credit services and branch
distribution, and excluding deposit products and services entirely, removes CRA recognition
for activities that many CDFI banks undertake every day to serve LMI communities. Access to
affordable deposit accounts, transaction services, financial education, and other retail banking
services often represents a consumer's first connection to the banking system and is an
important component of financial inclusion. CRA should continue to recognize institutions that
expand access to mainstream banking services for underserved households. CDBA
recommends retaining deposit products and services as a component of the service test.
 • "Incidental basis" standard for limited-purpose banks: The proposed 5% cap on incidental
lending by a bank evaluated solely on community development activity does not specify
whether the cap is measured by dollar volume, number of loans, or both. Because a bank could
be within the cap on one measure and above it on the other, CDBA requests that the agencies
clarify the metric (or metrics) that will govern this standard before finalizing the rule.
• Discriminatory or other illegal credit practices standard: CDBA supports efforts to provide
greater regulatory certainty and transparency when discriminatory or illegal credit practices
may affect a CRA rating. Any final standard should provide clear evidentiary standards and fair
notice to institutions while ensuring that CRA consequences remain tied to well-established
findings of unlawful discrimination. Such an approach would preserve strong protections
against discriminatory practices while providing institutions with greater certainty regarding
how supervisory concerns may affect CRA evaluations.
• Side Letters: The proposed rule does not expressly address the use of "side letters" among
multiple investors in a fund or activity, though its proposed allocation methodology could
accommodate the substance of such arrangements. Out of an abundance of caution, CDBA
recommends the final rule expressly acknowledge that appropriately structured side letters are
permissible, provided they include safeguards ensuring that duplicate CRA credit is not
claimed by multiple institutions for the same underlying asset.
Conclusion
CDBA appreciates the agencies' decision to pursue targeted amendments rather than a wholesale
restructure of the current CRA regulatory framework, and recognizes important elements of
regulatory relief in the proposal. At the same time, we urge the agencies to weigh the cumulative
negative effect of disruption in access to capital and undermining economic viability of LMI
communities that would likely occur under the proposal as written.
We welcome the opportunity to work with the agencies toward a final rule that achieves burden
reduction without weakening the incentives that continue to direct capital, deposits, and grants to the
communities CRA was designed to serve.
Please direct any questions regarding this letter to CDBA's Policy team.
Respectfully,

Jeannine Jacokes
Chief Executive Officer
Community Development Bankers Association

To Whom It May Concern:

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") put forth a Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, proposing significant revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). CRA has provided a long-standing incentive for banks to provide
loans, investments, grants, and services to strengthen economic drivers such as home ownership
and small business formation in the communities in which they do business.

We appreciate the agencies' intent to improve the CRA framework. At the same time, we have
concerns with several proposed changes that portend to have the unintended consequence of
diminishing the flow of capital needed to fuel such broad-based economic vitality. DreamSpring
is submitting this letter in response to the request for comments on the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation regarding the CRA.



2




DreamSpring is an award-winning nonprofit lender with a mission to increase access to business
credit and provide loans and support to propel entrepreneurs in realizing their business dreams.
Founded in 1994 in Albuquerque, New Mexico, DreamSpring has grown to serve entrepreneurs
in 27 states (Alabama, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas,
Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, North
Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Washington,
and Wyoming) across the country from coast to coast and hundreds of rural communities in
between. We work with existing and aspiring small business owners to provide the capital and
tools to grow vibrant small businesses. Our clients come from many backgrounds, geographies,
and industries, and include Main Street diners, agricultural producers, light manufacturers,
veteran-owned businesses, mechanic shops, childcare centers, eateries, and many more small
businesses that are both the bedrock and engine of our local economies.

Our organization provides loans as small as $1,000 and up to $2 million to entrepreneurs who are
committed to contributing to the American economy through small business ownership and
success. When our clients succeed as business owners, America's communities benefit from new
economic vitality and banks go on to welcome new commercial customers. DreamSpring is also
alongside small businesses when disaster strikes and has served as a Paycheck Protection
Program lender that helped tens of thousands of small businesses withstand the COVID-19
pandemic and a source of hurricane and fire relief loans assisting small businesses in affected
areas resume operations.

DreamSpring is certified by the U.S. Department of the Treasury as a Community Development
Financial Institution (CDFI) and is a Community Advantage lender through the U.S. Small
Business Administration. To date, DreamSpring has provided some 34,000 small businesses with
more than $585 million in credit for start-up, operations, and growth. Banks are critical partners
in DreamSpring's work. To fuel and fortify our impact, our organization borrows capital and
invests capacity-building grants from CRA-motivated banks that range from local community
banks to our nation's largest financial institutions. Without this CRA-motivated support,
DreamSpring would not be able to meet the credit needs of thousands of small businesses around
the country and the economic contributions of those entrepreneurs might never be realized.

General Feedback on the Proposal

As a partner to a range of banks reporting to the three entities charged with CRA regulation, we
see firsthand how a consistent regulatory framework across the three regulatory bodies benefits
communities. Consistent rules and enforcement give banks a stable foundation for making long-
term capital commitments to their communities. A rule proposed by two of the three CRA
regulators is likely to create inconsistency and confusion that will diminish CRA-related capital
flows and the small business growth that these flows make possible. The OCC and FDIC have
noted concern about rent-seeking behavior among non-profits, and an inconsistent regulatory
framework would lend itself to rent-seeking by for-profit banks seeking the regulatory



3

framework most easily satisfied by their operations. Any new CRA rule should apply across all
three regulators and if that consistency cannot be achieved, the rule should not be changed.

Specific Feedback on Numbered Questions

DreamSpring has only responded to the questions where it believes its experience and insight as
a nonprofit small business lender are particularly relevant.

Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less than $30
billion as a threshold for certain supervisory approaches, such as being considered a
community bank or being subject to the continuous examination process, should the
agencies consider adjusting the intermediate bank asset size threshold to include all banks
with an asset size of less than $30 billion that do not qualify as small banks? If the agencies
establish $30 billion as the appropriate threshold to delineate between intermediate banks
and large banks, should the agencies also adopt a larger threshold for small banks, such as
the $10 billion currently proposed as the intermediate bank threshold?

The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate
banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with
more than $10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate community development
test as intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose that requirement. Another
approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as large banks would become intermediate
banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment, and service tests and many associated
data-reporting requirements. We believe these changes would precipitously curtail capital flows
to small businesses that turn to CDFIs to meet their credit needs. The consequences may be
especially significant in rural and smaller markets, where there are fewer financial institutions
and fewer alternative sources of capital. In these communities, the loss of even one or two CRA-
motivated bank partners can materially affect whether businesses find financing to launch or
continue operations.

We also note that the original rule in 1977 had no asset thresholds. In terms of bank capacity to
serve CRA obligations and meet data burdens, it has never been easier given advances in
software and core banking systems. Even the smallest banks now have the means and tools to
readily target CRA activity and meet their obligations. And after 50 years of work, CRA
knowledge and expertise is now widespread across banks of all sizes.

Consideration of adjustment of the asset thresholds for banks is also justified in the Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking in relation to a desire to align the proportions of banks in different
categories historically with the proportions today. Given increasing industry consolidation,
maintaining those proportions seems vanishingly achievable. More importantly, it has not been
made clear why the proportion of banks in different categories should be an objective at all or
related to the setting of asset thresholds.

Question 9: Are there alternative standards the agencies should consider relying on in the
context of limiting indirect costs for CD grants? Do the proposed guardrails do enough to



4

ensure the majority of grant and donation funds go directly towards benefiting the bank's
assessment area(s)?

Before responding directly to this question, we would note that no objective evidence is
presented that a problem needs to be fixed and there is no indication analysis is underway to
determine whether the proposed remedy – changes to grant administration - has any benefit.
We oppose the proposed restrictions on community development (CD) grants. While we share
the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit communities, the
proposed requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and misunderstand
the role that flexible operating support plays in community development finance. For CDFIs,
staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk management, data systems,
financial management, technical assistance, and product development are not ancillary to
community development. They are the infrastructure that makes community development
lending possible.

Moreover, we oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA eligibility. An
organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for community impact.
Costs vary depending on an organization's size, geography, product mix, regulatory obligations,
technical-assistance model, and populations served. The cap could disproportionately affect
small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar loans, organizations
providing intensive borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new products or entering
underserved markets and organizations making necessary investments in technology,
compliance, data, and risk management.

The CRA rule does not review whether banks are efficient at meeting their obligations or how
they choose to operationalize lending efforts. It focuses only on results. It reviews whether
sufficient volume and dispersion of loans occur relative to the bank's deposits and business
model. This approach was a very intentional change made in 1995 to move from process focus to
results.

The same approach is the most effective for CD grants. If a bank believes a grant is an efficient
way to aid its community and fits its CRA strategy, then that should be sufficient evidence.
Requiring banks to measure and monitor indirect costs is an inefficient approach that will have
no discernible impact on bank assessment areas. The requirements to track and gather cost
information further impair efficiency by increasing the regulatory burden on banks. In fact, this
inefficiency may actually limit grants from going where they are most needed as banks may
prefer to avoid small grants in light of an associated documentation burden.

We recommend the agencies preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-
building grants as is currently in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage
flexibility for banks to provide the form of support that best responds to the identified
community needs instead of imposing undue compliance burdens.

Question 10: As an alternative, should the agencies eliminate all grants and donations from
CRA consideration?



5

As with Question 9, before responding directly to this question, we would note that no objective
evidence is presented that a problem needs to be fixed and there is no indication analysis is
underway to determine whether the proposed remedy – eliminating grants and donations from
CRA consideration - has any benefit. The agencies have not made clear the basis for the
proposal.

We strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and
donations from CRA consideration. It is essential to recognize there are many types of lending
and support that are positive for small businesses and the economy but which do not generate
sufficient profit to cover a providing entity's expenses. This is the reason banks choose to partner
with nonprofits and provide grants for CRA purposes – to help ensure impactful, yet not
immediately profitable, work occurs. As long as the work fits within the targets of CRA, grants
and donations are a proven way to reinvest in communities.

In closing, CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the
communities we serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility and
value the consideration of changes that would assuredly result in more capital reaching
communities with unmet credit needs, as the CRA statute was intended.

We therefore respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds
proposed and to withdraw the proposed restrictions on CD operating grants as well as the
proposed elimination of CD grants and donations.

Thank you for considering these proposed rulemaking comments.

Sincerely,

Dear Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
I am writing to ask the OCC and FDIC to preserve a strong Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) and the incentives it creates for banks to invest in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), small businesses, and communities that have historically had less access to capital.
The CRA has an important and straightforward purpose: banks should help meet the credit needs of the communities they serve, including low- and moderate-income communities. CDFIs help make that possible. I’m writing to share my support for a CDFI in my local community, WomenVenture.

CDFIs combine affordable capital with business support, relationships, and technical assistance so entrepreneurs have a better opportunity to start, stabilize, and grow their businesses. WomenVenture’s mission is to “help entrepreneurs and small business owners build profitable and sustainable businesses.” WomenVenture celebrates its 25th year as a CDFI serving Minnesota and Western Wisconsin. 

Bank partnerships are critical to this work. CRA has helped encourage banks to lend, invest, and provide other resources through CDFIs that know their communities and can help capital reach people and businesses that might otherwise be overlooked.

CRA and the Bucks County housing market
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework ensuring that banks
meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including LMI neighborhoods. In the Philadelphia
metro area, from 2010 to 2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA-qualified mortgage lending to LMI
borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA-qualified lending to small businesses.
Bucks County is part of that market, and CRA-motivated capital has helped finance affordable rental
housing (4 LIHTC projects in the last 2 years alone and 10 Habitat homes with mortgages for
homebuyers made possible through CRA).

Bucks County is often viewed as a uniformly affluent suburb. In practice, it is a county of sharply
different housing markets. Lower Bucks communities such as Bristol Borough and Township,
Bensalem, Falls Township, Morrisville and Levittown have older housing stock, lower household
incomes and pockets of concentrated need. Upper Bucks has small towns and rural areas with few bank
branches. Central Bucks has high housing costs that put homeownership out of reach for many working
households. Because incomes and prices are not uniform, aggregate county averages mask real need. In
Bucks County, home prices have risen far faster than incomes. Between 2019 and 2023, median
household income grew about 26 percent, while the average home price grew about 44 percent and
reached roughly $575,000 in 2024. Rents have climbed steadily as well, and more than a quarter of
households are ALICE (Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed). These working families earn
above the poverty line but still cannot afford the basic cost of living here. At the same time, supply is
tightening. Home sales and new permits have both fallen since 2021, and most of the County's land is
zoned for single-family use only. These countywide figures also mask greater need in Lower Bucks and
in the small towns of Upper Bucks.

The proposal would reduce investment
We are concerned that the proposal upends banks' incentives to invest in our communities. It suggests
that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to community development loans or
investments would be enough for a passing CRA rating. This is a dramatic reduction from what large
banks currently devote to community investments, and we fear it would operate as a ceiling rather than a
floor. The National Community Reinvestment Coalition estimates that annual CRA-related targets in
Pennsylvania would fall from approximately $3 billion to $1.1 billion.

Impact on LIHTC and affordable rental housing in Bucks County
The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) is the primary tool for producing affordable rental
housing in Bucks County. Industry estimates are that roughly 80 percent of Housing Credit investment is
motivated by CRA, so changes to CRA affect Housing Credit demand directly. The proposal would

This matters acutely in Bucks County for three reasons. First, the regional and community banks that

Impact on first-time homebuyers in Bucks County
Homeownership is the principal way working families build wealth, and entry into it is already difficult
in much of Bucks County. Rising prices, higher interest rates and limited starter-home inventory have
outpaced wage growth. First-time buyers depend on down-payment assistance, bank-sponsored special
purpose credit and affordable mortgage products, and on nonprofit housing counselors, all of which are
supported by CRA-motivated bank activity. In Lower Bucks, where older and more modestly priced
homes also need repairs, access to home-improvement credit is critical to preserving the housing stock.

Branches, deposit services and rural Upper Bucks
The proposal would limit the large-bank service test to credit services, removing deposit products such

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Housing Opportunities Made Equal of Greater Cincinnati (HOME) submits this comment in
opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above issued by the Office of the
Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because
it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before
making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-
income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the
agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
HOME is a private nonprofit fair housing organization serving Southwest Ohio. Since its
founding in 1968, HOME has spent more than 50 years working to promote stable, integrated
communities and eliminate illegal housing discrimination. HOME provides a wide range of
services including fair housing counseling, fair housing training for both residents and housing
providers, investigations into alleged instances of housing discrimination, and the filing of fair
housing complaints when violations do occur. HOME is a member of the National Community
Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC).
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, particularly the needs of low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress recognized that communities depend on equal access
to fair and non-predatory credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially
important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and
unequal access to mainstream financial services. The proposed rule would substantially reduce or
narrow CRA scrutiny for banks. We are concerned that these changes are being considered
without an adequate analysis of their effects on low- and moderate-income communities that
have historically experienced discrimination and disinvestment.

 Raised Asset Threshold Significantly Reduces CRA Obligations

The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determines how banks are
evaluated under CRA. In Ohio, eighteen banks representing 20.9% of all banks operating in the
state would lose community development obligations and would no longer have to invest in
critical local projects. Moreover, 43.2% of large-banks operating in Ohio would no longer be
considered large-banks under these new regulations. These large-banks would no longer be
required to maintain branches in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, volunteer with local
nonprofits, or report small business lending data each year.

In Cincinnati, banks have supported both the development of more affordable housing and the
preservation of existing housing stock and homeownership. The CRA drives affordable housing
investment both in the Cincinnati region and nationwide. CRA obligations are the primary
motivator of bank investment in Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) projects, and this
funding represents 85% of all LIHTC investment dollars nationwide. Community Development
Financial Institutions (CDFIs) also fund a considerable amount of this work in our region and
receive significant funding from banks as a result of the CRA. Many of these critical community
development projects would not be feasible without the support of these banks and the proposed
rule risks making that support harder to obtain. Raising the asset threshold would considerably
reduce CRA obligations and drastically weaken the incentive structure that motivates banks to
provide loans and make investments in the communities that they serve. The CRA should
continue to incentivize these types of investments for critical programs in underserved
communities.
These reduced regulations would also permit the closure of 176 branches serving LMI
communities in Ohio, representing a loss of over 25% of all LMI branches in the state.
Communities of color are similarly at risk with the proposed regulations jeopardizing nearly 10%
of bank branches located in their communities. These branches serve as a critical resource in
underserved communities, and their loss would be extremely consequential. Ohio already lags
behind the national average of branches in these communities and HOME's research into home
mortgage lending disparities further shows that LMI communities and communities of color are
still underserved with the current regulations. The proposed rule would only exacerbate this
issue.
Weakened Requirements for Infrastructure Projects Encourage Disinvestment

Under the current regulations, infrastructure projects in an LMI area receive CRA credit only
when they help keep or attract residents or businesses. The proposal allow credit for
infrastructure that "benefits or serves" a targeted area, even when the project delivers few
meaningful benefits to LMI residents and does not preserve or strengthen the community. This
means that a bank could seek CRA credit for a large regional infrastructure project that only
incidentally serves an LMI neighborhood, even if the project's benefits primarily flow to wealthy
communities or private companies. For example, a data center located in or connected to an LMI
community could qualify for CRA credit despite providing little direct benefit to residents.

 Proposed Rule Would Reduce Mortgage Lending
Over the last 15 years, banks have issued over $29.5 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending
to LMI borrowers and LMI census tracts in the Cincinnati MSA. These considerable investments
are essential to correcting the historic disinvestment these communities experienced and would
not have occurred without the CRA as it stands today. Under the current rule, large banks
are generally evaluated on their home mortgage, small business and small farm lending. The new
proposal outlines options for regulators to focus only on products designated as a bank's "major
product lines." This would allow weak performance in a lower volume business area to escape
meaningful scrutiny even when that lending is important locally. For example, a bank with a
high volume of business lending and extremely low home mortgage lending would not be
evaluated on their mortgage products even when the communities that bank serves demonstrate a
strong need for mortgage lending.
HOME's analysis of Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data shows that LMI
communities are consistently underrepresented in the lending process and there is a strong need
for more mortgage lending, particularly in communities of color. Census tracts with over 50%
people of color are also considerably underrepresented in the lending process. Despite
representing 33% of census tracts in Hamilton County, only 17% of mortgage lending occurred
in communities of color. Even when lending occurs in communities of color, the HMDA data
shows that over half (54%) of the borrowers receiving loans are white borrowers. However,
under the proposed rule if mortgage lending is not a major part of a bank's business, regulators
will not evaluate whether the bank is meeting this crucial community need. Absent such
evaluation, the bank will likely deprioritize making these loans.
Assessment of Fair Lending Compliance Would be Weakened Under the Proposed Rule
The proposed CRA rules weakens the criteria for what constitutes evidence of discriminatory or
other illegal credit practices and would effectively give banks a pass on unlawful discrimination,
redlining, and consumer protection. The proposed rule appears to attempt to remove redlining
violations from consideration for a downgrade in CRA performance rating. This is done by
subtly modifying the regulatory language to limit considerations of discriminatory conduct to
only "discrimination against applicants" compared to the existing regulation's consideration of
all relevant discriminatory conduct. If this reading is accurate, it is a particularly concerning
provision considering Southwest Ohio's documented history of redlining and other forms of
race-based housing and lending discrimination. A bank that is not complying with fair housing,
fair lending, or consumer protection law is by definition not serving the needs of the entire
community, regardless of how well it is meeting other tests related to low- and moderate-income
people in CRA regulations. However, under the proposed rule, some lenders may feel
empowered to deprioritize their fair lending obligations in light of the reduced oversight from
regulators.
HOME's analysis of lending practices in the region provides evidence of the ongoing impacts of
these policies and indicate that not all banks are meeting their fair lending obligations. HMDA
data for Hamilton County shows that Black households are consistently underrepresented in the
mortgage lending process. In Hamilton County (the county that contains Cincinnati, OH), Black
 borrowers represent 25% of the population yet they only represented 20% of total applications
and 16% of total originated loans. Beyond underrepresentation, HMDA data shows that Black
borrowers are still denied loans at nearly twice the rate of white borrowers. When controlling for
only upper-income applicants, upper-income Black applicants are 3.8 times more likely to be
denied compared to upper-income white applicants. These disparities provide strong evidence
that lenders are not meeting the needs of the entire community. Analysis of individual lender
activity further demonstrates that certain banks consistently fall behind their peers and fail to
meet fair lending performance metrics in our region.
The proposed rule also limits the types of evidence of unlawful discriminatory or otherwise
illegal credit practices that the agencies would consider. Under the proposal, evidence of fair
lending violations from individual lawsuits or enforcement actions by private organizations,
including qualified fair housing enforcement organizations, would not be considered in an
evaluation. This evidence must be assessed under the CRA for the law to achieve its purpose of
remedying the historic disinvestment these communities have faced. All fair lending violations
should be considered by examiners and should constitute a reason for a downgraded score.
Special Purpose Credit Programs
In a prior CRA rule, the FDIC and the OCC included special purpose credit programs authorized
under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) as part of the rule. That inclusion was
"universally" supported by commenters. The current proposal does not include mention of
special purpose credit programs. Special purpose credit programs have proven to be quite
beneficial for local communities, borrowers, and businesses. These programs have helped
strengthen the mortgage banking sector, expanding opportunities for consumers, and increasing
the breadth of mortgage products lenders can offer to people.
Special purpose credit programs are important tools for closing the homeownership gap and
ensuring that historically disadvantaged communities have fair and non-predatory access to
lending. As discussed above, the communities HOME serves have a history of racially
discriminatory housing and lending practices and the HMDA data presented in the previous
demonstrates that those historic polices still have an impact today. These communities need the
investments incentivized by the CRA to overcome these barriers. Special purpose credit
programs are specifically designed to benefit economically disadvantaged classes of people to
overcome historical segregation and discrimination. These programs empower banks to address
the unique financial needs of these communities and ensure that they have access to fair and non-
predatory lending.
From 2022-2024, special purpose credit programs backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac
helped nearly 58,000 economically disadvantaged persons fairly access homeownership and the
ability to build wealth for their families. According to the Federal Housing Finance Agency,
those loans generated $17.2 billion in positive economic impact. The OCC and FDIC should
continue to explicitly recognize special purpose credit programs as responsive credit products
under CRA.
Proposal Threatens to Significantly Reduce Philanthropic Grants
 We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants. Banks
often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling, workforce
programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants to
nonprofit organizations. These resources are incredibly important to local organizations that have
deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities. Our
organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants can play in supporting community
development as HOME receives funding from banks to perform crucial services in our
communities.
The proposed rule would considerably restrict how local organizations can use these funds by
requiring project-based budgets for CRA-eligible grants and putting limits on indirect costs. The
flexibility of CRA-eligible grants is a crucial factor in their success because it incentivizes banks
to fund important programs and initiatives that may not fit neatly into a project-based budget.
Many essential and ongoing community development activities require funding for general
operating support in addition to specific project-based funding. Banks would have far fewer
incentives to provide general operating funding, and many smaller and less resourced non-profits
would be unable to meet the increased regulatory burden to receive these grants. Even the OCC
itself acknowledges that these changes are likely to create greater difficulty for smaller
nonprofits, newer organizations, and organizations serving hard-to-reach populations. We are
concerned that these limits would reduce bank philanthropic support to nonprofit organizations
that will ultimately reduce services and resources to low- and moderate-income communities.
Conclusion
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not
have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. We therefore request that the
agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,

Elisabeth Risch, Executive Director
Housing Opportunities Made Equal

Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (the "NPRM"), published in the Federal Register on August 12,
2026, concerning the regulations that implement the Community Reinvestment Act (the "CRA").1
The NAIB represents the nation's industrial banks ("IBs"), which for more than a century have
provided specialized financial services to businesses and families across the United States and
driven innovation that enhances consumer welfare while maintaining capital standards and other
safety and soundness benchmarks that outpace many other banks. IBs proudly reinvest in the
states that charter them and the communities in which they operate; they regularly meet or exceed
their federal CRA requirements. The current CRA framework has a long track record in
producing strong CRA outcomes for IBs and the communities in which they operate.


Executive Summary

In general, the NAIB supports many of the updates to the CRA regulatory scheme contained in
the NPRM, such as the proposal to increase the asset size thresholds to categorize banks and tailor
