the regulations that apply to them, more accessible strategic plans, community development
qualifying activity confirmation process, and the ongoing consideration of community
development loans. Some proposals, however, risk causing more harm than good, or imposing
more burdens and costs than benefits. These include:

● Measuring IBs by share of loans made in their assessment area: IBs operate
nationwide but have limited physical footprints. Therefore, subjecting them to a retail
lending test that measures performance in their relatively small (compared to a nationwide
service area) assessment areas. Measuring IB retail lending in this way is incongruent with
the public policy underlying the CRA and could cause significant disruption in product
lines. These banks currently serve the needs of their communities, as measured by the
community development test.

● Eliminating or narrowing the limited purpose and wholesale designations: Many IBs
rely on the limited purpose or wholesale designation in the current CRA regulations.
Eliminating or narrowing these designations would cause banks to be measured under the
applicable asset size test, which includes a retail lending test. Many IBs would find it
difficult to meet the demands of a retail lending test.

● Collecting and reporting consumer data: If subjected to a retail lending test, IBs that
are considered large banks would be required to collect millions of consumer records and
data even if only a small fraction of their consumer lending is in their assessment area.
This would produce an enormous cost for a bank with only one office while offering no
meaningful data to a regulator.

● Departing from the long-standing treatment of consumer lending: The proposed
Major Product Lines test would evaluate all consumer lending in the aggregate whenever
it constitutes a majority of a bank's retail lending by both dollar amount and loan count.
This change would subject many IBs, without a limited purpose or wholesale designation,
to an evaluation the Agencies concluded just three years ago could not be performed
reliably: consumer loan income data is often unverified or not collected at all, no reliable
market benchmarks exist, and consumer products are too varied to compare across banks.

● Replacing long-standing broader statewide or regional area concept with
prescriptive metrics that create "hot spots:" The Agencies should retain the current
broader statewide or regional area concept. The proposed geographic flexibility standard
could direct an estimated billions of dollars a year into the Salt Lake County area alone,
worsening the "hot spot" concentration the Agencies seek to address and reducing support
for the regional and rural organizations that serve these communities.

● Excluding operating liquidity from economic development: The proposed definition
recognizes financing that "preserves" a small business's productive capacity or
employment base yet would exclude financing "primarily used for ongoing operating
liquidity," such as working capital that lets a business retain employees through a

The Uniqueness of IBs: Serving a National Customer Base from a Limited Physical Presence

In the 30 years since the CRA regulations were last amended, there has been immense change in
the character of the nation's banking sector. The banking landscape for which the three federal
banking agencies (including the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System) constructed
the present CRA regulations has been disrupted significantly by technology, most notably the
commercialization of an internet that allows a bank to reach customers in other states without
mediation by a branch. IBs have been particularly skilled in leveraging this technological progress
to offer specialty financial services on a nationwide basis while maintaining a modest physical
presence. The efficiencies of internet-based banking infrastructure have spurred greater
investment by IBs in product development, innovative underwriting, and decreases in consumer
lending rates. Today, the diversity of our nation's financial services sector enables consumers to
have access to the broadest set of financial products and services on the most competitive terms
than at any other time in American history.

While bank models have changed significantly since 1995, the obligation of banks of all shapes
and sizes to meet the needs of the communities in which they operate has not. The CRA remains
an important law with a strong moral quality and functions best when there is maximum
cooperation among a bank, its regulator, and its neighbors. Thus, regulatory tailoring is of
paramount importance for both a bank and its community, especially in the regulation of IBs that
present a special regulatory case due to their limited physical presence and nationwide consumer
base. Standardized, universal, one-size-fits-all regulation governing a bank's performance under
the CRA could have catastrophic consequences to an IB if, for example, the test were to examine
whether an IB's retail lending (national in scope) appropriately saturates its (extremely local)
assessment area in a manner similar to a more traditional community bank's lending.

While the NAIB thus appreciates that aspects of the NPRM seek to give more definition to CRA
provisions that may historically have been vague or construed differently by different regulators
(or even different regional offices of the same regulator), the Agencies should seek to avoid the
imposition of rigid bright-line performance tests that sacrifice the flexibility that a diverse
banking landscape currently relies on to meet its obligations. The CRA is an important
accountability statute. We are grateful the Agencies wish to set their expectations ex ante so as to




5
avoid the perils of ex post "regulation by enforcement." As discussed below, however, some
aspects of the NPRM create significant and material risk that banks will have to withdraw entire
product lines, create entirely new product lines, and/or create special direct lending programs
simply for the benefit of the primary assessment area that are not contemplated by their business
model and may not comport with safety and soundness, or simply fail their CRA assessments and
suffering the attendant consequences. The NPRM also proposes new data collection and reporting
rules that would place enormous regulatory burdens on IBs that presently lack the in-house staff
to collect millions of new customer data points, which seems especially unnecessary if only a
small fraction of those records are being reported to the regulator.


The Agencies Should Not Finalize a CRA Without the Federal Reserve

Before commenting on the substance of the NPRM, the NAIB respectfully suggests that the
Agencies should not promulgate a final rule unless or until the Board of Governors of the Federal
Reserve System (the "FRB") joins the rulemaking. A core strength of the American financial
system is the ability and willingness of its federal banking agencies to regulate the industry with
maximum coordination. While there will be always be minor differences in how banks are
regulated based on category (e.g., state-chartered vs. nationally chartered, or Federal Reserve
member vs. nonmember bank), the Agencies have historically proposed CRA amendments with
the FRB because doing so minimizes differences in the three regulators' approach to bank
regulation. That was true of the presently in-force regulations, dating from 1995, and was true as
well in the proposal and finalization of the 2023 attempt at CRA modernization (despite its never
having gone into effect due to judicial order). The current three-agency approach to CRA
regulation has created regulatory consistency that has reduced administrative burdens and caused
more lending, investment, and services delivered to the communities banks serve.

The conspicuous omission of the FRB's participation in this NPRM threatens the regulatory
harmony and the durability of any finalized changes to CRA regulations and would inject
unnecessary and artificial competition and charter-shopping into the banking system. First,
similarly situated banks, no matter their charter genetics or Federal Reserve membership, should
be subject to the same rules of the road and evaluated under substantially the same rubrics.2 This
is an important feature of a competitive banking landscape that keeps customer prices low and the
pace of innovation high. Regulatory consistency becomes a higher priority when, as discussed
below, changes to CRA regulations would have a substantial impact on the products and services
a bank regulated by the Agencies may offer (while a FRB-regulated community bank would not
be so affected). Second, IBs often partner with FRB-regulated community banks to fulfill CRA
obligations, such as in pooled affordable housing investments. Fragmentation of the CRA

The NPRM Should be Reproposed

The Administrative Procedure Act (the "APA") requires an agency to invite the public to
comment on any proposed change to legislative rules because public comment often improves the
quality of the final rule. So that the public can comment meaningfully on a proposal, the APA
does not permit an agency to finalize a rule unless it is substantially similar to the proposed rule.
The NAIB is concerned by the form of the NPRM for a variety of reasons and thus recommends
the Agencies repropose it (ideally, as discussed above, with the FRB) before proceeding to a final
rule. First, the NPRM's significant use of "optionality" does not present the public with a
cohesive or coherent proposal upon which it may comment. A menu-style approach to rulemaking
supposes the public is capable of considering numerous permutations and combinations and
commenting on every hypothetical regulatory outcome. To name a few: the NPRM proposes two
significantly different alternative options for a retail lending test; two different options for
"geographic flexibility standards"; and two options for how agencies will consider discriminatory
or other illegal credit practices. As the Agencies know, the CRA is an extremely complex law
with even more complex regulations. The pervasive use of optionality asks the public to zig-zag
through a maze of "what ifs" and thus deprives the public (and the Agencies) of the helpful
feedback mechanism contemplated by the APA. Perhaps a more appropriate forum for such
significant optionality would be in an advanced notice of proposed rulemaking or a request for
information.

The most significant concern with the format of the NPRM for the NAIB is the treatment of the
Agencies' proposal to summarily eliminate the "limited purpose" designation, which many IBs
rely on. In the Supplementary Information, the Agencies state: "In addition to the proposed major
product line standard, the [A]gencies are considering whether to eliminate the category of limited
purpose banks."3 Yet in the proposed regulatory text, the definition of "limited purpose bank or
savings association" is retained, as is § 25.25, outlining the community development test for such
banks. Elimination of this designation—and the consequence of subjecting IBs that currently
enjoy that designation to a retail lending test they simply cannot pass—is of paramount

A Retail Lending Test is Incongruent with the Unique IB Business Model

The Agencies have a long tenure of appreciation for the significant differences between the
business models of traditional banks and IBs, including in their CRA regulations. IBs often
maintain a limited physical presence yet provide specialty financial services and products on a
nationwide basis that, by definition, is much larger than a CRA assessment area. Historically,
however, IBs have been able to meet their CRA obligations using the community development
test or a Strategic Plan.

Yet in various ways discussed below, the effect of the NPRM will be to eliminate the community
development test and to subject IBs to a retail lending test (unless they operate under a Strategic
Plan) within their relatively small assessment area(s). This is a significant departure from what the
Agencies concluded just three years ago. In finalizing their 2023 CRA regulations, the Agencies
were sensitive to the unintended, negative consequences of subjecting limited purpose and other
IBs involved in consumer lending to a retail lending test that required significant distribution in
their assessment areas. At that time,

[t]he agencies also considered the potential unintended effects of a distribution analysis if
[consumer loans other than automobile loans] were evaluated under the Retail Lending Test—for
example, evaluation under a distribution analysis could inadvertently encourage a bank to issue
credit cards to customers who already have access to a consumer credit card, which may not be
responsive to community credit needs.4

Any test that applies a comparison or ratio of loans made into and beyond an assessment area
simply does not work for a nationwide lender with a limited physical presence and, often, a single
assessment area. For many IBs, the share of such loans in the assessment area would, by design
(as nationwide lenders), be a fraction of one percent. A retail lending test would thus turn on a

al.) (enjoined from taking effect by federal court order).

bank's business model, not its real-world ability to serve the needs of the community. This result
will squeeze IBs into one of three outcomes, each of them with negative consequences: (i) a
sudden need to graft an existing product line (or open a new line) with specific marketing and
execution into the bank's AA, regardless of safety and soundness principles; (ii) the closing of an
entire product line so as to avoid a failure to satisfy an AA-based retail lending test; or (iii) the
failure of the bank to meet its newly prescribed CRA requirements, even if it would have been
found to meet the needs of the community under the community development test. (As discussed
below, it would also cause a nationwide lender to collect millions of records on a nation-wide
basis that would provide the Agencies no useful information about the IB's consumer lending in
its assessment area.) For IBs that do not use a Strategic Plan, there are likely no IBs today whose
business would not need to undergo significant transformation to avoid failing the retail lending
test the NPRM would impose on them.

Moreover, subjecting IBs to a retail lending test by measuring lending in and outside of an
assessment area is incongruous with the public policy substrate of the CRA. The CRA was
enacted in large part to prevent a bank from taking advantage of a local community by collecting
deposits in the assessment area and making loans to a more remote community. Thus, for banks
that take deposits from their local community, an in/out ratio style test may be appropriate. But as
the Agencies recognized about IBs in the 1995 Community Reinvestment Act regulations,
wholesale and limited purpose banks "typically draw their resources from, and serve areas well
beyond, their immediate communities." The same is true of IBs that do not hold those
designations. A nationwide lender with a single assessment area may make a large number of
loans in that assessment area, enough to evaluate its borrower and geographic distribution and to
demonstrate that it serves its community well. Yet because those loans may represent only a small
fraction of its nationwide lending, its in/out ratio will be low regardless of how well it serves the
assessment area. The ratio measures the size of the bank's national business, not the quality or
volume of its local lending. The same is true of the loan-to-deposit ratio for a bank whose
deposits are not drawn from its assessment area. The NPRM would codify both measures as
standing criteria of the lending test, carrying this distortion into the new framework. As the
Agencies revise and codify the lending test, they should provide that, for nationwide lenders with
a single assessment area, neither the in/out ratio nor the loan-to-deposit ratio will be applied. Any
evaluation should instead be based on the number and dollar amount of the bank's loans in its
assessment area relative to the credit demand in that assessment area, not on those loans' share of
the bank's national portfolio. Indeed, under proposed Appendix A, a small or intermediate bank's
lending performance would be rated "satisfactory" only if, in general, "a majority of its loans are
in its assessment area(s)." For large banks, the proposed rating criteria likewise scale with the
share of loans made in the assessment area. "Outstanding" performance requires that "a
substantial majority" of loans in major product lines be made in the assessment area(s), while "a
very small percentage" is a criterion for "substantial noncompliance." A nationwide lender with a
single assessment area cannot meet these standards regardless of how well it serves that




9
assessment area. Under the large bank criteria, the share of its loans made in its assessment area
would point toward the lowest possible rating even where its local lending is excellent.


The Agencies Should Thus Retain the Limited Purpose/Wholesale Designation

In 1995, the Agencies tailored the present CRA regulations very well because they offer banks
like IBs to receive a "limited purpose" or "wholesale" designation ("LP/W Banks") if they
specialize in a limited set of consumer loans (in the case of a limited purpose bank) or if they
make no consumer loans at all (a wholesale bank). As the Agencies then noted, "A uniform
treatment of these institutions is therefore not practicable."5 LP/W Banks are examined under a
"community development" ("CD") performance test, an evaluation of "the record of these
institutions in helping to meet credit needs through community development lending, qualified
investments, and community development services."6 The Agencies chose to subject these banks
to this test because it recognized that "wholesale and limited purpose institutions typically draw
their resources from, and serve areas well beyond, their immediate communities."7

Importantly, the community development test does not subject a limited purpose or wholesale
bank to examination based on its retail lending in its assessment area because the data would
almost always present an inaccurate picture of the bank's CRA performance. A nationwide direct
consumer lender, for instance, may make only a fraction of a percent of its loans into its
assessment area, offering only statistically insignificant insight into whether the bank is meeting
the credit needs of the community through consumer lending alone. A different limited purpose
lender may make consumer loans only indirectly and as such would have no control over where
or to whom its loans are made (e.g., an automobile finance company that relies on dealerships to
offer and extend credit may not have an affiliated dealership in its assessment area). A wholesale
lender that makes only business-to-business loans offers no consumer loans at all (except,
perhaps, on an accommodation basis). A one-size-fits-all approach simply does not work for most
IBs, whether they are designated as LP/W banks or not.

The NPRM nevertheless proposes (or, as discussed above, at least considers) to eliminate the
limited purpose designation altogether. It also proposes to narrow the eligibility to be designated
as a wholesale bank (through the "incidental basis" test). The Agencies assert that because limited
purpose banks are, by definition, consumer lenders, they should be subjected to the generally
applicable (and proposed to be modified by the Major Product Lines concept) retail lending test

The Agencies Should Make Strategic Plans Easier to Obtain and Use

While the NAIB opposes the elimination or narrowing of the limited purpose and wholesale
designations, it supports the agencies' proposal "to make the Strategic Plan option a more viable
and less burdensome option for banks."8 Strategic Plans, which many IBs use today, are arguably
the most faithful manner of adhering to the CRA because they bespoke agreements negotiated in
good faith between banks and the communities in which they operate. They are thus bespoke and
tailored to the bank's model and the assessment area's specific needs.


8 NPRM, supra n.1, at 52120.




11
In adopting rules that promote more widespread adoption of Strategic Plans, however, the
agencies should resist two impulses. First, the Agencies should not view a more accessible
Strategic Plan program as a cure for eliminating or narrowing the limited purpose or wholesale
designation. Doing so would heighten the risk that a failure to negotiate a Strategic Plan would
force the bank to become subject to a retail lending test that it likely cannot pass—a regulatory
sword of Damocles. The Agencies should continue to permit limited purpose or wholesale banks
to use Strategic Plans, which allow for more granular tailoring to each community's unique needs
and an IB's unique business model. Second, the Agencies should include, as a hortatory statement
of policy in any final rule, an exhortation that the appropriate regulator should not require
approximations of the asset-size retail lending test in order to approve a Strategic Plan. Based on
recent experience, the NAIB believes that the Agencies may have a preference for a retail lending
component in a proposed Strategic Plan even if the bank does not engage in direct retail lending,
either at all or on a very limited basis within its assessment area. Formally or informally requiring
retail lending in Strategic Plans would frustrate the Agencies' stated goal of making such plans
more usable and accessible.

IBs using Strategic Plans have noted that regulators' regional office staff are often helpful
resources in drafting a plan and seeing it through to approval and implementation because they
know the characteristics of local assessment areas better than those who might review a proposed
plan in Washington, DC. The NAIB also requests clarification that Strategic Plans that are
effective if or when the Agencies publish a final rule in connection with this NPRM will remain
effective notwithstanding any changes to the Strategic Plan program made by a final rule.


Comments on Proposed Modifications to Community Development Activities

The NAIB supports the Agencies' attempt in the NPRM to give further definition to the meaning
of "community development" (CD) for purposes of meeting a bank's obligations under the CRA.
While a principles-based test has worked for many years, the NPRM rightly acknowledges that
subjectivity and inconsistent application has caused confusion (and likely foregone investment) in
what kinds of activities "count" and which do not. As with all regulation, more explicit
communication ex ante helps banks plan their CD activities, regardless of the test to which they
are subject under the CRA.

The NAIB opposes, however, the proposed change to the definition of "economic development"
that would expressly exclude "financing primarily used for ongoing operating liquidity."9 This
proposal substitutes a rigid, bright-line rule as a perceived upgrade to the vagueness of the present
"primary purpose" test, but it overshoots its mark.10 There are many operating liquidity loans in

9 See NPRM, supra n.1, at 52181 (proposing §25.12(3)(i)(B)).
10 See NPRM, supra n.1, at 52134 (propounding Question 29).
 12
place today that "preserve the business's or farm's productive capacity . . . or employment bases"
but the proposed regulatory text would inexplicably exclude all such loans from economic
development. There is no articulated need (or explanation in the Supplementary Information) to
summarily declare that all operating liquidity loans are de facto inconsistent with the first part of
the proposed regulatory text's definition of economic development; the form of the financing
should not prejudge its economic effect. Moreover, this exclusion would likely prevent thinly
capitalized businesses from growing in their communities, disadvantageous to the very businesses
the CRA was designed to assist. This proposed exclusion should be retracted. At a minimum, the
primary purpose test should be retained with respect to operating liquidity credit so that lenders
can demonstrate to the satisfaction of an examiner that such a loan is primarily for economic
development.

The NAIB supports the creation of new ___.13(b)(1), which would provide a means by which a
bank could pre-confirm that a proposed CD activity will meet the Agencies' CD criteria. The 90-
day timeframe is appropriate and helpful, though the NAIB would urge the Agencies not to grant
themselves an extension of time because there is a risk that after 90 days the opportunity for the
proposed CD activity may evaporate or expire. The proposed illustrative list concept will also
help banks understand the scope of CD activities as well and would hopefully, over time, decrease
the need for a bank to seek and receive pre-clearance. Additionally, the NAIB supports
considering community development loans like community development investments in each
evaluation period, in which they remain on the Bank's balance sheet. This change would create
parity between loans and investments and encourage the long-term financing that community
development projects require.

As noted above, because IBs typically have a limited physical presence, those that qualify under a
limited purpose or wholesale designation, as well as those that operate under a Strategic Plan,
often rely on their ability to satisfy the applicable community development test by performing
qualifying activities that may be outside the geographic bounds of their assessment area but that
nevertheless serve the assessment area. One benefit of this approach is that it prevents the
cramming of several IBs' CD activity into relatively limited census tracts (e.g. in Utah and
Nevada) by which a very limited population of communities would be served—an exacerbation of
the "hot spot" phenomenon the Agencies highlight. For the same reason, consideration of
community development activity that benefits the assessment area through a regional or statewide
channel ameliorates the "desert" phenomenon by extending CD funds to parts of a state that may
otherwise be underserved by the CRA. Many CD organizations operate on a regional or statewide
basis with a purpose mandate to benefit the assessment area. The Agencies should consider that
assistance to these organizations would decrease significantly if banks were required to channel
CD activity into the geographic bounds of an assessment area before any CRA credit would be
given for regional or statewide CD efforts that include the assessment area.





13
The NAIB thus opposes any new standard or rule that would have the effect of requiring
community development activity to be geographically located in an assessment area. Proposed
section 25.13(d)(1) appears to continue to contemplate activities that may occur on a statewide or
regional basis but that have "the purpose, mandate, or function of benefiting or serving the bank's
. . . assessment area(s)."11 The Supplementary Material, however, discusses a threshold a bank
would have to meet with in-area CD activity before out-of-area CD activity could be considered.
The NPRM contemplates a standard of 1.25% of Tier 1 capital for limited purpose and wholesale
banks (assuming those designations are preserved) and .625% for large banks. These percentages
are unreasonably high, and the Agencies provide no support or justification for this metric.
Informal calculations show that this metric would cause a surge of approximately $3 billion per
year to be directed to the Salt Lake County MSA (Utah), with a population of 1.2 million
residents, without any corresponding change in community need or demand. This amount for this
MSA would be highly disproportionate to the needs of the community. The NAIB therefore urges
Agencies to retain the broader statewide or regional area concept and to confirm in any final rule
that (i) an activity with a statewide or regional purpose, mandate, or function that encompasses
the assessment area satisfies § 25.13(d)(1)(ii) without expressly naming the assessment area; and
that (ii) for a bank with a single assessment area, such an activity receives full consideration in
that assessment area.

The NPRM's proposal to "permit the appropriate agency to determine based on performance
context that a bank that extended a lesser amount of CD loans or CD investments and CD grants,
as applicable, may nonetheless receive consideration for CD activities outside of its assessment
area(s)"—a highly subjective test—casts doubt on why the Agencies are proposing to establish a
bright-line test in the first place. Coupling an objective standard with broad regulatory permission
to deviate cuts against the laudable principles of certainty and predictability the Agencies seek to
pursue in publishing the NPRM.


The Agencies Should Increase the Asset Size Thresholds for Bank Categorization

The NAIB strongly supports the Agencies' proposal to increase the asset size thresholds for bank
categories. The Agencies rightly recognize that thresholds designed for 1995 do not produce a
similar distribution in the 2026 banking market. The proposed thresholds are such that "the
distribution of banks of different sizes across the performance tests and standards would be
substantially similar to the proportions of their distribution in 1995."12 Specifically, the proposal
to define "large bank" as one with more than $10 billion in assets is good policy. The NAIB
would support increasing this number to $30 billion, as contemplated in Question 1, for the
reasons set forth therein. The NAIB's support for this proposal derives not from any desire to

Other Comments

The NAIB also supports the Agencies' proposal to create an objective standard for determining
which practices will adversely affect evaluation of a bank's CRA performance. As proposed in
Option 1, the Agencies should consider only those violations that are cited in a public Federal or
state enforcement action or judicial order. The NAIB does, however, express concern with the
proposed addition of all Dodd-Frank section 1031 "UDAAP" citations if those citations involve
allegations of discrimination that an agency could not substantiate under otherwise applicable
antidiscrimination laws (e.g., the Equal Credit Opportunity Act). The Consumer Financial
Protection Bureau's UDAAP authority is important but should not be used as a roving anti-

technical enforcement action, particularly one involving self-identified and promptly remediated

that qualify as large banks (as proposed, more than $10 billion in assets) for consumer loans—a
burden that would be imposed by the proposed Major Product Lines test on IBs that engage in

require the hiring of several dozen staff dedicated solely to CRA compliance, thus directing
capital away from lending and toward compliance. Moreover, the "reporting" requirement would
tell the Agencies very little about a specific bank's CRA performance in the assessment area
because: (i) the bank may do only an insignificant amount of consumer lending in the assessment

area; (ii) the consumer loan product may not be tailored for LMI individuals; and/or (iii) there

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
The Office of Rural and Farmworker Housing submits this comment in opposition to
the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office
of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also
request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze
the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an
opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting
any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
The Office of Rural and Farmworker Housing (ORFH) is a 501c3 nonprofit based in
Yakima, WA. We provide affordable housing development services, including technical
assistance, to community partners seeking to expand affordable housing opportunities.
Our partners are primarily housing authorities and other nonprofit organizations. ORFH
provides the knowledge, tools and capacity to those who have the desire and the means to
operate affordable housing. Our development efforts began in earnest with farmworker
housing, but our portfolio of work has expanded to include housing for seniors, veterans,
and shelters for those experiencing homelessness or overcoming domestic violence.
ORFH is also a community loan fund and makes low-interest loans to our partners in
support of their affordable housing efforts. ORFH's development efforts directly provide
community support and enhancement.
1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 2
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In our service
area (rural Washington state), from 2010-2024, banks made over $1 billion in CRA
qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1
capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough
to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
Low- and moderate-income communities cannot withstand such a reduction in
community development investments and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for
banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the communities they serve, there could
be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in our community, banks often
provide investments in low income housing tax credits (LIHTC), construction loans and
gap financing for the creation of affordable rental housing opportunities. It is imperative
that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing
the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce
lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and
whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment
would be disproportionately affected.
2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks
surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625%
for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical
effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
 3
For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate
from access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families
can safely receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain
responsible credit. We are therefore concerned that under the proposal, examiners will no
longer evaluate whether banks that are still subject to the service test offer affordable
checking and savings accounts. By reducing the importance of deposit services and
branch performance in CRA evaluations, the proposal eliminates incentives for banks to
offer basic products that help unbanked and underbanked households. Before finalizing
these changes, the agencies should identify which communities would receive less
scrutiny of bank branches and services, determine whether the effects would fall
disproportionately on low- and moderate-income communities and explain why the
changes are justified despite those consequences.
We are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business
development, financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and
other community-based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with
nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local
organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific
needs of their communities.
ORFH is a small nonprofit organization with a full-time staff of 13. Bank grants,
scholarships and other special awards are a valuable investment in our ability to sustain
operations and provide a high level of capacity and support to the community sponsors
that we work with. Additionally, a great number of the affordable housing developments
that ORFH staff work on are also beneficiaries of bank support, ranging from investing in
low-income housing tax credits to interim construction loans and grants to operational
support. This support from local banking establishments particularly is vital to supporting
community revitalization efforts and ensuring that the members of those communities
have access to safe, affordable, well-managed housing.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect
costs and new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for
smaller organizations.3 For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be
unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses
are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also
have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or
redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with
limited administrative capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects
3 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 4
would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income communities
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of
reducing perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine
what the changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.
Under current guidance, infrastructure projects in an LMI area generally receive CRA
credit only when they help keep or attract residents or businesses. The proposal
would change the standard by allowing credit for infrastructure that "benefits or serves" a
targeted area, even when the project delivers little meaningful benefit to LMI residents
and does not help preserve or strengthen the community.4
This means that a bank could seek CRA credit for financing a large regional
infrastructure project that only incidentally serves an LMI neighborhood, even if most of
the project's benefits flow to affluent communities or private companies.
Before expanding what infrastructure projects qualify for CRA credit in this way, the
agencies should analyze the impact of expanding the types of projects that qualify for
CRA credit on people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income
communities, including whether it could result in a reduction in projects that preserve or
strengthen LMI communities. In addition, the agencies should explain why changing the
standard is consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting
the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income households.
It is worth noting that prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
●
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
scrutiny under the proposal;
●
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
●
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color; and
●
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability.
We believe that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough
analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely
needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
4 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,1335 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 5
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely,
Office of Rural and Farmworker Housing

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

Golden State Opportunity writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in
response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the
credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low and moderate income
(LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and
provide services in underserved communities, challenges related to redlining,
discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access remain.

Golden State Opportunity is a nonprofit dedicated to ending poverty by providing all
Californians with the tools to build financial well-being and thrive. As a nonprofit, we
receive state funds along with private grants, often from banks. We serve many LMI
communities throughout the state of California through free tax preparation, Earned
Income Tax Credit Outreach, and financial planning services. Having diversified streams of
revenue allows us to balance the extremely restrictive state grant requirements which
don't cover all our programmatic expenses or overhead costs. Without this funding, our
capabilities to provide these vital services would shrink, along with possibilities for new
partnerships and improved programs for the LMI communities we serve.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift. The
proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on LMI
communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional 60 days so

we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost to communities
because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

 Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring a
demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating that large banks
and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more than 15% of these grants
on overhead.[1] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and OCC question whether they should
end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller groups,
may be impacted.[2]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local needs.
They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and investment
products into communities inclined to trust long established local organizations. Many
nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment assistance programs, that
support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions to operate. Smaller, local, and
rural organizations will be least able to meet new reporting obligations, and they risk
losing bank support as a result. The proposal would also end impactful contributions from
banks for general operating support, sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps in their
own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower education, credit
building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job training and placement, tax
assistance, affordable housing and other services and programs which help residents
become stable and bankable so that banks can attract new deposits and make new loans
in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will focus
grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet their new FDIC
and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15% overhead
restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As one example, in
order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to pare down costs for

critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology,
impact measurement, product development, and borrower technical assistance. With less
support to sustain these operational functions, organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA activity
that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large negative
impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding, the harm it will
cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA, and the disruption it
will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to allow
for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of entities and
activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA was meant to support.
If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed, communities will also suffer
significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and CDFI support, more LMI
branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer community serving nonprofit
organizations, and increased bank discrimination and redlining with no CRA consequence.
The CRA will become further removed from its purpose of encouraging banks to support
LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to reconsider this proposal.


Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Very Truly Yours,







Amy Everitt
President
Golden State Opportunity

cc: Rise Economy






[1] Proposing a 15% ceiling on indirect costs is inconsistent with historic federal policy and practice as
the federal government routinely makes grant awards where more than 15% of the grant can be used
for indirect or overhead costs.

[2] The proposal notes, "The OCC also expects several potential second order impacts, including a
possible shift in CRA-motivated activity toward lending and credit services and away from certain CD
activities, in particular grants and deposit services." The proposal also notes that provisions "may
reduce CRA incentives for general operating-support grants, grants to intermediaries, or grants to
organizations with higher operating-cost ratios, which could affect nonprofit capacity and the distribution
of CRA motivated grant funding." And finally, "Some general operating support, capacity-building
grants, intermediary grants, or grants to smaller nonprofits may receive less CRA motivated funding."

Dear Comptroller Gould, Chairman Hill, and Agency Leadership,

On behalf of Oweesta Corporation, the national intermediary organization dedicated to supporting and
investing in Native Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) that work across Indian
County, we write to submit these comments on the proposed rule regarding the Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA).

While we have signed on to broader coalition comment letters addressing the overarching structural shifts
in this rulemaking, we are filing this dedicated comment letter to express our grave concern regarding
language and provisions that target financial intermediaries. Specifically, we want to articulate why our
role and work as a national financial intermediary for Native CDFIs is vital, unique, and irreplaceable —
a regulatory necessity rather than a supplementary option— and why policies restricting or discounting
intermediary models will inadvertently and dangerously sever capital access for the most underinvested
communities in the nation.

Background on Oweesta Corporation and Our Significance in Indian Country

For 26 years, Oweesta Corporation has served as a respected national financial intermediary connecting
institutional capital to Native CDFIs, Native nonprofits, and Tribal communities throughout Indian
Country. Operating under our mission to provide opportunities for Native people to develop financial
assets and create wealth by establishing strong, permanent institutions, Oweesta's central vision is to
ensure that Native communities possess the capacity and ingenuity to maintain sustainable, economic,
spiritual, and cultural well-being.


 2432 Main Street, 1st Floor | Longmont, CO 80501 | 303.774.8838 | info@oweesta.org | www.oweesta.org

Over the decades, Oweesta has persevered against severe structural and systemic headwinds—barriers
that many non-Native intermediaries have never had to face—to direct hundreds of millions of dollars
into Native communities. Under our mission-driven strategic plan, Oweesta remains steadfast in
facilitating significant capital deployment (targeting half a billion dollars of investment in Indian Country
by 2030) across critical areas including affordable housing, small business development, New Markets
Tax Credits, and economic sovereignty. By moving our capital where it's needed most, we will create
jobs and opportunity and boost economies across Tribal communities.

Comments on the Proposed Rule: The Irreplaceable Role of Intermediaries in Reaching
Underinvested Native Communities

We are particularly alarmed by provisions in the proposed rule that would require community
development grants to be used directly by the organization receiving bank funding, effectively barring
pass-through grant structures. Furthermore, for large banks, the proposal would impose strict caps
limiting indirect administrative costs to 15 percent while demanding extensive supporting documentation.

In practice, these restrictive provisions threaten to penalize or outright disqualify banks from receiving
CRA credit when they fund nonprofit intermediaries that distribute vital grants or low-cost capital to local
grassroots nonprofit organizations driving on-the-ground community development activities. For Indian
Country and other ultra-marginalized regions, cutting off the intermediary layer dismantles the exact
logistical and financial bridge required to deliver capital where it is most desperately needed.

We are deeply concerned that provisions targeting or restricting the recognition of financial
intermediaries will severely undermine capital flows to markets that have been neglected for far too long.
Our work demonstrates precisely why the intermediary structure is indispensable:

•
Expanding CRA Investment into Underinvested Native Communities: Oweesta serves as a
national financial intermediary connecting bank capital to Native CDFIs that often lack the size,
staffing, infrastructure, or direct banking relationships necessary to access CRA-motivated
investments independently. Many Native CDFIs operate in rural, remote, and reservation
communities where traditional financial institutions have limited or no presence. Oweesta bridges
this gap by aggregating capital and deploying it through Native-led institutions that understand
and serve their communities.

•
Reducing Barriers and Increasing the Impact of Bank Investments: Oweesta provides the
financial infrastructure, underwriting, portfolio management, compliance, reporting, and technical
assistance that allow banks to invest at scale while reaching smaller Native CDFIs. Rather than
requiring banks to establish and manage numerous individual investment relationships, Oweesta
offers an established intermediary through which capital can reach multiple Native communities.


 2432 Main Street, 1st Floor | Longmont, CO 80501 | 303.774.8838 | info@oweesta.org | www.oweesta.org
This structure reduces transaction costs, strengthens Native CDFI capacity, and makes CRA-
related investment opportunities more accessible and sustainable.

•
Preserving CRA Access and Advancing Native Economic Sovereignty: Native CDFIs face
unique geographic, economic, and structural barriers to attracting conventional bank investment.
CRA policies should explicitly recognize qualified investments made through Native CDFI
intermediaries, including Oweesta, so that Native communities are not inadvertently excluded
from capital intended to address financial inequities. Oweesta's intermediary model ensures that
capital reaches Native-controlled financial institutions, supporting locally determined priorities in
housing, small business development, community facilities, and economic development while
strengthening long-term Native economic sovereignty.

A Stark Reality: The Lack of Infrastructure and Banking Deserts in Indian Country

To understand why intermediaries like Oweesta are a regulatory necessity rather than a supplementary
option, one must look at the profound absence of traditional banking infrastructure in Native regions. For
example, the Navajo Nation spans more than 27,000 square miles (roughly the size of West Virginia)
across Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah. Within this vast territory, there are historically very few
traditional brick-and-mortar bank branches.

For many years, there was only one financial institution serving as the primary commercial bank
operating physical branches directly on the reservation—maintaining a total of just 5 traditional branches
to serve a population of tens of thousands of residents. This creates massive "banking deserts" where
community members are forced to drive dozens or even hundreds of miles for routine in-person banking.
Furthermore, these rare branches provide highly limited services: they largely handle basic deposits and
check-cashing, and they do not provide mortgage lending products.

In an environment characterized by such extreme scarcity of traditional financial institutions and a high
percentage of unbanked or underbanked households, Native CDFIs—backed and capitalized by national
intermediaries like Oweesta—are the only entities delivering mortgage credit, small business capital, and
financial capability training. Penalizing or discouraging the use of intermediaries under the CRA will
directly penalize these banking deserts, cutting off the single pipeline of capital capable of reaching them.

Conclusion

Oweesta urges the agencies to explicitly protect and encourage qualified investments and community
development activities executed through mission-driven intermediaries. Restricting intermediary credit
under the guise of technical modifications will not streamline community development; rather, it will wall
off remote, rural, and reservation communities from the capital they desperately need.




 2432 Main Street, 1st Floor | Longmont, CO 80501 | 303.774.8838 | info@oweesta.org | www.oweesta.org
Thank you for the opportunity to submit these comments and for your consideration of the unique
realities of Indian Country.


Sincerely,



Chrystel Cornelius, President and CEO

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; RIN 1557–AF57, RIN 3064–AG31
To Whom It May Concern:
The Wisconsin Bankers Association (WBA) is the largest financial trade association in
Wisconsin, representing nearly 180 state and nationally chartered banks, savings banks, and
savings and loan associations of all sizes located in Wisconsin, their branches, and over 30,000
employees. WBA appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) (collectively, the
Agencies) proposal to amend their Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules (proposal).

Based on the extensive feedback the agencies have received on the current rules, the results of
the litigation regarding the 2023 CRA rules, and the agencies' supervisory experience
examining banks for compliance with the CRA, they have proposed targeted changes to their
current rules. In particular, the proposal seeks to refocus CRA on its statutory objective of
encouraging banks to meet the credit needs of their communities, to better ensure that
community development grants reach the communities they are intended to benefit, to reduce
unnecessary burden, and to provide greater clarity on how to obtain CRA consideration.

While many aspects of the current regulatory framework continue to work well and should be
preserved, WBA supports updating the regulations to ensure that CRA evaluations remain
appropriately tailored to the diversity of the financial institutions subject to the CRA. WBA also
shares the Agencies' goal of aligning the regulation with the CRA statute, appreciates the
proposal's renewed focus on credit needs, and supports the Agencies' goal of reducing
regulatory burden.
Asset-Size Thresholds
WBA supports raising the Small and Intermediate Bank thresholds to at least $1 billion and $10
billion, respectively. As the Agencies acknowledge in the proposal, the current thresholds have
not kept pace with changes in the banking industry. According to the proposal, roughly 80
percent of banks qualified as small banks when the Agencies created the category in 1995.
Today, only about 57 percent of banks fall into the comparable small bank category. The
proposal would bring that figure back to about 80 percent, while the largest banks would still
hold roughly 85 percent of industry assets, much as they did in 1995.




WISCONSIN BANKERS ASSOCIATION | 4721 South Biltmore Lane | Madison, WI 53718 | P: 608-441-1200 | F: 608-661-9381 | wisbank.com
Generally speaking, a bank with $5 billion in assets should not be examined under the same
framework as a bank with $500 billion in assets. Yet under the current rules, both are evaluated
as Large Banks and must collect and report data, despite significant differences in scale,
staffing, and resources. In a joint trade letter, which WBA has joined, the history of these
thresholds and the case for realigning them is discussed in greater detail.
WBA also asks that both thresholds be adjusted annually and tied to nominal Gross Domestic
Product (GDP). Under the proposal, only the Small Bank threshold would adjust each year,
while the $10 billion Intermediate Bank cap would stay fixed and inevitably become outdated.
Nominal GDP reflects both inflation and economic growth, so it would help keep these
categories meaningful over time and reduce the need for repeated rulemakings.
These changes would not exempt any bank from the CRA. Every bank would continue to have
CRA responsibilities and would continue to be examined. Banks moving into the Intermediate
category would still be evaluated on their community development activities. They would simply
have more flexibility to choose the mix of loans and investments that best fits the needs of their
communities.
That said, the higher thresholds would eliminate the community development test for many
banks that are currently intermediate small banks and would move into the small bank category.
Many of WBA's small community bank members are heavily engaged in their communities,
serving on nonprofit boards, contributing to area nonprofits that support low- and moderate-
income (LMI) populations, and making community development loans to meet local credit
needs. With a $1 billion small bank threshold and a lending test only, those activities would no
longer be considered as a distinct part of the evaluation, which could impact these banks'
ratings.
On the alternatives the Agencies raised, WBA does not support tying the Small Bank threshold
to the Small Business Administration's size standard. CRA thresholds should be set by the
banking Agencies, not by an agency with no role in CRA supervision. WBA appreciates that the
Agencies are also considering a higher $30 billion threshold and encourages them to keep in
mind the overall regulatory burden community banks face as they finalize the rule.
Finally, the new thresholds raise some practical questions, which the joint trade letter addresses
in more detail. Banks moving from Large to Intermediate need clarity on how their exams will
work once they no longer report CRA data, including assurance that they won't be measured
against data reported by Large Banks. Small Banks with strong community development
programs should be able to choose evaluation under the Intermediate Bank test so that work is
recognized. And banks that change categories should be able to either move to the new
framework at the start of the next year or finish their current evaluation period under the existing
rules.
Other Aspects of the Proposal

WBA supports the joint trade letter's recommendations on the remaining aspects of the
proposal, except as noted below, and defers to that letter for a full discussion. However, WBA
would like to highlight a few points in its own letter.
First, banks, regulators, customers, and communities are all best served by a stable regulatory
framework. As discussed in the joint trade letter, history shows that CRA reforms last when they
are developed on an interagency basis. To that extent, WBA urges the OCC and the FDIC to
work with the Federal Reserve on a unified CRA rule.




WISCONSIN BANKERS ASSOCIATION | 4721 South Biltmore Lane | Madison, WI 53718 | P: 608-441-1200 | F: 608-661-9381 | wisbank.com
The final rule should also accommodate the different ways banks do business. Strategic plans
remain an important tool for aligning a bank's CRA responsibilities with both local community
needs and its business strategy. The Agencies should strengthen that option by preserving
flexibility, grandfathering existing plans, and providing consistent examiner support. Likewise,
the rule should keep the wholesale and limited purpose designations so that these specialized
institutions aren't forced into retail-focused exams that don't reflect how they operate.
When it comes to lending, CRA evaluations should focus on the lending that matters most to a
bank's business. Major product lines should be determined at the bank level. For consumer
lending, the Agencies should keep the existing "substantial majority" standard and define it as
75 percent of a bank's total lending, rather than lowering it to a simple majority as proposed.
WBA also appreciates that the proposal keeps the service evaluation focused on credit,
consistent with the CRA's focus on helping meet community credit needs.
On community development, the Agencies should refine the proposed definitions, including
those covering affordable housing, financial education, economic development, essential
infrastructure, disaster recovery, and grants. With respect to affordable housing, the joint trade
letter supports including middle-income housing in high-cost markets. WBA's preference is to
keep affordable housing focused on serving low- and moderate-income individuals. Including
middle-income housing would create an incentive for middle-income projects, which could be
more profitable, and may impact the reach of affordable housing in traditionally defined LMI
areas. Banks should have flexibility in how they allocate activities that benefit more than one
assessment area. They should also receive credit for activities outside their assessment areas if
they earned a Satisfactory or better rating on their prior exam. WBA also supports the Agencies
publishing a list of qualifying activities and creating a timely process for banks to confirm
whether an activity qualifies.
Assessment areas should continue to reflect the communities a bank can reasonably serve. Any
requirement to include full counties should apply only to Large Banks, and the Agencies should
keep flexibility in how the "substantial portion" standard is applied. On data, community
development information should continue to be collected and kept for exams, but the Agencies
should avoid new reporting requirements that add little supervisory value. Community
development grants should not be publicly reported.
Finally, banks need time to adjust. Large Banks should have at least two years before new data
collection and reporting requirements take effect. Apart from banks changing size categories,
exams should not switch between the old and new rules partway through an evaluation period.
The Agencies should provide updated guidance and examination procedures well before the
new rule takes effect.
Conclusion
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposal. WBA appreciates the efforts to
refresh CRA and take a closer look at reducing regulatory burden. The proposal is the third
attempt to revise the CRA rules in less than a decade, and the Agencies should use this
opportunity to adopt a framework that will be long-lasting. A final rule is most likely to stand the
test of time if it remains faithful to the CRA statute, reflects interagency consensus, relies on
transparent and well-supported standards, and provides flexibility for diverse bank business
models.
Thank you for considering our comments.

To Whom It May Concern:

On behalf of the City of Austin, thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the U.S. Department
of the Treasury Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC)'s notice titled "Community Reinvestment Act Regulations." The City values the
agencies' efforts to update and improve the regulatory framework governing the Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA), a law that plays an essential role in ensuring equitable access to credit and support community
development.

The City of Austin submits these comments to highlight several critical concerns about how the proposed
rule may affect affordable housing production, nonprofit capacity, and community development financing
within our community. Austin depends heavily on CRA-motivated lending and investment to support local
housing and economic mobility goals, and it is vital that any modernization of the CRA preserve and
strengthen this impact.

General Comments

The City of Austin strongly supports the statutory purpose of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA):
ensuring that financial institutions help meet the credit needs of all communities, including low-income and
moderate-income communities. Austin faces urgent housing affordability challenges, rapidly increasing
construction costs, rising land values, and significant disparities in access to credit and community
development projects.

Austin faces a shortage of roughly 55,000 units affordable to households who earn below 50% Median
Family Income (MFI), a gap that will require billions in investment to close. Meeting this need demands
strong partnerships with the private sector, and robust CRA obligations are essential to channeling the
lending and investment needed to support deeply affordable housing in our community Austin relies heavily
on CRA-motivated investment – in particular, the CRA-driven share of the Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit (LIHTC) market, which represents approximately 80% of all LIHTC investment nationwide. Any
rulemaking that reduces or weakens CRA obligations risks directly reducing the financing available to
develop, preserve, and rehabilitate affordable housing units in Austin.

The City also emphasizes the importance of maintaining nonprofit accessibility to CRA-motivated grants,
loans, and partnerships. Many community-based organizations – including small, emerging, and culturally
specific nonprofit – lack the administrative capacity to meet heightened documentation requirements or
overhead restrictions. Strong nonprofit organizations are essential to Austin's affordable housing pipeline,
supportive housing services, neighborhood revitalization strategies, and economic mobility initiatives.


 The City of Austin is committed to compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act.
Reasonable modifications and equal access to communications will be provided upon request.
The City appreciates the agencies' interest in reducing regulatory burden and increasing clarity. However,
these goals must be balanced against the need to preserve strong community development obligations across
institutions of all sizes. Any modernization efforts should safeguard the availability of CRA-motivated
financing, ensure parity across regulatory agencies, and avoid creating barriers for nonprofits or reducing
investment in historically underserved neighborhoods.
The City urges OCC and the FDIC to ensure that the final rule strengthens, rather than diminishes, the
CRA's effectiveness in meeting community credit needs – particularly in communities like Austin where
CRA investment is fundamental to local housing and development strategies.
