RE: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould:

ASIAN, Inc. writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) rules. As you know, the CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and
creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of
communities, including low- to moderate- income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully
encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved communities, challenges related
to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access remain.

Founded in San Francisco in 1971, ASIAN, Inc. is a non-profit organization that advances economic
opportunity and community empowerment for disadvantaged populations of all racial backgrounds, with
a focus on LMI households and business owners. As a HUD-approved Housing Counseling Agency, we
provide homebuyer education and counseling and connect LMI households to affordable
homeownership resources. Through our business development programs, we also facilitate access to
capital and markets by underserved microenterprises and other small businesses. We work with
financial institutions to expand access to credit, housing, and investment in communities that have
historically faced redlining. ASIAN, Inc. is a member of several organizations, including Rise Economy,
the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC), the National Coalition for Asian Pacific
American Community Development (National CAPACD), and we support strong CRA standards that
ensure financial institutions remain accountable to the communities both they and we serve.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift. The proposal does
not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on LMI communities. We request an
extension of the comment period for an additional 60 days so we have time to better understand how
much CRA activity may be lost to communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did
not conduct or provide.

The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved communities in
several ways.
1167 MISSION STREET, 4TH FLOOR ​
T: 415.928.5910 x122​
www.asianinc.org
SAN FRANCISCO, CA 94103 ​
F: 415.921.0182​
advocacy@asianinc.org


1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing and small businesses
will drop dramatically.

As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities that support critically
needed affordable housing and economic development projects. These activities often provide the
greatest CRA impact in communities as they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life,
and social health of residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large" Banks, such that
many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and expectation to serve the community
development needs of their communities.[1] According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition
(NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development Test responsibilities
entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical community development
programs that have had large impacts in LMI communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax
Credits (LIHTCs) which are a key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits
(NMTC) which fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity equivalent
investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) that provide small business
lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach, and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take
property off of the speculative market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting the critical
importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable housing.[3] Approximately half of
non-profit CDFI funding comes from CRA motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken
CD obligations if they adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over
$30 billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance even where they
remain subject to the Community Development and Investment Tests. The regulators signal to all banks
that they can do significantly less CD lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all
while seeking CRA credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1 capital were devoted
to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower than the percentage that NCRC
determined banks currently devote to community investments and loans. If each bank instead
conducted only the amount necessary to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by
approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have tremendous
negative impacts on affordable housing and small business development in our state. Asset thresholds
should not be raised.

2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.

The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain branches in LMI
and underserved neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a Large Bank to over $10 billion,
forty-five banks in California will no longer be subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that
their branches are serving LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in
LMI areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure due to this
proposal.[6]



Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities. Fewer branches
will result in less small business lending. These changes will be particularly hard hitting in rural areas of
our state where smaller banks originate a larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to offer deposit products
that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are a gateway to credit access, financial
stability, and wealth building, especially for families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory
financial institutions. As one important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low
fee bank accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based organizations, and local
governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are
underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of dollars in overdraft and
non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone, state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six
million dollars ($56 million) in OD and NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.

Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer banks will be
required to report data regarding their small business, small farm, and community development lending
activities. Such data is critical to understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the
needs of local markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA data
when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The loss of such data is
particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is walking back efforts to collect and disclose
detailed small business lending data under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will
disproportionately impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.

4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see sufficient benefits.

The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs of Native American
communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served by banks. The current rules focus CRA
obligations in areas where banks have branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near
Tribal lands and in rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related activities in "Indian
Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of bank CRA assessment areas. But many
members of Tribes in California will not benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country
or on Tribal or Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within particular geographies,
given the challenges and impacts associated with historic dispossession and federal policy. Instead,
CRA evaluations should also consider whether banks have established meaningful relationships with,
and provided direct benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access programs and
contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, non-profit organizations or
other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses that are majority-owned and
controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by providing:

●​ Active outreach and engagement
●​ Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and economic
development projects


●​ Small farm and small business loans
●​ Home mortgage loans
●​ Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes and support for
Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
●​ Support for cultural, health and other programs
●​ Bank branches
●​ Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
●​ The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship programs and
technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities outside of their
branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to encourage banks to engage in
CRA-related activity to directly benefit Tribes, non-profit organizations and other entities controlled by
Tribes, and Native-owned businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and responsiveness review
factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks whether banks have engaged in any CRA
activity directly with Tribes, Tribally controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know
they will be examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work with
Tribes.

5) Contributions to local non-profits that serve communities will suffer.

The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to non-profits by requiring a
demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating that large banks and their
grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if
this wasn't enough, the FDIC and OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank
grantmaking to non-profits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian measures will be
except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller groups, may be impacted.[14]

non-profits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local needs. They also can be
key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and investment products into communities inclined
to trust long established local organizations. Many non-profit organizations and programs, such as
downpayment assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions to
operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new reporting obligations, and
they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal would also end impactful contributions from
banks for general operating support, sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their communities on their
own. Most banks rely on non-profit partners to fill in the gaps in their own capacity – seeking assistance
with community outreach, borrower education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal
services, job training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can attract new deposits
and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will focus grantmaking
on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet their new FDIC and OCC-imposed
regulatory burdens.

Even where non-profits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15% overhead restriction will
negatively affect operations and organizational success. As one example, in order to secure CRA


grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as
underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and
borrower technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions, organizations
are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA activity that
contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large negative impact it will have on
non-profit organizations that rely on bank funding, the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are
meant to benefit from the CRA, and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-non-profit
partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.

There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link between CRA and LMI
impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their top two major product
lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in, and profiting from, communities, this
lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small
farm and consumer loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines from CRA oversight,
banks will have less incentive to consider how those products are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and soundness,
encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater trust in banks by the community.
Eliminating categories of loan products from scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test, which has
encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the definition of economic development.
The CRA should create greater incentives for banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family
sustaining wages for LMI workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would
provide CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit middle- and
upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA credit for large
scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for banks, would likely be financed without
CRA credit, and provide only incidental benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion
of what qualifies for CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing larger scale
infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative, smaller CDFI-led projects that
better meet local community needs (such as childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water
systems, or resilience projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA should require
banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments areas,[15] where they are subject to
more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes,
as noted above). Banks are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the
areas where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the 2023 CRA
Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit for projects in areas away from
their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of
their assessment areas, while providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes out of its way to
encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet their CRA responsibilities. The


Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions that operated under a unique business model that the
CRA rules were not designed to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input
and regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity they need to
engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with Strategic Plans tend to reinvest
less in the community and in less impactful ways. The OCC's guidance establishing low community
development thresholds for banks opting for the Strategic Plan[17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community development efforts with little
benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing, where units are affordable at a point in time but not
encumbered by deed or rent restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should
not give banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and communities is
unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it can be a driver of bank investment
in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if
the project is owned and operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are
LMI tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are compliant with
tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents can reasonably be expected to
retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA ratings downgrades.

The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline should not be allowed to
pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding" ratings. Under the previous Administration,
at least a dozen banks that passed their CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only
increase that number by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should consider any evidence
that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices
as part of their lending, deposit, branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered
regardless of its source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based on
data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation, etc.). We also urge the
regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit
Programs (SPCPs), and to once again encourage banks to develop SPCPs to better serve
communities that have been redlined, excluded, and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to allow for
meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of entities and activities, and will
undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the
same form as proposed, communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable
housing and CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer community
serving non-profit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and redlining with no CRA
consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its purpose of encouraging banks to support
LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,



Lamar Heystek
President

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Affordable Housing Clearinghouse (AHC) strongly encourages regulators to consider the potential impact these proposed CRA changes could have on low- and moderate-income communities and the nonprofit organizations serving them.

As a HUD-certified housing counseling organization serving Southern California, we see firsthand how CRA-supported lending, investments, grants, and partnerships help connect families with the education, financial resources, and opportunities needed to achieve and sustain homeownership. These investments are particularly important as rising housing costs, limited inventory, and economic pressures continue to create barriers for first-time and lower-income homebuyers.

We are concerned that raising bank size thresholds, reducing reporting and examination requirements, and establishing CD activity thresholds significantly below current levels could unintentionally reduce incentives for banks to invest in affordable housing, housing counseling, financial capability, and other community development activities.

CRA should continue to encourage meaningful, measurable investment in the communities where banks operate not simply establish a minimum floor for compliance. We urge regulators to preserve strong transparency, accountability, and incentives for banks to partner with community-based organizations that have the local expertise and trusted relationships necessary to translate CRA resources into real outcomes for LMI households.

has enjoyed tremendous success at encouraging and enabling financial institutions to meet
the needs of the local communities in which they operate. As a multifamily rental housing
developer and owner, we have partnered with banks, large and small, to fund the creation of
quality affordable homes, primarily using the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit or "Housing
Credit." We are concerned that the proposed changes to the CRA could undermine the law's
core objectives and discourage the investment and lending activity needed in America's
highest-need communities.








Mercy Housing, Inc., 1600 Broadway, Suite 2000, Denver, CO 80202 p | 866.338.0557
mercyhousing.org
Mercy Housing is sponsored by communities of Catholic Sisters

We ask that the OCC and FDIC reconsider the proposed threshold changes that would
reclassify many intermediate banks as small and an even higher proportion of large banks as
intermediate, thereby removing reclassified large banks from the Investment Tests and
Service Tests. These changes risk undermining recent federal efforts to address the housing
affordability crisis, including the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act and the expansion of the
Housing Credit in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

According to a recent report from CohnReznick, banks provide 75 to 80 percent of Housing
Credit equity, with at least 71 percent of that investment considered CRA-motivated. The
Investment Test has facilitated an active and competitive market for Housing Credit equity by
creating meaningful incentive for banks to invest in affordable housing. By substantially
reducing the number of institutions subject to the Investment Test, the proposed changes
could weaken the incentive at a time when additional investment is urgently needed to
create and preserve quality affordable homes. We are particularly concerned about the
impact on residents of rural areas and small towns, where regional banks currently play a
critical role in meeting credit needs.

Additionally, we ask that the agencies avoid threshold changes and restrictions that would
discourage community development grants. As a housing provider offering most residents free
onsite programming focused on financial stability and economic mobility, Mercy Housing
depends on CRA-motivated grants to support the delivery of resident services that often
cannot be resourced through lending or investment capital. These grants play a vital role in
Mercy Housing's ability to support individuals, families, and local economies by building
healthy housing communities where residents can achieve their goals. Rather than adopt the
proposal's more restrictive treatment of community development grants, we urge the
agencies to maintain broad CRA consideration for grants that help financial institutions meet
the diverse needs of the communities in which they serve.

Mercy Housing remains committed to partnering with the federal government to provide
quality affordable homes to families, seniors, and people with special needs. We urge the
agencies to reconsider the proposed changes and preserve the power of the Community
Reinvestment Act to hold financial institutions accountable for meeting local credit,
investment, and community development needs.

We thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on this proposal.

Live in Hope,

Ismael Guerrero, CEO and President
Mercy Housing

1




October 13, 2026

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
RIN 3064-AG31
Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations—Military Banks, Veterans, and Military Families
To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
The Association of Military Banks of America (AMBA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the
proposed revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. AMBA represents banks serving
servicemembers, veterans, and their families, including institutions operating on military installations and
banks serving these communities nationwide.
AMBA supports retaining provisions that recognize the distinctive customers and operating circumstances of
military banks. We are concerned, however, that the proposed exclusion of deposit products from retail
banking services consideration could undermine recognition of activities that bring unbanked and
underbanked veterans into the banking system. We urge the agencies to preserve meaningful consideration
of these activities and clarify how banks can receive consistent recognition for serving military and veteran
communities.
In his September 28, 2026 remarks at AMBA's Military Banking Summit, Comptroller Gould recognized the
needs of servicemembers relocating on military orders, military families purchasing homes, and veterans
transitioning to civilian life. He also invited feedback on the CRA proposal and remaining regulatory
obstacles. AMBA welcomes that invitation. The recommendations below seek to advance those objectives
by preserving recognition of banking access and clarifying how qualifying services to military and veteran
communities receive CRA consideration.
1. Preserve CRA consideration for banking access through programs such as the Veterans Benefits Banking
Program.
Through the Veterans Benefits Banking Program (VBBP), AMBA works with the Department of Veterans Affairs
and participating financial institutions to help veterans and other eligible VA beneficiaries obtain banking
services and receive their benefits through direct deposit.
For an unbanked or underbanked veteran, opening an accessible, affordable transaction account can be
an essential first step toward financial stability. It provides a means to receive benefits, pay bills, manage
household finances, and establish a banking relationship. These services also support access to appropriate
credit over time.
AMBA has worked with agency staff to understand how participating banks may document VBBP activities
for CRA consideration under the existing framework. Our published guidance identifies retail banking
services as a potential basis for that consideration, subject to applicable requirements and supervisory
evaluation.
The proposal would exclude deposit products from the retail services evaluation and supersede related
guidance. This creates uncertainty about whether and how banks would receive recognition for helping
unbanked and underbanked veterans establish and maintain accounts.


2

We request that the final rule retain CRA consideration of responsive deposit products and account-access
services, including qualifying activities conducted through programs such as VBBP. If the agencies proceed
with the proposed exclusion, they should establish an explicit alternative pathway that preserves meaningful
consideration of these activities.
Financial education can complement account access, but recognition of education alone would not
adequately address the distinct work involved in bringing an unbanked or underbanked individual into the
banking system.
If the agencies conclude that CRA does not permit consideration of these activities, AMBA requests that the
final rule explain the specific statutory limitation, distinguish deposit products from related credit-access and
financial capability services, and identify which components of programs such as VBBP remain eligible and
under which evaluation criteria.
2. Retain and harmonize the military-bank provisions.
AMBA supports recognition of current and former members of the armed forces and their dependents within
the military-bank definition. We also support the nationwide assessment-area option and related institution-
level evaluation provisions, which recognize the dispersed and mobile nature of military communities.
These provisions reflect priorities AMBA has raised in earlier rulemaking comments. Military customers
frequently relocate, transition between military and civilian employment, and maintain banking relationships
across state and national boundaries.
We request that OCC and FDIC adopt identical language defining when an institution predominantly serves
military customers. The OCC proposal uses "most important customer group," while the FDIC proposal uses
"primary customer group." A uniform qualitative standard would reduce uncertainty and support consistent
examinations.
The final rule or accompanying guidance should also clarify the treatment of services provided to eligible
military customers stationed overseas, including those using APO or FPO addresses which complicate
assessment area calculations.
3. Distinguish military-bank status from eligibility of military-serving activities.
Many banks that serve veterans and military families, including VBBP participants, may not satisfy the
definition of a military bank. Their activities should nevertheless be evaluated under clear and consistent
standards inasmuch as roughly six (6) percent of our current adult population are veterans.
We request guidance explaining how qualifying military- and veteran-serving activities may receive
consideration regardless of whether the participating institution qualifies as a military bank.
That guidance should address account access, financial counseling and education, affordable housing,
responsible lending, small-business development, and assistance during military-to-civilian transitions. It
should explain applicable income-targeting, geographic, and documentation requirements rather than
leaving banks to infer eligibility from the military-bank definition.
The agencies should also clarify the treatment of spouses, dependents, survivors, caregivers, and other
eligible VA beneficiaries. These categories are not necessarily interchangeable, and references to
dependents alone may not encompass the populations served by relevant programs.
4. Provide practical documentation and transition guidance.
Banks need predictable standards for documenting participation and demonstrating responsiveness to
community needs. The final rule should explain what evidence is appropriate for activities such as opening
and maintaining accounts, facilitating benefits deposits, providing counseling, and supporting qualifying
community organizations.


3

For nationwide programs, the agencies should explain how participating banks should identify eligible
beneficiaries, document their own contributions, and demonstrate the required relationship to applicable
assessment areas.
Where relevant information is already available to an agency, the agency should make it accessible to the
examination team and avoid requiring banks to submit it again. Guidance should distinguish information
supplied by the agency from documentation the bank must maintain.
Any change affecting previously recognized activities should include clear prospective implementation
guidance. Banks should understand how activities conducted under the existing framework will be
evaluated during the transition.
5. Address the remaining policy gap.
AMBA continues to pursue targeted legislation to provide clearer CRA recognition for financial services
benefiting veterans, servicemembers, and their families. The proposed military-bank provisions are valuable,
but they do not independently establish eligibility for the full range of activities or participating institutions
that this effort seeks to address.
We encourage the agencies to use their existing authority to provide the clearest available recognition and
to coordinate with the Federal Reserve to reduce inconsistent treatment across supervisory agencies.
AMBA would welcome continued engagement on regulatory language and practical examples that
preserve appropriate supervisory discretion while giving banks greater certainty. We respectfully urge the
agencies to retain military-bank protections and ensure that the final rule continues to encourage
meaningful banking access for veterans and military families.

Sincerely,


Omuso D. George
Brigadier General, U.S. Army (Retired)
President & CEO
Association of Military Banks of America

To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency:
LiftFund appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. LiftFund is a nonprofit Community
Development Financial Institution (CDFI) that provides capital and business support to
small businesses. Our perspective comes from decades of small business lending,
technical assistance, bank and CDFI partnerships, grant administration, and responses to
more than 50 disasters and major business disruptions.
In addition to commenting on relevant topics to a CDFI small business lender, we want to
draw additional attention to the role of CDFIs and banks in responding to the particular
needs of small businesses. Small businesses can lose the cash they need to operate even
when their premises remain intact. Among disaster-affected firms surveyed by the Federal
Reserve, 84% reported business interruption or lost sales, fewer than one-third had
insurance covering that loss, and only 4% of those who sought external funds received
enough to cover their losses. [1] LiftFund's Texas Hill Country flood relief program is designed
for businesses facing physical damage or economic injury and combines financial
assistance with technical support. That experience shows why recovery programs must
address operating costs as well as property damage, and why community partners need the
capacity to deliver assistance promptly and responsibly. [2]


 2 | P a g e

Banks can help communities meet these needs through established relationships with
CDFIs and other local partners. The final CRA rule should give banks clear grounds to provide
support before, during, and after a disaster, while preserving their obligation to meet needs
within their own assessment areas.
While we respond to specific questions below, the key points are as follows. LiftFund asks
the agencies to make disaster financing more responsive by recognizing documented state,
Tribal, county, and municipal emergencies. Additionally, with regard to disasters, the
agencies should recognize working capital, advance financing facilities, and qualifying
support outside assessment areas. We also ask the agencies to retain CRA consideration for
grants, replace the proposed 15% indirect cost cutoff with a documented reasonableness
standard, recognize public and private small business financing partnerships such as the
State Small Business Credit Initiative (SSBCI), and preserve meaningful community
development evaluation and useful information as bank asset thresholds change. These
recommendations reflect our work with bank partners across asset sizes and our shared
interest in practical CRA rules that support communities.
1. Recognize federally and locally declared disasters (Question 31)
LiftFund supports removing the existing exclusion for counties that receive only Federal
Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance Emergency Work Category A or
Category B assistance. The agencies should adopt the proposed change rather than retain
that exclusion and rely on individual exceptions. [3] Even disasters with these more limited
federal responses can severely impact small businesses, and we believe this change will
ensure capital flows more readily along with helping build out more comprehensive
partnerships with CDFIs.
The final rule should also recognize that state, Tribal, county, and municipal authorities may
declare an emergency or disaster that materially disrupts local commerce without a FEMA
Major Disaster Declaration. A prolonged utility failure, damaged infrastructure, or loss of
commercial access can threaten small businesses regardless of the declaration's source.
Local officials bring unique perspectives on the impact, and this approach of relying on local
officials also fits with other CRA community development definitions around revitalization
and stabilization that support, "any other area targeted by a government entity for
redevelopment..." (12 C.F.R. § 345.12, definition of "community development," paragraph
(4)(iv)).
We ask the agencies to establish a separate CRA path for activities responding to a formally
declared state, Tribal, county, or municipal disaster or emergency. Eligibility should require
an identified affected area, credible documentation of material economic or business
disruption, and a government recovery or stabilization plan or comparable official action.
 3 | P a g e

The bank and its partners will document a qualifying community development purpose, the
geography served, intended beneficiaries, and the use of funds. This would not give CRA
consideration to ordinary business financing solely because a local emergency was
declared. The proposed rule's recognition of government small business programs and
revitalization plans provides a foundation for this clarification, but its existing geographic
criteria do not resolve the issue for every locally declared emergency event. [3]
As part of ensuring the definition of community development around disasters is as clear as
possible, the agencies should clarify that disaster recovery plans do permit working capital
loans as part of the response. Disaster recovery often depends on liquidity. A business may
need to pay employees, rent, utilities, or suppliers before customers return or insurance
proceeds arrive. JPMorganChase Institute research found that half of the small businesses
it studied held fewer than 15 days of cash buffer. [4]
Additionally, the agencies should clarify that "activities that assist individuals and
communities...to prepare for, adapt to, or withstand natural disasters" can include arranging
and committing to financing in advance of a disaster. Because "preparing for" is by definition
before a declared disaster, the agency needs to clarify that a disaster need not be declared.
LiftFund supports the proposed 36-month period for designated disaster areas and the
agencies' authority to extend it in writing. [3] The agencies should provide a straightforward
way to request an extension when a government recovery plan, community needs
assessment, or economic data shows that material recovery needs persist. The agencies
previously extended CRA consideration for Hurricane Maria recovery activities. [6] Using the
same request process for the "publicly available non-exhaustive, illustrative list of example
CD activities" to request extension of the disaster declaration time frame would be a simple
remedy.
2. Allow qualifying disaster activity outside assessment areas (Question 34)
A disaster can overwhelm the financial capacity of banks located in the affected community.
The proposed rule provides a path for considering community development activities
outside a bank's assessment areas, generally conditioned on the bank meeting specified
standards within its assessment areas. [3] LiftFund asks the agencies to add a disaster
provision that allows qualifying activity outside assessment areas to receive consideration
at the appropriate state, multistate metropolitan statistical area, or bank level without first
meeting a mechanical geographic threshold, while requiring the bank to remain responsive
to needs in its own assessment areas.
There is precedent for geographic flexibility. After Hurricane Maria, the agencies described
CRA consideration for qualifying activities in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands by
 4 | P a g e

institutions elsewhere, subject to the institutions' continued responsiveness to their own
assessment areas. [5] A rule addressing the same issue in advance would make disaster
partnerships easier to arrange.
The clarification should expressly cover eligible grants as well as loans, investments, and
services. It should also explain how an examiner will document the area served and consider
a CDFI program that operates across more than one affected county or state.
3. Preserve grants and revise the 15% indirect cost condition (Questions 9 and 10)
LiftFund opposes eliminating grants and donations from CRA consideration, an alternative
on which the agencies expressly request comment. [3] Grants can fund technical
assistance, borrower preparation, disaster relief, interest subsidies, credit enhancements,
and support for businesses for which additional debt is unsuitable.
We also urge the agencies to revise the proposed condition under which a large bank's grant
loses CRA eligibility if the recipient's indirect costs for administering it exceed 15%. The
agencies themselves acknowledge that the proposed grant requirements may reduce
support for general operations, organizational capacity, and intermediaries that finance or
assist multiple projects. [3] These concerns are acute in disaster response, where verifying
eligibility, underwriting, preventing fraud, servicing, reporting, and guiding business owners
require trained staff and functioning systems.
The final rule should treat indirect costs of 15% or less of the grant amount as a safe harbor,
while permitting a higher amount when the recipient demonstrates that its costs are
reasonable and consistently allocated. The bank and recipient should be able to rely on a
standard set of records, such as a grant budget, established cost allocation method,
negotiated indirect cost rate, or comparable records, without having to develop a separate
review process for each grant. The records should identify the funded activities, affected
geography, intended beneficiaries, use of funds, and a practical way to report results. Costs
directly attributable to delivering the funded program should be treated as direct program
costs under a consistent accounting method.
The agencies cite the federal Uniform Guidance's 15% de minimis indirect cost rate in
support of the proposed limit. [3] The Uniform Guidance applies that optional rate to
modified total direct costs, while the proposal tests a recipient's indirect costs against the
grant amount. [3, 8] The federal de minimis option provides a simple way to recover indirect
costs; it does not establish that every organization can administer every qualifying program
within the proposed ceiling. The agencies can protect community benefit through
documentation of the grant's purpose, geography, activities, and costs without disqualifying
 5 | P a g e

an otherwise effective program solely because its reasonable indirect costs exceed that
figure.
If the agencies retain a limit, they should allow the qualifying portion of a grant to receive
consideration rather than disqualifying the entire grant. They should also confirm that grants
supporting the delivery capacity of a qualifying program can receive consideration when
their community development purpose and expected beneficiaries are documented.
The final rule should also clarify that a grant to a CDFI or other qualified intermediary can
satisfy the proposed direct use requirement when the recipient administers a qualifying
community development program. That work may include making grants to disaster-
affected businesses, providing technical assistance, and funding accountable local
partners. The bank and intermediary should document the program's purpose, affected
geography, use of funds, and intended beneficiaries. Requiring every dollar to pass directly
from the first recipient to the ultimate beneficiary would discourage the partnerships needed
to deliver assistance across a disaster area. The proposal itself acknowledges the risk of
reduced support for intermediaries. [3]
Finally, LiftFund supports the proposal's protection for activities that are qualified when
conducted. The final rule should state clearly how that protection applies to grants and
legally binding financing commitments made before new grant or documentation standards
take effect and provide a reasonable period to adapt future program agreements and
records. [3]
4. Recognize public and private small business financing partnerships (Question 26)
The final rule should expressly identify SSBCI as an example of a government program that
may support qualifying CRA activity, provided the underlying financing meets the applicable
community development requirements. [3, 7]
Public funds, philanthropy, CDFI capital, and bank financing can be combined through
guarantees, subordinated capital, loan loss reserves, and interest subsidies. These
structures are especially useful in a disaster, when shared risk can make affordable lending
possible while grants address needs that borrowers should not have to finance with more
debt.
5. Preserve community development information as thresholds change (Question 1)
LiftFund works with bank partners of different sizes and supports CRA examination and
reporting requirements that reflect their capacity and business models. Proportionate
requirements can allow banks to devote more resources to meeting community needs. As
the agencies consider the proposed asset thresholds and the $30 billion alternative raised
 6 | P a g e

in Question 1, we ask them to preserve a meaningful way to evaluate community
development activity and identify unmet small business credit needs. [3]
The FDIC estimates that, under the main proposal, 604 FDIC-supervised banks would move
from the intermediate to the small bank category and would no longer receive a separate
community development test. Another 250 would move from the large to the intermediate
bank category and would no longer have separate investment and service tests. [3] Urban
Institute's analysis of 2024 federal reporting data found that banks with assets between
$1.65 billion and $10 billion reported $30.3 billion in community development lending, while
banks between $10 billion and $30 billion reported $51.9 billion. These figures describe
existing lending across banks supervised by all three federal banking agencies; they are not
estimates of lending that would decline or disappear. Urban Institute estimates that, if the
thresholds applied nationwide, 22% to 38% of previously reported community development
lending would cease to be centrally reported. [9]
Before finalizing threshold changes, the agencies should assess the community
development activity and public reporting that would be affected. They should consider a
proportionate way to evaluate community development activity at banks moving into
simpler categories, preserve enough information to identify gaps in small business
financing, and explain how they will monitor outcomes after implementation. We seek
reporting that is useful for evaluating community needs and practical for banks of different
sizes.
Conclusion
The next major disaster should not require banks and community partners to assemble a
financing system from scratch. Clear CRA rules can support partnerships established in
advance, timely working capital, grants, technical assistance, and responsible lending
throughout a prolonged recovery.
LiftFund asks the agencies to adopt the proposed expansion of FEMA disaster eligibility; add
a documented path for state, Tribal, county, and municipal emergencies; clarify the
acceptance of disaster working capital and advance financing facilities; allow appropriate
consideration outside assessment areas; publish clear examples of qualifying activity;
preserve flexibility for long-term recovery; retain grants, including grants administered by
CDFIs; and replace the proposed 15% indirect cost ceiling with a documented
reasonableness standard. The final rule should also use proportionate community
development evaluation and reporting to monitor outcomes as new bank size standards take
effect.
 7 | P a g e

These changes would make it easier for banks to support small businesses when recovery
depends on timely capital and capable local partners, while maintaining CRA's focus on
community needs.
Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely,

Amy H. Hereford
President and Chief Executive Officer
LiftFund Inc.

OCC (Tracking No.: mv6-x4h8-mdh5). We respectfully request that this version be treated as
LiftFund's authoritative comment.

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID OCC -2026-0694)
To Whom It May Concern:
Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The Texas Affiliation of Affordable
Housing Providers (TAAHP) is the leading voice for affordable housing in Texas,
representing more than 900 professionals involved in the development, financing, and
management of affordable housing communities across the state. TAAHP members build
affordable rental housing with the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit), and
CRA-motivated bank investment is a large part of what makes those developments
possible.
The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable
rental housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. Banks provide
roughly 75 to 80 percent of Housing Credit equity, and at least 71 percent is CRA-driven,
according to the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC). Banks accept the
modest return on these investments in large part because the full CRA examination for
large banks includes a distinct investment test.
We are concerned that the OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with assets
ranging from $1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks
subject to the full CRA examination, including the investment test, could reduce
competition in the Housing Credit equity market, leading to lower pricing on credits and
less housing produced. AHTCC's survey of Housing Credit syndicators found that at least
108 investor banks in this asset range invested $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equi ty from
2021 to 2025.
The proposal would reach deep into Texas. In addition to raising the large bank threshold
to $10 billion, it would raise the small bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion,
removing the community development test entirely from banks below that line. According
to an analysis by the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL), Texas
would lose 84 of its 246 banks with CRA community development incentives. The number
of Texans living in community development deserts, where no bank with those incentives
serves the community, would rise from 74,000 to 124,000, and another 535,000 Texans
would newly live in areas served by five or fewer such banks. Seven Texas counties would
have no such bank at all. They include Jim Hogg, Duval, and Frio in S outh Texas, Mills in
Central Texas, Haskell and Knox in West Texas, and Donley in the Panhandle. If all three
bank regulators adopted these thresholds, 751,926 Texans would newly fall into thin
coverage or a community development desert, more than in any other state.
The consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to rural and smaller
communities. AHTCC found that approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity from
banks with $412 million to $10 billion in assets supported rural markets, compared with
 8.1 percent invested in nonmetro counties in CohnReznick's industry-wide sample, indicating that these banks play an
outsized role in investing in smaller communities. Texas has the largest rural population of any state, with more than
4.7 million rural residents counted in the 2020 Census, and TAAHP members build Housing Credit properties in rural
communities across the state.
NAAHL's analysis shows how exposed these communities already are. Today, 87 percent of rural census tracts in Texas
are served by five or fewer banks with community development incentives, or by none. Under the proposal, the share
of rural tracts with no such bank would rise from 8 to 13 percent, and the share of micropolitan tracts with five or fewer
or none would rise from 36 to 58 percent. Counties across the state would fall from six or more of these banks to five
or fewer, including Wharton on the Gulf Coast, Palo Pinto west of Fort Worth, and Kleberg and Jim Wells in the Coastal
Bend. In Kleberg County, the share of deposits held at these banks would drop from 94 percent to 29 percent.
The Rio Grande Valley shows what is at stake. In Hidalgo County, the median family income was $46,609 in the 2020
Census, and more than a quarter of families lived below the poverty level. Because Housing Credit rents are capped as
a share of area median income, a development in the Valley supports less debt than it would in a higher-income market,
and equity must cover more of its cost. International Bank of Commerce in Brownsville, which holds the largest share
of deposits in Hidalgo County, invested more than $37.5 million in a fund that combines Housing Credits with local tax
incentives, including more than $15.8 million that supported two developments in the county. With $4.0 billion in assets
at its 2024 CRA examination, the bank would become an intermediate bank with no investment test under the proposal.
Moreover, the proposal undercuts recent congressional action to expand the Housing Credit and bank investment in it.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act increased Housing Credit authority enough to finance an estimated 1.22 million affordable
rental homes over the next decade, while the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public
welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to increase their Housing Credit investments. The provision lifting the PWI cap
would mostly impact many of the same banks that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Texas will need more
equity investors to put its share of the expanded allocation to use.
The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal. The first would raise the large bank asset threshold
from $1.649 billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still cause harm but is substantially less disruptive to
Housing Credit investment than the primary proposal. According to AHTCC's survey, 108 Housing Credit investor banks
would be reclassified as intermediate banks if the threshold is set at $10 billion, while just 40 would be reclassified if it
is set at $3.252 billion. The banks that would remain subject to the separate investment test under a $3.252 billion
threshold account for approximately 86 percent of the Housing Credit equity from affected banks captured in the
AHTCC survey.
In Texas, the $3.252 billion alternative would reduce the number of banks losing community development incentives
from 84 to 65 and cut the increase in Texans living in community development deserts from 50,000 to 22,000, according
to NAAHL. Jim Hogg and Duval counties would still lose every such bank under either threshold.
The second alternative, a $30 billion threshold, would be the most damaging of the three for affordable rental housing
production. AHTCC estimates it would affect at least 142 Housing Credit investor banks and $4.5 billion in Housing
Credit equity, and NAAHL estimates that 17 states would see the number of large banks with investment requirements
cut by half or more.
TAAHP members have seen the impact of CRA firsthand. We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to leave the
thresholds as they currently stand under the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve, the third
bank regulator, appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA regulations, we strongly
urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for large banks and adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit
market in all communities, including rural and smaller markets.

Respectfully submitted,



Kathryn Saar

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes
Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,
Northern California Land Trust (NCLT) writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to
redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking
needs of communities, including low and moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has
successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved communities,
challenges related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access remain.
Founded in 1973, NCLT is a community land trust (CLT) that uses community ownership and control of
land to create and steward permanently affordable homes and community facilities. NCLT stewards
more than 20 projects, including affordable apartments, limited-equity condominiums, cooperatives,
 and nonprofit office space, in the San Francisco Bay Area. NCLT also provides education, training, and
technical assistance on community land trust and cooperative development through its Community Co-
Ownership Initiative, and supports regional and statewide coalitions, including the Bay Area CLT
Consortium and the California Community Land Trust Network.
The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift. The proposal does
not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on LMI communities. We request an
extension of the comment period for an additional 60 days so we have time to better understand how
much CRA activity may be lost to communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did
not conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved communities in
several ways.
1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing and small businesses will drop
dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities that support critically
needed affordable housing and economic development projects. These activities often provide the
greatest CRA impact in communities as they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life,
and social health of residents and communities.
The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large" Banks, such that
many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and expectation to serve the community
development needs of their communities.[1] According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition
(NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development Test responsibilities
entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to the Investment Test.[2]
The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical community development
programs that have had large impacts in LMI communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax
Credits (LIHTCs) which are a key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC)
which fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity equivalent
investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) that provide small business
lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach, and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take
property off of the speculative market.
Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting the critical importance
of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit
CDFI funding comes from CRA motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD
obligations if they adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.
Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance even where they
remain subject to the Community Development and Investment Tests. The regulators signal to all banks
that they can do significantly less CD lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all
while seeking CRA credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests that a
bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1 capital were devoted to CD
 loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower than the percentage that NCRC determined
banks currently devote to community investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the
amount necessary to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%.[5]
Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have tremendous
negative impacts on affordable housing and small business development in our state. Asset thresholds
should not be raised.
2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain branches in LMI and
BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five
banks in California will no longer be subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their
branches are serving LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure due to this
proposal.[6]
Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities. Fewer branches will
result in less small business lending. These changes will be particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our
state where smaller banks originate a larger portion of the small business loans.
The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to offer deposit
products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are a gateway to credit access,
financial stability, and wealth building, especially for families who are otherwise preyed upon by
predatory financial institutions. As one important example, the BankOn program has provided access to
no or low fee bank accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based organizations, and local
governments. The proposal jettisons this work.
Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are underbanked.[9]
National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees
in 2025, and in California alone, state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million)
in OD and NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]
3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer banks will be
required to report data regarding their small business, small farm, and community development lending
activities. Such data is critical to understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs
of local markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA data when
meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The loss of such data is particularly
harmful at a time when the Administration is walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small
business lending data under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make up a larger part of
the small business and small farm lending markets.
4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see sufficient benefits.
 The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs of Native American
communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served by banks. The current rules focus CRA
obligations in areas where banks have branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near
Tribal lands and in rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related activities in "Indian
Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of bank CRA assessment areas. But many
members of Tribes in California will not benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country
or on Tribal or Native lands, as defined.
CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within particular geographies,
given the challenges and impacts associated with historic dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA
evaluations should also consider whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and
provided direct benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes. Non-
federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access programs and contracts
with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes exist.
More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit organizations or
other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses that are majority owned and
controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by providing:
•
Active outreach and engagement
•
Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and economic
development projects
•
Small farm and small business loans
•
Home mortgage loans
•
Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes and support for
Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
•
Support for cultural, health and other programs
•
Bank branches
•
Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
•
The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship programs and
technical assistance support
While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities outside of their
branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to encourage banks to engage in CRA
related activity to directly benefit Tribes, nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes,
and Native-owned businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.
A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and responsiveness review factor
during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity
directly with Tribes, Tribally controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will
be examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work with Tribes.
5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will suffer.
 The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring a
demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating that large banks and their
grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if
this wasn't enough, the FDIC and OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank
grantmaking to nonprofits entirely.
Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian measures will be
except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller groups, may be impacted.[14]
Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local needs. They also can be
key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and investment products into communities inclined
to trust long established local organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as
downpayment assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions to
operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new reporting obligations, and
they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal would also end impactful contributions from
banks for general operating support, sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.
Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their communities on their
own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps in their own capacity – seeking assistance
with community outreach, borrower education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal
services, job training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and programs
which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can attract new deposits and make new
loans in LMI communities.
The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will focus grantmaking
on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet their new FDIC and OCC-imposed
regulatory burdens.
Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15% overhead restriction will
negatively affect operations and organizational success. As one example, in order to secure CRA grants
from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as
underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and
borrower technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions, organizations
are put at risk.
The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA activity that
contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large negative impact it will have on
nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding, the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are
meant to benefit from the CRA, and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit
partnerships.
6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link between CRA and LMI
impact in the name of easing bank burden.
Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their top two major product
lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in, and profiting from, communities, this lending
 by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and
consumer loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest product
lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines from CRA oversight, banks will
have less incentive to consider how those products are offered.
Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and soundness,
encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater trust in banks by the community.
Eliminating categories of loan products from scrutiny will have the opposite effect.
No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test, which has
encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the definition of economic
development. The CRA should create greater incentives for banks to support the creation of jobs that
pay family sustaining wages for LMI workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that
would provide CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit middle- and
upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the purpose of CRA.
Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA credit for large scale
community infrastructure products that generate profits for banks, would likely be financed without
CRA credit, and provide only incidental benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of
what qualifies for CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities. For
example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing larger scale infrastructure
projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative, smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local
community needs (such as childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or
resilience projects).
Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA should require banks to
focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous
regulatory oversight (with an exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted
above). Banks are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas where
they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the 2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the
proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit for projects in areas away from their branches,
lending and CRA responsibility. This will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their
assessment areas, while providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.
Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes out of its way to
encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic
Plan was meant for financial institutions that operated under a unique business model that the CRA
rules were not designed to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity they need to
engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less
in the community and in less impactful ways. The OCC's guidance establishing low community
development thresholds for banks opting for the Strategic Plan,[17] validates this perspective.
Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community development efforts with little
benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing, where units are affordable at a point in time but not
encumbered by deed or rent restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should
not give banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and communities is
 unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it can be a driver of bank investment in
problematic landlords and displacement. CRA credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the
project is owned and operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are compliant with tenant
rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents can reasonably be expected to retain their
