FDIC RIN 3064-AG31 (published Aug. 12, 2026)
Dear Sir or Madam:
The National Bankers Association ("NBA") submits these comments on the notice of proposed
rulemaking issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (together, the "Agencies") amending their regulations implementing the Community
Reinvestment Act ("CRA").
NBA supports the Agencies' objectives of reducing unnecessary burden on community banks and
providing greater clarity about qualifying activities. Many NBA member institutions would benefit
directly from the proposed relief, and we say so plainly. We write because the proposal's most
consequential effect on our members runs through a channel the proposal does not analyze: the CRA-
motivated capital that flows from other institutions into MDIs. Congress has twice directed that this
activity be encouraged — in section 804(b) of the CRA and, this past July, in the 21st Century ROAD to
Housing Act. Several elements of the proposal would narrow the practical operation of both directives at
the same moment Congress acted to widen them.
Our recommendations are summarized below and developed in the sections that follow.


 Summary of Recommendations
1. Retain the proposed $1 billion small bank threshold but adopt $3.252 billion, not $10
billion, as the upper bound of the intermediate bank category. This preserves the full measure
of relief the proposal offers the smallest institutions while retaining investment test coverage for
the regional banks on which MDI capital formation depends. NBA opposes a $30 billion
intermediate cap.
2. Exempt activities described in 12 U.S.C. § 2903(b) from the geographic flexibility standard,
so that investments and ventures with MDIs, women's depository institutions, and low-income
credit unions receive consideration without regard to assessment-area thresholds.
3. Conform this rulemaking to the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (P.L. 119-101),
including section 203's increase in the public welfare investment ceiling and section 906's
mentor-protégé program, and address the charter disparity their interaction creates.
4. Withdraw the proposed deletion of minority- and women-owned entity references from 12
C.F.R. part 24 (Docket ID OCC-2025-0075, RIN 1557-AF32), which would compound the
effect of this proposal.
5. Retain the requirement that intermediate banks achieve at least "satisfactory" on the
community development test to receive an overall "satisfactory" rating.
6. Permit recipients with a federally negotiated indirect cost rate to use that rate rather than
applying a flat 15% limitation to all community development grants.
7. Permit small banks to elect evaluation under the intermediate community development test.
8. Publish an MDI-specific impact analysis consistent with the Agencies' obligations under
section 308 of FIRREA before finalizing.
9. Coordinate with the Board of Governors to avoid charter-based divergence in CRA
supervision.
I. The Proposal Would Remove 376 Institutions from the Investment Test
The Agencies estimate that 126 OCC-supervised and 250 FDIC-supervised large banks would be
reclassified as intermediate banks, and that 194 OCC-supervised and 604 FDIC-supervised intermediate
small banks would be reclassified as small banks. Approximately 79.8% of all CRA-subject banks the
Agencies supervise would be evaluated as small banks.
The 376 institutions in the first group would no longer be subject to the investment test, the service test,
or large-bank data collection and reporting. It is the first of those that concerns us.
The investment test is the single most important regulatory driver of equity investments, deposits, loan
participations, and grants directed into MDIs. Congress made that connection explicit. Section 804(b) of
the CRA, 12 U.S.C. § 2903(b), provides that in assessing an institution's record, the appropriate agency
may consider capital investment, loan participation, and other ventures undertaken in cooperation with
minority- and women-owned financial institutions and low-income credit unions, where those activities
help meet local credit needs.
 That provision does not operate on its own. It operates through the tests. Removing 376 institutions from
the investment test does not merely reduce their reporting burden; it removes the examination context in
which § 2903(b) activity is identified, weighted, and rewarded. NBA members report that mid-size
regional institutions have been an important and growing source of MDI investment, in part because the
largest institutions tend to concentrate their MDI activity in a small number of high-profile transactions.
Recommendation. The Agencies have requested comment on an alternative pairing of $850 million and
$3.252 billion, and on a $30 billion intermediate cap. NBA recommends a hybrid: retain the proposed $1
billion small bank threshold, which delivers the full measure of relief to the smallest institutions, but
adopt $3.252 billion rather than $10 billion as the upper bound of the intermediate category. That
combination preserves every element of community-bank relief the Agencies have identified as their
objective while leaving investment test coverage in place for the regional institutions whose participation
the MDI sector depends on. NBA opposes a $30 billion intermediate cap, which would extend the
concern described above by an order of magnitude.
II. The Geographic Flexibility Standard Would Impede Statutorily Authorized MDI
Investment
The proposal would condition consideration for community development activities outside a bank's
assessment areas on the institution first meeting specified in-assessment-area thresholds — under Option
1, 0.625% of tier 1 capital for community development loans and 0.625% for investments and grants for
large banks, and 1.25% for intermediate, wholesale, and limited purpose banks.
MDI investment is characteristically out-of-assessment-area. An institution headquartered in one region
may invest in an MDI serving a community hundreds of miles away precisely because that community is
underserved and no local institution has the capacity to serve it. Section 2903(b) contains no geographic
limitation, and the Agencies have long recognized that cooperative activities with MDIs may be
considered regardless of location. Conditioning that consideration on satisfaction of an unrelated
assessment-area threshold would, as a practical matter, subordinate a standalone statutory provision to a
regulatory gate that Congress did not impose.
We note that the Agencies are not proposing significant changes to the assessment area framework itself.
The concern here is not how assessment areas are drawn; it is that activity Congress specifically
authorized without geographic limitation would become contingent on in-area performance.
Recommendation. Whichever option the Agencies adopt, the final rule should provide expressly that
activities described in 12 U.S.C. § 2903(b), including capital investment, loan participation, deposits,
technical assistance, and other ventures undertaken in cooperation with MDIs, women's depository
institutions, and low-income credit unions receive consideration without regard to the geographic
flexibility standard.



 III. The Proposal Is in Tension with the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act
Twenty days before the Agencies issued this proposal, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, P.L. 119-
101, became law. It took effect July 11, 2026.
Section 203 of the Act, the Community Investment and Prosperity Act, raises the statutory ceiling on
public welfare investments ("PWIs") from 15% to 20% of capital and surplus. It does so by amending 12
U.S.C. § 24(Eleventh) for national banks and section 9(23) of the Federal Reserve Act, 12 U.S.C. § 338a,
for state member banks. Section 203 also requires biennial reports from the OCC and the Board on such
investments. Section 906 codifies a Treasury mentor-protégé program for smaller financial institutions —
institutions that are, in substantial part, NBA's membership.
The public welfare investment authority is the mechanism through which a bank may hold equity in
another depository institution, an activity otherwise generally impermissible. It is, in practical terms, the
legal channel for direct equity investment in minority depository institutions. In raising the ceiling by a
third, Congress expanded that channel deliberately, by votes of 85 to 5 in the Senate and 358 to 32 in the
House.
The proposal moves in the opposite direction. By raising the large bank threshold to $10 billion, it
removes 376 institutions from the investment test — the examination framework that gives banks a
reason to use PWI capacity at all. Congress has enlarged the container; the Agencies propose to reduce
the incentive to fill it. We note further that investments above the former 15% level require approval or
non-objection from the OCC or the Board, so the Agencies control in substantial part whether the new
headroom is usable in practice.
Recommendations. First, the Agencies should confirm in the final rule that the amendments to the
OCC's Public Welfare Investments rule included in this proposal reflect the 20% ceiling now in force,
and conform them if they do not. Second, the Agencies should confirm that a mentor institution's
participation in the section 906 program receives CRA consideration under § 2903(b). Third, the biennial
PWI reports required by section 203 should break out investments in minority depository institutions as a
distinct category; without that breakout, neither Congress nor the Agencies will be able to observe the
effect of this rulemaking on MDI capital formation.
A three-way disparity across charter types
Section 203's increased PWI ceiling reaches national banks and state member banks. It does not reach
state nonmember banks. Layered onto a CRA proposal issued by the OCC and FDIC without the Board,
the combined effect is a three-way split among institutions of identical size and business model:
Charter

State nonmember bank

Proposed FDIC rule


 State nonmember institutions would hold the narrower investment authority and the narrowed
examination incentive. A substantial share of NBA's membership holds that charter. We do not suggest
that either Congress or the Agencies intended to disadvantage one charter class, but that is the arithmetic
of the two enactments read together. Adopting the $3.252 billion intermediate threshold recommended in
Section I would materially reduce the disparity by keeping a larger set of institutions within the
investment test regardless of charter.
IV. The Pending Part 24 Amendments Would Compound These Effects
On April 27, 2026, the OCC proposed to amend 12 C.F.R. part 24 to remove references to minority- and
women-owned entities (Docket ID OCC-2025-0075, RIN 1557-AF32). The proposed amendments would
strike "or minority-owned small business" from § 24.2(h); ", including minority- and women-owned
small businesses or small farms," from § 24.6(b)(2); ", including minority- and women-owned small
businesses," from § 24.6(d)(1); and "minority- and women-owned" from § 24.6(d)(4). The OCC's stated
rationale is that these references are not required by statute.
NBA addresses that proposal in this letter because its effect cannot be assessed in isolation from this one.
Taken together, three actions in a single year would: raise the statutory PWI ceiling (section 203); remove
from the implementing regulation the examples that identify minority-owned entities as qualifying
recipients of those investments (part 24 proposal); and remove 376 institutions from the examination test
that motivates the investments in the first place (this proposal). Each may be defensible standing alone.
The combination narrows, at three separate points, the only well-established channel through which
private capital reaches minority depository institutions and the businesses they serve.
That a statute does not compel a regulatory reference is not a reason to remove it. The references in part
24 are illustrative; they tell examiners and compliance officers what Congress had in mind, and their
removal will be read by the market as a signal, whatever the OCC intends. Section 2903(b) of the CRA
and section 308 of FIRREA both remain in force and both speak directly to minority-owned institutions.
Recommendation. The OCC should withdraw the proposed part 24 amendments insofar as they remove
references to minority- and women-owned entities. At minimum, the OCC should defer action on those
amendments until this rulemaking is final, so that their combined effect can be evaluated on a complete
record.
V. The Revised Intermediate Bank Rating Criteria Would Weaken Community
Development Incentives
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank must receive at least "satisfactory" on both the
lending test and the community development test to receive an overall "satisfactory" rating. The proposal
would require a satisfactory rating on the lending test alone.
Applied to the enlarged intermediate category, this change makes community development performance
effectively optional for a satisfactory outcome. NBA does not suggest the Agencies intend that result, but
it is the predictable consequence. Community development activity is the mechanism through which
many of these institutions engage with MDIs and CDFIs in their regions.
 Recommendation. Retain the current two-test requirement. If the Agencies wish to introduce flexibility,
a preferable approach would be to permit a "needs to improve" community development rating to be
offset by demonstrably strong lending performance, rather than to remove the community development
test from the rating calculus altogether.
VI. The 15% Indirect Cost Limitation Would Disqualify Capable Grant Recipients
The proposal would limit large-bank consideration for community development grants to recipients
whose indirect costs for administering the grant do not exceed 15%, calculated in accordance with the
Uniform Guidance for Federal Awards.
NBA shares the Agencies' concern that grant funds reach the communities they are intended to benefit.
But 15% is precisely the Uniform Guidance de minimis rate — the default available to organizations that
have not negotiated a rate with a federal agency. Federally negotiated indirect cost rates for established
community development organizations, including CDFIs and housing intermediaries that partner with
NBA members, commonly exceed that figure. As drafted, the limitation would disqualify an organization
for the sole reason that it has undergone federal cost-rate negotiation and operates at the rate the
government itself approved. That is the opposite of the sorting the Agencies intend.
Recommendation. Permit a recipient with a federally negotiated indirect cost rate to use that rate. Apply
the 15% figure only to recipients relying on the de minimis rate.
VII. Small Bank Reclassification and the Loss of the Community Development Record
Raising the small bank threshold to $1 billion will relieve a substantial number of NBA member
institutions of the community development test. For many members this is welcome, and NBA supports
it. For others, the community development test is where institutional mission is documented and where
they have earned "outstanding" ratings that support branch and merger applications, philanthropic
fundraising, and deposit-placement programs. For a mission-driven institution, the evaluation is an asset,
not only a burden.
Recommendation. Permit a small bank to elect evaluation under the intermediate community
development test. The election imposes nothing on institutions that do not want it and preserves the
evaluative record for institutions that do.
VIII. The Agencies Should Publish an MDI-Specific Impact Analysis
Section 308 of FIRREA directs the Agencies to preserve and promote minority depository institutions.
The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs has designated this proposal an economically
significant regulatory action, and the Agencies expect it to be deregulatory with total costs below zero.
The accompanying analysis does not, to our reading, address the proposal's effect on capital flows into
MDIs. A cost estimate that counts compliance savings to banks but not foregone investment in the
institutions those banks invest in is incomplete on its own terms.

 Recommendation. Before finalizing, the Agencies should publish an analysis estimating (i) the volume
of qualified investments and grants directed to MDIs and CDFIs by the 376 institutions that would move
from large bank to intermediate bank status, and (ii) the projected effect of the geographic flexibility
standard on out-of-assessment-area MDI activity. NBA is prepared to assist with member data.
IX. Charter-Based Divergence
The Board of Governors did not join this proposal, and absent further action will continue to apply the
1995 regulations. If this rule is finalized as proposed, state member banks will be subject to materially
different CRA requirements than national banks and state nonmember banks of identical size and business
model. NBA's membership spans all three supervisory categories. As described in Section III, this
divergence compounds a parallel disparity in public welfare investment authority.
Divergence of this kind creates competitive distortion, complicates charter and Federal Reserve
membership decisions for reasons unrelated to safety and soundness, and produces inconsistent
examination outcomes for institutions serving similar communities. NBA urges the Agencies to
coordinate with the Board toward a uniform framework. Failing that, the final rule should address how
institutions changing charter or membership status will be evaluated during transition, and should state an
applicability date and transition period, neither of which the proposal currently provides.
Conclusion
NBA supports burden relief for community institutions and welcomes the Agencies' attention to clarity in
the qualifying-activity standards. We ask only that the final rule be calibrated so that relief for community
banks is not purchased at the cost of the capital that sustains minority depository institutions — capital
that Congress acted three months ago to expand. The recommendations above are, we believe, consistent
with both objectives.
We would welcome the opportunity to meet with staff of either Agency to discuss these comments.
Respectfully submitted,

Nicole Elam
CEO, National Bankers Association
Executive Director, National Bankers Association Foundation

Our Nation has a troubled history of credit and housing discrimination in working-class
and lower-income communities. For decades, banks rejected lending to communities of color,
preventing working-class residents from buying homes and building small businesses. This
widespread practice came to be known as "redlining." Redlining prevented millions of people
from building wealth through home ownership and entrepreneurship.3

The Community Reinvestment Act was enacted to "prevent redlining and to encourage
banks to help meet the credit needs of all segments of their community, including LMI
neighborhoods and individuals."4 Under the CRA, financial institutions have a "continuing and
affirmative obligation" to meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they operate.5
The CRA is a core civil rights law, a product of the movement that also produced laws banning
credit discrimination like the Fair Housing Act and Equal Credit Opportunity Act. By passing
this suite of laws, Congress "created two distinct but complementary toolkits to fulfill" its goals
of ending discriminatory housing and credit practices.6

The importance of the CRA is underscored by a worsening housing crisis that
disproportionately affects low-income and historically marginalized communities. The National
Low Income Housing Coalition warns of a shortage of 7.2 million rental homes that are both
affordable and available for extremely low-income renters, defined as those with incomes at the
poverty level or below 30% of Area Median Income.7 Nationwide, housing cost burdens have
reached historical highs, with lower- and moderate-income households facing severe shortages of
available, affordable units. In California alone, over 50% of renters are cost-burdened—paying
more than 30% of their income on housing—while the state faces a shortfall of over 1.2 million
affordable homes for extremely low-income renters.8 The CRA serves as the fundamental
financial engine that leverages private banking capital into low-income housing production and

I.
Redlining, the CRA's Passage, and Ongoing Disparities

Congress' enactment of the CRA was driven by the twin and related phenomena of
racially driven redlining and disinvestment in urban communities.10 By 1977, Congress was
confronted with ample evidence of both practices, finding that banks were "export[ing] savings
despite sound local lending opportunities," and facing "nationwide demands that Congress do
something about redlining."11 For example, the Senate Banking Committee's two-year study
uncovered that only ten percent of money deposited by Washington, D.C. residents was
reinvested back in their communities.12

Neighborhoods in Los Angeles, New York, Cleveland, St. Louis, and Indianapolis
reported similar disinvestment.13 These practices were a direct result of the 1930s' Home Owners

II.
The CRA's Benefits to the States and Their Residents

Even as problems persist, the CRA has been a very successful tool in addressing the
inequalities described above, to the benefit of the States and our residents. The CRA has driven
more than $6 trillion worth of investments in LMI communities and communities of color
nationwide,28 including an estimated $2 trillion in small business and community development
loans since 1996.29 A recent report concluded that, in 2024 alone, the CRA incentivized more
than $430 billion in loans and investments for homeownership, small businesses, and affordable
housing and community development in LMI communities nationwide.30

One of the CRA's key accomplishments has been to unlock lending to small businesses.
For example, between 2010 and 2016 alone, the CRA expanded the number of small business
loans in LMI neighborhoods by 38%31; 95% of the small business loans and 79% of the small
farm loans originated under the CRA in 2024, the most recent year for which data is available,
were for amounts under $100,000.32 CRA loans reflect the needs of small businesses, the vast
majority of which earn under $1 million in annual revenue.33 Indeed, the greatest need for capital
is for small dollar amounts.34 Studies have made clear that banks "are responsive to the
incentives that CRA provides" relating to small-business lending, with areas that lose CRA
eligibility seeing precipitous drops in lending.35

IV.
The Proposed Rule Is Arbitrary and Capricious and Contrary to Law

Beyond weakening the CRA's policy goals, the Proposed Rule fails to satisfy the
requirements of reasoned decisionmaking under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and
departs from the CRA's statutory text. Under the APA, a court must set aside agency action that
is "arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law." 5
U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). If finalized, the Proposed Rule is vulnerable to challenge on both grounds.

A. The Proposed Rule Is Arbitrary and Capricious

An agency engages in reasoned decisionmaking only if it "examine[s] the relevant data
and articulate[s] a satisfactory explanation for its action including a 'rational connection between
the facts found and the choice made.'"101 An agency acts arbitrarily when it entirely fails to
consider an important aspect of the problem, offers an explanation that runs counter to the
evidence before the agency, or reverses a prior policy without adequately accounting for the facts
and reliance interests underlying that policy.102 The Proposed Rule fails this standard in at least
eight respects.

First, the agencies have not adequately grappled with the substantial body of evidence—
much of it cited in this letter and doubtless before the agencies in the rulemaking record—
showing that reduced CRA coverage causes measurable declines in small-business and mortgage
lending to LMI communities.103 An agency cannot simply disregard evidence "before the
agency" that cuts against its chosen course; it must confront that evidence and explain why it is
nonetheless proceeding.104 Nowhere does the Proposed Rule meaningfully engage with these
studies or explain why the loan-volume declines documented after prior CRA-coverage losses
will not recur—and likely occur at even greater scale—here.

Second, the agencies' own acknowledgment that narrowing the product lines evaluated
under the lending test "could raise concerns that banks would no longer be incentivized to
engage in those activities going forward, which could have a negative impact on
communities,"105 is itself evidence of arbitrary decisionmaking. An agency that identifies a harm
flowing directly from its rule must explain why that harm is justified or how it will be mitigated;
simply noting the harm and proceeding regardless—without further analysis—is precisely the
failure to "consider an important aspect of the problem" that State Farm forbids.

Third, the Proposed Rule represents a sharp reversal from the CRA's decades-long
regulatory trajectory, including the agencies' own 2023 CRA rule, without the reasoned

is changing position," show that the new policy is permissible, and give reasons adequate to the

serious reliance interests at stake."106 States, community development financial institutions,
LIHTC syndicators, and nonprofit housing developers have built multi-year investment pipelines
around the current thresholds, product-line coverage, and grant-eligibility rules described supra,

does it explain why the factual premises underlying the current framework—many of which the
agencies themselves previously endorsed—are now mistaken.

Fourth, the agencies cannot reconcile their claim that the Proposed Rule still serves the
CRA's purposes with the drastic reduction in the number of banks subject to public data
collection and reporting—to just 86 banks, or roughly 2.4% of covered institutions.107 Data
reporting is not incidental to the CRA's function; it is the mechanism by which regulators,
researchers, and the public verify whether banks are meeting their statutory obligations and
detect emerging patterns of disinvestment. An agency acts arbitrarily when it undermines the
very oversight tools necessary to accomplish the goals it claims to be pursuing, without
explaining how those goals will otherwise be verified or enforced.

Fifth, the Proposed Rule's structure raises serious concerns about adequate notice under 5
U.S.C. § 553(b)-(c). A final rule must be a "logical outgrowth" of the proposal such that
interested parties had fair notice of, and a genuine opportunity to comment on, what the agencies
might actually adopt.108 The Proposed Rule presents at least five unresolved, independent binary
or multi-option choices simultaneously—the small-bank threshold ($1 billion versus an SBA-
linked $850 million), the major-product-line methodology (Option 1 versus Option 2), the
geographic-flexibility standard for consideration of CD activities outside assessment areas (a
quantitative tier-1-capital standard versus a qualitative standard), the scope of discriminatory-
and illegal-credit-practices consideration (Option A versus Option B), and the intermediate-bank
asset cap ($10 billion versus an alternative $3.252 billion).109 Because several of these choices
interact substantively—for example, a bank near the small-bank threshold would face materially
different obligations depending on which product-line methodology and which threshold the
agencies ultimately pair together—the agencies could finalize any of a large number of
substantively different combinations without any single commenter having had a genuine
opportunity to address that specific combination. A comment addressing one option in isolation
does not necessarily provide fair notice of a final rule that combines that option with a different
choice on a separate, interacting axis. The agencies should clarify, and if necessary re-propose,
the specific combination of options they intend to adopt before finalizing this rule.

B. The Proposed Rule Is Contrary to Law

The APA separately requires courts to set aside agency action that is "not in accordance
with law" or "in excess of statutory jurisdiction, authority, or limitations."119 Following Loper
Bright,120 courts must determine the best reading of a statute using traditional tools of

cannot survive that independent review.

to help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they are chartered,"121 and
requires the agencies to assess an institution's record of "meeting the credit needs of its entire
community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods."122 By raising the "large bank"

Dear Comptroller Otting:

This letter is submitted on behalf of the States of California, Illinois, Iowa, Maryland,
Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania,
Oregon, Virginia, and the District of Columbia, in response to the Office of the Comptroller of
the Currency's (OCC) September 5, 2018 Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPR)1
regarding the agency's intentions to revise its Community Reinvestment Act regulations.

The States have a strong interest in ensuring that banks take affirmative steps to ensure
robust investment in, and fair treatment of, communities which have traditionally been poorly
served by the banking industry. We write to state our concern that the proposals contained
within the OCC's ANPR will significantly weaken banks' obligations under the CRA. The
proposed changes will lead to disinvestment in low- and moderate-income communities,
undermining the very purposes of the Act. A weakened CRA could result in a loss of up to $101
billion dollars of investment and lending activity nationally over the next five years, over $25
billion in California alone.2

Under the Act, financial institutions have a "continuing and affirmative obligation" to meet the
credit needs of the local communities in which they operate.4
Our Nation has a troubled history of credit and housing discrimination in working-class
and lower-income communities. For decades, banks rejected lending to communities of color,
preventing working-class residents from buying homes and building small businesses. This
widespread practice came to be known as "redlining." Redlining prevented millions of people
from building wealth through home ownership and entrepreneurship.
A landmark series of fair lending laws including the Fair Housing Act, Equal Credit
Opportunity Act, and the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act aimed to stop redlining. The
Community Reinvestment Act was passed as a companion to these laws. Its purpose was to
remedy redlining by requiring banks to affirmatively expand credit access in local communities.
The CRA has been transformative. Trillions of dollars have been reinvested in working-class
neighborhoods that for years were excluded from participating in the American Dream.
Unfortunately, credit access remains a problem for communities of color. From 2001 to
2016, African-American homeownership rates fell by 5% compared to only 1% for white
homeowners.5 In 2017, African-American and Hispanic applicants experienced higher denial
rates for conventional home purchase loans than comparable white applicants.6
Minority-owned businesses also still struggle to access credit. While African-American
owned businesses applied for credit in numbers 10% higher than white-owned companies, their
approval rates are 19% lower.7 And such disparities cannot be explained by differences in credit
scores; only 40% of minority-owned businesses with good credit received the full amount they
asked for compared to 68% of nonminority-owned firms.8
Thus, strong implementation of the CRA is still needed, and it has been effective at
ameliorating some of the ongoing disparities. For example, a 2017 study found that the CRA is
linked to increased small business lending in LMI communities.9 Any measures to modernize

II.
Rescind Lenient Guidance on Credit Discrimination.
We urge the OCC to rescind recently issued guidance that will weaken enforcement of credit
discrimination and consumer protection laws through the CRA. OCC Bulletin 2018-23
unnecessarily limits the impact that credit discrimination or consumer protection violations will
have on CRA exams in two ways. First, the OCC will only consider those violations that are
"directly relate[d]" or have a "logical nexus" to a bank's CRA lending activity.17 This means
that even significant violations of consumer protection or credit discrimination laws will not
affect a bank's CRA rating unless they fall within this narrow definition. This guidance ignores
the clearly negative implications that such violations have for the bank's entire operations as they
relate to consumers and members of protected classes.
Second, the OCC's guidance adopts a "general policy" that downgrades for violations of
credit discrimination and consumer protection laws will only be by "one rating level unless
illegal practices are found to be particularly egregious."18 This means that a bank with
substantial, non-technical violations that are not "egregious" could be, for example, only
downgraded from "Outstanding" to "Satisfactory." Such a minor downgrade will not impact
regulators' review of their mergers and acquisitions—the only real "stick" for CRA
compliance.19 Bank examiners should be able to levy meaningful consequences on banks who
not only fail to take the affirmative steps required to assist communities and consumers, but have
actively harmed them.
Additionally, OCC Bulletin 2018-1720 should be substantially revised. Historically, if a bank
was under investigation for credit discrimination by the OCC or another federal agency, the OCC
would delay release of the Bank's CRA exam results. This allowed examiners to incorporate
findings from that investigation and adjust the bank's final CRA rating accordingly. The
downside of this practice was that a particularly complex or serious investigation could delay the
final release of the results for years.
Bulletin 2018-17 ends this practice but creates a more serious problem. Now, the OCC will
not take findings of illegal credit discrimination practices into account in its assessment of the

III.
Reject a "One-Ratio" Approach to CRA Evaluation.
Under current examination procedures, banks are evaluated under both quantitative and
qualitative standards. The ANPR suggests that the OCC could evaluate a bank's compliance
with CRA requirements by simply measuring a bank's total CRA activities as a percentage of its
total assets, a so-called "one-ratio" approach which would severely undermine the CRA's
purpose of ensuring responsiveness to local community needs.21
Under current practice, a CRA examiner, through public comment and other methods,
evaluates priority needs for a given geography. While one area may, for example, need
affordable housing development due to rapidly increasing housing prices, another with high
unemployment may need to prioritize small business lending and job creation. Adopting a "one-
ratio" formula will make it more difficult for CRA examiners to evaluate how well banks are
responding to these local needs, as expressed by community members. A one-ratio formula
would likely incentivize banks to focus predominantly or exclusively on large-dollar loans and
investments that qualify under the CRA, enabling banks to bump up their ratios regardless of
whether these investments actually meet local credit needs (e.g., of LMI small businesses and
individuals) which can involve more challenging or labor-intensive efforts on the part of banks.
FDIC Director (and former Chairman) Martin J. Gruenberg recently emphasized that a single
ratio approach for CRA evaluation "could obscure the current community-based focus of [the]
CRA and undermine its basic purpose."22 He cautioned that a single ratio evaluation would
"fundamentally change the relationship between banks and local communities" because it will
"undermine the incentive that banks currently have to develop constructive partnerships with
community organizations."23 These partnerships, Director Gruenberg noted, "have been central
to community development in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods . . . around the
country." Lastly, he noted that a single ratio approach could potentially violate "the statutory
requirement that . . . [a] CRA evaluation be presented separately for each metropolitan area in
which a bank maintains one or more branches."24
Similarly, the Federal Reserve Board's Community Advisory Council (CAC) has urged
banking regulators, including the OCC, "not to adopt a single quantitative assessment to

IV.
Highlight Community Benefits Agreements as a Tool for CRA Compliance.

The OCC should e ncourage and recognize community benefits agreements as a positive
factor in CRA ratings.

Banks' applications for mergers and acquisitions are subject to public comment periods.
These comments often involve discussion of CRA performance ratings. Banks that receive
adverse comments have, on some occasions, entered into agreements with community groups to
demonstrate how they will meet local credit needs post-merger or acquisition. These community
benefit agreements include specific lending a nd investment goals in designated LMI
communities or commitments to not close certain branch locations, and are highly useful means
of injecting local public input into the CRA process.

Unfortunately, in a recent guidance document, the OCC failed to recognize the importance of
these agreements, allowing banks with failing CRA ratings to merge, acquire, or grow their
business without any requirement or incentive to enter into community benefits agreements or
otherwise respond to local community concerns.27 The OCC should remedy this failure in the
ANPR by affirming the important role that community benefits agreements can play in helping
banks with less than satisfactory CRA ratings to come into CRA compliance.

Federal policymakers have recommended that regulators formalize the use of these
agreements. Treasury's April 2018 CRA memorandum states that regulators should make clear
to banks that a community benefits agreement "can be an effective tool for banks with less than

VI.
Include Banks' Affiliates' Activities as Part of CRA Examinations.
Several banks own mortgage companies as affiliates. The current regulations give banks the
option of including their affiliates as part of any CRA examination, but does not require that the
activities of affiliates undergo CRA scrutiny.36 This loophole has created serious deficiencies in
the CRA examination process; for example, it allowed several banks' affiliate mortgage
companies with abusive practices to avoid examination for CRA compliance.37 A properly
modernized CRA would require the activities of bank affiliates to be considered in any
examination. Notably, Treasury commented negatively on this loophole in its April 2018
memorandum, and recommended that regulators take steps to address it.38
The undersigned States fundamentally disagree with the proposed ANPR. If adopted, the
ANPR's proposals will undermine the affirmative and continuing obligation banks have to meet
the credit needs of all of the communities they serve, in particular, low- and moderate-income
communities. We urge the OCC to withdraw the ANPR and rescind recently issued CRA
guidance. In the alternative, the changes recommended above should be considered as part of
any future joint rulemaking. Thank you for your consideration of our views.

Such changes must be undertaken with care, ensuring that any revisions keep to the
congressional promise that CRA would be an antidote to the pernicious practices of redlining and
disinvestment which have done lasting harm to LMI communities, particularly communities of
color. Such caution is particularly apt at a time of such economic turmoil and constriction in
credit caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. CRA's goals are more important than ever as LMI
communities seek to recover from the profound effects of this public health emergency.
Given the major changes in the banking landscape that have taken place over the past 25
years, thoughtful updates to CRA regulations—made with an eye to Congress's goals in enacting
the statute—are appropriate. Such reforms could help ensure that that LMI communities are not
left behind in an era of online and mobile banking, including the rise of "fintech" companies that
differ significantly from traditional banks.
Unfortunately, the Proposed Rule, far from thoughtfully modernizing CRA's
implementation to advance its core purposes, is inimical to them. It would shift the CRA's
incentive structure by discarding time-tested methods of assessing banks' performance in
meeting the investment, credit and deposit needs of LMI communities in favor of a narrow,
purely quantitative test to generate banks' presumptive ratings, using apparently arbitrary
benchmarks. This approach would encourage banks to shift their focus away from the actual
needs of the communities that the banks are purporting to serve and toward a myopic approach
with the dollar value of activities paramount. Further, under the Proposed Rule banks can receive
high CRA ratings while failing to meet the needs of almost half of the areas in which they do
business. Moreover, the Proposed Rule would greatly expand the activities that qualify for CRA
credit, including some activities that have little or no connection to CRA's core purposes. The
Rule also virtually eliminates the service test, contrary to CRA's explicit focus on banks meeting
the needs of depositors in their assessment areas. Finally, the OCC and FDIC have not cited any
concrete data supporting the major proposed changes. Tellingly, the Rule is a product of only
two of the three regulatory agencies tasked with oversight of CRA; the third—the Federal
Reserve Board of Governors (hereinafter the Board)—has indicated its fundamental
disagreement with the approach taken here. Instead, it has proposed an alternative framework—
and published supporting data—that would likely be much more consistent with the values that
Congress put into law when it passed the CRA. In short, the Proposed Rule is contrary to CRA's
purpose and text, will harm communities and the States, and should be withdrawn.

BACKGROUND ON CRA AND IMPORTANCE TO THE STATES
Congress' enactment of the CRA was driven by the twin and related phenomena of
racially driven redlining and disinvestment in urban communities.12 By 1977, Congress was
confronted with ample evidence of both practices, finding that banks were "export[ing] savings
despite sound local lending opportunities," and facing "nationwide demands that Congress do
something about redlining."13 For example, the Senate Banking Committee's two-year study
uncovered that only ten percent of money deposited by Washington, D.C. residents was
reinvested back in their communities.14 Neighborhoods in Los Angeles, New York, Cleveland,
St. Louis, and Indianapolis reported similar disinvestment.15 These practices were a direct result
of the 1930s' Home Owners Loan Corporation (HOLC) maps that demarcated communities as
credit worthy based on race,16 leading banks to adopt similar practices.17 Forty years after CRA's
passage, historical vestiges of inequality and racism continue, as does the need for CRA to
remedy them; today, 74% of the neighborhoods once graded high-risk or hazardous and shaded
red on the HOLC maps are LMI neighborhoods.18

THE RULE IS FUNDAMENTALLY FLAWED
The Proposed Rule is flawed in multiple respects. Each of these is problematic in its own
right, but even more troublingly, these problems interact in a way that causes harm to CRA's
core purposes, LMI communities, and the States.
I.
THE PROPOSED RATING SYSTEM WILL UNDERMINE CRA'S CORE PURPOSES
At the heart of the Proposed Rule is the OCC and FDIC's radical proposal to replace the
existing CRA rating system with one that is ostensibly more "quantitative," but which is rigidly
formulaic and ignores the fact that CRA activity can and should be measured in ways beyond
raw dollar figures. This proposal would be a serious threat to CRA's continuing vitality as a
driver of economic progress and justice in LMI communities for the reasons discussed below.
A.
The Proposed Formulaic Test Is Seriously Flawed
Under current practice and historically, regulators have examined large banks' CRA
compliance through three distinct lenses, known as the lending, services, and investment tests.
Banks must perform well in each category to receive a positive CRA rating.47
The Proposed Rule would discard this approach in favor of a formulaic test, which experts
have called an "aggregate balance sheet ratio"48 approach. Under this test, the examiner would
evaluate a bank's compliance with CRA requirements by simply measuring the dollar value of a
bank's total CRA activities as a percentage of its deposits.49 Although the Proposed Rule would

degree, and have a greater proportion of African American residents relative to their peer
communities that have been less affected."60

B.
Banks Are Not Sufficiently Downgraded for Discrimination
While the Proposed Rule does provide that banks' ratings can be impacted by
"discriminatory or other illegal credit practices,"88 the OCC has taken other actions that could
lead to banks which have been found to have engaged in discriminatory practices not facing
serious consequences to their CRA rating. Most directly, the OCC has reduced the negative
impact of violations of federal credit discrimination or consumer protection law on a bank's
CRA rating.89 This means that a bank with substantial, non-technical violations that are not
"egregious" could be, for example, only downgraded from "Outstanding" to "Satisfactory." Such
a minor downgrade will not impact regulators' review of their mergers and acquisitions—the
only real "stick" for CRA compliance.90 Further, the OCC has narrowed the universe of
consumer protection or credit discrimination violations that will affect banks' ratings.91 Bank
examiners should be able to levy meaningful consequences on banks who not only fail to take
the affirmative steps required to assist communities and consumers, but have actively harmed
them.

V.

VI. THE PROPOSED RULE IS UNLAWFUL
As discussed above, Congress's purpose in adopting the CRA was two-fold: combatting
redlining and meeting the credit and deposit needs of communities. The CRA was inspired by the
need to address the "stark lending disparities across the country" where only a small percentage
of deposits remained in underserved communities, while banks loaned a majority of the assets
deposited there to businesses and individuals outside the community.137 The Proposed Rule runs
contrary to those purposes and the plain text of the CRA. This is not only bad policy, it is
unlawful.
A.
The Proposed Rule Is Contrary to Law
Multiple of the Proposed Rule's provisions are contrary to clear Congressional intent and
frustrate the policies that Congress sought to implement in passing the CRA. Thus, the Proposed
Rule is subject to being struck down by courts.138
The Proposed Rule is contrary to the CRA's intended purposes of meeting the credit and
deposit needs of LMI communities in particular,139 as well as its mandate that regulators examine
how well a given bank is meeting the needs "of its entire community, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods"140 in multiple ways.
The Rule gives no consideration to how banks are meeting LMI communities' need
for deposit accounts and other retail products, effectively eliminating the retail test which has
been one of CRA's pillars. The Proposed Rule eliminates the current regulations requiring

B.
The Proposed Rule Is Arbitrary and Capricious
Under the APA, courts must "hold unlawful and set aside agency action, findings, and
conclusions found to be . . . arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in
accordance with law."143 Agency action is "arbitrary and capricious if the agency has [1] relied
on factors which Congress has not intended it to consider, [2] entirely failed to consider an
important aspect of the problem, [3] offered an explanation for its decision that runs counter to
the evidence before the agency, or [4] is so implausible that it could not be ascribed to a
difference in view or the product of agency expertise."144 When an agency reverses course by
changing a prior policy, the agency must provide a "reasoned explanation," and show that "the
new policy is permissible under the statute, that there are good reasons for it, and that the agency
believes it to be better."145 The Proposed Rule fails this test in numerous respects.
First, as discussed above, the OCC and FDIC relied on factors that Congress did not intend
when they crafted the Proposed Rule by deviating from the CRA's statutory focus on LMI
communities and the importance of retail services in those areas.

THE BOARD MUST ENSURE THAT ONCE-IN-A-GENERATION CRA REFORM
MEETS THE NEEDS OF LMI COMMUNITIES
It has been over twenty years since the Board, OCC and Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC) last engaged in significant joint CRA rulemaking. As mentioned above, in
2020, the OCC adopted its own rule—alone, without the support of the other two regulatory
agencies (OCC Rule). A group of Attorneys General opposed the OCC Rule for a number of
reasons,1 including that the Rule: (1) was inimical to CRA's core purposes; (2) shifted CRA's
incentive structure and discarded time-tested methods of assessing banks' performance in
meeting the investment, credit and deposit needs of LMI communities in favor of a narrow,
purely quantitative test to generate banks' presumptive ratings, using arbitrary benchmarks
without the support of a robust data set; (3) created a rating system that diverted the focus away
from the actual needs of LMI communities and toward a myopic approach that rewarded the
dollar value of activities; (4) expanded qualifying activities to include those with little or no
connection to CRA's core purposes—and virtually eliminated the service test—contrary to
CRA's explicit focus on banks meeting the needs of depositors in their assessment areas; and
(5) shut the communities that CRA was intended to serve out of the evaluation process.
The Board's ANPR stands in stark contrast to the OCC's misguided rule, and offers
a chance to return to a regulatory regime that advances CRA's objectives. First, the ANPR
appropriately acknowledges that any rulemaking must be rooted in CRA's core purpose of
meeting the credit and deposit needs of LMI communities, and cognizant of CRA's aim to
stop racial redlining.2 The signatory States agree that the Board must focus on CRA's
historical context and understanding that CRA operates as a "crucial mechanism for
addressing persistent systemic inequity in the financial system for LMI and minority
individuals and communities."3 Second, the States support the Board's evaluation
framework, which maintains distinct retail and community development evaluations,
recognizing the value of these services to communities in addressing the CRA's aims.
Additionally, the States support the Board's plan to assess retail services and deposit
products separately under the ANPR's Retail Services Subtest. The ANPR includes
proposals that zero in on areas where credit and deposit needs are unmet, focuses on
addressing needs of the smallest businesses and those in rural areas, and includes proposals
to promote financial inclusion in Indian Country and other underserved areas, including
investments in Minority Depository Institutions and Community Development Financial
Institutions. Overall, States are encouraged that the Board's ANPR rejects the OCC Rule's
harmful one ratio approach. For example, in the case of mortgage lending, the ANPR
proposes evaluating a bank's retail lending in its major product lines using metrics that
measure the number of loans a bank makes, not the dollar value of these loans. Further, the

CONCLUSION
Low-income communities and communities of color continue to face inequities and
discrimination like those that prompted Congress to pass the CRA. As the OCC rule change
demonstrated, regulations implementing the CRA's requirements can be used to subvert the
explicit purpose of the Act. Therefore, the most pressing objective must be maintaining fidelity
to CRA's core purpose of remedying disinvestment in low-income communities and the
lingering impact of racially-driven redlining. The States agree that the Board's ANPR is an
"important step forward in laying a foundation for the [regulatory] agencies to build a shared,
modernized CRA framework that has broad support."76 To meet CRA's mandate during a

I.
Focus on Systemic Racial Inequities.
For the Final Rule to truly reflect CRA's remedial purpose of addressing racist lending
and banking practices such as redlining, it must address persistent systemic inequalities and the
entrenched intergenerational effects of discrimination.3 For example, while lending to LMI
homeowners falls significantly short of their overall share of homeownership, lending to Black
homeowners is even more deficient.4 More generally, the racial wealth gap between Black and
white Americans remains roughly the same today as it had been two years before the Civil
Rights Act was passed in 1964.5 A CRA modernization effort is incomplete without examining
the impact of modern-day lending discrimination, redlining, and continued neighborhood
segregation.6

nearly all former redlined neighborhoods nationwide remain racially segregated. And two-thirds

The Final Rule must incentivize efforts to keep LMI communities housed, encourage

To Whom It May Concern:
The Connecticut Bankers Association (CBA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of
the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed
amendments to their regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), published at
91 Fed. Reg. 52114 (August 12, 2026).
CBA represents banks of all sizes and business models, including community, regional, and larger
institutions operating in Connecticut. Our member banks have longstanding commitments to meeting the
credit needs of their communities, including low- and moderate-income individuals and neighborhoods.
These commitments extend beyond traditional lending to include affordable housing investments,
partnerships with nonprofit organizations and other community development activities.
CBA generally supports the agencies' efforts to modernize the CRA regulations, reduce unnecessary
regulatory burdens, and provide greater clarity and predictability in CRA examinations. At the same
time, we believe regulatory relief should not diminish recognition of the meaningful contributions banks
make through community development lending, investments, grants, and services. A successful final
rule should accomplish both objectives while preserving the flexibility necessary to accommodate
differences in institutional size, business model, and local community needs.
With these principles in mind, CBA offers the following recommendations.
 2

1. Support Increased Asset Thresholds While Preserving Recognition of Community Development
Activities
CBA supports the proposed increases in the CRA asset thresholds, which would classify banks with less
than $1 billion in assets as Small Banks, banks with between $1 billion and $10 billion in assets as
Intermediate Banks, and banks with more than $10 billion in assets as Large Banks.
Under the proposed framework, Small Banks and Intermediate Banks would be evaluated under the
same Lending Test. Intermediate Banks would also undergo a separate Community Development Test,
while Small Banks would not be required or allowed to do so. As discussed below, CBA supports
allowing Small Banks to elect an opt-in approach to the Intermediate Bank framework, including its
separately rated Community Development Test. Large Banks would remain subject to separate Lending,
Investment, and Service Tests. CBA supports tailoring these examination requirements to banks' size
and resources while preserving meaningful recognition of their community development activities.
The proposed thresholds would provide meaningful regulatory relief to community and midsize banks
without eliminating their CRA obligations. CBA also supports adjusting both asset thresholds annually
based on nominal Gross Domestic Product so they remain appropriate as the banking industry and
broader economy evolve.
At the same time, CBA recognizes that some community banks that will move to the proposed Small
Bank category under this proposal have established significant community development programs.
These institutions may provide community development loans, invest in affordable housing projects,
contribute to nonprofit organizations serving low- and moderate-income populations, and provide
financial expertise through qualifying community development services. Under the current proposal,
these activities would no longer be evaluated under a separate Community Development Test for those
banks and could receive less recognition in determining a bank's overall CRA rating.
CBA therefore supports permitting banks that qualify for the Small Bank framework to elect
examination under the Intermediate Bank framework, including its separate Community Development
Test. This option would allow banks with substantial community development programs to seek separate
recognition for those activities while preserving the Small Bank framework for banks that do not make
the election.
Similarly, banks moving from the Large Bank framework to the Intermediate Bank framework would no
longer be subject to separate Investment and Service Tests. Instead, qualifying community development
activities would be evaluated together under the Intermediate Bank Community Development Test.
CBA supports this combined approach, which would give banks greater flexibility to determine the
appropriate mix of community development loans, investments, grants, and services based on the needs
and opportunities in their communities.
The agencies should confirm that all qualifying activities, including affordable housing investments, will
continue to receive meaningful consideration under the combined test.
 3

Reducing unnecessary regulatory burden is an important objective, but the final rule must continue to
recognize and encourage the community development activities and partnerships that banks have
established over many years. 1
2. Improve Predictability and Consistency Across Examiners, Regulators, and Charter Types
One of the most important objectives of CRA modernization should be to provide banks with greater
certainty regarding how their activities will be evaluated.
Banks should be able to plan and undertake lending, investment, and community development activities
with confidence that the applicable standards will be interpreted and applied consistently. A bank's CRA
evaluation should not depend materially on which examiner conducts the examination, which federal
agency supervises the institution, or whether the institution holds a state or federal charter.
CBA urges the agencies to work together (including with the Federal Reserve) toward a uniform
interagency framework and to establish common examination procedures, interpretive guidance, and
examiner training. Greater consistency is particularly important for community development activities,
where banks may commit substantial resources based on their reasonable expectation that an activity
will qualify for CRA consideration.
We support the proposed illustrative list of qualifying activities and the process for obtaining advance
confirmation of CRA eligibility. These mechanisms should be administered consistently across
agencies, provide timely responses, and permit banks to rely on eligibility determinations made in good
faith when activities are undertaken.
The proposed Intermediate Bank category would encompass institutions ranging from $1 billion to $10
billion in assets. Banks within this broad range may differ significantly in financial resources, business
models, branch networks, lending capacity, and local market conditions. CBA therefore urges the
agencies to provide clear guidance on the selection and use of similarly situated lenders in CRA
examinations. Where comparative information is considered, examiners should use appropriately
tailored peer groups reflecting meaningful similarities among institutions, rather than treating the entire
Intermediate Bank category as a single peer group. Such comparisons should inform an examiner's
assessment of a bank's performance context, not serve as independent benchmarks or substitute for
evaluating the bank's own record of meeting community credit needs.
3. Preserve Flexibility in Assessment Area Requirements
CBA urges the agencies to ensure meaningful flexibility in how banks delineate their CRA assessment
areas and to ensure that this flexibility is respected in examinations. Assessment areas should reflect the

1 CBA understands that other industry commenters may recommend higher asset thresholds than those proposed. Regardless
of the thresholds ultimately adopted, banks classified as Small Banks should be permitted to elect examination under the
Intermediate Bank framework, including its separately rated Community Development Test.
 4

communities a bank can reasonably serve based on its branch network, lending activity, size and
capacity, business model, and local market conditions.
CBA strongly opposes requiring all banks to delineate entire counties (or regional planning districts –
see below) regardless of their size, capacity, or geographic footprint. Small and Intermediate Banks in
particular must retain the flexibility to delineate assessment areas that reasonably reflect the
communities they serve, and the banks' capacity to serve them.
This is not a theoretical concern. CBA has seen instances in which examiners have directed banks to
include an entire county because a branch was located just across the county line. These expectations
have created confusion, significant compliance pressure, and uncertainty about how a bank with a
limited presence in the county is expected to serve communities throughout it. A branch serving a
neighboring community should not, by itself, be treated as evidence that the bank can reasonably serve
an entire additional county.
This has historically been a particular concern in New England, where county boundaries do not
necessarily correspond to the local communities a bank can reasonably serve. Federal statistical practice
has recognized city- and town-based areas as alternatives to county-based metropolitan areas. A bank
may serve adjoining towns on both sides of a county line without having the capacity or geographic
reach to serve every community within both counties.
The concern is especially relevant in Connecticut, where county governments ceased functioning in
1960 and the state's nine planning regions now serve as county-equivalent geographic units.2 Requiring
a bank to include an entire planning region in its assessment area could create unreasonable expectations
where the bank operates in only a portion of that region. CBA urges the agencies to expressly recognize
county-equivalent geographic areas and make clear that the same flexibility available for delineating
partial counties applies to those areas.
The proposal itself recognizes that even a Large Bank with a single branch or deposit-taking ATM at the
edge of a geographically expansive or populous county may have limited capacity to serve the entire
county.3 That concern is at least as significant for smaller institutions. General assurances that examiners
will consider performance context do not provide the upfront certainty these banks need.
The final rule and examination guidance should expressly prohibit requiring Small or Intermediate
Banks to include an entire county (or county-equivalent area) solely because they maintain a branch
there. Any required expansion should be supported by a documented, institution-specific analysis of the
bank's capacity, geographic reach, and applicable assessment-area requirements, not an examiner's
preference for whole-county boundaries.
CBA also supports preserving flexibility in the treatment of qualifying community development
activities outside a bank's assessment areas. Banks that received an overall CRA rating of "Satisfactory"
or better on their most recent examination should receive consideration for qualifying community

3 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52114, 52154 (Aug. 12, 2026).
 5

development activities outside their assessment areas, without having to satisfy the proposed geographic
flexibility standards, whether measured annually or over the full examination period.
This flexibility can be particularly important for affordable housing investments and community
development financing arrangements that serve broader geographic areas or multiple communities. CRA
requirements should encourage participation in these activities rather than unnecessarily restrict the
locations where banks may provide support.

4. Preserve Support for Community Development Nonprofits and Provide Practical
Accommodations for Smaller Organizations
CBA is concerned that the proposal's treatment of community development grants could discourage
bank support for nonprofit organizations, including those providing affordable housing and essential
services to low- and moderate-income communities.
Banks have longstanding relationships with nonprofit organizations throughout Connecticut. These
partnerships often involve more than funding individual projects. Banks provide ongoing financial
support, contribute professional expertise, and help nonprofit organizations maintain the capacity
necessary to deliver services over time.
The proposed rule would generally limit CRA consideration to grants directly used for a particular
community development program, project, or initiative. For Large Banks, it would also condition CRA
consideration on a recipient organization's indirect administrative costs not exceeding 15% of the grant
amount, together with additional documentation requirements.
While CBA appreciates the agencies' objective of ensuring that community development funding
benefits its intended recipients, we are concerned that these requirements could unnecessarily restrict
support for organizations carrying out important community development work.
First, CBA urges the agencies to preserve CRA consideration for reasonable general operating
support provided to qualifying community development nonprofits. Organizations providing
affordable housing, financial education, small business assistance, and other community services depend
on funding for personnel, facilities, technology, and administration. These expenditures are often
essential to delivering the programs and services that benefit low- and moderate-income communities.
A grant should not be excluded from CRA consideration solely because it supports the general
operations of an organization whose primary mission and activities qualify as community development,
rather than being earmarked for a discrete project. Banks should be permitted to demonstrate the grant's
community development purpose through reasonable documentation of the organization's mission,
activities, and use of funds.
Second, CBA urges the agencies to eliminate the proposed 15% indirect-cost limitation and
associated documentation requirements. Administrative costs are not necessarily evidence of
 6

inefficiency, and nonprofits differ substantially in how they organize, deliver, and account for their
services. CRA consideration should focus on whether a grant supports a qualifying community
development purpose, rather than whether the recipient satisfies a fixed administrative-cost threshold.
These concerns are particularly significant for smaller community-based nonprofits, many of which
operate with limited staff and financial resources. Such organizations may lack the accounting systems
necessary to separately calculate and document indirect costs using the methodology contemplated by
the proposal. Some also are not required to file a full IRS Form 990 and may not ordinarily prepare the
financial records requested under the proposed requirements.
The result could be that banks become less willing to support smaller, locally focused nonprofit
organizations because of uncertainty regarding whether their grants will receive CRA consideration.
That outcome would be particularly unfortunate for organizations with longstanding bank partnerships
and demonstrated records of serving local communities.
These alternatives do not alter CBA's recommendation that the agencies eliminate the proposed
limitation and related prescriptive documentation requirements. If the agencies nevertheless retain the
proposed 15% limitation or additional documentation requirements, CBA recommends the following
accommodations to reduce the burden on banks and the nonprofit organizations they support:
•
Small nonprofit exemption. Grants to nonprofit organizations below a reasonable annual
revenue or operating-budget threshold should be exempt from the 15% indirect-cost limitation.
The agencies should also consider an exemption for smaller-dollar grants, where the costs of
compliance may be disproportionate to the funding provided.
•
Good-faith safe harbor. Banks should receive CRA consideration when they conduct
reasonable due diligence and rely in good faith on a nonprofit recipient's representations
regarding its community development mission, intended use of grant funds, and compliance with
applicable requirements. A bank should not lose CRA credit solely because a nonprofit
subsequently experiences an increase in administrative costs or cannot satisfy technical
accounting requirements, provided the bank had no knowledge or reason to know of misuse of
funds or other material concerns.
•
Simplified documentation. Smaller nonprofits should be permitted to provide basic
documentation of their mission, activities, and intended use of funds rather than detailed indirect-
cost calculations, annual operating budgets, and financial reports that they may not ordinarily
prepare.
CBA also opposes public reporting of individual community development grants, including the
identities of recipients and amounts awarded. Banks should maintain appropriate grant
documentation for CRA examination purposes, but public disclosure could create unnecessary pressure
on banks' grantmaking decisions and discourage support for local nonprofit organizations.
 7

These recommendations would preserve appropriate safeguards while ensuring that CRA requirements
do not unintentionally discourage bank support for smaller nonprofit organizations that often provide
essential services in their local communities.
Conclusion
CBA appreciates the agencies' efforts to establish a clearer, more durable, and appropriately tailored
CRA framework. We believe the final rule can reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens while preserving
meaningful incentives for banks of all sizes to meet the credit and community development needs of the
communities they serve.
In particular, we encourage the agencies to adopt the proposed asset thresholds while preserving
meaningful recognition of community development activities, promote consistent examinations across
regulators and charter types, preserve assessment area flexibility, and ensure that community
development grant requirements do not discourage support for affordable housing and other qualifying
nonprofit organizations.
CBA believes these recommendations would help achieve the agencies' regulatory modernization
objectives while supporting the longstanding relationships between banks and the communities they
serve.
Thank you for considering our comments. We welcome the opportunity to provide additional
information as the agencies work toward a final rule.
Sincerely,

Thomas S. Mongellow

The Mayor’s Office of Housing and Community Development (MOHCD) and the Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector in the City and County of San Francisco appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)'s proposed rule to amend Community Reinvestment Act (CRA or "the Act") regulations. 
CRA-motivated lending and investments fill financing gaps left by limited public resources, allowing projects and programs like affordable housing, workforce development, and small businesses to move forward. When that private capital disappears, public dollars are not enough to replace it, leaving projects with larger financing gaps and longer delays that ultimately render them infeasible. This means fewer affordable housing projects, small businesses, and community-serving programs. 
We support efforts to provide greater clarity and predictability in CRA examinations. However, several provisions of the proposed rule would substantially weaken incentives for investments in these activities. The potential impacts are particularly significant for San Francisco’s affordable housing pipeline. Low-Income Housing Tax Credit equity is a major source in new affordable housing development financed through local funds, and changes in investor pricing translate directly into a need for increased public subsidies required to make those projects feasible. Recent underwriting from MOHCD illustrates the scale of this exposure. Projects moving through the City’s pipeline in 2025 assumed federal tax credit pricing of approximately $0.94 to $0.97 per dollar of credit. Since then, national LIHTC pricing has softened, with recent market data showing average pricing in the low-to-mid $0.80 range. Reducing CRA incentives for financial institutions to make affordable housing investments could further constrain investor demand, reduce the amount of equity generated by each tax credit award, and increase the local subsidy required to deliver San Francisco’s affordable housing pipeline. 
We also encourage the agencies to consider community reinvestment broadly, including the financial services that enable low- and moderate-income households to participate safely in the financial system. San Francisco’s experience with Bank On San Francisco demonstrates the importance of access to safe, affordable accounts and appropriate financial products. CRA should continue to recognize activities that address these foundational community needs, not only the volume or complexity of lending.  As such, we submit the feedback in the attached file in response to the proposal's questions.
