To whom it may concern,
The Mayor's Office of Housing and Community Development (MOHCD) and the Office of the
Treasurer & Tax Collector in the City and County of San Francisco appreciate the opportunity to
comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC)'s proposed rule to amend Community Reinvestment Act (CRA or "the Act")
regulations.
CRA-motivated lending and investments fill financing gaps left by limited public resources,
allowing projects and programs like affordable housing, workforce development, and small
businesses to move forward. When that private capital disappears, public dollars are not enough to
replace it, leaving projects with larger financing gaps and longer delays that ultimately render them
infeasible. This means fewer affordable housing projects, small businesses, and community-
serving programs.
We support efforts to provide greater clarity and predictability in CRA examinations. However,
several provisions of the proposed rule would substantially weaken incentives for investments in
these activities. The potential impacts are particularly significant for San Francisco's affordable
housing pipeline. Low-Income Housing Tax Credit equity is a major source in new affordable
housing development financed through local funds, and changes in investor pricing translate
directly into a need for increased public subsidies required to make those projects feasible. Recent
underwriting from MOHCD illustrates the scale of this exposure. Projects moving through the City's
pipeline in 2025 assumed federal tax credit pricing of approximately $0.94 to $0.97 per dollar of
credit. Since then, national LIHTC pricing has softened, with recent market data showing average
pricing in the low-to-mid $0.80 range. Reducing CRA incentives for financial institutions to make
 affordable housing investments could further constrain investor demand, reduce the amount of
equity generated by each tax credit award, and increase the local subsidy required to deliver San
Francisco's affordable housing pipeline.
We also encourage the agencies to consider community reinvestment broadly, including the
financial services that enable low- and moderate-income households to participate safely in the
financial system. San Francisco's experience with Bank On San Francisco demonstrates the
importance of access to safe, affordable accounts and appropriate financial products. CRA should
continue to recognize activities that address these foundational community needs, not only the
volume or complexity of lending. As such, we submit the feedback below in response to the
proposal's questions.
Questions 1-3: We encourage utilizing alternate metrics or creating a graduated framework so
incentives for affordable housing are maintained. The proposed increases would remove hundreds
of multibillion-dollar institutions from the large bank examination, directly contradicting the core
CRA objective to help meet local community credit needs. Mechanically trying to reproduce prior
distributions by asset size alone would inversely create an imbalance in examinations.
Further, moving banks out of the large bank examination would remove them from the investment
test, which is the core motivator for banks to participate in the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
(LIHTC) market. LIHTC is the primary capital investment program for affordable housing, and is a
complex market requiring specialized staff and ongoing compliance monitoring. Removing banks
from this requirement would result in a significant departure from the LIHTC market, meaning
fewer investments that historically lead to lower credit pricing. Decreases in the corporate tax rate
and increased availability of 4% LIHTC (one of the two program types) have already contributed to
steady decreases in LIHTC pricing. Further decreases will drastically reduce the production and
rehabilitation of affordable housing, since fewer projects would pencil and states/localities would
have to concentrate their limited resources in fewer projects to make up the difference. Therefore,
we strongly encourage removing or amending this provision to prevent further decreasing vital
investments in affordable housing.
Questions 4-7, 23: We discourage narrowing evaluations to the two largest major project lines
across all asset threshold sizes. This approach may help smaller or specialized banks with
administrative burden but for larger and intermediate banks this limited concentration risks
diminishing the value of maintaining robust and diverse portfolios of loan services. We also urge
the agencies to avoid narrowing large-bank service tests to credit services only. Basic banking
products noninclusive of credit services directly affect housing stability. People need accessible
accounts to pay rent and mortgages, establish savings, avoid predatory financial products, and
manage the costs of moving, purchasing, or maintaining a home. CRA should continue
incentivizing these critical community services.
In particular, we strongly recommend retaining deposit services within the retail banking services
evaluation. Safe, affordable deposit accounts are foundational to economic stability: they allow
households to receive income, pay bills, save, and avoid costly alternative financial services. San
 Francisco's Bank On program was created to expand access to accounts with features such as no
overdraft fees, no minimum balance requirements, and flexible account opening. CRA should not
incentivize institutions to prioritize credit services while reducing accountability for the availability
and quality of basic deposit services.
Questions 9 & 10: We strongly oppose the proposal to either deny CRA consideration for grants
from large banks where the recipient's indirect costs associated with administering the grant
exceed 15 percent or alternatively eliminate all grants and donations from CRA consideration. This
limitation is arbitrary and does not reflect the actual cost structure of many effective nonprofit
organizations. MOHCD has extensive experience in administering grants under other federal
programs and establishing this arbitrary cap would simply shift the administrative burden from
financial institutions to the grant recipients. Further, a flexible, outcomes-based standard is the
best method for evaluating whether a grant has a primary community-development purpose, not a
desultory absolute value that overlooks the actual impacts of these grants.
Questions 11-17: We support clarifying when affordable housing activities qualify for CRA
consideration, particularly recognition of projects undertaken in conjunction with other public
affordable housing programs. Such provisions can provide useful certainty to lenders and investors
partnering with public agencies and nonprofit housing organizations. In jurisdictions like San
Francisco, public affordable housing programs depend on private lending and investment to
leverage scarce public dollars. A regulatory change that nominally clarifies eligibility while
simultaneously subjecting fewer financial institutions to meaningful community-development
evaluation could result in a net reduction in affordable housing investment. CRA consideration
should avoid an overreliance on whether a project fits within a narrow product category or
produces an immediate financial return. The relevant question should be whether the activity
responds meaningfully to identified housing and community-development needs.
The definition of affordable housing should not be expanded to cover unsubsidized units. There is
no assurance or proof that unsubsidized projects directly support LMI households, and thus this
definition is too broad and will move funding away from projects that explicitly support low- to
moderate-income (LMI) households.
More broadly, we recommend that CRA place greater weight on responsiveness to identified
community needs than on the technical complexity of an activity. A straightforward product or
service can have substantial community impact and should not receive less consideration simply
because it is less complex. For example, safe and affordable deposit accounts like a Bank On
certified account may not involve complex financing structures but can provide substantial
benefits to low- and moderate-income households. CRA should preserve meaningful recognition
for these activities based on their demonstrated community impact and responsiveness.
Questions 18-20: We strongly support expanding the definition of affordable housing to include
rental housing for middle-income households in high-cost areas. We also support consideration of
the cost of providing housing as a component of a bank's evaluation. Projects serving households
around 80 to 120% AMI are in high demand but often have difficulty accessing the same subsidy
 and tax-credit tools available to lower-income housing. Giving banks CRA consideration for
financing that segment could make workforce or middle-income projects easier to capitalize. In
determining the definition of a "high-cost area," we urge the agencies to be wary of raising the cost-
burden threshold above 40% and to include additional factors such as available land for
development and construction costs to ensure greater accuracy than cost-burden alone.
Questions 21-22: We request revisions that ensure any naturally occurring affordable housing
nonprofit partnerships have clear, long-term affordability restrictions upon acquisition. Deed
restrictions are the only way to ensure projects permanently serve LMI households.
Question 34: Geographic flexibility should not allow institutions to substitute investments outside
their assessment areas for meaningful performance in the communities they serve. We
recommend incentivizing against this by clearly defining when a community's needs are
"substantially met" and providing greater weight for community development activities within an
assessment area, thus treating activity outside of the area as additive instead of substitutive.
Questions 35-54: We oppose broadly reversing the existing regulatory framework to the strategic-
plan model proposed. Strategic plans should remain a narrowly tailored option for when the
generally applicable performance tests may not provide a reasonable evaluation outcome.
Creating multiple sources of truth and allowing banks to set their own goals undermines the
agencies' priorities of consistency and accountability. At a minimum, strategic plans should also
be required to demonstrate why the generally applicable performance tests are inappropriate, and
any alternative goals should provide protections and expectations at least as rigorous as those
standards, if not more so.
Where strategic plans are permitted, we also recommend clear expectations for meaningful
community engagement. Public posting alone is not sufficient. Banks should provide advance
notice, make proposed goals and performance information accessible, allow sufficient time for
public input, and demonstrate how community feedback informed the plan. Engagement should
include organizations and residents representing low- and moderate-income communities.
Questions 56 & 57: We support establishing clearer and more objective quantitative geographic
assessment standards. While a radius-based approach may reduce opportunities to selectively
exclude certain census tracts, it risks overlooking online, centralized, or otherwise branch-
independent lending channels that provide critical services in underserved areas. Assessment
areas should reflect where institutions meaningfully conduct economic activityin addition to the
location of physical facilities.
Questions 58-63: We are generally supportive of these provisions. The Interagency Questions and
Answers will continue to be valuable. Transition provisions should be included for particularly
complex changes. Public information should still be maintained physically, but adopting a website
requirement would make it more readily accessible and reduce the need for public information to
be maintained at all branch locations. Non-compliant assessment areas should be clarified, but a
bank should still be required to revise its delineation to maintain integrity and accountability.
 Further, updating the cross reference detailed in Question 63 would meet our recommendation to
focus on community development and impact.
We support making CRA information available online, but recommend that it be accessible and
usable, not simply posted. CRA performance information should be searchable, downloadable,
and presented in a format that allows community organizations, local governments, and the public
to understand and compare institutions' performance. Online access should complement, rather
than entirely replace, reasonable options for people who face barriers to digital access.
For these reasons, we urge the withdrawal or substantial revision of the proposed rule. At a
minimum, any rule proposal should maintain robust community development obligations for
institutions with substantial assets and ensure continued incentives for critical affordable housing
programs.
Thank you for your consideration of this response.

The Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) is a landmark law that passed Congress in 1977. It came
about from a groundswell of grassroots organizing by residents of communities that had seen banks
gladly accept their deposits but repeatedly reject their loan applications.
Now, as the CRA approaches its 50th birthday next year, rather than inviting us to celebrate the law's
successes and better leverage its power for communities moving forward, this Administration is
forcing us to fight against an effort to water down the CRA. It is a tall order for community-based
organizations and nonprofit advocacy organizations like Woodstock Institute, only made more
difficult by the abrupt 60-day comment period.
A more appropriate name for this proposed rule would be the Community Disinvestment Act.
Taken together, the changes in this proposal would threaten billions of dollars in community
development. This rule proposal undercuts the work done by Congress this year in passing the
bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act to address some of the challenges in today's housing
market and to better support creation of affordable housing supply for all communities. This
proposal also runs counter to the Administration's own stated priority of supporting affordable
housing for Americans.
Woodstock Institute has selected a sample of high-priority problems in this proposed rule for our
comment letter. Many of our partner organizations have written more exhaustive letters, and we
echo their concerns as well.
Procedural Failings & Mischaracterization of Community Development Landscape
Before addressing the more specific definition and test-level changes in this proposed rule,
Woodstock Institute asserts that the procedural elements and framing of this proposal are deeply
flawed. Procedurally, there is a baseline failure to assess the potential impact of this rule. The
Agencies spend an awful lot of time in this proposed rule harping on the supposedly onerous

2

regulatory burden imposed by the CRA. We at Woodstock Institute find that positioning very
puzzling. At least to our knowledge, no failed bank has cited the costs associated with CRA
compliance as a reason for its downfall. On the contrary, banks currently operate under rules that
were put in place in 1995. If a bank hasn't figured out how to comply with those regulations by now
while the rest of its competitors have, that is a problem rooted in bank management, not community
development obligations.
Moreover, as the Agencies work to lighten regulatory burden under this proposed rule, they provide
no meaningful cost-benefit analysis when it comes to the communities served by the CRA. Any
effort to lessen regulatory burden must consider how effective and important those regulations are
to protecting consumers and serving the needs of communities. As indicated by the billions of
dollars of community development investments that would be threatened by this proposal, the harm
to communities would be catastrophic. Had the Agencies bothered to do a meaningful cost-benefit
analysis on this proposed rule, they would have found that the costs to community far outweigh the
supposed benefit to the regulated entities.
Instead, the proposed rule is insultingly dismissive of the needs of LMI communities served by the
CRA. The Agencies acknowledge a likely shift in CRA-motivated activity "away from certain CD
activities, in particular grants and deposit services," which are crucial to the broader community
development landscape. The Agencies also expect "downstream effects on LMI communities, small
business, small farms, nonprofit organizations, and other community development stakeholders, but
the direction and magnitude of those effects are uncertain" [emphasis added]. LMI communities, small
businesses, and small farms are the target beneficiaries of the CRA according to the statute. It is
appallingly irresponsible to propose, let alone implement, a rule without knowing whether it will
harm those populations and if so, how much. This failure to assess the potential cost to the target
beneficiaries of the law is arguably a direct violation of the law and an abdication of the Agencies'
duty to implement the laws passed by Congress.
Consistent with that disregard for the harm to communities, throughout this rule runs an
undercurrent of disdain for the community-based organizations and capacity-building nonprofits
that utilize CRA-eligible funding to serve the needs of LMI communities. The rule characterizes
them as "rent extractors" and "middlemen" diverting funds away from LMI communities,
demonstrating a fundamental misunderstanding of the infrastructure necessary to deploy community
development funds to individual consumers and communities.
Take housing counseling as just one example. In order to provide housing counseling services,
counselors must be trained and must be paid during their training. In order to train counselors, we
need organizations to offer training and pay their trainers. In order to keep pace with the evolving
homebuying landscape, trainings must be able to incorporate new information to protect hopeful
homebuyers and existing homeowners from novel predatory products that stand to strip them of
wealth rather than support wealth building through homeownership – this requires organizations
that can monitor the marketplace. In order to reach the consumers and households that would take
advantage of housing counseling, agencies must conduct outreach activities and have sufficient web

3

presence and technology to support client intake. And since not all consumers are web-savvy or
have reliable access to internet for virtual counseling, agencies must have a physical space to provide
in-person counseling as necessary.
To support all of these activities, housing counseling agencies rely on a diverse funding ecosystem,
of which grant funding from banks, both project-specific and general operating, is a key part. Banks
rely on housing counseling agencies for a pipeline of mortgage-ready borrowers; they are not
equipped to provide the level of individualized attention and detailed education that housing
counselors provide. It is counterproductive and destructive to limit the ways in which banks can
support the ecosystem of housing counseling and homebuyer education – yet that is exactly what
this proposed rule does with its 15% cap on overhead expenses and exclusion of general operating
funding from CRA consideration.
Asset Size Thresholds
The proposed changes to the asset size thresholds for each category of bank are drastic and
unreasonable. The Agencies propose changing the Large bank threshold from the current $1.6
billion to $10 billion in assets; and the current Intermediate Small bank threshold of $416 million to
a Medium bank threshold of $1 billion. What's more, the Agencies ask in the requests for feedback
whether $30 billion and $10 billion, respectively, would be more appropriate. Needless to say, that
larger change would be even worse for community development.
In Woodstock's home state of Illinois, this would result in approximately 50 of the 81 OCC and
FDIC-supervised Large banks moving down into the Medium category, thereby losing their small
business loan data reporting requirements and individual consideration of community development
lending and investments separately. An additional 68 Intermediate Small banks would move down
into the new Small category and lose CRA evaluation of their community development activities
entirely. At a time when policymakers in Congress and the Illinois legislature are working to
incentivize more community development, we in Illinois will see significantly fewer banks held
accountable to community development needs.
It is important to note that many rural and non-metropolitan areas of Illinois largely rely on banks
smaller than $10 billion in assets, as the biggest banks have mostly retreated from those markets.
This trend is not unique to Illinois. This proposed rule would result in the vast majority of such
banks serving rural and non-metropolitan areas either having limited CRA examination of
community development activities, or no CRA examination of community development activities at
all. These rural communities will have fewer tools to be able to advocate for their financial service
needs and, as the Agencies acknowledge in their so-called cost-benefit analysis, would likely see less
community development lending and investment from banks.
Small Business Lending Data
An additional consequence of raising the asset-size thresholds is a loss of publicly available data.
Only Large banks are required to report data on their small business lending under the CRA. This

4

data is not as geographically detailed as the mortgage data reported under the Home Mortgage
Disclosure Act (HMDA). But, until the data reporting requirements established under Section 1071
of the Dodd-Frank Act are finally implemented, this CRA data is the best data source available for
small business lending patterns. It forms the basis of Woodstock's small business lending data
analysis, including our series of "Patterns of Disparity" reports and our Community Lending Data
Portal. Raising the Large bank size threshold so dramatically would also severely limit the small
business lending data reported, and would impede communities' ability to advocate for their needs
as well as policymakers' ability to implement smart and efficient data-informed policy. It also hinders
banks' ability to compare themselves to peers, resulting in their inability to accurately assess market
share against similarly situated financial institutions.
Small Farm Lending Implications
The proposal introduces the concept of "Major Product Line" as a form of regulatory relief by
limiting the lending focus of CRA exams to the two loan product lines with the greatest volume. For
most financial institutions, mortgage and small business lending greatly outweigh small farm lending
activity, which means it would not be examined during a CRA exam. In a quick assessment of the
top small farm lenders using 2024 data, only John Deere Financial has more small farm loans
originated than small business loans. The rest show small farm lending activity as a miniscule
percentage of overall small business lending volume including but not limited to JPMorgan Chase
(2.2 million small business loans to 30 thousand small farm loans), Bank of America (500 thousand
small business loans to 3 thousand small farm loans), and Capital One (500 thousand small business
loans to 8 thousand small farm loans). The proposed Major Produce Line concept will hide small
farm lending from additional oversight, scrutiny, and transparency, and once again,
disproportionately harm rural communities. The downside for geographies where agriculture is an
important economic driver is not worth the virtually non-existent regulatory relief associated with
this specific proposal.
Weakening of Community Development Test Standards
The proposed rule weakens the importance and effectiveness of the Community Development
components of CRA exams. First, the proposed rule would allow Medium banks to receive a
Satisfactory rating on their exam even if they fail either the Lending Test or the Community
Development Test. Given that lending activities are more closely aligned with the most profit-driven
parts of a bank's business model, it is reasonable to conclude that it will be the Community
Development Test performance that will suffer under this structure. Failing the Community
Development Test should have a corresponding and appropriate negative impact on a bank's exam
score overall – but this proposed rule would disregard such a failure entirely.
Further, the proposed rule would set a disturbingly low bar for a presumptive satisfactory level of
community development lending and investment. Currently, banks may receive consideration on
their CRA exams for community development activities that do not fit neatly within their
assessment areas (AA), but still meaningfully address community needs. The proposed rule
formalizes this allowance, but takes it a step further by setting minimum inside-AA performance

5

levels, measured by percentage of Tier 1 capital invested or lent, to allow for consideration of
outside-AA activities. In practice, these will be viewed as presumptive Satisfactory levels of
community development lending and investment. The minimums designated in the proposal are a
fraction of typical bank performance. Furthermore, they are lower even than the standards that the
OCC set in its proposal last year for sample elective Satisfactory goals for a bank opting to operate
under a CRA strategic plan – goals that were themselves too low, as Woodstock outlined in our
comment letter on that proposal. Setting such low standards will inevitably result in a race to the
bottom among banks, and it will be LMI communities that suffer the consequences.
Conclusion
Operating a bank charter is a privilege. It is eminently reasonable to expect banks afforded such a
privilege to operate according to high standards in terms of customer service and community
reinvestment. CRA compliance is tied to FDIC insurance because, so long as taxpayers are serving
as the backstop for the safety of a bank's deposits, banks should be serving our communities well.
This rule would undo decades of progress in community development and would severely hamper
our economy's ability to address new community development challenges in the years to come. For
all the reasons summarized in this letter, Woodstock Institute demands that the Agencies discard
this rule proposal and continue on with the existing 1995 CRA regulations.
Should you have any questions regarding our letter, please contact jdoyle@woodstockinst.org.

Sincerely,
Woodstock Institute

B.​ Long-Term Economic Security and Safety for Survivors15

Approximately 84% of survivors report that not having enough money to support themselves or
their children is their biggest barrier to safety.16 The stark reality is that GBV is financially
devastating for survivors, making long-term safety incredibly expensive. The Center for
Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that the average lifetime cost of abuse for a
ciswoman survivor in the U.S. is a staggering $135,000.17 On top of this financial burden, 99%
of survivors are subjected to economic abuse18 – control over their financial resources – by a
harm-doer.19 Economic abuse tactics include harm-doers preventing survivors from going to
work, controlling or restricting survivors' access to cash, monitoring or withdrawing from
survivors' bank accounts, and incurring debt in survivors' names without their knowledge or
consent through credit cards or loans (i.e., coerced or fraudulent debt). In fact, up to 60% of
survivors lose their jobs as a result of GBV-related harm.20 Additionally, 58% of survivors report
that a harm-doer has monitored, accessed, withdrawn from, or otherwise controlled their bank
account;21 and at least 52% of survivors are subjected to coerced or fraudulent debt.22

figures in costs, no cash or income, fraudulent debt, damaged credit, and no further supports. As
such, survivors are 4 times more likely to have experienced material hardship compared to

C.​ The Federal Government Must Better Support Survivors

As GBV is a systemic economic issue, state regulators must support survivors in obtaining
long-term safety and financial freedom. In FreeFrom's first-of-its-kind National Survivor
Financial Security Policy Map and Scorecard, FreeFrom found that only 3 states currently
supports survivors' financial security and only 19 more are "taking steps" to do so,37 meaning
that there is a strong need for the federal government to implement policies that prioritize
survivors' financial security nationwide.

Despite the lack of adequate support, survivors trust the Federal Government, reporting it
among the safest, most convenient places for them to seek financial assistance.38
Accordingly, the Federal Government – including federal agencies – must address GBV beyond
traditional methods.

Given the financial devastation of GBV and economic abuse, federal agencies must support
survivors and their families in building the financial security necessary to heal, recover,
and stay safe. Advancing survivor-informed rulemaking is one crucial way to achieve this.

III.​
FREEFROM'S
COMMENTS
ON
OCC
AND
FDIC'S
PROPOSED
RULEMAKING ON THE CRA

FreeFrom appreciates the opportunity to respond to the invitation for comments from the OCC
and FDIC regarding regulatory changes to the CRA. The CRA was enacted nearly 50 years ago
to ensure banks and other financial institutions met the credit and investment needs of the
communities they serve, including those that have historically experienced barriers to savings
and financing due to unfair and discriminatory policies like redlining and gentrification. This
proposal follows guidance OCC issued last year on a simplified strategic plan process for
community banks to comply with the CRA,39 and subsequent litigation on the 2023 interagency
CRA rule.40

If implemented, this proposal could severely limit community bank investments, make banking
and other financial services less accessible, and keep nonprofit and community-based
organizations from providing necessary support. FreeFrom submits these comments to urge that
this rule be withdrawn, and ensure any future rulemaking reflects the unique financial and safety
needs of survivors and their families.

A.​ Importance of Financial Access for Survivors and Others Experiencing Systemic Harm

Access to savings and financing enables communities enduring the economic impacts of
systemic oppression to build financial stability and security. CRA-related individual and
community development programs have expanded access to homeownership, entrepreneurship,
health and education services for many borrowers and families who've historically been denied
access to the financial system and in turn, lifelong prosperity.

For survivors dealing with the economic consequences of GBV, this financial access is critical to
building the savings and credit necessary to get and stay safe. By weakening current protections,
this proposed rule risks exacerbating disparities that prevent survivors and their families from
securing lasting safety.

B.​ Impact of Proposed Changes

The agencies propose several changes to CRA rules, including:

1.​ Increasing the asset-size thresholds used by regulators to determine how financial
institutions are examined under federal banking laws.

The assets threshold for small banks would go up to nearly $1 billion (formerly,
less than $412 million); for intermediate banks (currently known as "intermediate
small"), the asset threshold would increase from $1 billion – $10 billion
(formerly, $412 million – $1.649 billion); and for large banks, the asset threshold
would exceed $10 billion (formerly, more than $1.649 billion). This would
reclassify over 1,200 banks, including 800 intermediate banks that would now be
considered small banks and over 400 large banks that would be newly treated as
intermediate banks.

This is significant because under current CRA rules, small banks are evaluated
only under the lending test, focused on individual and retail loans like mortgages,
car loans, credit cards, and business loans; and not the community development
test, which is focused on broader community investments like affordable housing,
community health and education services, and workforce development, used in
part to assess large and mid-sized banks. Large banks, by contrast, are evaluated
under a more robust framework that includes the lending test (for both retail and
community development loans); the service test, which assesses the availability
and accessibility of banking products, services, and branch networks; and the
investment test, which evaluates the scale and effectiveness of community
development financing, as well as technical assistance provided to local
organizations. Together, these form key components of CRA-bank evaluations
that help assess local economic growth and financial stability, especially for
communities experiencing systemic harm.

These threshold changes would result in hundreds of fewer banks having
community development obligations, reducing or eliminating financing for


community projects and services across the country. By the agencies' own
estimates, 79.8% of all banks subject to the CRA would now be classified as
small banks, risking over half a billion dollars annually in community
investments,41 including those tied to the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
(LIHTC), which banks rely on as part of their community development
activities.42 Raising the large bank threshold would also eliminate separate branch
evaluations – which review the performance of local bank offices – for these
newly classified intermediate banks. According to the National Community
Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC), more than 5,000 branches in low-and-moderate
income (LMI) census tracts (approximately 30% of all LMI-branches nationwide)
and over 4,000 branches in majority BIPOC census tracts (23% of all such
branches) would lose needed accountability measures.43 Without these branch
obligations, the number of local banking offices maintained by banks in
LMI-areas could decline drastically, furthering banking deserts – or areas without
a local bank – that exacerbate financial inequality.

For survivors, these changes would adversely affect their long-term safety and
well-being. Safe housing, affordable healthcare, and secure employment have
consistently ranked among survivors' top reported needs.44 Survivors have also
indicated that banks and other financial institutions are among the safest,
most convenient places for them to seek financial assistance45 – highlighting
the unique role they play in supporting survivors navigate the financial
devastation of harm, including through individual and community investments.
These changes could prevent survivors from accessing the necessary resources –
like safe bank accounts and affordable loans – to recover, heal, and rebuild.

2.​ Changing CRA grant requirements that would make it harder for nonprofit and
community-based organizations to meet individual and community needs,
including those of survivors.

Specifically, the proposal would direct CRA-grants be directly used for "a plan,
project, or initiative whose primary purpose is community development", which
would be narrowly limited to "affordable housing, civic assistance, economic
development, or revitalization and stabilization". It would also require large banks
to document that grant recipients' administrative costs don't exceed 15%.

This would restrict flexible operating funds for nonprofit and community-based
organizations to cover ongoing staff and tech costs to ensure grant compliance
and provide support to borrowers and communities. The strict overhead limit
would also make grants harder to access, potentially disincentivizing these groups
from seeking them. As a result, these changes could prevent organizations from

building and maintaining the necessary infrastructure to meet community needs,
including those of survivors. Given the high prevalence of GBV, this would leave

3.​ Reducing data collection and reporting requirements for banks.

Banks that move from large to intermediate banks would no longer be required to
collect and report data on certain small business loans, community-development
loans, and assessment areas. According to the NCRC, this would result in nearly
an 11% loss in reporting data.46

This would make it harder to understand and respond to community credit needs,
including those of survivors and others experiencing systemic harm. Without this
data, survivors and other changemakers – including legislators, financial
regulators, bank officials, and community advocates – have less insight into
community development financing to identify and address gaps, and ensure
lasting safety for all.

C.​ The Need to Strengthen Financial Protections

To address the enduring economic impacts of systemic oppression – including GBV – we must
pursue policies rooted in financial equity and inclusion. Accordingly, FreeFrom urges OCC and
FDIC to withdraw this proposed rule, and to meaningfully engage survivors and advocates in
future rulemaking.

IV.​
CONCLUSION

Financial insecurity is a top obstacle to survivors' safety. We cannot disrupt the cycle of GBV
in the U.S. unless we prioritize and protect survivors' financial security – and that includes
survivors' access to financial support and relief. It is imperative that federal agencies consider
the unique financial and safety needs of survivors and families, and safeguard their interests.

As a team of survivors, FreeFrom encourages OCC and FDIC to work with us to ensure every
survivor has access to the financial resources necessary to support individual, intergenerational,
and collective healing – including safe banking and community-driven financial investments.

If you have any questions or would like to discuss FreeFrom's comments further, please contact
FreeFrom's Systems Change Team at policy@freefrom.org. Thank you very much for your
consideration.

Sincerely,
FreeFrom

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
On behalf of the Hamilton County, Ohio, Board of County Commissioners, thank you for the
opportunity to comment on the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
regulations published August 12, 2026.
Hamilton County is the anchor county of the Cincinnati region, with a central city, older first-ring
suburbs, and neighborhoods with significant low- and moderate-income populations. The
county relies on partnerships with banks to finance affordable housing, small businesses,
community facilities, and economic development. These partnerships depend in large part on
the incentives the CRA creates.
The scale of those incentives is significant. In 2024 alone, the CRA encouraged more than $430
billion in loans and investments in low- and moderate-income communities nationwide. CRA-
motivated banks also provide more than 80 percent of the annual equity for Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit and New Markets Tax Credit projects, the primary tools for building
affordable housing and financing development in communities like ours. At a time when
Hamilton County faces rising housing costs and limited public resources, the CRA should
continue to strengthen these partnerships.
The county also invests directly in small businesses, and those investments depend on bank
credit to succeed. Since 2022, the county's Office of Small Business has provided one-on-one
support to more than 1,700 small businesses, most of them sole proprietors or firms with 10 or
fewer employees, including more than 500 businesses in 2025 alone. Through its Down
Payment Match Program, the county matched $200,000 in 2024 and 2025 to help four small
Todd B. Portune Center for County Government, 138 East Court Street, Room 603, Cincinnati, Ohio 45202
Phone: 513-946-4400 | www.hamiltoncountyohio.gov
 businesses buy their own buildings, helping unlock more than $7.9 million in total project
investment. In 2025, the county also awarded $250,000 in façade grants to improve business
districts in Cheviot, Wyoming, Colerain Township, and Springfield Township. County dollars are
designed to close gaps, not carry projects alone. These programs work only when local banks
are willing to finance the rest.
We urge you to ensure that the final rule does the following:
I. Maintain meaningful community development responsibilities for banks of all sizes. The
proposal would raise the large bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion in assets, leaving
only about 86 banks nationwide subject to the full lending, investment, and service tests. It
would also remove the community development test for banks between $412 million and $1
billion. Mid-size regional and community banks are often among the most active local partners
on affordable housing and small business projects, and they know local markets well. Reducing
their community development responsibilities would leave fewer partners available to finance
county priorities. We urge the agencies to retain the current large bank threshold or, at minimum,
adopt the alternative intermediate bank cap of $3.252 billion described in the proposal, and to
keep a community development test for banks between $412 million and $1 billion.
II. Preserve strong expectations for community development lending and investment. Loans
and investments are not interchangeable. Equity investments make Housing Credit and New
Markets Tax Credit projects possible in ways conventional lending cannot. Under the proposal,
an intermediate bank could receive an overall "satisfactory" rating based on its lending test
alone, even with weaker community development performance. This change would reduce the
importance of community development investment in a bank's rating. The final rule should keep
a balanced role for both lending and investment so that support for affordable housing and
economic development does not decline.
III. Protect grants and other support for nonprofit and community-based organizations.
Nonprofits in Hamilton County provide housing counseling, financial education, small business
assistance, food access, and other services that residents depend on, and many rely on bank
grants to operate. The proposal would limit CRA credit for grants to those used directly for
program activities and, for large banks, would exclude grants to recipients whose indirect costs
exceed 15 percent. Staff, facilities, and administrative capacity are what allow these
organizations to deliver services, particularly smaller organizations taking on difficult work.
These limits, along with new documentation requirements, could lead banks to reduce grant
support. We ask the agencies to set a more realistic limit or to recognize documented
administrative costs that directly support program delivery.
IV. Keep low- and moderate-income people and communities at the center of the CRA, as
intended by statute. The proposal would remove the requirement that economic development
financing create, preserve, or improve jobs for low- and moderate-income people or
communities. More than one in four Americans live in a low- or moderate-income census tract,
and the need for affordable housing and access to capital remains greatest there. Removing this

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

On behalf of The Alden Foundation, I am writing to comment on the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.  

The Alden Foundation is a developer of Affordable Independent Senior Living facilities.  At present, The Alden Foundation has 14 facilities in the greater Chicago, Illinois area, including adjoining suburban areas.  The 15th facility under construction will host a ribbon cutting in the spring of 2027.  Approximately 1,100 seniors reside in the 14 Alden Foundation facilities.

The demand for Affordable Senior Living is great.  When The Alden Foundation announces a project, and before a formal interest / waiting list is developed, many seniors are calling and request being considered for admission.  

CRA has played an important role in encouraging financial institutions to meet the credit and community development needs of the communities they serve.  Bank lending, investments, grants, and services supported through CRA help finance affordable housing, small business, community facilities, CDFIs, nonprofit organizations, and other activities that strengthen local economies.

We are concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule, particularly when considered together, could significantly reduce the incentives for banks to support these activities.  We urge your agencies to consider not only how individual provisions affect financial institutions, but also their cumulative impact on the communities, projects, and organizations that rely on CRA-incentivized capital and partnerships.

The OCC and FDIC proposal to reclassify banks with assets ranging from $1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks subject to the full CRA examination, including the investment test, could reduce competition in the Housing Credit equity market, leading to lower pricing on credits and less housing produced.

The intent of Congress in H. R. 1, through Affordable Housing initiatives in the approved legislation, was to increase Affordable Housing production, not decrease production, as could occur as a result of the proposed rules.

We appreciate your agencies’ efforts to provide greater clarity and proportionality within the CRA framework.  At the same time, changes intended to reduce regulatory burden should not inadvertently reduce the lending, investment, grants, and services that CRA helps bring to communities.

The Alden Foundation strongly encourages the OCC and FDIC to leave the banking thresholds as they currently stand under the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve – the third bank regulator – appears to be taking.  If the OCC and FDIC move forward with the changes to CRA regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for large banks and adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including rural and smaller markets.

We urge the OCC and FDIC to preserve strong incentives for the full range of community development activities and to consider the cumulative effects of the proposed changes on affordable housing, small businesses, CDFIs, nonprofit organization, and communities across the country.

Thank you very much for consideration of our comments.

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

East Bay Housing Organizations (EBHO) writes to you to oppose the proposed
amendments to the regulations guiding the implementation of the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) as published in the Federal Register on August 12, 2026.
By reducing accountability measures for financial institutions subject to the CRA,
eliminating requirements for financial institutions to offer certain community
services, and restricting the types of grants and donations that institutions may
count towards their CRA requirements, these proposed rule changes would seriously
undermine the impactful role the CRA has played in California and across the
country.

EBHO is the leading advocacy organization addressing issues of affordable housing
in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties in California. Since 1984, we have brought
together a coalition of low income community members, affordable housing
developers, nonprofit service providers, faith institutions, and community
organizations to advocate for the production and preservation of affordable housing,
along with protections that allow renters and homeowners to maintain their
housing. Our organization is also a member of the Rise Economy coalition and have
worked with them for many years to realize the promise of just banking in
California.


The CRA was created in 1977 to address the history of financial institutions
discriminating directly against low income communities and communities of color.
The CRA has been highly effective in ensuring that more affordable homes get built
in underserved communities and that low-income community members have access
to critical banking services. However, much work remains to be done. In the
absence of an effective CRA, our nation's affordable housing shortage will intensify,
inequality will deepen, and community organizations seeking to ameliorate these
issues will be undermined. Curtailing the CRA in the proposed manner at this
moment is "like throwing away your umbrella in a rainstorm because you're not
getting wet."

While the CRA addresses many types of community investments, EBHO is
particularly familiar with the role the CRA has played in supporting the development
of affordable housing in our region. The Bay Area's affordable housing crisis is
immediate and well documented. Close to half of all Bay Area residents spend more
than 30% of their income on rent or mortgage.1 A much higher proportion, 81%, of
low income residents in the Bay Area spend more than 30% of their income on
housing, and 53% of this group spends more than half of their income on housing.
The California Housing Partnership estimates that close to 1.3 million low income
households in the Bay Area do not have access to an affordable home.2

The CRA has played a key role in addressing the affordable housing crisis in our
region. Over the past 5 years, more than 58,000 affordable homes have been
constructed in the region, almost all of them supported by grants, loans, or
tax-credit investments made by financial institutions meeting CRA requirements.3
EBHO members who are affordable housing developers have consistently stated
that the majority, if not all, of their projects would be impossible to finance without
CRA-motivated donations and investments.

The proposed changes to the CRA regulations would drastically reduce the amount
of funding and investments available for affordable housing development in the Bay
Area and across the country. The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small,"
"Intermediate" and "Large" Banks, such that many banks will be subject to
substantially less CRA scrutiny and expectation to serve the community
development needs of their communities. According to National Community
Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks would see their
3 Ibid.
2 https://calhousingpartnership.org/housing-needs/
1 https://www.bayareaequityatlas.org/indicators/housing-burden

reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal.4 Twenty-five California banks
would shed their Community Development Test responsibilities entirely, and 45
California banks would no longer be subject to the Investment Test.5

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several two main
community development programs that contribute directly to financing affordable
housing: Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) and EQ2 equity equivalent
investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) that provide
small business lending including to Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take
property off of the speculative market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
housing.6 Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA motivated
banks.7 The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they adopt the
alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30 billion in
assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.8

Because a limited number of Low-Income Housing Tax Credits are available, when a
large number of financial institutions are motivated to invest in them (via the CRA)
the price of the investments goes up, which means affordable housing developers
are in a stronger position to finance their projects. The problem with banks not
being motivated to purchase LIHTCs is not only that fewer projects will receive

7 https://nextcity.org/urbanist-news/a-critical-few-weeks-ahead-for-community-development-finance
6 https://nationalmortgageprofessional.com/news/cra-proposal-could-reshape-bank-lending-and-affordable-housing-investment
5 Ibid.
4 https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending

financing, but also that the projects that do receive financing will be financed at a
lower rate.

At the same time that the proposed rules would make it more difficult for specific
affordable housing and community development projects to receive funding, they
make it more difficult for nonprofits providing other community benefits to receive

and mandating that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will

FDIC and OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank
grantmaking to nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller

In EBHO's case, donations and grants from CRA-motivated financial institutions are
critical to our organization's financial stability. While the donations we receive are
small compared to the investments banks make directly in affordable housing
developments, our work is critical in ensuring that those projects are actually
constructed. Our advocacy work ensures that local programs are in place to provide
gap funding and permit affordable housing in a timely manner. We ensure that
preservation and tenant protection programs exist to keep residents stably housed
once affordable housing is built. And we conduct educational campaigns which help
developers connect with financers and residents connect with affordable housing
that meets their needs. Undermining the funding an organization like ours may
receive is just as harmful to the community as cutting down the amount of LIHTC
investments an affordable housing developer is likely to see.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to allow for
meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of entities and
activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA was meant to
support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed, communities will

suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and CDFI support,
more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer community serving
nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and redlining with no
CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its purpose of
encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to
reconsider this proposal.

Sincerely,

Policy Manager, East Bay Housing Organizations​

To Whom It May Concern:

This letter is submitted on behalf of Woda Cooper Companies, Inc. to provide our comments on the joint notice
of proposed rulemaking to strengthen and modernize the regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA).

As a vertically integrated affordable housing developer, construction company, and property management firm
operating across 19 states, Woda Cooper Companies has a unique, ground-level perspective on how regulatory
frameworks dictate private capital flows. Ranked 7th in the nation among Developers and 17th among Owners
in 2025 by Affordable Housing Finance magazine, our portfolio includes more than 375 communities and 19,000
units operating or under construction. Today, we are proud to provide safe, high-quality affordable housing to more
than 30,000 people.

Because our business relies entirely on pairing federal incentives with private bank capital, we commend the
agencies' proposal to grant automatic CRA eligibility to Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) investments.
However, as an active practitioner, we are deeply concerned that several structural elements of this proposal will
severely restrict equity demand, increase our development gaps, and directly hinder our ability to build homes in
the 19 states we serve.

We urge the agencies to modify the proposed rule based on the following critical developer and owner insights:



614.396.3200
www.wodagroup.com
 .

1. The Real-World Reality of the Capital Stack: Separate Lending and Investment Tests Are Essential

As a developer, we emphasize that debt and equity are completely non-interchangeable components of affordable
housing finance. We strongly oppose consolidating the lending and investment tests into a single community
development financing test.

Housing Credit properties strictly limit rents to keep them affordable for low-income families. Because of these
restricted rents, our properties do not generate the substantial cash flows required to service heavy commercial
mortgages. Typically, our developments utilizing 9% Housing Credits can only sustain permanent debt covering 10
to 25 percent of total costs (rising to 15 to 30 percent for 4% credits). The remaining 60 to 80 percent of the capital
stack must be funded via private equity investments from banks.

By eliminating a standalone investment test, the proposal creates a dangerous regulatory loophole. Because
commercial loans are less complex, more liquid, and require half the Tier 1 capital reservation of equity under Basel
III, banks will naturally shift capital toward lending. Without robust equity pricing driven by a dedicated investment
test, developers like Woda Cooper will face severe financing gaps, stalling projects across our multi-state footprint.

2. Guarding Regional and Rural Supply: Adopt the $3.252 Billion Asset Threshold

Woda Cooper's extensive operational footprint covers a diverse array of urban, suburban, and rural communities.
We are particularly concerned about the proposal to raise the large bank asset threshold to $10 billion, which would
reclassify 376 financial institutions into the intermediate framework and exempt them from separate investment
metrics.

Data shows that regional and community banks under $10 billion contribute up to $2 billion in LIHTC equity over
a five-year period, with an astonishing one-third of that capital directly funding rural developments (compared
to an 8 percent industry average). In smaller and mid-sized markets across our 19-state operating area, these regional
institutions are frequently the primary or sole investors available to clear a project's equity needs.

•
Our Recommendation: To prevent creating severe affordable housing "deserts" in regional markets, the
agencies should adopt the inflation-adjusted $3.252 billion alternative threshold. This compromise
protects 63 percent of the at-risk bank investors.

•
Reject the $30 Billion Threshold: We strongly urge the regulators to discard the alternative $30 billion
threshold, which would put up to $4.5 billion in critical affordable housing equity at risk nationwide.

3. Ensure Equal 50/50 Test Weighting and Meaningful Thresholds

We recommend an equal 50/50 scoring split between the Retail and Community Development tests, replacing the
proposed 60/40 retail bias. A 60/40 formula allows financial institutions to secure a "Satisfactory" overall score
through retail channels while neglecting complex, high-impact community investments like affordable housing. A
bank should not be granted a satisfactory overall rating without achieving a satisfactory score on both components
independently.

4. Protect Income Mixing, Deep Affordability, and Property Sustainability

The final rule must explicitly name LIHTC equity investments as a positive impact review factor under the

 .

Woda Cooper Companies houses more than 30,000 Americans today, but the ongoing supply crisis demands that

the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
to reconsider provisions that would weaken accountability for meeting community credit
needs, diminish transparency, and undermine investment in affordable housing, small
businesses, and economically distressed communities.

FWCDC is a local nonprofit organization working to expand economic opportunity and
improve the quality of life for low- and moderate-income Texans. Our mission is:

•
To provide affordable housing options to the impoverished in the greater Central Texas
area through the construction, rehabilitation, and preservation of safe and sanitary
housing for low- to moderate-income individuals and families.
•
To combat the deterioration of the community and to contribute to its overall physical
and economic improvement.
•
To provide educational services related to affordable home purchasing, including
housing counseling regarding pre-purchase, post-purchase, foreclosure prevention,
financial literacy, and credit education.

We understand firsthand that community development depends on a functioning
partnership among banks, nonprofit organizations, public agencies, and mission-driven
The CRA is a foundational mechanism for encouraging banks to participate in these
partnerships and help meet the credit needs of the communities they serve.


 T 512.385.1500 • F 512.385.1503 • 2200 E. MARTIN LUTHER KING JR. BLVD, SUITE 300 • AUSTIN, TX 78702
WWW.FRAMEWORKSCDC.ORG







A HUD-Approved Housing Counseling Agency

Although we support reasonable efforts to simplify regulations and provide greater clarity to
financial institutions, the proposed rulemaking is not reasonable, and regulatory efficiency
must not come at the expense of meaningful community investment and public accountability.

I. The CRA Must Continue to Promote Meaningful Investment in Affordable Housing and
Community Development

Affordable housing remains a critical need across Texas. CDCs develop and preserve
affordable rental housing, support homeownership, rehabilitate deteriorating properties, and
revitalize neighborhoods where private capital alone frequently fails to meet community
needs. These activities often depend on complex financing structures that combine bank
loans, grants, philanthropic resources, public funding, and specialized financing from CDFIs.
The CRA helps encourage banks to participate in these transactions by recognizing the value
of lending, investments, and services that support community development. Weakening that
incentive could make it more difficult for nonprofit developers to assemble viable financing
packages, increase the cost of affordable housing production, and limit the ability of
communities to preserve existing affordable units.

FWCDC is particularly concerned that changes intended to narrow or redirect qualifying
community development activities could create uncertainty for banks and their nonprofit
partners. Banks need clear, predictable rules that recognize the full range of legitimate
community development activities, including affordable housing development and
preservation, rehabilitation of distressed neighborhoods, and financing for community facilities
serving low-income populations.

We urge the agencies to preserve broad, practical eligibility for activities that demonstrably
benefit low- and moderate-income communities. Any qualifying-activity framework should be
transparent, sufficiently flexible to accommodate local needs, and responsive to the realities of
financing affordable housing and community development projects.

II. Excluding Deposit Services Would Overlook an Important Dimension of Community
Reinvestment

The proposed rule would narrow the range of retail banking services considered in CRA
evaluations by excluding deposit services. FWCDC opposes this approach. Access to safe,
affordable banking is an important component of economic stability. Low-income households
and small businesses need accessible deposit accounts to receive income, save for
emergencies, manage expenses, and establish financial relationships that can support future
borrowing.

In communities where traditional banking access is limited, the availability and affordability of
deposit services can be particularly important. Although deposit services are not a substitute

providing meaningful access to basic banking services in the neighborhoods they serve.

FWCDC urges the agencies to retain a comprehensive assessment of retail banking services,
including deposit access, affordability, accessibility, and responsiveness to the needs of low-
and moderate-income communities. CRA evaluations should encourage banks to expand
responsible banking relationships, not limit the definition of community service to a narrower
set of activities.

FWCDC is concerned about the proposal to exempt banks with $10 billion or less in assets
from certain CRA data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements. We recognize
that smaller institutions have fewer resources to devote to compliance. However, reducing
reporting requirements without adequate safeguards could make it harder for regulators and
the public to determine whether community credit needs are being met. TACDC and our
members do not want to see any changes to the current bank asset-size classifications.
Reliable data help identify underserved neighborhoods, evaluate lending patterns, measure
access to credit, and determine whether community development investments are reaching
the people and places with the greatest need. For nonprofit housing developers and CDFIs,
transparent information about lending and investment patterns can also support effective
partnerships with financial institutions.

Texas includes large metropolitan areas alongside rural communities, smaller cities, and
regions experiencing persistent economic challenges. Aggregate information can obscure
significant differences in access to capital within these areas. Without appropriate data, gaps
in mortgage lending, small-business financing, and community development investment may
be more difficult to identify and address.

IV. Protect the Role of CDFIs and Community-Based Lending Partnerships

CDFIs are essential partners in expanding access to capital for small businesses,
entrepreneurs, and communities that are underserved by conventional financial institutions.
FWCDC members use specialized lending, technical assistance, and local knowledge to
support businesses that create jobs, strengthen neighborhood economies, and provide goods
and services in underserved areas.

 T 512.385.1500 • F 512.385.1503 • 2200 E. MARTIN LUTHER KING JR. BLVD, SUITE 300 • AUSTIN, TX 78702
WWW.FRAMEWORKSCDC.ORG



A HUD-Approved Housing Counseling Agency

These institutions frequently collaborate with banks to structure financing, extend credit to
borrowers with limited collateral or credit histories, and support projects that may not proceed
through conventional underwriting alone. CRA incentives can encourage banks to provide
loans, investments, and other support that enable these partnerships to operate effectively.

The agencies should ensure that the regulations recognize the community development value
of financing delivered through qualified CDFIs and other mission-driven intermediaries. The
proposed rules do not accomplish this. Community development lending should not be
evaluated so narrowly that it discourages banks from partnering with organizations that
possess specialized expertise and established relationships with underserved borrowers.
The final rule should clearly recognize qualifying loans, investments, and other eligible support
that help CDFIs finance affordable housing, small businesses, and community revitalization. It
should also preserve a workable process for confirming eligibility so that banks can make
informed commitments without unnecessary uncertainty or delay.

V. Ensure Community Development Grants Reach Communities Without Undermining
Effective Organizations

FWCDC supports appropriate safeguards to ensure that community development grants
benefit their intended recipients and produce meaningful community outcomes. However,
rules governing grants and donations should recognize that effective nonprofit organizations
require qualified staff, sound financial management, compliance systems, and other
reasonable operating resources to deliver those outcomes.

Restrictions that fail to distinguish between excessive administrative costs and necessary
organizational capacity will weaken the organizations responsible for delivering affordable
housing, small-business financing, and essential services. Smaller community-based
organizations will be especially vulnerable to rules that impose rigid requirements without
accounting for differences in organizational size, mission, and operating model.
We encourage the agencies to adopt clear, practical standards that prevent misuse of grant
funding while recognizing reasonable administrative and operational expenses necessary to
achieve community development objectives. The focus should remain on measurable
community benefits, sound stewardship, and effective delivery of services to underserved
populations.

WWW.FRAMEWORKSCDC.ORG



A HUD-Approved Housing Counseling Agency

VI. Recommendations and Conclusion

FWCDC respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to revise the proposed rule to:

1. Preserve strong CRA accountability by ensuring that regulatory simplification does not
diminish banks' responsibility to meet the credit needs of their entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
2. Retain consideration of deposit services as part of a comprehensive evaluation of
access to affordable, responsible retail banking.
3. Maintain meaningful data transparency through proportionate reporting requirements
and appropriate safeguards that allow regulators and the public to identify unmet credit
needs and disparities in access to capital.
4. Protect community development financing partnerships by recognizing qualifying
activities conducted through CDFIs, CDCs, and other mission-driven organizations that
serve low-income communities and small businesses.
5. Support effective nonprofit capacity by ensuring that grant and donation standards
distinguish necessary operating expenses from improper diversion of funds.
6. Provide clear and inclusive qualifying-activity standards that recognize the diversity
of affordable housing, community revitalization, and economic development needs across
Texas.

The Community Reinvestment Act is more than a regulatory framework. It is an important
public policy tool for encouraging the financial resources of the banking system to help meet
community needs. For Texas communities facing housing shortages, limited access to small-
business capital, and persistent economic disparities, a strong and effective CRA remains
essential.

FWCDC urges the OCC and FDIC to reconsider the proposed changes identified in this letter
and adopt a final rule that preserves meaningful incentives for community investment,
supports effective partnerships between banks and community-based organizations, and
maintains transparency and accountability for the communities the CRA was enacted to serve.

Thank you for considering our comments and for the opportunity to represent the perspectives
of Texas's community development sector.


Sincerely,


Joyce McDonald

new documentation requirements to demonstrate compliance. A 15% cap on overhead and administrative costs

Happen Bank, National Association ("Happen Bank," "we," or "our") respectfully submits this

Background

The CRA, passed in 1977, generally requires insured depository institutions to engage in investment,
lending, and service activities that help meet the credit needs of their designated assessment
areas—particularly low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities and small businesses and farms,
insured depository institutions receive a rating from the banking regulators based on their
performance. The first set of regulations to implement the CRA was issued in 1978 and then revised
in 1995 and 2005. In 2020-2025, the agencies attempted, in various proposals and rules to modernize
CRA regulations.

The banking landscape has fundamentally evolved since the 1995 CRA framework was adopted.
Digital banks now supplement traditional branch-based banking by serving millions of consumers
nationwide through digital channels and business models, expanding access to financial services in
underserved markets and underbanked consumers. A framework that treats all banks identically —
regardless of their business model or where their customers reside — risks creating misaligned
incentives that prioritize regulatory compliance over community impact. The Proposed Rule offers
an opportunity to strengthen the CRA by recognizing how digital banks serve LMI consumers
nationwide, well beyond the reach of their current assessment areas.
The Happen Bank Perspective

Happen Bank supports several key elements of the Proposed Rule that represent meaningful
improvements to the existing CRA framework. Specifically, we commend the agencies' efforts to
enhance strategic plan flexibility by (i) permitting banks greater discretion in structuring measurable
goals, (ii) allowing for the combination of lending, investments, grants, and services within a single
plan, and (iii) establishing a more collaborative pre-filing process. These improvements recognize
that not all banks operate through identical business models and that CRA effectiveness depends on
evaluation frameworks tailored to institutional capacity and community needs.

We ask the agencies to preserve the strategic plan option and limited purpose bank designation as
viable, flexible, evaluation pathways and to ensure that performance context continues to inform
CRA evaluations. If the agencies nevertheless eliminate the limited purpose designation — a change

We also support the Proposed Rule's emphasis on clarity regarding qualifying community

appropriately concentrates examination resources on activities that meaningfully reflect a bank's
service to its communities. We believe these reforms — if properly implemented and combined with

However, we are concerned that certain provisions in the Proposed Rule, though seemingly narrow,
