To Whom It May Concern,
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies")
promulgated a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the
regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). CRA has helped create a
durable incentive for banks to provide loans, investments, grants, and services in
communities that have historically lacked access to capital.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support
some of the agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase
responsible capital in underserved communities. However, we have significant
concerns with the increases in the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on operating grants. We also have concerns
with several interacting provisions that could further weaken community development
incentives that will undoubtedly impair the flow of much needed capital in the most
underserved communities.
Founded in 1985, BlueHub Loan Fund, Inc. is a certified community development
finance institution (CDFI) with an A+ rating from S&P Global Ratings, working in 25
states, Washington, DC and Puerto Rico. In addition to our core markets in New
England, the East Coast and Mid-Atlantic states, we work in strategic locations across
the country where partners are seeking additional mission-driven capital. We are a
nonprofit CDFI that provides flexible, often first-in financing for affordable housing,
charter schools, early education and childcare centers, community health centers,
other community facilities, and small businesses, primarily in low- and moderate-
income (LMI) neighborhoods. We frequently finance projects at stages where
conventional lenders are not yet willing to participate, such as acquisition and
predevelopment.


2 | P a g e

Banks are critical partners in our work. Over the last 40 years with support from our
bank partners, BlueHub Loan Fund has deployed more than $1.5 billion in LMI
communities. This has helped to support the creation or preservation of more than
39,100 affordable homes and 37,800 jobs and to serve over 59,000 children at high-
quality schools and early education facilities and 294,900 patients at community
health centers, with most of the financing deployed in LMI communities.
We have strong relationships with banks, some for multiple decades, that provide us
with senior and subordinated debt capital. These partnerships provide approximately
53% of our total borrowed capital, enabling us to manage our currently $350 million
portfolio of loans that support over 150 community development projects.

These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital
and resources to CDFIs, banks rely on CDFIs like BlueHub Loan Fund to reach
underserved communities, develop borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers.
Affordable housing developers, charter schools, and community health centers that
first borrow from BlueHub Loan Fund, often when no bank will lend for their project,
will frequently be able to obtain conventional bank financing for later projects once
they have established a track record. Our unsecured predevelopment loans are one
example. We recently made a $1.75 million predevelopment loan to a longtime
nonprofit partner to cover architectural, legal, and engineering costs for a mixed-
income, mixed-use development in Boston's Roxbury neighborhood with 64 affordable
rental units and 42 affordable homeownership units. Capital at this early stage, when
bank financing is rarely available, positions projects to secure follow-on construction
financing, often from banks. The CRA has long helped create the incentives for banks
to build and sustain these relationships, strengthening the broader community
development ecosystem. We are therefore concerned that several provisions in the
proposal could weaken these incentives, reducing bank engagement with CDFIs and
ultimately the flow of capital to the communities we serve.
Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development
Finance: Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 1–3
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets,
intermediate banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large
banks as institutions with more than $10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face
a separate community development test as intermediate small banks would become
small banks and lose that requirement. Another approximately 400 banks that are
currently evaluated as large banks would become intermediate banks, losing the
separate large-bank lending, investment, and service tests and many associated
data-reporting requirements.
In Massachusetts, where we are headquartered, it is estimated that 23 banks,
comprising 24% of banks with community development obligations, would no longer
be required to reinvest in local community development projects such as affordable
housing, small business support, workforce development, community healthcare and
education services. Twenty-seven (27) banks, comprising 50% of all large banks,
would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing lending, investment, and
services in LMI census tracts across Massachusetts.

3 | P a g e

The consequences may be especially significant in smaller markets, where there are
fewer financial institutions and fewer alternative sources of capital. Much of our
lending is in smaller cities and older industrial communities, such as Massachusetts'
Gateway Cities, where a few regional and community banks often account for most of
the locally available community development capital. In these communities, the loss
of even one or two CRA-motivated bank partners can materially affect whether
projects are financed. For communities with fewer financial institutions and fewer
sources of private capital to begin with, losing even a handful of CRA-motivated
lenders and investors could have an outsized effect on whether affordable housing,
small businesses, and community facilities get financed.
Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance
These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development
performance is evaluated and therefore affect the strength of banks' incentives to
engage in community development. The agencies acknowledge in the proposal that
when banks become subject to a CD test under the current framework, the explicit
evaluation of their CD activities typically results in banks adjusting their CRA
programs.
Banks moving down asset sizes and losing incentives for community development
activities would have a direct impact on our partnerships. We estimate that $17
million of our senior and subordinated debt capital would be at risk from our bank
funders that are currently considered large or intermediate that would transition into
lower asset categories. This represents critical risk aligned capital in our funding
structure.
For example, below-market capital from a national bank partner helped BlueHub Loan
Fund finance two health centers. One is a $2.29 million participation to expand a
Federally Qualified Health Center in rural Maine, where more than half of patients
have incomes at or below 200% of the federal poverty level. Another is an $8.1
million construction loan for a new health center in a medically underserved
community in Indiana that will double its capacity to more than 16,000 patients a
year. Bank capital makes up about 53% of our borrowed capital. Even a modest bank
commitment goes far to enable our lending and losing even one bank partner could
reduce our capacity to finance projects like these. CDFIs frequently rely on regional
and community banks for patient debt, deposits, investments, lines of credit, grants,
and other forms of capital that allow us to reach borrowers and projects that
conventional financial institutions cannot efficiently serve directly.
Misalignment with Congressional Priorities on Affordable Housing and New
Markets Tax Credit (NMTC)
The change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) which are two
bipartisan, popular federal tax tools with a long track record of success in our
communities. While Congress expanded LIHTC and made NMTC permanent, the
proposal undermines these important investment tools.

LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the
standalone investment test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-

4 | P a g e

weighted component of their CRA evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving
banks into the lower size category would mean these transitioned banks would only
be subject to a diluted evaluation that considers all community development (CD) in
one test. This means a bank may have greater ability to emphasize CD lending rather
than maintain the same level of LIHTC or NMTC investment because investment
performance no longer receives a separate rating. Through this weakened regulatory
incentive, bank demand for these investments would decrease.

Our organization frequently provides early stage or bridge financing for affordable
housing and economic development projects that require LIHTC or NMTC investments
to be financially feasible. Banks are primary investors in these tax credits, and their
participation in these credit markets is a material driver of credit pricing and deal
feasibility. A reduction of bank investments in these credits will, inevitably, jeopardize
these transactions. The recent improvements of the LIHTC program via the OBBBA
has demonstrated the impact of low tax credit demand by increasing the supply of
credits in response to the nationwide affordable housing crisis. The resulting gap
between tax credit supply and investor demand has resulted in decreased pricing,
increased funding gaps and inability to attract investors, particularly in areas that do
not have high volumes of deposits from CRA-regulated banks.
Recommendation
For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds
and reject all alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised
for consideration in Question 1). The current thresholds are already annually indexed
to CPI-W, so they are not beholden to 1995 asset levels. Moreover, the justification of
"restoring proportionality to 1995" that the agencies use in the proposal does not
adequately explain why raising asset thresholds better serve the statutory intent of
the CRA—which is to ensure that credit needs of LMI communities are met. For the
small bank threshold, the proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the
number of banks such that nearly 80% of all banks would be considered small, similar
to what it was in 1995. While that's true, by the same logic, nearly 20% of banks in
1995 were considered large whereas under the proposed large bank threshold, only a
little over 2% of all banks would be considered large. Instead, the agencies selectively
use total banking industry share to justify the large bank threshold saying large banks
would under this proposal, and similar to 1995 cover about 85% of all total bank
industry's assets. Matching a 1995 distribution through either method does not
necessarily demonstrate that the resulting categories are appropriate for the modern
banking system. The industry has consolidated dramatically, bank business models
and geographic reach have changed. Banks with several billion dollars in assets today
may have substantially greater lending, investment, data, and operational capacity
than institutions that were treated as small or intermediate, three decades ago. The
fact that assets happen to sit above a chosen threshold does not by itself establish
that banks below that threshold should lose the separate investment/service tests or
associated data requirements.


5 | P a g e

Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C,
"Community Development Activities — CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants
which: 1) requires a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a
program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of community development; 2)
for large banks, caps grant recipient's indirect administrative costs to 15%; 3)
requires that large banks obtain documentation from grant recipients including
written commitments regarding use of funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form
990s, and operating and program budgets. We also strongly oppose the alternative
contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and donations from CRA
consideration entirely.
While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants
meaningfully benefit communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of
effective grantmaking and misunderstand the role that flexible operating support
plays in community development finance. For CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, risk management, data systems, financial management,
technical assistance, and product development are not ancillary to community
development. They are the infrastructure that makes community development lending
possible.
Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of
CRA eligibility. An organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate
proxy for community impact. Costs vary depending on an organization's size,
geography, product mix, regulatory obligations, technical-assistance model, and
populations served. The cap could disproportionately affect small and emerging
CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar loans, organizations providing
intensive borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new products or entering
underserved markets and organizations making necessary investments in technology,
compliance, data, and risk management.
Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-
building grants as currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should
encourage flexibility for banks to provide the form of support that best responds to
the identified community needs instead of imposing undue compliance burdens.
Interacting Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community
Development Incentives
Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance:
Section IV.B, "Performance Tests — Intermediate Bank Ratings"
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at
least a Satisfactory rating on both its lending test and its CD test to receive an overall
Satisfactory rating. The proposal would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test
rating but would allow lending performance to compensate for weaker CD
performance.

6 | P a g e

This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset
thresholds, which would move hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-
bank framework into the intermediate category. If weak CD performance does not
prevent an overall Satisfactory rating, banks may have less regulatory incentive to
make CDFI loans and investments, provide grants, or undertake other community
development activities. We urge the agencies to retain a requirement that
intermediate banks demonstrate at least Satisfactory CD performance to receive an
overall Satisfactory rating.
In our experience, the community development component of a bank's CRA
evaluation is a key driver of bank engagement with CDFIs. Bank partners regularly
cite their community development test performance when deciding whether to renew
or expand commitments to BlueHub Loan Fund. Over the last 5 years, BlueHub Loan
Fund has secured and renewed over $200 million in CRA-motivated lending capital to
support our community development financing activities.
Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section
IV.E, "Consideration of Community Development Activities — CD Activities
Outside Assessment Areas"; proposed § __.13(e); Question 34
We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with
significant unmet needs but relatively few bank assessment areas. Greater geographic
flexibility could be particularly beneficial for reaching CRA deserts.
BlueHub Loan Fund serves communities across the Southeast in Mississippi,
Louisiana, Alabama, and Tennessee, where few banks maintain branches or
assessment areas and where CRA-motivated capital can be difficult to attract, even
though credit needs are substantial.
However, flexibility should supplement rather than displace CD activity in banks' own
assessment areas. The agencies are considering both quantitative and qualitative
approaches for determining when a bank has sufficiently served its assessment areas
to receive consideration for outside-Assessment Area activity.
With respect to Question 34, we support greater geographic flexibility where it can
help direct CRA-motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other
underserved areas that may fall outside traditional assessment areas. However, that
flexibility should only become available after a bank has demonstrated meaningful
community development performance within its own assessment areas.
We are concerned that the quantitative standard proposed under Option 1 is too low
to meet that objective. For large banks, the proposal would allow outside-
assessment-area consideration once a bank reaches 0.625% of allocated Tier 1
capital in community development loans and 0.625% in community development
investments and grants. The agencies themselves explain that these thresholds
generally reflect the minimum level of activity needed to avoid a "Needs to Improve"
rating and are not, by themselves, sufficient to demonstrate satisfactory community
development performance.

7 | P a g e

Recent analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) further
illustrates the gap between the proposed thresholds and current bank activity. Among
69 large OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks analyzed by NCRC, current annual
assessment-area community development lending, investments, and grants totaled
approximately $102 billion. Applying the proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital thresholds to
those same institutions yielded a benchmark of approximately $14.8 billion—roughly
85% below current activity. NCRC also found median assessment-area community
development lending equal to 6.83% of Tier 1 capital and median qualified
investments and grants equal to 3.5%, both substantially above the proposed
0.625% benchmarks.
A standard intended to determine when a bank has adequately served its own
communities should therefore be calibrated to meaningful, satisfactory community
development performance—not merely the minimum necessary to avoid a failing
rating. We encourage the agencies to adopt a more rigorous standard that considers
both the level of activity and its responsiveness to identified community needs. We
further caution against allowing a broadly defined "substantially met" standard to
weaken this safeguard. Any exception should be narrowly tailored to circumstances in
which a documented lack of community development opportunities or other
performance-context factors explain the shortfall, rather than simply allowing weaker
community development performance in individual assessment areas to be offset by
activity elsewhere.
Allocation of CD activities across assessment areas: Section IV.E, "CD
Activities in Assessment Areas, Assessment Area Allocation, Assigning
Assessment Area Weights"
We support greater flexibility in allocating CD activities that benefit or serve multiple
assessment areas. This could better accommodate statewide and regional CDFIs
whose community impact is not accurately represented by the physical location of
their headquarters.
For example, BlueHub Loan Fund has loans in more than 25 states, Washington, D.C.,
and Puerto Rico with 79% of our $350 million outstanding portfolio deployed in states
other than where we are headquartered in Massachusetts. Assigning an entire bank
investment to our headquarters location would not accurately represent the
communities benefiting from the capital.
Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community
Development Finance
Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD
Loans"; Question 8
We strongly support providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain
outstanding from prior evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-
period investments. Community development borrowers frequently need long-term,
patient financing. CRA should encourage banks to structure loans around community
needs rather than examination cycles.

8 | P a g e

With respect to Question 8, we recommend evaluation period-based consideration
because it better recognizes patient, long-term CD financing and provides a more
representative measure of capital committed throughout the CRA examination period
than an annual snapshot and brings parity to the treatment of loans and investments.
The agencies should base consideration on the average outstanding balance or
otherwise account for both the amount and duration of the outstanding exposure and
should treat repeated renewals of substantially the same loan as a single exposure.
Conclusion
CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the
communities we serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and
flexibility. Modernization, however, should result in more responsible capital reaching
communities with unmet credit needs, as the CRA statute was intended.
We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to:
1. Retain the current asset thresholds, which sustain bank investment in CDFIs
and in LIHTC and NMTC projects, and reject the higher alternatives under
consideration;
2. Withdraw the proposed restrictions on community development grants and
preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building
support;
3. Retain the requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate at least
Satisfactory community development performance; and
4. Adopt a more rigorous standard for out-of-assessment-area consideration.
We support the proposals to consider prior-period community development loans and
to provide greater flexibility in allocating activities across assessment areas.
Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the
proposed changes on the communities we serve.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

The Massachusetts Housing Partnership (MHP), a public nonprofit organization founded in 1985, works
with communities to create innovative policy and financing solutions that provide affordable homes and
better lives for the people of Massachusetts. For over 40 years, MHP has partnered with policymakers,
municipalities, housing developers, and the banking industry to expand affordable housing opportunities
across the Commonwealth. MHP's SoftSecond and ONE Mortgage programs have helped more than
26,400 low- and moderate-income Massachusetts households purchase their first homes, leveraging
more than $5.4 billion in private mortgage financing. MHP has also provided over $2.2 billion in
financing for more than 33,000 multifamily apartments across Massachusetts. The overwhelming
majority of this financing has been provided by Massachusetts banks. As a result, changes that affect
banks' incentives to engage in community development lending and investment have direct implications
for MHP's ability to support affordable housing and homeownership opportunities across the
Commonwealth. Our work depends heavily on partnerships with banks regulated by the OCC, FDIC, and
Federal Reserve, and we have firsthand experience with the role CRA plays in supporting affordable
housing, community development, and homeownership opportunities throughout Massachusetts.

We appreciate the agencies' efforts to modernize CRA regulations, provide greater clarity, and reduce
unnecessary regulatory burden. Several elements of the proposal could improve CRA administration,
including clearer standards for qualifying activities, CRA consideration for community development



loans originated in prior examination periods that remain outstanding, and greater transparency
regarding CRA eligibility determinations. We also support maintaining incentives for community
development activities beyond a bank's immediate assessment area when local needs are being met.
These targeted improvements can strengthen CRA implementation while preserving flexibility for banks
and community development partners.

At the same time, we are concerned that several proposed changes, taken together, could substantially
reduce the incentives that currently drive affordable housing and community development investment.

CRA remains one of the nation's most successful mechanisms for channeling private capital into low-
and moderate-income communities. In 2024 alone, CRA incentivized more than $430 billion in loans and
investments benefiting low- and moderate-income households and communities. CRA-motivated
investors provide the majority of equity supporting both the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit and New
Markets Tax Credit programs, making CRA a foundational component of the nation's affordable housing
and community development finance system.

Our primary concern is the proposal to raise asset thresholds and reduce the number of institutions
subject to meaningful community development responsibilities. Banks below $30 billion in assets
account for more than one-third of community development lending nationally and a majority of
community development loans by count. In many smaller markets and rural communities, these
institutions are among the most important sources of affordable housing and community development
financing.

The implications are particularly significant in Massachusetts. Based on recent analyses of the proposal's
impact on Massachusetts institutions, 39 of the 62 Massachusetts-based banks regulated by the OCC or
FDIC would face reduced CRA obligations if the proposal is adopted. Twenty-one banks currently
evaluated as large institutions would be reclassified as intermediate banks, and eighteen additional
institutions would move from intermediate-bank status to small-bank status and no longer receive a
separate community development evaluation. Only two Massachusetts-based OCC- or FDIC-regulated
institutions would remain subject to the large-bank CRA framework.

We are also concerned that the proposal would both expand the number of institutions evaluated under
the intermediate-bank framework and reduce the importance of community development performance
within that framework. Community development lending, investments, grants, and services are not
incidental activities. They are central to financing affordable housing, supporting community
development financial institutions and community development corporations, strengthening nonprofit
capacity, and addressing unmet credit needs. An institution should not be able to achieve a satisfactory
CRA rating while demonstrating weak performance in community development activities that are
fundamental to the purposes of CRA. The agencies should maintain meaningful community
development expectations for intermediate banks and continue to require satisfactory performance in
both lending and community development.

For Massachusetts, these changes would have direct implications for housing production. CRA remains
one of the most important drivers of bank participation in LIHTC investments and community



development lending. Reduced CRA incentives could translate into lower demand for affordable housing
investments, weaker pricing for housing credit equity, and greater reliance on scarce public subsidy
resources. The result would likely be fewer affordable housing developments moving forward at a time
when policymakers at every level of government are seeking to increase housing production and
improve housing affordability. Any changes that reduce incentives for affordable housing investment
warrant substantial caution.

We are similarly concerned about proposed restrictions on grants to nonprofit organizations. Flexible
operating support often allows nonprofit organizations, community development corporations, and
CDFIs to provide the technical assistance, borrower support, project development, housing counseling,
and organizational infrastructure that make successful lending and investment possible. More restrictive
standards and documentation requirements could discourage support for the very organizations that
help create community development opportunities and lending pipelines. Smaller organizations serving
rural and underserved communities may be particularly affected.

Finally, MHP remains concerned about the prospect of divergent CRA frameworks among the federal
banking agencies. Because the Federal Reserve is not participating in this proposal, adoption of
substantially different regulatory approaches could result in institutions serving the same communities
being evaluated under different federal standards. This concern is especially significant in
Massachusetts, where OCC-, FDIC-, and Federal Reserve-regulated institutions often compete directly in
the same markets and participate in the same affordable housing and community development
transactions. The existence of separate federal frameworks, layered on top of Massachusetts CRA
requirements for state-chartered institutions, would introduce additional complexity for banks,
regulators, and community stakeholders. MHP has long supported the development of a consistent
interagency CRA framework and continues to believe that uniformity among the federal banking
agencies should remain an important objective.

MHP supports thoughtful modernization of CRA regulations that improves clarity, transparency, and
administration. However, we encourage the agencies to revise the proposed rule to preserve
meaningful community development responsibilities for banks of all sizes, maintain strong community
development expectations for intermediate banks, preserve flexible support for nonprofit and
community development partners, and work toward a consistent interagency CRA framework.

Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

Sincerely,



Mark Curtiss
Managing Director

RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations – A Proposed Rule by the Comptroller of the Currency
and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (Docket ID: OCC-2026-0694 / RIN 3064-AG31)

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould:

The National Center for American Indian Enterprise Development (The National Center) – a 501(c)(3) non-profit
organization with more than 50 years of experience assisting Tribal Nations, Alaska Native Corporations, their
enterprises, and businesses owned by Native people with advancing their business, economic, and community
development priorities – welcomes this opportunity to provide comments to the FDIC and OCC regarding their
Proposed Rule governing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

For decades, The National Center has assisted hundreds of Tribal Nations and thousands of Native people
pursuing commercial business, government contracts, and financing to support their endeavors. We have
worked and advocated for increasing the flow of capital to Indian country to support business and economic
development and growth and catalyze domestic and international commerce in and with Native communities.
The National Center also operates the largest Apex Accelerator serving Indian Country, enhancing the ability
of Native-owned businesses across 33 states to compete for federal contracts through no-cost guidance,
training, and technical assistance. Recently, we established Native Edge Finance, an emerging Native
community development financial institution (CDFI), to address the acute financing gap facing Native
businesses and communities across the United States.

The CRA: A Five-Decade Record of Failing Tribal Nations and Native Communities

Congress passed the CRA in 1977 to encourage banking institutions to serve the credit needs of the communities
in which they operate, specifically low- and moderate-income areas and populations. The Act also aimed to curb
discriminatory credit and lending practices against those populations, a practice commonly known as "redlining."
With many Native communities located in the poorest parts of the country, and much of our Native populations


deemed to be low or moderate income, CRA implementation should have significantly enhanced the ability of
Tribal Nations, their enterprises, Native-owned small businesses, Native homebuyers, and Native consumers to
access capital and credit through CRA-qualifying banking institutions.

Unfortunately, to date, the CRA has largely failed to compel or effectively incentivize adequate investment by
banking institutions in Tribal Nations and Native communities. As the CDFI Fund's landmark "Access to Capital
and Credit in Native Communities" report points out, while the CRA "was not intended to exclude Native
Communities living on tribal lands...in practice it often does," and banks under the Act's current regulations can
easily satisfy CRA requirements without having to do business in or with Native nations and communities if they
so choose (as most do), and they are not required to affirmatively disclose that they have failed to make CRA-
qualified investments in Tribal Nations and Native communities.1

This lax attention to CRA requirements has contributed to predictable, persistent, and sobering outcomes. With
the CRA largely overlooking Tribal Nations and Native communities, large swaths of Indian country continue to
suffer as credit desert epicenters with no locally available banking services. Given this banking void, many Native
people are left to turn to nearby high-cost predatory lenders that trap them in endless debt cycles and rob them
of their ability to grow their personal and familial assets. As the Native American Finance Officers Association
explains, "An alignment of a banking and credit deserts map with a map of tribal communities reveals a crisis for
tribal citizens and governments attempting to access cost-effective capital and banking services."2 A recent study
of this state of affairs in Arizona and New Mexico, meanwhile, found that (among other things) traditional
mortgage lending is failing Native families "egregiously," Tribal lands received less than one cent for each dollar
loaned to small businesses in those two states, and Tribal areas have far higher quantified financial need than
other rural areas.3

The CRA Proposed Rule: What It Will Mean for Indian Country

Based on our analysis of the Proposed Rule and how its provisions likely would specifically impact Tribal Nations
and Native communities, we are opposed to the Proposed Rule on three primary grounds:

(1) it will structurally and dramatically de-incentivize bank lending and investment in Tribal Nations and
Native communities generally and Native CDFIs specifically, all but eliminating the modest benefits the
CRA currently generates for these recipients;

(2) it will make it impossible to track the nature and degree of CRA-qualifying bank activity involving Tribal
Nations, Native communities, and Native CDFIs at a national, local, or individual bank level, further
reducing banks' public accountability to Indian Country under the CRA; and

(3) it will make it exceedingly difficult to amend the CRA regulations in the future to strengthen CRA to
increase bank lending and investment in Indian Country (the Proposed Rule, coupled with the agencies'
current effort to secure court decisions that would prevent future administrations from amending CRA
regulations to examine lending beyond banks' footprints or evaluate deposit products, threatens to
restrict the CRA's reach permanently).

Our Position on the Overarching Provisions of the Proposed Rule

We oppose finalization of the Proposed Rule in its current form based on our analysis of how the Rule's key
provisions will specifically manifest themselves across Indian Country. Below is a detailed explanation of several
ways the CRA Proposed Rule will reduce CRA-qualified lending and investment in Tribal Nations, Native
communities, and Native CDFIs:

1. Substantially reduces the number of banks required to satisfy the CRA's most rigorous requirements
by increasing bank asset thresholds: Under the Proposed Rule, banks with less than $1 billion in assets would
be considered "small banks" (up from the current threshold of $412 million), while banks with between $1 billion
and $10 billion (up from $1.649 billion) in assets would be considered intermediate small (hereafter, intermediate)


banks. Combined, these two new thresholds would dramatically reduce the number of large banks under CRA,
meaning far fewer would remain subject to the full large bank CRA examination with its separate lending,
investment, and service tests. Removal of these accountability measures will de-incentivize hundreds of regional
and community banks from channeling vitally needed CRA-qualified capital into Indian country and other rural
areas. For Native CDFIs, fewer banks subject to the most rigorous CRA requirements will mean fewer banks
inclined to pursue loans, investments, deposits, grants, and other partnerships with Native CDFIs, especially for
younger, emerging ones like Native Edge Finance that have yet to build up a sound lending track record.

Of grave concern is the significant reduction in bank accountability to invest in community development that
these proposed asset threshold changes will cause. First, raising the ceiling threshold for small banks from $412
million to $1 billion would eliminate community development evaluations under CRA for roughly 814 banks, or
about 40% of the banks currently subject to that requirement, which is projected to prompt the loss of at least
$500 million dollars annually in CRA-qualifying community development loans and investments from those
banks.4 Meanwhile, the more than 400 banks moving from large bank to intermediate bank status would eliminate
the separate investment and service tests they must now satisfy and combine community development loans,
investments and services into one evaluation, reducing their distinct scrutiny purposes. As a result, only the
largest 6% of banks would face separate reviews of their community development loans/investments and branch
services or of their CRA small-business loan reporting requirements.

Also concerning is proposed Option 1 in the Proposed Rule, which would allow a large bank to qualify for broader
geographic consideration of community development loans after meeting a benchmark equal to 0.625% of Tier
1 capital allocated to its assessment areas. The same 0.625% benchmark would apply separately to CD
investments and grants. A recent analysis concluded that Option 1 could endanger as much as 85% of the
current CRA-based community development activity.5

Together, these provisions also could jeopardize financing for affordable housing, especially in smaller markets
that include much of Indian country, worsening the nation's housing crisis. Notably, the Proposed Rule would
reduce demand for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) at a time when Congress just increased the
supply of LIHTCs through the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (which won't matter much if more than 800
banks no longer have community development requirements, with another 400 no longer being separately
evaluated for investments). The cumulative harm to community development financing would be particularly
severe across Indian country.

2. Reduces bank branches in LMI areas: Raising the classification threshold for large banks six-fold to $10
billion would eliminate a total of 417 banks from the service test that currently examines the distribution, opening,
and closing of bank branches and whether they are adequately accessible to LMI communities. More than 5,000
branches of these banks are located in LMI census tracts (30% of all LMI branches nationwide) and more than
4,000 of their branches are located in majority-people-of-color census tracts (23% of all such branches) – these
branches would no longer be evaluated by this vital accountability measure. CRA's branching requirements are
a primary reason that banks have maintained the share of their branches located in LMI communities at relatively
steady levels – about 24% nationwide. With this compulsory mechanism removed, the number and share of
branches maintained by affected banks in LMI areas would likely decline precipitously. Such a decline would
particularly harm Indian country, where bank branch access is already extremely limited. Across the nation,
Majority-Native American counties average just two bank branches, compared with nine in rural counties
generally and 27 across all counties.

3. Decreases bank investment in Native CDFIs and non-profit organizations: Currently, some Native CDFIs
and CDFI intermediaries and a greater number of Native non-profits like The National Center receive CRA-based
investments from banks in the form of grants and donations designed to support qualifying community
development initiatives. Often these investments are for general operating support to help these entities sustain
and grow their operations and diversify and expand the lending and other services they provide to meet their
communities' evolving needs. Under the existing CRA regulations, there is no cap on what the recipients of those
investments can spend on indirect or administrative costs, which in the case of Indian county gives Native entities
great flexibility to tailor those dollars to meet Native communities' distinct needs most impactfully.



The Proposed Rule, however, requires grant funds from all banks to be tied to a specific community development
project or program to receive CRA credit. It also institutes a 15% cap on indirect and administrative costs that is
bound to disincentivize large banks' investments in Native CDFIs and non-profits, particularly smaller ones who
need these investments most but whose indirect and administrative costs comprise a larger – and under the
Proposed Rule, disqualifying – percentage of their annual operational budgets. This cap will compel Native
CDFIs and non-profits to spend more time pursuing project-specific grants from banks and less on designing
and offering critical CRA-eligible community development services, such as helping families become first-
generation homeowners and providing technical assistance to small businesses. It also will make Native CDFIs
and non-profits more vulnerable to economic downturns by making it more difficult to cover fixed overhead costs
when there are reductions in other sources of revenue.

4. Elevates bank strategic plans that will serve to reduce community development financing: The
Proposed Rule expands the ability of – and incentives for – banks to opt to be evaluated under a regulator-
approved CRA strategic plan instead of the normal CRA tests. In addition, it allows CRA regulators to coach
banks on the adequacy of their proposed strategic plan goals before public input is solicited and gathered,
diminishing the importance of the public comment process, and allows banks that fail to achieve their self-
selected goals to fall back on the regular CRA test. Meanwhile, recently the OCC issued guidance fixing annual
community development loans and investments equal to just 0.12% to 0.24% of assets as "Satisfactory" and
0.20% to 0.40% as "Outstanding," percentages that are significantly lower than the historical medians of 0.70%
for OCC-supervised banks with assets of $30 billion or less and 0.64% for banks with assets of $1 billion or less.6
Combined, the Proposed Rule and the OCC guidance would enable banks to commit substantially less to
communities and still earn passing, or even outstanding, CRA ratings. For example, if just 10% of banks reduced
their annual activity from their historical median level to the OCC's new 0.24% benchmark, nearly $100 million
in community development financing would be lost annually.7

5. Reduces transparency of banks' CRA performance by decreasing required small business and other
lending data: Currently under CRA, large banks generally must collect and report data on small business loans,
small farm loans, community development loans, and assessment areas, which is critical for understanding
where, how, and to what degree those banks are investing in LMI communities. Under the Proposed Rule,
however, a significant number of once-large banks would no longer be required to collect and share this data
with federal regulators. As a result, for example, CRA small business lending data would decrease by an
estimated 11% nationally, with particularly large losses in rural states. Losing CRA data from regional and
community banks would make it harder for The National Center, Tribal Nations, Native CDFIs, and their
advocates to: (1) determine which banks are lending in Indian Country, where, and in what amounts; (2) compare
banks' institutional commitments to Indian country; (3) identify credit gaps; and (4) demonstrate unmet needs
during CRA exams, mergers, or community-benefit negotiations. The data loss would be especially significant in
rural Western and Plains states where smaller banks make up a larger share of the banking market.

6. Lessen the impact of CRA-qualifying dollars by diluting the definition of "economic development":
Under the current CRA regulations governing economic development, an activity must generally satisfy both a
size test and a purpose test, including showing that it creates, retains or improves jobs for LMI people, benefits
LMI areas, or works through qualifying intermediaries. However, the Proposed Rule weakens this standard for
earning CRA credit for economic development activities by eliminating the purpose test – meaning banks would
be able to receive CRA credit without proving that the business financing they are providing actually creates,
preserves, or improves jobs for LMI people or communities. For example, a bank could receive CRA credit for
financing a limited liability company (LLC) established by a wealthy business owner in an upper-income census
tract, even if the business creates no jobs for low- and moderate-income people – which is wholly contrary to the
CRA's original intent. Specific to Indian country, this would directly harm the employment prospects of Tribal
citizens, as Tribal and non-Tribal businesses reliant on CRA-qualified start-up or growth capital that are located
in or near Native communities or otherwise dependent on Native labor would no longer be attractive to banks for
CRA purposes.



7. Disincentivize bank investments in critically needed infrastructure projects for LMI people and in LMI
communities: Currently, bank investments in infrastructure projects in an LMI area typically will receive CRA
credit only when they work to retain or attract residents or businesses to that area. The Proposed Rule weakens
this LMI accountability measure by enabling banks to get credit for such projects that benefit or serve a targeted
area, even when they produce few if any meaningful benefits for LMI residents or the community writ large. This
means banks could get CRA credit for infrastructure projects that primarily benefit affluent communities or private
companies at the expense of LMI people and communities. For Indian country, this would actively suppress
place-based infrastructure development, which is the prerogative of Tribal Nations and Native communities, and
ensure reduced opportunities for Tribal Nations and Native CDFIs to attract private financing for desperately
needed large-scale infrastructure projects that benefit not just Tribal but also surrounding communities.

Our Position on Specific Questions Posed in the Proposed Rule

Question 55: Are there alternative approaches the agencies should consider to encourage banks to meet the
credit needs of Indian country and other Tribal and native lands? For example, should the agencies use the
definition of Native Lands in the 2023 CRA rules? Are there any difficulties or unintended consequences that
banks might encounter with the definitions as proposed?

Yes, if the FDIC and OCC ultimately decide to advance this Proposed Rule, it should be substantively overhauled
to integrate the key provisions contained in the 2023 CRA Final Rule8 explicitly designed to increase bank
investment in Tribal Nations and Native communities. These include:

1. The 2023 rule's establishment of "Native Land Areas" (NLAs) as a stand-alone CRA place-based
category investment area and, critically, its additional consideration for branches and further
incentivizing community development activity benefiting Native communities. As referenced above,
"Indian country" and "other Tribal and Native lands" exhibit significant disparities in access to capital and bank
services. For example, the National Community Reinvestment Coalition recently found that the average census
tract on Tribal land received just five small business loans, compared to 82 such loans made on average in non-
Tribal tracts.9 The OCC and FDIC acknowledge that "communities in Indian country or other Tribal and native
lands face significant and unique CD [community development] challenges", but their proposed rule's approach
to addressing those challenges falls short in comparison to the 2023 CRA Final Rule.10 The OCC and FDIC are
currently offering to include "Indian country or other Tribal and native lands" as an eligible geography under the
revitalization and stabilization category of community development, but the 2023 CRA Final Rule took it a critical
step further by awarding additional qualitative consideration for bank branches on Native Lands and creating an
impact and responsiveness factor for community development activity that "benefits or serves residents of Native
Land Areas" (see below).11 CRA performance evaluations under the 2023 rule would have included how much
of a bank's community development activities fit into each impact and responsiveness factor, creating a
meaningful incentive for banks to pursue community development in Native Lands and other high-need areas
so as to avoid having nothing to report in specific categories.12 The 2023 rule also would have made it easier for
banks to pursue community development financing outside of their branch networks by not requiring banks to
first demonstrate they have adequately served their assessment areas and instead to weight activities inside
and outside facility-based assessment areas based on where a bank lends and takes deposits.13 Given these
factors, we request the OCC and FDIC use the 2023 rule's definition of Native land areas as it is more
comprehensive.14 This definition also should be expanded to cover the formal service areas of certified Native
CDFIs that fall outside of these lands.

2. The 2023 rule's conferral of automatic, enhanced CRA credit for a bank's entire loan, grant, investment,
or service if it involves a Treasury-certified Native CDFI.15 It is critical that this automatic credit not be
abridged or limited in any way by any other, potentially conflicting provisions contained within the FDIC and
OCC's Final Rule.

3. Inclusion of CDFIs and NLAs among the CRA's impact and responsiveness review factors: In the 2023
Final Rule, two of the 12 factors considered in evaluating the impact and responsiveness of a bank's community


development loan, investment, or service was whether it (1) "supports a...CDFI, excluding certificates of deposit
with a term of less than one year" and (2) "benefits or serves residents of Native Land Areas."

We believe the Proposed Rule should be amended to require banks, as part of their CRA evaluations, to collect
and report data on their community development financing activities in "Indian country" and "Other Tribal and
native lands" and with entities such as Tribal governments and Native CDFIs that serve American Indian, Alaska
Native, and Native Hawaiian communities. The agencies should publicly share that data with Tribal governments,
Native CDFIs, economic development-supporting Native non-profits like The National Center, and other key
Indian country stakeholders annually, and should annually provide to these groups an updated longitudinal
analysis of CRA-qualified community development financing activity trends within those lands and involving
American Indians, Alaska Natives, and Native Hawaiians.

Furthermore, banks should be required to collect and report data as part of their CRA evaluations that documents
where within "Indian country" and "Other Tribal and native lands" their CRA-qualified activities took place (specific
geographic location, whether an activity took place on Tribal trust land or non-trust land, etc.). This disaggregated
data will enable Tribal governments, Native CDFIs, economic development-supporting Native non-profits, and
other key Indian country stakeholders to evaluate the true commitment of a particular bank in practice to invest
in the most underserved and under-resourced parts of Indian country and hold accountable those banks that are
not living up to the spirit of the CRA.

Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less than $30 billion as a threshold
for certain supervisory approaches, such as being considered a community bank or being subject to the
continuous examination process, should the agencies consider adjusting the intermediate bank asset size
threshold to include all banks with an asset size of less than $30 billion that do not qualify as small banks? If the
agencies establish $30 billion as the appropriate threshold to delineate between intermediate banks and large
banks, should the agencies also adopt a larger threshold for small banks, such as the $10 billion currently
proposed as the intermediate bank threshold?

No. We categorically oppose the proposal to adjust "the intermediate bank asset size threshold to include all
banks with an asset size of less than $30 billion that do not qualify as small banks," as we oppose the Proposed
Rule's raising of the asset threshold size for large banks to $10 billion. We also, therefore, categorically oppose
the ensuing proposal to "adopt a larger threshold for small banks, such as the $10 billion currently proposed as
the intermediate bank threshold." If the $30 billion threshold was adopted, it would jeopardize over $26 billion in
community development loans and $267 million in investments per year, while 42 states would have their number
of banks with local community development requirements cut in half or more, and 21 states would lose two thirds
of the banks currently required to reinvest in local community development under CRA.

Question 9: Are there alternative standards the agencies should consider relying on in the context of limiting
indirect costs for CD grants? Do the proposed guardrails do enough to ensure the majority of grant and donation
funds go directly towards benefiting the bank's assessment area(s)?

As discussed in detail in point #3 on pages 3-4 of this comment letter, the agencies should remove this
problematic provision from the Proposed Rule altogether, as it would significantly harm the ability of Native non-
profits and CDFIs to secure bank investments that will help them meet the distinct needs of their service
communities.

Question 10: As an alternative, should the agencies eliminate all grants and donations from CRA consideration?

No. Grants and donations currently constitute an important source of CRA-qualifying support for LMI
communities and organizations that serve them, and they should be retained as pathways to achieve CRA credit.

Question 25: Should the agencies retain the requirement that the activity create, improve, or retain jobs for LMI
individuals or in an LMI area in the first category of economic development?



Yes, for the reasons outlined in points #6 and #7 on pages 4-5 of this comment letter.

Question 30: Are there other programs that should be presumed to promote economic development, such as
programs that support Indian country residential development? Alternatively, should these activities be presumed
to qualify as community development but instead be considered as a revitalization and stabilization activity that
helps to attract or retain businesses or residents (see discussion of revitalization and stabilization activities
below)?

Programs that support Indian country residential development should be presumed to promote economic
development and community development under CRA guidelines, as should any other bank lending and
investments in Tribal Nations, Native communities, Native non-profit organizations, and Native CDFIs.

Conclusion

On the whole, the Proposed Rule would greatly weaken CRA's accountability to Indian country; instead that
accountability desperately needs to be strengthened. The CRA is one of many vehicles through which the federal
government can and should fulfill its eternal trust and treaty obligations to Tribal Nations, their citizens, and, by
extension, Native entities like non-profits and CDFIs that serve and support them. Any changes to the regulations
governing CRA, therefore, should be formulated in partnership with Tribal Nations through meaningful, ongoing
consultation, and should be precisely designed to shift the calculus to compel banks to prioritize lending and
investment in Tribal Nations and Native communities as opposed to the status quo of banks considering such
lending and investment as a luxury or last resort.

We look forward to continuing to engage directly with the FDIC and OCC to ensure that any new CRA regulations
fully – and finally – incentivize substantially increased investments by banks in Tribal Nations and Native
communities across this country.

Sincerely,

Chris James
President and CEO
National Center for American Indian Enterprise Development

Introduction and ANHD Context

The Association for Neighborhood and Housing Development (ANHD) submits this comment in
opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the
Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC),1 as it aims to weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) significantly. In addition,
given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC,
before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and
moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the
agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.
ANHD is a nonprofit membership-based organization made up of over 80+ community-based
organizations across New York City. Our mission is to build community power to secure affordable
housing and create thriving, equitable neighborhoods for all New Yorkers. We also convene the
Equitable Reinvestment Committee (ERC), a member-led body that holds financial institutions
accountable for economic, geographic, and racial inequities. Through years of responsible banking
efforts, ANHD has seen firsthand how the CRA remains essential to ensuring financial institutions
serve all communities, particularly those historically excluded from access to banking and credit.
Since 2010, banks have lent nearly $5 trillion in CRA-qualified mortgages and small business loans
nationwide, including an estimated $368 billion in the New York City Metropolitan Statistical Area

(MSA) alone.2 These investments have financed affordable housing, small businesses, and
community infrastructure, creating jobs and projects that strengthen local economies and ensure
economic prosperity for all New Yorkers. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia
found that when census tracts lose CRA eligibility, home purchase lending drops by 10%3, and
small-business lending declines by nearly 10% in urban areas.4 This shows CRA's impact and how
crucial it has been in creating both pathways to access credit and wealth building.
New York City illustrates why strong CRA implementation remains necessary. NYC is home to some
of the nation's largest financial institutions and financial markets, yet access to affordable credit,
banking services, homeownership, small-business financing, and community development capital
remains a challenge in our city. The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA

considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income
communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination, disinvestment, and
redlining. For ANHD and our members, the CRA is an important law for ensuring that financial
institutions remain accountable to, and reinvest in, the communities in which they operate.
I. Reduction in Community Investment Expectations for All Banks

The proposed CRA rule aims to upend banks' incentives to invest in communities. For example, it
suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community

percentage is far lower than the percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC)
determined the largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC, of which ANHD is a member organization, analyzed the most recent CRA performance
evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC and FDIC-supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets.
The findings show that banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community

II. Raising Asset Thresholds Would Reduce Meaningful CRA Scrutiny

ANHD and its members are concerned that substantially raising the asset thresholds used to
determine how banks are evaluated could reduce the depth of CRA scrutiny applied to financial
institutions in New York City. The relevant question is not simply how many banks would be
reclassified nationwide. Regulators should examine where those institutions operate, which
communities they serve, and which lending, investment, service, and community development
activities would consequently receive less scrutiny. For context, the rulemaking proposal would
substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how regulators evaluate banks under CRA.
Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while banks with assets between
$1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less demanding intermediate-bank
framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to large banks.8 The proposal would also
eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks
for institutions with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on small-business and
community development lending.9
Nationwide, approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation
because the proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion.10 The 417
banks newly classified as intermediate rather than large banks would no longer be examined under
separate CRA investment and service tests. Instead, their community development loans,
investments, and services would be evaluated under a combined community development test. These
reclassifications, and the resulting reduction in community development scrutiny, could have
significant consequences for affordable housing and community development, including a reduction
in incentives for banks to invest in Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC).
For New York City specifically, these changes could further exacerbate our housing and affordability
crisis by creating fewer incentives for financial institutions to meaningfully invest in the communities
they serve. The potential impact across New York is significant. According to NCRC's state-level
analysis of the proposed CRA changes:
●​ 21.7% of banks would lose their community development obligation;
●​ 40.4% of banks would lose their large-bank status.

housing, supporting community-based organizations, providing small-business credit, and investing
in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, the consequences could be significant. At a time when
New Yorkers continue to face a severe housing and affordability crisis, federal regulators should be
strengthening incentives for meaningful community reinvestment, not reducing the level of
accountability applied to financial institutions.
The existence of New York State's own Community Reinvestment Act further highlights the
importance of maintaining strong reinvestment laws. New York has continued to recognize the role
that financial institutions play in meeting local credit and community development needs. Strong
state oversight, however, should complement rather than fill in for federal CRA obligations.
Weakening the federal framework could leave fewer institutions subject to robust community
development scrutiny and ultimately reduce the tools available to communities to hold financial
institutions accountable.
III. Branches, Deposit Services, and Banking Access Remain Essential in New York City
Access to physical bank branches and affordable banking services remains essential to meeting the
credit and financial service needs of low- and moderate-income communities. While banking has
increasingly shifted toward digital services, brick-and-mortar branches continue to serve an important
role for small businesses, seniors, and households that may face barriers to accessing digital banking
services. The proposed changes to CRA service evaluations risk reducing scrutiny of branch access
and deposit services at a time when significant disparities in access to mainstream banking continue
to exist in New York City.
ANHD's analysis of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) found that the summary of
deposit data shows that New York City's branch network has continued to contract. Across the five
boroughs, the number of FDIC-reported banking branches declined from 1,478 in June 2023 to 1,393
in June 2026, a net decline of 85 locations, or approximately 5.8 percent.11
At the same time, disparities in access to mainstream banking remain. Recent research from the New
York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection found that approximately 238,900 New
York City households, or 7.0 percent, were unbanked in 2023, compared with 4.2 percent nationally.
The disparity is particularly significant in the Bronx, where 13.5 percent of households were
unbanked, more than three times the national rate.12 These figures show that branch count alone does

CRA examinations should continue to meaningfully evaluate branch distribution, branch openings

but it should supplement rather than replace banks' responsibility to maintain meaningful and

IV. Community Development Rules Should Not Undermine Support for Local
Organizations
ANHD is concerned that the proposal's treatment of community development grants could
discourage banks from supporting smaller community-based organizations that play an essential role
in meeting the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
Under the proposal, a grant or donation would receive CRA consideration only if it is directly used
for a program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of community development and meets
applicable geographic requirements. For large banks, the proposal would also require that a
recipient's indirect costs for administering the grant or donation not exceed 15 percent. The
agencies state that this requirement is intended to ensure that grant dollars directly support
community development activities rather than organizational overhead.
Our experience demonstrates why this distinction is not so simple in practice. ANHD receives direct
financial support from financial institutions, including general operating grants, that help sustain our
work across housing, small business, responsible banking, research and data, education, technical
assistance, etc. This flexible support helps maintain the staff, systems, and organizational capacity
necessary to carry out community development work.
We see this dynamic from the grantmaking side as well. ANHD administered and distributed funding
through the New York Community Cares Fund (NYCC), which grew out of commitments associated
with New York Community Bank's acquisition of Flagstar Bank. Through NYCC, ANHD typically
distributes grants of approximately $12,500 to 10 to 15 ANHD member organizations each year. The
flexibility of these grants allows organizations to support staffing, outreach, research, technical
assistance, housing work, and general operating needs while filling financial gaps that more restricted
funding won't cover.
Recent NYCC grantees demonstrate the impact of these relatively modest financial resources.
Chhaya Community Development Corporation used NYCC support in connection with tenant
outreach and education that reached more than 150 tenants, including approximately 60
Mandarin-speaking tenants, while providing interpretation to expand participation. Another member
organization, Fifth Avenue Committee, used its support for eviction-prevention counseling and tenant
outreach, including work that helped tenants secure stable leases and needed repairs. Asian American
for Equality (AAFE) reported that NYCC funding helped support a housing team that provided 300
one-on-one housing counseling services alongside tenant education and multilingual housing
assistance.
These experiences inform our concern with a 15 percent indirect-cost threshold. Smaller
community-based organizations often operate with limited financial and administrative capacity. Staff
 7

time, rent, technology, accounting, compliance, and other operating expenses are part of the
infrastructure needed to deliver housing counseling, tenant education, small-business assistance,
financial education, and other community development services. A rigid threshold could make
smaller organizations more difficult for banks to support under CRA and encourage funding
decisions based on which organizations are at a threshold that would grant them CRA credit rather
than which are best positioned with established rapport across NYC neighborhoods.
ANHD and its members urge the agencies to reconsider the proposed 15 percent indirect-cost
requirement and avoid grant eligibility standards that could discourage flexible support for smaller
community-based organizations. At minimum, the agencies should evaluate how the requirement
would affect organizations of different sizes and administrative capacities and whether it could
redirect funding away from organizations serving low- and moderate-income communities. CRA
should encourage banks to support organizations that are best positioned to meet community
needs, not simply those that are easiest for banks to document.
V. CRA Credit Should Demonstrate Meaningful Benefit to LMI Communities;
Eliminating "Purpose Test" Does the Opposite
ANHD and its members have consistently emphasized that the CRA should evaluate impact, not
simply activity. Financing should have a meaningful connection to the people and communities CRA
is intended to serve. Broadening CRA credit eligibility for economic development or infrastructure
projects without sufficient attention to potential ripple effects on low- and moderate-income
communities creates space to distance and eliminate financial capital where our city needs it most.
A project's location in or proximity to an LMI neighborhood should not be the sole criterion in
determining meaningful community benefit. Regulators should maintain standards that require banks
to show how their activity and lending respond to community needs and create tangible economic
benefits for low- and moderate-income communities.
Under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not automatically constitute
economic development. The activity must also satisfy a requirement known as the "purpose test,"
meaning it must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation, retention, or
improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.
The proposed rule aims to eliminate the "purpose test," and thus under the proposal, banks could earn
CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs for low-
and moderate-income communities. Instead, financing could qualify as economic development based
primarily on the type and size of the business and whether the financing expands, improves, or
preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence, or employment base.
Our members are concerned that this change would weaken the connection between CRA
economic-development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to benefit.
 8

Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase
economic opportunity in an underserved neighborhood, or address the needs of low- and
moderate-income communities.
Our CDFI and community-based members demonstrate how targeted capital can translate into
measurable community benefit. Renaissance Economic Development Corporation, an ANHD
member serving low- and moderate-income communities and under-resourced entrepreneurs, reports
providing more than 2,500 small-business loans, deploying nearly $66 million in loan capital into
New York City communities, helping create or retain more than 7,000 New York City jobs, and
providing technical assistance to more than 10,000 small-business owners and entrepreneurs.15
Another ANHD member, the Leviticus Fund, reports making $337 million in loans for housing and
community development since 1983, with 75 percent of that lending supporting housing for low-,
very low-, or extremely low-income households.16 These examples demonstrate the importance of
maintaining a CRA framework that incentivizes financial institutions to direct capital toward
organizations with a demonstrated ability to reach the most underserved.
Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods. The
agencies themselves acknowledge that eliminating the purpose test would expand the universe of
activities eligible for CRA credit.
Instead of eliminating the purpose test, the agencies should first analyze what additional activities
would qualify under the new definition, where those activities are likely to occur, and whether bank
financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs for low- and moderate-income
people or in low- and moderate-income communities. The agencies should also explain why
eliminating the existing connection to these outcomes is consistent with CRA's requirement to assess
banks' records of meeting the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income communities.
VI. Proposal Will Narrow the Activities Subject to CRA Examination and Hide Lending
Gaps.
Under the current rule, large banks are generally evaluated on their home mortgage and
small-business lending. The proposal outlines two options for focusing examinations on products
designated as a bank's "major product lines": either evaluating the two largest product lines based on
overall lending volume or determining major product lines based on the lending a bank conducts
within a particular assessment area. Either approach could allow weak performance in a

lower-volume product to escape meaningful scrutiny even when that type of credit is important to the
local community.
This is particularly concerning for small-business lending in New York City. In 2014, of the city's
roughly 220,000 businesses, 98 percent employ fewer than 100 people, and 89 percent employ fewer
than 20.17 Yet significant disparities in access to credit remain. As ANHD documented in our analysis
of small-business lending, only 32 percent of Black-owned businesses are fully approved for
financing compared with 56 percent of white-owned businesses, while 40 percent of Black-owned
businesses are completely denied loans or credit compared with 18 percent of white-owned
businesses.18 Research from Accompany Capital conducted in 2023, cited by ANHD, also found that
only 15 percent of women entrepreneurs surveyed received start-up capital, and only half of that
funding came from bank loans.19 These needs do not become less important simply because
small-business lending represents a smaller share of a particular bank's business.
Before any narrowing of the activities subject to CRA examination, the agencies should analyze the
impact these changes would have on low- and moderate-income people and communities, including
whether they could reduce lending that responds to demonstrated community needs. The agencies
should not allow a bank's business model to determine which community credit needs receive
CRA scrutiny. The agencies should also explain why these changes are consistent with CRA's
requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of their entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
VII. CRA Reporting Data and Transparency Are Necessary for Community Input and
Accountability.
ANHD and our members are concerned that the proposal would significantly reduce the CRA data
available to communities, regulators, and researchers. Under the current framework, banks above the
applicable threshold annually collect and report data on small-business, small-farm, and community
development lending. The proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10
billion in assets, meaning hundreds of banks would no longer be required to report this information.20
For ANHD and our members, access to reliable lending data is essential to understanding whether
financial institutions are meeting local credit and community development needs.

Conclusion
ANHD and our members have long relied on the Community Reinvestment Act as an accountability
tool to evaluate whether banks are meeting the credit and community development needs of New
York City neighborhoods. Through ANHD's Responsible Banking work, we use lending and branch
data, CRA examinations, community input, research, and direct engagement with financial
institutions to identify gaps and advance greater investment in low- and moderate-income
communities. These tools have supported work ranging from small-business and mortgage lending to
affordable housing preservation and partnerships among community organizations, financial
institutions, regulators, and public agencies.
The proposal would make significant changes to that framework, yet the agencies have not
sufficiently demonstrated what those changes would mean for the communities CRA is intended to
