COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Carolina Community Impact (CCI) respectfully submits its comments in response to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking published on August 12, 2026, proposing significant revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

The proposed changes to asset thresholds, grant restrictions, intermediate-bank rating standards, and data requirements would, taken together, significantly weaken CRA incentives across the board. CCI urges the OCC and FDIC to:
- Retain the current CRA asset thresholds;
- Preserve CRA eligibility for flexible operating and capacity-building grants;
- Maintain the requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate Satisfactory community development performance;
- Preserve robust CRA data collection and public transparency; and
- Ensure that CRA modernization strengthens, rather than reduces, the flow of responsible capital to underserved communities.

Carolina Community Impact has built the relationships, infrastructure, and trust necessary to move capital into communities that conventional financial institutions do not always reach directly. That work depends on a CRA framework that continues to create meaningful incentives for banks to be partners in it.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Carolina Community Impact (CCI) respectfully submits these comments in response to the Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking published on August 12, 2026, proposing significant revisions to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
We note at the outset that this proposal was not joined by the Federal Reserve, and that the resulting
framework — applied differently across the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve — risks creating
inconsistent incentives for community development finance depending solely on which agency
supervises a given bank. CCI urges the OCC and FDIC to consider the systemic effects of a fractured
regulatory framework as they finalize this rule.
About Carolina Community Impact
Carolina Community Impact is a North Carolina nonprofit community development organization
certified by the U.S. Department of the Treasury as a Community Development Financial Institution
(CDFI).
We currently maintain active partnerships with six banks that collectively provide millions in
investment across the state of North Carolina. These bank investments support loans, grants, and
technical assistance to small businesses, and housing counseling to support homeownership and
housing stability.
These partnerships are foundational to our work. CRA has created durable incentives that make these
relationships possible and sustainable. We are therefore writing to express serious concern that

Page 2 of 4
several provisions of the proposed rule would weaken those incentives in ways that would have direct,
measurable consequences for the communities CCI serves.
The Proposed Asset Threshold Increases Would Reduce Capital Available to Communities
The proposed rule would redefine bank size categories — small banks as institutions with less than $1
billion in assets, intermediate banks between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks above $10
billion. This restructuring would move approximately 800 banks currently subject to a separate
community development test into a lower evaluation category, and would move approximately 400
large banks into the intermediate category, reducing their obligations under the lending, investment,
and service tests and eliminating associated data-reporting requirements. The scale of this reduction
matters: under the proposed thresholds, more than 75% of all banks could be exempt from the
community development test entirely.
National analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition puts the consequences in
concrete terms. NCRC examined the 69 largest OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks and found that they
currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development loans and
investments inside their assessment areas. If those same institutions reduced their activity to the
proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital benchmark — the level the agencies describe as sufficient for a
passing rating — combined activity would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually. That is a
reduction of roughly $87 billion per year, or 85%. Even if actual behavior does not reach that floor, the
agencies would be establishing an explicit passing threshold that banks can reasonably use to justify
scaling back. That has real consequences for organizations like CCI.
The impact is also not distributed evenly. Of the approximately 800 banks that would be newly
classified as small, 47% are headquartered in rural areas where there are already fewer financial
institutions and fewer alternative sources of capital. In smaller and rural markets like those in North
Carolina that we serve, the loss of even one or two CRA-motivated bank partners can determine
whether a small business gets the financing it needs to start, hire its first employee, buy equipment,
invest in property, or recover from a natural disaster.
For CCI, this is not an abstract regulatory question. The banks we work with — many of them in the $1
billion to $10 billion asset range — made a deliberate decision to partner with us in part because of
their CRA obligations. If those obligations are reduced or eliminated, we expect some of those
partnerships to erode.We estimate that approximately 30% of our total capital base comes from
institutions that would be reclassified under the proposed thresholds. The loss or reduction of this
capital would directly constrain our ability to originate loans in North Carolina's rural and underserved
communities.
The agencies should not assume that raising asset thresholds will have no effect on community
development activity. The agencies themselves acknowledge in the proposal that when banks
become subject to a community development test, they typically adjust their CRA programs. The
inverse is equally true: when that obligation is reduced, so is the incentive to maintain it.
CCI's Recommendation: Retain the current CRA asset thresholds. The current thresholds are already
indexed annually and are therefore not frozen at 1995 levels. Raising them dramatically would not
"restore proportionality" — it would reduce accountability at a time when community development
needs are growing, not shrinking.

Page 3 of 4
Restrictions on Operating Grants Misunderstand How Community Development Works
The proposed rule would place new restrictions on CRA-eligible grants, including: (1) requiring that
grants be directly used for a program or project with a primary purpose of community development; (2)
capping indirect administrative costs at 15% for large-bank grants; and (3) requiring extensive
documentation including written fund-use commitments, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s,
and program budgets. The proposal also raises the possibility, in Question 10, of eliminating grants
from CRA consideration entirely.
CCI urges the agencies to reject all three of these restrictions and to firmly reject the alternative of
eliminating grants altogether.
The proposed 15% cap on indirect costs would be particularly harmful to smaller CDFIs, rural
organizations, and organizations like CCI that provide intensive technical assistance alongside
lending. Our cost structure reflects the reality of our work, not inefficiency. An arbitrary cap tied to an
administrative cost percentage is not an appropriate measure of community impact.
CCI's Recommendation: Preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building
grants under the current 1995 framework. CRA should encourage banks to provide the type of support
that best responds to demonstrated community needs — and in many cases, flexible operating
support is exactly that.
Weakening Intermediate-Bank Community Development Requirements Would Compound the
Harm
The proposal would also change how intermediate banks' CRA ratings are calculated, allowing strong
lending performance to compensate for weaker community development performance. Under the
current framework, an intermediate bank must receive a Satisfactory rating on both its lending test
and its CD test to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
This change, in combination with the proposed threshold increases, would compound the negative
effects on CCI and organizations like us. If hundreds of banks move from the large-bank to the
intermediate-bank category, and intermediate banks are then allowed to substitute lending
performance for community development activity, the incentive structure that supports CDFI
partnerships — grants, investments, deposits, loan participations — becomes significantly weaker.
CCI's Recommendation: Retain the requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate at least
Satisfactory community development performance to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act has worked in our communities because it creates a durable,
meaningful incentive for banks to do more than they would otherwise do. It works not only through the
direct activities of individual banks but through the networks of CDFIs, intermediaries, and mission
lenders — like Carolina Community Impact — that those banks support. Since 2010, CRA has helped
drive nearly $5 trillion in qualifying mortgages and small business loans to LMI communities. The
proposed changes would put that track record at risk.
The proposed changes to asset thresholds, grant restrictions, intermediate-bank rating standards,
and data requirements would, taken together, weaken those incentives across the board. CCI urges
the OCC and FDIC to:

Page 4 of 4
•
Retain the current CRA asset thresholds;
•
Preserve CRA eligibility for flexible operating and capacity-building grants;
•
Maintain the requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate Satisfactory community
development performance;
•
Preserve robust CRA data collection and public transparency; and
•
Ensure that CRA modernization strengthens, rather than reduces, the flow of responsible
capital to underserved communities.
Carolina Community Impact has built the relationships, infrastructure, and trust necessary to move
capital into communities that conventional financial institutions do not always reach directly. That
work depends on a CRA framework that continues to create meaningful incentives for banks to be
partners in it.

billion threshold invested $2 billion in LIHTC equity. Without the CRA's

survey, more than 140 banks falling under this proposed threshold invested
more than $4.5 billion in LIHTC equity over a five-year period.

investment from banks, who are motivated by the CRA. Banks provided 80% of

adopt a lower large bank threshold. The $3.252 billion threshold would at
least be less damaging to our industry than the $10 and, worse, $30
billion thresholds.

incentives are weakened, equity pricing per credit would be sure to drop.

any reduction in pricing would significantly slow the development of
affordable housing.

regulatory agencies consider a variety of approaches, including the

organizations.

This documentation is formatted exclusively for review under IRS Form 211 whistleblower provisions.

**RE: Comments on Proposed Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57; RIN 3064-AG31]**

To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC):

We are submitting this comment in response to the notice of proposed rulemaking regarding the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations detailed in the document OCC-2026-0694-0001_content.pdf. We recognize the agencies' stated goals of aligning the CRA regulatory framework with the statutory mandate to meet community credit needs, improving clarity, and reducing unnecessary regulatory burden. Our commentary focuses on the structural changes to asset-size thresholds, the treatment of retail lending product lines, and the revised standards for community development (CD) grants.

**I. Asset-Size Threshold Revisions**
The proposal significantly reclassifies bank asset-size thresholds. Specifically, the definition of a "small bank" would increase from the current threshold of less than $412 million to less than $1 billion in total assets. The "intermediate small bank" category would be replaced with an "intermediate bank" category for institutions with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion, and the "large bank" threshold would increase from greater than $1.649 billion to greater than $10 billion.

While we recognize that these adjustments reflect changes in the banking industry and inflation, raising the large bank threshold to $10 billion effectively exempts a substantial number of institutions from the comprehensive large bank data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements. Data transparency is critical to validating whether banks are fulfilling their affirmative obligations under the CRA. We urge the agencies to rigorously assess whether reducing data reporting for banks between $1.649 billion and $10 billion will impede the public's and the agencies' ability to objectively evaluate community investment performance.

**II. Retail Lending and the Major Product Line Standard**
We note the agencies' proposal to adopt a major product line approach for evaluating retail lending across all banks, focusing on the two largest product lines by dollar volume and loan count (Option 1). Evaluating only major product lines could reduce regulatory burden by focusing on the most meaningful components of a bank's business model. However, eliminating the evaluation of non-major product lines may inadvertently reduce a bank's incentive to offer certain credit products that, while not constituting a majority of the bank's portfolio, are vital to addressing the specific credit needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities and small businesses.

**III. Community Development Grants and the 15% Indirect Cost Cap**
We strongly support the agencies' focus on ensuring that CD grants directly benefit communities and are not depleted by excessive administrative overhead. The proposed requirement that large banks limit CD grant consideration to recipients whose indirect costs do not exceed 15% (calculated consistent with the Uniform Guidance for Federal Awards, 2 CFR part 200) is a necessary and mathematically verifiable standard to prevent rent extraction. This metric ensures that the vast majority of grant funding is deployed directly into LMI neighborhoods, affordable housing, and economic development initiatives. We recommend that this indirect cost standard be strictly enforced through the required IRS Form 990 documentation.

**Conclusion**
We appreciate the agencies' efforts in OCC-2026-0694-0001_content.pdf to modernize the CRA framework. We recommend balancing the desire for burden reduction with the necessity of maintaining robust data reporting and comprehensive lending evaluations to ensure that the statutory purpose of the CRA is fully realized.

Respectfully submitted,
Cold Blood and Steel Consulting

RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 3064-AG31)
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Generation Housing submits these comments in strong opposition to the
proposed amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
Generation Housing is a housing policy and advocacy nonprofit based in Santa Rosa,
serving Sonoma County and the North Bay. We were launched in 2020 by
community leaders who came together after the 2017 Sonoma Complex wildfires
and concluded that the greatest barrier to affordable housing in our county was not
only a lack of capital, but a lack of public and political will to build. Our mission is
more, more diverse, and more affordable housing. In five years, we have endorsed
5,566 proposed homes, over half of the projects 100% affordable, and led efforts to
attract $170 million to Sonoma County for affordable and climate-smart housing.





​


Our annual State of Housing in Sonoma County reports document a region still
recovering from several disasters and short tens of thousands of homes:
●​ Wildfires since 2017 destroyed just under 5,000 homes, and most recovery
funding has now been allocated. The county still needs roughly 38,000 homes
to make up for past deficits.
●​ A household now needs to earn upwards of $160,000 to afford median
housing costs, up nearly $50,000 from the late 2010s. The median monthly
mortgage payment jumped from $2,400 in 2022 to just under $4,000 in 2025.
●​ Workers earning the median wage in six of the county's most common
occupations can afford about $1,000 a month in rent, while median rents
exceed $1,900.
●​ The lowest-earning households have faced cost burden rates near 80% for two
decades.
●​ Market-rate rentals under $1,000 a month have fallen from 19,000 to just 9,000,
a 52% drop, and the true vacancy rate sits near 1.5%, far below a healthy 5-10%.
●​ School enrollment has fallen nearly 10% as families with young children leave
the county.
The CRA requires banks to help meet "the credit needs of the local communities in
which they are chartered." For nearly 50 years, it has been one of the most important
tools for bringing private capital into affordable housing and community
development. In our region, CRA-motivated loans, investments, and grants have
financed affordable homes, sustained the nonprofits that plan, advocate for, build,
and preserve them, and helped communities rebuild after repeated wildfires.
This proposal would weaken the CRA at every level. It would release most mid-sized
banks from the investment test, let banks pass their examinations on lending alone,
sharply restrict the grants that fund nonprofit capacity, and broaden what counts as
"affordable housing" without ensuring lasting benefit to low- and moderate-income
(LMI) households. The result would be fewer dollars for affordable housing, fewer
organizations able to help projects succeed, and less investment staying in the
communities where banks take deposits. We urge the agencies to withdraw or
substantially revise the proposal.
Bank Thresholds and Ratings
The proposal would raise the large bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion,
removing banks in that range from the standalone investment test, the primary
driver of bank investment in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit equity. Banks under $1
billion "would no longer be subject to the CD test," and intermediate banks could
earn a "satisfactory" rating "on only the lending test." Together, these changes would
release most of the community and regional banks that finance housing in smaller
markets like ours from meaningful community development obligations.





We ask the agencies to retain the current thresholds or, at minimum, adopt the
$3.252 billion alternative; reject the $30 billion alternative in Question 1; and require
intermediate banks to pass both the lending and community development tests.
Community Development Grants
The proposal would count only grants "directly used by the recipient for a program,
project, or initiative," cap large-bank grant recipients' indirect costs at 15%, and
require each recipient to supply commitments, attestations, and IRS Form 990s
regardless of grant size. The agencies also ask whether to "eliminate all grants and
donations from CRA consideration" (Question 10). Their own analysis concedes these
rules "may reduce CRA incentives for general operating support, capacity-building
grants, or grants to intermediaries."
General operating support for policy and community education is critical to realizing
CRA's brick-and-mortar investments. A fully financed affordable project can still fail
on the ground. Bad policy, a slow and risk-averse regulatory culture, and organized
public opposition can delay good projects for years, driving up costs and sometimes
causing them to collapse, along with the CRA loans and investments behind them.
Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson document this pattern in their 2025 book
Abundance. Gen H was founded precisely because our community found that the
lack of public and political will, not only capital, was blocking affordable housing.
Policy and education groups work upstream of every bank transaction, clearing the
path for many projects at once, which is why this work cannot fit a single-project
"directly used" test. Investing in it makes CRA lending and investment more efficient
and more reliably impactful.
We ask the agencies to reject Question 10; expressly recognize general operating
support, policy, research, and community education as qualifying uses; and withdraw
the 15% cap, which turns the federal government's minimum default indirect cost
rate into a ceiling.
Affordable Housing Definition
The proposal would credit unsubsidized housing based on rents "at the time of the
transaction," with no requirement that it remain affordable after a sale or turnover,
and would extend credit to housing affordable at up to 120% of area median income
in "high-cost areas," a term defined only in the preamble. The agencies themselves
acknowledge this "could reduce the emphasis on activities that serve LMI individuals
more directly."
We ask the agencies to require a recorded long-term affordability commitment for
any unsubsidized housing credit, including middle-income housing, and to define
"high-cost area" in the rule text. We support the proposal's pro rata credit for
mixed-income housing and ask the agencies to confirm it covers density bonus and
inclusionary units.




Minimum Activity Standard
The proposed geographic flexibility standard of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital is described by
the agencies as "the minimum level of CD activity... to not receive a 'needs to
improve' rating." A minimum framed this way will become the target. Banks could
meet it locally and send the rest of their community development dollars to
wherever deals are easiest, away from high-cost, high-need regions like the North
Bay.
The CRA works because it asks banks to reinvest in the communities where they
take deposits. This proposal would weaken that obligation for most banks and
cut off support for the organizations that help affordable housing get approved
and built. Generation Housing strongly opposes the proposal as drafted and
urges the agencies to withdraw or substantially revise it.
In partnership,




Jen Klose
Executive Director, Generation Housing

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Habitat for Humanity International appreciates the opportunity to share our perspective on the
proposed rulemaking changes to the Community Reinvestment Act put forward by the Office of
the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation.
Habitat for Humanity works in communities throughout the U.S. and worldwide to ensure that
everyone has access to a safe and affordable place to call home. Since our founding in 1976 as
a Christian organization, together we have helped more than 65 million people globally build
their futures on their own terms through access to decent housing. We've done that by working
alongside people of all walks of life to build, repair and finance their homes, by innovating new
ways of financing and building, and by investing in neighborhoods to create vibrant
communities where everyone can thrive.
Habitat's U.S. network includes more than 950 local Habitat organizations working in rural,
urban and suburban communities across all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto
Rico to build stronger communities and help low-income households access and sustain
affordable homeownership. Through this work on the ground, Habitat has gained a broad and
deep perspective on the credit needs of low-income families and under-invested communities.




Office of Government Relations and Advocacy | 1310 L St. NW, Suite 350, Washington, DC 20005 advocacy@habitat.org
The proposed rulemaking includes helpful changes that give banks more flexibility in where
they can receive CRA credit. We support these. However, we are concerned that other
elements of the proposed rulemaking would reduce flexibility and undermine the intent of the
CRA to ensure that financial institutions serve the full credit and investment needs of all
communities—including the need for capital and resources that support affordable home
construction and greater opportunities for homeownership.
While we recognize the value of reducing unnecessary burdens on banks, any streamlining of
the CRA must retain strong incentives for banks to provide residents of all neighborhoods,
including low- and moderate-income communities, with adequate access to mortgage capital
and other essential financial resources and services. We believe the proposed rulemaking, as
currently drafted, falls short in this regard.
This letter shares Habitat for Humanity's responses to specific questions posed by the
regulatory agencies (the "Agencies"), followed by additional comments about the proposed
rulemaking. We start by describing how banks work with Habitat to bring greater investment to
underserved communities.
Banks Partner with Habitat for Humanity in Multiple Ways to Advance CRA Aims
Since its enactment, the CRA has been instrumental in Habitat for Humanity's success in
addressing the credit needs of low- and moderate-income homebuyers and homeowners in
underserved communities. The CRA plays an essential role in facilitating partnerships between
banks and Habitat organizations that significantly strengthen our capacity to provide affordable
mortgages to qualified lower-income families, construct new affordable homes, and deliver
home repairs and other services that improve housing stability for existing homeowners.
Motivated by the CRA, banks work with local Habitat organizations in various ways to bring
financial opportunities to communities across the country:
• Mortgage origination – Banks originate nearly a third of Habitat's low-cost mortgages to
homebuyers, meaning local Habitat organizations do not need to hold these mortgages
on their balance sheets and can create more affordable homeownership opportunities
for more hard-working families.
• Construction financing – Many banks offer low-cost construction financing that helps
Habitat build and rehabilitate homes at lower cost, so these homes can better support
an affordable mortgage.




Office of Government Relations and Advocacy | 1310 L St. NW, Suite 350, Washington, DC 20005 advocacy@habitat.org
• Loan purchases – Banks purchase roughly a quarter of Habitat's below-market-rate
mortgages to partner families. These loan sales enable our local network to create many
more homes and attainable homeownership opportunities than would otherwise be
possible. For some Habitat organizations, this annually frees up tens of millions of
dollars for building additional affordable homes.
• Programmatic grants – Banks further address critical community credit needs by
making grants to directly support Habitat's local programmatic work. This includes
crucial support for home construction and home repair activities serving low- and
moderate-income homebuyers and homeowners. It also includes support for affiliates'
homebuyer counseling, financial capability, and related community programming, as
well as disaster recovery initiatives.
• Operating support grants – For a substantial share of the Habitat organizational
network, bank grants are an important source of general operating support that is
fundamental to achieving programmatic impact in the communities they work in. This
includes grant support for construction management, volunteer coordination,
technology improvements, predevelopment, facility spaces, and homebuyer and
homeowner education activities not tied to a dedicated program.
• Volunteer services – Local bank partnerships facilitated by the CRA also provide
volunteers who serve as board members, directly assist affordable homebuilding and
home repair activities, provide financial education services to the community, and
more.
Raising Asset-Size Thresholds Would Substantially Reduce CRA Incentives for Banks and
Greatly Diminish Habitat's Ability to Serve Families and Communities
(Response to Question 1)
We recommend that the Agencies do not pursue their default proposal for changing the asset-
size thresholds used to determine bank expectations under the CRA. Nor should they consider
higher thresholds still, such as establishing $30 billion as the minimum threshold for
classifying a bank as "large."
The default proposal from the OCC and FDIC for revising asset-size thresholds would mean
that:
1. Banks with assets of $1.65 billion–$10 billion, currently considered "large," would be
reclassified as "intermediate," with reduced CRA expectations and scrutiny.




Office of Government Relations and Advocacy | 1310 L St. NW, Suite 350, Washington, DC 20005 advocacy@habitat.org
2. Banks with assets of $412 million–$1 billion, currently considered "intermediate,"
would be reclassified as "small," bringing even lower expectations and scrutiny.
For a substantial share of the banks that Habitat works with, these changes would significantly
reduce or eliminate bank obligations for investing in "community development" activities —
which include loans and grants for affordable housing. Many of these banks are the only banks
operating in the communities we serve.
In a 2026 survey of the Habitat network, we found that:
• Two-thirds (66%) of surveyed Habitat organizations work with at least one "large" bank
that would be reclassified as "intermediate," meaning reduced community
development scrutiny and other CRA expectations because they would no longer be
subject to the separate lending, investment and service tests that are part of large-bank
examinations.
• Nearly a third (31%) of surveyed Habitat organizations work with at least one
"intermediate" bank that would be reclassified as "small," eliminating any community
development expectations for those banks.
• Overall, reduced CRA expectations caused by proposed bank size reclassifications
would impact 71% of surveyed Habitat organizations.
• Rural-serving Habitat organizations would be disproportionately impacted by
reduced CRA obligations, as a greater share of their banking relationships are with
institutions that would be reclassified downward. Reducing community development
responsibilities for these banks would have an outsized impact on financing and
investment on not just rural areas, but smaller communities generally.
Bank size reclassification would similarly have a profound impact on CRA incentives for
community development and affordable housing investment nationwide. According to an
analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition, the proposed asset-size changes
above would mean:
• Approximately 800 fewer banks would lose their community development obligations
under the CRA because they would be reclassified from "intermediate" to "small."
• Another 417 banks would be reclassified from "large" to "intermediate," and thus have
reduced incentives for community development investments.




Office of Government Relations and Advocacy | 1310 L St. NW, Suite 350, Washington, DC 20005 advocacy@habitat.org
If the most aggressive changes put forth in the proposed rule are adopted, (i.e., raising the large
bank threshold to $30 billion and the small bank threshold to $10 billion), NCRC estimates that
$26 billion in community development loans would be jeopardized annually, along with $267
million in community development investments. Under this more aggressive proposal, more
than a third of all banks, roughly 1,500 banks, would no longer have any CRA expectations to
provide community development loans or investments, according to analysis by the National
Association of Affordable Housing Lenders.
The data above underscore the scale of our concern. If adopted, the proposed changes would
remove or substantially reduce community development obligations for hundreds of banks and
could place billions of dollars in community development lending and investment at risk. For
Habitat, this would translate into fewer lending and investment partnerships and diminished
access to affordable capital, greatly hindering our local network's ability to scale affordable
home production and increase access to affordable home mortgages.
Ultimately, the consequences would be borne not by Habitat organizations alone, but by the
families and communities we serve. Fewer CRA-motivated investments mean fewer affordable
homes built, fewer homeowners able to access critical repairs, fewer opportunities for first-
time homebuyers to achieve homeownership, and fewer resources flowing into communities
that already face significant housing challenges. At a time when the nation is confronting a
persistent housing crisis, weakening incentives for community development investment would
move us further away from, rather than closer to, meeting the housing needs of the nation.
Lastly, we don't believe the Agencies have made a compelling case for increasing bank asset-
size thresholds, especially given the significant potential for negative impacts on access to
capital for home construction, repairs and affordable mortgages. If the Agencies' concern is
compliance burden for banks, the significant rise in overall bank assets since the 1990s would
suggest that more banks have the resources to comply now – not fewer.
Restricting CRA Credit for Community Development Grants Would Have Additional
Negative Impacts
(Response to Question 9 and Question 10)
Preserve credit for community development investments that indirectly support community
development programming.
The Agencies should preserve existing flexibility under the CRA for how community
development grants can be used, rather than limiting these grants to directly supporting
community development projects or programs. Credit should be available for grants that




Office of Government Relations and Advocacy | 1310 L St. NW, Suite 350, Washington, DC 20005 advocacy@habitat.org
support clear community development purposes – whether directly or indirectly. And the
Agencies should certainly not eliminate community development grants from CRA
consideration.
Many Habitat organizations receive community development grants for direct program support
as well as general operating assistance that indirectly supports their programming. Non-
program-specific grants support critical functions such as construction management,
volunteer coordination, outreach to hard-to-reach homebuyers and homeowners, facility
space, technological improvements, predevelopment costs, accounting, and homebuyer and
homeowner education activities not tied to a dedicated program.
Narrowing the types of community development grants eligible for CRA credit would eliminate
support for critical operating costs, organizational capacity, and non-program-specific
services that enable effective community development. For many Habitat organizations and
other community-based nonprofits, these grants support the operational infrastructure
necessary to deliver housing and community development programs effectively and at scale. In
many communities, these organizations serve as the primary, and sometimes only, entities
providing affordable homeownership, housing counseling, home repair and disaster recovery
services. Limiting support for these foundational functions could weaken their long-term
sustainability, reduce their capacity to serve the families in their communities and ultimately
diminish the impact of CRA investments in the communities they are intended to benefit.
Intermediary entities play a critical role in helping banks reach underserved, small and rural
communities.
The proposed rulemaking would also bar community development grantees from making sub-
grants to other nonprofits. This would have substantial negative impacts for smaller and rural
communities, and for affordable housing and homeownership activities in these communities.
Any new CRA rulemaking should preserve the ability of banks to work through qualified
intermediaries where there is clear accountability, transparency and qualifying community
development activity. What matters is that these grants are ultimately used to increase access
to financial resources and reinvestment for underserved communities – not whether they are
assisted by grantees providing sub-grants.
Habitat for Humanity International and state Habitat organizations serve as trusted
intermediary partners that help banks efficiently deploy community development investments
to local Habitat organizations working in thousands of communities nationwide. Habitat




Office of Government Relations and Advocacy | 1310 L St. NW, Suite 350, Washington, DC 20005 advocacy@habitat.org
intermediaries often serve as a first point of contact for banks, connecting them to well-
matched, high-impact opportunities for investment, and providing an efficient platform for
distributing resources to support homebuilding and other community development programs
operated by local Habitat organizations—particularly in underserved and rural communities.
At the national level, HFHI provides the infrastructure for larger bank partners operating across
multiple markets to manage a significant national investment while ensuring that funding and
impact remain local. The value added for banks includes:
• Standardized funding agreements, due diligence, measurement and reporting.
• Transparency and traceability of funds to local communities.
• Consolidated reporting of local impact.
• Reduced administrative burden for both bank partners and local Habitat organizations.
Through longstanding partnerships with national financial institutions, HFHI consolidates
significant investments that support affordable homeownership programs across hundreds of
local Habitat organizations, providing an efficient and accountable structure for directing
resources to communities nationwide.
State-level Habitat organizations play a similar role in securing larger grants to assist smaller
affiliates that don't have the administrative or compliance capacity to pursue individual grants,
especially in rural areas.
For example, Habitat Iowa has a long-term relationship with a large bank that used to provide
small grants directly to each Habitat organization in the state. But when the bank shifted its
grantmaking to a more efficient approach of providing fewer, larger grants, most of the state's
smaller and rural affiliates – and their communities – were at risk of being left out. To remedy
this, Habitat Iowa over the past six years has successfully submitted a single-grant request that
divides the assistance among the smaller/rural Habitat organizations to support their local
programming. By consolidating grant requests, Habitat Iowa preserves the opportunity for
more communities to benefit from affordable housing grant funding while enabling the bank to
make its grantmaking more efficient.
Serving as intermediaries, HFHI and state Habitat organizations increase the reach, efficiency,
and impact of local CRA investments, ensuring resources are leveraged and delivered to the
communities that need them most.
If sub-grants from intermediaries are disallowed, we expect hundreds of Habitat organizations
across the country to be adversely affected, with the greatest impact falling on Habitat and




Office of Government Relations and Advocacy | 1310 L St. NW, Suite 350, Washington, DC 20005 advocacy@habitat.org
other organizations serving rural and smaller communities. Faced with additional
administrative burdens and fewer efficient pathways for distributing resources, banks will
understandably concentrate their community development investments among a smaller
number of larger organizations and markets. As a result, smaller and rural communities will
receive less investment.
Focus CRA Credit on Activities that Provide Clear Benefit To LMI Households
(Response to Question 18)
We would discourage the Agencies from providing CRA credit for middle-income rental
housing. We believe it would be most helpful to keep the CRA's focus on LMI households and
addressing their considerable need for greater credit access and affordable housing. Allowing
credit for middle-income rental housing could shift critical private capital away from serving
these LMI households.
For similar reasons, we would not support providing CRA consideration for community
infrastructure investments if banks no longer have to demonstrate how the investment
ultimately helps attract, retain or benefit LMI residents or businesses. Historically, many
infrastructure investments, including highways, parking garages and public facilities, displaced
low-income residents rather than benefitting them. It is important that community
infrastructure investments seeking CRA credit show how LMI residents in these communities
will be able to share in the benefits.
Preserve CRA Incentives for Mortgage Loans to LMI households
(Response to Question 23)
We recommend against modifying the definition of affordable housing such that home
mortgage loans provided to LMI households would qualify for consideration as Community
Development loans if not evaluated as a major product line under a bank's Retail Lending test.
These mortgages are essentially retail loans, not community development. Treating them
under Community Development risks marginalizing their importance.
Expand Where CRA Credit is Available
(Response to Question 31 and Question 34)
Habitat supports responsible, geographic flexibility regarding where banks can receive CRA
credit for helping meet the needs of underserved communities.




Office of Government Relations and Advocacy | 1310 L St. NW, Suite 350, Washington, DC 20005 advocacy@habitat.org
We support the Agencies' proposal to expand the definition of designated disaster areas to
include counties designated to receive only FEMA Public Assistance Emergency Work Category
A (Debris Removal) and/or Category B (Emergency Protective Measures). This would create
additional opportunities for local Habitat organizations to secure bank financing for housing
recovery and resilience, particularly in communities where residential impacts and repair
needs are not fully reflected in FEMA assistance designations.
We also believe that it would be helpful to allow banks to receive credit for community
development activities outside their assessment areas – including credit at the state,
multistate MSA level or bank level – on the condition that they have first adequately met
community development needs inside their assessment areas. Community development
lending and grants from out-of-region banks are especially important to Habitat affiliates in
smaller/rural communities.
Lastly, for community development activities related to "revitalization or stabilization of
targeted geographic areas," we support the proposal to include under this header "any other
area targeted by a government entity for redevelopment that qualifies for significant economic
incentives, such as tax credits, tax abatements, or grants." This would capture more
communities where Habitat operates that have significant community reinvestment needs.
Expand Eligible Activities to Include Investment in Disaster Preparedness
We support the proposal to provide CRA credit for community development activities that help
individuals and communities in targeted, disaster-impacted areas prepare for, adapt to, or
withstand natural disasters, including retrofitting affordable housing to withstand future
disasters.
Explicit recognition of disaster preparedness and resilience activities could help local Habitat
organizations attract bank support for home hardening, including roof strengthening, window
replacements, flood mitigation, and wildfire-resistant improvements. This aligns closely with
Habitat's efforts to expand resilience through existing home preservation programs.
Continue to Allow CRA Credit for Volunteer Services Indirectly Tied to Financial Services
The Agencies propose to narrow CRA consideration for community development volunteer
services to those "related to the provision of financial services or the employee's area of
expertise at the bank." Bank volunteer teams are a big part of how our local Habitat
organizations build. Bank volunteers contribute thousands of hours volunteering on the build




Office of Government Relations and Advocacy | 1310 L St. NW, Suite 350, Washington, DC 20005 advocacy@habitat.org
site each year with Habitat affiliates across the nation. For example, one of our national bank
partners has provided more than 10,000 volunteers over the past five years to help build over
2,000 homes and repair or rehab an additional 500 homes. These are meaningful contributions.
CRA credit should at least be available for volunteering that contributes to the development or
rehabilitation of affordable homes that support homebuyers' access to affordable mortgages.
Give Community Development Sufficient Weight in Overall CRA Evaluations
The Agencies propose to change bank ratings for intermediate banks such that they would only
need a "Satisfactory" rating on the lending test to receive an overall Satisfactory rating, as
opposed to needing a Satisfactory rating on both the lending and community development test,
as currently is the case. We recommend not pursuing this proposal, as it would further
compound disincentives in the proposed rulemaking for community development investments.
This change would also disincentivize construction lending for affordable housing, since it
appears that the proposed rule would treat construction loans for affordable housing as part of
"Community Development."
The Lack of Participation by the Federal Reserve Will Create a Fragmented and Confusing
Regulatory Landscape for Banks and Communities
The Federal Reserve Board did not join the OCC and the FDIC in issuing their proposed CRA
rulemaking. If the proposed changes are implemented as-is, banks overseen by the Federal
Reserve will face a different set of rules than banks regulated by the OCC or FDIC. We believe
this could cause confusion and inefficiency for both banks and local stakeholders that
ultimately leads to less investment in underserved communities.
The OCC and FDIC should work with the Federal Reserve to develop a revised proposal that
has consensus support from all three agencies while presenting a single, consistent
framework.
Proposed CRA Changes Would Undermine the Goals of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing
Act and Recent Administrative Executive Orders
By reducing incentives for banks to support community development activities, the proposed
CRA changes described above would inadvertently undercut the objectives of the recently
passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. These changes could limit private-sector
investment in affordable housing development and homeownership opportunities, making it




Office of Government Relations and Advocacy | 1310 L St. NW, Suite 350, Washington, DC 20005 advocacy@habitat.org
more difficult to achieve the legislation's goal of expanding the supply of affordable homes in
communities across the country, including those that have been underserved.
Similarly, CRA changes that reduce banks' incentives for investing in affordable home
development would appear inconsistent with the Administration's broader efforts to increase
the nation's housing supply and improve housing affordability. Recent executive actions have
emphasized reducing barriers to housing production to encourage the construction of
additional homes to help address the nation's housing shortage.
While both the historic 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act and recent Administrative Executive
Orders helpfully clear many regulatory barriers to affordable housing development, fewer of
these homes will actually get built if the CRA reduces banks' incentives to invest in these
affordable housing developments.
The CRA has long served as an important catalyst for bank investment in affordable housing
and community development, helping to ensure that capital reaches the communities where it
is needed most. Weakening these incentives risks blunting the impact of both the 21st Century
ROAD to Housing Act and the Administration's housing supply agenda by reducing the private-
sector investment necessary to translate policy goals into actual homes, homeowners, and
stronger communities.
Closing
Thank you for the opportunity to share Habitat's feedback on the proposed rulemaking. We
appreciate your consideration of these comments.
As you evaluate changes to the CRA framework, we urge you to preserve the incentives that
drive investment in affordable housing, homeownership, and community development. We
welcome the opportunity to discuss these recommendations further and to be a constructive
partner in advancing a CRA framework that delivers meaningful results for families and
communities nationwide.
In partnership,
Robert Hickey
Director, Housing Policy Development and Analysis
Habitat for Humanity International

Thank you for your invitation to comment on the OCC and FDIC proposed rulemaking on CRA. Attached is the CRA comment letter from the Metropolitan Milwaukee Fair Housing Council.

Bethany Sanchez

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0625_09000064b966c536.pdf:
1



October 13, 2026

Via electronic submission to: Federal eRulemaking Portal https://regulations.gov/.
Via email to Comments@fdic.gov

Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219

Attn: Chief Counsel's Office
Travis Hill, Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC)
550 17th Street, NW
Washington, DC 20429
Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
I am writing on behalf of the Metropolitan Milwaukee Fair Housing Council, to
comment in opposition to the changes to the Community Reinvestment Act
described in the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM)
issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1. We believe that the changes would significantly
weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we believe
that before making any of the proposed changes, it would be important for the OCC
and FDIC to carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-
income (LMI) communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and
evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and provide a comment
deadline of at least 90 days for subsequent invitations for the public to comment.
The Metropolitan Milwaukee Fair Housing Council (MMFHC) is a 49-year-old
nonprofit whose mission is to promote fair housing throughout the State of
Wisconsin by combating illegal housing discrimination and by creating and
maintaining racially and economically integrated housing patterns. Central to this
mission is expanding housing choice for all Wisconsinites. MMFHC's Fair Lending
Program staff works with banks and other home lenders to help them expand their
markets, and connect with otherwise-underserved populations. We are active

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 2
members of the National Community Reinvestment Coalition and our concerns echo
NCRC's regarding the proposed CRA changes.
The Metropolitan Milwaukee Fair Housing Council and CRA were born in the same
year. In the nearly 50 years since they were created, CRA has been an important
tool for MMFHC's work with community partners to address the harmful effects of
redlining, disinvestment, and unequal access to mainstream financial services. CRA
is a central part of the federal framework for our work to ensure that banks meet
the lending, investment, and financial services needs of their entire communities,
including LMI neighborhoods. Working in multiple partnerships with banks that
have CRA incentives has produced positive changes in home lending in particular,
as well as in small business lending, and it has increased impactful investments in
LMI neighborhoods in Milwaukee, and indeed across the country.
We are concerned that the proposed changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities
and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and
disinvestment. Federal data shows us that nationally, the CRA has been successful
at ensuring working-class borrowers and neighborhoods have access to
homeownership and entrepreneurship, with nearly $5 trillion in CRA-qualifying
mortgages and small business loans made from 2010-2024.
In the Milwaukee Metropolitan Statistical Area, during that same 2010-2024
period, banks made:
• $15,924,167,000 in home mortgages to LMI borrowers, or on homes in LMI
census tracts
• $9,408,064,000 in loans to business in LMI census tracts,
• $6,541,456,000 in small business loans.
These CRA-qualified loan products are often the result of banks listening to the
needs of residents and community advocates.
This home lending, often using downpayment assistance and/or innovative
programs (for example, the Milwaukee Community Land Trust), enables credit-
worthy renters with modest incomes to purchase newly constructed or fully
rehabbed homes, at amounts that they can afford.
Affordable mortgages to credit-worthy borrowers are important to a wide range of
borrowers. For example, they allow parents to focus their attention on their
children, instead of needing to have 2-3 jobs just to pay the mortgage; and help
full-time workers afford decent, stable housing while they are finishing their
educational degrees. Having access to banks' small business loans helps
entrepreneurs finance their business needs, and pursue their dreams.
Under the current rule, large banks are generally evaluated on their
home mortgage, small business and small farm lending. The proposal outlines two
 3
options for regulators to focus on as products designated as a bank's "major
product lines," based either on the largest two product lines by all lending volume,
or based on the type of lending a bank does more of in a particular assessment
area.2 Either option would allow weak performance in a lower volume product to
escape meaningful scrutiny even when that credit is important locally.
For example, in rural areas of Wisconsin, there is a strong need for home mortgage
and small farm lending. But if the proposal is implemented, and small farm lending
is not a major part of a large bank in Wisconsin's business, regulators will not
evaluate whether the bank is meeting this crucial community need. Absent such
evaluation, the bank will likely deprioritize making such loans.
When CRA was passed, Congress recognized that communities depend on access to
both credit and deposit services. These financial services remain especially
important in communities whose residents have experienced discrimination and
who have previously been shut out of access to mainstream financial services. The
number of bank branches located in Milwaukee's LMI neighborhoods have
increased significantly since CRA was enacted – especially during the past 25 years.
We have seen banks' physical presence in LMI neighborhoods:
• help residents to avoid predatory check-cashing and payday loans, as well as
predatory home loans, and
• address small businesses' deposit needs, and provide them with reasonably-
priced bank loans, helping them avoid being preyed upon by internet
lenders.

NCRC's data shows that under this current proposal, in Wisconsin, 45.9% of bank
branches in LMI neighborhoods, and 32.9% of branches in communities of color
could be at risk.

The branches located in Milwaukee's LMI neighborhoods have spurred growth and
stability in the immediate neighborhoods as well as the surrounding areas. We have
made a lot of progress, but many LMI communities are still banking desserts. To
increase the economic and social benefits that CRA has brought to Milwaukee - and
more broadly, to the State of Wisconsin - we need more bank branches in urban
LMI neighborhoods, as well as in rural areas that have no financial institutions at all.
We believe that the proposed changes would weaken CRA regulations that
incentivize bank branches in LMI geographies.
In our experience in Milwaukee, CRA-inspired activity has helped banks understand
that not only do LMI communities benefit, but the banks reap new relationships,
new customers, new lines of business, and new loans. Working in collaboration with
community partners such as Milwaukee's homeownership consortium called Take
Root Milwaukee, and the Bank On-Greater Milwaukee coalition, now more than ever,
bank employees are listening to the credit, capital and financial services needs of
the communities they serve - and they are acting on that input, designing helpful

2 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52123 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 4
loan products, working with the local organizations to provide Community
Development investments in affordable housing and resident-inspired
developments in LMI neighborhoods, and designing new user-friendly banking
products for their customers.
Community Development investments are deeply appreciated by the local
communities, as well as the cities or counties in which the developments are
located. Like the bank branches, the impact of the investments spurs growth and
stability in a wider geographical area.
As a result, we are deeply concerned about the effects of the proposal to reduce
the number of banks that would have a Community Development (CD) test on their
CRA Performance Evaluation. NCRC's research shows that if this proposal is
enacted, among the banks doing business in Wisconsin
• 46 of the 106 (43.4%) would lose their CD obligations and
• 22 of the 40 (55%) large banks would lose their large banks status, and
have reduced CD obligations
As NCRC's analysis notes, "The agencies have not shown that these community
needs become less significant simply because a bank falls below a higher asset
threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA obligations and scrutiny applied to
these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that would move into less
rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those institutions
serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and
moderate-income communities or communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment."
We agree with NCRC's contention that "Low- and moderate-income communities
and those that have experienced historic discrimination cannot withstand such a
reduction in community development investments and loans. If regulators lower the
expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the communities
they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities."
In Milwaukee, banks working to comply with CRA have benefited communities in the
following ways:
• Developing new home loan programs for credit-worthy first-time homebuyers,
including people of modest means and people of color.
• Offering down payment assistance for credit-worthy first-time homebuyers,
including people of modest means and people of color.
• Offering home repair programs for homeowners of modest means.
• Providing financial assistance for nonprofit organizations that provide free or low-
cost home repairs for extremely low income, elderly or disabled homebuyers.
• Providing financial support for nonprofit homebuyer counseling agencies that
have helped thousands of people to access the American Dream.
 5
• Providing bank staff to volunteer with organizations that provide financial
counseling, homebuyer counseling, affordable housing development, or small
business development.
• Providing loans and/or investments in dozens of affordable housing or mixed
income housing developments.
• Providing loans and/or investments in community facilities located in LMI
neighborhoods.
• Providing financial support and technical assistance to minority business
development organizations.
• Providing support to workforce development programs, and nonprofit
organizations that help with employment readiness.
• Providing investments and technical support to CDFIs (Community Development
Financial Institutions), mission-driven, nonprofit lenders that focus their lending on
programs and developments that the banks will not lend directly to.
• Providing office space to nonprofits that serve low and moderate income people
and neighborhoods.
• Providing low-cost checking accounts for entry-level customers.
• Participating in foreclosure prevention programs.
• Participating in Take Root Milwaukee, which is our homeownership consortium
that works to move residents from renters to successful, sustainable
homeownership.
Before CRA was established, very few banks did these things. Indeed, they openly
discriminated against people of color, and redlined low-income neighborhoods,
especially neighborhoods where people of color and immigrants lived. Some banks
may still have a long way to go. But when the community works with the banks,
listens to input that helps them understand the unmet needs of the people in their
assessment areas, it has successfully lead to the above list of positive outcomes – in
Milwaukee, and across the country.
In conclusion, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
• identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less
CRA scrutiny under the proposal;
• quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and
community development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
• assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color;
• consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden
without sacrificing meaningful community accountability.

Given their failure to do so, and the concerns described above, MMFHC believes
that the OCC and FDIC should reconsider this proposal, craft a thorough analysis of
its impacts and release it for public comment. We believe that this proposal likely
needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

 6
The Community Reinvestment Act remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that
banks are accountable for meeting community credit needs. The agencies should
not finalize changes that materially weaken that accountability without first
demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the
credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income people
and neighborhoods.

Sincerely,

Bethany Sanchez

Bethany Sanchez
Senior Administrator, Fair Lending

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
The Chicago Community Loan Fund (CCLF) is pleased to submit its comments on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) to the Community Reinvestment (CRA) regulations promulgated by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). The CRA has been a pivotal, but imperfect, tool in transforming historically underserved and marginalized communities for nearly 50 years. By spurring investment in overlooked low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities, the CRA is integral to fully realizing a just economy that affords people from all walks of life a tangible opportunity to thrive. Proposed Changes that Will Reduce Community Development Incentives

As noted previously, several proposed changes within the NPR would negatively impact CDFIs and
community development in general.

Entity Size Threshold Changes
The CRA examination process consists of a tiered system of examination and scrutiny based on the
asset size of the regulated entity. The categories previously consisted of small banks (under $416
million in assets, intermediate small banks (between $416 million and $1.6 billion in assets), and large
banks ($1.6 billion and above in assets). These bands were adjusted incrementally each year to account
for inflation. In this NPR, the regulators proposed drastically shifting these classes by redefining small
banks as less than $1 billion in assets, renaming the middle tier of banks from intermediate small banks
to intermediate banks and shifting that threshold to between $1 billion and $10 billion in assets, and
raising the threshold for the large bank designation to $10 billion and above.

While it is important that regulators take steps to properly calibrate these threshold ranges to ensure
that bank CRA requirements are commensurate with their size and reach, this considerable jump would
mean that 800 banks formerly considered intermediate small banks would no longer receive a
community development evaluation as they would now be considered small banks under the proposed
definition and 417 banks, previously considered large, would no longer be examined under separate
CRA investment and services tests and instead would be evaluated based on their combined
community development loans, investments and services, under the intermediate bank threshold.8 In
Illinois specifically, this would translate to 118 out of the 171 banks in our state losing core community
development obligations. 68 of these banks would move from the intermediate small bank designation
to the small bank designation losing all their current community development obligations. An

Community Development Performance and Lending Activity
Questions 12-17: Complexity Definition
Overall, this NPR relies too heavily on lending activity as the benchmark for meeting community
development needs and fails to fully account for the nuance of how bank activity supports community
development. This proposal ties the definition of complexity for CD investments, grants, and services
primarily to whether the activity is a necessary or beneficial component of a multicomponent financing
transaction involving a loan. For CDFIs, this narrow definition misses the vital work we do to provide
specialized expertise, layered capital, subordinate positions, public subsidies, risk sharing, guarantees,
tax-credit structures, patient repayment terms, or other features that make transactions complex even
when they are not directly paired with a particular bank loan. Complexity isn't automatically more
responsive to community needs than innovation, flexibility or impact. It is our hope that the agencies
would prioritize the characteristics and community value of the activity, including complexity,
innovativeness, flexibility, impact, and responsiveness over whether it is associated with a lending
transaction.

Section IV.B: Intermediate Bank Performance Tests
Currently, intermediate small banks are required to perform at a level of Satisfactory on both their
lending test and CD test in order to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. This proposal would not only

evaluation entirely but it would also allow a bank to perform below a Satisfactory grade on their CD test
and still receive an overall Satisfactory rating if they were able to score a Satisfactory or better grade on
their lending test. Deemphasizing the CD test would lessen the likelihood for banks to partner with
CDFIs, provide grants, or engage in other community development activities. It is imperative that we
keep the standards for CD activity high, particularly as the need for CDFI partnership is continuing to
increase, according to a 2025 report from the Federal Bank of Richmond.19

within the bank assessment area. According to analysis conducted by NCRC, of the 69 largest banks
regulated by the OCC and FDIC, the median amount of Tier 1 capital dedicated to community
development lending was 6.83%; for community development grants and investments, the median was
3.58%. Both of these marks sit well above the default line created by the NPR and could create a race to
the bottom and a sharp decline in bank community development performance in areas that they have
the most direct duty to serve.

Questions 4–7: Retail Product Lending and Protecting Specialized CD Lending
The NPR proposes to shift the bank retail lending evaluation to focus only on activity in a bank's major
product lines. For large banks in particular, this could potentially create a significant mismatch between
evolving community needs and bank lending priorities. For example, a community in great need of
home mortgages could conflict with the priorities of the large banks in their area who might be
primarily focused on other activities, further camouflaging the economic development gaps in that
community. It also would allow a loan in a retail product line outside of a bank's major product lines to
receive consideration as a CD loan if the loan otherwise satisfies the community development
definition. While this could be helpful in some cases, there is a risk that banks could use this as
opportunity to substitute ordinary course of business activity for more specialized development lending
that depends more directly on CRA incentives.

Conclusion

This NPR comes at a time of great economic uncertainty and the vulnerable communities that the CRA
has been entrusted to protect need more intentional care, not less. The FDIC and OCC included several
pivotal changes that could benefit marginalized communities, and CCLF is very supportive of these.
However, other proposed changes would harm vulnerable populations if this proposal goes forward as
is. This proposal would cost these LMI communities billions of dollars in investment and does not do
enough to actively center their needs. We urge the FDIC and OCC to withdraw this proposal in favor
working collaboratively with the FRB to create a unified regulatory regime that will maintain the intent
of the authors of the CRA by putting the needs of our most underserved and overlooked citizens first.

The CRA holds the key to creating widespread economic mobility and putting this nation on track for
enduring greatness. Realizing President Trump's vision of "a new era of soaring incomes. Skyrocketing
wealth. Millions and millions of new jobs and a booming middle class" requires us to deepen our
investment in historically underserved communities.20 It is our hope that the OCC, FDIC, and the FRB will

2024/

consider these factors when reviewing NPR comments and deciding how to improve the next iteration
of this regulation.

Again, we thank you all for the opportunity to comment on this very important proposed rulemaking
and for your thoughtful consideration of our comments and recommendations. If you have any
questions, please do not hesitate to contact me at rtucker@cclfchicago.org or CCLF's Policy and

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

Fair Housing Advocates of Northern California (FHANC) writes to object to the harmful
changes proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by
Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help
meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low and moderate income
(LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest, and
provide services in underserved communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination,
underinvestment, and lack of access remain.

Fair Housing Advocates of Northern California (FHANC) is a private nonprofit organization
dedicated to assisting individuals experiencing housing discrimination and educating the
community, including tenants, housing providers, and government employees, as to their rights
and responsibilities under federal and state fair housing laws. The mission of FHANC is to
ensure equal housing opportunity and to educate the community on the value of diversity in
housing.

FHANC provides free comprehensive fair housing counseling services to individuals alleging
housing discrimination in the North Bay counties of Marin, Napa, Solano, and Sonoma. FHANC
also provides prepurchase and foreclosure prevention services as well as fair housing trainings to
housing providers and the general community, in the North Bay and other neighboring counties.
In addition to counseling and education services, FHANC recruits, trains, and employs fair
housing testers in order to investigate claims of housing discrimination and to assist in
conducting systemic investigations.

For more than 25 years, FHANC has conducted multiple telephone, in-person, and email audits
in several Bay Area counties designed to measure the extent of discrimination in housing against
members of protected classes, particularly ethnic and racial minorities. Historically, the results of
these audits suggest that unlawful discrimination based on race, national origin, gender, and
familial status continues to be pervasive. FHANC periodically conducts fair lending and
redlining investigations. A fair lending audit is a way to assess lenders' compliance or non-
compliance with federal and state fair housing laws. It is a controlled measurement of the
difference in quality, quantity, and content of information and services afforded to borrowers by
lenders.

In the last decade, there has been an increase in complaints alleging gender and familial status
discrimination by borrowers on maternity leave. In many of these cases, complainants alleged
that lenders denied or delayed loans to working women because they were pregnant or on
maternity leave or required women to end their maternity leave and return to work in order to be
approved for a home purchase loan. In 2021, FHANC conducted an audit to determine whether
lenders would require women (testers) to return to work before closing on a home purchase loan,
a prime example of discrimination based on gender and familial status. Of the ten match-paired
tests conducted, 60% showed at least some evidence of discrimination based on race, national
origin, gender, and/or familial status. In 2022, this audit expanded on that investigation to
determine whether lenders are more likely to discriminate against women on maternity leave if
they are Black or Latinx. Half of all the tests conducted revealed at least some evidence of race
or national origin discrimination, 40% of which were based on clear evidence. Strikingly, 80% of
the five match-paired tests conducted in which the protected tester was a Black woman revealed
at least some evidence of race discrimination. Existing data already shows that Black and Latinx
borrowers are less likely to be approved for mortgage loans than white borrowers.

In 2023-2024, FHANC evaluated each lender on seven different criteria to determine whether there
was a correlation between outreach activities (language access services, branch location, and/or

The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Redlining investigations usually focus on three risk
factors for lenders: lending disparities, gerrymandered Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)

lender has a high redlining risk overall.

A lender has a high risk of lending disparities if there are significant differences in the percentage
of mortgage applications or originations from majority minority census tracts compared to peer
lenders in the same area. A lender has a high risk of having a gerrymandered CRA assessment area

around but not within these minority areas.

Fair housing laws protect homeowners from discriminatory behavior from appraisers, lenders,

provision of housing or credit. FHANC has represented several clients around the Bay Area who

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
The Illinois CDFI Coalition (Coalition) is pleased to submit its comments on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) to the Community Reinvestment (CRA) regulations promulgated by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). For nearly 50 years, the CRA has been a pivotal tool in transforming historically underserved and marginalized communities by spurring investment in overlooked low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities, across urban, suburban, and rural landscapes. The CRA is integral to ensuring that all Americans have access to the vital economic resources. We are thankful for the opportunity to provide comments that will help regulators better understand the implications of the proposed rule changes to the CRA and its impact on the communities that we represent.
