To Whom it May Concern:

The Illinois CDFI Coalition (Coalition) is pleased to submit its comments on the Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) to the Community Reinvestment (CRA) regulations promulgated by
the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC). For nearly 50 years, the CRA has been a pivotal tool in transforming historically
underserved and marginalized communities by spurring investment in overlooked low- and
moderate-income (LMI) communities, across urban, suburban, and rural landscapes. The CRA is
integral to ensuring that all Americans have access to the vital economic resources. We are
thankful for the opportunity to provide comments that will help regulators better understand the
implications of the proposed rule changes to the CRA and its impact on the communities that we
represent.

The Illinois CDFI Coalition is a consortium of U.S. Treasury-certified Community Development
Financial Institutions (CDFIs) who deploy responsible, flexible, and patient capital in numerous
underserved communities across the state. Our work focuses on conducting joint research,
business, and advocacy initiatives aimed at bolstering opportunities for equitable community
development statewide and to aid in eliminating geographic wealth gaps statewide. Our lending
bolsters small business entrepreneurship, creates and preserves affordable housing, develops
commercial retail spaces, catalyzes social enterprises that support nonprofit entities, and
establishes critical community facilities, like health care centers and educational centers, that serve


LMI populations in Illinois. From 2005 to 2021, CDFIs, as a whole, poured over $4.525 billion into
Illinois. In that same timeframe, the need for CDFIs has continued to grow with lending increasing
annually by an average of 25%. From 2020 to 2025, members of our Coalition alone invested over
$1.05 billion into nearly 6,600 wide-ranging community development projects. Many of these
projects would not have been possible without the collaboration of CRA-regulated banks who
often look to our industry as trusted community partners who are able to direct capital into
geographies that they struggle to reach. Based on an internal assessment of IL CDFI Coalition
members, the proposed changes to the CRA would jeopardize between 21% - 41% of the
respondent CDFI's total funding.

The comments we provide here are on behalf of the Illinoisans that we serve, many of whom live
in communities that are part of the legacy of disinvestment that prompted the creation of the
CRA itself. 402 bank branches, representing roughly $1.37 trillion in total bank assets, are at risk of
closing due to these proposed changes. Most of these branches are located in our state's poorest
neighborhoods. Based on analysis by the Center for American Progress of data collected from the
US Census Bureau, from 2019 to 2024, Illinois consistently ranked in the bottom half of the nation
in poverty.1 Zooming in on our most populated city, Chicago, 17% of its residents were living
below the poverty line with over a third of those individuals living in what is known as deep
poverty, surviving on less than $21 per day in 2024.2 The most heavily impacted of these
geographies is the Auburn-Gresham neighborhood on Chicago's south side in which 1-in-5
residents live in deep poverty. This neighborhood is marked for the type of sorely needed
collaborative community investment that could be jeopardized by imbalanced changes to CRA
that don't prioritize the needs of the current neighborhood residents.

We appreciate the desire of both the OCC and the FDIC to formulate updated rules that would
advance the legacy of this landmark legislation. Based on our analysis of the NPR, we believe this
proposal has several key community benefits including uplifting innovative programs like
Opportunity Zones that have demonstrated a positive impact, pairing an "illustrative" list of
qualified activities with an established process for confirmation of Community Development (CD)
activity, recognizing disaster preparedness and resilience as CD activity, providing consideration
for prior-period CD loans to highlight patient capital, and elevating CD activity in Indian and tribal
lands communities with the aim of alleviating chronic underinvestment. We applaud these
proposals.

However, we are concerned about the impact that other proposed changes would have on
underserved geographies, particularly the shift in regulated bank asset size thresholds, which have
a myriad of downstream repercussions. Some of the unintended consequence of this proposal
include drawing vital dollars away from the areas in greatest need through asset threshold
changes and the cap on bank grantmaking activity, shrinking community development in rural
communities, discouraging small business entrepreneurship and job creation, fracturing
regulatory structures both at the federal and the state level, and exacerbating disinvestment in the
development of affordable housing and community facilities. The aforementioned changes also
serve to limit the effectiveness of several federal, state, and local economic development
initiatives, several of which are part of long-standing policy priorities for this administration to

Positive Gains for Community Development Incentives

Questions 32–33: Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process:
"Illustrative List" and "Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"
We greatly support the creation of a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of eligible
CD activities as paired with a thoughtful, formal process for advanced confirmation of eligibility.
This process would address both a longstanding request from banking institutions for clarity
regarding eligible CD activity and concerns about transparency from community development
organizations. Simultaneously, this would ensure that banks and their community partners, like
CDFIs, have the flexibility to meet the unique capital needs of the communities they serve. This
approach would work best if all the prudential regulators (the OCC, FDIC, and the FRB) worked
collaboratively to maintain consistent standards and establish a single interagency
illustrative list. We urge the regulators to adopt a 30-day response period with a publication of
determinations to ensure community needs are being addressed in a timely fashion.

Question 30: Recognize Opportunity Zones, "Revitalization and Stabilization"
We support the inclusion of Opportunity Zones (OZs) within the revitalization and stabilization
category of community development. Nationally, since its nascence in 2017, the "OZ designation
[has] produced a large, sustained [housing] supply increase in designated low-income tracts, with
an estimated effect of over 416,000 additional active/vacant addresses through 2025Q1,
averaging 47.5 addresses per treated tract" and reflects "new development, not reallocation from
nearby non-OZ areas, showing place based capital-gains tax incentives can stimulate private
investment that increases local housing supply, according to research from the Economic
Innovation Group."3

We have seen firsthand the transformative power of the OZ tool. In 2020, the Chicago Community
Loan Fund (CCLF), a Coalition member, created the Chicagoland Opportunity Zones Consortium
(COZC), bringing together nonprofit, private, and public sector organizations focused on
enhancing community development opportunities in the 183 Opportunity Zones within the City of
Chicago and suburban Cook County. Its membership includes several CDFIs, representatives from
state and local government, academic institutions, and philanthropic organizations, including ones
led by CRA regulated banks. Through its matchmaking, education, and technical assistance work,
COZC has contributed to the creation of over 600 units of affordable housing in underinvested
areas across Chicagoland. The work being done here is becoming a national model with diverse
interest from community development entities and investors from across the country. We believe
that adding this investment incentive through CRA will only serve to heighten the catalytic success
we are currently witnessing.

Question 54: Recognize Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands,"Revitalization
and Stabilization"; "Indian Country and Other Tribal and Native Lands";
We are supportive of expressly recognizing Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands as
targeted geographies within the revitalization and stabilization component of community
development. The long history of these geographies struggling to access credit continues even
today with "none of the three largest home lenders in the US [issuing] federally-guaranteed
mortgages for the construction of new permanent homes within tribal lands".4 Here in Illinois, on
March 24, 2025, the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation was able reclaim part of its lost territory in
Shabbona Lake State Park, a 1,500-acre tract in southern DeKalb County that largely overlaps the
tribe's original home, becoming the first federally recognized tribal reservation in Illinois. This
need for community development investment in this area is strong as evidenced by the $5.45
million that has been invested by CDFIs from our Coalition in this area that has supported over 70
community development projects in this area over the last five years.

Question 31: Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: "Revitalization and
Stabilization — Designated Disaster Areas";
Recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt to, and withstand
natural disasters is an essential step towards creating thriving and resilient communities. CDFIs
frequently provide financing before and after disasters to affordable housing developments,
homeowners, small businesses, and community facilities. We often pair this with well-rounded
technical assistance and lending expertise that helps communities build responsibly with long-
term sustainability in mind. Joining that proactive approach with CRA recognition will strengthen
the caliber of investment necessary to ensure vulnerable communities are more prepared before
disasters occur, lessening the burden on these already distressed geographies during recovery.

The cost and frequency of natural disasters is only climbing. According to the National Oceanic
and Atmospheric Agency (NOAA), "from 1980-2024, there were 403 confirmed weather/climate
disaster events with losses exceeding $1 billion each to affect United States."5 While the overall
average during that time period was nine billion-dollar disaster events per year, isolating just the
final five years of that arc from 2020-2024, the US averaged 23 billion-dollar disaster events per
year. In Illinois, the average for these events jumps from 2.8 per year overall to 7.8 from 2020-
2024. Illinois has faced several severe storms this summer and is currently leading the nation in
tornadoes with 243 preliminary tornado reports this year, establishing a new national record.6

Proposed Changes that Will Reduce Community Development Incentives

As noted previously, several proposed changes within the NPR would negatively impact CDFIs and
community development in general.

Entity Size Threshold Changes
The CRA examination process consists of a tiered system of examination and scrutiny based on
the asset size of the regulated entity. The categories previously consisted of small banks (under
$416 million in assets, intermediate small banks (between $416 million and $1.6 billion in assets),
and large banks ($1.6 billion and above in assets). These bands were adjusted incrementally each
year to account for inflation. In this NPR, the regulators proposed drastically shifting these classes
by redefining small banks as less than $1 billion in assets, renaming the middle tier of banks from
intermediate small banks to intermediate banks and shifting that threshold to between $1 billion
and $10 billion in assets, and raising the threshold for the large bank designation to $10 billion
and above.

While it is important that regulators take steps to properly calibrate these threshold ranges to
ensure that bank CRA requirements are commensurate with their size and reach, this considerable
jump would mean that 800 banks formerly considered intermediate small banks would no longer
receive a community development evaluation as they would now be considered small banks
under the proposed definition and 417 banks, previously considered large, would no longer be
examined under separate CRA investment and services tests and instead would be evaluated
based on their combined community development loans, investments and services, under the
intermediate bank threshold.7 In Illinois specifically, this would translate to 118 out of the 171
banks in our state losing core community development obligations. 68 of these banks would
move from the intermediate small bank designation to the small bank designation losing all their
current community development obligations. An additional 50 banks serving this state would see
their community development obligations severely diminished by moving from the large bank
designation to the new intermediate bank designation.

If the aforementioned entity size thresholds were adopted, it would exacerbate CRA coverage
deserts across the country but particularly here in Illinois. Research conducted by the National
Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) indicates that our state would have the 2nd greatest
loss of CRA regulated banks with CD obligations in the country.8 Across Illinois, this change would
grow the percentage of census tracts that were either in a CD desert or had thin coverage by 50%,

Misalignment with State, Local, and Federal Policy Priorities on Affordable Housing and
Economic Development
One of the most vital parts of the CRA is that it serves as a catalyst for the public-private
partnership that has become a requirement for state, local, and federal programs to work. In
Chicago, several of the city's economic development and housing programs, like the City's
Housing and Economic Development Bond, require participants to prove substantial private
sector backing, often from banks, is available in order to unlock public funds. Another example
would be the Illinois State Small Business Credit Initiative (known as Advantage Illinois) which is
intended to support small business owners who have struggled to attract conventional capital.
Backed by the U.S. Treasury and operated by the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic
Opportunity (DCEO), Advantage Illinois requires proof of private sector investment before DCEO
can invest. Small business applicant eligibility is directly tied to CRA compliance. Because of our
status as trusted community members and our technical assistance and lending expertise, CDFIs
are often the lynchpin to operationalizing the public and private sector partnerships that both
policymakers and financial institutions depend on to achieve their economic development goals.

 Impact on Federal Tax Credit Incentives
Federally, this NPR would weaken the impact of both the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC)
and the NMTC programs, which have been instrumental in the creation and preservation of
affordable housing, building homeownership opportunities, and supporting cornerstone

Several CDFIs within our Coalition have utilized NMTCs, either as direct recipients or in

CRA Data Collection and Transparency
Proper data collection is an essential part of CRA examinations and grading. The asset threshold
changes proposed by the NPR would substantially reduce the number of banks required to
submit large-bank CRA data. In Illinois, it would be nearly a 40% reduction in the amount of
available data. This change would make the community development landscape more opaque
and make it harder for community stakeholders, CDFIs, policymakers, and regulators at all levels
to accurately address community needs, assess credit gaps, compare bank performance, and
identify geographic disparities. Maintaining high standards for data collection is the only way to
tell whether bank performance is laudatory or in need of correction.

This impact of this missing data would be particularly harmful to small business development.
Given the limited data on small business lending and the pending status of section 1071 of the
Dodd-Frank, the information that comes from these CRA exams is the most reliable publicly
available small business lending data. These proposed changes will result in an 11% reduction in
CRA small business lending data nationally and a 14% reduction in our state. In Illinois, small
businesses, in addition to being excellent economic engines, are also primary job creators.
According to the Illinois Policy Institute, as of November 2025, small businesses created virtually
all of the jobs in Illinois' largest county, Cook County, since the COVID-19 pandemic. "Nationwide,
businesses with fewer than 20 employees have been responsible for 81% of job growth since the
pandemic, statewide the figure is 99% and in Cook County 100%."17 The small business data
generated by CRA is central to making sure that all Americans are able to have stable
employment and generate wealth.

Community Development Performance and Lending Activity
Questions 12-17: Complexity Definition
Overall, this NPR relies too heavily on lending activity as the benchmark for meeting community
development needs and fails to fully account for the nuance of how bank activity supports
community development. This proposal ties the definition of complexity for CD investments,
grants, and services primarily to whether the activity is a necessary or beneficial component of a
multicomponent financing transaction involving a loan. For CDFIs, this narrow definition misses
the vital work we do to provide specialized expertise, layered capital, subordinate positions,
public subsidies, risk sharing, guarantees, tax-credit structures, patient repayment terms, or
other features that make transactions complex even when they are not directly paired with a
particular bank loan. Complexity isn't automatically more responsive to community needs than
innovation, flexibility or impact. It is our hope that the agencies would prioritize the characteristics
and community value of the activity, including complexity, innovativeness, flexibility, impact, and
responsiveness over whether it is associated with a lending transaction.

Section IV.B: Intermediate Bank Performance Tests
Currently, intermediate small banks are required to perform at a level of Satisfactory on both their
lending test and CD test in order to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. This proposal would not
only move many of the current banks with these obligations into the small bank category
removing this evaluation entirely but it would also allow a bank to perform below a Satisfactory
grade on their CD test and still receive an overall Satisfactory rating if they were able to score a
Satisfactory or better grade on their lending test. Deemphasizing the CD test would lessen the
likelihood for banks to partner with CDFIs, provide grants, or engage in other community
development activities. It is imperative that we keep the standards for CD activity high, particularly
as the need for CDFI partnership is continuing to increase, according to a 2025 report from the
Federal Bank of Richmond.20

Large Bank CD Performance
For the banks that would retain their large bank designation under the NPR, they will continue to
be permitted to receive CRA credit for community development activities outside of their
assessment areas provided they meet the newly formalized standards for how much community
development activity those banks must do within their assessment areas first. The baseline the
NPR establishes of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital in community development grants and investments
and 0.625% in community development lending to avoid a failing exam rating creates an implicit
Satisfactory level of performance within the bank assessment area. According to analysis
conducted by NCRC, of the 69 largest banks regulated by the OCC and FDIC, the median amount
of Tier 1 capital dedicated to community development lending was 6.83%; for community
development grants and investments, the median was 3.58%. Both of these marks sit well above
the default line created by the NPR and could create a race to the bottom and a sharp decline in
bank community development performance in areas that they have the most direct duty to serve.

Question 34: Flexibility Across and Outside of Assessment Areas
Creating greater flexibility in the allocation of CD activities across multiple assessment areas could
be exceedingly beneficial for bank investment in CDFIs that have a statewide, regional, or national
focus. One-third of the current Coalition membership have a meaningful portion of their work
outside of the area in which they are headquartered. Assigning an entire bank investment to their
respective headquarters locations would not accurately represent the communities benefiting
from the capital. Regarding geographic flexibility for CD activities outside of assessment areas,
this kind of activity should be additive and complementary and in no way disruptive or displacive
of core activity happening within assessment areas. This is most helpful when working to fill
community development gaps in CRA deserts.

Questions 4–7: Retail Product Lending and Protecting Specialized CD Lending
The NPR proposes to shift the bank retail lending evaluation to focus only on activity in a bank's
major product lines. For large banks in particular, this could potentially create a significant
mismatch between evolving community needs and bank lending priorities. For example, a
community in great need of home mortgages could conflict with the priorities of the large banks
in their area who might be primarily focused on other activities, further camouflaging the
economic development gaps in that community. It also would allow a loan in a retail product line
outside of a bank's major product lines to receive consideration as a CD loan if the loan otherwise
satisfies the community development definition. While this could be helpful in some cases, there
is a risk that banks could use this as opportunity to substitute ordinary course of business activity
for more specialized development lending that depends more directly on CRA incentives.

Prioritizing Community Infrastructure and Facilities in Community Development Definition
CRA consideration for essential community facilities and infrastructure is particularly helpful
in rural communities, Indian Country, distressed areas, and other markets with limited access
to conventional capital. The proposed eligibility for essential community infrastructure and
facilities serving specified targeted areas is overly broad and would obviate banks of their
responsibility to demonstrate that these projects would help attract or retain businesses or
residents. It would also allow community-wide infrastructure to receive CRA consideration without
ensuring that a specified share is allocated to benefit to LMI individuals. A major unintended
consequence here is that large infrastructure transactions routinely financed in the conventional
market could compete with harder to finance opportunities that need additional support like
affordable housing, CDFI financing, small business lending, and other activities more dependent
on CRA incentives. We urge that any flexibility given regarding community infrastructure and
facilities financing doesn't displace highly targeted CD activity for infrastructure transactions that
can easily find support through traditional means.

Questions 38–46 and 53: Strategic Plan Guardrails
Given the level of latitude that strategic plans provide to banks in developing their individualized
CRA performance standards, it is incumbent upon the regulators to provide firm guardrails that
certify banks are living up to the letter and intent of the CRA. These bright-line requirements
should prioritize responsiveness to community needs and have a transparent and measurable
verification method to keep them compliant with what would be expected under the standard
CRA tests. Verification should be subject to meaningful public engagement and evaluated against
clear benchmarks for determining whether the goals adequately address assessment-area credit
needs. We particularly urge the agencies to establish strong standards in responding to Question
53, which asks when measurable goals should be considered inadequate to address assessment-
area needs.



Conclusion

When asked why PNC Bank and other CRA-regulated financial institutions chose to stand with
CDFIs despite the challenges that the industry has faced over the past few years, Thurman "Tony"
Smith, Senior Vice President of Community Development–Midwest at PNC Bank, gave a very
simple answer, "the results speak for themselves. CDFI's work! And that work is so much more
than remarkable!"21 As the regulators consider how to improve the CRA for vulnerable
communities during this time of great economic uncertainty, we urge them to prioritize and

To whom it may concern:

Texas Housers appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed rule
regarding Community Reinvestment Act Regulations.

Texas Housers is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization founded in 1988 that advocates alongside
low-income Texans for housing that is affordable, stable, dignified, and fair. Our mission is to
support low-income Texans' efforts to achieve the dream of a decent, affordable home in a
quality neighborhood of their choosing. We work toward these goals through research, policy,
and collaboration with community organizations. Texas Housers offers the following comments.

Texas Housers strongly opposes the proposed rule to weaken requirements under the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) and urges the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC) and Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) to withdraw this rule in its entirety.

The proposed rule should be withdrawn because it will cause the following harms:

THREATENS FUNDING FOR AFFORDABLE HOUSING
The proposed rule will significantly reduce incentives for investments in affordable housing.
Redefining asset thresholds would remove community development investment obligations for
81 banks in Texas (48 regulated by the FDIC, 32 by the OCC), more than any other state.1
Question 1 proposes going even further to redefine asset thresholds, risking even more
investment. This would have a significant negative impact on the ability to finance affordable
units, particularly deeply affordable units and units in smaller metropolitan areas and rural
markets.

1 https://ncrc.org/cra/


Texas Housers frequently works with low-income tenants of affordable rental housing funded
through investments incentivized by CRA requirements, particularly properties that receive
Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs). As a result, we closely monitor state programs and
are heavily involved in the annual update to Texas' Qualified Allocation Plan that guides the
award of LIHTC funding. The proposed changes would reduce the demand for LIHTCs,
countering the positive changes increasing funding and investment in the 21st Century ROAD
to Housing Act. LIHTC is a key source of funding for affordable housing that provides a lifeline
for many tenants struggling with housing stability, including those with Housing Choice
Vouchers. LIHTC properties must accept vouchers, making them an important resource for
voucher holders given the lack of federal or state source of income protections.

LIHTC is far from the only federal program that depends on private investment in order to build
affordable housing. The proposal would not only severely harm the ability to secure financing
for development, but would upend incentives that drive private investment that many federal
programs rely on to function (e.g., match funds for the HOME Investment Partnerships
Program).

We are currently experiencing a housing shortage that most severely impacts the
lowest-income residents. Among renters, households making at or below 50% AMI are those
most in need of affordable housing and the need is particularly severe for households making
at most 30% AMI. Per the National Low Income Housing Coalition's Gap Report, there are just
26 affordable and accessible units for every 100 ELI households.2 That number drops to just 17
units in the Houston MSA and 18 units in the Dallas-Fort Worth MSA.

We regularly hear from tenants in "affordable" units that still cannot afford their housing. Texas
desperately needs more rental units affordable and available to households making less than or
equal to 30% AMI, but these units are also the most difficult to finance. Incentives like those
currently in the CRA are essential to create or preserve deeply affordable units.

ENABLES DISINVESTMENT IN LOW-INCOME COMMUNITIES OF COLOR
The CRA was created to require banks to support the needs of all members of the community
in the wake of redlining. Weakening CRA requirements will drive disinvestment in the same
vulnerable communities the CRA was passed to protect and strengthen.

The proposal will put 643 branches in low- to moderate-income (LMI) communities and 1,191
branches in communities of color at risk, more than any other state.3 These branch closures
have direct impacts on low-income families. Access to branches and affordable banking
services can determine whether families are able to receive income, build savings, establish
banking relationships, and obtain responsible credit. Branch closures may increase the use of
3 https://ncrc.org/cra/
2 https://nlihc.org/gap/state/tx

alternative, often predatory, financial services such as payday lenders and check-cashing
services.

These closures exacerbate existing vulnerabilities. Many lower-income, rural, older, and
disabled consumers prefer in-person banking and communities of color are already losing bank
branches at a disproportionate rate.4 While use of online banking services is on the rise,
households without internet access are more likely to be lower-income, rural, and older, as well
as people of color.

Branch closures also have ripple effects. Closing bank branches has been shown to reduce
small business lending.5 While availability of mobile apps can reduce the impact, this effect is
most pronounced for high-income census tracts and high-rated apps. This means that the
proposed rule will disproportionately impact small business lending for lower-income
communities.

Branch closures are also associated with increases in eviction filings, primarily in urban areas.6
Evictions (which disproportionately impact communities of color) negatively impact
employment, financial stability, future housing stability, and increase the risk of homelessness.7
Evictions are not just destabilizing at the household level; they have community-level health
impacts.8

Eliminating the "purpose test" removes requirements that investments promote economic
development through permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for LMI individuals.
Expanding qualifying infrastructure area-benefit projects could result in projects with little
benefit to low-income individuals. These proposals weaken the connection between
CRA-driven investment and meaningful community and economic development.

An investment alone is not enough to revitalize a community or spur further development.
Similar issues with the LIHTC program led the IRS to issue a notice stating that properties only
qualify for the "concerted community revitalization plan"preference if "...there is an added
benefit to the neighborhood in the form of the project's contribution to a concerted community
revitalization plan."9 The proposal weakens and eliminates requirements that support more
meaningful and impactful investment.

8 https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0277953623008535

Disinvestment driven by weakened CRA requirements could even increase neighborhood flood

already vulnerable neighborhoods, leaving them more vulnerable to disaster damage, less able
to recover, and less able to proactively mitigate damage from future disasters.

CONCLUSION
A strong and effective CRA is necessary to drive investment to underserved communities.
While there is room to improve current CRA requirements, this proposal is a step in the wrong

The FDIC and OCC should rescind this rule to preserve CRA requirements that ensure equal

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN
3064-AG31]

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould,

On behalf of New Jersey Citizen Action (NJCA), we submit this comment in opposition to the Notice
of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would
significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of
the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any
proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income
communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify
supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.

New Jersey Citizen Action is a statewide community- and coalition-based organization that works to
empower, organize and mobilize communities through issue advocacy, education, and the provision of
free direct services in an effort to eliminate social, racial and economic inequities so that all New
Jerseyans have opportunities to thrive and prosper. As a longtime member of the National Community
Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC), for more than four decades NJCA has worked to ensure banks
serving New Jersey families comply with the spirit of the federal Community Reinvestment Act and its
requirement for affirmative, equitable lending and investment in historically redlined communities,
specifically by negotiating CRA agreements totaling more than $45 billion in commitments for
affordable lending, economic and small business development across the Garden State. In addition to
these efforts, NJCA provides free direct services to nearly 20,000 low- and moderate-income families
across the state each year. These services, which are an extension of our economic justice work, are


1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).


2


designed to lift families out of poverty and promote economic opportunities for all and in many ways
would not be possible without the Community Reinvestment Act, and the access it provides to basic
banking and credit within the low-and moderate-income communities we serve.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that
banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and
deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced
redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change
how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit
organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis
of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have
experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

REDUCTION IN COMMUNITY INVESTMENT EXPECTATIONS FOR ALL BANKS

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In New Jersey, from 2010-
2024, banks made $87.9 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI
census tracts and $35.6 billion in CRA qualified lending to small businesses. Overall, during this time
banks lent nearly $138 billion in CRA-qualified mortgages and small business loans across the state.
Without CRA, there would be significantly less opportunities for homeownership and
entrepreneurship.

New Jersey Citizen Action is concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest
in communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted
to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA
rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the percentage the National Community
Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the largest banks currently devote to community
investments and loans.

NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC and FDIC
supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently conduct
approximately $102 billion annually in community development loans and investments inside their
assessment areas, and that the median percentage of annual community development lending in
assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital, and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA
qualified investments.3 If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate
thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined


2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks surpass a
benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625% for investments. 91 Fed.
Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical effect of this proposal is that the
benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept. 10, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-risk/.


3


activity would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make their CRA
compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set strategic plan
benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of community development activity.4

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If regulators
lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the communities they
serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, across New Jersey low-
and moderate-income families continue to face significant affordability challenges driven by rising
housing costs, the highest property taxes in the nation, healthcare expenses, and inflation. According to
the National Low Income Housing Coalition, full-time New Jersey workers must earn $39.99 per hour
to afford a modest 2-bedroom apartment, while on average, they earn only $23.97 per hour, making
New Jersey the seventh most expensive state for renters. Nearly half of New Jersey renter households
are considered cost-burdened, spending over 30 percent of their income on housing, while affordable
housing supply remains far below demand. In fact, across New Jersey there is a shortage of at least
240,000 affordable rental units. Rising rent and home prices have increasingly impacted not only low-
income residents but also working- and moderate-income families struggling to remain in the
communities where they work. As housing costs continue to outpace wage growth, many families face
reduced financial stability, difficulty saving for homeownership, and increased risk of housing
insecurity. These conditions disproportionately impact communities of color, with the New Jersey
Institute of Social Justice reporting that New Jersey's stark racial wealth gap, which is one of the
largest in the country, has doubled in the last decade from $300,000 to $640,000. Such a reduction in
community development investments and loans would only further the homeownership and racial
wealth gaps across our state, as affordable loans would become less available to traditionally
underserved communities, with many LMI families instead turning to high-cost financial products and
services. It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs.
Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce
lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether
communities that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be
disproportionately affected.

LESS COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT SCRUTINY OF BANKS

The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated
under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while banks with
assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less demanding
intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to large banks.5 The
proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently


4 NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept 1, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.

5 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,120–23 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).


4


applicable to large banks for institutions with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on small-
business, small-farm and community development lending.6

Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation because the
proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion.7 The 417 banks newly
classified as intermediate rather than large would no longer be examined under separate CRA
investment and services tests and instead would be evaluated based on their combined community
development loans, investments and services. These reclassifications and resulting eliminations of
community development obligations for over 800 banks and separate investment evaluations for 400
banks, may worsen the housing crisis by reducing the demand for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC). In New Jersey, the impact would be devastating for low- and moderate-income communities
across the state: 13 of 82 banks, or 15.9 percent would lose their community development obligations.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-income
communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable mortgage credit and
homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business financing; and
neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small businesses and other
community development. For example, in 2025 the average home price was $680,000 as reported by
New Jersey's Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency, with home prices continuing to rise while
housing inventory fell by more than 20 percent from 2020 levels. These high prices and upfront costs
make it harder for first-time and LMI new Jersey buyers to qualify and save for a down payment.
Moreover, according to Census data at $2,797 per month New Jersey ranked among the states with the
highest monthly homeownership costs, including mortgage payments, property taxes, insurance and
other selected expenses. As indicated above, these conditions disproportionately impact communities
of color, as New Jersey has one of the largest racial wealth gaps in the country at $640,000 as reported
by the New Jersey Institute of Social Justice.

The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply because a
bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA obligations and
scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that would move into less
rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those institutions serve, analyze the
lending and community development activity that would receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the
effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income communities or communities that have
experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

BANK BRANCHES AND ACCESS TO BANKING SERVICES

By raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion, 417 banks would no longer receive the full large-
bank examination, including a separate service test that evaluates branch delivery systems and banking
services. We are concerned that approximately 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census

6 Id. at 52,120.
7 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-
cra-rollbacks/.


5


tracts would no longer be evaluated as part of the large-bank CRA service test under the proposal, and
more than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census tracts would also lose CRA
consideration. In 28 states, at least one-third of branches located in LMI census tracts would no longer
receive any CRA evaluation.8 In New Jersey, 28 of 63 banks, or 44.4 percent, would lose their large-
bank status and 70 of 462 LMI branches, or 15.2 percent, would be jeopardized. Additionally, 136 of
741 branches, or 18.4 percent of branches in communities of color would be jeopardized.

The proposal would also narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service test. Today,
examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information about the costs
and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit services, removing
deposit products such as checking and savings accounts from direct evaluation under the service test.9
As such, examiners would no longer evaluate whether those products are affordable and responsive to
community needs even though 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.10 CRA review of the cost and features of deposit products has played an important
role in encouraging banks to address these disparities by providing affordable products.
Our organization works with communities where access to mainstream banking services remains a
serious concern. For many of the 20,000 low- and moderate-income individuals and families that
access our services each year, including the nearly 6,000 families who receive free tax preparation
services from our Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) program annually, many of these families
often rely on high-cost fringe financial products and services, including check cashers, high-cost tax
preparation services, and/or other alternative financial services. For the people we serve, bank branches
and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from access to credit and economic opportunity. They
can determine whether families can safely receive income, build savings, establish banking
relationships and obtain responsible credit.
New Jersey Citizen Action is therefore concerned that under the proposal, examiners will no longer
evaluate whether banks that are still subject to the service test offer affordable checking and savings
accounts. By reducing the importance of deposit services and branch performance in CRA evaluations,
the proposal eliminates incentives for banks to offer basic products that help unbanked and
underbanked households. Before finalizing these changes, the agencies should identify which
communities would receive less scrutiny of bank branches and services, determine whether the effects
would fall disproportionately on low- and moderate-income communities or communities of color, and
explain why the changes are justified despite those consequences.



8 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-
cra-rollbacks/.
9 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,126 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
10 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-
cra-rollbacks/.



6

SUPPORT FOR LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS
New Jersey Citizen Action is also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community
development grants and nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-
business development, financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and
other community-based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit
organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep
relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.11 For
smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying
program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources over which to
spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may
not maintain financial records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would
need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more
difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities
are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can play in
supporting community development. For a state like New Jersey, there is a small but competitive
network of private foundations. For these reasons, nonprofit service providers rely heavily on
partnerships with financial institutions, and more specifically, grant funding from large banks. For
New Jersey Citizen Action, our free financial empowerment programs and services, including our
statewide HUD-certified housing counseling program, tax preparation services, and financial coaching
program, among others, rely heavily on bank support, especially at a time when federal funding
opportunities have become more limited.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community development
activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond the banks
themselves.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed documentation
requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or redirect bank support away from
smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with limited administrative capacity. The agencies
must also determine whether those effects would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and
moderate-income communities. More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule
primarily in terms of reducing perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also
determine what the changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.

11 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).


7

CONCLUSION
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under
the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development
activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color;
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability; and
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the OCC
and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and
released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant
declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The
proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank
classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other
core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from community
organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated
regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected organizations to
evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and
provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base any final rule. New Jersey Citizen
Action therefore requests that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least
60 days.

Sincerely,



Leila Amirhamzeh
Director of Community Reinvestment
New Jersey Citizen Action

To Whom it May Concern:
The Legal Defense Fund (LDF) submits this comment to strongly oppose the Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) (collectively, "agencies") regarding proposed
changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The CRA plays a crucial role in
advancing equity in housing, credit, and lending for Black people and other communities of
color as well as low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. The proposed changes would
weaken community development oversight, reduce lending-data transparency, and exclude
deposit services from the service test, thereby undermining efforts to address persistent racial
inequities in access to financial services. In particular, the changes to the asset size threshold
classification would decrease financial opportunities for Black communities by omitting
institutions with fewer assets from several requirements including data collection, maintenance,
and reporting. Also, proposed changes to the service test fail to help comprehensively assist in
meeting the needs of Black communities. The agencies also fail to adequately account for
reliance interests arising from longstanding examination requirements and community
partnerships and to recognize Special Purpose Credit Programs (SPCPs) as critical mechanisms
enabling lenders to proactively create pathways to credit for underserved populations. The
proposed changes to the CRA regulations would deepen racial discrimination in lending
practices and violate the intent of the statute. LDF strongly urges the agencies to withdraw the
proposed rule.
Founded in 1940 by Thurgood Marshall, LDF is the nation's premier racial justice law
organization. LDF has long fought for racial and economic justice for Black communities and
people of color, including by leading advocacy against redlining and discrimination in housing,
credit, and lending. LDF lawyers, for example, have worked on fair housing and economic
justice efforts early on through cases including Shelley v. Kraemer (1948) and McGhee v. Sipes
(1948).1 Today, economic justice remains a critical concern of Black communities, and LDF has

I.
The CRA Remains Critical to Addressing Redlining and Persistent Racial
Inequity
A. Congress Enacted the CRA to Address Discriminatory Access to Credit in Lending and
Investments
Although the 1968 Fair Housing Act and 1974 Equal Credit Opportunity Act outlawed racial
discrimination in housing and credit sectors, the practice of redlining nonetheless persisted well
into the following decades.4 Banks continued to discriminate against Black, and other non-white
neighborhoods based on Federal Housing Administration (FHA) mortgage criteria labeling
predominantly Black neighborhoods as "risky."5 Despite enacted civil rights statutes, redlining
persisted, leading to the long-term withholding of investment in Black and other neighborhoods
and preventing Black families from accessing credit and wealth-building opportunities, such as
through homeownership.6 As discussed below, the legacy of redlining continues to limit Black
communities' economic stability and opportunity.
Congress passed the CRA to address gaps in the other civil rights legislation which "did not
tackle geographic forms of discrimination that left entire communities destitute."7 The CRA
requires regulators to assess a financial institution's record of "meeting the credit needs of the
entire community, including low-and moderate-income [LMI] neighborhoods."8 Regulators
evaluate banks' qualifying activities, such as mortgage, consumer, and business lending, in the
areas where they have deposit-taking operations. Regulators then use these evaluations to issue

In passing the CRA, Congress intended to target racial discrimination in credit access
and lending, including those intended for home mortgages and businesses, which perpetuates
disinvestment.10 The goal of the CRA was to "protect consumer interests"11 and tackle the
nefarious effects of redlining and racial discrimination in the economic sphere. Notably, the
CRA's legislative history emphasizes a demand for private institutions—namely, banks—to help
remediate harms of redlining, rather than relegating this responsibility to the public sector
alone.12 The CRA's framework is grounded in prioritizing implementation of community
feedback, along with banks' roles in meaningfully serving their local communities.13 To
effectuate the CRA's intent and meet the community's needs, the CRA framework solicits public
and community comment and input on banks' actions, including on merger applications and
anticipated impacts on local communities.14 Banks, in return, must consider and be responsive
to this feedback—they are indeed mandated to do so given their enjoyment of distinct benefits
and profit from their local communities.15

Community Organizations Have a Reliance Interest in the CRA Framework

the past decades—including through increased mortgage grants,16 encouraging investment in
Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC),17 and generating "more than $1 trillion in loans for
community development and $1 trillion for small businesses located in low- and moderate-
income census tracts." Additionally, the CRA's current regulations have created a substantial
reliance interest in banks subject to CRA regulations. When organizations or banks make
substantial investments or structural changes based on existing federal rules, agencies must

Community groups have successfully negotiated CBAs across a wide range of settings and issue

finalized, community groups would have fewer levers to use when bargaining with financial
institutions because many banks would be reclassified based on asset thresholds and would no
longer face separate investment and service tests, while banks reclassified as small would no
longer be subject to a community development evaluation. The proposed changes would also
prevent the collection and evaluation of evidence to demonstrate unmet need and ongoing
lending disparities. The CRA was intended to help increase credit access for Black and LMI
communities and CBAs have helped advance this goal. The agencies should not adopt proposed
changes that will impede the creation and success of CBAs and thus frustrate the intent of the
CRA.

II.
The Proposed Higher Asset Size Thresholds and Changes to the Service
Test Lack a Reasoned Basis and Will Further Entrench Racial Inequity
In order for an agency action to be valid under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), it
must be the product of "reasoned decision making."37 Agency actions, including regulations, are
arbitrary and capricious in violation of the APA when, among other things, the agency has
"entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem, offered an explanation for its
decision that runs counter to the evidence before the agency, or is so implausible that it could
not be ascribed to a difference in view or the product of agency expertise."38 Here, the agencies
proposed changes to asset size threshold and excluding deposit services are arbitrary and
capricious because the agency fails to offer a sufficient justification for such a drastic change,
which also frustrates the CRA's original intent.
A. Changes to Asset Size Threshold
Under the NPRM's proposed changes, the agencies would substantially increase the asset
size thresholds governing bank classifications, potentially worsening the racial wealth gap. CRA
regulations provide banks are evaluated under different CRA examination procedures based on
their asset-size threshold amounts. Under the current thresholds, small banks have assets below
$412 million, intermediate small banks have assets from $412 million to less than $1.649 billion,
and large banks have assets of $1.649 billion or more. The proposal would raise the small-bank
threshold to $1 billion and classify banks with assets from $1 billion through $10 billion as
intermediate banks; only banks with assets exceeding $10 billion would be classified as large
banks. Small banks are generally evaluated using the "Retail Lending Test" under the CRA.39
The Retail Lending Test evaluates a bank's record of helping to meet the credit needs of its
entire community through the bank's origination and purchase of home mortgage loans,
multifamily loans, small business loans, and small farm loans.40 Intermediate Small Banks
(ISBs) are evaluated under the Community Development (CD) test in addition to the small bank
retail lending test. The CD test measures the extent to which an institution engages in
community development activities. In evaluating the responsiveness of a bank's community
development activities, examiners review the volume, mix, and qualitative aspects of community
development loans, of qualified investments, and of community development services.41 The CD
test focuses on determining whether an institution understands and is responsive to the
community development needs of its assessment area(s).42

B. Excluding Deposit Services from the Service Test
Under the NPRM's proposed changes, the Service Test will only evaluate credit services
rather than deposit services. A service test evaluates a bank's record of helping to meet
community credit needs by assessing the bank's services and community development services.
Any proposed change potentially leading to restricted access to deposit services will prevent
Black communities from building wealth and savings. The statutory text of the CRA clearly
states financial institutions are required to meet "the credit needs of its entire community."61
However, a sole focus on credit services while excluding deposit services will likely lead to the
failure of institutions meeting the needs of entire communities. Under the reformed Service
Test, banks would be disincentivized to provide and expand access to deposit services. However,
in order to advance racial justice and overcome present-day barriers, banks must ensure access
to deposit services, particularly among Black communities, which are disproportionately
underbanked compared to white communities.62
Because of past historical lending practices, Black communities are more likely to utilize
alternative financial services—such as check cashers, cash advance loans, check advance loans,
and payday lenders–which are notoriously predatory, and have significantly higher interest
rates and service fees.63 Black households experience significantly higher rates of being
unbanked or underbanked compared to white households64 and this proposed change would
further deepen this disparity. On the contrary, increasing banking depository access could save
Black and Hispanics up to $40,000 over their lifetime.65 The proposed changes to the service
test could impact depository services Black communities depend on in their daily lives. The

III.
The Agencies Should Explicitly Recognize Special Purpose Credit
Programs
In the 2023 CRA final rule, the agencies included Special Purpose Credit Programs (SPCPs)
authorized under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA).66 The current proposed CRA rule
omits SPCPs, which have proven to be quite beneficial for local communities and financial
intuitions to increase opportunities for economically disadvantaged communities. SPCPs are a
targeted lending or credit product that allows for favorable credit terms to economically
disadvantaged or historically underserved groups who might otherwise be denied credit.67
SPCPs are explicitly authorized under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) and Regulation
B as a legal exception to general anti-discrimination laws, provided they are properly designed
and documented.68 From 2022-2024, SPCPs backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac helped
nearly 58,000 economically disadvantaged persons fairly access homeownership and the ability
to build wealth for their families. According to the Federal Housing Finance Agency, those loans
generated $17.2 billion in positive economic impact.69 Given the success SPCPs have had at
increasing credit opportunities for economically disadvantaged communities the agencies fail to
meet the needs of the community by excluding SPCPs as responsive credit products under CRA.
If the agencies were to add SPCPs as responsive credit products offered under the CRA more
banks and financial institutions would be open to creating their own SPCPs and increase credit
access for economically disadvantaged communities.
IV.
Discriminatory Lending Must Meaningfully Affect CRA Ratings
LDF opposes limiting consideration of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices to
violations cited in public enforcement actions or judicial orders involving a Federal or State
agency. This approach would exclude violations identified through supervision unless they
result in such public action, allowing CRA ratings to overlook documented harm to Black
borrowers and communities. The agencies' alternative option would preserve consideration of
violations cited in examination reports and nonpublic enforcement actions while protecting
confidential supervisory information.70 The agencies should retain this flexibility and ensure
discriminatory lending meaningfully affects overall CRA ratings and relevant performance-test
and geographic ratings.71

A. Congress Enacted the CRA to Address Discriminatory Access to Credit in Lending and

discrimination in housing and credit sectors, the practice of redlining nonetheless persisted well
into the following decades.4 Banks continued to discriminate against Black, and other non-white
neighborhoods based on Federal Housing Administration (FHA) mortgage criteria labeling
predominantly Black neighborhoods as "risky."5 Despite enacted civil rights statutes, redlining
persisted, leading to the long-term withholding of investment in Black and other neighborhoods
and preventing Black families from accessing credit and wealth-building opportunities, such as
through homeownership.6 As discussed below, the legacy of redlining continues to limit Black
communities' economic stability and opportunity.
Congress passed the CRA to address gaps in the other civil rights legislation which "did not
tackle geographic forms of discrimination that left entire communities destitute."7 The CRA
requires regulators to assess a financial institution's record of "meeting the credit needs of the
entire community, including low-and moderate-income [LMI] neighborhoods."8 Regulators

II.
The Proposed Higher Asset Size Thresholds and Changes to the Service
Test Lack a Reasoned Basis and Will Further Entrench Racial Inequity
In order for an agency action to be valid under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), it
must be the product of "reasoned decision making."37 Agency actions, including regulations, are
arbitrary and capricious in violation of the APA when, among other things, the agency has
"entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem, offered an explanation for its
decision that runs counter to the evidence before the agency, or is so implausible that it could
not be ascribed to a difference in view or the product of agency expertise."38 Here, the agencies
proposed changes to asset size threshold and excluding deposit services are arbitrary and
capricious because the agency fails to offer a sufficient justification for such a drastic change,
which also frustrates the CRA's original intent.
A. Changes to Asset Size Threshold
Under the NPRM's proposed changes, the agencies would substantially increase the asset
size thresholds governing bank classifications, potentially worsening the racial wealth gap. CRA
regulations provide banks are evaluated under different CRA examination procedures based on
their asset-size threshold amounts. Under the current thresholds, small banks have assets below
$412 million, intermediate small banks have assets from $412 million to less than $1.649 billion,
and large banks have assets of $1.649 billion or more. The proposal would raise the small-bank
threshold to $1 billion and classify banks with assets from $1 billion through $10 billion as
intermediate banks; only banks with assets exceeding $10 billion would be classified as large
banks. Small banks are generally evaluated using the "Retail Lending Test" under the CRA.39
The Retail Lending Test evaluates a bank's record of helping to meet the credit needs of its
entire community through the bank's origination and purchase of home mortgage loans,
multifamily loans, small business loans, and small farm loans.40 Intermediate Small Banks
(ISBs) are evaluated under the Community Development (CD) test in addition to the small bank
retail lending test. The CD test measures the extent to which an institution engages in
community development activities. In evaluating the responsiveness of a bank's community
development activities, examiners review the volume, mix, and qualitative aspects of community
development loans, of qualified investments, and of community development services.41 The CD
test focuses on determining whether an institution understands and is responsive to the
community development needs of its assessment area(s).42

In the 2023 CRA final rule, the agencies included Special Purpose Credit Programs (SPCPs)
authorized under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA).66 The current proposed CRA rule
omits SPCPs, which have proven to be quite beneficial for local communities and financial
intuitions to increase opportunities for economically disadvantaged communities. SPCPs are a
targeted lending or credit product that allows for favorable credit terms to economically
disadvantaged or historically underserved groups who might otherwise be denied credit.67
SPCPs are explicitly authorized under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) and Regulation
B as a legal exception to general anti-discrimination laws, provided they are properly designed
and documented.68 From 2022-2024, SPCPs backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac helped
nearly 58,000 economically disadvantaged persons fairly access homeownership and the ability
to build wealth for their families. According to the Federal Housing Finance Agency, those loans
generated $17.2 billion in positive economic impact.69 Given the success SPCPs have had at
increasing credit opportunities for economically disadvantaged communities the agencies fail to
meet the needs of the community by excluding SPCPs as responsive credit products under CRA.
If the agencies were to add SPCPs as responsive credit products offered under the CRA more
banks and financial institutions would be open to creating their own SPCPs and increase credit
access for economically disadvantaged communities.

To Whom it May Concern,
The National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders (NALCAB) is a
nonpartisan Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) intermediary
and national network that represents and serves over 200 economic development
organizations across the country. We help build our members' capacity to drive
economic growth in their communities by providing affordable capital through our
lending and grantmaking practice alongside technical assistance focused on
organizational development and leadership training. We appreciate the opportunity
to comment on the FDIC and OCC's proposed changes to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA).
Enacted in 1977, the CRA was intended to address the history of financial exclusion
that limited minority and low- to moderate-income (LMI) communities' access to
capital and financial services. Congress asserted that the privileges of a bank
charter, namely low-cost deposit insurance from the FDIC and inexpensive credit
from the Federal Reserve and the Federal Home Loan Banks, obligate chartered
banks to meet the needs of all communities they serve. With the passage of the
CRA, Congress sought to ensure that, consistent with the safe and sound operation
of such institutions, banks fulfill an affirmative obligation to serve the credit needs
of the local communities where they conduct business.
Importantly, Congress designed the CRA as an incentive-based framework rather
than a punitive mandate. Neither the original 1977 statute nor subsequent
regulatory revisions established lending quotas or mandatory lending targets.
Instead, a bank's record of community development lending, investment, and
service is positively considered when regulators evaluate applications for mergers,
acquisitions, and branch expansion. CRA performance has always been evaluated

within the context of local market conditions and the safe and sound operation of

While critics characterize the CRA as an unwelcome regulatory burden, research
suggests the opposite: requiring banks to adequately serve their local communities
opens access to budding lending markets they would not otherwise enter without
subjecting these communities to undue risk. For example, a 2018 study by the
Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia found that CRA-covered banks received more
small business loan applications and originated more of these loans in LMI
communities than would have in the absence of CRA.1 This research suggests that
by requiring institutions to serve overlooked borrowers and communities, the CRA
actually opens up sound lending opportunities that would otherwise go unnoticed.
Economic development organizations, such as community lenders and affordable
housing developers, work collaboratively with banks to help deliver capital and
services to underserved communities. These organizations leverage on-the-ground
experience and deep community ties to maximize the impact of banks' CRA
investments. These investments are not intended to benefit community
development organizations themselves, but rather to address the legacy of financial
exclusion that continues to constrain economic opportunity in communities of color
and LMI communities.
NALCAB's members and partners see the effects of these dynamics every day.
When well-designed and informed by communities, CRA rules strengthen the
partnerships through which banks and community organizations direct capital to

IV. Proposed Limits to Operational Expenses for Community Grants
NALCAB is deeply concerned by the proposed cap on operational expenses for
community development (CD) grants. The rule calls for a strict 15 percent cap on
indirect expenses for qualifying community development grants made by large
banks looking to receive CRA credit. It also places a more subjective restriction on
small and intermediate sized banks, requiring that their CD grants be "directly
used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of
community development." The proposed rule justifies this change by arguing it
would help ensure grant dollars are benefiting local communities directly rather
than subsidizing nonprofit grantees who deliver these CD services. It also argues
that indirect grants given to intermediary nonprofit organizations that support
other nonprofits, rather than provide community services themselves, siphon off
funds that would otherwise directly benefit LMI communities.
As such, the proposed rule frames intermediaries as unnecessary middlemen, but
without them, many banks would have difficulty directing resources to the LMI
communities CRA is meant to support. Intermediaries identify and evaluate local
partners, coordinate funding from multiple sources, build organizational capacity,
and ensure accountability. As a CDFI intermediary, NALCAB channels bank
capital to a national network of trusted nonprofits and provides hands-on support
that strengthens these organizations' operations and impact. This gives banks an
efficient way to meet their CRA obligations while ensuring capital reaches the
communities it is meant to serve. By potentially disallowing CRA credit for
investment in intermediaries, the proposed rule could sever the connection between
banks and the local organizations best positioned to serve LMI communities.
Additionally, direct service providers depend on accompanying administrative and
operational infrastructure to deliver grant-funded programs; without
administrative, accounting, and compliance functions sustaining day-to-day
operations, these programs could not function. Recognizing this reality, indirect
costs have traditionally accounted for approximately 25 to 30 percent of community
development grants. A 15 percent cap fails to reflect the true cost of delivering these
services. Moreover, this change thrusts an additional layer of compliance on banks
seeking to receive CRA credit for community development grants. Under the
proposed rule, large banks would be required to strictly verify that operational
expenses incurred by a grantee fall under the proposed 15 percent cap. This poses
two additional risks to the sustainability of CD financing: nonprofits may decide
these grants are no longer financially viable, which would affect their ability to
continue delivering much needed services, and banks may stop pursuing CRA credit
through these grants due to the complexity of compliance reporting.

• permanent job creation, retention, and/or improvement
o for low- or moderate-income persons;
o in low- or moderate-income geographies;
o in areas targeted for redevelopment by Federal, state, local, or tribal governments;
