To Whom It May Concern,
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). The CRA has created a durable incentive for banks to provide loans,
investments, grants, and services in communities that have historically lacked access to
capital.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support some of the
agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in
underserved communities. However, we have grave concerns with the increases in the asset
thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on
operating grants. We also have concerns with several interacting provisions that could further
weaken community development incentives that will undoubtedly impair the flow of much
needed capital in the most underserved communities.
We are a community development finance institution (CDFI) working in California's Inland
Empire and the broader Southern California market. We operate a community-based housing
developer, a non-profit community loan fund, a HUD-certified homeownership counseling
center, and a research arm focused on improving wealth building opportunities for all low-
income, rural, senior, and veteran communities. Founded in 1991 in the City of Montclair,
NPHS is now one of the primary CDFIs serving homeowners in southern California, with the
only dedicated resilience financing program, a renowned down payment assistance program,
and a growing presence in construction lending.
Banks are critical partners in our work. We currently have relationships with banks that
provide EQ2 investments, general operating support grants, technical assistance on initiatives
like broadening outreach, recruiting staff, etc. These partnerships provide approximately $2-3
million per annum of our total grant/investment capital support which have helped us support
the creation of hundreds of homeowners annually, the production of dozens of new housing
 Page 2
units, and the successful retrofit of numerous of homes. Through the support we receive from
banks, we prove a competitive force for bringing public dollars to our region of California,
which in turn attracts further private investment in our lending and construction portfolios.
These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital and
resources to CDFIs, banks rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, develop
borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers. While interest rates have remained stubbornly
high, a number of our banking partners have reached out to ask if our targeted loan products
can help them create more homeowners and keen the mortgage market running smoothly.
The CRA has long helped create the incentives for banks to build and sustain these
relationships, strengthening the broader community development ecosystem. We are therefore
concerned that several provisions in the proposal could weaken these incentives, reducing
bank engagement with CDFIs and ultimately the flow of capital to the communities we serve.
Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance:
Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 1–3
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets,
intermediate banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as
institutions with more than $10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate
community development test as intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose
that requirement. Another approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as large
banks would become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment,
and service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements.
In the state of California where we serve, it is estimated that 25 of 132 banks, comprising
18.9% of all the banks in the state would no longer be required to reinvest in local community
development projects such as affordable housing, small business support, workforce
development, community healthcare and education services. About 45 of 89 banks, comprising
50.6% of all banks in the state would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing 16.8%
of low-and moderate-income (LMI) census tracts in California.1
Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance
These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development performance
is evaluated and therefore affect the strength of banks' incentives to engage in community
development. The agencies acknowledge in the proposal that when banks become subject to a
CD test under the current framework, the explicit evaluation of their CD activities typically
results in banks adjusting their CRA programs. This acknowledgment begs the question of
whether or not being subject to the CD test is seen by the agencies as a positive force or a
negative one. At NPHS, we believe that being subject to the CD test is important for the
maintenance of strong investment in CDFIs.
1 National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) Interactive CRA Map. https://ncrc.org/cra/
 Page 3
Banks moving down asset sizes and losing incentives for community development activities
would have a direct impact on our partnerships. We estimate that 10% of our operating grants
would be at risk from our bank funders that are currently considered large or intermediate that
would transition into lower asset categories. If the agencies were to increase the ceiling of the
intermediate threshold to $30 billion, as suggested in Question 1, then several of our banking
partners would face decreased obligations despite controlling billions of dollars of community-
sourced capital.
One prime example of the impact that bank investments have had on NPHS is our ADU Go loan
product, which helps low-income households produce extra housing on land they own. Without
the support of large banks and community banks, our fund would not have been capitalized to
the degree it was. Even the general operating support grants we receive from intermediate
banks were instrumental in ensuring we had the staff capacity to support our employees as
they developed the product, and began the process of educating homeowners about its
availability. CDFIs frequently rely on regional and community banks for patient debt, deposits,
investments, lines of credit, grants, and other forms of capital that allow us to reach borrowers
and projects that conventional financial institutions cannot efficiently serve directly.
Misalignment with Congressional Priorities on Affordable Housing and New Markets
Tax Credit (NMTC)
The change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) which are two bipartisan, popular federal
tax tools with a long track record of success in our communities. While Congress expanded
LIHTC and made NMTC permanent, the proposal undermines these important investment
tools.
LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the standalone
investment test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted component of
their CRA evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into the lower size
category would mean these transitioned banks would only be subject to a diluted evaluation
that considers all CD in one test. This means a bank may have greater ability to emphasize CD
lending rather than maintain the same level of LIHTC or NMTC investment because investment
performance no longer receives a separate rating. Through this weakened regulatory incentive,
bank demand for these investments would decrease.
Our organization, for example, has worked with banks where they provided deep equity
investments into LIHTC projects like our homeless housing project, Sunrise at Bogart. Losing
the investment incentives for banks would likely lead to a decline in the investment appetite
banks current express for our multi-family affordable housing projects.
Recommendation
For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and
reject all alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for
consideration in Question 1). The current thresholds are already annually indexed to CPI-W,
so they are not beholden to 1995 asset levels. Moreover, the justification of "restoring
 Page 4
proportionality to 1995" that the agencies use in the proposal does not adequately explain why
raising asset thresholds better serve the statutory intent of the CRA, which is to ensure that
credit needs of LMI communities are met. For the small bank threshold, the proportionality
metric rests on the distribution of the number of banks such that nearly 80% of all banks
would be considered small, similar to what it was in 1995. While that's true, by the same logic,
nearly 20% of banks in 1995 were considered large whereas under the proposed large bank
threshold, only a little over 2% of all banks would be considered large. Instead, the agencies
selectively use total banking industry share to justify the large bank threshold saying large
banks would under this proposal, and similar to 1995 cover about 85% of all total bank
industry's assets. Matching a 1995 distribution through either method does not necessarily
demonstrate that the resulting categories are appropriate for the modern banking system. The
industry has consolidated dramatically, bank business models and geographic reach have
changed. Banks with several billion dollars in assets today may have substantially greater
lending, investment, data, and operational capacity than institutions that were treated as small
or intermediate, three decades ago. The fact that assets happen to sit above a chosen
threshold does not by itself establish that banks below that threshold should lose the separate
investment/service tests or associated data requirements.
Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community
Development Activities — CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which: 1)
requires a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or
initiative with a primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, caps grant
recipient's indirect administrative costs to 15%; 3) requires that large banks obtain
documentation from grant recipients including written commitments regarding use of funds,
indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and operating and program budgets. We also
strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and donations
from CRA consideration entirely.
While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit
communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and
misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in community development
finance. For CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk
management, data systems, financial management, technical assistance, and product
development are not ancillary to community development. They are the infrastructure that
makes community development lending possible.
Neighborhood Partnership Housing Services (NPHS) uses operating grants to hire staff that
build our capacity to serve our region, develop new products that de-risk lending for our
banking partners, and even support initiatives like our research into credit gaps in our
community. Without general operating support, NPHS would be a smaller organization with
less capacity to serve the myriads of homeowners in our region who need support. We've
pioneered nation-leading load products and maintained a robust HUD Counseling department
to counsel our loan recipients, even as federal funding was cut this year. Our work is more
than just one project after another and recognizing the need for ongoing operating support is
 Page 5
essential to protect communities across the United States from losing access to responsive
capital.
Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA
eligibility. An organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for
community impact. Costs vary depending on an organization's size, geography, product mix,
regulatory obligations, technical-assistance model, and populations served. The cap could
disproportionately affect small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar
loans, organizations providing intensive borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new
products or entering underserved markets and organizations making necessary investments in
technology, compliance, data, and risk management.
Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building
grants as currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage flexibility for
banks to provide the form of support that best responds to the identified community needs
instead of imposing undue compliance burdens.
Interacting Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community
Development Incentives
Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section
IV.B, "Performance Tests — Intermediate Bank Ratings"
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a
Satisfactory rating on both its lending test and its CD test to receive an overall Satisfactory
rating. The proposal would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would allow
lending performance to compensate for weaker CD performance.
This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset thresholds,
which would move hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-bank framework into
the intermediate category. If weak CD performance does not prevent an overall Satisfactory
rating, banks may have less regulatory incentive to make CDFI loans and investments, provide
grants, or undertake other community development activities. We urge the agencies to retain
a requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate at least Satisfactory CD performance to
receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
Due to nearly $2-3 million in annual CRA investments into our CDFI, the NPHS team is
extremely concerned that weakened incentives for CD performance will force us to rely on a
small number of large banks, rather than a wide array of banking partners of each and every
size. We ask that the agencies, in this regard, contemplate the potential for a consolidation of
large bank influence over CDFIs that in turn makes community-driven capital harder to access.
 Page 6
Essential community infrastructure and facilities should retain a meaningful CD
nexus: Section IV.D, "Community Development Definition — Revitalization and
Stabilization", Question 25
We support CRA consideration for essential community facilities and infrastructure, particularly
in rural communities, Indian Country, distressed areas, and other markets with limited access
to conventional capital. The proposal, however, would broaden eligibility for essential
community infrastructure and facilities serving specified targeted areas. These activities would
no longer necessarily need to demonstrate that they help attract or retain businesses or
residents, and community-wide infrastructure may receive consideration without allocating a
particular share of the benefit to LMI individuals.
We are concerned that large infrastructure transactions routinely financed in the conventional
market could compete with affordable housing, CDFI financing, small-business lending, and
other activities more dependent on CRA incentives. The agencies should preserve flexibility
where infrastructure addresses a genuine community development or financing gap while
ensuring that ordinary-course infrastructure transactions do not displace more targeted CD
activity.
Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E,
"Consideration of Community Development Activities — CD Activities Outside
Assessment Areas"; proposed § __.13(e); Question 34
We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with significant
unmet needs but relatively few bank assessment areas. Greater geographic flexibility could be
particularly beneficial for reaching CRA deserts.
NPHS serves California's Inland Empire, a region inclusive of the largest County in the United
States, San Bernardino County, as well as Riverside County, a large jurisdiction in its own
right. Communities in San Bernardino and Riverside Counties include cities, suburban zones,
and a vast rural region. Many of these rural communities lack meaningful bank footprints.
At NPHS, we believe that flexibility should supplement rather than displace CD activity in
banks' own assessment areas. The agencies are considering both quantitative and qualitative
approaches for determining when a bank has sufficiently served its assessment areas to
receive consideration for outside-AA activity.
With respect to Question 34, we support greater geographic flexibility where it can help direct
CRA-motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas that
may fall outside traditional assessment areas. However, that flexibility should only become
available after a bank has demonstrated meaningful community development performance
within its own assessment areas.
We are concerned that the quantitative standard proposed under Option 1 is too low to meet
that objective. For large banks, the proposal would allow outside-assessment-area
consideration once a bank reaches 0.625 percent of allocated Tier 1 capital in community
 Page 7
development loans and 0.625 percent in community development investments and grants. The
agencies themselves explain that these thresholds generally reflect the minimum level of
activity needed to avoid a "Needs to Improve" rating and are not, by themselves, sufficient to
demonstrate satisfactory community development performance.
Recent analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition further illustrates the gap
between the proposed thresholds and current bank activity. Among 69 large OCC- and FDIC-
supervised banks analyzed by NCRC, current annual assessment-area community development
lending, investments, and grants totaled approximately $102 billion. Applying the proposed
0.625% Tier 1 capital thresholds to those same institutions yielded a benchmark of
approximately $14.8 billion—roughly 85% below current activity. NCRC also found median
assessment-area community development lending equal to 6.83% of Tier 1 capital and median
qualified investments and grants equal to 3.5%, both substantially above the proposed
0.625% benchmarks.
A standard intended to determine when a bank has adequately served its own communities
should therefore be calibrated to meaningful, satisfactory community development
performance, not merely the minimum necessary to avoid a failing rating. We encourage the
agencies to adopt a more rigorous standard that considers both the level of activity and its
responsiveness to identified community needs. We further caution against allowing a broadly
defined "substantially met" standard to weaken this safeguard. Any exception should be
narrowly tailored to circumstances in which a documented lack of community development
opportunities or other performance-context factors explain the shortfall, rather than simply
allowing weaker community development performance in individual assessment areas to be
offset by activity elsewhere.
Allocation of CD activities across assessment areas: Section IV.E, "CD Activities in
Assessment Areas, Assessment Area Allocation, Assigning Assessment Area
Weights"
We support greater flexibility in allocating CD activities that benefit or serve multiple
assessment areas. This could better accommodate statewide and regional CDFIs whose
community impact is not accurately represented by the physical location of their headquarters.
For example, NPHS is headquartered in Rancho Cucamonga, a city located in suburban San
Bernardino County, but over 90% of our lending falls outside of Rancho Cucamonga, and over
50% of our financing is deployed outside of San Bernardino County. Assigning an entire bank
investment to our headquarters location would not accurately represent the communities
benefiting from the capital.
Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process: Section IV.E,
"Illustrative List" and "Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions 32–33
We strongly support establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of eligible
CD activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of eligibility. The OCC, FDIC, and
 Page 8
Federal Reserve should seek to maintain consistent standards and, ideally, a single
interagency illustrative list.
With respect to Questions 32–33, we support requiring banks to retain eligibility
determinations for as long as the applicable activity remains on their balance sheet and
establishing a maximum 30-day extension beyond the proposed 90-day review period.
We also encourage the agencies to pair this with a confirmation process that provides timely
certainty while maintaining accountability for genuine community development impact.
Eligibility determinations should include a clear written rationale and, where appropriate,
identify the facts or conditions on which eligibility depends. The agencies should provide a
process for reconsideration where banks or community development partners can supply
additional information, as well as a mechanism for community stakeholders to raise material
concerns regarding activities that have been determined eligible. Nonconfidential or
anonymized determinations and their rationales should be made public to promote
transparency and consistent treatment across institutions. Eligibility determinations should
also remain subject to verification during CRA examinations where the activity is ultimately
implemented differently than represented.
Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and
Stabilization — Designated Disaster Areas"; Question 31
We support expressly recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt
to, and withstand natural disasters. CDFIs frequently provide financing before and after
disasters to affordable housing developments, homeowners, small businesses, and community
facilities. CRA should recognize responsible investments that strengthen vulnerable
communities before disasters occur, not only financing provided after damage occurs.
NPHS is the first CDFI in the nation to develop a resilience-oriented loan product that is
specifically tailored to meet insurer recommendations and provide not only insurability, but
also ensure homeowners can secure a mortgage. By helping homeowners defend their homes
from disasters, we ensure the American Dream cannot be lost due to a fire, flood, earthquake,
or hurricane. Millions of American families have built wealth through homeownership, and
crediting disaster preparedness investments would help ensure banks continue investing in
mitigation that saves homes and reduces future cost burdens on all levels of government.
By expanding the scope of qualifying activities to include mitigation-oriented lending, the
agencies can also help promote what CDFIs do best; functioning as the research-and-
development labs that test financial products, identify new lending avenues, and de-risk
lending through standardization. Through support for disaster preparedness lending, we also
allow banks to play a more active role in the de-risking of our housing stock, thus introduce
greater stability across the real estate, insurance, and energy markets.
 Page 9
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act has helped create a powerful partnership among banks,
CDFIs, and the communities we serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity
and flexibility. Modernization, however, should result in more responsible capital reaching
communities with unmet credit needs, as the CRA statute was intended.
We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds proposed and to
withdraw the restrictions on CD operating grants while still expanding eligible activities to
include disaster preparedness, the allocation of CD activities beyond headquarter location, and
the publishing of illustrative non-exhaustive lists of CD activities.
By focusing on decreasing burdens and increasing community investments, the agencies can
ensure that banks remain important stewards of economic growth in every community across
our Country.
Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed
changes on the communities we serve.
Sincerely,
Clemente Mojica
President and CEO
Neighborhood Partnership Housing Services (NPHS)

can help them create more homeowners and keen the mortgage market running smoothly.
The CRA has long helped create the incentives for banks to build and sustain these
relationships, strengthening the broader community development ecosystem. We are therefore
concerned that several provisions in the proposal could weaken these incentives, reducing
bank engagement with CDFIs and ultimately the flow of capital to the communities we serve.
Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance:
Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 1–3
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets,
intermediate banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as
institutions with more than $10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate
community development test as intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose
that requirement. Another approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as large
banks would become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment,
and service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements.
In the state of California where we serve, it is estimated that 25 of 132 banks, comprising
18.9% of all the banks in the state would no longer be required to reinvest in local community
development projects such as affordable housing, small business support, workforce
development, community healthcare and education services. About 45 of 89 banks, comprising
50.6% of all banks in the state would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing 16.8%
of low-and moderate-income (LMI) census tracts in California.1
Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance
These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development performance
is evaluated and therefore affect the strength of banks' incentives to engage in community
development. The agencies acknowledge in the proposal that when banks become subject to a
CD test under the current framework, the explicit evaluation of their CD activities typically
results in banks adjusting their CRA programs. This acknowledgment begs the question of
whether or not being subject to the CD test is seen by the agencies as a positive force or a
negative one. At NPHS, we believe that being subject to the CD test is important for the
maintenance of strong investment in CDFIs.
1 National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) Interactive CRA Map. https://ncrc.org/cra/
 Page 3
Banks moving down asset sizes and losing incentives for community development activities
would have a direct impact on our partnerships. We estimate that 10% of our operating grants
would be at risk from our bank funders that are currently considered large or intermediate that
would transition into lower asset categories. If the agencies were to increase the ceiling of the
intermediate threshold to $30 billion, as suggested in Question 1, then several of our banking
partners would face decreased obligations despite controlling billions of dollars of community-
sourced capital.
One prime example of the impact that bank investments have had on NPHS is our ADU Go loan
product, which helps low-income households produce extra housing on land they own. Without
the support of large banks and community banks, our fund would not have been capitalized to
the degree it was. Even the general operating support grants we receive from intermediate
banks were instrumental in ensuring we had the staff capacity to support our employees as
they developed the product, and began the process of educating homeowners about its
availability. CDFIs frequently rely on regional and community banks for patient debt, deposits,
investments, lines of credit, grants, and other forms of capital that allow us to reach borrowers
and projects that conventional financial institutions cannot efficiently serve directly.
Misalignment with Congressional Priorities on Affordable Housing and New Markets
Tax Credit (NMTC)
The change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) which are two bipartisan, popular federal
tax tools with a long track record of success in our communities. While Congress expanded
LIHTC and made NMTC permanent, the proposal undermines these important investment
tools.
LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the standalone
investment test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted component of
their CRA evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into the lower size
category would mean these transitioned banks would only be subject to a diluted evaluation
that considers all CD in one test. This means a bank may have greater ability to emphasize CD
lending rather than maintain the same level of LIHTC or NMTC investment because investment
performance no longer receives a separate rating. Through this weakened regulatory incentive,
bank demand for these investments would decrease.
Our organization, for example, has worked with banks where they provided deep equity
investments into LIHTC projects like our homeless housing project, Sunrise at Bogart. Losing
the investment incentives for banks would likely lead to a decline in the investment appetite
banks current express for our multi-family affordable housing projects.
Recommendation
For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and
reject all alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for
consideration in Question 1). The current thresholds are already annually indexed to CPI-W,
so they are not beholden to 1995 asset levels. Moreover, the justification of "restoring
 Page 4
proportionality to 1995" that the agencies use in the proposal does not adequately explain why
raising asset thresholds better serve the statutory intent of the CRA, which is to ensure that
credit needs of LMI communities are met. For the small bank threshold, the proportionality
metric rests on the distribution of the number of banks such that nearly 80% of all banks
would be considered small, similar to what it was in 1995. While that's true, by the same logic,
nearly 20% of banks in 1995 were considered large whereas under the proposed large bank
threshold, only a little over 2% of all banks would be considered large. Instead, the agencies
selectively use total banking industry share to justify the large bank threshold saying large
banks would under this proposal, and similar to 1995 cover about 85% of all total bank
industry's assets. Matching a 1995 distribution through either method does not necessarily
demonstrate that the resulting categories are appropriate for the modern banking system. The
industry has consolidated dramatically, bank business models and geographic reach have
changed. Banks with several billion dollars in assets today may have substantially greater
lending, investment, data, and operational capacity than institutions that were treated as small
or intermediate, three decades ago. The fact that assets happen to sit above a chosen
threshold does not by itself establish that banks below that threshold should lose the separate
investment/service tests or associated data requirements.
Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community
Development Activities — CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which: 1)
requires a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or
initiative with a primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, caps grant
recipient's indirect administrative costs to 15%; 3) requires that large banks obtain
documentation from grant recipients including written commitments regarding use of funds,
indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and operating and program budgets. We also
strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and donations
from CRA consideration entirely.
While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit
communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and
misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in community development
finance. For CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk
management, data systems, financial management, technical assistance, and product
development are not ancillary to community development. They are the infrastructure that
makes community development lending possible.
Neighborhood Partnership Housing Services (NPHS) uses operating grants to hire staff that
build our capacity to serve our region, develop new products that de-risk lending for our
banking partners, and even support initiatives like our research into credit gaps in our
community. Without general operating support, NPHS would be a smaller organization with
less capacity to serve the myriads of homeowners in our region who need support. We've
pioneered nation-leading load products and maintained a robust HUD Counseling department
to counsel our loan recipients, even as federal funding was cut this year. Our work is more
than just one project after another and recognizing the need for ongoing operating support is
 Page 5
essential to protect communities across the United States from losing access to responsive
capital.
Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA
eligibility. An organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for
community impact. Costs vary depending on an organization's size, geography, product mix,
regulatory obligations, technical-assistance model, and populations served. The cap could
disproportionately affect small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar
loans, organizations providing intensive borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new
products or entering underserved markets and organizations making necessary investments in
technology, compliance, data, and risk management.
Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building
grants as currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage flexibility for
banks to provide the form of support that best responds to the identified community needs
instead of imposing undue compliance burdens.
Interacting Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community
Development Incentives
Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section
IV.B, "Performance Tests — Intermediate Bank Ratings"
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a
Satisfactory rating on both its lending test and its CD test to receive an overall Satisfactory
rating. The proposal would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would allow
lending performance to compensate for weaker CD performance.
This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset thresholds,
which would move hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-bank framework into
the intermediate category. If weak CD performance does not prevent an overall Satisfactory
rating, banks may have less regulatory incentive to make CDFI loans and investments, provide
grants, or undertake other community development activities. We urge the agencies to retain
a requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate at least Satisfactory CD performance to
receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
Due to nearly $2-3 million in annual CRA investments into our CDFI, the NPHS team is
extremely concerned that weakened incentives for CD performance will force us to rely on a
small number of large banks, rather than a wide array of banking partners of each and every
size. We ask that the agencies, in this regard, contemplate the potential for a consolidation of
large bank influence over CDFIs that in turn makes community-driven capital harder to access.
 Page 6
Essential community infrastructure and facilities should retain a meaningful CD
nexus: Section IV.D, "Community Development Definition — Revitalization and
Stabilization", Question 25
We support CRA consideration for essential community facilities and infrastructure, particularly
in rural communities, Indian Country, distressed areas, and other markets with limited access
to conventional capital. The proposal, however, would broaden eligibility for essential
community infrastructure and facilities serving specified targeted areas. These activities would
no longer necessarily need to demonstrate that they help attract or retain businesses or
residents, and community-wide infrastructure may receive consideration without allocating a
particular share of the benefit to LMI individuals.
We are concerned that large infrastructure transactions routinely financed in the conventional
market could compete with affordable housing, CDFI financing, small-business lending, and
other activities more dependent on CRA incentives. The agencies should preserve flexibility
where infrastructure addresses a genuine community development or financing gap while
ensuring that ordinary-course infrastructure transactions do not displace more targeted CD
activity.
Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E,
"Consideration of Community Development Activities — CD Activities Outside
Assessment Areas"; proposed § __.13(e); Question 34
We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with significant
unmet needs but relatively few bank assessment areas. Greater geographic flexibility could be
particularly beneficial for reaching CRA deserts.
NPHS serves California's Inland Empire, a region inclusive of the largest County in the United
States, San Bernardino County, as well as Riverside County, a large jurisdiction in its own
right. Communities in San Bernardino and Riverside Counties include cities, suburban zones,
and a vast rural region. Many of these rural communities lack meaningful bank footprints.
At NPHS, we believe that flexibility should supplement rather than displace CD activity in
banks' own assessment areas. The agencies are considering both quantitative and qualitative
approaches for determining when a bank has sufficiently served its assessment areas to
receive consideration for outside-AA activity.
With respect to Question 34, we support greater geographic flexibility where it can help direct
CRA-motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas that
may fall outside traditional assessment areas. However, that flexibility should only become
available after a bank has demonstrated meaningful community development performance
within its own assessment areas.
We are concerned that the quantitative standard proposed under Option 1 is too low to meet
that objective. For large banks, the proposal would allow outside-assessment-area
consideration once a bank reaches 0.625 percent of allocated Tier 1 capital in community
 Page 7
development loans and 0.625 percent in community development investments and grants. The
agencies themselves explain that these thresholds generally reflect the minimum level of
activity needed to avoid a "Needs to Improve" rating and are not, by themselves, sufficient to
demonstrate satisfactory community development performance.
Recent analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition further illustrates the gap
between the proposed thresholds and current bank activity. Among 69 large OCC- and FDIC-
supervised banks analyzed by NCRC, current annual assessment-area community development
lending, investments, and grants totaled approximately $102 billion. Applying the proposed
0.625% Tier 1 capital thresholds to those same institutions yielded a benchmark of
approximately $14.8 billion—roughly 85% below current activity. NCRC also found median
assessment-area community development lending equal to 6.83% of Tier 1 capital and median
qualified investments and grants equal to 3.5%, both substantially above the proposed
0.625% benchmarks.
A standard intended to determine when a bank has adequately served its own communities
should therefore be calibrated to meaningful, satisfactory community development
performance, not merely the minimum necessary to avoid a failing rating. We encourage the
agencies to adopt a more rigorous standard that considers both the level of activity and its
responsiveness to identified community needs. We further caution against allowing a broadly
defined "substantially met" standard to weaken this safeguard. Any exception should be
narrowly tailored to circumstances in which a documented lack of community development
opportunities or other performance-context factors explain the shortfall, rather than simply
allowing weaker community development performance in individual assessment areas to be
offset by activity elsewhere.
Allocation of CD activities across assessment areas: Section IV.E, "CD Activities in
Assessment Areas, Assessment Area Allocation, Assigning Assessment Area
Weights"
We support greater flexibility in allocating CD activities that benefit or serve multiple
assessment areas. This could better accommodate statewide and regional CDFIs whose
community impact is not accurately represented by the physical location of their headquarters.
For example, NPHS is headquartered in Rancho Cucamonga, a city located in suburban San
Bernardino County, but over 90% of our lending falls outside of Rancho Cucamonga, and over
50% of our financing is deployed outside of San Bernardino County. Assigning an entire bank
investment to our headquarters location would not accurately represent the communities
benefiting from the capital.
Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process: Section IV.E,
"Illustrative List" and "Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions 32–33
We strongly support establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of eligible
CD activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of eligibility. The OCC, FDIC, and
 Page 8
Federal Reserve should seek to maintain consistent standards and, ideally, a single
interagency illustrative list.
With respect to Questions 32–33, we support requiring banks to retain eligibility
determinations for as long as the applicable activity remains on their balance sheet and
establishing a maximum 30-day extension beyond the proposed 90-day review period.
We also encourage the agencies to pair this with a confirmation process that provides timely
certainty while maintaining accountability for genuine community development impact.
Eligibility determinations should include a clear written rationale and, where appropriate,
identify the facts or conditions on which eligibility depends. The agencies should provide a
process for reconsideration where banks or community development partners can supply
additional information, as well as a mechanism for community stakeholders to raise material
concerns regarding activities that have been determined eligible. Nonconfidential or
anonymized determinations and their rationales should be made public to promote
transparency and consistent treatment across institutions. Eligibility determinations should
also remain subject to verification during CRA examinations where the activity is ultimately
implemented differently than represented.
Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and
Stabilization — Designated Disaster Areas"; Question 31
We support expressly recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt
to, and withstand natural disasters. CDFIs frequently provide financing before and after
disasters to affordable housing developments, homeowners, small businesses, and community
facilities. CRA should recognize responsible investments that strengthen vulnerable
communities before disasters occur, not only financing provided after damage occurs.
NPHS is the first CDFI in the nation to develop a resilience-oriented loan product that is
specifically tailored to meet insurer recommendations and provide not only insurability, but
also ensure homeowners can secure a mortgage. By helping homeowners defend their homes
from disasters, we ensure the American Dream cannot be lost due to a fire, flood, earthquake,
or hurricane. Millions of American families have built wealth through homeownership, and
crediting disaster preparedness investments would help ensure banks continue investing in
mitigation that saves homes and reduces future cost burdens on all levels of government.
By expanding the scope of qualifying activities to include mitigation-oriented lending, the
agencies can also help promote what CDFIs do best; functioning as the research-and-
development labs that test financial products, identify new lending avenues, and de-risk
lending through standardization. Through support for disaster preparedness lending, we also
allow banks to play a more active role in the de-risking of our housing stock, thus introduce
greater stability across the real estate, insurance, and energy markets.
 Page 9
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act has helped create a powerful partnership among banks,
CDFIs, and the communities we serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity
and flexibility. Modernization, however, should result in more responsible capital reaching
communities with unmet credit needs, as the CRA statute was intended.
We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds proposed and to
withdraw the restrictions on CD operating grants while still expanding eligible activities to
include disaster preparedness, the allocation of CD activities beyond headquarter location, and
the publishing of illustrative non-exhaustive lists of CD activities.
By focusing on decreasing burdens and increasing community investments, the agencies can
ensure that banks remain important stewards of economic growth in every community across
our Country.
Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed
changes on the communities we serve.

I am an attorney and I submit this comment in my individual capacity. I oppose the notice of
proposed rulemaking on the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations (the Proposal)1
because its changes, taken together, would reduce the scrutiny banks receive for serving low- and
moderate-income (LMI) communities, and the record the agencies have assembled does not show
what those changes would do to the communities the statute exists to protect. I urge the agencies
to withdraw the Proposal or, at a minimum, to publish an analysis of its effects on LMI
communities and re-propose it for public comment.
I write as a lawyer who values the rule of law and who believes that communities long shut out of
the financial mainstream need workable tools to build wealth and opportunity. The CRA is one of
those tools. It is also a statute with a defined mandate, and agencies implementing it must stay
within that mandate and explain their choices on the record.
I. The statute requires attention to credit and deposit services and to LMI neighborhoods
Congress found that regulated financial institutions have a continuing and affirmative obligation
to help meet the credit needs of the communities in which they are chartered, and that "the
convenience and needs of communities include the need for credit services as well as deposit
services."2 Congress directed the agencies to assess each institution's record of meeting the credit
needs of its entire community, "including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods," consistent
with safe and sound operation.3

The Proposal defends several of its changes, most notably its limitation of the service test to "credit
services," by pointing to the statutory focus on "credit needs."4 But the same statutory findings
state that community needs include deposit services. An agency that relies on one half of
Congress's finding while setting aside the other has not reckoned with the statute's text. More
broadly, every change that reduces scrutiny of banks must be justified against the statute's purpose
of encouraging institutions to meet the needs of their entire communities, including LMI
neighborhoods, and not merely against a goal of reducing burden.
II. The record does not show what the Proposal would do to LMI communities
Agency action must rest on reasoned decisionmaking that considers the important aspects of the
problem and offers an explanation consistent with the evidence.5 The most important aspect of this
problem is the effect on the communities CRA protects. On that question the Proposal's own
analysis is candid, and it is not reassuring. The OCC states that it "expects the proposed changes
could have downstream effects on LMI communities, small business, small farms, nonprofit
organizations, and other community development stakeholders, but the direction and magnitude
of those effects are uncertain."6 The OCC also anticipates "a possible shift in CRA-motivated
activity toward lending and credit services and away from certain CD activities, in particular grants
and deposit services."7 And its summary table acknowledges that the Proposal "[d]ecreases data
availability for certain banks" and "[d]ecreases regulatory oversight into how banks are performing
within their non-major products," which the OCC concedes "may be meaningful to" some banks'
communities.8
These are costs borne by the very communities the CRA is meant to serve, and the agencies identify
them without quantifying them. Before finalizing any rule, the agencies should: (1) identify the
banks that would move into less rigorous evaluation categories and the communities those banks
serve; (2) quantify the branches, loans, investments, grants and services that would receive less or
no CRA scrutiny; (3) assess whether those effects are concentrated in LMI, rural, Tribal or

III. Specific provisions of concern
A. Higher asset thresholds
The Proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion and the large-
bank threshold from about $1.649 billion to $10 billion. Small banks would rise from about 57.0
percent to about 79.8 percent of covered banks, and only about 86 banks (2.4 percent) would
remain "large."9 The National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) estimates that roughly
814 banks would lose a community development evaluation, that 417 banks would move out of
the large-bank framework, that more than 5,000 branches in LMI census tracts (about 30 percent
of those branches) would lose a separate branch evaluation, and that in 28 states at least one-third
of LMI-tract branches would lose evaluation.10
The agencies justify the new thresholds largely by comparing the share of industry assets held by
each size class with the 1995 distribution.11 But a bank's share of national assets measures its
economic weight, not whether a particular community depends on it. Banks below $10 billion in
assets may be the principal source of credit and services in many smaller and rural communities,
and the Proposal does not examine that question. The Proposal would also allow an intermediate
bank to receive an overall "satisfactory" rating on the strength of its lending test alone, and would
eliminate consideration of small and intermediate banks' responses to written complaints.12 In
response to Questions 1 and 2, the agencies should not extend the intermediate category to banks
with up to $30 billion in assets.
B. Deposit services and branch access
The Proposal would limit the service test's retail-banking criterion to "credit services" and would
supersede interagency guidance under which examiners consider deposit products, transaction
fees, and the costs and features of accounts.13 As discussed above, that choice is hard to square
with Congress's finding that community needs include deposit services. It also matters in practice.
According to FDIC survey data summarized by NCRC, 5.6 million U.S. households are unbanked
and more than 19 million are underbanked.14 For these households, whether a nearby bank offers
an affordable checking or savings account is not separate from access to credit. The OCC itself
anticipates a shift of activity away from deposit services. The agencies should retain consideration
of deposit products in the service test and should not finalize this change without analyzing its
effect on unbanked and underbanked households.

The Proposal would credit a grant by a large bank only if the recipient's indirect costs do not
exceed 15 percent, and would require a written commitment, an attestation, and the recipient's IRS

staff and modest records, and overhead such as rent, accounting and technology is frequently
necessary to deliver the program itself. The agencies' own footnote states that the OMB 15 percent

compensated for their overhead costs."16 A rate designed to protect small recipients' overhead
recovery is a poor basis for excluding those recipients from bank support. The Proposal's concern

grants from CRA consideration.

Under current guidance, small-business financing counts as economic development only if it meets
both a size test and a "purpose test" tied to creating, retaining or improving jobs for LMI persons

definition "would expand the activities that would qualify as economic development."19 The
agencies' stated reason is that the test is subjective, but subjectivity can be addressed with clearer

individuals or in LMI areas.
Similarly, the Proposal would give credit for essential infrastructure that "benefits or serves"
targeted areas, whereas current guidance credits such activity in LMI tracts only if it helps attract

industrial parks and similar projects provided through public-private partnerships.21 Large projects
that serve a wide region may incidentally touch an LMI tract while delivering little to its residents.

Congress found that regulated financial institutions have a continuing and affirmative obligation
to help meet the credit needs of the communities in which they are chartered, and that "the
convenience and needs of communities include the need for credit services as well as deposit
services."2 Congress directed the agencies to assess each institution's record of meeting the credit
needs of its entire community, "including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods," consistent
with safe and sound operation.3

On behalf of the Central California Hispanic Chamber of Commerce (CCHCC), I appreciate the opportunity to
submit comments regarding the proposed amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
For more than four decades, the Central California Hispanic Chamber of Commerce has worked to promote
entrepreneurship, strengthen small businesses, and advance economic opportunities throughout California's
Central Valley. Our mission is to support businesses from startup to success by providing access to education,
networking opportunities, financial resources, and partnerships that foster sustainable economic growth. As an
organization dedicated to advancing the success of Hispanic-owned businesses and the broader small business
community, we understand the challenges entrepreneurs face when seeking affordable financing, building
credit, and accessing the resources necessary to establish and expand their businesses.
We recognize the importance of regulatory efficiency and reasonable requirements for financial institutions.
However, we are concerned that certain proposed CRA changes could unintentionally weaken incentives for
community development investment, reduce support for Community Development Financial Institutions
(CDFIs), and limit the availability of technical assistance and affordable capital in underserved communities.
1. Preserving Access to Capital for Small Businesses
Access to affordable financing remains one of the most significant challenges facing entrepreneurs throughout
the Central Valley. Many Hispanic-owned businesses, first-generation entrepreneurs, startups, and businesses in
rural or low- and moderate-income communities encounter barriers to conventional lending. These challenges
include limited credit histories, insufficient collateral, language barriers, and difficulties navigating traditional
banking requirements. The 2022 Fresno Small Business Capital Flows and Gaps Analysis, commissioned by

Nicolas Madrigal Madrigal
President
Access Plus Capital and its partners, estimated at least $3 billion in annual unmet small business financing
demand in Fresno County. This estimate included both unmet financing applications and demand from
businesses discouraged from applying for credit. This finding illustrates the importance of continued investment
in responsible lending programs and community partnerships that address financing gaps. We respectfully
encourage the OCC and FDIC to preserve meaningful CRA incentives that encourage financial institutions to
expand responsible small business lending and improve access to capital in historically underserved
communities.
2. Maintaining Community Development Investment and Banking Partnerships
Community and regional banks are essential partners in Central California's economic development ecosystem.
Through investments, lending relationships, and community partnerships, financial institutions help support
CDFIs, nonprofit organizations, and business development programs that provide resources to entrepreneurs
who may not qualify for traditional financing. We are concerned that the proposed increase in bank
classification thresholds to $1 billion for small banks and $10 billion for large banks could reduce community
development expectations for certain financial institutions. Although changes in regulatory classifications do
not necessarily result in reduced lending or investment, they may influence future decisions regarding
community development financing, grant funding, and partnerships with organizations serving underserved
businesses. We respectfully request that the agencies carefully evaluate the potential effects of these proposed
thresholds on regional small business financing and preserve meaningful community development expectations
for banks with the capacity to support these activities.
3. Supporting Community Development Financial Institutions
CDFIs play a critical role in expanding access to capital for small businesses that face barriers to conventional
financing. In the Central Valley, organizations such as Access Plus Capital provide financing and business
development services that help entrepreneurs launch, sustain, and expand their businesses. These organizations
often serve business owners who need smaller loans, flexible financing arrangements, or additional assistance
preparing for traditional bank financing. Bank investments, loans, and grants help CDFIs maintain the lending
capacity and organizational resources necessary to meet these needs. We encourage the OCC and FDIC to
preserve CRA consideration for qualifying CDFI investments, financing arrangements, and grants that
demonstrate meaningful community development benefits. Maintaining strong partnerships between financial
institutions and CDFIs is essential to expanding responsible access to capital and supporting sustainable small
business growth.

Access to capital alone is not sufficient to ensure long-term business success. Entrepreneurs also require
business planning assistance, financial education, credit preparation, bookkeeping support, cash-flow
management, and guidance navigating lending requirements. Chambers of commerce, CDFIs, Small Business

Hispanic entrepreneurs and first-generation business owners, these organizations serve as trusted sources of

on CRA consideration for certain operating and capacity-building grants, including the proposed 15 percent
administrative or overhead limitation for grants from large banks. Organizations providing technical assistance
must maintain adequate staffing, outreach, infrastructure, and operational capacity to deliver effective services.

building grants when recipients can demonstrate a clear community development purpose and measurable
benefits to underserved businesses. Evaluations should consider outcomes such as entrepreneurs served,

businesses receiving technical assistance, financing readiness, and access to responsible lending opportunities
rather than relying exclusively on administrative cost classifications.
5. Addressing the Unique Needs of Central Valley Communities
California's Central Valley is home to a diverse and entrepreneurial population that contributes significantly to
the region's economic vitality. Small businesses operating in agriculture, construction, retail, hospitality, food
service, professional services, and other industries support local employment and community prosperity.
However, rural communities and underserved urban neighborhoods continue to face challenges accessing
financial services and business development resources. For many small business owners, relationships with
trusted community organizations are essential to understanding available financing options and preparing for
responsible borrowing. We encourage the agencies to maintain meaningful opportunities for community input
and preserve sufficient small business lending data to identify financing gaps across the region. A strong CRA

partnerships that respond to the needs of the communities they serve.

I. The Proposed Asset Thresholds Suit Their Main Purpose
The Proposal sets the new tiers by matching the 1995 distribution of banks and assets. In 1995,
small banks were 80.4 percent of banks and held 13.8 percent of assets; large banks were 19.6
percent of banks and held 86.2 percent (Proposal at 52120). Under the Proposal, small banks
would be about 79.8 percent of the banks the agencies supervise, small and intermediate banks
together would hold 14.6 percent of assets, and the 86 large banks (2.4 percent) would hold 85.4
percent (id. at 52120, 52122). The agencies describe these shares as "substantially similar to the
proportions of their distribution in 1995" (id. at 52120).
The case for resetting the lines is strong. The number of insured institutions fell from 12,354 in
June 1995 to 4,411 at the end of 2025, and the agencies acknowledge that annual inflation
adjustments "have not been sufficient to keep up with changes in the industry, including its
overall growth and consolidation" (id. n.96). For deciding how closely to examine a bank, assets
are a sensible measure, because size tracks complexity and the capacity to absorb a more detailed
exam. I support the $1 billion and $10 billion thresholds.
II. One Asset Line Now Does Two Jobs
The line that sets the exam also sets the data duty. As the Proposal explains, "large banks are
subject to data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements while small banks, including
intermediate small banks, are not" (Proposal at 52122). Raising the large bank line from $1.649
billion to $10 billion therefore does two things at once. It gives banks between those sizes a
lighter exam, which is its stated aim. It also ends their small business and small farm data
reporting, a consequence the economic analysis acknowledges in general terms but does not
measure. The agencies estimate that 376 banks would leave the large bank category (126
supervised by the OCC and 250 by the FDIC) and describe the result as "a significant
compliance cost savings for affected banks" (id. at 52160; see id. at 52166).
A basic rule of policy design, associated with Jan Tinbergen, holds that each independent target
needs its own instrument. The intensity of an exam and the scope of public lending data are
separate targets. Assets are a good guide to the first. For the second, the question is where the
lending is, and the asset line answers that question poorly, as the next section shows. The
agencies "invite feedback regarding the methodology and data used to set thresholds for small,
intermediate, and large banks" (id. at 52120). My answer is that the methodology is right for
exams and should be paired with a lending measure for data.

1995 asset share does not match the 1995 lending share, and the gap is widest for farm loans.
Consolidation has pulled the two distributions apart. The Proposal compares the two periods only
