Under the Proposal, coverage of small business lending would fall from 78.2 percent to 63.1
percent, below the 1995 level. Coverage of small farm lending would fall from 35.8 percent to
17.8 percent, about half its current level and well below the 1995 level of 23.2 percent. These
figures assume that state member banks stay under the 1995 rules, since the Federal Reserve did
not join the Proposal (Covington & Burling, Aug. 12, 2026). If the Board later adopts the same
thresholds, coverage would fall further.
Reporting banks disclose, for each census tract, the number and dollar amount of their small
business and small farm loans by loan size, and the number and amount made to businesses and
farms with gross annual revenue of $1 million or less. Call Reports give only bank-wide totals.
In 2005 the agencies themselves noted that Call Report data lack "the loan-location and
business-size information in the CRA data" (70 Fed. Reg. 44256, 44258 (Aug. 2, 2005)). The
Proposal's economic analysis recognizes that the change "may also reduce information available
to community organizations, researchers, local governments, and other public users seeking to
compare CRA performance across banks or geographies" (Proposal at 52163).
The 2005 change is the closest precedent, and it has been studied. It moved banks with assets
between $250 million and $1 billion out of data reporting. In June 2005 that size class held 7.8
percent of bank assets, 21.2 percent of small business loan dollars, and 21.8 percent of small
farm loan dollars. The banks leaving reporting now hold 6.6 percent of all bank assets, 15.1
percent of small business loan dollars, and 18.0 percent of small farm loan dollars. In both cases
the group's share of this lending is between 2.3 and 2.8 times its share of assets. Sydney Kim,
Oktay Urcan, and Hayoung Yoon examined what followed the 2005 change, using data for 2002
to 2007. They estimate that in CRA-targeted zip codes where more than half of the newly exempt
banks stopped disclosing, the number of business establishments fell by about 2 percent, new
firm formation by about 3 percent, and average wages by about 1.5 percent. The study is a
working paper, and I give its estimates that weight. It nonetheless suggests that public disclosure
itself, and not only the exam, matters in the places the CRA is meant to serve.
In 2005 the agencies heard the objection that the change "would reduce public data on small
business, small farm, and community development loans" (70 Fed. Reg. at 44258) and concluded
that "the costs of the mandatory data collection and reporting by intermediate small banks,
including the fixed costs that weigh more heavily on smaller banks, outweigh the benefits" (id. at
4
 44259). That judgment came before any evidence on what losing the data did. The banks at issue
now are also several times larger, so fixed costs weigh less on them, and the trigger proposed
here would not restore reporting for the whole group, only for the few banks that hold most of its
lending.
A court has since examined a similar trade-off. In National Community Reinvestment Coalition v.
CFPB, No. 20-cv-2074 (BAH) (D.D.C. Sept. 23, 2022), the court vacated the CFPB's 2020
increase in the HMDA closed-end reporting threshold from 25 to 100 loans. It found that the
CFPB "did not engage appropriately with the nonquantifiable 'harms'" of the change and held
that its conclusion that the benefits outweighed the harms was arbitrary and capricious; it upheld
the open-end threshold. I cite the case not to suggest that the Proposal is unlawful, but because it
shows the kind of record expected when an agency raises a reporting threshold: an estimate of
the data lost, weighed against the savings.
V. Keeping the Data From the Banks That Matter Costs Little
The agencies estimate 219 hours a year for an OCC-supervised bank and 100 hours for an
FDIC-supervised bank to collect and maintain the data, plus 8 hours to report it (Proposal at
52177). That is 108 to 227 hours per bank, or 5.2 to 10.9 percent of one full-time employee's
year of 2,080 hours. On the agencies' figures, the 376 banks leaving reporting would save about
55,600 hours a year (126 × 227 + 250 × 108 = 55,602).
A dollar trigger set at the 1995 coverage level would keep about 35 banks reporting for small
business lending and about 6 for farm lending. Even if no bank met both tests and every one bore
the higher OCC estimate, the cost would be at most 41 × 227 = 9,307 hours, or 16.7 percent of
the savings. Banks as a group would keep at least 83 percent of the relief the Proposal offers.
The cost would also fall on the banks best able to bear it. Compliance costs are largely fixed, so
their weight declines with size. In a 2015 survey of community banks, compliance costs were 8.7
percent of noninterest expense at banks under $100 million in assets and 2.9 percent at banks
between $1 billion and $10 billion (Dahl, Meyer & Neely, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis,
2016). The banks the trigger would reach are among the largest small business and farm lenders
below $10 billion, and each of them collects and reports these data today. The trigger asks them
to continue an existing process, not to build a new one.
VI. Section 1071 Will Not Fill the Gap
The agencies "intend to leverage section 1071 data and discontinue duplicative CRA data
collection and reporting requirements," and they ask whether it is feasible to "partially or fully
discontinue CRA data collection for small business loans and small farm loans and rely
exclusively on section 1071 data" (Proposal at 52147). Duplicate reporting should end once
Section 1071 data can do the job. They cannot do it yet, and for farm loans they never will.
Timing. Section 1071 compliance begins on January 1, 2028, with a grace period through
December 31, 2028 (91 Fed. Reg. 23530 (May 1, 2026)). There will be no Section 1071 data on
lending in 2026 or 2027, and no full year of data can be public before 2029.
Coverage by count, not dollars. The CFPB's rule applies to lenders with at least 1,000 covered
originations in each of the two preceding calendar years and estimates that this threshold
captures "92 to 93 percent of small business loans by depository institutions" (id. at 23535). That
5
 figure counts loans. When the CFPB proposed the threshold, its coverage estimates by dollar
value were approximately 60.3 to 62.0 percent (90 Fed. Reg. 50970, tbl. 1 (2025), as summarized
by the SBA Office of Advocacy, comment letter of Dec. 15, 2025, at 5). A count threshold favors
high-volume, small-ticket lenders, which are the banks that will keep reporting CRA data
anyway. Mid-sized banks that make fewer, larger loans are the ones most likely to fall below it.
Different definitions. Section 1071 now defines a small business as one with gross annual
revenue of $1 million or less, down from $5 million, and excludes loans of $1,000 or less (91
Fed. Reg. at 23544). CRA data cover all loans of $1 million or less to businesses of any size and
report the subset made to firms with revenue of $1 million or less separately. In 2024 that subset
was 53.8 percent of CRA small business loans by number but only 34.6 percent by dollar amount
(FFIEC). The two data sets measure different lending.
Farm lending is excluded. The CFPB excluded agricultural lending to "avoid covering a
distinct and specialized lending sector that is already subject to a different regulatory reporting
scheme" (91 Fed. Reg. at 23542), and among the existing frameworks it cites is CRA small farm
reporting (id. at 23543). The Proposal, in turn, asks whether CRA small farm data could give
way to Section 1071 data. If each rule relies on the other, no one collects the data. For OCC- and
FDIC-supervised banks below $10 billion, no tract-level farm lending data would remain. Farm
Credit System lenders, which held almost half of farm real estate loans in 2022, are also outside
Section 1071 (id. at 23532; USDA Economic Research Service, Aug. 2024), so bank data are
much of what the public can see.
For small business data, the trigger is a bridge: it should end once Section 1071 data are public
and the agencies confirm that they cover the same lending. For small farm data, there is nothing
to bridge to, and the trigger should be permanent.
VII. Design of the Trigger
The rule. An intermediate bank would collect and report small business and small farm loan data
for a calendar year if, in each of the two preceding calendar years, its originations of small
business loans exceeded a small business trigger amount or its originations of small farm loans
exceeded a small farm trigger amount. The two-year test follows the look-back the rule already
uses for asset thresholds and keeps a single unusual year from changing a bank's obligations. A
bank that meets either test should report both data types, since the agencies "consider small
business and small farm data to be a single data set" (Proposal at 52149).
Calibration. Each trigger should be set so that reporting banks hold about the share of bank
lending that reporting banks held under the 1995 rule: about 67 percent of small business loan
dollars and about 23 percent of small farm loan dollars. On December 2025 data, ranking
intermediate OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks by small business loans held, the top 35 restore
67.2 percent coverage; the 35th holds about $550 million of such loans. For farm loans, the top 6
restore 23.2 percent; the sixth holds about $206 million. None of these banks is new to reporting.
The agencies should set the final amounts from CRA origination data, which they hold and
which measure new lending rather than loans on the books. The 1995 benchmark is conservative:
coverage was higher in 1996 (69.0 and 24.9 percent) and 1997 (70.6 and 28.0 percent).
Why dollars. The burden of reporting is largely fixed per bank, so the goal is the most coverage
for the fewest banks, and a dollar test ranks banks directly by what coverage measures. A count
6
 trigger set to the same small business coverage would need about 45 banks, three of them new to
reporting. Because each small business loan is at most $1 million and each small farm loan at
most $500,000, any trigger in the tens of millions of dollars guarantees well over the 30 loans the
agencies regard as enough for "a meaningful analysis" (id. at 52125). The agencies already
identify major product lines by where a bank "did the most lending by dollar amount and loan
count" (id. at 52123), and Question 6 asks whether to "rely on dollar volume, loan count, or
both" (id. at 52125). For the data trigger, dollars are the better measure.
Keeping it current. The trigger amounts should be indexed for inflation in the same way as the
asset thresholds, and the agencies should recheck coverage every five years. The gap between
assets and lending has widened with consolidation and may keep moving.
VIII. Two Backstops: Review and Published Waivers
First, the agencies should review the effect of the new thresholds on public data within three
years and retain the authority to restore reporting if coverage falls further than expected. Second,
waivers under proposed § __.42(h) should be published. The provision allows a waiver "upon
written request" where the data are "not necessary for evaluating the bank's . . . performance or
more than minimally useful to the agencies' overall data collection" (Proposal at 52194–95
(OCC); id. at 52212–13 (FDIC)). The agencies "would generally expect use of this waiver to be
rare" (id. at 52149). Publishing each waiver with its reason costs little and lets the public see
whether that expectation holds.
IX. Likely Objections
The agencies settled this in 2005. That judgment preceded the evidence on its effects, the banks
now at issue are several times larger, and the trigger reaches only a few dozen of them.
Section 1071 will make CRA data redundant. For small business data, eventually, which is
why that trigger should end. Not before 2029, and never for farm data.
Fixed costs fall hardest on smaller banks. That is why the trigger reaches only the largest
lenders among intermediate banks, all of which report today.
Large banks already make most small business loans. By number. By dollars, smaller
reporters made 29.3 percent of reported dollars in 2024, and the banks leaving reporting hold
15.1 percent of all bank small business loans and 18.0 percent of small farm loans.
The industry has changed since 1995. It has. The Proposal itself uses 1995 proportions to set
the asset lines, and applying the same benchmark to lending asks only that the rule be consistent.
Banks can opt in. The OCC expects only "a handful" of banks to opt into large bank evaluation,
noting that "upwards of a dozen" non-large banks do so now (Proposal n.227). Opting in cannot
be relied on to preserve coverage.
Responses to Specific Requests
Threshold methodology (Proposal at 52120). Keep the asset method for exams and add a
lending trigger for data.
Question 1 (at 52122–23). A higher large bank line, such as $30 billion, would move still more
of this lending out of reporting and make a lending trigger more important.
7
 Question 6 (at 52125). For major product lines, use both measures. For the data trigger, use
dollars.
Section 1071 (at 52147). Rely on Section 1071 for small business data only after the data are
public and shown to cover the same lending. Do not rely on it for farm data.
Question 59 (at 52155). Banks reached by the trigger report today and need no transition. A
bank that later meets the trigger should begin collecting data on January 1 of the following year.
Question 61 (at 52155). Index the trigger amounts in the same way as the asset thresholds.
Waivers (at 52149). Publish waivers and the reasons for them.
Paperwork Reduction Act (at 52178). On item (a), the data have practical utility, as the
Proposal's own analysis of lost public information recognizes (at 52163). On item (b), the
agencies' per-bank estimates imply that the trigger would retain at most 9,307 of the 55,602
hours saved.
Conclusion
The Proposal's asset thresholds are a reasonable reset for exams. Applied to data, the same line
would push public coverage of small business lending below its 1995 level and cut coverage of
small farm lending by about half, with no replacement for farm data in prospect. A dollar trigger
calibrated to the agencies' own 1995 benchmark would restore that coverage by keeping at most
41 banks in a reporting process they already run, while preserving more than four-fifths of the
burden relief. I urge the agencies to adopt the thresholds together with that trigger.
Thank you for considering these comments.
Respectfully submitted,​
​
Nicholas Pruett

The Ongoing Affordable Housing Crisis

A. Our National Shortage is Harming Families Across the Country

The United States has a "serious and intractable housing shortage" particularly
of units "affordable to households with low and moderate incomes."1 Congress
has recently recognized the seriousness of this issue and, with overwhelming
bipartisan support, enacted an extensive set of reforms to begin responding.2 The
express aim of that legislation—known as the 21st Century Road to Housing Act—
was to "increase the supply of housing in America."3 And it included numerous
initiatives specifically focused on boosting affordable housing development.

This is undoubtedly a step in the right direction, but housing experts broadly
agree that much more legislative action is needed to solve the affordability
crisis.4 That is largely due to the severity of the housing shortage nationwide and
the grave toll it exacts on people across both state lines and income brackets.
While households with the lowest incomes feel the pain most acutely, the strain
on middle income households has been steadily growing.

significant increase to the large bank threshold. Raising that threshold to $10

Coalition, 42% of respondents indicated that eliminating the separate Investment

majority Black communities, the practice of denying communities of color and lower-income
neighborhoods equal access to loans, investments and other critical financial services.1 The law,
while imperfect, has required that banks lend to all communities in which they are chartered to do
business and has also proven to be a critical tool to combat decades of discriminatory banking and

II.
The Proposed Rule Would Fundamentally Undermine the Statutory Goals
Underlying the Community Reinvestment Act

The Community Reinvestment Act was enacted due to public and congressional concerns
about the deteriorating condition of America's cities, particularly lower-income neighborhoods
and communities with significant numbers of Black residents.3 Before the implementation of the
CRA, although many mainstream financial institutions were willing to accept deposits from
households and small businesses in lower-income neighborhoods, they were unwilling to lend or
invest in those same neighborhoods, even controlling for credit worthiness.4 Congress established
that regulated financial institutions are required to meet the needs of the communities in which
they are chartered to do business, including equal access to credit.5

The CRA must therefore be implemented in a manner that meaningfully evaluates whether
banks are meeting the financial needs of the communities they serve, including LMI communities.
However, the Proposed Rule significantly weakens evaluations and reduces the availability of
information necessary to access bank performance, thus undermining the goals and effectiveness
of the CRA. In short, the Proposed Rule would reduce the ability of regulators and the public to
determine whether banks are fulfilling their community reinvestment obligations.

to credit, and assess whether regulatory safeguards are working as intended.
The absence of consistent reporting requirements would make it more difficult to identify parts

Black communities, and communities of color, are being equally served. This concern is especially
significant for LMI neighborhoods and communities of color, where access to affordable credit

economic stability.

IV.
The Proposed Rule Will Limit Access to Essential Banking Services for Black
and Lower-Income Communities
The proposal would narrow the retail banking services considered in CRA evaluations by
focusing the assessment on credit-related services. This approach raises concerns about whether
banks' broader roles in providing essential banking services, such as accepting deposits, will
receive adequate oversight.
Access to deposit services, convenient banking locations, and reliable service-delivery options
are vital to individuals and small businesses, particularly in communities with limited access to
traditional banking institutions. These services can support household financial stability and
facilitate participation in the broader economy. Their importance should not be diminished simply
because they do not directly involve extending credit.
Indeed, in adopting the CRA, Congress expressly recognized that community needs encompass
both credit and deposit services.6 The NAACP believes that it is critical that agencies preserve an
evaluation framework that accounts for the availability, accessibility, and effectiveness of essential
banking services, right alongside assessment of access to lending services.
The NAACP recommends that the agencies retain meaningful consideration of deposit access,
branch availability and branch closures, and alternative delivery systems when evaluating CRA
performance. Any proposed revisions to the CRA should assess whether banks are meeting the
financial needs of their communities as a whole rather than focusing narrowly on select credit-
related activities.
V.
Recommendation

For the reasons outlined above, the NAACP opposes the adoption of the Proposed Rule. The
combined effect of reduced reporting requirements, narrower consideration of banking services,
and more restrictive grant eligibility criteria will prevent regulators and the public from being
able to meaningfully evaluate whether community reinvestment needs are being met. These
proposed changes warrant more time for close analysis, careful examination and significant
modification.

The CRA remains an important federal safeguard intended to end modern day redlining, reduce
the racial wealth gap and encourage regulated financial institutions to equitably meet the credit
needs of all communities, including LMI neighborhoods. Its effectiveness depends on a regulatory
framework that promotes meaningful oversight, transparency, and accountability while
recognizing the full range of financial needs within those communities. Our preliminary review
shows that the Proposed Rule will significantly reduce access to information about bank
performance, narrow the services considered in CRA evaluations, and impose restrictions that will
likely affect community development grant recipients. The agencies should not adopt changes

6 12 U.S.C. § 2901(a)(2).

without adequately addressing these concerns and demonstrating how any revised framework will
continue to fulfill the important goals codified within the CRA.

Accordingly, the NAACP objects to the Proposed Rule. Alternatively, we encourage the
agencies to extend the comment period for 120 days so that we can fully assess the impact that the
proposed rule would have on community reinvestment obligations, and on LMI communities and
communities of color that stand to be denied equal access to essential financial services and
community development resources.

If you have any questions or wish to discuss the NAACP's concerns further, please
contact Assistant General Counsel Quiana-Joy Ochiagha at qochiagha@naacpnet.org.









Regards,

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

On behalf of MyPath, I write to object to the harmful changes proposed to the Community

the CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved

We request an extension of the comment period for an additional 60 days so we have time to

As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities that support

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large" Banks, such

community development needs of their communities.[1] According to National Community
Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks would see their reinvestment
obligations reduced under the proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their
Community Development Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer
be subject to the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical community
development programs that have had large impacts in LMI communities. These include Low
Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a key driver of affordable housing finance; New
Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which fuel economic development projects in tribal and other

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting the critical
importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable housing.[3] Approximately
MyPathUS.org
415-206-0846


half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have tremendous

The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain branches in
LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a Large Bank to over $10

that 245 branches in LMI areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities. Fewer

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to offer deposit

415-206-0846


home to several BankOn coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks,

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are

The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs of Native

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within particular

acknowledged by, and are able to access programs and contracts with, various local and state

●​ Support for cultural, health and other programs

5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring a
demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating that large banks and

overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and OCC question whether they should end CRA

MyPathUS.org
415-206-0846



Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian measures
will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller groups, may be
impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local needs. They also
can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and investment products into
communities inclined to trust long established local organizations. Many nonprofit
organizations and programs, such as downpayment assistance programs, that support CRA

The proposal would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15% overhead restriction

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA activity that

that are meant to benefit from the CRA, and the disruption it will cause to constructive

MyPathUS.org
415-206-0846


6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link between CRA and
LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their top two major
product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in, and profiting from,
communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates must be evaluated. Further,
certain products, such as small farm and consumer loans, are important in many communities,
but may not be among a bank's largest product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and soundness,
encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater trust in banks by the

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test, which has

only benefit middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA credit for
large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for banks, would likely be
financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental benefits to LMI residents and
communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's
impact on LMI residents and communities. For example, banks might choose to more profitably
earn CRA credit by financing larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing
less lucrative, smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA should require

serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and
MyPathUS.org
415-206-0846


deposit needs in the areas where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to

banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while providing no
accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks opting for
the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

residents and communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it

demonstrate that the transaction and the property are compliant with tenant rights and

housing.

or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its source (public or private

415-206-0846


parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based on data, testing results, comment

encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to reconsider
this proposal.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chair Hill,

The Center for New York City Neighborhoods opposes the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) rule because it negates all the core goals of the original 1977 law: stopping discriminatory credit
practices and expanding access to banking services in underserved and low- and moderate-income (LMI)
communities. In fact, the proposed rule would weaken banks' obligations to invest, lend and provide
services to communities in need while simultaneously reducing transparency and accountability.

The Center is a non-profit that promotes and protects affordable homeownership in New York so that
middle- and working-class families are able to live in strong, thriving communities. Established by public
and private partners, the Center meets the diverse needs of homeowners throughout New York state by
offering free, high-quality housing services. Since our founding in 2008, we have provided more than $60
million in funding to community-based partners and have assisted over 200,000 homeowners.

The proposed increased asset thresholds for banks will have disastrous effects by weakening or
completely eliminating CRA requirements. Under the proposed rule, only large banks with assets over
$10 billion will be subject to the full CRA examination. Large banks make up just 2.4% of banks under the
CRA, meaning that the other 97.6% will no longer have obligations to report their investments and
services or participate in community development requirements. Without requirements around data
collection and reporting on lending data, transparency and accountability will significantly be weakened,

making it more difficult for communities and policymakers to identify credit gaps and hold banks
accountable.

Raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion would also eliminate separate branch evaluations for 417
banks. More than 5,000 branches in LMI census tracts (which make up 30% of all LMI branches
nationwide) and over 4,000 branches in majority people of color communities (23% of all branches
nationwide) would lose crucial accountability measures.1 This is significant because local bank branches
are already disappearing nationally. Following the 2008 financial crisis, banks began reducing their
presence in many communities of color, contributing to the emergence of "banking deserts,"2 often
described in activist and academic literature as "modern-day redlining."3 Since the COVID-19 pandemic,
branch closures have accelerated further. Nationally, one-third of bank branches that closed between
2017 and 2021 were located in LMI or majority-minority neighborhoods.4 In New York City alone, more
than 100 bank branches closed in 2020, including 27% located in LMI census tracts and 20% in majority
Black or Hispanic census tracts.5

CRA branching obligations are the primary reason that banks have maintained any branches in LMI and
communities of color at all, and are crucial for fighting disparities in underbanked communities. The
proposed rule would restrict the large bank service test to credit services while excluding depository
services from consideration. This will reduce incentives to offer basic banking products to help unbanked
and underbanked households. According to the FDIC, 4.2% (5.6 million) households are unbanked across
the United States, with an additional 14.2% (over 19 million) households remaining underbanked. New
York City's unbanked numbers are even higher at 7.6%, with higher demographic disparities even while
controlling for income. Black and Hispanic households in NYC had unbanked rates of 10.9% and 14.5%,
respectively. This is compared to an unbanked rate of 3.5% for New York City's white, non-Hispanic
households.6 CRA review of the cost and features of depository products plays a crucial role in
encouraging banks to address disparities. The proposed elimination of depository services from the

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. Since its inception in 2017, ELOM has
leveraged the Low-income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) to preserve, build, and rehab
approximately 1,800 units.

For nearly half a century, CRA has driven banks to extend private capital financing to local
communities they serve, but its impact is more pronounced than the effect CRA has had on
the production of affordable rental housing through the Housing Credit program.

The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for producing affordable rental
housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80
percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated

bank investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm CohnReznick.1 Banks
make these investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax
advantages associated with investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because the
full CRA examination for large banks includes a distinct investment test. Because Housing
Credit investment yields are typically modest, large banks often could get a more
substantial yield from making other forms of investment, but often still choose to invest in
the Housing Credit because Housing Credit investments help banks meet their CRA
obligations.

We are concerned that OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with assets ranging
from $1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks subject to
the full CRA examination, including the investment test, could reduce competition in the
Housing Credit equity market, leading to lower pricing on credits and less housing
produced. Of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain
that designation under the proposal—a decline of over 60 percent, according to the banks in
the current large bank classification subject to the full CRA exam. According to a

1 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study, CohnReznick

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no
longer need to invest in the low- and moderate-income communities they are supposed to
serve because they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having
more general community development obligations as an intermediate-sized bank. This is
because banks often find it easier to support community development activities through
lending than through equity investment.

Moreover, the CRA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) undercuts recent congressional
action to strengthen and expand the Housing Credit and facilitate more bank investment in
the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts
Act) included a substantial increase in Housing Credit authority and expanded the 4

Percent Housing Credit program to increase supply, while the 215t Century ROAD to
Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to
increase their Housing Credit investments. The provision lifting the PWI cap would mostly
affect the same banks that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus, the CRA
changes under consideration by the OCC and FDIC could greatly dilute these

legislative accomplishments and undercut congressional goals of providing more
affordable rental homes.

This proposal would most harm smaller communities that now benefit from being in the
CRA assessment area of one or more large banks but may no longer be if the OCC and FDIC
change the definition of large bank as proposed. A survey by AHTCC finds that
approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity invested through

syndicators by banks in the $412 million — $10 billion asset range supported rural markets
between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these banks play an outsized role in investing in

developments because of overlapping assessment areas—tends to be much higher than
pricing in rural and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment areas for

ELOM LLC has spoken with several investors who said this change would drop pricing

directly into Housing Credit projects. Additionally, many Rural properties will no longer be
able to attract any investment if the banks that serve those areas are not required by the

not enough CRA-driven investors were involved in the transaction. If this Change occurred,
we would not have an investor.

Alternatives to the Primary Proposal
The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new CRA

thresholds for various bank size classifications. The first would raise the large bank
asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still have far-

substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the primary proposal to

According to AHTCC's survey of bank investment in the Housing Credit, 108 banks would

The second alternative proposal would be far more damaging for affordable rental housing

Conclusion

Rural transaction that was 15 minutes from a large metro.

under the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve—the third bank
regulator—appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA

 If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no longer need to invest in the
low and moderate-income communities they are supposed to serve because they would no longer be subject to
the investment test, despite still having more general community development obligations as an intermediate-
sized bank. This is because, for various reasons, it is often easier for banks to support community development
activities through lending rather than equity investment.

Moreover, the CRA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) undercuts recent congressional action to strengthen
and expand the Housing Credit and facilitate more bank investment in the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act
(also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts Act) included a substantial increase in Housing Credit authority and
expanded the 4 Percent Housing Credit program to increase supply, while the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act
raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to increase their Housing Credit
investments. The provision lifting the PW! cap would mostly impact many of the same banks that would be
reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus, the CRA changes under consideration by the OCC and FDIC could greatly
dilute these legislative accomplishments and undercut congressional goals of providing more affordable rental
homes.

The consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to smaller communities that now benefit from being
in the CRA assessment area of one or more large banks but may no longer be if the OCC and FDIC change the
definition of large bank as proposed. A survey by AHTCC finds that approximately one-third of Housing Credit
equity invested through syndicators by banks in the $412 million — $10 billion asset range supported rural markets
between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these banks play an outsized role in investing in smaller communities.
Credit pricing for properties in many urban areas—which are more likely to have at least one and often multiple
banks competing to invest in Housing Credit developments because of overlapping assessment areas—tends to be
much higher than pricing in rural and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment areas for large
banks subject to the investment test.

Having developed affordable communities across both high-competition metro areas and underserved rural
footprints, | have seen firsthand how CRA motivation dictates whether a project is viable. The pricing gap between
a CRA-driven bank investor and an economic-only buyer routinely ranges between 10% and 12% in net equity per
credit dollar. On a typical 70-to-80-unit development with a multi-million-dollar tax credit allocation, that spread
translates directly to an equity gap of $1.5 million to over $2.0 million. In secondary and rural markets already
operating on thin financial margins, losing that bank competition creates an insurmountable funding hole that soft
funds and state gap financing simply cannot absorb.

Alternatives to the Primary Proposal

The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new thresholds for various bank size
classifications related to CRA. The first would raise the large bank asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $3.252
billion. This alternative would still have far-reaching negative consequences compared to the current large bank
threshold but is substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the primary proposal to raise the
large bank threshold to $10 billion.

According to AHTCC's survey of bank investment in the Housing Credit, 108 banks would be reclassified as
intermediate banks rather than large banks if the threshold is set at $10 billion, while just 40 would be reclassified
as intermediate banks if the large bank threshold is set at $3.252 billion. Moreover, the banks that would remain
subject to the separate investment test under a $3.252 billion threshold account for approximately 86 percent of
 the Housing Credit equity investment by OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks captured in the AHTCC survey with assets
between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

The second alternative proposal would be far more damaging for affordable rental housing production than either
the primary or first alternative proposals. NAAHL estimates that, under a $30 billion large bank threshold, 17
states would see the number of large banks with investment requirements cut by half or more. According to
AHTCC, banks with assets between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as much Housing Credit
debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

Conclusion

| have witnessed firsthand how sensitive affordable rental production is to bank examination standards. Over
three decades of delivering housing across the Southwest and Midwest, we have repeatedly seen that without a
dedicated investment test compelling institution-level participation, private capital gravitates toward frictionless
lending rather than complex, long-term equity commitments. Narrowing the large bank pool will inevitably
convert today's competitive communities into tomorrow's CRA deserts.

We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under the 1995 CRA rule,
consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve—the third bank regulator—appears to be taking. If the OCC and
FDIC move forward with changes to CRA regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold
for large banks and adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including rural
and smaller markets.

Dear Comptroller and Members of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed amendments to the regulations
implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), published at 91 Fed. Reg. 52114 on
August 12, 2026.
I recognize that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) have legitimate interests in reducing unnecessary
compliance costs, clarifying regulatory expectations, and ensuring that community
development funding reaches its intended beneficiaries.
However, regulatory efficiency should not come at the expense of meaningful public
accountability. The central question is whether the proposed changes will help banks meet
the credit and banking needs of their communities or instead make it easier for institutions
to receive satisfactory assessments without adequately addressing those needs.
I urge the agencies to withdraw the proposal and undertake a more comprehensive,
evidence-based review before developing replacement regulations.
1. Preserve meaningful community development evaluations
The proposal would materially increase the asset thresholds determining which CRA
evaluation standards apply to banks.
Under the proposed framework, banks with assets below $1 billion would no longer be
subject to a separate community development test. The intermediate-bank category would
extend to $10 billion in assets, reducing the scope of separate investment and service
evaluations for institutions moving out of the large-bank category.
The agencies' own analysis estimates that hundreds of FDIC-supervised institutions would
move into categories with fewer evaluation requirements.
These changes should not be finalized without a transparent assessment of their
consequences.
The agencies should disclose the affected institutions, their existing CRA performance,
their community development lending and investment activities, and the communities
 potentially affected by reduced scrutiny. The analysis should explain what public benefits
are expected to compensate for the reduction in separate evaluations.
If the agencies believe that less intensive oversight will not weaken community investment,
they should demonstrate that conclusion through evidence rather than assumption.
2. Retain deposit services within CRA evaluations
The proposal would exclude deposit services from the range of retail banking services
considered in CRA evaluations.
I urge the agencies to reconsider this change.
Communities need more than access to loans. Households and small businesses also
depend on affordable deposit accounts, practical transaction services, and banking
facilities that meet their needs.
A framework that examines lending while excluding deposit services risks overlooking an
important part of the relationship between a bank and the communities it serves.
This issue warrants particular attention given the agencies' acknowledgment that the
proposal could shift CRA-motivated activity away from deposit services and certain
community development activities.
At a minimum, the agencies should retain deposit services in the service test unless they
can demonstrate, through a reasoned analysis, that the proposed exclusion would not
materially weaken the CRA's effectiveness.
3. Prevent lending evaluations from overlooking important local markets
The proposed major-product-line approach is intended to reduce the burden of evaluating
lending categories that do not represent a significant part of a bank's overall business.
That objective should not become a justification for ignoring material credit needs in
particular communities.
A lending category can be relatively small across an institution's national portfolio while
remaining important to borrowers in a specific assessment area. Consumer lending, small-
business lending, small-farm lending, and home mortgage lending can serve different
groups with different financing needs.
The agencies should therefore consider lending activity at the assessment-area level and
preserve examiner authority to investigate material lending categories where local
conditions or potential discriminatory practices warrant further examination.
 The evaluation framework should identify whether banks are meeting the actual needs of
the communities they serve, rather than allowing the overall composition of a bank's
portfolio to determine which local credit needs receive meaningful scrutiny.
4. Evaluate community development grants on their merits
I support appropriate safeguards to ensure that community development grants benefit
their intended recipients and communities.
Nevertheless, a fixed 15% ceiling on indirect costs may exclude otherwise beneficial
projects without establishing that their expenses are excessive or their outcomes
inadequate.
Legitimate operating costs—including accounting, technology, administration, facilities,
and compliance—can be necessary to deliver services and protect the funds entrusted to
community organizations.
The agencies should distinguish between unnecessary administrative expenditure and
reasonable costs necessary to deliver effective programs.
I recommend replacing a rigid overhead ceiling with transparent cost reporting,
proportionate documentation, appropriate audit safeguards, and evidence of community
benefit. The proposed direct-use requirement should likewise distinguish arrangements
that divert funds from those that enable smaller organizations to provide effective services.
This would protect public accountability without unnecessarily restricting funding for
worthwhile community development initiatives.
5. Preserve meaningful data collection and public transparency
Effective oversight requires sufficient information to determine whether banks are meeting
their statutory obligations.
The agencies should retain meaningful collection and reporting of community
development, small-business, small-farm, and other relevant lending information for
institutions that would otherwise become subject to less comprehensive evaluations.
They should also publish an assessment of how the proposed changes would affect
community lending, branch access, deposit services, grants, and investments.
The assessment should identify the limitations of the available evidence and explain how
those limitations affect the agencies' conclusions.
A reduction in reporting requirements should not automatically become a reduction in the
public's ability to determine whether banks are meeting community needs.
 If the agencies cannot demonstrate that the proposed changes will preserve meaningful
accountability, they should not proceed without further analysis and public consultation.
6. Preserve consistency and reasoned regulatory decision-making
The absence of the Federal Reserve from this proposal raises an additional concern about
regulatory consistency.
Differences in CRA requirements among institutions may complicate compliance,
complicate comparisons of performance, and create uncertainty about how similar
community obligations will be evaluated.
I encourage the OCC and FDIC to coordinate with the Federal Reserve and explain how
differences in regulatory treatment would affect institutions and the communities they
serve.
I also urge the agencies to ensure that the final administrative record adequately explains
the evidence supporting each material change. The Administrative Procedure Act requires
reasoned decision-making, and substantial changes in regulatory coverage should be
accompanied by a clear explanation of their expected benefits, costs, and consequences.
I do not suggest that every provision of the proposal is necessarily unlawful. Rather, the
agencies should ensure that their statutory interpretations and factual conclusions are
adequately explained and supported before adopting changes that could reduce public
accountability.
7. Requested action
For these reasons, I respectfully request that the OCC and FDIC:
1. Withdraw the proposal and develop a replacement after a comprehensive
assessment of the CRA's current performance and shortcomings.
2. Retain meaningful community development, investment, service, and lending
evaluations rather than substantially reducing scrutiny through higher asset
thresholds.
3. Retain deposit services within CRA assessments and ensure that important local
lending categories cannot be excluded merely because they represent a smaller
share of an institution's overall business.
4. Replace rigid grant-cost restrictions with proportionate safeguards that promote
financial transparency, responsible expenditure, and measurable community
benefits.
 5. Preserve relevant data collection and public reporting so that regulators,
researchers, and members of the public can assess bank performance and the
effects of regulatory changes.
6. Publish a comprehensive impact assessment addressing potential changes in
lending, community development financing, deposit services, branch access, and
the availability of financial services to low- and moderate-income communities.
7. Reopen the comment period for an appropriate period after publication of the
additional analysis, allowing the public to evaluate the evidence and respond
meaningfully.
8. Coordinate with the Federal Reserve to address regulatory fragmentation and
promote consistent, transparent assessment standards.
The Community Reinvestment Act reflects an important public responsibility: regulated
financial institutions should be evaluated on how they meet the needs of the communities
they serve.
The objective should not be to maximize regulatory burden. It should be to ensure that
regulatory requirements are proportionate, effective, and supported by evidence while
preserving meaningful public accountability.
The agencies should not weaken those safeguards without demonstrating that the resulting
framework will continue to identify and address unmet community credit and banking
needs.
I respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposal and pursue a more
transparent, empirically supported, and accountable approach to CRA modernization.
Respectfully,
Robert E. Rutkowski

The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) submits this comment in opposition to
the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office
of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC).1 The CRA NPRM would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) and should be withdrawn. If the agencies nevertheless continue to consider
changes to the CRA regulations, they should, at a minimum, supplement the record with
a meaningful assessment of the likely effects on community development financing,
affordable housing, small business lending, disaster recovery financing, and other forms
of credit that CRA was enacted to encourage, provide the public an opportunity to
comment on that assessment before proposing or finalizing any changes, and extend the
comment period by an additional 60 days to ensure stakeholders have a meaningful
opportunity to review and respond to that assessment.
Congress enacted the Community Reinvestment Act to ensure that regulated financial
institutions help meet the credit needs of the communities they serve, including LMI
communities. The statute expressly recognizes that insured depository institutions have
a "continuing and affirmative obligation" to help meet local credit needs and directs
federal banking agencies to use their supervisory authority to encourage such activity.2
Accordingly, when revising CRA regulations, the agencies should evaluate not only
changes in compliance burden for supervised institutions but also the effect of those
changes on the availability of credit, investment, and financial services in underserved

communities. The CRA NPRM contains extensive discussion of burden reduction but
provides little analysis of how the proposed changes may affect the flow of capital to
community development activities that CRA was designed to encourage.
NRDC is an international nonprofit environmental organization with more than 3
million members and online activists. Since 1970, our lawyers, scientists, economists,
and other environmental specialists have worked to protect the world's natural
resources, people, and environment. NRDC has offices in New York City, Washington

communities to benefit from the climate transition.
Summary of Comments
Our comments address the failure of the agencies to consider LMI community-level
effects in their crafting of the CRA NPRM. We discuss our opposition to the proposed (1)
Asset Size Thresholds and (2) definition for Community Development Activities,
specifically the changes to community development grantmaking. NRDC strongly
opposes these changes because they would reduce LMI communities' access to credit by
decreasing capital available to the community development financing ecosystem. In
practice, these changes would drastically undermine banks' ability "to meet the credit
needs of their communities," which – as the agencies recognize – underpins the CRA. By
weakening banks' longstanding obligations under the CRA and, in turn, scaling back the
flow of capital to community development, the CRA NPRM would cut off vital funding
that facilitates credit access to countless families and small businesses in communities
across the country.
Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) provide finance and
affordability solutions for redlined, underbanked, and disaster-stricken communities.3
Furthermore, they are one of the primary channels through which CRA capital reaches
LMI communities: CRA-obligated banks co-lend or directly invest in CDFIs, enabling
them to lend to households, small businesses, and affordable housing projects that
private banks otherwise could not reach due to smaller project sizes, inflexible
underwriting criteria, and other reasons. In turn, banks receive CRA consideration for
their support, which encompasses $15-$25 billion in capital annually.4 The proposed
asset thresholds and restrictions on community development activities will weaken
incentives for banks to provide capital to CDFIs, especially capital that enables lending
to LMI communities.
We are concerned that the agencies failed to analyze the full economic impact of the
proposed changes on LMI communities in favor of only emphasizing reduced regulatory

The Agencies Have Not Adequately Assessed Community-Level Effects
The CRA NPRM discusses anticipated reductions in regulatory burden but does not

CDFIs and How They Support Lending in LMI Communities: CDFIs emerged

supported the creation of new CDFIs through capitalization funding. Intentionally timed
together, these two policy tools supported the emergence of a local ecosystem of CDFIs
that could serve as financial intermediaries for newly motivated CRA investment.10

CRA-obligated banks, in partnership with CDFIs, facilitate affordable housing

Disaster Relief and Recovery
CDFIs are "financial first responders" when disaster strikes.15 As locally-based
institutions with a mission-first mandate, CDFIs can deploy flexible dollars to help small
businesses and individuals recover from natural disasters, emergencies, and economic
crises. This role has been recognized by Congress, which established the Emergency
Capital Investment Program (ECIP) and the CDFI Rapid Response Program (RRP) in
2021. These two programs collectively disbursed $9.82 billion to CDFIs to provide
financial services in COVID-19-impacted regions.16 CDFIs effectively leveraged these
dollars into recovery and economic stabilization: CDFIs receiving ECIP disbursements
originated over $58.3 billion in loans between 2022-2023, while CDFI Fund awardees
receiving RRP dollars originated over $85.64 billion in 2022.17
The CRA incentivizes private banks to provide disaster relief and CDFIs have emerged
as an on-the-ground partner for banks in making these types of community
investments.18 Banks provide flexible funding to CDFIs, which then redeploy funding
through their direct access with impacted communities. For example, in 2025, a large
national bank committed $10 million to CDFIs to support LA fire recovery efforts.
The role of CDFIs and CRA capital to help communities recover from hurricanes,
flooding, and wildfires will become increasingly important as climate change worsens.
Scientists have noted that the frequency and severity of these events are becoming
worse, and these impacts disproportionately impact LMI communities. A study
commissioned by the San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank found that 57% of current
disaster-impacted counties have census tracts where banks may receive consideration
for CRA credit.19
If enacted, the proposed changes to CRA requirements would directly weaken local
lenders' capacity to provide financial assistance during and after disasters and
undermine the agencies' own proposed changes to consider recovery and resiliency
investments in CRA examinations.20 This would leave families and small businesses in
the lurch after unforeseeable crises.

Energy Costs
Finally, CDFIs provide financing to expand access to energy efficiency and renewable
energy technologies. These products are typically structured with below-market
financing and smaller loan amounts than a private bank would issue. These financing
products provide much needed relief to households by lowering utility bills during a
period of rising energy costs driven by increased energy demand and international
conflicts impacting supply.21
The flexible capital CDFIs receive from CRA-obligated banks has given CDFIs the fiscal
space to develop innovative products that deliver clean and cheap energy, with these
products reaching the communities the CRA targets.22
At a time when energy bills are skyrocketing, local lenders need more resources – not
less – to help families and small businesses make ends meet. By limiting capital for
projects that help communities deploy cost-saving energy technologies, the proposed
changes to CRA requirements would undermine these lenders' ability to address the
affordability crisis head-on.
CRA Proposed Changes will Undermine Agencies' Goals of Meeting
Community Credit Needs Through Increased Lending (Questions 1, 9, 10)
Asset Threshold (Question 1)
To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less than $30 billion
as a threshold for certain supervisory approaches, such as being considered a
community bank or being subject to the continuous examination process, should the
agencies consider adjusting the intermediate bank asset size threshold to include all
banks with an asset size of less than $30 billion that do not qualify as small banks? If
the agencies establish $30 billion as the appropriate threshold to delineate between
intermediate banks and large banks, should the agencies also adopt a larger threshold
for small banks, such as the $10 billion currently proposed as the intermediate bank
threshold?
We strongly oppose the proposed Asset Threshold changes as well as the additional
proposed $30 billion threshold posed in question 1. These changes will reduce the
amount of capital that flows to and in coordination with CDFIs, ultimately decreasing
lending activity in LMI communities.

Large Bank Threshold
The proposed large bank threshold is estimated to lead to the reclassification of 417
banks.23 The proposed $30 billion threshold would further reduce the number of large
banks. As the agencies are aware, these banks would no longer be subject to the separate
investment and lending test and would only be evaluated under the combined
community development test. In effect, this would incentivize banks moving into the
intermediate classification to rely on revenue-generating debt products for community
development test compliance.
Downstream, banks will be less likely to extend investments in the form of capital grants
and deposits to CDFIs. These investments provide the liquidity and balance sheet
strength to CDFIs that enable specialized lending to LMI communities. Ultimately,
weakening incentives to provide this capital flow will decrease the pace, scale, and dollar
amount of lending that CDFIs typically achieve in CRA census tracts, undermining CRA
goals and harming communities.
Furthermore, banks will face weaker incentives to provide direct investment into
priority sectors, such as affordable housing. The threats to affordable housing
investment are especially urgent: these proposed changes will depress the Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit market and subsequently create insurmountable financing gaps in
affordable housing projects. By making projects in this sector unbankable, the proposed
rulemaking will further depress the amount of lending activity in LMI communities. In
the long term, this will reduce housing supply, exacerbating the on-going housing
affordability crises.
Intermediate Small Bank Threshold
The proposed intermediate bank threshold eliminates community development testing
entirely for 814 banks.24 These banks would no longer have CRA incentives to provide
community development investments and community development loans to CDFIs,
resulting in negative impacts on LMI communities.
Bank debt supports capitalization for mid-size and small CDFIs, with mid-size CDFIs
receiving up to 48.9% of their debt from private banks.25 This debt is structured around
a model of revolving capital and allows CDFIs to provide lending for affordability
solutions. If a subset of CRA-obligated banks are no longer receiving CRA credit for
providing this capital, CDFIs could risk losing a significant percentage of their capital
base. Without proper capitalization, CDFIs will be restricted in their ability to provide
consumer and small business lending to LMI communities, act as "financial first
responders" following disasters, or innovate new affordability solutions, such as clean
energy lending.

The loss of debt capital could delay or eliminate financing solutions that support LMI
communities in absorbing energy price shocks, living in healthier homes, and being

Community Development Grant Limitation Will Weaken LMI Community Credit Access
(Question 9 and 10)
Are there alternative standards the agencies should consider relying on in the context
of limiting indirect costs for CD grants? Do the proposed guardrails do enough to
ensure the majority of grant and donation funds go directly towards benefiting the
bank's assessment area(s)?
As an alternative, should the agencies eliminate all grants and donations from CRA
consideration?
We strongly oppose the proposal to narrow CRA consideration for grants or donations.
Specifically, we oppose the language that restricts banks from receiving CRA credit for
grants that are used for administrative costs. Furthermore, we urge the agencies against
outright eliminating grants and donations from CRA consideration.
Grantmaking is a central part of CRA consideration, as CRA regulations expressly
recognize community development loans, investments (including grants), and services
as relevant elements of CRA performance evaluation.27
In practice, CDFIs are common recipients of unrestricted grants from CRA-obligated
banks. The grants help CDFIs build internal capacity, train staff, build internal
networks, and free up resources for CDFIs to reach end-use borrowers. By limiting this
source of flexible capital, the proposed language will restrict the flexibility of CDFIs to
facilitate lending to LMI communities.
CRA grantmaking also benefits Community Benefit Organizations, key players in
building project pipelines. Like CDFIs, Community Benefit Organizations rely on
administrative grants to provide community development services at the local level. In
addition, their proximity to communities makes them effective at identifying priority
projects for investment and intermediating between lenders, government, and
communities throughout the project development process. Restricting flexible funding
to these organizations would not only preclude them from maximizing community
impact but would also prevent them from supporting pipeline development by limiting
their internal capacity to engage on projects. Ultimately, this would hamper lending in
LMI communities through the dwindling of vetted, community-supported projects.

The agencies have proposed this language as part of their prioritization on CRA lending

CRA NPRM Contradicts Agencies' Goals and Agencies Fail to Fully Consider Impact on
LMI Communities
It is clear from the agencies' economic analysis that they did not properly consider the
impact of the rulemaking on LMI communities. While the agencies acknowledge their
proposed changes will induce a "possible shift in CRA-obligated activity... away from
certain CD activities," the agencies fail to consider the downstream impacts of the
changes in the distribution of CRA capital to LMI communities beyond claiming the
"direction and magnitude of...effects are uncertain."28
However, available evidence indicates the impacts of the CRA NPRM: it will harm LMI
communities and the families and small businesses within them. While there are
multiple mechanisms in which the proposed changes will harm the communities it
purports to aid, our letter specifically outlines how the NPRM will disincentivize
investment in the community development financial ecosystem, resulting in decreased
credit access to communities.
In light of these concerns, we urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposal. If the
agencies elect to continue considering changes to the CRA regulations, they should first
assess the likely impact of such changes on community development financing,
affordable housing, small business lending, disaster recovery financing, and other
activities that CRA was enacted to encourage, provide the public an opportunity to
comment on that assessment before proposing or finalizing any changes, and extend the
comment period by 60 days following publication of that assessment to ensure
stakeholders have a meaningful opportunity to evaluate and respond to the analysis.

Proposed CRA Changes will Reduce Affordable Housing and Community Development
Investments and Financing, Especially in Rural Markets

As a state with significant rural geography, including hundreds of small cities with a population of
5,000 and less, Minnesotans will experience significant negative impacts from the proposed changes,
especially those who lived in rural and other underserved communities.
The proposed rule would eliminate or weaken CRA requirements for hundreds of Minnesota banks
while expanding CRA credit for activities unrelated to low- and moderate-income communities.
According to the National Community Reinvestment Coalition
• 46.7% of Minnesota banks, or 50 of a total of 107 banks, many in rural communities, will no
longer have community development obligations – the second highest percent of banks
losing community development obligations for any state in the nation.
• 52.8% of Minnesota banks will lose their "large-bank" status, meaning fewer requirements
and oversight; and
• 49.6% of Minnesota bank branches in low- and moderate-income communities, a total of
170 branches, would be at risk of closure. Again, a significant number of these bank
branches are located in rural areas of Minnesota.

In short, the proposed rule will likely result in significantly fewer investments, financial service
products, and small business loans serving low- and moderate-income people in Minnesota,
dramatically impacting banking services and programs serving Minnesotans.

In Minnesota, housing undersupply and the high cost of housing have created a tenuous housing
situation, impacting families from rural towns to metropolitan areas. Currently, Minnesota has a
shortfall of just under 100,000 homes, with the greatest impact of that shortfall felt by Minnesotans
with low incomes. Further underinvestment, as is likely with the proposed CRA rule, will increase
our housing shortfall that most impacts families with low and moderate incomes.

Of great concern is that the proposed CRA rules undercut recent efforts to expand and strength the
Low Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Tax Credit). H.R. 1, also known as the Working Families
Tax Cuts Act, included an increase to the Housing Tax Credit and expanded the 4 percent Housing
Tax Credit program. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public
welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to increase their Housing Tax Credit investments.

The Housing Tax Credit has been a critical tool in addressing the need for affordable homes, but
encouraging private investment in affordable rental housing. In Minnesota, since the Housing Tax
Credit was created in 1986, it has helped develop or preserve almost 80,000 homes, served over
186,000 households with low incomes, supported 140,300 jobs, and generated $5.77 billion in tax
revenue. The CRA has been critical to these successful results – and the changes proposed will
jeopardize that.


MHP : : 2446 University Avenue West, Ste 106 : : Saint Paul, MN 55114 : : 651-649-1710 : : mhponline.org
The Housing Tax Credit – the most important tool for affordable housing production in the U.S. --
relies on investments from banks subject to CRA. Banks make these investments in part because the
full CRA examination for large banks includes a distinct investment test. Because Housing Credit
investment yields are typically modest, large banks often could get a more substantial yield from
making other forms of investment, but often still choose to invest in the Housing Credit because
Housing Credit investments help banks meet their CRA obligations

 The CRA changes could greatly dilute these legislative accomplishments and undercut congressional
goals of providing more affordable rental homes. The consequences of this proposal would be most
damaging to smaller rural communities that now benefit from being in the CRA assessment area of
one or more large banks but may no longer be if the OCC and FDIC change the definition of large
bank as proposed. As well, housing tax credit pricing for properties in many urban areas—which are
more likely to have at least one and often multiple banks competing to invest in Housing Credit
developments because of overlapping assessment areas—tends to be much higher than pricing in
rural and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment areas for large banks subject to
the investment test.

Conclusion

We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under the
1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve—the third bank regulator—
appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA regulations, we
strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for large banks and adopting policies to
strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including rural and smaller markets.
